chapters.title: Chapter 1 — Loomings
paragraphs: Call me Ishmael. Some years ago — never mind exactly how long — with little or no money in my purse and nothing in particular to hold my interest on land, I decided I would sail around for a while and see the watery part of the world. It's my way of chasing off the gloom and keeping my circulation in order. Whenever I notice my mouth setting into a grim line; whenever it's a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I catch myself stopping without meaning to in front of coffin warehouses, and tagging along at the back of every funeral I pass; and above all whenever my low spirits get such a grip on me that only a strong moral principle keeps me from walking deliberately into the street and methodically knocking people's hats off — then I know it's high time to get to sea as fast as I can. This is my substitute for pistol and bullet. Cato, with a philosophical flourish, throws himself on his sword; I quietly go to sea. There's nothing surprising in this. If they only realized it, nearly all men, each in his own degree, at one time or another feel almost exactly what I feel toward the ocean.

There now is your island city of the Manhattoes, belted around by wharves as the Indian isles are by coral reefs — commerce surrounds it with her surf. Right and left, the streets lead you toward the water. Its farthest downtown point is the Battery, where that noble mole, or seawall, is washed by waves and cooled by breezes that a few hours earlier were out of sight of land. Look at the crowds of water-gazers there.

Walk around the city on a dreamy Sunday afternoon. Go from Corlears Hook to Coenties Slip and then north by way of Whitehall. What do you see? Standing like silent sentinels all around the town are thousands upon thousands of mortal men fixed in ocean reveries. Some lean against the pilings; some sit on the pier heads; some gaze over the sides of ships from China; some perch high in the rigging, as if trying to get an even better view of the sea. But these are all landlocked people — weekdays they're penned up in plaster and wood, chained to counters, nailed to benches, clamped to desks. What's going on? Have all the green fields vanished? What are they doing here?

But look! Here come more crowds, pacing straight for the water, seemingly bound for a dive. Strange! Nothing will satisfy them but the very outermost edge of the land; loitering in the shady lee of those warehouses over there won't do. No. They must get just as near the water as they possibly can without falling in. And there they stand — miles of them — leagues. Inlanders all, they come from lanes and alleys, streets and avenues — north, east, south, and west. Yet here they all unite. Tell me, does the magnetic power of the compass needles of all those ships draw them here?

One more example. Say you're in the country, somewhere in high lake land. Take nearly any path you like, and ten to one it will lead you down into a valley and leave you beside a pool in the stream. There's magic in it. Take the most absent-minded man alive, sunk in his deepest daydream — stand him up, get his feet moving, and he will lead you to water without fail, if there is any water in that whole region. If you're ever thirsty in the Great American Desert, try this experiment, provided your caravan happens to include a professor of metaphysics. Yes, as everyone knows, meditation and water are wedded for good.

But here is an artist. He wants to paint you the dreamiest, shadiest, quietest, most enchanting piece of romantic landscape in the whole valley of the Saco. What is the main element he relies on? There are his trees, each with a hollow trunk, as though a hermit and a crucifix were hidden inside; here his meadow sleeps, and there his cattle sleep; and from that cottage in the distance a sleepy smoke drifts up. A winding path twists deep into far-off woods, reaching toward overlapping spurs of mountains steeped in their hillside blue. Yet though the picture lies there in its trance, and though this pine tree sheds its sighs like leaves onto this shepherd's head, it would all be for nothing unless the shepherd's gaze were fixed on the magic stream in front of him. Visit the Prairies in June, when for scores upon scores of miles you wade knee-deep through tiger lilies — what is the one charm that's missing? Water — there isn't a drop of water there! If Niagara were nothing but a waterfall of sand, would you travel your thousand miles to see it? Why did the poor poet of Tennessee, when he suddenly came into two handfuls of silver, hesitate over whether to buy himself a coat, which he badly needed, or spend the money on a walking trip to Rockaway Beach? Why does almost every strong, healthy boy with a strong, healthy soul in him go crazy at some point to go to sea? Why, on your own first voyage as a passenger, did you feel such a mystical thrill when you were first told that you and your ship were now out of sight of land? Why did the ancient Persians consider the sea holy? Why did the Greeks give it a god of its own, and make him Jove's own brother? Surely none of this is without meaning. And deeper still is the meaning of the story of Narcissus, who, unable to grasp the tormenting, gentle image he saw in the fountain, plunged into it and drowned. But we ourselves see that same image in every river and ocean. It is the image of the ungraspable phantom of life; and this is the key to it all.

Now, when I say I go to sea whenever my eyes grow hazy and I become too aware of my own breathing, don't imagine I ever go as a passenger. To go as a passenger you need a purse, and a purse is just a rag unless there's something in it. Besides, passengers get seasick, grow quarrelsome, don't sleep at night, and generally don't enjoy themselves much. No, I never go as a passenger; nor, though I know my way around a ship, do I ever go as a Commodore, Captain, or Cook. I leave the glory and distinction of such positions to those who want them. I personally despise all honorable, respectable labor, trials, and tribulations of every kind whatsoever. I have quite enough to do just looking after myself without looking after ships, barques, brigs, schooners, and what not. And as for going as cook — though I confess there's considerable glory in that, a cook being a sort of officer on board — somehow I never much liked the idea of broiling chickens. Though once broiled, properly buttered, judiciously salted and peppered, there's no one who speaks of a broiled chicken with more respect — even reverence — than I do. It's because of the ancient Egyptians' idolatrous doting on broiled ibis and roasted hippopotamus that you find mummies of those creatures in their enormous bake-houses, the pyramids.

No, when I go to sea, I go as a simple sailor, right before the mast, down into the forecastle, up to the royal masthead. True, they order me around and make me jump from spar to spar like a grasshopper in a May meadow. At first, this kind of thing is unpleasant enough. It stings your pride, especially if you come from an old established family — the Van Rensselaers, or Randolphs, or Hardicanutes. And even more so if, just before dipping your hand into the tar bucket, you'd been lording it as a country schoolteacher, making the tallest boys tremble before you. The transition from schoolmaster to sailor is a sharp one, I assure you, and requires a strong dose of Seneca and the Stoics to help you grin and bear it. But even this wears off in time.

So what if some crusty old sea captain orders me to get a broom and sweep down the decks? What does that indignity amount to, weighed, I mean, on the scales of the New Testament? Do you think the archangel Gabriel thinks any the less of me because I promptly and respectfully obey that old grouch in that particular instance? Who isn't a slave? Tell me that. Well, then, however the old sea captains may order me about — however they may thump and punch me about — I have the satisfaction of knowing that it is all right; that everybody else is served in much the same way, one way or another — from either a physical or a metaphysical point of view, that is; and so the universal thump is passed around, and all hands should rub each other's shoulder blades and be content.

Besides, I always go to sea as a sailor, because they make a point of paying me for my trouble, while as far as I've ever heard they never pay passengers a single penny. Quite the reverse — passengers have to pay. And there is all the difference in the world between paying and being paid. Paying is perhaps the most uncomfortable punishment those two orchard thieves, Adam and Eve, left us with. But being paid — what can compare with that? The gracious readiness with which a man accepts money is truly remarkable, considering how earnestly we believe money is the root of all earthly evils, and that a moneyed man can on no account get into heaven. Ah, how cheerfully we sign ourselves over to damnation!

Finally, I always go to sea as a sailor because of the healthy exercise and pure air of the forecastle deck. For as in this world headwinds are far more common than winds from astern (that is, if you never violate the Pythagorean maxim), so for the most part the Commodore on the quarter-deck gets his air secondhand from the sailors on the forecastle. He thinks he breathes it first; but not so. In much the same way the common people lead their leaders in many other things, while the leaders little suspect it. But why it was that, after repeatedly smelling the sea as a merchant sailor, I should now take it into my head to go on a whaling voyage — that the invisible police officer of the Fates, who keeps me under constant surveillance, secretly dogs my steps, and influences me in some unaccountable way, can answer better than anyone else. And no doubt my going on this whaling voyage formed part of the grand program of Providence that was drawn up a long time ago. It came in as a sort of brief interlude and solo between more extensive performances. I take it that this part of the playbill must have run something like this:
"GRAND CONTESTED ELECTION FOR THE PRESIDENCY OF THE UNITED STATES." "WHALING VOYAGE BY ONE ISHMAEL." "BLOODY BATTLE IN AFFGHANISTAN."

Though I can't say exactly why those stage managers, the Fates, cast me in this shabby part of a whaling voyage, when others were given magnificent parts in high tragedies, short and easy parts in genteel comedies, and jolly parts in farces — though I can't say exactly why; still, now that I recall all the circumstances, I think I can see a little into the springs and motives that were cunningly presented to me under various disguises and led me to take on the part I did — besides fooling me into the delusion that it was a choice I made by my own unbiased free will and discriminating judgment.

The chief of these motives was the overwhelming idea of the great whale himself. A monster so ominous and mysterious stirred all my curiosity. Then there were the wild, far-off seas where he rolled his island-sized bulk; the untold, nameless dangers of the whale; these, together with all the marvels that come with a thousand Patagonian sights and sounds, helped push me toward what I wanted. For other men, perhaps, such things would have been no attraction at all; but as for me, I am tormented by a never-ending itch for faraway things. I love to sail forbidden seas and land on barbarous coasts. I don't overlook what is good, but I'm quick to spot a horror, and I could still be on social terms with it — if they would let me — since it's only sensible to be friendly with all the inmates of the place you're lodging in.

For all these reasons, the whaling voyage was welcome. The great floodgates of the wonder-world swung open, and in the wild fantasies that drove me toward my purpose, two by two there floated into my deepest soul endless processions of whales — and in the middle of them all, one grand hooded phantom, like a snow hill in the air.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — The Carpet-Bag
paragraphs: I stuffed a shirt or two into my old carpet-bag, tucked it under my arm, and headed for Cape Horn and the Pacific. Leaving the good city of old Manhatto, I duly arrived in New Bedford. It was a Saturday night in December. I was very disappointed to learn that the little packet boat to Nantucket had already sailed, and that there would be no way of getting there until the following Monday.

Since most young candidates for the pains and penalties of whaling stop at this same New Bedford, to embark on their voyage from there, I may as well say that I, for one, had no intention of doing so. My mind was made up to sail in nothing but a Nantucket craft, because there was a fine, boisterous something about everything connected with that famous old island that pleased me amazingly. Besides, though New Bedford has lately been gradually monopolizing the whaling business, and though poor old Nantucket is now far behind her in this matter, Nantucket was her great original — the Tyre of this Carthage — the place where the first dead American whale was stranded. Where else but from Nantucket did those aboriginal whalemen, the Red-Men, first sally out in canoes to give chase to the Leviathan? And where but from Nantucket, too, did that first adventurous little sloop set out, partly loaded with imported cobblestones — so the story goes — to throw at the whales, in order to find out when they were near enough to risk a harpoon from the bowsprit?

Now, with a night, a day, and still another night ahead of me in New Bedford before I could embark for my intended port, the question of where I was to eat and sleep in the meantime became a matter of concern. It was a very dubious-looking — no, a very dark and dismal — night, bitingly cold and cheerless. I knew no one in the place. With anxious grappling hooks I had sounded my pocket, and brought up only a few pieces of silver. So, wherever you go, Ishmael, I said to myself, as I stood in the middle of a dreary street shouldering my bag and comparing the gloom to the north with the darkness to the south — wherever in your wisdom you may decide to lodge for the night, my dear Ishmael, be sure to ask the price, and don't be too particular.

With halting steps I paced the streets, and passed the sign of "The Crossed Harpoons" — but it looked too expensive and jolly there. Farther on, from the bright red windows of the "Sword-Fish Inn" came such fervent rays that they seemed to have melted the packed snow and ice from in front of the house, for everywhere else the congealed frost lay ten inches thick in a hard, asphalt-like pavement — rather tiring for me when I struck my foot against the flinty ridges, because after hard, remorseless service the soles of my boots were in a most miserable state. Too expensive and jolly, I thought again, pausing a moment to watch the broad glare in the street and hear the tinkling of glasses inside. But go on, Ishmael, I said at last; don't you hear? Get away from the door; your patched boots are blocking the way. So on I went. I now followed by instinct the streets that led me toward the water, for there, no doubt, were the cheapest, if not the cheeriest, inns.

What dreary streets! Blocks of blackness, not houses, on either side, and here and there a candle, like a candle moving about in a tomb. At this hour of the night, on the last day of the week, that part of town proved all but deserted. But soon I came to a smoky light coming from a low, wide building, whose door stood invitingly open. It had a careless look, as if it were meant for the use of the public; so, going in, the first thing I did was stumble over an ash-box in the porch. Ha! I thought, ha, as the flying particles almost choked me — are these ashes from that destroyed city, Gomorrah? But "The Crossed Harpoons," and "The Sword-Fish"? — then this must be the sign of "The Trap." However, I picked myself up, and, hearing a loud voice inside, pushed on and opened a second, inner door.

It seemed like the great Black Parliament sitting in Tophet, the biblical hell. A hundred black faces turned around in their rows to peer; and beyond, a black Angel of Doom was beating a book in a pulpit. It was a negro church; and the preacher's text was about the blackness of darkness, and the weeping and wailing and teeth-gnashing there. Ha, Ishmael, I muttered, backing out — wretched entertainment at the sign of "The Trap"!

Moving on, I at last came to a dim sort of light not far from the docks and heard a forlorn creaking in the air. Looking up, I saw a swinging sign over the door with a white painting on it, faintly representing a tall, straight jet of misty spray, and these words underneath: "The Spouter Inn — Peter Coffin."

Coffin? Spouter? Rather ominous in that particular connection, I thought. But it's a common name in Nantucket, they say, and I suppose this Peter here is an emigrant from there. Since the light looked so dim, and the place looked quiet enough for the time being, and the dilapidated little wooden house itself looked as if it might have been carted here from the ruins of some burned district, and since the swinging sign had a poverty-stricken sort of creak to it, I thought this was the very spot for cheap lodgings and the best of pea coffee.

It was an odd sort of place — a gable-ended old house, one side palsied, as it were, and leaning over sadly. It stood on a sharp, bleak corner, where that tempestuous wind Euroclydon kept up a worse howling than it ever did around poor Paul's storm-tossed ship. Euroclydon, nevertheless, is a mighty pleasant breeze to anyone indoors, with his feet on the hearth, quietly toasting them before bed. "In judging of that tempestuous wind called Euroclydon," says an old writer — of whose works I possess the only surviving copy — "it makes a marvelous difference whether you look out at it from a glass window where the frost is all on the outside, or whether you observe it from that sashless window, where the frost is on both sides, and of which that fellow Death is the only glazier." True enough, I thought, as this passage came to mind — old black-letter book, you reason well. Yes, these eyes are windows, and this body of mine is the house. What a pity they didn't stop up the chinks and crannies, though, and stuff in a little lint here and there. But it's too late to make any improvements now. The universe is finished; the copestone is on, and the chips were carted off a million years ago. Poor Lazarus there, chattering his teeth against the curbstone for his pillow, and shaking off his tatters with his shivering — he might plug up both ears with rags and put a corncob in his mouth, and still that would not keep out the tempestuous Euroclydon. Euroclydon! says old Dives, in his red silk robe (he had a redder one afterward) — pooh, pooh! What a fine frosty night; how Orion glitters; what northern lights! Let them talk of their Eastern summer climates of everlasting conservatories; give me the privilege of making my own summer with my own coals.

But what does Lazarus think? Can he warm his blue hands by holding them up to the grand northern lights? Wouldn't Lazarus rather be in Sumatra than here? Wouldn't he far rather lay himself down lengthwise along the line of the equator — yes, you gods! — even go down to the fiery pit itself, to keep out this frost?

Now, that Lazarus should be lying stranded there on the curb outside Dives's door is more astonishing than if an iceberg were moored to one of the Moluccas. And yet Dives himself also lives like a czar in an ice palace built of frozen sighs, and since he is president of a temperance society, the only thing he drinks is the lukewarm tears of orphans.
But no more of this blubbering now — we're going whaling, and there's plenty of that still to come. Let's scrape the ice from our frosted feet and see what sort of place this "Spouter" may be.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — The Spouter-Inn
paragraphs: Entering that gable-ended Spouter-Inn, you found yourself in a wide, low, straggling entry with old-fashioned wood paneling, reminding you of the bulwarks of some condemned old ship. On one side hung a very large oil painting so thoroughly blackened by smoke, and defaced in every way, that in the uneven crosslights by which you viewed it, it was only by diligent study, a series of systematic visits, and careful inquiry of the neighbors that you could arrive at any understanding of its purpose. There were such unaccountable masses of shades and shadows that at first you almost thought some ambitious young artist, in the time of the New England witches, had tried to depict chaos bewitched. But by dint of much earnest contemplation and oft-repeated pondering, and especially by throwing open the little window toward the back of the entry, you at last came to the conclusion that such an idea, however wild, might not be altogether unwarranted.

But what most puzzled and confounded you was a long, limber, portentous, black mass of something hovering in the center of the picture over three blue, dim, perpendicular lines floating in a nameless yeast. A boggy, soggy, squelchy picture truly, enough to drive a nervous man to distraction. Yet there was a sort of indefinite, half-attained, unimaginable sublimity about it that fairly froze you to it, until you involuntarily swore an oath to yourself to find out what that marvelous painting meant. Every now and then a bright but, alas, deceptive idea would dart through you. — It's the Black Sea in a midnight gale. — It's the unnatural combat of the four primal elements. — It's a blasted heath. — It's a Hyperborean winter scene, from the far frozen north. — It's the breaking-up of the icebound stream of Time. But at last all these fancies yielded to that one portentous something in the middle of the picture. Once that was found out, all the rest would be plain. But wait; doesn't it bear a faint resemblance to a gigantic fish? Even the great leviathan himself?

In fact, the artist's design seemed to be this — a final theory of my own, partly based on the combined opinions of many old people I talked with on the subject. The picture shows a Cape-Horner — a ship rounding Cape Horn — in a great hurricane; the half-foundered ship is wallowing there with only its three dismantled masts visible; and an exasperated whale, intending to spring clean over the vessel, is in the enormous act of impaling himself on the three mastheads.

The opposite wall of this entry was hung all over with a heathenish array of monstrous clubs and spears. Some were thickly set with glittering teeth resembling ivory saws; others were tufted with knots of human hair; and one was sickle-shaped, with a vast handle sweeping around like the curve a long-armed mower cuts in new-mown grass. You shuddered as you gazed, and wondered what monstrous cannibal and savage could ever have gone death-harvesting with such a hacking, horrifying implement. Mixed with these were rusty old whaling lances and harpoons, all broken and deformed. Some were storied weapons. With this once-long lance, now wildly bent at the elbow, Nathan Swain killed fifteen whales between one sunrise and sunset fifty years ago. And that harpoon — so like a corkscrew now — was thrown in Javan seas, and run away with by a whale that was killed years afterward off the Cape of Blanco. The original iron entered near the tail and, like a restless needle wandering around in the body of a man, traveled a full forty feet, and at last was found embedded in the hump.

Crossing this dusky entry, and going on through that low-arched way — cut through what in old times must have been a great central chimney with fireplaces all around — you enter the public room. This is an even duskier place, with such low, ponderous beams above and such old wrinkled planks beneath that you would almost imagine you were treading some old ship's cockpits, especially on such a howling night, when this corner-anchored old ark rocked so furiously. On one side stood a long, low, shelf-like table covered with cracked glass cases, filled with dusty rarities gathered from the remotest nooks of this wide world. Projecting from the farther corner of the room stands a dark-looking den — the bar — a crude attempt at a right whale's head. Be that as it may, there stands the vast arched bone of the whale's jaw, so wide that a coach might almost drive beneath it. Inside are shabby shelves lined with old decanters, bottles, and flasks; and in those jaws of swift destruction, like another cursed Jonah (which indeed is what they called him), bustles a little withered old man who, for their money, sells the sailors delirium and death at a dear price.

Abominable are the tumblers into which he pours his poison. Though they were true cylinders outside, inside, the villainous green goggling glasses tapered deceitfully downward to a cheating bottom. Parallel meridians, crudely pecked into the glass, circle these robbers' goblets. Fill to this mark, and your charge is only a penny; to this one, a penny more; and so on up to the full glass — the Cape Horn measure, which you may gulp down for a shilling.

When I entered the place I found a number of young seamen gathered around a table, examining by a dim light various specimens of skrimshander — sailors' carved bone and ivory work. I looked for the landlord, and when I told him I wanted a room, he answered that his house was full — not a bed unoccupied. "But hold on," he added, tapping his forehead, "you ain't got no objections to sharing a harpooner's blanket, have you? I s'pose you're goin' whaling, so you'd better get used to that sort of thing."

I told him I never liked sleeping two to a bed; that if I ever did, it would depend on who the harpooner turned out to be; and that if he (the landlord) really had nowhere else to put me, and the harpooner wasn't downright objectionable, then rather than wander any farther around a strange town on such a bitter night, I would settle for half of any decent man's blanket.
"Thought so. All right, have a seat. Supper? You want supper? Supper'll be ready directly."

I sat down on an old wooden bench carved all over like a seat on the Battery. At one end, a ruminative sailor was further decorating it with his jackknife, stooping over and working diligently at the space between his knees. He was attempting a ship under full sail, but he wasn't making much headway, I thought.

At last some four or five of us were summoned to our meal in an adjoining room. It was cold as Iceland — no fire at all; the landlord said he couldn't afford it. Nothing but two dismal tallow candles, each wrapped in a winding sheet of dripped tallow. We had to button up our monkey jackets and hold cups of scalding tea to our lips with our half-frozen fingers. But the food was of the most substantial kind — not only meat and potatoes, but dumplings; good heavens! Dumplings for supper! One young fellow in a green box coat went at these dumplings in a most alarming manner.
"My boy," said the landlord, "you'll have nightmares to a dead certainty."
"Landlord," I whispered, "that ain't the harpooner, is it?"
"Oh, no," he said, looking sort of diabolically funny, "the harpooner is a dark-complexioned chap. He never eats dumplings, he don't — he eats nothing but steaks, and he likes 'em rare."
"The devil he does," I said. "Where is that harpooner? Is he here?"
"He'll be here before long," was the answer.

I couldn't help it: I started to feel suspicious of this "dark-complexioned" harpooner. At any rate, I decided that if it turned out we really had to share a bed, he would have to undress and get in before I did.
After supper, the company returned to the bar room. Having nothing else to do, I decided to spend the rest of the evening as a spectator.

Soon a riotous noise was heard outside. Jumping up, the landlord cried, "That's the Grampus's crew. I seen her reported in the offing this morning — a three years' voyage, and a full ship. Hurrah, boys; now we'll have the latest news from the Fijis."

We heard sea boots tramping in the entry; the door was flung open, and in rolled a wild enough bunch of sailors. Bundled in shaggy watch coats, their heads wrapped in woolen scarves darned all over and ragged, and their beards stiff with icicles, they looked like a horde of bears erupting out of Labrador. They had just come ashore from their boat, and this was the first house they had walked into. No wonder, then, that they steered straight for the whale's mouth — the bar — where the wrinkled little old Jonah on duty soon poured them all brimming glasses. One of them complained of a bad head cold, so Jonah mixed him a potion like pitch, of gin and molasses, which he swore was a sure cure for any cold or catarrh whatever, no matter how long you'd had it, or whether you'd caught it off the coast of Labrador or on the windward side of an ice island.
The liquor quickly went to their heads, as it usually does with even the heaviest drinkers who've just come ashore, and they began leaping about wildly.

I noticed, however, that one of them held somewhat apart, and though he seemed anxious not to spoil his shipmates' hilarity with his own sober face, on the whole he refrained from making as much noise as the rest. This man interested me at once; and since the sea-gods had ordained that he should soon become my shipmate (though only a sleeping-partner one, as far as this narrative is concerned), I will venture a little description of him here. He stood a full six feet tall, with noble shoulders and a chest like a coffer-dam. I have seldom seen such brawn in a man. His face was deeply browned and sunburnt, which made his white teeth dazzling by contrast; while in the deep shadows of his eyes floated some memories that did not seem to give him much joy. His voice at once announced that he was a Southerner, and from his fine stature I thought he must be one of those tall mountaineers from the Alleghanian Ridge in Virginia. When the revelry of his companions had reached its height, this man slipped away unobserved, and I saw no more of him until he became my comrade on the sea. Within a few minutes, however, his shipmates missed him, and since he was, it seems, for some reason a huge favorite with them, they raised a cry of "Bulkington! Bulkington! Where's Bulkington?" and dashed out of the house after him.

It was now about nine o'clock. The room felt almost supernaturally quiet after all that carousing, and I began congratulating myself on a little plan that had occurred to me just before the sailors arrived.

Nobody actually prefers sleeping two in a bed. In fact, you'd much rather not share one even with your own brother. I don't know why, but people like privacy when they sleep. And when it comes to sleeping beside a stranger you don't know, in a strange inn, in a strange town — and that stranger a harpooner — your objections multiply without end. Nor was there any earthly reason why I, as a sailor, should share a bed any more than anyone else; sailors at sea no more sleep two in a bed than bachelor kings do on land. True, they all sleep together in one room, but you have your own hammock, you cover yourself with your own blanket, and you sleep in your own skin.

The more I pondered this harpooner, the more I loathed the thought of sleeping with him. It was fair to assume that, being a harpooner, his linen or woolens, as the case might be, would not be of the tidiest, and certainly not of the finest. I began to twitch all over. Besides, it was getting late, and my decent harpooner ought to be home and heading for bed. Suppose, now, he should tumble in on me at midnight — how could I tell what vile hole he had been coming from?
"Landlord! I've changed my mind about that harpooner. I won't sleep with him. I'll try the bench here."

"Just as you please. I'm sorry I can't spare you a tablecloth for a mattress, and it's a plaguy rough board here" — feeling the knots and notches. "But wait a bit, Skrimshander; I've got a carpenter's plane there in the bar — wait, I say, and I'll make you snug enough." So saying, he fetched the plane, first dusted the bench with his old silk handkerchief, and set to vigorously planing away at my bed, grinning like an ape all the while. The shavings flew right and left, until at last the plane blade came bump against an indestructible knot. The landlord nearly sprained his wrist, and I told him for heaven's sake to quit — the bed was soft enough to suit me, and I didn't know how all the planing in the world could make eiderdown out of a pine plank. So, gathering up the shavings with another grin and throwing them into the great stove in the middle of the room, he went about his business and left me lost in a brown study.

Next I measured the bench and found it was a foot too short, though a chair could fix that. But it was also a foot too narrow, and the other bench in the room stood about four inches higher than the planed one, so there was no hitching the two together. Then I set the first bench lengthwise along the only clear stretch of wall, leaving a small gap between for my back to settle into. But I soon discovered that such a cold draft blew over me from under the windowsill that this plan was no good at all — especially since another current coming from the rickety door met the one from the window, and the two of them together whipped up a series of little whirlwinds right around the spot where I had meant to spend the night.

The devil take that harpooner, I thought. But wait — couldn't I steal a march on him: bolt his door on the inside and jump into his bed, not to be woken by the most violent knocking? It seemed no bad idea; but on second thought I dismissed it. For who could tell but that the next morning, as soon as I popped out of the room, the harpooner might be standing in the entry, all ready to knock me down!

Still, looking around me again and seeing no possible chance of spending a bearable night except in some other person's bed, I began to think that I might, after all, be harboring unwarranted prejudices against this unknown harpooner. I'll wait a while, I thought; he must be dropping in before long. I'll have a good look at him then, and perhaps we may become jolly good bedfellows after all — there's no telling.
But though the other boarders kept coming in by ones, twos, and threes and going to bed, there was still no sign of my harpooner.
"Landlord!" I said. "What sort of fellow is he — does he always keep such late hours?" It was now close to twelve o'clock.

The landlord chuckled again with his lean chuckle, and seemed mightily tickled at something beyond my comprehension. "No," he answered, "generally he's an early bird — early to bed and early to rise — yes, he's the bird what catches the worm. But tonight he went out a-peddling, you see, and I don't see what on earth keeps him so late, unless, maybe, he can't sell his head."

"Can't sell his head? What sort of a bamboozling story is this you're telling me?" I said, getting into a towering rage. "Do you mean to say, landlord, that this harpooner is actually busy this blessed Saturday night, or rather Sunday morning, peddling his head around this town?"
"That's exactly it," said the landlord, "and I told him he couldn't sell it here. The market's overstocked."
"Overstocked with what?" I shouted.
"With heads, of course. Aren't there too many heads in the world?"
"Look here, landlord," I said, quite calmly, "you'd better stop spinning that yarn to me. I'm not green."
"Maybe not," he said, taking out a stick and whittling a toothpick, "but I rather guess you'll be done brown if that there harpooner hears you a-slanderin' his head."
"I'll break it for him," I said, now flying into a rage again at the landlord's incomprehensible nonsense.
"It's broke already," he said.
"Broke?" I said. "Broke, do you mean?"
"Sartain, and that's the very reason he can't sell it, I guess."

"Landlord," I said, going up to him as cool as Iceland's volcano Mount Hekla in a snowstorm — "landlord, stop whittling. You and I must understand one another, and without delay, too. I come to your house and want a bed; you tell me you can only give me half of one; that the other half belongs to a certain harpooner. And about this harpooner, whom I have not yet seen, you persist in telling me the most mystifying and exasperating stories, which tend to give me an uncomfortable feeling toward the man you intend for my bedfellow — a sort of connection, landlord, which is an intimate and confidential one in the highest degree. I now demand that you speak out and tell me who and what this harpooner is, and whether I shall be safe in every respect spending the night with him. And in the first place, you will be so good as to take back that story about selling his head, which, if true, I take to be good evidence that this harpooner is stark mad; and I've no idea of sleeping with a madman; and you, sir — you, I mean, landlord — you, sir, by trying to get me to do so knowingly, would thereby make yourself liable to criminal prosecution."

"Well," said the landlord, fetching a long breath, "that's a purty long sermon for a chap that swears a little now and then. But be easy, be easy — this here harpooner I been tellin' you of has just arrived from the South Seas, where he bought up a lot of 'balmed New Zealand heads (great curios, you know), and he's sold all of 'em but one, and that one he's trying to sell tonight, 'cause tomorrow's Sunday, and it wouldn't do to be sellin' human heads about the streets when folks is goin' to church. He wanted to, last Sunday, but I stopped him just as he was goin' out the door with four heads strung on a string, for all the world like a string of onions."

This explanation cleared up what would otherwise have been an unaccountable mystery, and showed that the landlord hadn't meant to fool me after all. But at the same time, what was I to think of a harpooner who stayed out on a Saturday night straight through into the holy Sabbath, doing such cannibal business as selling dead idolaters' heads?
"Depend on it, landlord, that harpooner is a dangerous man."

"He pays reg'lar," was the reply. "But come, it's getting dreadful late; you'd better be turning flukes — turning in. It's a nice bed; Sal and me slept in that there bed the night we were spliced. There's plenty of room for two to kick about in that bed; it's an almighty big bed, that. Why, before we gave it up, Sal used to put our Sam and little Johnny in the foot of it. But I got to dreaming and sprawling about one night, and somehow Sam got pitched on the floor and came near breaking his arm. After that, Sal said it wouldn't do. Come along here, I'll give you a light in a jiffy." And so saying, he lit a candle and held it toward me, offering to lead the way. But I stood undecided; when, looking at a clock in the corner, he exclaimed, "I vow, it's Sunday — you won't see that harpooner tonight; he's come to anchor somewhere. Come along, then; do come; won't you come?"

I considered the matter a moment, and then up the stairs we went, and I was shown into a small room, cold as a clam, and furnished, sure enough, with a prodigious bed, almost big enough, in fact, for any four harpooners to sleep side by side.

"There," said the landlord, setting the candle on a crazy old sea chest that did double duty as a washstand and center table. "There, make yourself comfortable now, and good night to you." I turned around from eyeing the bed, but he had disappeared.

Folding back the counterpane, I bent over the bed. Though not the most elegant, it stood up to inspection tolerably well. I then glanced around the room; and besides the bedstead and the center table, I could see no other furniture belonging to the place but a crude shelf, the four walls, and a papered fireboard showing a man striking a whale. Of things not properly belonging to the room, there was a hammock lashed up and thrown on the floor in one corner; also a large seaman's bag, containing the harpooner's wardrobe, no doubt, in place of a land trunk. There was also a bundle of outlandish bone fishhooks on the shelf over the fireplace, and a tall harpoon standing at the head of the bed.

But what's this on the chest? I picked it up, held it near the light, felt it, sniffed it, and tried every way I could think of to reach some satisfying conclusion about it. The only thing I can compare it to is a big doormat, trimmed around the edges with little tinkling tags rather like the dyed porcupine quills on an Indian moccasin. There was a hole or slit in the middle of this mat, the kind you see in South American ponchos. But could any sober harpooner really climb into a doormat and parade through the streets of a Christian town dressed like that? I put it on to try it, and it dragged me down like a hamper, being unusually shaggy and thick, and, I thought, slightly damp, as if this mysterious harpooner had worn it on a rainy day. Wearing it, I went over to a scrap of mirror stuck on the wall, and I never saw such a sight in my life. I pulled myself out of it in such a rush that I gave myself a crick in the neck.

I sat on the edge of the bed and started thinking about this head-peddling harpooner and his doormat. After thinking a while there on the bedside, I got up, took off my monkey jacket, and stood in the middle of the room, thinking. Then I took off my coat and thought some more in my shirtsleeves. But I was beginning to feel very cold, half undressed as I was, and I remembered the landlord saying the harpooner wouldn't be coming home at all that night, since it was so very late; so without any more fuss I jumped out of my trousers and boots, blew out the light, tumbled into bed, and committed myself to heaven's care.

Whether that mattress was stuffed with corncobs or broken dishes, I can't say, but I tossed and turned a good deal and lay awake for a long time. At last I drifted into a light doze, and had very nearly made a good offing toward the land of Nod, when I heard a heavy tread in the passage and saw a glimmer of light come into the room under the door.

Lord save me, I thought, that must be the harpooner, the infernal head-peddler. But I lay perfectly still, and resolved not to say a word until spoken to. Holding a light in one hand, and that same New Zealand head in the other, the stranger entered the room and, without looking toward the bed, placed his candle a good way off from me on the floor in one corner, and then began working away at the knotted cords of the large bag I mentioned before as being in the room. I was all eagerness to see his face, but he kept it turned away for some time while busy unlacing the bag's mouth. This done, however, he turned around — when, good heavens! What a sight! Such a face! It was of a dark, purplish, yellow color, stuck over here and there with large blackish-looking squares. Yes, it's just as I thought: he's a terrible bedfellow; he's been in a fight, got dreadfully cut, and here he is, just back from the surgeon. But at that moment he happened to turn his face toward the light in such a way that I plainly saw those black squares on his cheeks could not be sticking-plasters at all. They were stains of some sort or other. At first I didn't know what to make of this; but soon an inkling of the truth occurred to me. I remembered a story of a white man — a whaleman, too — who, falling among the cannibals, had been tattooed by them. I concluded that this harpooner, in the course of his distant voyages, must have met with a similar adventure. And what is it, after all, I thought! It's only his outside; a man can be honest in any sort of skin. But then, what to make of his unearthly complexion — the part of it, I mean, lying round about, and completely independent of, the squares of tattooing? To be sure, it might be nothing but a good coat of tropical tanning; but I never heard of a hot sun tanning a white man into a purplish yellow one. However, I had never been in the South Seas; and perhaps the sun there produced these extraordinary effects on the skin. Now, while all these ideas were passing through me like lightning, this harpooner never noticed me at all. But after some difficulty in opening his bag, he began fumbling in it, and soon pulled out a sort of tomahawk and a sealskin wallet with the hair still on. Placing these on the old chest in the middle of the room, he then took the New Zealand head — a ghastly enough thing — and crammed it down into the bag. He now took off his hat — a new beaver hat — when I came near crying out with fresh surprise. There was no hair on his head — none to speak of, at least — nothing but a small scalp-knot twisted up on his forehead. His bald purplish head now looked for all the world like a mildewed skull. If the stranger had not stood between me and the door, I would have bolted out of it quicker than I ever bolted a dinner.

Even so, I half thought of slipping out through the window, but this was the second floor, at the back. I'm no coward, but what to make of this head-peddling purple rascal was completely beyond me. Ignorance is the parent of fear, and since I was utterly baffled and bewildered by the stranger, I admit I was now as frightened of him as if the devil himself had broken into my room like this in the dead of night. In fact, I was so scared of him that just then I didn't have the nerve to speak to him and demand a satisfactory explanation of what seemed so inexplicable about him.

Meanwhile he kept on undressing, and at last uncovered his chest and arms. As I live, those hidden parts of him were checkered with the same squares as his face; his back was covered in the same dark squares too; he looked as if he had fought in a Thirty Years' War and just escaped with a shirt of sticking plaster. What's more, even his legs were marked, as if a crowd of dark green frogs were running up the trunks of young palm trees. It was now perfectly clear that he must be some abominable savage or other who had signed onto a whaler in the South Seas and so ended up in this Christian country. I shook at the thought. A head peddler, too — maybe the heads of his own brothers. He might take a liking to mine — heavens! Look at that tomahawk!

But there was no time for shuddering, because the savage now started on something that absolutely riveted my attention and convinced me he really must be a heathen. He went to his heavy grego, or wrap-all, or dreadnaught — a thick sea coat — which he had hung on a chair earlier, rummaged in the pockets, and finally brought out a strange little misshapen figure with a hump on its back, exactly the color of a three-day-old Congo baby. Remembering the embalmed head, I nearly thought at first that this black manikin was a real baby preserved in some similar way. But seeing that it wasn't flexible at all, and that it gleamed a lot like polished ebony, I decided it must be just a wooden idol, which is exactly what it turned out to be. For now the savage goes over to the empty fireplace, takes away the papered fire-board, and sets this little hunchbacked figure up between the andirons like a bowling pin. The sides of the chimney and all the bricks inside were thick with soot, so I thought this fireplace made a very fitting little shrine or chapel for his Congo idol.

I now squinted hard toward the half-hidden image, feeling quite uneasy all the while, to see what would come next. First he takes about two handfuls of wood shavings out of his grego pocket and lays them carefully in front of the idol; then he puts a piece of ship's biscuit on top, holds the lamp flame to it, and lights the shavings into a sacrificial blaze. After a while, following many quick grabs into the fire and even quicker retreats of his fingers (which he seemed to be burning badly), he finally managed to pull the biscuit out; then, blowing off a bit of the heat and ash, he politely offered it to the little negro. But the little devil didn't seem to care for such dry fare at all; he never moved his lips. All these strange antics came with even stranger throaty noises from the worshipper, who seemed to be praying in a singsong, or else singing some pagan psalm or other, while his face twitched in the most unnatural way. At last he put out the fire, picked up the idol without any ceremony, and bagged it in his grego pocket again as casually as a hunter bagging a dead woodcock.

All these strange doings made me increasingly uncomfortable. Seeing that he was now showing every sign of concluding his business operations and jumping into bed with me, I decided it was high time — now or never, before the light was put out — to break the spell I'd been under for so long.

But the moment I spent working out what to say proved fatal. He picked up his tomahawk from the table, looked at its head for an instant, and then, holding it to the light with his mouth on the handle, puffed out great clouds of tobacco smoke. The next moment the light went out, and this wild cannibal, tomahawk between his teeth, leaped into bed with me. I shouted — I couldn't help it now — and with a sudden grunt of astonishment he began feeling me.

Stammering out something, I don't know what, I rolled away from him against the wall, and then begged him, whoever or whatever he might be, to keep quiet and let me get up and light the lamp again. But his guttural replies convinced me at once that he only poorly understood what I meant.
"Who-e debel you?" he said at last. "You no speak-e, dam-me, I kill-e." And so saying, he began flourishing the lighted tomahawk about me in the dark.
"Landlord, for God's sake! Peter Coffin!" I shouted. "Landlord! Watchman! Coffin! Angels! Save me!"

"Speak-e! Tell-ee me who-ee be, or dam-me, I kill-e!" the cannibal growled again, while his horrid flourishings of the tomahawk scattered the hot tobacco ashes about me until I thought my shirt would catch fire. But thank heaven, at that moment the landlord came into the room, light in hand, and leaping from the bed I ran up to him.
"Don't be afraid now," he said, grinning again. "Queequeg here wouldn't harm a hair of your head."
"Stop your grinning," I shouted, "and why didn't you tell me that that infernal harpooner was a cannibal?"

"I thought you knowed it — didn't I tell you he was a-peddlin' heads around town? But turn flukes again and go to sleep. Queequeg, look here — you sabbee me, I sabbee — you this man sleepe you — you sabbee?"
"Me sabbee plenty," grunted Queequeg, puffing away at his pipe and sitting up in bed.

"You gettee in," he added, motioning to me with his tomahawk and throwing the bedclothes to one side. He really did this in not only a civil but a truly kind and charitable way. I stood looking at him a moment. For all his tattooing, he was on the whole a clean, comely-looking cannibal. What's all this fuss I've been making about? I thought to myself. The man's a human being just as I am; he has just as much reason to fear me as I have to be afraid of him. Better sleep with a sober cannibal than a drunken Christian.

"Landlord," I said, "tell him to stash his tomahawk there, or pipe, or whatever you call it — tell him to stop smoking, in short, and I'll turn in with him. But I don't fancy having a man smoking in bed with me. It's dangerous. Besides, I ain't insured."
When this was told to Queequeg, he at once complied, and again politely motioned me to get into bed — rolling over to one side as much as to say, "I won't touch a leg of you."
"Good night, landlord," I said. "You may go."
I turned in, and never slept better in my life.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — The Counterpane
paragraphs: Waking the next morning around daylight, I found Queequeg's arm thrown over me in the most loving and affectionate manner. You would almost have thought I was his wife. The counterpane was patchwork, full of odd little multicolored squares and triangles; and this arm of his, tattooed all over with an endless Cretan labyrinth of a figure, no two parts of which were exactly the same shade — owing, I suppose, to his keeping his arm at sea unmethodically in sun and shade, his shirtsleeves rolled up irregularly at various times — this same arm of his, I say, looked for all the world like a strip of that same patchwork quilt. Indeed, with the arm lying partly on it as it was when I first woke, I could hardly tell it from the quilt, they blended their colors together so; and it was only by the sense of weight and pressure that I could tell that Queequeg was hugging me.

My sensations were strange. Let me try to explain them. When I was a child, I well remember, something somewhat similar happened to me — whether it was real or a dream, I could never entirely settle. It was this. I had been up to some mischief or other — I think it was trying to crawl up the chimney, as I had seen a little chimney sweep do a few days before; and my stepmother, who somehow or other was always whipping me or sending me to bed without supper — my mother dragged me by the legs out of the chimney and packed me off to bed, though it was only two o'clock in the afternoon of the 21st of June, the longest day of the year in our hemisphere. I felt dreadful. But there was no help for it, so upstairs I went to my little room on the third floor, undressed as slowly as possible to kill time, and with a bitter sigh got between the sheets.

I lay there dismally calculating that sixteen entire hours must pass before I could hope for a resurrection. Sixteen hours in bed! The small of my back ached to think of it. And it was so light, too — the sun shining in at the window, a great rattling of coaches in the streets, and the sound of cheerful voices all over the house. I felt worse and worse. At last I got up, dressed, and, going softly downstairs in my stocking feet, sought out my stepmother and suddenly threw myself at her feet, begging her as a particular favor to give me a good slippering for my misbehavior — anything, indeed, but condemning me to lie in bed for such an unendurable length of time. But she was the best and most conscientious of stepmothers, and back I had to go to my room. For several hours I lay there wide awake, feeling a great deal worse than I have ever felt since, even from the greatest later misfortunes. At last I must have fallen into a troubled nightmare of a doze; and slowly waking from it — half steeped in dreams — I opened my eyes, and the room that had been sunlit was now wrapped in outer darkness. Instantly I felt a shock run through my whole frame; nothing was to be seen, and nothing was to be heard; but a supernatural hand seemed placed in mine. My arm hung over the counterpane, and the nameless, unimaginable, silent form or phantom to which the hand belonged seemed to be sitting close by my bedside. For what seemed ages piled on ages, I lay there, frozen with the most awful fears, not daring to drag my hand away, yet always thinking that if I could only stir it one single inch, the horrid spell would be broken. I don't know how this awareness at last slipped away from me; but waking in the morning, I shudderingly remembered it all, and for days and weeks and months afterward I lost myself in bewildering attempts to explain the mystery. Indeed, to this very hour, I often puzzle over it.

Now, take away the awful fear, and my sensations at feeling the supernatural hand in mine were very similar, in their strangeness, to those I experienced on waking up and seeing Queequeg's pagan arm thrown around me. But at length all the events of the past night soberly came back, one by one, in fixed reality, and then I was alive only to the comical predicament. For though I tried to move his arm — to unlock his bridegroom clasp — yet, sleeping as he was, he still hugged me tightly, as though nothing but death should part us two. I now tried to rouse him — "Queequeg!" — but his only answer was a snore. I then rolled over, my neck feeling as if it were in a horse collar, and suddenly felt a slight scratch. Throwing aside the counterpane, there lay the tomahawk sleeping by the savage's side, as if it were a hatchet-faced baby. A pretty pickle, truly, I thought; in bed here in a strange house in broad daylight, with a cannibal and a tomahawk! "Queequeg! In the name of goodness, Queequeg, wake up!" At length, by dint of much wriggling, and loud and incessant protests about the unseemliness of his hugging a fellow male in that matrimonial sort of style, I succeeded in extracting a grunt; and presently he drew back his arm, shook himself all over like a Newfoundland dog just out of the water, and sat up in bed, stiff as a pikestaff, looking at me and rubbing his eyes as if he did not altogether remember how I came to be there, though a dim awareness of knowing something about me seemed slowly to be dawning over him. Meanwhile, I lay quietly eyeing him, having no serious misgivings now, and intent on closely observing so curious a creature. When at last his mind seemed made up about the character of his bedfellow, and he had become, as it were, reconciled to the fact, he jumped out onto the floor, and by certain signs and sounds gave me to understand that, if I liked, he would dress first and then leave me to dress afterward, leaving the whole room to myself. Queequeg, I thought, under the circumstances this is a very civilized overture; but the truth is, these savages have an innate sense of delicacy, say what you will; it is marvelous how essentially polite they are. I pay this particular compliment to Queequeg because he treated me with so much civility and consideration, while I was guilty of great rudeness — staring at him from the bed and watching all his dressing motions, my curiosity for the time getting the better of my upbringing. Still, a man like Queequeg you don't see every day; he and his ways were well worth unusual attention.

He began dressing at the top by putting on his beaver hat — a very tall one, by the way — and then, still without his trousers, he hunted up his boots. What under heaven he did it for, I can't tell, but his next move was to crush himself — boots in hand and hat on — under the bed; and from various violent gaspings and strainings, I inferred he was hard at work booting himself, though by no law of propriety that I ever heard of is any man required to be private when putting on his boots. But Queequeg, you see, was a creature in the transition stage — neither caterpillar nor butterfly. He was just civilized enough to show off his outlandishness in the strangest possible ways. His education was not yet complete. He was an undergraduate. If he had not been a little civilized, he very probably would not have bothered himself with boots at all; but then, if he had not still been a savage, he would never have dreamed of getting under the bed to put them on. At last he emerged with his hat badly dented and crushed down over his eyes, and began creaking and limping about the room, as if, not being much used to boots, his pair of damp, wrinkled cowhide ones — probably not made to order, either — rather pinched and tormented him at the start of a bitter cold morning.

Seeing now that there were no curtains on the window, and that, the street being very narrow, the house opposite had a plain view into the room, and noticing more and more what an indecent figure Queequeg made, stomping about with little else on but his hat and boots, I begged him as well as I could to hurry his dressing somewhat, and especially to get into his trousers as soon as possible. He complied, and then proceeded to wash himself. At that time in the morning any Christian would have washed his face; but Queequeg, to my amazement, was content to restrict his washing to his chest, arms, and hands. He then put on his waistcoat, and, picking up a piece of hard soap from the washstand center table, dipped it in water and began lathering his face. I was watching to see where he kept his razor, when lo and behold, he takes the harpoon from the bed corner, slips off the long wooden shaft, unsheathes the head, whets it a little on his boot, and, striding up to the bit of mirror against the wall, begins a vigorous scraping — or rather harpooning — of his cheeks. Queequeg, I thought, this is using Rogers's best cutlery with a vengeance. Afterward I wondered less at this operation, when I came to know what fine steel the head of a harpoon is made of, and how extremely sharp its long straight edges are always kept.
The rest of his grooming was quickly finished, and he marched proudly out of the room wrapped in his great pilot monkey jacket, carrying his harpoon like a marshal's baton.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — Breakfast
paragraphs: I quickly followed suit and went down to the bar room, greeting the grinning landlord very pleasantly. I bore him no grudge, though he had played more than a few pranks on me in the matter of my bedfellow.

However, a good laugh is a mighty good thing, and rather too scarce a good thing — more's the pity. So if any man, in his own proper person, provides material for a good joke to anybody, let him not hold back, but let him cheerfully allow himself to spend and be spent in that way. And the man who has anything bountifully laughable about him — be sure there is more in that man than you perhaps think.

The bar room was now full of the boarders who had been dropping in the night before, and whom I had not yet had a good look at. They were nearly all whalemen — chief mates, second mates, third mates, sea carpenters, sea coopers, sea blacksmiths, harpooners, and ship keepers; a brown and brawny company with bushy beards — an unshaven, shaggy set, all wearing monkey jackets for morning robes.

You could tell pretty plainly how long each one had been ashore. This young fellow's healthy cheek is the color of a sun-toasted pear, and would seem to smell almost as musky; he can't have been three days landed from his Indian voyage. The man next to him looks a few shades lighter; you might say there is a touch of satinwood in him. In the complexion of a third there still lingers a tropical tan, though slightly bleached by now; he, no doubt, has stayed whole weeks ashore. But who could show a cheek like Queequeg's? Barred with various tints, it seemed like the western slope of the Andes, showing in one array contrasting climates, zone by zone.
"Grub, ho!" the landlord now cried, flinging open a door, and in we went to breakfast.

They say that men who have seen the world become quite at ease in manner, quite self-possessed in company as a result. Not always, though: Ledyard, the great New England traveler, and Mungo Park, the Scottish one — of all men, they had the least assurance in the parlor. But perhaps merely crossing Siberia in a sledge drawn by dogs, as Ledyard did, or taking a long solitary walk on an empty stomach in the negro heart of Africa, which was the sum of poor Mungo's achievements — this kind of travel, I say, may not be the very best way of acquiring a high social polish. Still, for the most part, that sort of polish is to be had anywhere.

These reflections are prompted just here by the fact that after we were all seated at the table, and I was preparing to hear some good stories about whaling, to my no small surprise nearly every man kept a profound silence. And not only that, but they looked embarrassed. Yes, here was a set of sea dogs, many of whom had, without the slightest bashfulness, boarded great whales on the high seas — entire strangers to them — and dueled them dead without blinking; and yet here they sat at a social breakfast table — all of the same calling, all of kindred tastes — looking around at each other as sheepishly as though they had never been out of sight of some sheepfold among the Green Mountains. A curious sight — these bashful bears, these timid warrior whalemen!

But Queequeg sat among them — at the head of the table, as it happened — cool as an icicle. To be sure, I can't say much for his breeding. His greatest admirer couldn't have heartily justified his bringing the harpoon to breakfast and using it without ceremony — reaching across the table with it, endangering many heads, and hooking the beefsteaks toward himself. But that he certainly did very coolly, and everyone knows that in most people's estimation, to do anything coolly is to do it genteelly.

We won't dwell on all of Queequeg's peculiarities here — how he avoided coffee and hot rolls and devoted his full attention to beefsteaks, done rare. Enough to say that after breakfast he withdrew like the others to the public room, lit his tomahawk-pipe, and sat there quietly digesting and smoking with his inseparable hat on, while I headed out for a walk.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — The Street
paragraphs: If I'd been astonished at first seeing someone as outlandish as Queequeg strolling through the polite society of a civilized town, my surprise quickly vanished during my first daylight walk through New Bedford's streets.

In the streets near the docks, any sizable seaport will often put on view the strangest-looking nondescripts from foreign parts. Even on Broadway and Chestnut Street, Mediterranean sailors will sometimes jostle the frightened ladies. Regent Street is no stranger to Lascars and Malays; and at Bombay, on the Apollo Green, live Yankees have often scared the natives. But New Bedford beats every Water Street and Wapping. In those last-mentioned haunts you see only sailors; but in New Bedford, actual cannibals stand chatting on street corners — savages outright, many of whom still carry unholy flesh on their bones. It makes a stranger stare.

But besides the Fijians, Tongatobooarrs, Erromanggoans, Pannangians, and Brighggians, and besides the wild specimens of the whaling trade who reel unnoticed about the streets, you will see other sights still more curious, and certainly more comical. Every week scores of green Vermonters and New Hampshire men arrive in this town, all thirsting for gain and glory in the fishery. They are mostly young, with stalwart frames — fellows who have felled forests and now want to drop the axe and snatch up the whale-lance. Many are as green as the Green Mountains they came from. In some things you would think them only a few hours old. Look there! That fellow strutting around the corner. He wears a beaver hat and a swallow-tailed coat, belted with a sailor's belt and sheath-knife. Here comes another in a sou'wester and a bombazine cloak.

No town-bred dandy can compare with a country-bred one — I mean a downright bumpkin dandy, a fellow who in the dog-days of summer will mow his two acres in buckskin gloves for fear of tanning his hands. Now when a country dandy like this takes it into his head to make himself a distinguished reputation, and joins the great whale fishery, you should see the comical things he does when he reaches the seaport. Ordering his sea outfit, he has bell-buttons put on his waistcoats and straps on his canvas trousers. Ah, poor Hay-Seed! How bitterly those straps will burst in the first howling gale, when you are driven, straps, buttons, and all, down the throat of the tempest.

But don't think that this famous town has only harpooners, cannibals, and bumpkins to show its visitors. Not at all. Still, New Bedford is a strange place. If it hadn't been for us whalemen, that tract of land might to this day be in as howling a condition as the coast of Labrador. As it is, parts of its back country are enough to frighten you, they look so bony. The town itself is perhaps the most expensive place to live in all New England. It is a land of oil, true enough — but not like Canaan, a land also of corn and wine. The streets do not run with milk; nor in springtime do they pave them with fresh eggs. Yet in spite of this, nowhere in all America will you find more patrician-looking houses, or more opulent parks and gardens, than in New Bedford. Where did they come from? How were they planted on this once scraggy cinder-heap of a country?

Go and gaze at the iron harpoons set as emblems around that lofty mansion over there, and your question will be answered. Yes; all these fine houses and flowery gardens came from the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans. One and all, they were harpooned and dragged up here from the bottom of the sea. Can Herr Alexander, the stage conjurer, perform a trick like that?

In New Bedford, they say, fathers give whales to their daughters as dowries, and portion off their nieces with a few porpoises apiece. You must go to New Bedford to see a brilliant wedding; for, they say, they have reservoirs of oil in every house, and every night recklessly burn spermaceti candles down to their full length.

In summertime the town is sweet to see, full of fine maples — long avenues of green and gold. And in August, high in the air, the beautiful and bountiful horse-chestnuts, like candelabra, offer the passer-by their tapering upright cones of clustered blossoms. So all-powerful is art, which in many a district of New Bedford has laid bright terraces of flowers over the barren refuse rocks thrown aside on creation's final day.

And the women of New Bedford bloom like their own red roses. But roses bloom only in summer; the fine carnation of their cheeks is perennial as sunlight in the seventh heaven. Nowhere else can you match that bloom — except in Salem, where they say the young girls breathe such musk that their sailor sweethearts can smell them miles offshore, as if they were approaching the fragrant Moluccas instead of the Puritan sands.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — The Chapel
paragraphs: In this same New Bedford stands a Whaleman's Chapel, and few moody fishermen, shortly bound for the Indian Ocean or Pacific, fail to pay it a Sunday visit. I certainly didn't.

Returning from my first morning stroll, I set out again on this particular errand. The sky had changed from clear, sunny cold to driving sleet and mist. Wrapping myself in my shaggy jacket of the cloth called bearskin, I fought my way through the stubborn storm. Inside, I found a small, scattered congregation of sailors and sailors' wives and widows. A muffled silence reigned, broken only at times by the shrieks of the storm. Each worshipper seemed deliberately sitting apart from the others, as if each grief were an island, incommunicable. The chaplain hadn't arrived yet. These silent islands of men and women sat steadfastly gazing at several marble tablets with black borders, set into the walls on either side of the pulpit. Three of them read something like this, though I don't pretend to quote exactly:

SACRED TO THE MEMORY OF JOHN TALBOT, Who, at the age of eighteen, was lost overboard, Near the Isle of Desolation, off Patagonia, November 1st, 1836. THIS TABLET Is erected to his Memory BY HIS SISTER.

SACRED TO THE MEMORY OF ROBERT LONG, WILLIS ELLERY, NATHAN COLEMAN, WALTER CANNY, SETH MACY, AND SAMUEL GLEIG, Forming one of the boats' crews OF THE SHIP ELIZA Who were towed out of sight by a Whale, On the Off-shore Ground in the PACIFIC, December 31st, 1839. THIS MARBLE Is here placed by their surviving SHIPMATES.

SACRED TO THE MEMORY OF The late CAPTAIN EZEKIEL HARDY, Who in the bows of his boat was killed by a Sperm Whale on the coast of Japan, August 3d, 1833. THIS TABLET Is erected to his Memory BY HIS WIDOW.

Shaking the sleet from my ice-glazed hat and jacket, I took a seat near the door, and on turning sideways I was surprised to find Queequeg close by. The solemnity of the scene had affected him, and his face wore a wondering look of disbelieving curiosity. This savage was the only one there who seemed to notice me come in, because he was the only one who couldn't read, and so wasn't reading those cold inscriptions on the wall. Whether any relatives of the seamen named there were in the congregation now, I couldn't tell; but the fishery has so many unrecorded accidents, and several of the women present so plainly wore the look, if not the mourning dress, of some unending grief, that I feel certain the people gathered in front of me were those in whose unhealing hearts the sight of those bleak tablets, in sympathy, made the old wounds bleed again.

Oh! You whose dead lie buried beneath the green grass, who can stand among flowers and say — here, right here, lies my beloved — you do not know the desolation that broods in hearts like these. What bitter blanks in those black-bordered marbles that cover no ashes! What despair in those immovable inscriptions! What deadly voids and unbidden infidelities in lines that seem to gnaw at all Faith, and refuse resurrection to beings who have perished nowhere, without a grave. Those tablets might as well stand in the cave of Elephanta as here.

In what census of living creatures are the dead of mankind included? Why does a universal proverb say of them that they tell no tales, though they hold more secrets than the Goodwin Sands? How is it that to the name of someone who departed yesterday for the other world we prefix so significant and unbelieving a word, and yet give him no such title if he merely embarks for the remotest Indies of this living earth? Why do the Life Insurance Companies pay out death-forfeitures on immortals? In what eternal, unstirring paralysis and deadly, hopeless trance does ancient Adam still lie, who died sixty full centuries ago? How is it that we still refuse to be comforted for those whom we nevertheless maintain are dwelling in unspeakable bliss? Why do all the living strive so hard to hush all the dead? Why does the mere rumor of a knocking in a tomb terrify a whole city? None of these things is without its meaning.
But Faith, like a jackal, feeds among the tombs, and even from these dead doubts she gathers her most vital hope.

I hardly need to tell with what feelings, on the eve of a Nantucket voyage, I looked at those marble tablets, and by the murky light of that darkened, doleful day read the fate of the whalemen who had gone before me. Yes, Ishmael, the same fate may be yours. But somehow I grew merry again. Delightful inducements to embark, a fine chance for promotion, it seems — yes, a stove-in boat will make me an immortal by brevet, an honorary rank. Yes, there is death in this business of whaling — a speechlessly quick, chaotic bundling of a man into Eternity. But what then? I think we have hugely mistaken this matter of Life and Death. I think that what they call my shadow here on earth is my true substance. I think that in looking at spiritual things, we are too much like oysters observing the sun through the water, and thinking that thick water the thinnest of air. I think my body is only the dregs of my better being. In fact, take my body whoever will — take it, I say — it is not me. And therefore three cheers for Nantucket; and let a stove boat and a stove body come when they will, for stave in my soul Jove himself cannot.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 — The Pulpit
paragraphs: I had not been sitting very long before a man of a certain venerable robustness came in. The moment the storm-pelted door flew back to admit him, the whole congregation's quick, respectful eyeing of him was enough to show that this fine old man was the chaplain. Yes, it was the famous Father Mapple, as the whalemen called him, among whom he was a very great favorite. He had been a sailor and a harpooner in his youth, but for many years past had dedicated his life to the ministry. At the time I am writing of, Father Mapple was in the hardy winter of a healthy old age — the sort of old age that seems to be merging into a second, flowering youth, for among all the fissures of his wrinkles there shone certain mild gleams of a newly developing bloom, the spring green peeping out even beneath February's snow. No one who had not heard his history beforehand could see Father Mapple for the first time without the greatest interest, because there were certain clerical peculiarities grafted onto him, owing to the adventurous seagoing life he had led. When he came in, I noticed that he carried no umbrella, and certainly had not come in his carriage, for his tarpaulin hat was running with melting sleet, and his great pilot-cloth jacket seemed almost to drag him to the floor with the weight of the water it had soaked up. However, hat and coat and overshoes were taken off one by one and hung up in a little space in a nearby corner; and then, dressed in a decent suit, he quietly approached the pulpit.

Like most old-fashioned pulpits, it was a very lofty one, and since a regular staircase to such a height would, by its long slant across the floor, seriously shrink the already small area of the chapel, the architect, it seemed, had acted on a hint from Father Mapple and finished the pulpit without a staircase, substituting a perpendicular side ladder, like those used for climbing aboard a ship from a boat at sea. The wife of a whaling captain had provided the chapel with a handsome pair of red worsted man-ropes for this ladder, which was itself neatly capped with knobs and stained a mahogany color; considering what kind of chapel it was, the whole contrivance seemed by no means in bad taste. Pausing for an instant at the foot of the ladder, with both hands grasping the ornamental knobs of the man-ropes, Father Mapple cast a look upward, and then, with a truly sailor-like yet still reverent dexterity, hand over hand, mounted the steps as if climbing to the main-top of his ship.

The upright parts of this side ladder, as is usually the case with swinging ones, were made of cloth-covered rope, and only the rungs were of wood, so that at every step there was a joint. At my first glimpse of the pulpit, I had noticed that however convenient these joints might be on a ship, in this case they seemed unnecessary. For I was not prepared to see Father Mapple, after reaching the top, slowly turn around, stoop over the pulpit, and deliberately drag up the ladder step by step, until the whole of it was stowed inside, leaving him impregnable in his little Quebec.

I pondered for some time without fully understanding the reason for this. Father Mapple had such a wide reputation for sincerity and holiness that I could not suspect him of courting notoriety by any mere stage tricks. No, I thought, there must be some sober reason for this; what's more, it must symbolize something unseen. Can it be, then, that by that act of physical isolation he signifies his spiritual withdrawal, for the time being, from all outward worldly ties and connections? Yes, for to the faithful man of God, replenished with the meat and wine of the word, this pulpit, I see, is a self-contained stronghold — a lofty Ehrenbreitstein, with a never-failing well of water within its walls.

But the side ladder was not the only strange feature of the place borrowed from the chaplain's former seafaring. Between the marble cenotaphs on either side of the pulpit, the wall that formed its back was adorned with a large painting of a gallant ship beating against a terrible storm off a lee coast of black rocks and snowy breakers. But high above the flying scud and dark rolling clouds there floated a little island of sunlight, from which an angel's face beamed out; and this bright face shed a distinct spot of radiance on the ship's tossed deck, something like the silver plate now set into the Victory's planking where Nelson fell. "Ah, noble ship," the angel seemed to say, "beat on, beat on, you noble ship, and keep a hardy helm; for look! The sun is breaking through; the clouds are rolling off — the most serene blue is at hand."
