The pulpit itself also showed traces of the same seafaring taste that had produced the ladder and the painting. Its paneled front was shaped like a ship's bluff bows, and the Holy Bible sat on a jutting piece of scrollwork modeled on a ship's fiddle-headed beak.

What could be more full of meaning? For the pulpit is always this earth's foremost part; all the rest comes behind it; the pulpit leads the world. From there the storm of God's quick wrath is first sighted, and the bow must bear the first brunt. From there the God of breezes fair or foul is first called on for favorable winds. Yes, the world's a ship on its passage out, and not a completed voyage; and the pulpit is its prow.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 — The Sermon
paragraphs: Father Mapple rose, and in a mild voice of unassuming authority ordered the scattered people to close up. "Starboard gangway, there! Side away to port — port gangway to starboard! Midships! Midships!"
There was a low rumbling of heavy sea boots among the benches and an even slighter shuffling of women's shoes, and then all was quiet again, every eye on the preacher.

He paused a moment, then kneeled in the bow of the pulpit, folded his large brown hands across his chest, raised his closed eyes, and offered a prayer so deeply reverent that he seemed to be kneeling and praying at the bottom of the sea.

When he finished, in prolonged, solemn tones — like the continuous tolling of a bell on a ship foundering at sea in fog — he began reading the following hymn. But as he reached the final stanzas, his manner changed, and he burst forth with pealing joy and exultation:
"The ribs and terrors in the whale / Arched over me a dismal gloom, / While all God's sunlit waves rolled by, / And lifted me deepening down to doom.
"I saw the opening jaws of hell, / With endless pains and sorrows there; / Which none but those who feel can tell — / Oh, I was plunging to despair.
"In black distress, I called my God, / When I could hardly think him mine; / He bent his ear to my complaints — / No more the whale did me confine.
"Swiftly he flew to my relief, / As though on a shining dolphin borne; / Fearsome, yet bright, as lightning shone / The face of my Deliverer God.
"My song forever shall record / That terrible, that joyful hour; / I give the glory to my God, / His all the mercy and the power."

Nearly everyone joined in singing this hymn, which swelled high above the howling of the storm. A brief pause followed; the preacher slowly turned over the pages of the Bible, and at last, laying his hand flat on the proper page, said: "Beloved shipmates, clinch the last verse of the first chapter of Jonah — 'And God had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah.'"

"Shipmates, this book, containing only four chapters — four yarns — is one of the smallest strands in the mighty cable of the Scriptures. Yet what depths of the soul Jonah's deep sea-line sounds! What a pregnant lesson this prophet is to us! What a noble thing is that canticle in the fish's belly! How billow-like and boisterously grand! We feel the floods surging over us; we sound with him to the kelpy bottom of the waters; seaweed and all the slime of the sea is around us! But what is this lesson that the book of Jonah teaches? Shipmates, it is a two-stranded lesson: a lesson to us all as sinful men, and a lesson to me as a pilot of the living God. As sinful men, it is a lesson to us all, because it is a story of the sin, the hard-heartedness, the suddenly awakened fears, the swift punishment, the repentance, the prayers, and finally the deliverance and joy of Jonah. As with all sinners among men, the sin of this son of Amittai lay in his willful disobedience of the command of God — never mind now what that command was, or how it was conveyed — which he found a hard command. But all the things that God would have us do are hard for us to do — remember that — and so he more often commands us than tries to persuade us. And if we obey God, we must disobey ourselves; and it is in this disobeying of ourselves that the hardness of obeying God consists.

"With this sin of disobedience in him, Jonah flouts God still further by trying to flee from Him. He thinks that a ship made by men will carry him into countries where God does not reign, but only the Captains of this earth. He skulks about the wharves of Joppa, and looks for a ship that's bound for Tarshish. Perhaps there lurks a meaning here that no one has noticed until now. By all accounts Tarshish could have been no other city than the modern Cadiz. That's the opinion of learned men. And where is Cadiz, shipmates? Cadiz is in Spain; as far by water from Joppa as Jonah could possibly have sailed in those ancient days, when the Atlantic was an almost unknown sea. Because Joppa, the modern Jaffa, shipmates, is on the most easterly coast of the Mediterranean, the Syrian coast; and Tarshish, or Cadiz, is more than two thousand miles to the west of that, just outside the Straits of Gibraltar. Don't you see, then, shipmates, that Jonah sought to flee the whole width of the world from God? Miserable man! Oh! Most contemptible and worthy of all scorn; with slouched hat and guilty eye, skulking from his God; prowling among the shipping like a vile burglar hurrying to cross the seas. His look is so disordered and self-condemning that if there had been policemen in those days, Jonah would have been arrested on the mere suspicion of something wrong before he touched a deck. How plainly he's a fugitive! No baggage, not a hat-box, valise, or carpetbag — no friends come with him to the wharf to say goodbye. At last, after much dodging search, he finds the Tarshish ship taking on the last items of her cargo; and as he steps on board to see its Captain in the cabin, all the sailors stop hoisting in the goods for the moment, to take note of the stranger's evil eye. Jonah sees this; but in vain he tries to look all ease and confidence; in vain he attempts his wretched smile. The sailors' strong intuitions about the man assure them he can be no innocent. In their playful but still serious way, one whispers to another — 'Jack, he's robbed a widow'; or, 'Joe, do you see him? He's a bigamist'; or, 'Harry lad, I guess he's the adulterer that broke jail in old Gomorrah, or maybe one of the missing murderers from Sodom.' Another runs to read the notice that's stuck up against the post on the wharf where the ship is moored, offering five hundred gold coins for the capture of a parricide, and giving a description of his person. He reads, and looks from Jonah to the notice; while all his sympathetic shipmates now crowd around Jonah, ready to lay their hands on him. Frightened Jonah trembles, and summoning all his boldness into his face, only looks all the more a coward. He will not admit that he is suspected; but that in itself is strong grounds for suspicion. So he makes the best of it; and when the sailors find that he is not the man in the notice, they let him pass, and he goes down into the cabin.

"'Who's there?' cries the Captain at his busy desk, hurriedly making out his papers for the Customs — 'Who's there?' Oh! How that harmless question mangles Jonah! For an instant he almost turns to flee again. But he rallies. 'I want a passage in this ship to Tarshish; how soon do you sail, sir?' So far the busy Captain had not looked up at Jonah, though the man now stands in front of him; but no sooner does he hear that hollow voice than he darts a searching glance at him. 'We sail with the next tide,' he answered at last, slowly, still eyeing him intently. 'No sooner, sir?' — 'Soon enough for any honest man who goes as a passenger.' Ha! Jonah, that's another stab. But he swiftly calls the Captain away from that scent. 'I'll sail with you,' he says — 'the passage money, how much is that? I'll pay now.' For it is particularly written, shipmates, as if it were a thing not to be overlooked in this history, 'that he paid the fare thereof' before the ship sailed. And taken with the context, this is full of meaning.

"Now Jonah's Captain, shipmates, was one whose discernment detects crime in anyone, but whose greed exposes it only in the penniless. In this world, shipmates, sin that pays its way can travel freely, and without a passport; whereas Virtue, if a pauper, is stopped at every frontier. So Jonah's Captain gets ready to test the length of Jonah's purse before he judges him openly. He charges him three times the usual sum; and Jonah agrees to it. Then the Captain knows that Jonah is a fugitive; but at the same time he resolves to help a flight that paves its trail with gold. Yet when Jonah actually takes out his purse, prudent suspicions still trouble the Captain. He rings every coin to find a counterfeit. 'Not a forger, anyway,' he mutters; and Jonah is entered for his passage. 'Show me my stateroom, sir,' says Jonah now; 'I'm travel-weary; I need sleep.' 'You look it,' says the Captain; 'there's your room.' Jonah goes in, and would lock the door, but the lock has no key. Hearing him foolishly fumbling there, the Captain laughs quietly to himself, and mutters something about how the doors of convicts' cells are never allowed to be locked from inside. All dressed and dusty as he is, Jonah throws himself into his berth, and finds the little stateroom's ceiling almost resting on his forehead. The air is close, and Jonah gasps. Then, in that cramped hole, sunk too beneath the ship's waterline, Jonah feels a foreboding, like a herald, of that stifling hour when the whale will hold him in the smallest of the prison wards of his bowels.

"Screwed at its axis against the side, a swinging lamp gently oscillates in Jonah's room; and as the ship heels over toward the wharf with the weight of the last bales taken on, the lamp, flame and all, though slightly moving, still keeps a permanent slant in relation to the room; though in truth, being itself unfailingly straight, it only makes obvious the false, lying levels among which it hangs. The lamp alarms and frightens Jonah; as he lies in his berth his tormented eyes roll around the place, and this so far successful fugitive finds no refuge for his restless glance. But that contradiction in the lamp appalls him more and more. The floor, the ceiling, and the side are all awry. 'Oh! So my conscience hangs in me!' he groans. 'Straight upward it burns; but the chambers of my soul are all in crookedness!'

"Like one who after a night of drunken revelry hurries to his bed, still reeling, but with his conscience still pricking him, just as the plunging of the Roman racehorse only strikes the steel tags hung on it all the deeper into its flesh; like one who in that miserable plight still turns and turns in giddy anguish, praying God for annihilation until the fit has passed; and at last, amid the whirl of woe he feels, a deep stupor steals over him, as over a man who bleeds to death, for conscience is the wound, and there is nothing to stanch it; so, after sore wrestlings in his berth, Jonah's prodigy of ponderous misery drags him drowning down to sleep.

"And now the time of the tide has come; the ship casts off her cables; and from the deserted wharf the uncheered ship for Tarshish, heeling far over, glides out to sea. That ship, my friends, was the first smuggler on record! The contraband was Jonah. But the sea rebels; it will not bear the wicked burden. A dreadful storm comes on; the ship is about to break up. But now, when the boatswain calls all hands to lighten her; when boxes, bales, and jars are clattering overboard; when the wind is shrieking, and the men are yelling, and every plank thunders with trampling feet right over Jonah's head; in all this raging tumult, Jonah sleeps his hideous sleep. He sees no black sky and raging sea, does not feel the reeling timbers, and little does he hear or heed the distant rush of the mighty whale, which even now, with open mouth, is cleaving the seas after him. Yes, shipmates, Jonah had gone down into the sides of the ship — a berth in the cabin, as I take it — and was fast asleep. But the frightened master comes to him, and shrieks in his dead ear, 'What do you mean, O sleeper? Arise!' Startled from his lethargy by that dreadful cry, Jonah staggers to his feet, and stumbling up to the deck, grasps a shroud, one of the ropes bracing the mast, to look out at the sea. But at that moment a panther of a billow leaps over the bulwarks and springs on him. Wave after wave leaps into the ship like this, and finding no quick way out, runs roaring fore and aft, until the sailors come close to drowning while still afloat. And every time the white moon shows her frightened face from the steep gullies in the blackness overhead, aghast Jonah sees the rearing bowsprit pointing high upward, but soon beaten downward again toward the tormented deep.

"Terrors upon terrors run shouting through his soul. In all his cringing postures, the God-fugitive is now too plainly recognized. The sailors take note of him; their suspicions of him grow more and more certain, and at last, to test the truth fully by referring the whole matter to high Heaven, they fall to casting lots, to see on whose account this great tempest has come upon them. The lot is Jonah's; and once that is discovered, how furiously they mob him with their questions. 'What is your occupation? Where do you come from? Your country? What people?' But note now, my shipmates, the behavior of poor Jonah. The eager sailors only ask him who he is, and where he is from; yet they receive not only an answer to those questions, but also an answer to a question they did not put; and that unasked answer is forced from Jonah by the hard hand of God that is upon him.

"'I am a Hebrew,' he cries — and then — 'I fear the Lord, the God of Heaven, who has made the sea and the dry land!' Fear Him, O Jonah? Yes, well might you fear the Lord God then! Right away he goes on to make a full confession; at which the sailors become more and more appalled, but still they pity him. For when Jonah, not yet begging God for mercy, since he knew all too well the darkness of what he deserved — when wretched Jonah cries out to them to take him and throw him into the sea, for he knew that it was for his sake this great tempest was upon them, they mercifully turn from him, and look for other ways to save the ship. But all in vain; the indignant gale howls louder; then, with one hand raised to God in prayer, with the other they, not without reluctance, lay hold of Jonah.

"And now see Jonah lifted up like an anchor and dropped into the sea; and at once an oily calm drifts in from the east, and the sea goes still, as Jonah takes the gale down with him and leaves smooth water behind. He sinks into the whirling heart of such a masterless turmoil that he barely notices the moment he drops, seething, into the gaping jaws that wait for him; and the whale slams all his ivory teeth shut on his prison, like so many white bolts. Then Jonah prayed to the Lord from the belly of the fish. But look at his prayer, and learn a weighty lesson. For sinful as he is, Jonah doesn't weep and wail to be rescued outright. He feels that his terrible punishment is just. He leaves his rescue entirely to God, and is content with this: that despite all his pains and pangs, he will still look toward His holy temple. And here, shipmates, is true and faithful repentance; not loudly demanding pardon, but grateful for punishment. And how much this conduct of Jonah's pleased God is shown when He finally delivers him from the sea and the whale. Shipmates, I don't set Jonah before you to be imitated in his sin; but I do set him before you as a model of repentance. Don't sin; but if you do, make sure you repent of it the way Jonah did."

While he spoke these words, the howling of the shrieking, slanting storm outside seemed to add new power to the preacher. Describing Jonah's storm, he seemed tossed by a storm himself. His deep chest heaved like a ground swell; his tossed arms seemed the warring elements at work; and the thunder rolling from his dark brow and the light leaping from his eyes made every simple listener watch him with a strange, quick fear.
Then a lull came over his expression as he silently turned the pages of the Book once more. At last, standing motionless with closed eyes, he seemed for a moment to be communing with God and himself.
But again he leaned toward the congregation, and bowing his head low, with an expression of the deepest yet manliest humility, he spoke these words:

"Shipmates, God has laid just one hand on you; both his hands press down on me. By whatever murky light I have, I have read you the lesson that Jonah teaches all sinners; and so to you, and still more to me, because I am a greater sinner than you. And now how gladly I would come down from this masthead and sit on the hatches there where you are sitting, and listen as you listen, while one of you read me that other and more awful lesson — the one Jonah teaches me, as a pilot of the living God. How Jonah — an anointed pilot-prophet, or speaker of true things, commanded by the Lord to sound those unwelcome truths in the ears of wicked Nineveh — appalled at the hostility he would stir up, fled from his mission, and tried to escape his duty and his God by taking ship at Joppa. But God is everywhere; Jonah never reached Tarshish. As we have seen, God came down on him in the whale and swallowed him into living gulfs of doom, and with swift, slanting plunges dragged him 'into the midst of the seas,' where the swirling depths sucked him ten thousand fathoms down, and 'the weeds were wrapped about his head,' and the whole watery world of woe rolled over him. Yet even then, beyond the reach of any plumb line — 'out of the belly of hell' — when the whale ran aground on the ocean's deepest bones, even then God heard the swallowed, repenting prophet when he cried out. Then God spoke to the fish; and up from the shuddering cold and blackness of the sea the whale came breaching toward the warm and pleasant sun and all the delights of air and earth, and 'vomited out Jonah upon the dry land'; and the word of the Lord came a second time; and Jonah, bruised and beaten — his ears, like two seashells, still murmuring with the ocean's countless voices — Jonah did what the Almighty told him. And what was that, shipmates? To preach the Truth to the face of Falsehood! That was it!

"This, shipmates, this is that other lesson; and woe to the pilot of the living God who takes it lightly. Woe to the man whom this world lures away from his Gospel duty! Woe to the man who tries to pour oil on the waters when God has brewed them into a gale! Woe to the man who tries to please rather than to appall! Woe to the man whose good name matters more to him than goodness! Woe to the man who, in this world, does not court dishonor! Woe to the man who would not be true, even if being false meant salvation! Yes, woe to the man who, as the great Pilot Paul says, preaches to others and is himself a castaway!"

He dropped and fell away from himself for a moment; then, lifting his face to them again, he showed a deep joy in his eyes, as he cried out with a heavenly enthusiasm: "But oh! Shipmates! On the starboard hand of every woe there is a sure delight; and the top of that delight is higher than the bottom of the woe is deep. Is not the main-truck at the masthead higher than the kelson is low? Delight is to him — a far, far upward and inward delight — who against the proud gods and commodores of this earth always stands forth as his own inexorable self. Delight is to him whose strong arms still hold him up when the ship of this base, treacherous world has gone down beneath him. Delight is to him who gives no quarter in the truth, and kills, burns, and destroys all sin, though he pluck it out from under the robes of Senators and Judges. Delight — top-gallant delight is to him who acknowledges no law or lord but the Lord his God, and is only a patriot to heaven. Delight is to him whom all the waves of the billows of the seas of the boisterous mob can never shake from this sure Keel of the Ages. And eternal delight and deliciousness will be his who, coming to lay himself down, can say with his final breath — O Father! — known to me chiefly by Your rod — mortal or immortal, here I die. I have striven to be Yours, more than to be this world's, or my own. Yet this is nothing: I leave eternity to You; for what is man that he should live out the lifetime of his God?"
He said no more. Slowly waving a benediction, he covered his face with his hands and remained kneeling until every person had left and he was alone in the place.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 — A Bosom Friend
paragraphs: Returning to the Spouter-Inn from the Chapel, I found Queequeg there quite alone, as he had left the Chapel some time before the benediction. He was sitting on a bench in front of the fire, with his feet on the stove hearth, and in one hand he was holding that little negro idol of his close up to his face, peering hard into its face, and gently whittling away at its nose with a jackknife, meanwhile humming to himself in his heathenish way.

When I interrupted him, he put the idol away. Soon he went to the table, picked up a large book, placed it on his lap, and began counting the pages with careful regularity. At every fiftieth page — as I imagined — he'd stop, look vaguely around, and let out a long, gurgling whistle of astonishment. Then he'd start again at the next fifty, seeming to begin at one each time, as if he couldn't count past fifty — and it was only the sheer number of fifties that amazed him.

I sat watching him with great interest. Savage though he was, and hideously marred about the face — at least to my taste — his face still had something in it that was by no means disagreeable. You cannot hide the soul. Through all his unearthly tattooings, I thought I saw the traces of a simple, honest heart; and in his large, deep eyes, fiery black and bold, there seemed to be signs of a spirit that would dare a thousand devils. And besides all this, there was a certain lofty bearing about the Pagan, which even his uncouthness could not altogether spoil. He looked like a man who had never cringed and never had a creditor. Whether it was also that, his head being shaved, his forehead stood out in freer and brighter relief, and looked broader than it otherwise would, I will not venture to decide; but it was certain that his head was phrenologically an excellent one. It may seem ridiculous, but it reminded me of General Washington's head, as seen in the popular busts of him. It had the same long, regularly graded slope retreating from above the brows, which likewise projected a great deal, like two long promontories thickly wooded on top. Queequeg was George Washington cannibalistically developed.

While I was scanning him so closely, half-pretending all the while to be looking out the window at the storm, he never paid attention to my presence, never bothered himself with so much as a single glance, but seemed wholly occupied with counting the pages of the marvelous book. Considering how sociably we had slept together the night before, and especially considering the affectionate arm I had found thrown over me when I woke in the morning, I thought this indifference of his very strange. But savages are strange beings; at times you do not know exactly how to take them. At first they are overawing; the calm self-collectedness of their simplicity seems a Socratic wisdom. I had also noticed that Queequeg never mixed at all, or only very little, with the other seamen in the inn. He made no advances whatever, and seemed to have no desire to widen his circle of acquaintances. All this struck me as mighty peculiar; yet on second thought there was something almost sublime in it. Here was a man some twenty thousand miles from home — by way of Cape Horn, that is, which was the only way he could get there — thrown among people as strange to him as if he were on the planet Jupiter; and yet he seemed entirely at his ease, keeping the utmost serenity, content with his own company, always equal to himself. Surely this was a touch of fine philosophy, though no doubt he had never heard there was such a thing. But perhaps, to be true philosophers, we mortals should not be conscious of living or striving that way. As soon as I hear that such-and-such a man sets himself up as a philosopher, I conclude that, like the dyspeptic old woman, he must have "broken his digester."

As I sat in that now-lonely room — the fire burning low, in that gentle stage when, having warmed the air, it just glows to be looked at; the evening shadows and phantoms gathering at the windows, peering in at us, a silent, solitary pair; the storm booming outside in solemn swells — I began to feel strange sensations. Something was melting in me. My splintered heart and furious fist were no longer turned against the wolfish world. This soothing savage had redeemed it. There he sat, his very indifference revealing a nature free of civilized hypocrisies and smooth deceits. Wild he was — a sight of sights to see. Yet I began to feel myself mysteriously drawn to him. And the very things that would have repelled most people were the magnets that attracted me. I'll try a pagan friend, I thought, since Christian kindness has proved to be hollow courtesy. I moved my bench closer and made friendly signs and hints, doing my best to talk with him. At first he barely noticed, but when I mentioned his hospitality the night before, he managed to ask whether we'd be bedfellows again. I said yes, and he seemed pleased — perhaps a little flattered.

We turned over the book together, and I tried to explain the purpose of printing and the meaning of the few pictures in it. This caught his interest, and from there we moved on to chattering as best we could about the various sights to see in this famous town. Soon I suggested we smoke together. He produced his pouch and tomahawk-pipe and quietly offered me a puff. And then we sat, exchanging puffs from that wild pipe of his, passing it regularly back and forth.

If any ice of indifference toward me was still hiding in the Pagan's heart, this pleasant, friendly smoke of ours soon melted it and left us pals. He seemed to take to me just as naturally and spontaneously as I did to him; and when we had finished smoking, he pressed his forehead against mine, clasped me around the waist, and told me that from then on we were married — which, in the idiom of his country, meant we were bosom friends; he would gladly die for me if it came to that. In one of my own countrymen, such a sudden flare of friendship would have seemed far too hasty, and much to be distrusted; but those old rules didn't apply to this simple savage.

After supper and another sociable chat and smoke, we went to our room together. He gave me his embalmed head as a present; then he took out his huge tobacco pouch, felt around under the tobacco, and pulled out about thirty dollars in silver. Spreading the coins on the table, he mechanically split them into two equal piles, pushed one toward me, and said it was mine. I was about to object, but he cut me off by pouring them into my trouser pockets. I let them stay there. Then he began his evening prayers, took out his idol, and removed the paper fireboard. From certain signs and hints, I thought he seemed eager for me to join him; but knowing perfectly well what would follow, I considered for a moment whether, if he asked me, I would go along with it or not.

I was a good Christian, born and bred in the bosom of the infallible Presbyterian Church. How then could I join this wild idolator in worshipping his piece of wood? But what is worship? I thought. Do you suppose now, Ishmael, that the magnanimous God of heaven and earth — pagans and all included — can possibly be jealous of an insignificant bit of black wood? Impossible! But what is worship? To do the will of God — that, and nothing else, is worship. And what is the will of God? To do to my fellow man what I would have my fellow man do to me — that, and nothing else, is the will of God. Now, Queequeg is my fellow man. And what do I wish this Queequeg would do to me? Why, join me in my own particular Presbyterian form of worship. Consequently, I must then join him in his; therefore, I must turn idolator. So I lit the shavings; helped prop up the innocent little idol; offered him burnt biscuit with Queequeg; salaamed, bowing low before him, two or three times; kissed his nose; and that done, we undressed and went to bed, at peace with our own consciences and all the world. But we did not go to sleep without a little chat.

How it is, I don't know; but there is no place like a bed for confidential disclosures between friends. Man and wife, they say, open the very bottom of their souls to each other there; and some old couples often lie and chat over old times till nearly morning. So, then, in our hearts' honeymoon, Queequeg and I lay there — a cozy, loving pair.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 — Nightgown
paragraphs: We had lain in bed chatting and napping in short intervals, with Queequeg now and then affectionately throwing his brown tattooed legs over mine and drawing them back. We were so entirely sociable and free and easy together. At last, our confabulations chased away what little nappishness remained in us, and we felt like getting up — though dawn was still some way off.

We grew so wide awake that lying down became tiresome. Little by little we sat up, bedclothes tucked snugly around us, leaning against the headboard with our four knees drawn up close together and our two noses bent over them, as if our kneecaps were warming pans. We felt wonderfully cozy, especially since it was so cold outside — and outside the blankets too, since there was no fire in the room. To truly enjoy bodily warmth, some small part of you must be cold, because no quality in this world exists except by contrast. Nothing exists in itself. If you flatter yourself that you've been comfortable all over for a long time, then you can no longer be said to be comfortable at all. But if, like Queequeg and me in that bed, only the tip of your nose or the crown of your head is slightly chilled, then in your general consciousness you feel most delightfully and unmistakably warm. For this reason, a bedroom should never have a fire — that's one of the luxurious discomforts of the rich. The height of this kind of bliss is having nothing but the blanket between your warmth and the cold outside air. Then you lie like the one warm spark in the heart of an arctic crystal.

We had been sitting hunched like this for some time when all at once I decided to open my eyes. When I'm between sheets, day or night, awake or asleep, I tend to keep my eyes shut to concentrate the snugness of being in bed. Because no person can truly feel their own identity unless their eyes are closed — as if darkness were the proper element of our essence, though light suits our clay better. Opening my eyes and leaving my own pleasant, self-created darkness for the imposed, coarse outer gloom of an unlit midnight, I felt a disagreeable jolt. Nor did I object at all when Queequeg hinted that perhaps we had better light a lamp, since we were wide awake and he badly wanted a few quiet puffs from his tomahawk pipe. I should mention that I'd been dead set against his smoking in bed the night before; yet see how elastic our stiff prejudices become once love starts to bend them. Now I liked nothing better than having Queequeg smoke beside me — even in bed — because he seemed so full of serene, domestic contentment. I no longer worried about the landlord's fire insurance. I was alive only to the condensed, confidential comfort of sharing a pipe and a blanket with a real friend. With our shaggy jackets around our shoulders, we passed the tomahawk pipe back and forth until a blue hanging canopy of smoke slowly gathered above us, glowing in the flame of the newly lit lamp.

Whether it was that this undulating canopy of smoke carried the savage away to far-distant scenes, I don't know, but he now spoke of his native island; and, eager to hear his history, I begged him to go on and tell it. He gladly agreed. Though at the time I understood quite a few of his words only poorly, later disclosures, after I had grown more familiar with his broken phrasing, now allow me to present the whole story, such as it may prove to be, in the mere skeleton I give here.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 — Biographical
paragraphs: Queequeg was a native of Rokovoko, an island far away to the west and south. It isn't on any map; true places never are.

When he was a new-hatched savage running wild about his native woodlands in a grass loincloth, followed by the nibbling goats as if he were a green sapling — even then, a strong desire lurked in Queequeg's ambitious soul to see something more of Christendom than a sample whaler or two. His father was a High Chief, a King; his uncle a High Priest; and on his mother's side he boasted aunts who were the wives of unconquerable warriors. There was excellent blood in his veins — royal stuff; though sadly spoiled, I fear, by the cannibal appetite he nourished in his untutored youth.

A Sag Harbor ship visited his father's bay, and Queequeg asked for a passage to Christian lands. But the ship, having her full complement of seamen, rejected his request; and not all the influence of the King his father could prevail. But Queequeg vowed a vow. Alone in his canoe, he paddled off to a distant strait which he knew the ship must pass through when she left the island. On one side was a coral reef; on the other a low tongue of land, covered with mangrove thickets that grew out into the water. Hiding his canoe, still afloat, among these thickets, with its prow toward the sea, he sat down in the stern, paddle held low in his hand; and when the ship was gliding by, he darted out like a flash; reached her side; capsized and sank his canoe with one backward kick of his foot; climbed up the chains; and throwing himself full length on the deck, grabbed a ring-bolt there, and swore not to let go of it even if he were hacked to pieces.

In vain the captain threatened to throw him overboard and held a cutlass over his naked wrists; Queequeg was the son of a King, and Queequeg did not budge. Struck by his desperate daring, and his wild desire to visit Christendom, the captain at last relented, and told him he might make himself at home. But this fine young savage — this sea Prince of Wales — never saw the Captain's cabin. They put him down among the sailors, and made a whaleman of him. But like Czar Peter, content to toil in the shipyards of foreign cities, Queequeg scorned no apparent humiliation, if by it he might gain the power of enlightening his untutored countrymen. For at bottom — so he told me — he was moved by a profound desire to learn from the Christians the arts by which to make his people still happier than they were; and more than that, still better than they were. But alas! The practices of whalemen soon convinced him that even Christians could be both miserable and wicked — infinitely more so than all his father's heathens. Arriving at last in old Sag Harbor, and seeing what the sailors did there, and then going on to Nantucket and seeing how they spent their wages in that place too, poor Queequeg gave it up for lost. It's a wicked world in every meridian, he thought; I'll die a pagan.

So, though still an old idolater at heart, he lived among these Christians, wore their clothes, and tried to speak their gibberish. That explains his odd ways, even though he had been away from home for some time now.

Through hints, I asked him whether he did not intend to go back and have a coronation, since he might now consider his father dead and gone, as he had been very old and feeble at last report. He answered no, not yet; and added that he was afraid Christianity, or rather Christians, had made him unfit to ascend the pure and undefiled throne of thirty pagan Kings before him. But by and by, he said, he would return — as soon as he felt himself baptized again. For the time being, however, he intended to sail about and sow his wild oats in all four oceans. They had made a harpooner of him, and that barbed iron now served him in place of a scepter.

I asked him what his immediate plans might be. He answered: to go to sea again, in his old calling. At this, I told him that whaling was my own design, and told him of my intention to sail out of Nantucket, as the most promising port for an adventurous whaleman to embark from. He at once resolved to go with me to that island, ship aboard the same vessel, get into the same watch, the same boat, the same mess as me — in short, to share my every fortune, and with both my hands in his, boldly dip into the potluck of both worlds. To all this I joyfully agreed; for besides the affection I now felt for Queequeg, he was an experienced harpooner, and as such could not fail to be very useful to someone who, like me, was wholly ignorant of the mysteries of whaling, though well acquainted with the sea as merchant seamen know it.

His story finished with his pipe's last dying puff. Queequeg embraced me, pressed his forehead against mine, and blowing out the light, we rolled away from each other, this way and that, and were soon asleep.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 — Wheelbarrow
paragraphs: Next morning, Monday, after disposing of the embalmed head to a barber, for use as a wig block, I settled my own and my comrade's bill — using, however, my comrade's money. The grinning landlord, as well as the boarders, seemed amazingly tickled by the sudden friendship that had sprung up between me and Queequeg — especially as Peter Coffin's cock-and-bull stories about him had earlier alarmed me so much about the very person I now kept company with.

We borrowed a wheelbarrow, and loading our things into it, including my own poor carpetbag and Queequeg's canvas sack and hammock, off we went down to "the Moss," the little Nantucket packet schooner moored at the wharf. As we went along, people stared — not so much at Queequeg, for they were used to seeing cannibals like him in their streets, but at seeing him and me on such confidential terms. But we paid them no attention, going along wheeling the barrow by turns, with Queequeg now and then stopping to adjust the sheath on his harpoon barbs. I asked him why he carried such a troublesome thing with him ashore, and whether all whaling ships did not supply their own harpoons. To this, in substance, he replied that though what I suggested was true enough, he had a particular affection for his own harpoon, because it was made of reliable stuff, well tried in many a mortal combat, and deeply intimate with the hearts of whales. In short, like many inland reapers and mowers who go into the farmers' meadows armed with their own scythes — though in no way obliged to supply them — just so Queequeg, for his own private reasons, preferred his own harpoon.

Shifting the barrow from my hand to his, he told me a funny story about the first wheelbarrow he had ever seen. It was in Sag Harbor. The owners of his ship, it seems, had lent him one to carry his heavy chest to his boarding house. So as not to seem ignorant about the thing — though in truth he was entirely ignorant of exactly how to manage a barrow — Queequeg puts his chest on it, lashes it fast, and then shoulders the barrow and marches up the wharf. "Why, Queequeg," I said, "you might have known better than that, one would think. Didn't the people laugh?"

At this, he told me another story. The people of his island of Rokovoko, it seems, at their wedding feasts press the fragrant water of young coconuts into a large stained calabash like a punchbowl; and this punchbowl always forms the great central ornament on the braided mat where the feast is held. Now a certain grand merchant ship once touched at Rokovoko, and its commander — by all accounts a very stately, punctilious gentleman, at least for a sea captain — this commander was invited to the wedding feast of Queequeg's sister, a pretty young princess just turned ten. Well, when all the wedding guests were assembled at the bride's bamboo cottage, this Captain marches in, and being given the place of honor, sets himself opposite the punchbowl, between the High Priest and his majesty the King, Queequeg's father. Grace being said — for those people have their grace as well as we do, though Queequeg told me that unlike us, who at such times look down at our plates, they, on the contrary, copying the ducks, glance upward to the great Giver of all feasts — grace, I say, being said, the High Priest opens the banquet with the immemorial ceremony of the island; that is, dipping his consecrated and consecrating fingers into the bowl before the blessed drink goes around. Seeing himself placed next to the Priest, and noting the ceremony, and thinking that he — being Captain of a ship — plainly took precedence over a mere island King, especially in the King's own house, the Captain coolly proceeds to wash his hands in the punchbowl, taking it, I suppose, for a huge finger bowl. "Now," said Queequeg, "what you tink now? Didn't our people laugh?"

Finally, with our fare paid and our luggage safe, we stood on board the schooner. She hoisted sail and slid down the Acushnet River. On one side New Bedford climbed in terraces of streets, the ice-coated trees all sparkling in the clear, cold air. Enormous hills and mountains of casks upon casks were stacked on her wharves, and side by side the world-roaming whale ships lay silent and at last safely moored; while from others came the sounds of carpenters and coopers, mixed with the noise of fires and forges melting pitch — all signs that new voyages were getting under way; that the end of one long and deeply dangerous voyage only begins a second, and the end of the second only begins a third, and so on, forever and ever. Such is the endlessness — yes, the unbearableness — of all earthly effort.

Once we reached the more open water, the bracing breeze grew fresh; the little Moss tossed the quick foam from her bows, as a young colt tosses his snortings. How I sniffed that Tartar air! How I spurned that turnpike earth — that common highway dented all over with the marks of slavish heels and hoofs — and turned to admire the magnanimity of the sea, which will permit no records.

Queequeg seemed to drink and reel with me at the same foam-fountain. His dusky nostrils swelled apart; he showed his filed and pointed teeth. On, on we flew; and once we had gained the offing, the Moss paid homage to the blast, ducking and diving her bows like a slave before the Sultan. Leaning sideways, we darted sideways; every rope-yarn tingling like a wire; the two tall masts buckling like Indian canes in land tornadoes. We were so full of this reeling scene, as we stood by the plunging bowsprit, that for some time we did not notice the jeering glances of the passengers, a lubberly crowd, who marveled that two fellow beings should be so companionable — as though a white man were anything more dignified than a whitewashed negro. But there were some boobies and bumpkins there who, by their intense greenness, must have come from the very heart and center of all green growing things. Queequeg caught one of these young saplings mimicking him behind his back. I thought the bumpkin's hour of doom had come. Dropping his harpoon, the brawny savage caught him in his arms, and with an almost miraculous dexterity and strength sent him bodily high into the air; then, with a slight tap on his rear in mid-somersault, the fellow landed on his feet with bursting lungs, while Queequeg, turning his back on him, lit his tomahawk pipe and passed it to me for a puff.
"Capting! Capting!" yelled the bumpkin, running toward that officer. "Capting, Capting, here's the devil."
"Hey, you there, sir," cried the Captain, a gaunt rib of the sea, stalking up to Queequeg, "what in thunder do you mean by that? Don't you know you might have killed that fellow?"
"What him say?" said Queequeg, mildly turning to me.
"He say," I said, "that you came near kill-e that man there," pointing to the still-shivering greenhorn.
"Kill-e," cried Queequeg, twisting his tattooed face into an unearthly look of disdain, "ah! him very small-e fish-e; Queequeg no kill-e so small-e fish-e; Queequeg kill-e big whale!"
"Look here," roared the Captain, "I'll kill-e you, you cannibal, if you try any more of your tricks aboard here; so mind your eye."

But just then, as it happened, it was high time for the Captain to look out for himself. The enormous strain on the mainsail had snapped the weather-sheet, and the huge boom was now swinging wildly from side to side, sweeping clean across the whole after part of the deck. The poor fellow Queequeg had treated so roughly was knocked overboard; the whole crew panicked; and trying to grab the boom to stop it looked like madness. It flew from right to left and back again in hardly more than a single tick of a watch, and every instant it seemed about to shatter into splinters. Nobody did anything, and nothing seemed possible to do; the people on deck ran toward the bows and stood staring at the boom as if it were the lower jaw of an enraged whale. In the middle of this alarm, Queequeg dropped neatly to his knees, crawled under the path of the boom, grabbed a rope, made one end fast to the bulwarks, then flung the other end like a lasso and caught it around the boom as it swept over his head; at the next jerk the spar was trapped, and everything was safe. The schooner was turned into the wind, and while the crew were clearing away the stern boat, Queequeg, stripped to the waist, shot off the side in a long, living arc of a leap. For three minutes or more he could be seen swimming like a dog, flinging his long arms straight out ahead of him, his powerful shoulders showing now and then through the freezing foam. I looked at this grand and glorious fellow, but saw no one to save. The greenhorn had gone under. Launching himself straight up out of the water, Queequeg glanced around him for an instant, and appearing to grasp exactly how things stood, dove down and vanished. A few minutes later he came up again, one arm still stroking, the other dragging a lifeless body. The boat soon picked them both up. The poor bumpkin was brought back to life. The whole crew declared Queequeg a noble trump; the captain begged his pardon. From that hour I stuck to Queequeg like a barnacle — yes, until poor Queequeg took his last long dive.

Was there ever such unself-consciousness? He did not seem to think that he in any way deserved a medal from the Humane and Magnanimous Societies. He only asked for water — fresh water — something to wipe the brine off; that done, he put on dry clothes, lit his pipe, and leaning against the bulwarks and mildly eyeing those around him, seemed to be saying to himself: "It's a mutual, joint-stock world, in all meridians. We cannibals must help these Christians."

chapters.title: Chapter 14 — Nantucket
paragraphs: Nothing else noteworthy happened during the crossing, so after a fine run, we arrived safely in Nantucket.

Nantucket! Take out your map and look at it. See what a real corner of the world it occupies; how it stands there, far offshore, lonelier than the Eddystone lighthouse. Look at it — a mere hillock, an elbow of sand; all beach, with no background. There is more sand there than you would use in twenty years as a substitute for blotting paper. Some playful fellows will tell you that they have to plant weeds there, since they don't grow naturally; that they import Canada thistles; that they have to send overseas for a wooden plug to stop a leak in an oil cask; that pieces of wood in Nantucket are carried about like bits of the true cross in Rome; that people there plant toadstools in front of their houses, to get under the shade in summertime; that one blade of grass makes an oasis, and three blades in a day's walk a prairie; that they wear quicksand shoes, something like Laplander snowshoes; that they are so shut in, belted about, enclosed every way, surrounded, and made an utter island of by the ocean, that small clams will sometimes be found sticking to their very chairs and tables, as to the backs of sea turtles. But these extravaganzas only show that Nantucket is no Illinois.

Now consider the marvelous traditional story of how the red men came to settle this island. The legend goes like this. Long ago an eagle swooped down on the New England coast and carried off an Indian baby in his talons. Wailing loudly, the parents watched their child carried away out of sight over the wide waters. They decided to follow in the same direction. They set out in their canoes, and after a dangerous crossing they found the island, and there they found an empty ivory casket — the poor little Indian's skeleton.

What wonder, then, that these Nantucketers, born on a beach, should take to the sea for a living! First they caught crabs and quahogs in the sand; grown bolder, they waded out with nets for mackerel; more experienced, they pushed off in boats and caught cod; and at last, launching a navy of great ships on the sea, they explored this watery world, put an unceasing belt of circumnavigations around it, peeped in at the Bering Strait, and in all seasons and all oceans declared everlasting war on the mightiest animated mass that has survived the flood — most monstrous and most mountainous! That Himalayan, salt-sea Mastodon, clothed with such an ominous weight of unconscious power that his very panics are more to be dreaded than his most fearless and malicious attacks!

And so these naked Nantucketers, these hermits of the sea, swarming out of their anthill in the ocean, have overrun and conquered the watery world like so many Alexanders, carving up the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans among themselves the way the three pirate powers carved up Poland. Let America add Mexico to Texas and stack Cuba on top of Canada; let the English swarm over all of India and hang their blazing flag from the sun; two thirds of this globe of land and water belong to the Nantucketer. For the sea is his; he owns it as emperors own empires, while other seamen have only a right of way through it. Merchant ships are nothing but extension bridges; warships nothing but floating forts; even pirates and privateers, though they follow the sea the way highwaymen follow the road, only rob other ships — other fragments of the land like themselves — without trying to make their living from the bottomless deep itself. The Nantucketer alone lives and revels on the sea; he alone, in the Bible's words, goes down to it in ships, plowing it back and forth as his own private plantation. That is his home; that is where his business lies, a business that Noah's flood would not interrupt, even if it drowned all the millions in China. He lives on the sea as prairie chickens live on the prairie; he hides among the waves, and he climbs them the way chamois hunters climb the Alps. For years at a time he doesn't know the land, so that when he finally reaches it, it smells like another world, stranger than the moon would smell to an earthling. Like the landless gull, which folds her wings at sunset and is rocked to sleep between the swells, the Nantucketer at nightfall, out of sight of land, furls his sails and lies down to rest, while under his very pillow herds of walruses and whales rush past.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 — Chowder
paragraphs: It was quite late in the evening when the little Moss came snugly to anchor and Queequeg and I went ashore; so we could attend to no business that day, at least none but a supper and a bed. The landlord of the Spouter-Inn had recommended us to his cousin Hosea Hussey of the Try Pots, who, he claimed, ran one of the best-kept hotels in all Nantucket; and he had also assured us that Cousin Hosea, as he called him, was famous for his chowders. In short, he plainly hinted that we could not possibly do better than try potluck at the Try Pots. But the directions he had given us — keep a yellow warehouse on our starboard hand till we came in sight of a white church to port, then keep that on the port hand till we made a corner three points to starboard, and that done, ask the first man we met where the place was — these crooked directions of his puzzled us very much at first, especially as, right at the start, Queequeg insisted that the yellow warehouse, our first point of departure, must be left on the port hand, whereas I had understood Peter Coffin to say it was on the starboard. However, by beating about a little in the dark, and now and then knocking at a peaceable inhabitant's door to ask the way, we at last came to something there was no mistaking.

Two enormous wooden pots painted black, hung by asses' ears, swung from the cross-trees of an old topmast planted in front of an old doorway. The horns of the cross-trees had been sawed off on the other side, so that this old topmast looked not a little like a gallows. Perhaps I was oversensitive to such impressions at the time, but I could not help staring at this gallows with a vague misgiving. I got a sort of crick in my neck as I gazed up at the two remaining horns — yes, two of them, one for Queequeg and one for me. It's ominous, I think. A Coffin for my innkeeper on landing in my first whaling port; tombstones staring at me in the whalemen's chapel; and here a gallows! And a pair of prodigious black pots too! Are these last throwing out oblique hints about Tophet, that biblical place of fire?

These thoughts were interrupted by the sight of a freckled woman with yellow hair and a yellow dress, standing on the inn's porch beneath a dim red lamp that swung there looking a lot like an injured eye, and briskly scolding a man in a purple woolen shirt.
"Get along with you," she said to the man, "or I'll be combing you!"
"Come on, Queequeg," I said, "all right. There's Mrs. Hussey."

And so it turned out; Mr. Hosea Hussey was away from home, but had left Mrs. Hussey entirely competent to attend to all his affairs. When we made known our wish for a supper and a bed, Mrs. Hussey, putting off further scolding for the present, showed us into a little room, and seating us at a table spread with the remains of a recently finished meal, turned around to us and said: "Clam or Cod?"
"What's that about Cods, ma'am?" I said, very politely.
"Clam or Cod?" she repeated.
"A clam for supper? A cold clam; is that really what you mean, Mrs. Hussey?" says I. "But that's a rather cold and clammy reception in wintertime, ain't it, Mrs. Hussey?"

But she was in a great hurry to get back to scolding the man in the purple shirt, who was waiting for it in the entry, and she seemed to have heard nothing but the word "clam"; so Mrs. Hussey rushed toward an open door into the kitchen, yelled out "clam for two," and vanished.
"Queequeg," I said, "do you think we can make a supper for both of us out of one clam?"

However, a warm, savory steam from the kitchen served to contradict the apparently cheerless prospect before us. But when that smoking chowder came in, the mystery was delightfully explained. Oh, sweet friends, listen to me! It was made of small juicy clams, hardly bigger than hazelnuts, mixed with pounded ship biscuit and salt pork cut up into little flakes, the whole enriched with butter and plentifully seasoned with pepper and salt. Our appetites being sharpened by the frosty voyage, and Queequeg in particular seeing his favorite fishing food in front of him, and the chowder being surpassingly excellent, we dispatched it with great speed; then, leaning back a moment and remembering Mrs. Hussey's clam-and-cod announcement, I thought I would try a little experiment. Stepping to the kitchen door, I uttered the word "cod" with great emphasis, and went back to my seat. In a few moments the savory steam came out again, but with a different flavor, and in good time a fine cod chowder was placed before us.

We got back to business; and while plying our spoons in the bowl, I thought to myself, I wonder now if this here has any effect on the head? What's that stultifying saying about chowder-headed people? "But look, Queequeg, ain't that a live eel in your bowl? Where's your harpoon?"

Of all fishy places, the Try Pots was the fishiest, and it fully earned its name, because its pots were always boiling chowders. Chowder for breakfast, chowder for dinner, and chowder for supper, until you started watching for fish bones to poke through your clothes. The ground in front of the house was paved with clamshells. Mrs. Hussey wore a polished necklace of codfish vertebrae, and Hosea Hussey had his account books bound in fine old sharkskin. The milk had a fishy taste too, which I couldn't explain at all, until one morning I happened to stroll along the beach among some fishermen's boats and saw Hosea's brindled cow eating fish scraps and marching along the sand with each foot stuck in a cod's severed head, looking very slipshod, I can tell you.

Supper over, we received a lamp from Mrs. Hussey, and directions for the nearest way to bed; but as Queequeg was about to go up the stairs ahead of me, the lady reached out her arm and demanded his harpoon; she allowed no harpoon in her bedrooms. "Why not?" I said. "Every true whaleman sleeps with his harpoon — but why not?" "Because it's dangerous," says she. "Ever since young Stiggs, coming from that unfort'nate v'yage of his, when he was gone four years and a half with only three barrels of ile, was found dead in my first-floor back room with his harpoon in his side — ever since then I allow no boarders to take sich dangerous weepons into their rooms at night. So, Mr. Queequeg" (for she had learned his name), "I'll just take this here iron and keep it for you till morning. But the chowder — clam or cod tomorrow for breakfast, men?"
"Both," says I, "and let's have a couple of smoked herring for variety."

chapters.title: Chapter 16 — The Ship
paragraphs: That night in bed, we worked out our plans for the next day. But to my surprise and no small concern, Queequeg now gave me to understand that he had been diligently consulting Yojo — the name of his little black god — and Yojo had told him two or three times over, and strongly insisted on it in every way, that instead of the two of us going together among the whaling fleet in the harbor and choosing our ship jointly — instead of this, I say, Yojo earnestly directed that the choice of the ship should rest entirely with me, since Yojo meant to befriend us. To that end he had already picked out a vessel which I, Ishmael, left to myself, would be certain to hit upon, exactly as though it had happened by chance. And I was to sign on to that vessel immediately, leaving Queequeg out of it for the present.

I have forgotten to mention that, in many things, Queequeg placed great trust in the excellence of Yojo's judgment and his surprising foresight. He regarded Yojo with considerable esteem, as a fairly decent sort of god who perhaps meant well enough on the whole, but who did not, in all cases, succeed in his well-meaning plans.

Now, this plan of Queequeg's — or rather Yojo's — about choosing our ship: I didn't like that plan at all. I had counted a good deal on Queequeg's shrewdness to point out the whaler best fitted to carry us and our fortunes safely. But since all my objections had no effect on Queequeg, I had to give in; and so I got ready to go at the business with a determined, rushing sort of energy and vigor that would quickly settle that trifling little affair. Early the next morning, I left Queequeg shut up with Yojo in our little bedroom — for it seemed that for Queequeg and Yojo that day was some sort of Lent or Ramadan, a day of fasting, humiliation, and prayer. How it worked I never could find out, because though I applied myself to it several times, I never could master his liturgies and his Thirty-Nine Articles. Leaving Queequeg, then, fasting over his tomahawk pipe, and Yojo warming himself at his sacrificial fire of wood shavings, I set out among the shipping. After a long stretch of wandering and many random inquiries, I learned that there were three ships taking on crews for three-year voyages — the Devil-dam, the Tit-bit, and the Pequod. Devil-Dam, I don't know the origin of; Tit-bit is obvious; Pequod, you will no doubt remember, was the name of a celebrated tribe of Massachusetts Indians, now as extinct as the ancient Medes. I peered and pried around the Devil-dam; from her I hopped over to the Tit-bit; and finally, going aboard the Pequod and looking around her for a moment, I decided that this was the very ship for us.

You may have seen many a quaint craft in your day, for all I know — square-toed luggers, mountainous Japanese junks, butter-box galliots, and whatnot. But take my word for it, you never saw such a rare old craft as this same rare old Pequod. She was a ship of the old school, rather small if anything, with an old-fashioned, claw-footed look about her. Long seasoned and weather-stained in the typhoons and calms of all four oceans, her old hull's complexion was darkened like that of a French grenadier who has fought in both Egypt and Siberia. Her venerable bows looked bearded. Her masts — cut somewhere on the coast of Japan, where her original ones were lost overboard in a gale — her masts stood stiffly up like the spines of the three old kings of Cologne. Her ancient decks were worn and wrinkled, like the pilgrim-worshipped flagstone in Canterbury Cathedral where Becket bled. But to all these old antiquities of hers were added new and marvelous features, belonging to the wild business she had followed for more than half a century. Old Captain Peleg, for many years her chief mate before he commanded a vessel of his own, and now a retired seaman and one of the principal owners of the Pequod — this old Peleg, during his time as chief mate, had built upon her original grotesqueness and inlaid it all over with a quaintness of both material and design unmatched by anything, unless it be Thorkill-Hake's carved buckler or bedstead. She was decked out like some barbaric Ethiopian emperor, his neck heavy with pendants of polished ivory. She was a thing of trophies. A cannibal of a craft, dressing herself up in the carved bones of her enemies. All around, her unpaneled, open bulwarks were garnished like one continuous jaw with the long, sharp teeth of the sperm whale, set there as pins to fasten her old hempen sinews and tendons to. Those sinews did not run through lowly blocks of land wood but traveled deftly over sheaves of sea-ivory. Scorning a turnstile wheel at her reverend helm, she sported a tiller there; and that tiller was in one piece, curiously carved from the long, narrow lower jaw of her hereditary foe. The helmsman who steered by that tiller in a storm felt like the Tartar holding back his fiery steed by clutching its jaw. A noble craft, but somehow a most melancholy one! All noble things are touched with that.

When I looked around the quarter-deck for someone in authority, so as to offer myself as a candidate for the voyage, at first I saw nobody. But I couldn't very well overlook a strange sort of tent, or rather wigwam, pitched a little behind the mainmast. It seemed to be only a temporary structure used in port. It was cone-shaped, some ten feet high, made of the long, huge slabs of flexible black bone taken from the middle and highest part of the right whale's jaws. A circle of these slabs, planted with their broad ends on the deck and laced together, sloped in toward one another and joined at the top in a tufted point, where the loose, hairy fibers waved back and forth like the topknot on the head of some old Pottowottamie Sachem, or chief. A triangular opening faced the bow of the ship, so that whoever sat inside had a complete view forward.

Half hidden in this strange shelter, I finally found someone who looked like he had authority. It was noon, the ship's work was paused, and he was enjoying a break from the burden of command. He sat in an old-fashioned oak chair, wriggling all over with curious carving, its seat formed of a stout interlacing of the same springy material as the wigwam.

There was nothing so very remarkable, perhaps, about the appearance of the elderly man I saw. He was brown and muscular, like most old seamen, and heavily bundled in blue pilot-cloth cut in the Quaker style. The only notable thing was a fine, almost microscopic network of the tiniest wrinkles around his eyes, which must have come from years of sailing through hard gales and always squinting into the wind — that habit tightens the muscles around the eyes. Wrinkles like that are very effective in a scowl.
"Is this the Captain of the Pequod?" I said, stepping up to the entrance of the tent.
"Supposing it is the captain of the Pequod, what do you want with him?" he demanded.
"I was thinking of signing on."
"Were you now? I can see you're no Nantucketer. Ever been in a stove boat?"
"No, Sir, I never have."
"Don't know anything at all about whaling, I suppose — eh?"
"Nothing, Sir, but I have no doubt I'll learn quickly. I've made several voyages in the merchant service, and I think that —"

"Merchant service be damned. Don't talk that lingo to me. See that leg? I'll take that leg off your stern if you ever talk of the marchant service to me again. Marchant service indeed! I suppose now you feel considerable proud of having served in those marchant ships. But flukes! Man, what makes you want to go whaling, eh? It looks a little suspicious, doesn't it, eh? You haven't been a pirate, have you? Didn't rob your last captain, did you? Not thinking of murdering the officers once you get to sea?"

I protested my innocence. I could see that behind the mask of these half-humorous insinuations, this old seaman, as an insulated, Quakerish Nantucketer, was full of his insular prejudices. He was rather suspicious of all outsiders unless they came from Cape Cod or the Vineyard.
"But what draws you to whaling? I want to know that before I think about signing you on."
"Well, sir, I want to see what whaling is. I want to see the world."
"Want to see what whaling is, eh? Have you set eyes on Captain Ahab?"
"Who is Captain Ahab, sir?"
"That's what I thought. Captain Ahab is the captain of this ship."
"I'm mistaken then. I thought I was speaking to the captain himself."

"You're speaking to Captain Peleg — that's who you're speaking to, young man. It's my job, mine and Captain Bildad's, to see the Pequod fitted out for the voyage and supplied with everything she needs, including crew. We're part owners and agents. But as I was saying, if you want to know what whaling is, as you say you do, I can show you a way to find out before you commit yourself past backing out. Take a look at Captain Ahab, young man, and you'll find he has only one leg."
"What do you mean, sir? Was the other one lost by a whale?"
"Lost by a whale! Young man, come closer to me: it was devoured, chewed up, crunched by the most monstrous parmacetty that ever chipped a boat! — ah, ah!"

I was a little alarmed by his intensity, and perhaps also a little moved by the genuine grief in that final exclamation. But I said as calmly as I could, "What you say is no doubt true enough, sir. But how could I have known there was anything especially ferocious about that particular whale, though I might have guessed as much from the simple fact of the accident?"
"Look here, young man, your lungs are sort of soft, do you see; you don't talk shark a bit. Sure you've been to sea before now? Sure of that?"
"Sir," said I, "I thought I told you that I'd been on four voyages in the merchant —"

"Hard down out of that! Mind what I said about the marchant service — don't aggravate me — I won't have it. But let's understand each other. I've given you a hint about what whaling is; do you still feel inclined for it?"
"I do, sir."
"Very good. Now, are you the kind of man who'd throw a harpoon down a live whale's throat and then jump in after it? Answer quick!"
"I am, sir, if it were absolutely necessary and there were no alternative — which I don't believe is actually the case."

"Good again. So you not only want to go whaling to find out what it's like, but you also want to see the world? Wasn't that what you said? I thought so. Well then, just step forward there and take a look over the weather bow. Then come back and tell me what you see."

For a moment I stood puzzled by this odd request, not sure whether to take it as a joke or seriously. But when Captain Peleg concentrated all his crow's feet into one fierce scowl, he sent me on my way.

Walking forward and looking over the weather bow, I saw that the ship, swinging on her anchor with the rising tide, was now pointing at a slant toward the open ocean. The view was unlimited but utterly monotonous and forbidding. Not the slightest variety that I could see.
"Well, what's the report?" said Peleg when I came back. "What did you see?"
"Not much," I replied. "Nothing but water. Plenty of horizon, though, and there's a squall coming up, I think."
"Well, what do you think now about seeing the world? Still want to go around Cape Horn to see more of it, eh? Can't you see the world right where you stand?"

I was a little taken aback, but go whaling I must and would. The Pequod was as good a ship as any — I thought the best — and I repeated all this to Peleg. Seeing how determined I was, he agreed to sign me on.
"You might as well sign the papers right now," he added. "Come along." And with that, he led the way below deck into the cabin.

Sitting on the stern bench was what struck me as a most unusual and surprising figure. This turned out to be Captain Bildad, who along with Captain Peleg was one of the largest owners of the vessel. The remaining shares, as is sometimes the case in these ports, were held by a crowd of old pensioners — widows, orphaned children, and wards of the court — each owning about the value of a timber head, a foot of plank, or a nail or two in the ship. People in Nantucket invest their money in whaling vessels the same way that you invest yours in approved state stocks that bring in good interest.

Now, Bildad, like Peleg and indeed many Nantucketers, was a Quaker. The island had originally been settled by that sect, and to this day its inhabitants generally retain Quaker peculiarities to an unusual degree, though strangely modified by completely foreign influences. Some of these Quakers are the most bloodthirsty of all sailors and whale hunters. They are fighting Quakers — Quakers with a vengeance.

So there are cases among them of men who were given Scripture names — a remarkably common fashion on the island — and who in childhood naturally absorbed the stately, dramatic "thee" and "thou" of the Quaker idiom; yet, from the audacious, daring, and boundless adventure of their later lives, they strangely blend with these peculiarities they never outgrew a thousand bold dashes of character not unworthy of a Scandinavian sea-king or a poetical pagan Roman. And when these things unite in a man of greatly superior natural force, with a globular brain and a ponderous heart; who has also, through the stillness and seclusion of many long night watches in the remotest waters, beneath constellations never seen here in the north, been led to think untraditionally and independently; receiving all nature's sweet or savage impressions fresh from her own virgin, voluntary, and confiding breast, and thereby chiefly, though with some help from accidental advantages, learning a bold, sinewy, lofty language — that man makes one in a whole nation's census: a mighty pageant creature, formed for noble tragedies. Nor will it detract from him at all, seen dramatically, if either by birth or by other circumstances he has what seems a half-willful, overruling morbidness at the bottom of his nature. For all men who are tragically great are made so through a certain morbidness. Be sure of this, O young ambition: all mortal greatness is only disease. But we are not yet dealing with such a man — rather with quite another; and still a man whose peculiarity, if he is indeed peculiar, again results only from another phase of the Quaker, modified by individual circumstances.

Like Captain Peleg, Captain Bildad was a well-to-do, retired whaleman. But unlike Captain Peleg — who didn't care a straw for what are called serious things, and in fact considered those very same serious things the most trifling of all trifles — Captain Bildad had not only been raised from the first in the strictest sect of Nantucket Quakerism, but all his later life at sea, and the sight of many unclothed, lovely island creatures round the Horn — all that had not moved this native-born Quaker one single jot, had not so much as altered one angle of his vest. Still, for all this unchangeableness, there was some lack of plain consistency about worthy Captain Bildad. Though he refused, from conscientious scruples, to bear arms against invaders on land, he had himself boundlessly invaded the Atlantic and the Pacific; and though a sworn enemy of human bloodshed, he had, in his straight-bodied coat, spilled tuns upon tuns of leviathan gore. How the pious Bildad, now in the contemplative evening of his days, reconciled these things in memory, I don't know. But it didn't seem to concern him much, and very probably he had long since come to the wise and sensible conclusion that a man's religion is one thing and this practical world quite another. This world pays dividends. Rising from a little cabin boy in short clothes of the drabbest drab to a harpooner in a broad shad-bellied waistcoat; from that to boat-header, chief mate, and captain, and finally ship owner — Bildad, as I hinted before, had concluded his adventurous career by retiring wholly from active life at the goodly age of sixty and devoting his remaining days to the quiet receiving of his well-earned income.

Now, Bildad, I'm sorry to say, had the reputation of being a hopeless old miser, and in his sea-going days, a bitter, hard taskmaster. They told me in Nantucket, though it certainly seems a curious story, that when he sailed the old Categut whaler, his crew, upon arriving home, were mostly all carried ashore to the hospital, utterly exhausted and worn out. For a pious man, especially a Quaker, he was certainly rather hard-hearted, to say the least. He never swore at his men, they said. But somehow he got an enormous amount of cruel, unrelenting hard work out of them. When Bildad was chief mate, having his drab-colored eye fixed intently on you made you feel completely nervous until you could grab something — a hammer or a marlinspike — and go to work like a madman at something or other, never mind what. Laziness and idleness withered before him. His own body was the perfect expression of his utilitarian character. On his long, gaunt frame, he carried no spare flesh and no unnecessary beard — just a soft, economical fuzz on his chin, like the worn nap of his broad-brimmed hat.

Such was the person I saw sitting on the stern bench when I followed Captain Peleg down into the cabin. The space between the decks was small. There, bolt upright, sat old Bildad, who always sat that way and never leaned — this to preserve his coat tails. His broad-brimmed hat was placed beside him. His legs were stiffly crossed. His drab clothes were buttoned up to his chin. And with spectacles on his nose, he seemed absorbed in reading from a heavy volume.
"Bildad," cried Captain Peleg, "at it again, Bildad, eh? You've been studying those Scriptures now for the last thirty years, to my certain knowledge. How far have you got, Bildad?"
As if long accustomed to such irreverent talk from his old shipmate, Bildad paid no attention to the disrespect. He quietly looked up, saw me, and glanced inquiringly at Peleg.
"He says he's our man, Bildad," said Peleg. "He wants to sign on."
"Does thee?" said Bildad, in a hollow tone, turning to face me.
"I does," I said, unconsciously mimicking him — he was that intense a Quaker.
"What do you think of him, Bildad?" said Peleg.
"He'll do," said Bildad, looking me over. Then he went on spelling his way through his book in a mumbling tone, quite audible.

I thought him the strangest old Quaker I'd ever seen, especially since Peleg, his friend and old shipmate, seemed like such a blowhard. But I said nothing, only looking around me sharply. Peleg threw open a chest, pulled out the ship's articles, set pen and ink before him, and sat down at a small table. I began to think it was time to figure out what terms I'd accept for the voyage. I already knew that in the whaling business they paid no wages. Instead, everyone, including the captain, received shares of the profits called lays. These lays were proportional to the importance of each man's duties. I also knew that as a green hand at whaling, my own lay wouldn't be large. But considering that I was used to the sea, could steer a ship, splice a rope, and all that, I had no doubt, from everything I had heard, that I would be offered at least the 275th lay — that is, the 275th part of the clear net proceeds of the voyage, whatever that might amount to. And though the 275th lay was what they called a rather long lay, it was better than nothing. If we had a lucky voyage, it might nearly cover the cost of the clothes I'd wear out, to say nothing of three years' food and board, for which I wouldn't have to pay a penny.

You might think this was a poor way to pile up a princely fortune — and so it was, a very poor way indeed. But I'm one of those people who never fuss about princely fortunes, and I'm quite content if the world is ready to feed and house me while I'm putting up at this grim sign of the Thunder Cloud. All things considered, I thought the 275th lay would be about the fair thing, though I wouldn't have been surprised to be offered the 200th, given my broad-shouldered build.

But one thing, nevertheless, made me a little uneasy about getting a generous share of the profits. Ashore, I had heard about both Captain Peleg and his strange old crony Bildad — how, being the principal owners of the Pequod, the other, lesser and scattered owners left nearly all management of the ship's business to these two. And for all I knew, stingy old Bildad might have a great deal of say in hiring the crew, especially since I now found him aboard the Pequod, completely at home in the cabin, reading his Bible as if by his own fireside. While Peleg was vainly trying to sharpen a pen with his jackknife, old Bildad — to my considerable surprise, given that he was such an interested party in these proceedings — paid us no attention at all. He just went on mumbling to himself from his book: "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth —"
"Well, Captain Bildad," Peleg interrupted, "what do you say? What lay shall we give this young man?"
"You know best," came the sepulchral reply. "The seven hundred and seventy-seventh wouldn't be too much, would it? — 'where moth and rust do corrupt, but lay —'"

Lay indeed, I thought, and such a lay! The seven hundred and seventy-seventh! Well, old Bildad, you're determined that I, for one, shall not lay up many lays here below, where moth and rust do corrupt. That was an exceedingly long lay indeed.
