And though the size of the figure might at first deceive a landsman, the slightest thought will show that though seven hundred and seventy-seven is a pretty large number, yet when you come to make a "teenth" of it — a fraction — you will see, I say, that the seven hundred and seventy-seventh part of a farthing is a good deal less than seven hundred and seventy-seven gold doubloons. And so I thought at the time.
"Why, blast your eyes, Bildad," cried Peleg, "you don't want to swindle this young man! He must have more than that."
"Seven hundred and seventy-seventh," Bildad said again, without lifting his eyes. Then he went on mumbling: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."
"I'm putting him down for the three hundredth," said Peleg. "Do you hear that, Bildad? The three hundredth lay, I say."

Bildad laid down his book and, turning solemnly toward him, said, "Captain Peleg, you have a generous heart. But you must consider the duty you owe to the other owners of this ship — widows and orphans, many of them — and that if we reward the labors of this young man too abundantly, we may be taking the bread from those widows and those orphans. The seven hundred and seventy-seventh lay, Captain Peleg."

"You Bildad!" roared Peleg, starting up and clattering about the cabin. "Blast you, Captain Bildad, if I had followed your advice in these matters, I'd have had a conscience by now to lug around that would be heavy enough to founder the largest ship that ever sailed round Cape Horn."

"Captain Peleg," said Bildad steadily, "your conscience may be drawing ten inches of water, or ten fathoms — I can't tell. But since you are still an impenitent man, Captain Peleg, I greatly fear your conscience is only a leaky one, and will in the end sink you, foundering, down to the fiery pit, Captain Peleg."

"Fiery pit! Fiery pit! You insult me, man — past all natural bearing, you insult me. It's an all-fired outrage to tell any human creature that he's bound for hell. Flukes and flames! Bildad, say that again to me, and start my soul-bolts, but I'll — I'll — yes, I'll swallow a live goat with all his hair and horns on. Out of the cabin, you canting, drab-colored son of a wooden gun — a straight wake with you!"
As he thundered this out, he rushed at Bildad. But with a marvelous sideways, sliding quickness, Bildad dodged him that time.

Alarmed by this terrible outburst between the two principal and responsible owners of the ship, and half thinking of giving up the whole idea of sailing on a vessel so questionably owned and temporarily commanded, I stepped aside from the door to let Bildad escape. Surely he'd want to flee from Peleg's wrath. But to my astonishment, he sat back down on the bench very quietly and showed not the slightest intention of leaving. He seemed completely used to impenitent Peleg and his ways. As for Peleg, after blowing off his rage, he seemed to have no more left in him. He too sat down like a lamb, though he twitched a little, as if still nervously agitated. "Whew!" he finally whistled. "The squall's blown off to leeward, I think. Bildad, you used to be good at sharpening a lance — sharpen that pen for me, will you? My jackknife needs a grindstone. That's it — thank you, Bildad. Now then, young man, Ishmael's your name, didn't you say? Well then, down you go here, Ishmael, for the three hundredth lay."
"Captain Peleg," said I, "I have a friend who wants to sign on too — shall I bring him down tomorrow?"
"Of course," said Peleg. "Bring him along and we'll have a look at him."
"What lay does he want?" groaned Bildad, glancing up from the book in which he had again buried himself.
"Oh, never mind about that, Bildad," said Peleg. "Has he ever whaled?" he asked, turning to me.
"Killed more whales than I can count, Captain Peleg."
"Well, bring him along then."
And after signing the papers, off I went, fully confident that I had done a good morning's work and that the Pequod was the very ship Yojo had chosen to carry Queequeg and me around the Cape.

But I hadn't gone far before it struck me that the captain I was to sail with still remained unseen. In many cases, a whale ship will be completely fitted out and take on her entire crew before the captain shows up to take command. Sometimes these voyages last so long, and the time ashore between them is so short, that if the captain has a family or any pressing personal matters, he doesn't bother much with his ship in port but leaves everything to the owners until she's ready for sea. Still, it's always wise to have a look at him before irrevocably putting yourself in his hands. Turning back, I found Captain Peleg and asked where Captain Ahab might be.
"And what do you want with Captain Ahab? Everything's fine — you're signed on."
"Yes, but I'd like to see him."

"I don't think you'll be able to right now. I don't know exactly what's the matter with him, but he stays shut up inside his house. He's a sort of sick, and yet he doesn't look it. Actually, he isn't sick — but he isn't well either. Anyway, young man, he won't always see even me, so I don't suppose he'll see you. He's a strange man, Captain Ahab — so some think — but a good one. Oh, you'll like him well enough, no fear. He's a grand, ungodly, god-like man, Captain Ahab. He doesn't talk much, but when he does, you'd better listen. Be warned: Ahab is above the common run. He's been in colleges as well as among cannibals. He's faced deeper wonders than the waves and driven his fiery lance into mightier, stranger enemies than whales. His lance! The keenest and truest that ever came from all our island! Oh, he's not Captain Bildad, no, and he's not Captain Peleg. He's Ahab, boy. And Ahab of old, as you know, was a crowned king!"
"And a very wicked one. When that evil king was killed, the dogs licked his blood, did they not?"

"Come here — closer, closer," said Peleg, with a look in his eye that nearly startled me. "Listen, lad. Never say that aboard the Pequod. Never say it anywhere. Captain Ahab did not name himself. It was a foolish, ignorant whim of his crazy, widowed mother, who died when he was only a year old. And yet the old squaw Tistig, at Gay Head, said the name would somehow prove prophetic. And perhaps other fools like her may tell you the same. I want to warn you — it's a lie. I know Captain Ahab well. I've sailed with him as mate, years ago. I know what he is — a good man. Not a pious, good man like Bildad, but a swearing good man — something like me — only there's a good deal more of him. I'll admit he was never very cheerful. And I know that on the way home last voyage, he was a little out of his mind for a while. But that was the sharp, shooting pains in his bleeding stump — anyone could see that. I know, too, that ever since he lost his leg on the last voyage to that accursed whale, he's been moody — desperately moody, and savage sometimes. But that will pass. And once and for all, let me tell you and assure you, young man: it's better to sail with a moody good captain than a laughing bad one. So goodbye — and don't wrong Captain Ahab just because he happens to have a wicked name. Besides, my boy, he has a wife — married not three voyages ago — a sweet, resigned girl. Think about that. By that sweet girl, the old man has a child. Can you hold, then, that there's any utter, hopeless harm in Ahab? No, no, my lad. Stricken and blasted as he may be, Ahab has his humanities!"

As I walked away, I was full of thoughtfulness. What had been incidentally revealed to me about Captain Ahab filled me with a certain wild, vague painfulness concerning him. And somehow, at the time, I felt a sympathy and a sorrow for him, though for what I don't know, unless it was the cruel loss of his leg. And yet I also felt a strange awe of him; but that sort of awe, which I can't describe at all, was not exactly awe. I don't know what it was. But I felt it, and it didn't turn me against him, though I felt impatient at what seemed like mystery in him, known to me as imperfectly as he was then. Eventually, though, my thoughts were carried off in other directions, so that for the present dark Ahab slipped my mind.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 — The Ramadan
paragraphs: Since Queequeg's Ramadan, or Fasting and Humiliation, was to continue all day, I chose not to disturb him until toward nightfall. For I have the greatest respect for everybody's religious obligations, never mind how comical, and I couldn't find it in my heart to look down on even a congregation of ants worshipping a toadstool — or on those other creatures in certain parts of our earth who, with a degree of footman-like servility quite unheard of on other planets, bow down before the torso of a deceased landed proprietor merely because of the enormous possessions still owned and rented in his name.

I say, we good Presbyterian Christians should be charitable about these things. We shouldn't consider ourselves so vastly superior to other people — pagans and whoever else — because of their half-crazy ideas on these subjects. There was Queequeg, certainly holding the most absurd beliefs about Yojo and his Ramadan — but so what? Queequeg thought he knew what he was doing, I suppose. He seemed content, and there I should let him be. All our arguing with him wouldn't help. Let him be, I say, and Heaven have mercy on us all — Presbyterians and Pagans alike — for we are all somehow dreadfully cracked in the head and badly need mending.

Toward evening, when I felt sure all his rituals must be over, I went up to his room and knocked on the door. No answer. I tried to open it, but it was locked from inside. "Queequeg," I said softly through the keyhole. All silent. "I say, Queequeg! Why don't you answer? It's me — Ishmael." But everything stayed still as before. I started to worry. I had given him plenty of time. I thought he might have had a stroke. I looked through the keyhole, but since the door opened into an odd corner of the room, the keyhole view was only a crooked and sinister one. I could only see part of the footboard of the bed and a strip of wall, nothing more. I was surprised to see the wooden shaft of Queequeg's harpoon leaning against the wall — the landlady had taken it from him the previous evening, before we went up to the room. That's strange, I thought. But since the harpoon was there, and he hardly ever went anywhere without it, he must be inside. No question about it.

"Queequeg! — Queequeg!" — still nothing. Something must have happened. A stroke! I tried to force the door open, but it held firm. Running downstairs, I quickly explained my fears to the first person I met — the chambermaid. "Oh my!" she cried. "I thought something must be wrong. I went to make the bed after breakfast and the door was locked. Not a mouse to be heard, and it's been just as silent ever since. But I thought maybe you'd both gone out and locked your things in for safekeeping. Oh my, ma'am! — Mistress! Murder! Mrs. Hussey! A stroke!" And with those cries she ran toward the kitchen, with me right behind her.

Mrs. Hussey soon appeared, with a mustard pot in one hand and a vinegar bottle in the other, having just broken off from attending to the castors (the stands that hold the table's condiment bottles) and scolding her little black boy at the same time.

"The woodshed!" I cried. "Which way to it? Run, for God's sake, and get something to pry open the door — the axe! The axe! He's had a stroke, I'm sure of it!" And saying this, I was rushing back upstairs in no sort of order, empty-handed, when Mrs. Hussey blocked my way with the mustard pot, the vinegar bottle, and the entire condiment stand of her face.
"What's the matter with you, young man?"
"Get the axe! For God's sake, someone run for the doctor while I pry it open!"

"Look here," said the landlady, quickly putting down the vinegar bottle to free up a hand. "Look here — are you talking about prying open one of my doors?" And with that she grabbed my arm. "What's the matter with you? What's the matter with you, shipmate?"

As calmly and quickly as I could, I explained the situation. Unconsciously pressing the vinegar bottle against one side of her nose, she thought for a moment, then exclaimed, "No! I haven't seen it since I put it there." Running to a small closet under the stairs, she looked inside, came back, and told me Queequeg's harpoon was missing. "He's killed himself," she cried. "It's that poor Stiggs all over again — there goes another bedspread — God pity his poor mother! It'll be the ruin of my house. Does the poor lad have a sister? Where's that girl? — there, Betty, go to Snarles the Painter, and tell him to paint me a sign: 'No suicides permitted here, and no smoking in the parlor.' Might as well kill both birds at once. Kill? The Lord be merciful to his ghost! What's that noise up there? You, young man, stop right there!"
And running up after me, she caught me as I was again trying to force the door open.

"I don't allow it; I won't have my premises spoiled. Go for the locksmith — there's one about a mile from here. But wait!" putting her hand in her side pocket, "here's a key that'll fit, I guess; let's see." And with that, she turned it in the lock; but, alas! Queequeg's extra bolt stayed shot on the inside.

"Have to break it down," I said, and was running back down the hall to get a running start when the landlady grabbed me again, insisting I not break down her property. But I tore free and, with a sudden full-body charge, threw myself against the door.

With a tremendous crash the door flew open, the knob slamming into the wall and sending plaster to the ceiling. And there — good heavens! — there sat Queequeg, perfectly cool and composed, right in the middle of the room, squatting on his heels, holding Yojo on top of his head. He looked neither one way nor the other but sat like a carved statue with barely a sign of life.
"Queequeg," I said, going up to him, "Queequeg, what's the matter with you?"
"He hasn't been sitting like that all day, has he?" said the landlady.

But no matter what we said, we couldn't drag a single word out of him. I almost felt like pushing him over just to change his position, which was almost unbearable to look at — so painfully and unnaturally stiff. Especially since, in all likelihood, he had been sitting that way for upwards of eight or ten hours, going without his regular meals the whole time.
"Mrs. Hussey," said I, "he's alive, at any rate. So leave us, please, and I'll deal with this strange business myself."

Closing the door on the landlady, I tried to get Queequeg to sit in a chair, but it was useless. There he sat. Despite all my polite efforts and coaxing, he wouldn't budge an inch, say a single word, look at me, or show the slightest awareness that I was there.

I wonder, I thought, if this could be part of his Ramadan. Do they fast while squatting like this on his native island? It must be so. Yes, it's part of his religion, I suppose. Well, let him be. He'll get up sooner or later. It can't last forever, thank God. And his Ramadan only comes once a year — and I don't think it's very punctual even then.

I went down to supper. After sitting a long time listening to the rambling stories of some sailors who had just come from a "plum-pudding voyage," as they called it — meaning a short whaling trip in a schooner or brig, limited to waters north of the equator in the Atlantic Ocean — after listening to these plum-puddingers until nearly eleven o'clock, I went upstairs to bed, feeling quite sure by then that Queequeg must have finished his Ramadan. But no — there he was, exactly where I had left him. He hadn't moved an inch. I started getting annoyed with him. It seemed so utterly senseless and insane to sit there all day and half the night on his heels in a cold room, holding a piece of wood on his head.
"For heaven's sake, Queequeg, get up and move around. Get up and have some supper. You'll starve. You'll kill yourself, Queequeg." But not a word did he reply.

Giving up on him, I decided to go to bed and sleep. No doubt he would follow before long. But before turning in, I took my heavy bearskin jacket and threw it over him, since it promised to be a very cold night and he had nothing but his ordinary short sailor's jacket on. For some time, no matter what I did, I couldn't fall asleep. I had blown out the candle, and the mere thought of Queequeg — not four feet away — sitting in that miserable position, completely alone in the cold and dark — it made me truly wretched. Think of it: sleeping all night in the same room with a wide-awake pagan squatting in this dreary, inexplicable Ramadan!

But somehow I drifted off at last and knew nothing more until daybreak. Looking over the side of the bed, there squatted Queequeg, as if he had been bolted to the floor. But as soon as the first rays of sun entered the window, up he got, with stiff and creaking joints but a cheerful face. He limped over to where I lay, pressed his forehead against mine again, and said his Ramadan was over.

Now, as I mentioned before, I have no objection to anyone's religion, whatever it may be, as long as that person doesn't kill or insult anyone else for not sharing it. But when a person's religion becomes truly fanatical — when it's a source of real torment, and when, in short, it makes this earth of ours an uncomfortable place to live — then I think it's high time to take that individual aside and have a serious talk.

And that's exactly what I did with Queequeg. "Queequeg," I said, "get into bed and lie down and listen to me." I then launched into a review, beginning with the rise and development of primitive religions and working my way down to the various religions of today. Throughout, I tried to show Queequeg that all these Lents, Ramadans, and long hours of squatting in cold, cheerless rooms were complete nonsense — bad for the health, useless for the soul, and contrary to the basic laws of hygiene and common sense. I told him that since he was in other respects such an extremely sensible and shrewd savage, it pained me — deeply pained me — to see him being so foolish about this ridiculous Ramadan of his. Besides, I argued, fasting weakens the body, which weakens the spirit, and all thoughts born of fasting are necessarily half-starved. This is the reason why most dyspeptic religious people — those with chronic indigestion — cherish such gloomy notions about their hereafters. In a word, Queequeg, I said, getting somewhat off track: hell is an idea first born from an undigested apple dumpling, and has been perpetuated ever since through the hereditary indigestion caused by Ramadans.

I then asked Queequeg whether he himself was ever troubled with indigestion, putting the question very plainly so he could understand. He said no — except on one memorable occasion. It was after a great feast given by his father, the king, celebrating a great battle in which fifty of the enemy had been killed by about two in the afternoon and all cooked and eaten that very evening.

"No more, Queequeg," I said, shuddering. "That will do." I knew what he was implying without him spelling it out. I had met a sailor who had visited that very island, and he told me that when a great battle was won there, the custom was to barbecue all the slain in the victor's yard or garden. Then, one by one, they were placed on great wooden platters, garnished around like a pilaf with breadfruit and coconuts, and with parsley in their mouths, were sent round with the victor's compliments to all his friends — just as though these gifts were so many Christmas turkeys.

In the end, I don't think my remarks about religion made much of an impression on Queequeg. In the first place, he seemed somewhat deaf to that particular subject, unless it was approached from his own point of view. In the second place, he didn't understand more than a third of what I said, no matter how simply I put it. And finally, he no doubt believed he knew a good deal more about true religion than I did. He looked at me with a sort of condescending pity and compassion, as though he thought it a great shame that such a sensible young man should be so hopelessly lost to evangelical pagan piety.

At last we got up and dressed. Queequeg ate a tremendously hearty breakfast of chowders of every kind, making sure the landlady wouldn't profit too much from his Ramadan. Then we headed out to board the Pequod, strolling along and picking our teeth with halibut bones.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 — His Mark
paragraphs: As we walked down the wharf toward the ship, Queequeg carrying his harpoon, Captain Peleg loudly called out to us from his wigwam in his gruff voice. He said he hadn't realized my friend was a cannibal, and he didn't allow any cannibals on board unless they could produce their papers first.
"What do you mean by that, Captain Peleg?" said I, jumping up onto the ship's rail and leaving my companion standing on the wharf.
"I mean," he replied, "he has to show his papers."

"Yes," said Captain Bildad in his hollow voice, poking his head out from behind Peleg's in the wigwam. "He must prove he's been converted. Son of darkness," he added, turning to Queequeg, "are you currently in communion with any Christian church?"
"Why," said I, "he's a member of the First Congregational Church." Let it be said here that many tattooed savages who sail in Nantucket ships end up at last being converted into the churches.

"First Congregational Church!" cried Bildad. "What! The one that meets in Deacon Deuteronomy Coleman's meeting house?" And saying this, he took out his spectacles, wiped them with his big yellow handkerchief, put them on very carefully, came out of the wigwam, and, leaning stiffly over the rail, took a good long look at Queequeg.
"How long has he been a member?" he then said, turning to me. "Not very long, I'd guess, young man."
"No," said Peleg, "and he hasn't been properly baptized either, or it would have washed some of that devil's blue off his face."
"Is that so?" cried Bildad. "Is this Philistine really a member of Deacon Deuteronomy's congregation? I never saw him there, and I pass it every Lord's day."
"I don't know anything about Deacon Deuteronomy or his meeting," said I. "All I know is that Queequeg here is a born member of the First Congregational Church. He's a deacon himself, Queequeg is."
"Young man," said Bildad sternly, "you are skylarking with me — explain yourself, you young Hittite. What church do you mean? Answer me."

Finding myself pushed this hard, I replied, "I mean, sir, the same ancient Catholic — that is, universal — Church to which you and I, and Captain Peleg there, and Queequeg here, and all of us, every mother's son and soul of us, belong: the great and everlasting First Congregation of this whole worshipping world. We all belong to that; only some of us cherish some odd crotchets that in no way touch the grand belief. In that, at least, we all join hands."

"Splice — you mean splice hands," cried Peleg, coming closer. "Young man, you'd better sign on as a missionary instead of a common sailor. I never heard a better sermon. Deacon Deuteronomy — why, Father Mapple himself couldn't beat it, and he's considered something. Come aboard, come aboard — never mind about the papers. I say, tell Quohog there — what do you call him? Tell Quohog to step along. By the great anchor, what a harpoon he's got there! Looks like good stuff, that, and he handles it just right. I say, Quohog, or whatever your name is, have you ever stood in the bow of a whale-boat? Have you ever struck a whale?"

Without saying a word, Queequeg, in his wild way, jumped up onto the ship's rail, from there into the bow of one of the whale-boats hanging alongside, and then, bracing his left knee and balancing his harpoon, cried out something like this:

"Cap'ain, you see him small drop tar on water there? You see him? Well, s'pose him one whale eye — well, then!" And taking sharp aim at it, he darted the iron right over old Bildad's broad brim, clean across the ship's decks, and struck the glistening tar spot out of sight.
"Now," said Queequeg, calmly hauling in the line, "suppose that whale eye. Well, then — that whale dead."

"Quick, Bildad," said Peleg, his partner, who had retreated toward the cabin entrance, shaken by how close the flying harpoon had come. "Quick, I say, Bildad — get the ship's papers. We need Hedgehog there — I mean Quohog — in one of our boats. Listen, Quohog, we'll give you the ninetieth lay, and that's more than any harpooner out of Nantucket has ever been given."
So down we went into the cabin, and to my great joy, Queequeg was soon enrolled in the same ship's company as me.

When all the formalities were done and Peleg had everything ready for signing, he turned to me and said, "I guess Quohog there doesn't know how to write, does he? I say, Quohog — blast you! Do you sign your name or make your mark?"

But Queequeg, who had taken part in similar ceremonies two or three times before, looked not at all embarrassed. Taking the offered pen, he copied onto the paper, in the proper place, an exact replica of a strange round figure tattooed on his arm. So, thanks to Captain Peleg's stubborn error with his name, it looked something like this:
Quohog. his X mark.

Meanwhile, Captain Bildad sat earnestly and steadfastly eyeing Queequeg. At last he rose solemnly, fumbled in the huge pockets of his broad-skirted drab coat, and pulled out a bundle of tracts. Selecting one titled "The Latter Day Coming; or No Time to Lose," he placed it in Queequeg's hands. Then, grasping those hands and the tract with both of his own, he looked earnestly into his eyes and said, "Son of darkness, I must do my duty by you. I am part owner of this ship, and I feel concerned for the souls of all its crew. If you still cling to your Pagan ways, which I sadly fear, I beg you, do not remain forever a bondsman of Belial. Spurn the idol Bell, and the hideous dragon; turn from the wrath to come; mind your eye, I say; oh! goodness gracious! steer clear of the fiery pit!"
Something of the salt sea still lingered in old Bildad's speech, oddly mixed with scriptural and domestic phrases.

"Hold on there, hold on there, Bildad — stop spoiling our harpooner," cried Peleg. "Pious harpooners never make good voyagers — it takes the shark out of them; no harpooner is worth a straw who isn't pretty sharkish. There was young Nat Swaine, once the bravest boat-header out of all Nantucket and the Vineyard; he joined the meeting, and never came to any good. He got so frightened about his plaguy soul that he shrank and sheered away from whales, for fear of what might come after, in case he got stove and went to Davy Jones."

"Peleg! Peleg!" said Bildad, lifting his eyes and hands. "You yourself, as well as I, have seen many a perilous time. You know, Peleg, what it is to have the fear of death. How, then, can you prattle in this ungodly way? You belie your own heart, Peleg. Tell me — when this same Pequod here had her three masts overboard in that typhoon off Japan, that same voyage when you went as mate with Captain Ahab, didn't you think of Death and the Judgment then?"

"Hear him! Hear him now!" cried Peleg, marching across the cabin and thrusting his hands deep into his pockets. "Hear him, all of you. Think of that! When every moment we thought the ship would go down! Death and the Judgment then? What? With all three masts making such an endless thundering against the hull, and every wave breaking over us fore and aft? Think of Death and the Judgment then? No! No time to think about death. Life was what Captain Ahab and I were thinking about — and how to save every hand on board. How to rig jury-masts (makeshift masts). How to reach the nearest port. That was what I was thinking about."

Bildad said no more. He buttoned up his coat and walked out on deck, where we followed him. There he stood, very quietly watching some sailmakers who were mending a topsail amidships. Now and then he stooped to pick up a patch or save a length of tarred twine that might otherwise have been wasted.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 — The Prophet
paragraphs: "Shipmates, have you signed on to that ship?"

Queequeg and I had just left the Pequod and were strolling away from the water, each lost in his own thoughts, when a stranger spoke these words to us. Pausing in front of us, he aimed his heavy forefinger at the ship in question. He was shabbily dressed in a faded jacket and patched trousers, with a rag of a black handkerchief around his neck. A confluent smallpox, the kind whose sores run together, had flowed over his face in every direction and left it like the complicated, ribbed bed of a torrent after the rushing waters have dried up.
"Have you signed on to her?" he repeated.
"You mean the ship Pequod, I suppose," said I, trying to buy a little more time for a good look at him.
"Yes, the Pequod — that ship there," he said, pulling his whole arm back and then thrusting it straight out, his pointed finger aimed like a bayonet at the vessel.
"Yes," said I, "we've just signed the articles."
"Anything in there about your souls?"
"About what?"

"Oh, maybe you haven't got any," he said quickly. "No matter though. I know plenty of fellows who haven't got any — good luck to them. They're all the better off for it. A soul is a sort of fifth wheel on a wagon."
"What are you going on about, shipmate?" said I.
"He's got enough soul, though, to make up for what's missing in other men," the stranger said abruptly, placing a nervous emphasis on the word "he."
"Queequeg," said I, "let's go. This fellow has escaped from somewhere. He's talking about something and somebody we don't know."
"Stop!" cried the stranger. "You spoke true — you haven't seen Old Thunder yet, have you?"
"Who's Old Thunder?" said I, riveted again by the insane earnestness of his manner.
"Captain Ahab."
"What! The captain of our ship, the Pequod?"
"Yes, some of us old sailor types call him that. You haven't seen him yet, have you?"
"No, we haven't. They say he's sick, but getting better, and he'll be fine again before long."
"Fine again before long!" the stranger laughed — a solemn, mocking kind of laugh. "Listen: when Captain Ahab is fine, then this left arm of mine will be fine. Not before."
"What do you know about him?"
"What did they tell you about him? Tell me that!"
"They didn't say much of anything about him. I've only heard he's a good whale-hunter and a good captain to his crew."

"That's true, that's true — yes, both true enough. But you must jump when he gives an order. Step and growl; growl and go — that's the word with Captain Ahab. But nothing about that thing that happened to him off Cape Horn, long ago, when he lay like dead for three days and nights? Nothing about that deadly skrimmage with the Spaniard before the altar in Santa? Heard nothing about that, eh? Nothing about the silver calabash — the gourd-shaped bowl — he spat into? And nothing about his losing his leg last voyage, according to the prophecy? Didn't you hear a word about those matters, and something more, eh? No, I don't think you did; how could you? Who knows it? Not all Nantucket, I guess. But however that may be, maybe you've heard tell about the leg, and how he lost it; yes, you've heard of that, I dare say. Oh yes, that everyone knows, almost — I mean they know he's got only one leg, and that a parmacetti took the other off."

"My friend," said I, "I have no idea what all this rambling of yours is about, and I don't much care. It seems to me you must be a little damaged in the head. But if you're talking about Captain Ahab of that ship there, the Pequod, then let me tell you — I know all about the loss of his leg."
"All about it, eh? Sure you do? All?"
"Pretty sure."

With finger pointed and eye fixed on the Pequod, the beggar-like stranger stood a moment, as if in a troubled daydream. Then, starting slightly, he turned and said: "So you've signed on, have you? Names down on the papers? Well, well, what's signed is signed. And what's to be will be — and then again, maybe it won't be after all. Anyway, it's all fixed and arranged already. Some sailors or other have to go with him, I suppose — might as well be you as anyone. God pity them! Good morning to you, shipmates, morning. The ineffable heavens bless you. I'm sorry I stopped you."
"Look here, friend," said I, "if you have something important to tell us, out with it. But if you're just trying to trick us, you've picked the wrong men. That's all I have to say."

"And well said — I like hearing a man speak up like that. You're just the right sort for him — exactly the type. Good morning, shipmates, morning! Oh! And when you get there, tell them I've decided not to make one of them."
"Ah, my friend, you can't fool us that way — you can't fool us. It's the easiest thing in the world for a man to act as though he carries a great secret."
"Good morning, shipmates, morning."
"Morning it is," said I. "Come along, Queequeg, let's leave this crazy man. But stop — tell me your name, will you?"
"Elijah."

Elijah! I thought. And we walked away, both commenting, each in his own fashion, on this ragged old sailor, and agreed that he was nothing but a humbug trying to be a bugbear. But we had not gone perhaps more than a hundred yards when, happening to turn a corner and looking back as I did so, who should I see but Elijah following us, though at a distance. Somehow the sight of him struck me so that I said nothing to Queequeg about his being behind us, but walked on with my companion, anxious to see whether the stranger would turn the same corner we did. He did; and then it seemed to me that he was dogging us, but with what purpose I could not for the life of me imagine. This, together with his ambiguous, half-hinting, half-revealing, shrouded sort of talk, now bred in me all kinds of vague wonderings and half-fears, all connected with the Pequod; and Captain Ahab; and the leg he had lost; and the Cape Horn fit; and the silver calabash; and what Captain Peleg had said of him when I left the ship the day before; and the prediction of the squaw Tistig; and the voyage we had bound ourselves to sail; and a hundred other shadowy things.

I decided to find out for certain whether this ragged Elijah was truly following us. Queequeg and I crossed to the other side of the street and retraced our steps. But Elijah walked straight past without seeming to notice us. This was a relief, and once more — and finally, as it seemed to me — I decided in my heart that he was nothing but a humbug.

chapters.title: Chapter 20 — All Astir
paragraphs: A day or two passed, and there was great activity aboard the Pequod. Old sails were being mended, new sails were coming on board, along with bolts of canvas and coils of rigging. Everything indicated that the ship's preparations were hurrying to a close. Captain Peleg seldom or never went ashore, but sat in his wigwam keeping a sharp eye on the crew. Bildad handled all the purchasing and provisioning at the shops. And the men working in the hold and up in the rigging kept at it long after dark.

The day after Queequeg signed the articles, word was sent to all the inns where the crew was staying that their sea chests had to be on board before nightfall — there was no telling how soon the ship might sail. So Queequeg and I brought our belongings down, though we planned to sleep ashore until the last possible night. But it seems they always give very long notice in these cases, and the ship didn't actually sail for several more days. No surprise there — there was a great deal to be done, and no telling how many details needed attending to before the Pequod was fully equipped.

Everyone knows what a multitude of things — beds, saucepans, knives and forks, shovels and tongs, napkins, nutcrackers, and whatnot — are indispensable for running a household. It's just the same with whaling, which requires three years of housekeeping on the open ocean, far from all grocers, costermongers (street sellers of fruit and vegetables), doctors, bakers, and bankers. This is true of merchant ships too, but nowhere near to the same extent as with whalers. Besides the great length of the voyage and the many specialized items needed for the whale hunt, and the impossibility of replacing them at the remote harbors these ships usually visit, you have to remember that of all ships, whalers are the most exposed to accidents of every kind — especially the destruction and loss of the very equipment on which the voyage's success depends. Hence the spare boats, spare spars, spare lines and harpoons, and spare almost everything — everything but a spare captain and a duplicate ship.

By the time we arrived at the island, most of the Pequod's heavy stores had already been loaded — her beef, bread, water, fuel, iron hoops, and barrel staves. But as I mentioned, there was a constant stream of odds and ends, both large and small, being carried on board.

Chief among those doing this ferrying was Captain Bildad's sister, a thin old lady of fierce and tireless determination, but genuinely kindhearted. She seemed resolved that, if she had anything to say about it, nothing would be found lacking on the Pequod once the ship was fairly at sea. One time she came aboard with a jar of pickles for the steward's pantry. Another time with a bunch of quill pens for the chief mate's desk, where he kept his log. Another with a roll of flannel for the small of someone's rheumatic back. No woman ever better deserved her name, which was Charity — Aunt Charity, as everyone called her. And like a sister of charity, this charitable Aunt Charity bustled here and there, ready to turn her hand and heart to anything that promised safety, comfort, or consolation to everyone aboard a ship in which her beloved brother Bildad had an interest, and in which she herself owned a score or two of well-saved dollars.

But it was startling to see this kind-hearted Quaker woman come aboard on the last day carrying a long oil ladle in one hand and an even longer whaling lance in the other. Nor were Bildad and Captain Peleg any less busy. Bildad carried a long checklist of needed supplies, and at every delivery, he made a mark next to that item on his list. Every now and then, Peleg hobbled out of his whalebone den, roaring at the men down the hatchways, roaring up at the riggers on the masthead, and then concluded by roaring back into his wigwam.

During these days of preparation, Queequeg and I often visited the ship, and each time I asked about Captain Ahab — how he was and when he planned to come aboard. They always answered that he was getting better and better and was expected any day. In the meantime, the two captains, Peleg and Bildad, could handle everything needed to ready the vessel. If I had been truly honest with myself, I would have seen plainly that I only half liked the idea of being committed to such a long voyage without once laying eyes on the man who would be its absolute dictator the moment the ship reached open sea. But when a man suspects something is wrong, it sometimes happens that, if he is already caught up in the matter, he unconsciously tries to cover up his suspicions even from himself. And that's exactly what I did. I said nothing and tried to think nothing.
At last the word came that the ship would definitely sail the next day. So the following morning, Queequeg and I got a very early start.

chapters.title: Chapter 21 — Going Aboard
paragraphs: It was nearly six o'clock, but only a gray, imperfect, misty dawn when we approached the wharf.
"There are some sailors running ahead there, if I'm seeing right," said I to Queequeg. "Those can't be shadows. She must be leaving by sunrise, I think. Come on!"

"Stop!" cried a voice. Its owner came up close behind us, laid a hand on both our shoulders, and then slipped himself in between us. Stooping forward slightly in the uncertain twilight, he peered strangely from Queequeg to me. It was Elijah.
"Going aboard?"
"Hands off, will you," said I.
"Look here," said Queequeg, shaking himself free, "go away!"
"Not going aboard, then?"
"Yes, we are," said I, "but what business is that of yours? Do you know, Mr. Elijah, that I consider you rather rude?"
"No, no, no — I wasn't aware of that," said Elijah, slowly and wonderingly looking from me to Queequeg and back with the strangest glances.
"Elijah," said I, "you would do my friend and me a favor by going away. We're heading to the Indian and Pacific Oceans and would prefer not to be delayed."
"Are you, are you? Coming back before breakfast?"
"He's crazy, Queequeg," said I. "Come on."
"Hello there!" cried Elijah, standing where he was and calling after us when we had gone a few steps.
"Ignore him," said I. "Queequeg, come on."
But he crept up to us again and, suddenly clapping his hand on my shoulder, said, "Did you see anything that looked like men heading toward that ship a little while ago?"
Struck by this straightforward, matter-of-fact question, I answered, "Yes, I thought I saw four or five men, but it was too dim to be sure."
"Very dim, very dim," said Elijah. "Morning to you."
Once more we left him behind. But once more he came softly after us, and touching my shoulder again, said, "See if you can find them now, will you?"
"Find who?"

"Morning to you! Morning to you!" he called back, moving off again. "Oh! I was going to warn you against — but never mind, never mind — it's all one, all in the family too. Sharp frost this morning, isn't it? Goodbye to you. Won't be seeing you again very soon, I guess — unless it's before the Grand Jury." And with those wild words he finally departed, leaving me for the moment in no small amazement at his frantic boldness.

At last, stepping aboard the Pequod, we found everything in deep quiet. Not a soul was moving. The cabin entrance was locked from inside. The hatches were all closed and piled with coils of rigging. Going forward to the forecastle, we found the scuttle slide open. Seeing a light, we went down and found only an old rigger there, wrapped in a tattered pea jacket. He was stretched out full length across two sea chests, face down, his head buried in his folded arms. The deepest sleep had taken hold of him.

"Those sailors we saw, Queequeg — where could they have gone?" said I, looking doubtfully at the sleeper. But it seemed that Queequeg hadn't noticed what I was referring to when we were on the wharf. I would have thought I was seeing things, if not for Elijah's otherwise inexplicable question. But I pushed the thought aside. Looking again at the sleeper, I jokingly suggested to Queequeg that perhaps we should sit up with the body, and told him to make himself comfortable. He put his hand on the sleeper's rear end, as if testing whether it was soft enough, and then, without further hesitation, sat right down on it.
"Good gracious! Queequeg, don't sit there," said I.
"Oh! Very good seat," said Queequeg. "My country way. Won't hurt him face."

"Face!" said I. "You call that his face? A very benevolent face, then. But listen to how hard he's breathing — he's heaving up and down. Get off, Queequeg, you're heavy. It's grinding the face of the poor. Get off, Queequeg! Look, he'll throw you off any second. I'm amazed he doesn't wake up."

Queequeg moved himself just past the sleeper's head and lit his tomahawk pipe. I sat at the feet. We passed the pipe back and forth over the sleeper between us. Meanwhile, when I questioned him, Queequeg explained in his broken way that in his land, due to the complete lack of benches and sofas, the king, chiefs, and important people had the custom of fattening some of the lower orders to serve as ottomans; and to furnish a house comfortably in that respect, you only had to buy up eight or ten lazy fellows and lay them around in the wall spaces between the windows and in the alcoves. Besides, they were very convenient on outings — much better than those garden chairs that fold into walking sticks. On occasion, a chief would simply call his attendant and order him to make himself into a bench under a spreading tree, perhaps in some damp marshy spot.
While telling these stories, every time Queequeg took the tomahawk from me, he flourished the hatchet end of it over the sleeper's head.
"What's that for, Queequeg?"
"Very easy, kill him. Oh! Very easy!"

He was going on with some wild memories about his tomahawk-pipe, which had apparently both brained his enemies and soothed his soul, when we were suddenly drawn to the sleeping rigger. The thick smoke had completely filled the cramped space and was starting to affect him. He breathed with a sort of muffled sound, then seemed bothered in his nose, then rolled over once or twice, then sat up and rubbed his eyes.
"Hey there!" he finally wheezed. "Who are you smokers?"
"Signed-on crew," I answered. "When does she sail?"
"Oh, you're going on her, are you? She sails today. The captain came aboard last night."
"What captain — Ahab?"
"Who else?"
I was about to ask him more questions about Ahab when we heard noise on deck.

"Hey! Starbuck's up and about," said the rigger. "He's a sharp chief mate, that one — good man and religious. But he's fully awake now, so I've got to get to work." And with that he went up on deck, and we followed.

It was now clear sunrise. Soon the crew came aboard in twos and threes. The riggers got to work. The mates were busy giving orders. And several people from shore were bringing various last things on board. Meanwhile, Captain Ahab remained invisibly enshrined within his cabin.

chapters.title: Chapter 22 — Merry Christmas
paragraphs: At length, toward noon, after the ship's riggers were finally dismissed, and after the Pequod had been hauled out from the wharf, and after the ever-thoughtful Charity had come out in a whale-boat with her last gifts — a nightcap for Stubb, the second mate and her brother-in-law, and a spare Bible for the steward — after all this, the two captains, Peleg and Bildad, emerged from the cabin. Turning to the chief mate, Peleg said:
"Now, Mr. Starbuck, are you sure everything is ready? Captain Ahab is all set — just spoke to him — nothing more to get from shore, eh? Well, call all hands, then. Gather them aft here — blast them!"
"No need for profane words, however great the hurry, Peleg," said Bildad. "But off with you, friend Starbuck, and carry out our orders."

How about that! Here at the very moment of departure, Captain Peleg and Captain Bildad were running the show on the quarter-deck, just as if they were going to be the joint commanders at sea as well as, to all appearances, in port. As for Captain Ahab, there was still no sign of him. They said he was in the cabin. But the idea was that his presence wasn't at all necessary for getting the ship underway and steering her well out to sea. That was really the pilot's job, and since he hadn't fully recovered — so they said — Captain Ahab stayed below. All of this seemed natural enough, especially since in the merchant service many captains never show themselves on deck for some time after the anchor is raised, but stay at the cabin table having a farewell party with their shore friends before those friends leave the ship for good with the pilot.
But there wasn't much time to think it over, because Captain Peleg was now fully energized. He seemed to do most of the talking and commanding, not Bildad.
"Get back here, you sons of bachelors!" he cried, as the sailors lingered at the mainmast. "Mr. Starbuck, drive them aft."

"Strike the tent!" was the next order. As I mentioned before, this whalebone shelter was only set up in port. Aboard the Pequod, for thirty years, the order to strike the tent was well known to be the step right before raising the anchor.
"Man the capstan! Blood and thunder — jump!" was the next command, and the crew sprang for the handspikes.

Now, when getting underway, the pilot usually stations himself at the front of the ship. And there was Bildad, who — along with Peleg, you should know — was one of the port's licensed pilots in addition to his other roles. He was suspected of having got himself licensed just to save the Nantucket pilot fee for every ship he had a stake in, since he never piloted any other vessel. Bildad, I say, could now be seen looking over the bow for the approaching anchor, and at intervals singing what seemed a dismal verse of a psalm to cheer the men at the windlass. They roared out some sort of chorus about the girls in Booble Alley, with hearty good will. This despite the fact that not three days before, Bildad had declared that no profane songs would be permitted aboard the Pequod, especially while getting underway. And Charity, his sister, had placed a small, choice copy of Watts, the hymn-writer, in each seaman's berth.

Meanwhile, overseeing the other end of the ship, Captain Peleg raged and swore astern in the most frightful manner. I almost thought he'd sink the ship before the anchor could be raised. I involuntarily paused at my handspike and told Queequeg to do the same, thinking of the dangers we faced in starting a voyage with such a devil for a pilot. I was comforting myself with the thought that pious Bildad might offer some salvation, despite his seven hundred and seventy-seventh lay, when I felt a sudden sharp jab in my rear. Turning around, I was horrified to see Captain Peleg withdrawing his leg from my immediate vicinity. That was my first kick.

"Is that the way they heave in the marchant service?" he roared. "Spring, you sheep-head; spring, and break your backbone! Why don't you spring, I say, all of you — spring! Quohog! Spring, you fellow with the red whiskers; spring there, Scotch-cap; spring, you green pants. Spring, I say, all of you, and spring your eyes out!" And with that, he moved along the windlass, using his leg very freely here and there, while the imperturbable Bildad kept leading off with his psalm-singing. Captain Peleg, thinks I, must have been drinking something today.

At last the anchor was up, the sails were set, and off we glided. It was a short, cold Christmas Day. As the brief northern daylight merged into night, we found ourselves nearly out on the wintry ocean, whose freezing spray coated us in ice like polished armor. The long rows of whale teeth along the bulwarks gleamed in the moonlight. And like the white ivory tusks of some enormous elephant, vast curving icicles hung from the bow.

Gaunt Bildad, as pilot, headed the first watch. And again and again, as the old ship plunged deep into the green seas and sent shivering frost everywhere, and the winds howled, and the rigging sang, his steady voice could be heard:
"Sweet fields beyond the swelling flood, Stand dressed in living green. So to the Jews old Canaan stood, While Jordan rolled between."

Never did those sweet words sound more beautiful to me than at that moment. They were full of hope and fulfillment. Despite this frigid winter night on the wild Atlantic, despite my wet feet and even wetter jacket, it seemed to me there were still many pleasant harbors ahead — meadows and glades so eternally springlike that the grass that shot up in the spring remains, untrodden and unwilted, at midsummer.
At last we reached such a distance from shore that the two pilots were no longer needed. The sturdy sailboat that had accompanied us came alongside.

It was curious, and not unpleasing, how Peleg and Bildad were affected at this point, especially Captain Bildad. For, loath to depart just yet, very loath to leave for good a ship bound on so long and perilous a voyage — beyond both stormy Capes; a ship in which some thousands of his hard-earned dollars were invested; a ship in which an old shipmate sailed as captain, a man almost as old as himself, setting out once more to meet all the terrors of the pitiless jaw; loath to say goodbye to a thing so brimful in every way of every interest to him — poor old Bildad lingered long. He paced the deck with anxious strides; ran down into the cabin to speak another farewell word there; came on deck again and looked to windward; looked toward the wide and endless waters, bounded only by the far-off, unseen Eastern Continents; looked toward the land; looked aloft; looked right and left; looked everywhere and nowhere; and at last, mechanically coiling a rope on its pin, he convulsively grasped stout Peleg by the hand and, holding up a lantern, stood for a moment gazing heroically into his face, as much as to say, "Nevertheless, friend Peleg, I can stand it; yes, I can."

As for Peleg, he took it more philosophically. But for all his composure, there was a tear glistening in his eye when the lantern came too close. And he, too, kept running from cabin to deck — a word below, then a word with Starbuck, the chief mate.

But at last he turned to his companion with a final sort of look about him. "Captain Bildad — come, old shipmate, we must go. Back the main yard there! Boat ahoy! Stand by to come alongside now! Careful, careful — come, Bildad, old friend — say your last. Good luck to you, Starbuck. Good luck, Mr. Stubb. Good luck, Mr. Flask. Goodbye and good luck to you all — and three years from today, I'll have a hot supper waiting for you in old Nantucket. Hurrah and away!"

"God bless you, and have you in His holy keeping, men," murmured old Bildad, almost incoherently. "I hope you'll have fine weather now, so that Captain Ahab may soon be moving among you — a pleasant sun is all he needs, and you'll have plenty of that on the tropic voyage you're making. Be careful in the hunt, you mates. Don't stave the boats needlessly, you harpooners; good white cedar plank has gone up a full three percent within the year. Don't forget your prayers, either. Mr. Starbuck, mind that cooper doesn't waste the spare staves. Oh! The sail needles are in the green locker! Don't whale it too much on the Lord's days, men; but don't miss a fair chance either — that's rejecting Heaven's good gifts. Keep an eye on the molasses cask, Mr. Stubb; it was a little leaky, I thought. If you touch at the islands, Mr. Flask, beware of fornication. Goodbye, goodbye! Don't keep that cheese too long down in the hold, Mr. Starbuck; it'll spoil. Be careful with the butter — twenty cents a pound it was, and mind you, if —"
"Come, come, Captain Bildad — stop chattering — away!" And with that, Peleg hurried him over the side, and both dropped into the boat.

Ship and boat parted ways. The cold, damp night breeze blew between them. A screaming gull flew overhead. The two hulls rolled wildly. We gave three heavy-hearted cheers and plunged blindly, like fate, into the lonely Atlantic.

chapters.title: Chapter 23 — The Lee Shore
paragraphs: Some chapters back, a man named Bulkington was mentioned — a tall, recently landed sailor encountered at the inn in New Bedford.

When, on that shivering winter's night, the Pequod thrust her vengeful bows into the cold, malicious waves, who should I see standing at her helm but Bulkington! I looked at the man with sympathetic awe and dread. Here was someone who, in midwinter, having just landed from a dangerous four-year voyage, could so restlessly push off again for yet another stormy term at sea. The land seemed to scorch his feet. The most wondrous things are always the ones that cannot be spoken; deep memories yield no epitaphs; this six-inch chapter is the stoneless grave of Bulkington. Let me say only that it went with him as with the storm-tossed ship that drives miserably along a lee shore. The port would gladly give shelter; the port is compassionate; in the port there is safety, comfort, a hearth, supper, warm blankets, friends — everything that is kind to our mortal selves. But in that gale, the port, the land, is that ship's direst danger. She must flee all hospitality. One touch of land, even if it only grazed the keel, would make her shudder through and through. With all her might she crowds on every sail to get offshore, and in doing so fights the very winds that would gladly blow her homeward. She seeks the lashed sea's landlessness again, rushing forlornly into danger for the sake of refuge — her only friend her bitterest enemy!

Do you understand now, Bulkington? Do you seem to catch glimpses of that mortally unbearable truth — that all deep, earnest thinking is nothing but the brave effort of the soul to keep the open independence of her sea, while the wildest winds of heaven and earth conspire to cast her on the treacherous, enslaving shore?

But since the highest truth lives only in landlessness — shoreless and boundless as God — it is better to perish in that howling infinity than to be ingloriously dashed against the lee shore, even if that shore meant safety! For who, worm-like, would crawl like a coward to land! Terrors of the terrible! Is all this agony in vain? Take heart, take heart, O Bulkington! Bear up grimly, demigod! Up from the spray of your ocean death — straight up — leaps your apotheosis!

chapters.title: Chapter 24 — The Advocate
paragraphs: Since Queequeg and I are now properly launched in this business of whaling, and since whaling has somehow come to be seen by people on land as a rather unpoetic and disreputable trade, I am anxious to convince you landlubbers of the injustice done to us whale hunters.

First, it may seem unnecessary to establish the fact that, among the general public, whaling is not considered on the same level as the so-called liberal professions. If a stranger were introduced into any mixed gathering of city society, it would hardly raise the general opinion of his merits to present him as a harpooner. And if, in imitation of naval officers, he were to add the letters S.W.F. (Sperm Whale Fishery) after his name on his business card, that would be considered extremely presumptuous and ridiculous.

No doubt one main reason the world refuses to honor us whalemen is this: people think that, at best, our occupation amounts to a butchering sort of business, and that when we're actively at work, we're surrounded by every kind of filth. Butchers we are — that's true. But butchers, too, and butchers of the bloodiest badge, have been all the military commanders whom the world invariably loves to honor. And as for the alleged uncleanliness of our business, you'll soon be let in on certain facts that until now have been pretty generally unknown, and which, on the whole, will triumphantly place the sperm whale ship at least among the cleanest things on this tidy earth. But even granting the charge to be true — what messy, slippery decks of a whale ship can compare with the unspeakable carrion of those battlefields from which so many soldiers return to drink in the applause of every lady? And if the idea of danger so greatly enhances the popular admiration of the soldier's profession, let me assure you that many a veteran who has freely marched up to a cannon battery would quickly recoil at the sight of a sperm whale's vast tail fanning the air above his head into eddies. For what are the terrors of man, which we can understand, compared with the interlinked terrors and wonders of God!

But though the world looks down on us whale hunters, it unknowingly pays us the deepest tribute — indeed, an overwhelming devotion! For almost all the candles, lamps, and tapers that burn around the globe burn, like offerings before so many shrines, to our glory!
But look at this from other angles. Weigh it on every scale. See what we whalemen are and have been.

Why did the Dutch in De Witt's time have admirals of their whaling fleets? Why did Louis XVI of France, at his own personal expense, fit out whaling ships from Dunkirk, and politely invite a score or two of families from our own island of Nantucket to that town? Why did Britain, between the years 1750 and 1788, pay her whalemen upwards of £1,000,000 in bounties? And lastly, how is it that we American whalemen now outnumber all the rest of the world's whalemen banded together; sail a navy of upwards of seven hundred vessels, manned by eighteen thousand men, consuming $4,000,000 a year, the ships worth $20,000,000 at the time of sailing; and every year bring into our harbors a well-reaped harvest of $7,000,000? How does all this come about, if there isn't something mighty in whaling?
But that's only half of it. Look again.

I freely assert that the cosmopolitan philosopher cannot, for the life of him, point to one single peaceful influence that, within the last sixty years, has worked more powerfully upon the whole broad world, taken all together, than the high and mighty business of whaling. One way and another, it has produced events so remarkable in themselves, and so continuously momentous in their consequences, that whaling may well be regarded as that Egyptian mother who bore offspring that were themselves pregnant from her womb. It would be a hopeless, endless task to catalogue all these things. Let a handful be enough. For many years past the whale ship has been the pioneer in ferreting out the remotest and least known parts of the earth. She has explored seas and archipelagoes that had no chart, where no Cook or Vancouver had ever sailed. If American and European warships now ride peacefully in once savage harbors, let them fire salutes to the honor and glory of the whale ship, which first showed them the way and first interpreted between them and the savages. They may celebrate as they like the heroes of Exploring Expeditions, your Cooks, your Krusensterns; but I say that scores of anonymous captains have sailed out of Nantucket who were as great as your Cook and your Krusenstern, and greater. For in their unaided, empty-handed state, in heathenish, shark-filled waters and by the beaches of unrecorded, javelin-throwing islands, they battled with virgin wonders and terrors that Cook, with all his marines and muskets, would not willingly have dared. All that is made such a flourish of in the old South Sea Voyages was only the lifelong commonplace of our heroic Nantucketers. Often, adventures to which Vancouver devotes three chapters, these men thought unworthy of being set down in the ship's ordinary log. Ah, the world! Oh, the world!

Until the whale fishery rounded Cape Horn, no trade but colonial, and hardly any contact but colonial, was carried on between Europe and the long line of wealthy Spanish provinces on the Pacific coast. It was the whaleman who first broke through the jealous policy of the Spanish crown regarding those colonies. And if space allowed, it could be clearly shown how, from those whalemen, there at last came the liberation of Peru, Chile, and Bolivia from the yoke of Old Spain, and the establishment of the eternal democracy in those parts.

That great America on the other side of the globe, Australia, was given to the enlightened world by the whaleman. After its first blunder-born discovery by a Dutchman, all other ships long shunned those shores as pestilently barbarous; but the whale ship called there. The whale ship is the true mother of that now mighty colony. Moreover, in the infancy of the first Australian settlement, the emigrants were several times saved from starvation by the benevolent biscuit of a whale ship that luckily dropped anchor in their waters. The countless islands of all Polynesia confess the same truth, and pay commercial homage to the whale ship, which cleared the way for the missionary and the merchant, and in many cases carried the first missionaries to their destinations. If that double-bolted land, Japan, is ever to become hospitable, it is the whale ship alone that will deserve the credit — for she is already on the threshold.

But if, despite all this, you still insist that whaling has no aesthetically noble associations, then I am ready to shiver fifty lances with you on that point, and unhorse you with a split helmet every time.
The whale has no famous author, and whaling no famous chronicler, you say.

The whale no famous author, and whaling no famous chronicler? Who wrote the first account of our Leviathan? Who but mighty Job! And who composed the first narrative of a whaling voyage? Who but no less a prince than Alfred the Great, who with his own royal pen took down the words of a man named Other, the Norwegian whale hunter of those times! And who delivered our glowing eulogy in Parliament? Who but Edmund Burke!
True enough, you say, but whalemen themselves are poor devils; they have no good blood in their veins.

No good blood in their veins? They have something better than royal blood there. The grandmother of Benjamin Franklin was Mary Morrel, afterward, by marriage, Mary Folger, one of the old settlers of Nantucket and the ancestress of a long line of Folgers and harpooners — all kith and kin to noble Benjamin — who to this day are darting the barbed iron from one side of the world to the other.
Fine, you say, but everyone agrees that whaling somehow just isn't respectable.
Whaling not respectable? Whaling is imperial! By old English statutory law, the whale is declared "a royal fish."*
Oh, that's in name only! The whale itself has never figured in anything grand or imposing.

The whale never figured in anything grand or imposing? In one of the mighty triumphs given to a Roman general upon his entry into the world's capital, the bones of a whale, brought all the way from the Syrian coast, were the most conspicuous object in the cymbal-clashing procession.*
*See later chapters for something more on this subject.
All right, since you bring it up. But say what you will, there's no real dignity in whaling.

No dignity in whaling? The very heavens bear witness to the dignity of our calling. Cetus is a constellation in the southern sky! Enough said! Jam your hat down firmly in the presence of the Czar, and take it off to Queequeg! Enough said! I know a man who, in his lifetime, has taken three hundred and fifty whales. I consider that man more honorable than that great captain of antiquity who boasted of taking as many walled towns.

And as for me, if by any possibility there is some as yet undiscovered prime quality in me; if I ever deserve any real reputation in that small but lofty, hushed world to which I might not unreasonably aspire; if hereafter I do anything that, on the whole, a man would rather have done than have left undone; if, when I die, my executors — or more accurately, my creditors — find any precious manuscripts in my desk, then here and now I ascribe all the honor and the glory to whaling in advance; for a whale ship was my Yale College and my Harvard.

chapters.title: Chapter 25 — Postscript
paragraphs: In defense of the dignity of whaling, I would prefer to offer nothing but proven facts. But after marshaling his facts, an advocate who entirely suppressed a not unreasonable guess that might speak eloquently for his cause — would such an advocate not be to blame?

It is well known that at the coronation of kings and queens, even modern ones, a certain curious process of seasoning them for their duties is gone through. There is a so-called salt cellar of state, and there may be a castor of state, a ceremonial cruet. How exactly they use the salt — who knows? What I am certain of, however, is that a king's head is solemnly oiled at his coronation, just like a head of salad. Could it be, though, that they anoint it so that its interior will run well, the way one oils machinery? Much could be pondered here about the essential dignity of this royal process, because in ordinary life we think meanly and contemptuously of a fellow who oils his hair and plainly smells of it. In truth, a grown man who uses hair oil, unless for medical reasons, probably has a boggy spot in him somewhere. As a general rule, he can't amount to much taken as a whole.

But the only question to consider here is this: what kind of oil is used at coronations? It certainly can't be olive oil, or macassar oil, or castor oil, or bear's oil, or train oil, or cod-liver oil. What then can it possibly be, but sperm oil in its unprocessed, unpolluted state — the sweetest of all oils?
Think about that, you loyal Britons! We whalemen supply your kings and queens with their coronation stuff!

chapters.title: Chapter 26 — Knights and Squires
paragraphs: The chief mate of the Pequod was Starbuck, a native of Nantucket and a Quaker by descent. He was a long, earnest man, and though born on an icy coast, he seemed well suited to endure hot latitudes, his flesh being as hard as twice-baked biscuit. Carried to the Indies, his living blood would not spoil like bottled ale. He must have been born in some time of general drought and famine, or on one of those fast days for which his state is famous. He had seen only some thirty arid summers, and those summers had dried up everything superfluous in his body. But this thinness of his, so to speak, seemed no more a sign of wasting anxieties and cares than of any bodily disease. It was simply the condensation of the man. He was by no means bad-looking — quite the contrary. His clean, tight skin was an excellent fit; and closely wrapped up in it, and embalmed with inner health and strength, like an Egyptian mummy brought back to life, this Starbuck seemed prepared to endure for long ages to come, and to endure always as he was now. For whether in polar snow or torrid sun, like a patent chronometer, his inner vitality was guaranteed to do well in all climates. Looking into his eyes, you seemed to see there the still-lingering images of the thousandfold dangers he had calmly faced throughout his life. A staid, steadfast man, whose life for the most part was an eloquent pantomime of action, not a tame chapter of sounds. Yet for all his hardy sobriety and fortitude, there were certain qualities in him which at times affected, and in some cases seemed almost to outweigh, all the rest. Uncommonly conscientious for a seaman, and endowed with a deep natural reverence, he was strongly inclined by the wild, watery loneliness of his life toward superstition — but toward that sort of superstition which in some minds seems, somehow, to spring from intelligence rather than from ignorance. Outward omens and inward premonitions were his. And if at times these things bent the welded iron of his soul, much more did his far-away memories of home, of his young Cape Cod wife and child, bend him still further from the original ruggedness of his nature, and open him still further to those hidden influences which, in some honest-hearted men, hold back the gush of daredevil daring so often shown by others in the more dangerous turns of the fishery. "I will have no man in my boat," said Starbuck, "who is not afraid of a whale." By this he seemed to mean not only that the most reliable and useful courage is the kind that arises from a fair estimate of the danger faced, but that an utterly fearless man is a far more dangerous comrade than a coward.

"That's right," said Stubb, the second mate. "Starbuck there is as careful a man as you'll find anywhere in this business." But we shall soon see what the word "careful" means when used by a man like Stubb, or almost any other whale hunter.

Starbuck was no crusader after dangers; in him courage was not a sentiment but a thing simply useful to him, and always at hand on every practical occasion where life and death were at stake. Besides, he thought, perhaps, that in this business of whaling, courage was one of the great staple supplies of the ship, like her beef and her bread, and not to be foolishly wasted. So he had no liking for lowering the boats for whales after sundown, nor for persisting in fighting a whale that persisted too much in fighting him. For, thought Starbuck, I am here on this critical ocean to kill whales for my living, and not to be killed by them for theirs; and Starbuck knew well that hundreds of men had been killed that way. What fate had been his own father's? Where, in the bottomless depths, could he find the torn limbs of his brother?

With memories like these in him, and given, moreover, to a certain superstitiousness, as has been said, the courage of this Starbuck, which could nevertheless still flourish, must indeed have been extreme. But it was not in reasonable nature that a man built this way, with such terrible experiences and memories as he had — it was not in nature that these things should fail to breed, hidden in him, an element which, under suitable circumstances, would break out of its confinement and burn all his courage up. And brave as he might be, his was chiefly the sort of bravery, seen in some fearless men, which, while generally holding firm in the conflict with seas, or winds, or whales, or any of the ordinary irrational horrors of the world, cannot withstand those more terrible, because more spiritual, terrors which sometimes threaten you from the concentrated brow of an enraged and mighty man.

But if the coming narrative were to reveal, in any instance, the complete collapse of poor Starbuck's fortitude, I would hardly have the heart to write it; for it is a most sorrowful thing — no, a shocking one — to expose the fall of valor in the soul. Men may seem detestable as joint-stock companies and nations; there may be knaves, fools, and murderers; men may have mean and meager faces; but man, in the ideal, is so noble and so sparkling, such a grand and glowing creature, that over any shameful blemish in him all his fellows should run to throw their costliest robes. That immaculate manliness we feel within ourselves, so far within us that it remains intact even when all the outer character seems gone, bleeds with the keenest anguish at the unrobed spectacle of a man whose valor is ruined. Nor can piety itself, at such a shameful sight, completely stifle her reproaches against the stars that permitted it. But this majestic dignity I speak of is not the dignity of kings and robes, but that abounding dignity which has no robed investiture. You shall see it shining in the arm that wields a pick or drives a spike; that democratic dignity which, on all sides, radiates without end from God — Himself! The great God absolute! The center and circumference of all democracy! His omnipresence, our divine equality!

If, then, I shall hereafter ascribe high qualities, though dark ones, to the meanest sailors, and renegades and castaways; if I weave tragic graces around them; if even the most mournful, perhaps the most degraded among them all, shall at times lift himself to the exalted mountaintops; if I touch that workman's arm with some ethereal light; if I spread a rainbow over his disastrous sunset — then against all mortal critics bear me out in it, you just Spirit of Equality, who have spread one royal mantle of humanity over all my kind! Bear me out in it, you great democratic God! You who did not refuse the pale, poetic pearl to the swarthy convict, Bunyan; you who clothed the stumped and poverty-stricken arm of old Cervantes with doubly hammered leaves of finest gold; you who picked up Andrew Jackson from the pebbles, who hurled him onto a warhorse, who thundered him higher than a throne! You who, in all your mighty earthly marchings, always gather your choicest champions from the kingly commons — bear me out in it, O God!

chapters.title: Chapter 27 — Knights and Squires
paragraphs: Stubb was the second mate. He came from Cape Cod, and so, by local custom, was called a Cape-Cod-man. He was happy-go-lucky, neither coward nor hero, meeting dangers as they came with an air of indifference; and in the tightest crisis of the chase he would keep working away, calm and collected, like a journeyman carpenter hired by the year. Good-humored, relaxed, and carefree, he ran his whale-boat as if the deadliest encounter were just a dinner party and his crew all invited guests. He was as fussy about arranging his end of the boat comfortably as an old stagecoach driver is about how snug his seat is. When close up to the whale, in the very death-lock of the fight, he handled his merciless lance coolly and casually, the way a whistling tinker handles his hammer. He would hum his old rigadig tunes while side by side with the most furious monster. For this Stubb, long habit had turned the jaws of death into an easy chair. What he thought about death itself, nobody can say. Whether he ever thought about it at all might be a fair question; but if he ever did happen to turn his mind that way after a comfortable dinner, then no doubt, like a good sailor, he took it as a kind of call of the watch to tumble up aloft and get busy there with something he would find out about when he obeyed the order, and not before.

What, perhaps, along with other things, made Stubb such an easygoing, unfearing man, so cheerily trudging along with the burden of life in a world full of grave peddlers all bowed to the ground by their packs — what helped to bring about that almost impious good humor of his — that thing must have been his pipe. For, like his nose, his short, black little pipe was one of the regular features of his face. You would almost as soon have expected him to turn out of his bunk without his nose as without his pipe. He kept a whole row of pipes there, ready loaded, stuck in a rack within easy reach of his hand; and whenever he turned in, he smoked them all out one after another, lighting each from the last to the very end; then loaded them again to be ready once more. For when Stubb dressed, instead of first putting his legs into his trousers, he put his pipe into his mouth.

I say this constant smoking must have been one cause, at least, of his peculiar temperament. For everyone knows that the earthly air, whether on land or sea, is terribly infected with the nameless miseries of the countless people who have died breathing it. And just as during a cholera outbreak some people walk around pressing camphor-soaked handkerchiefs to their mouths, so too, against all mortal troubles, Stubb's tobacco smoke may have served as a kind of disinfectant.

The third mate was Flask, a native of Tisbury, on Martha's Vineyard. A short, stout, ruddy young fellow, very pugnacious about whales, who somehow seemed to think that the great leviathans had personally and hereditarily insulted him; and therefore it was a sort of point of honor with him to destroy them whenever he met them. So utterly lost was he to all sense of reverence for the many marvels of their majestic bulk and mystic ways, and so dead to anything like a sense of possible danger from encountering them, that in his poor opinion the wondrous whale was only a species of magnified mouse, or at least water rat, requiring only a little outmaneuvering and some small expense of time and trouble in order to kill and boil. This ignorant, unconscious fearlessness of his made him a little waggish on the subject of whales; he followed these fish for the fun of it; and a three-year voyage around Cape Horn was only a jolly joke that lasted that long. As a carpenter's nails are divided into wrought nails and cut nails, so mankind may be divided in the same way. Little Flask was one of the wrought ones, made to clinch tight and last long. They called him King-Post on board the Pequod, because in shape he could well be likened to the short, square timber known by that name in Arctic whalers, which, by means of many radiating side timbers set into it, serves to brace the ship against the icy shocks of those battering seas.

Now these three mates — Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask — were important men. By universal tradition, they commanded three of the Pequod's boats as headsmen. In the grand battle formation in which Captain Ahab would likely arrange his forces to descend on the whales, these three headsmen were like company captains.
