Or, armed with their long, keen whaling lances, they were a chosen trio of lancers, just as the harpooners were throwers of javelins.

And since in this famous fishery each mate or headsman, like a Gothic knight of old, is always accompanied by his boat-steerer or harpooner, who at certain moments hands him a fresh lance when the first has been badly twisted or bent into an elbow in the attack; and since, moreover, a close intimacy and friendship generally exists between the two, it is only fitting that we set down here who the Pequod's harpooners were, and to which headsman each of them belonged.
First was Queequeg, whom Starbuck, the chief mate, had chosen as his squire. But Queequeg is already known to us.

Next was Tashtego, an unmixed Indian from Gay Head, the westernmost promontory of Martha's Vineyard, where there still exists the last remnant of a village of red men, which has long supplied the neighboring island of Nantucket with many of her most daring harpooners. In the fishery, they usually go by the general name of Gay Headers. Tashtego's long, lean, sable hair, his high cheekbones, and his black, rounded eyes — for an Indian, Oriental in their largeness, but Antarctic in their glittering expression — all this was enough to proclaim him an heir of the untainted blood of those proud warrior-hunters who, in quest of the great New England moose, had scoured the primeval forests of the mainland, bow in hand. But no longer sniffing the trail of the wild beasts of the woodland, Tashtego now hunted in the wake of the great whales of the sea, the unerring harpoon of the son fittingly replacing the infallible arrow of the fathers. Looking at the tawny brawn of his lithe, snaky limbs, you would almost have credited the superstitions of some of the earlier Puritans, and half-believed this wild Indian to be a son of the Prince of the Powers of the Air. Tashtego was the squire of Stubb, the second mate.

Third among the harpooners was Daggoo, a gigantic, coal-black negro-savage, with a lion-like tread — an Ahasuerus to behold. Hanging from his ears were two golden hoops, so large that the sailors called them ring-bolts, and would talk of securing the topsail halyards to them. In his youth Daggoo had voluntarily signed aboard a whaler lying in a lonely bay on his native coast. And having never been anywhere in the world but Africa, Nantucket, and the pagan harbors most visited by whalemen, and having now led for many years the bold life of the fishery in the ships of owners unusually careful about what sort of men they shipped, Daggoo kept all his barbaric virtues, and, erect as a giraffe, moved about the decks in all the pomp of six feet five in his socks. There was a bodily humility in looking up at him; and a white man standing before him seemed a white flag come to beg a truce of a fortress. Curious to say, this imperial negro, Ahasuerus Daggoo, was the squire of little Flask, who looked like a chess piece beside him. As for the rest of the Pequod's company, let it be said that at the present day not one in two of the many thousand men before the mast employed in the American whale fishery are American-born, though nearly all the officers are. In this the American whale fishery is the same as the American army and the military and merchant navies, and the engineering forces employed in building the American canals and railroads. The same, I say, because in all these cases the native American liberally provides the brains, and the rest of the world as generously supplies the muscles. No small number of these whaling seamen belong to the Azores, where the outward-bound Nantucket whalers often call to fill out their crews from the hardy peasants of those rocky shores. In the same way, the Greenland whalers sailing out of Hull or London put in at the Shetland Islands to take on their full complement of crew, and on the passage home they drop them there again. How it is, there is no telling, but islanders seem to make the best whalemen. They were nearly all islanders in the Pequod — Isolatoes too, as I call them, not acknowledging the common continent of men, but each Isolato living on a separate continent of his own. Yet now, federated along one keel, what a set these Isolatoes were! An Anacharsis Clootz deputation from all the isles of the sea and all the ends of the earth, accompanying old Ahab in the Pequod to lay the world's grievances before that bar from which not very many of them ever come back. Black little Pip — he never did — oh, no! he went before. Poor Alabama boy! On the grim Pequod's forecastle you shall soon see him, beating his tambourine; a prelude to the eternal time when, sent for to the great quarter-deck on high, he was told to strike in with the angels and beat his tambourine in glory; called a coward here, hailed a hero there!

chapters.title: Chapter 28 — Ahab
paragraphs: For several days after leaving Nantucket, nothing was seen of Captain Ahab above the hatches. The mates regularly relieved each other at the watches, and for all that could be seen to the contrary, they seemed to be the only commanders of the ship; only, they sometimes came out of the cabin with orders so sudden and peremptory that it was plain, after all, that they were only commanding on someone else's behalf. Yes, their supreme lord and dictator was there, though so far unseen by any eyes not permitted to penetrate the now sacred retreat of the cabin.

Every time I came up on deck from my watches below, I instantly looked aft to see if any strange face was visible; for my first vague uneasiness about the unknown captain, now in the seclusion of the sea, had become almost an agitation. This was strangely heightened at times by the ragged Elijah's diabolical, incoherent ramblings, which came back to me uninvited, with a subtle energy I could not have imagined before. I could only poorly withstand them, much as in other moods I was almost ready to smile at the solemn whims of that outlandish prophet of the wharves. But whatever apprehension or uneasiness — to call it that — I felt, whenever I came to look around me in the ship, it seemed against all reason to cherish such feelings. For though the harpooners, with the great body of the crew, were a far more barbaric, heathenish, and motley set than any of the tame merchant-ship companies I had known before, I still put this down — and rightly — to the fierce uniqueness of the very nature of that wild Scandinavian calling in which I had so recklessly embarked. But it was above all the look of the three chief officers of the ship, the mates, that was most strongly fitted to allay these colorless misgivings and to inspire confidence and cheerfulness about every prospect of the voyage. Three better, more promising sea-officers and men, each in his own different way, could not easily be found, and every one of them was American: a Nantucketer, a Vineyarder, a Cape man. Now, since it was Christmas when the ship shot out of her harbor, for a while we had biting polar weather, though all the time we were running away from it to the southward; and with every degree and minute of latitude we sailed, we gradually left that merciless winter and all its intolerable weather behind us. It was on one of those mornings of the transition, less threatening but still gray and gloomy enough, when with a fair wind the ship was rushing through the water with a vengeful sort of leaping and melancholy speed, that I climbed to the deck at the call of the forenoon watch; and the moment I leveled my gaze toward the taffrail at the stern, foreboding shivers ran over me. Reality outran apprehension: Captain Ahab stood upon his quarter-deck.

There seemed to be no sign of ordinary bodily illness about him, nor of recovery from any. He looked like a man cut down from the stake when the fire has swept over and withered all the limbs without consuming them, or taking away one particle of their compact, aged robustness. His whole tall, broad form seemed made of solid bronze, and shaped in an unalterable mold, like Cellini's cast Perseus. Threading its way out from among his gray hairs, and continuing right down one side of his tawny, scorched face and neck until it disappeared into his clothing, you saw a slender, rod-like mark, livid and whitish. It resembled that vertical seam sometimes made in the straight, lofty trunk of a great tree when the lightning from above darts tearing down it, and, without wrenching off a single twig, peels and grooves out the bark from top to bottom before running off into the soil, leaving the tree still green and alive, but branded. Whether that mark was born with him, or whether it was the scar left by some desperate wound, no one could say for certain. By some unspoken agreement, little or no mention was made of it throughout the voyage, especially by the mates. But once Tashtego's senior, an old Gay Head Indian among the crew, superstitiously asserted that Ahab was not branded that way until he was a full forty years old, and that it came upon him not in the fury of any mortal fight, but in an elemental struggle at sea. Yet this wild hint seemed, by inference, to be contradicted by what a gray Manxman hinted — an old, sepulchral man who, having never sailed out of Nantucket before, had never until now laid eyes on wild Ahab. Nevertheless, the old sea traditions, the immemorial credulities, popularly credited this old Manxman with preternatural powers of discernment. So no white sailor seriously contradicted him when he said that if Captain Ahab should ever be laid out peacefully — which might hardly come to pass, so he muttered — then whoever performed that last office for the dead would find a birthmark on him from crown to sole.

So powerfully did the whole grim aspect of Ahab affect me, and the livid brand which streaked it, that for the first few moments I hardly noticed that not a little of this overpowering grimness was owing to the barbaric white leg on which he partly stood. I had heard earlier that this ivory leg had been fashioned at sea from the polished bone of the sperm whale's jaw. "Aye, he was dismasted off Japan," the old Gay Head Indian once said, "but like his dismasted ship, he shipped another mast without coming home for it. He has a quiver of them."

I was struck by the singular posture he maintained. On each side of the Pequod's quarter-deck, and pretty close to the mizzen shrouds, an auger hole had been bored about half an inch or so into the plank. His bone leg was steadied in that hole. One arm raised, holding onto a shroud, Captain Ahab stood erect, staring straight out beyond the ship's ever-pitching bow. There was an infinity of the firmest fortitude, a determined, unsurrendering willfulness, in the fixed and fearless, forward dedication of that gaze. He spoke not a word, nor did his officers say anything to him. Yet by their every small gesture and expression, they clearly showed the uneasy, if not painful, awareness of being under a troubled master's eye. And more than that — moody, stricken Ahab stood before them with a crucifixion in his face, with all the nameless, regal, overpowering dignity of some mighty grief.

Soon after his first appearance on deck, he withdrew to his cabin. But after that morning, he was visible to the crew every day — either standing in his pivot-hole, or sitting on an ivory stool he had, or walking heavily across the deck. As the sky grew less gloomy and even began to turn a little mild, he became less and less of a recluse, as if, when the ship first sailed from home, nothing but the dead winter bleakness of the sea had kept him shut away. Gradually, he was almost constantly in the open air. But for all he said or visibly did on the deck, sunny at last, he seemed as unnecessary there as an extra mast. The Pequod was only making a passage, not actively cruising. The mates were fully capable of handling nearly all the whaling preparations that needed overseeing. So there was little or nothing outside of himself to occupy or excite Ahab now, and so to chase away, for that one interval, the clouds that were piled layer upon layer on his brow — just as all clouds always choose the loftiest peaks to pile themselves upon.

Nevertheless, before long, the warm, warbling persuasiveness of the pleasant holiday weather we came into seemed gradually to charm him out of his mood. For as when the red-cheeked dancing girls, April and May, come tripping home to the wintry, misanthropic woods, even the barest, most rugged, most thunder-split old oak will at least send out a few green sprouts to welcome such glad-hearted visitors, so Ahab did, in the end, respond a little to the playful enticements of that girlish air. More than once he put forth the faint blossom of a look which, in any other man, would soon have flowered into a smile.

chapters.title: Chapter 29 — Enter Ahab; to Him, Stubb
paragraphs: Some days passed, and with ice and icebergs all astern, the Pequod now went rolling through the bright Quito spring — the endless spring of that city on the equator — which at sea reigns almost perpetually on the threshold of the eternal August of the Tropic. The warmly cool, clear, ringing, perfumed, overflowing, abundant days were like crystal goblets of Persian sherbet, heaped up — flaked up — with rose-water snow. The starry, stately nights seemed like haughty ladies in jeweled velvets, nursing at home in lonely pride the memory of their absent conquering Earls, the golden-helmeted suns! For a sleeping man, it was hard to choose between such winsome days and such seductive nights. But all the enchantments of that unfading weather did not merely lend new spells and powers to the outer world. They turned inward upon the soul, especially when the still, mild hours of evening came on; then memory shot out her crystals as clear ice forms most readily in noiseless twilights. And all these subtle influences worked more and more upon the fabric of Ahab.

Old age is always wakeful, as if the longer a man is linked with life, the less he has to do with anything that looks like death. Among sea captains, the old graybeards are the ones who most often leave their beds to visit the night-wrapped deck. So it was with Ahab, except that lately he seemed to live so much in the open air that, truly speaking, his visits were more to the cabin than from it. "It feels like going down into one's tomb," he would mutter to himself, "for an old captain like me to be descending this narrow hatch to my grave-dug bed."

So almost every twenty-four hours, when the night watches were set and the men on deck stood guard over the sleep of the men below; and when, if a rope had to be hauled on the forecastle, the sailors did not fling it down roughly, as by day, but dropped it carefully into its place for fear of disturbing their sleeping shipmates; when this sort of steady quiet would begin to settle in, the silent helmsman would habitually watch the cabin hatch; and before long the old man would emerge, gripping the iron railing to help his crippled way. There was some considerate touch of humanity in him; for at times like these he usually refrained from patrolling the quarter-deck, because to his weary mates, trying to rest within six inches of his ivory heel, the echoing crack and din of that bony step would have been such that their dreams would have been of the crunching teeth of sharks. But once, the mood was on him too deep for ordinary consideration; and as with a heavy, lumbering pace he was measuring the ship from the taffrail to the mainmast, Stubb, the old second mate, came up from below and, with a certain unsure, apologetic humor, hinted that if Captain Ahab was pleased to walk the planks, then no one could say no; but there might be some way of muffling the noise — hinting something vaguely and hesitantly about a ball of tow, and inserting the ivory heel into it. Ah, Stubb, you did not know Ahab then.

"Am I a cannonball, Stubb," said Ahab, "that you'd wad me like that? But go your way — I forgot. Down to your nightly grave, where the likes of you sleep wrapped in shrouds, getting used to the one you'll fill at last. Down, dog, and to your kennel!"

Startled by the unforeseen closing exclamation of the so suddenly scornful old man, Stubb was speechless for a moment; then said excitedly, "I'm not used to being spoken to that way, sir; I like it less than half, sir."
"Enough!" Ahab growled through clenched teeth, moving violently away as if to avoid some passionate temptation.
"No, sir, not yet," said Stubb, growing bolder. "I won't meekly accept being called a dog, sir."
"Then be called ten times a donkey, and a mule, and an ass, and get out of my sight, or I'll rid the world of you!"
As he said this, Ahab advanced on him with such overpowering menace in his bearing that Stubb involuntarily backed away.

"I was never served like that before without giving a hard blow for it," muttered Stubb, as he found himself going down the cabin hatch. "It's very queer. Stop, Stubb; somehow, now, I don't quite know whether to go back and hit him, or — what's that? — get down here on my knees and pray for him? Yes, that was the thought coming up in me; but it would be the first time I ever really did pray. It's queer; very queer; and he's queer too; aye, take him fore and aft, he's about the queerest old man Stubb ever sailed with. How he flashed at me! — his eyes like powder-pans! Is he mad? Anyway, there's something on his mind, as sure as there must be something on a deck when it cracks. He isn't in his bed now, either, more than three hours out of the twenty-four; and he doesn't sleep then. Didn't that Dough-Boy, the steward, tell me that in the morning he always finds the old man's hammock clothes all rumpled and tumbled, and the sheets down at the foot, and the coverlet almost tied into knots, and the pillow a sort of frightful hot, as though a baked brick had been on it? A hot old man! I guess he's got what some folks ashore call a conscience; it's a kind of Tic-Dolly-row, they say — worse than a toothache. Well, well; I don't know what it is, but the Lord keep me from catching it. He's full of riddles; I wonder what he goes into the after hold for every night, as Dough-Boy tells me he suspects; what's that for, I'd like to know? Who's made appointments with him in the hold? Isn't that queer, now? But there's no telling; it's the old game. Here goes for a snooze. Damn me, it's worth a fellow's while to be born into the world, if only to fall right asleep. And now that I think of it, that's about the first thing babies do, and that's sort of queer, too. Damn me, but all things are queer, come to think of them. But that's against my principles. Think not, is my eleventh commandment; and sleep when you can, is my twelfth. So here goes again. But how's that? Didn't he call me a dog? Blazes! He called me ten times a donkey, and piled a lot of jackasses on top of that! He might as well have kicked me, and been done with it. Maybe he did kick me, and I didn't notice it, I was so taken aback by his brow, somehow. It flashed like a bleached bone. What the devil's the matter with me? I don't stand right on my legs. Running afoul of that old man has sort of turned me inside out. By the Lord, I must have been dreaming, though — how? how? how? — but the only way is to stow it; so here goes to the hammock again; and in the morning I'll see how this plaguey hocus-pocus looks when I think it over by daylight."

chapters.title: Chapter 30 — The Pipe
paragraphs: When Stubb had gone, Ahab stood for a while leaning over the bulwarks. Then, as had been his habit lately, he called a sailor of the watch and sent him below for his ivory stool, and also his pipe. Lighting the pipe at the binnacle lamp (the lamp by the compass) and planting the stool on the weather side of the deck, he sat and smoked.

In old Norse times, the thrones of the sea-loving Danish kings were made, so tradition says, of the tusks of the narwhal. How could anyone look at Ahab then, seated on that tripod of bones, without thinking of the royalty it symbolized? For Ahab was a Khan of the plank, and a king of the sea, and a great lord of Leviathans.

Some moments passed, during which the thick smoke came from his mouth in quick, constant puffs that blew back into his face. "How now," he said to himself at last, taking the stem from his mouth, "this smoking no longer soothes. Oh, my pipe! Things must be going hard with me if your charm is gone! Here I have been unknowingly toiling, not taking pleasure — aye, and ignorantly smoking to windward all the while; to windward, and with such nervous whiffs, as if, like the dying whale, my final spouts were the strongest and fullest of trouble. What business do I have with this pipe? This thing is meant for serenity, to send up mild white vapors among mild white hairs, not among torn iron-gray locks like mine. I'll smoke no more —"

He tossed the still-lit pipe into the sea. The fire hissed in the waves. At the same instant, the ship shot past the bubble the sinking pipe made. With his hat pulled low, Ahab lurched across the planks.

chapters.title: Chapter 31 — Queen Mab
paragraphs: The next morning, Stubb approached Flask.

"I never had such a queer dream, King-Post. You know the old man's ivory leg? Well, I dreamed he kicked me with it; and when I tried to kick back, upon my soul, my little man, I kicked my leg right off! And then, presto! Ahab seemed to be a pyramid, and I, like a blazing fool, kept kicking at it. But what was still more curious, Flask — you know how curious all dreams are — through all this rage I was in, I somehow seemed to be thinking to myself that, after all, it wasn't much of an insult, that kick from Ahab. 'Why,' thinks I, 'what's the row? It's not a real leg, only a false leg.' And there's a mighty difference between a living thump and a dead thump. That's what makes a blow from the hand, Flask, fifty times more savage to bear than a blow from a cane. The living limb — that's what makes the living insult, my little man. And all the while, mind you, I was thinking to myself, while I was stubbing my silly toes against that cursed pyramid — so confoundedly contradictory was it all — all the while, I say, I was thinking to myself, 'What's his leg now but a cane — a whalebone cane? Yes,' thinks I, 'it was only a playful cudgeling — in fact, only a whaleboning he gave me — not a low kick. Besides,' thinks I, 'just look at it: why, the end of it — the foot part — what a small sort of end it is; whereas if a broad-footed farmer kicked me, now there's a devilish broad insult. But this insult is whittled down to a point only.' But now comes the biggest joke of the dream, Flask. While I was battering away at the pyramid, a sort of badger-haired old merman with a hump on his back takes me by the shoulders and swings me round. 'What are you up to?' says he. Lord! man, but I was frightened. Such a mug! But somehow, the next moment I was over the fright. 'What am I up to?' says I at last. 'And what business is that of yours, I'd like to know, Mr. Humpback? Do you want a kick?' By the Lord, Flask, no sooner had I said that than he turned his stern to me, bent over, and, dragging up a lot of seaweed he wore for a loincloth — what do you think I saw? — why, thunder alive, man, his stern was stuck full of marlinspikes, with the points out. Says I, on second thought, 'I guess I won't kick you, old fellow.' 'Wise Stubb,' said he, 'wise Stubb,' and kept muttering it all the time, a sort of chewing on his own gums like an old hag by the chimney. Seeing he wasn't going to stop saying over his 'wise Stubb, wise Stubb,' I thought I might as well go back to kicking the pyramid. But I had only just lifted my foot for it when he roared out, 'Stop that kicking!' 'Hello,' says I, 'what's the matter now, old fellow?' 'Look here,' says he; 'let's argue the insult. Captain Ahab kicked you, didn't he?' 'Yes, he did,' says I — 'right here it was.' 'Very good,' says he — 'he used his ivory leg, didn't he?' 'Yes, he did,' says I. 'Well then,' says he, 'wise Stubb, what have you got to complain of? Didn't he kick with right good will? It wasn't a common pitch-pine leg he kicked with, was it? No, you were kicked by a great man, and with a beautiful ivory leg, Stubb. It's an honor; I consider it an honor. Listen, wise Stubb. In old England the greatest lords think it a great glory to be slapped by a queen and made Knights of the Garter; but let your boast be, Stubb, that you were kicked by old Ahab and made a wise man of. Remember what I say: be kicked by him; count his kicks as honors; and on no account kick back; for you can't help yourself, wise Stubb. Don't you see that pyramid?' With that, all of a sudden, he seemed somehow, in some queer fashion, to swim off into the air. I snored, rolled over, and there I was in my hammock! Now, what do you think of that dream, Flask?"
"I don't know. Seems kind of silly to me, though."

"Maybe. Maybe. But it's made a wise man of me, Flask. Do you see Ahab standing there, looking sideways over the stern? Well, the best thing you can do, Flask, is leave the old man alone. Never speak to him, no matter what he says. Wait! What's that he's shouting? Listen!"
"Masthead, there! Look sharp, all of you! There are whales around here!"
"If you see a white one, scream your lungs out for him!"

"What do you think of that now, Flask? Isn't there a small drop of something queer about that, eh? A white whale — did you catch that, man? Look here — there's something special in the wind. Be ready for it, Flask. Ahab has something bloody on his mind. But shh — he's coming this way."

chapters.title: Chapter 32 — Cetology
paragraphs: Already we are boldly launched upon the deep, but soon we shall be lost in its shoreless, harborless immensities. Before that happens — before the Pequod's weedy hull rolls side by side with the barnacled hulls of the leviathan — it is only sensible, at the outset, to attend to a matter almost indispensable to a thorough and appreciative understanding of the more special leviathanic revelations and allusions of all sorts that are to follow.

What I would now like to put before you is some systematized exhibition of the whale in his broad genera. Yet it is no easy task. Nothing less is attempted here than the classification of the constituents of a chaos. Listen to what the best and latest authorities have laid down.
"No branch of Zoology is so confused as that which is called Cetology," says Captain Scoresby, 1820.

"It is not my intention, were it in my power, to enter into the inquiry as to the true method of dividing the cetacea into groups and families. * * * Utter confusion exists among the historians of this animal" (sperm whale), says Surgeon Beale, 1839.

"Unfitness to pursue our research in the unfathomable waters." "Impenetrable veil covering our knowledge of the cetacea." "A field strewn with thorns." "All these incomplete indications but serve to torture us naturalists."

Thus speak of the whale the great Cuvier, and John Hunter, and Lesson, those lights of zoology and anatomy. Nevertheless, though there is little real knowledge, there are plenty of books; and so it is, in some small degree, with cetology, the science of whales. Many men, small and great, old and new, landsmen and seamen, have written about the whale, at length or in brief. Run over a few: the Authors of the Bible; Aristotle; Pliny; Aldrovandi; Sir Thomas Browne; Gesner; Ray; Linnaeus; Rondeletius; Willoughby; Green; Artedi; Sibbald; Brisson; Marten; Lacépède; Bonneterre; Desmarest; Baron Cuvier; Frederick Cuvier; John Hunter; Owen; Scoresby; Beale; Bennett; J. Ross Browne; the Author of Miriam Coffin; Olmstead; and the Rev. T. Cheever. But to what ultimate generalizing purpose all these have written, the extracts cited above will show.

Of the names on this list of whale authors, only those after Owen ever saw living whales, and only one of them was a real professional harpooner and whaleman. I mean Captain Scoresby. On the separate subject of the Greenland or right whale, he is the best authority there is. But Scoresby knew nothing and says nothing of the great sperm whale, compared with which the Greenland whale is hardly worth mentioning. And let it be said here that the Greenland whale is a usurper on the throne of the seas. He is not even by any means the largest of the whales. Yet because his claims go back so far, and because of the profound ignorance that, until some seventy years ago, surrounded the then fabulous or utterly unknown sperm whale — an ignorance that to this day still reigns everywhere except in a few scientific retreats and whaling ports — this usurpation has been complete in every way. A look at nearly all the allusions to leviathan in the great poets of past days will satisfy you that the Greenland whale, without a single rival, was to them the monarch of the seas. But the time has at last come for a new proclamation. This is Charing Cross (where London's royal proclamations were read); hear this, good people all — the Greenland whale is deposed — the great sperm whale now reigns!

There are only two books in existence that claim to present the living sperm whale and actually succeed to any degree. Those are Beale's and Bennett's. Both authors were surgeons on English South Sea whale ships, and both are accurate, reliable men. The original material about the sperm whale in their volumes is necessarily small, but what there is of it is excellent in quality, though mostly limited to scientific description. As yet, however, the sperm whale — whether scientific or poetic — lives complete in no literature. Far above all other hunted whales, his is an unwritten life.

Now the various species of whales need some sort of popular, comprehensive classification, if only a rough outline for now, to be filled in later by others. Since no better person steps forward, I offer my own humble efforts. I promise nothing complete, because anything human that claims to be complete must for that very reason be infallibly faulty. I won't attempt detailed anatomical descriptions of the various species — not here, at least — or much description of any kind. My object here is simply to project the draft of a systematization of cetology. I am the architect, not the builder.

But it is a weighty job; no ordinary letter-sorter at the Post Office is up to it. To grope down to the bottom of the sea after them; to have your hands among the unspeakable foundations, ribs, and very pelvis of the world — this is a fearful thing. Who am I to attempt to hook the nose of this leviathan! The terrible taunts in Job might well appall me. Will he (the leviathan) make a covenant with thee? Behold the hope of him is vain! But I have swum through libraries and sailed through oceans; I have dealt with whales with these very hands you can see; I am serious; and I will try. There are some preliminaries to settle.

First: The uncertain, unsettled state of this science of Cetology is shown right in the entrance hall by the fact that in some quarters it is still a moot point whether a whale is a fish. In his System of Nature, 1776, Linnaeus declares, "I hereby separate the whales from the fish." But from my own knowledge, I know that down to the year 1850, sharks and shad, alewives and herring, against Linnaeus's express edict, were still found sharing possession of the same seas with the Leviathan.

The grounds on which Linnaeus would have banished the whales from the waters he states as follows: "On account of their warm two-chambered heart, their lungs, their movable eyelids, their hollow ears, penem intrantem feminam mammis lactantem," and finally, "ex lege naturae jure meritoque" (by the law of nature, justly and deservedly). I submitted all this to my friends Simeon Macey and Charley Coffin, of Nantucket, both messmates of mine on a certain voyage, and they were united in the opinion that the reasons set forth were altogether insufficient. Charley profanely hinted they were humbug.

Let it be known that, setting aside all argument, I take the good old-fashioned position that the whale is a fish, and I call on holy Jonah to back me up. With this fundamental point settled, the next question is: in what internal way does the whale differ from other fish? Linnaeus has given you the details above. But in brief, they are these: lungs and warm blood, whereas all other fish are lungless and cold-blooded.

Next: how shall we define the whale by his obvious external features, so as to label him unmistakably for all time? To be brief, then: a whale is a spouting fish with a horizontal tail. There you have him. However condensed, that definition is the result of expanded meditation. A walrus spouts much like a whale, but the walrus is not a fish because he is amphibious. The last part of the definition is even more decisive when paired with the first. Almost anyone has noticed that all fish familiar to landsmen have not a flat but a vertical — that is, an up-and-down — tail. Whereas among spouting fish, the tail, though it may be similarly shaped, always assumes a horizontal position.

By this definition of what a whale is, I do not in any way shut out of the leviathanic brotherhood any sea creature that the best-informed Nantucketers have so far counted as a whale; nor, on the other hand, do I admit into it any fish that authorities have so far treated as foreign to it.* So all the smaller fish that spout and have horizontal tails must be included in this ground plan of Cetology. Now, then, for the great divisions of the whole host of whales.

*I am aware that, even now, many naturalists count the fish called Lamatins (that is, manatees) and Dugongs (the Pig-fish and Sow-fish of the Coffins of Nantucket) among the whales. But since these pig-fish are a noisy, contemptible lot, mostly skulking in river mouths and feeding on wet hay, and above all since they don't spout, I reject their credentials as whales, and have handed them their passports to leave the Kingdom of Cetology.
First: according to size, I divide the whales into three primary BOOKS (named, like printed books, by size, and subdivided into CHAPTERS), which shall include them all, both small and large.
I. THE FOLIO WHALE; II. THE OCTAVO WHALE; III. THE DUODECIMO WHALE.
As the type of the FOLIO I present the Sperm Whale; of the OCTAVO, the Grampus; of the DUODECIMO, the Porpoise.

FOLIOS. Under this heading I include the following chapters: I. The Sperm Whale; II. The Right Whale; III. The Fin-Back Whale; IV. The Humpbacked Whale; V. The Razor Back Whale; VI. The Sulphur Bottom Whale.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER I (Sperm Whale). — This whale, vaguely known among the English of old as the Trumpa whale, the Physeter whale, and the Anvil Headed whale, is the present Cachalot of the French, the Pottsfich of the Germans, and the Macrocephalus of the Long Words. He is, without doubt, the largest inhabitant of the globe; the most formidable of all whales to encounter; the most majestic in appearance; and lastly, by far the most valuable in commerce, since he is the only creature from which that valuable substance, spermaceti, is obtained. All his peculiarities will be enlarged upon in many other places. It is chiefly his name that concerns me now. Considered philologically, it is absurd. Some centuries ago, when the Sperm whale was almost wholly unknown in his own proper individuality, and when his oil was only accidentally obtained from stranded fish, spermaceti, it would seem, was popularly supposed to come from a creature identical with the one then known in England as the Greenland or Right Whale. It was also thought that this same spermaceti was that quickening humor of the Greenland Whale which the first syllable of the word literally expresses. In those times, too, spermaceti was exceedingly scarce, being used not for light but only as an ointment and medicine. It could only be had from the druggists, the way you buy an ounce of rhubarb nowadays. When, as I suppose, the true nature of spermaceti became known in the course of time, the dealers still kept its original name — no doubt to enhance its value by a notion that so strangely signified its scarcity. And so the name must at last have come to be given to the whale from which this spermaceti was really derived.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER II (Right Whale). — In one respect this is the most venerable of the leviathans, being the first to be regularly hunted by man. It produces the substance commonly known as whalebone or baleen, and the oil known as "whale oil," an inferior product commercially. Among fishermen, he is indiscriminately called by all the following names: The Whale; the Greenland Whale; the Black Whale; the Great Whale; the True Whale; the Right Whale. There is considerable confusion about the identity of the species so multiply baptized. What, then, is the whale I include as the second species of my Folios? It is the Great Mysticetus of the English naturalists, the Greenland Whale of the English whalemen, the Baleine Ordinaire of the French whalemen, and the Growlands Walfish of the Swedes. It is the whale that for more than two centuries has been hunted by the Dutch and English in the Arctic seas, and the whale that American fishermen have long pursued in the Indian Ocean, on the Brazil Banks, on the Northwest Coast, and various other parts of the world designated by them as Right Whale Cruising Grounds.

Some claim to see a difference between the Greenland whale of the English and the right whale of the Americans. But they agree precisely in all their major features, and no one has yet presented a single definitive fact on which to base a real distinction. It is by endless subdivisions based on the most inconclusive differences that some branches of natural history become so repulsively complicated. The right whale will be treated elsewhere at some length, as a way of shedding light on the sperm whale.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER III (Fin-Back). — Under this heading I count a monster which, under the various names of Fin-Back, Tall-Spout, and Long-John, has been seen in almost every sea, and is commonly the whale whose distant jet is so often spotted by passengers crossing the Atlantic on the New York packet routes. In the length he reaches, and in his baleen, the Fin-Back resembles the right whale, but he is less portly in girth and lighter in color, approaching olive. His great lips have a cable-like look, formed by the intertwisting, slanting folds of large wrinkles. His grand distinguishing feature, the fin from which he gets his name, is often a conspicuous object. This fin is some three or four feet long, growing vertically from the rear part of the back, angular in shape, and with a very sharp-pointed end. Even when not the slightest other part of the creature is visible, this isolated fin will at times be seen plainly projecting from the surface. When the sea is moderately calm and lightly marked with spherical ripples, and this gnomon-like fin stands up and casts shadows on the wrinkled surface, it may well be supposed that the watery circle around it somewhat resembles a dial, with its style (the dial's upright pointer) and wavy hour-lines engraved on it. On that Ahaz-dial (the sundial on which, in the Bible, the shadow miraculously went backward) the shadow often goes back. The Fin-Back is not gregarious. He seems a whale-hater, as some men are man-haters. Very shy; always going solitary; rising unexpectedly to the surface in the remotest and most sullen waters; his straight and single lofty jet rising like a tall misanthropic spear on a barren plain; gifted with such wondrous power and speed in swimming as to defy all present pursuit by man — this leviathan seems the banished and unconquerable Cain of his race, bearing as his mark that style upon his back. Because he has baleen in his mouth, the Fin-Back is sometimes grouped with the right whale in a theoretical species called Whalebone whales, that is, whales with baleen. Of these so-called Whalebone whales there would seem to be several varieties, most of which, however, are little known. Broad-nosed whales and beaked whales; pike-headed whales; bunched whales; under-jawed whales and rostrated whales — these are the fishermen's names for a few sorts.

In connection with this name of "Whalebone whales," it is of great importance to mention that, however convenient such a nomenclature may be for referring to some kinds of whales, it is useless to attempt a clear classification of the Leviathan based on either his baleen, or hump, or fin, or teeth — even though those marked parts or features very obviously seem better suited to form the basis of a regular system of Cetology than any other separate bodily distinctions that the whale, in his various kinds, presents. How so? Baleen, hump, back-fin, and teeth: these are things whose peculiarities are scattered indiscriminately among all sorts of whales, without any regard to what their structure may be in other and more essential respects. Thus the sperm whale and the humpbacked whale each has a hump; but there the likeness ends. Then this same humpbacked whale and the Greenland whale each has baleen; but there again the likeness ends. And it is just the same with the other parts mentioned above. In the various sorts of whales, they form such irregular combinations — or, taken one by one, such irregular isolation — as utterly to defy any general system built on such a basis. On this rock every one of the whale-naturalists has split.

But perhaps, you might think, in the whale's internal parts — his anatomy — there we could find the right classification. Not so. What feature of the Greenland whale's anatomy is more striking than his baleen? Yet we have seen that the Greenland whale cannot be correctly classified by his baleen. And if you descend into the bowels of the various leviathans, why, there you will not find distinctions even a fiftieth as useful to the systematizer as the external ones already listed. What remains? Nothing but to take hold of the whales physically, in their full liberal volume, and boldly sort them that way. And this is the bibliographical system I adopt here. It is the only one that can possibly work, for it alone is practical. Let us proceed.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER IV (Humpback). — This whale is often seen off the northern American coast. He has been frequently captured there and towed into harbor. He has a great pack on him like a peddler; or you might call him the Elephant and Castle whale. In any case, his popular name doesn't sufficiently distinguish him, since the sperm whale also has a hump, though a smaller one. His oil is not very valuable. He has baleen. He is the most playful and lighthearted of all the whales, making more joyful foam and white water than any other.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER V (Razor Back). — Of this whale, little is known but his name. I have seen him at a distance off Cape Horn. Of a retiring nature, he eludes both hunters and philosophers. Though no coward, he has never shown any part of himself but his back, which rises in a long, sharp ridge. Let him go. I know little more of him, and neither does anyone else.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER VI (Sulphur Bottom). — Another retiring gentleman, with a brimstone belly, doubtless acquired by scraping along the Tartarian tiles of the underworld in some of his deeper dives. He is seldom seen; at least I have never seen him except in the remoter southern seas, and then always at too great a distance to study his countenance. He is never chased; he would run away with whole rope-walks of line. Marvels are told of him. Farewell, Sulphur Bottom! I can say nothing more that is true of you, and neither can the oldest Nantucketer.
Thus ends BOOK I (Folio), and now begins BOOK II (Octavo).
OCTAVOES.* — These include the whales of middling size, among which may at present be counted: I. the Grampus; II. the Black Fish; III. the Narwhale; IV. the Thrasher; V. the Killer.

*Why this book of whales isn't called the Quarto is quite plain. It's because the whales of this order, though smaller than those of the previous order, still keep a proportional resemblance to them in shape, whereas the bookbinder's Quarto volume, in its dimensions, does not keep the shape of the Folio volume — but the Octavo volume does.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER I (Grampus). — Though this fish, whose loud, sonorous breathing, or rather blowing, has furnished a proverb to landsmen, is so well known a dweller of the deep, he is not popularly classed among whales. But since he possesses all the grand distinctive features of the leviathan, most naturalists have recognized him as one. He is of moderate octavo size, varying from fifteen to twenty-five feet in length, and of corresponding dimensions around the waist. He swims in herds; he is never regularly hunted, though his oil is considerable in quantity, and pretty good for light. Some fishermen regard his approach as a forewarning of the advance of the great sperm whale.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER II (Black Fish). — I give the fishermen's everyday names for all these fish, since as a rule they are the best. Where a name happens to be vague or says little, I'll point that out and suggest another. I do so now with the so-called Black Fish, because blackness is the rule among nearly all whales. So call him the Hyena Whale, if you like. His greed is well known, and since the inner corners of his lips curve upward, he wears a permanent Mephistophelean grin. This whale runs to about sixteen or eighteen feet long on average. He turns up in almost every latitude. He has an odd way of showing his hooked dorsal fin as he swims, which looks rather like a Roman nose. When they have nothing more profitable to do, the sperm whale hunters sometimes catch the Hyena whale to keep up their supply of cheap oil for household use — just as some thrifty housekeepers, when no guests are present and they are entirely on their own, burn smelly tallow instead of sweet-scented wax. Though their blubber is very thin, some of these whales will give you more than thirty gallons of oil.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER III (Narwhale), that is, Nostril whale. — Another instance of a curiously named whale, so named, I suppose, because his peculiar horn was originally mistaken for a peaked nose. The creature is some sixteen feet in length, while its horn averages five feet, though some exceed ten, and even reach fifteen feet. Strictly speaking, this horn is only a lengthened tusk, growing out from the jaw in a line slightly depressed from the horizontal. But it is only found on the sinister side — the left — which has an ill effect, giving its owner something like the look of a clumsy left-handed man. What precise purpose this ivory horn or lance serves, it would be hard to say. It does not seem to be used like the blade of the swordfish and billfish, though some sailors tell me that the Narwhale uses it as a rake for turning over the bottom of the sea for food. Charley Coffin said it was used as an ice-piercer; for the Narwhale, rising to the surface of the Polar Sea and finding it sheeted with ice, thrusts his horn up and so breaks through. But you cannot prove either of these guesses correct. My own opinion is that however the Narwhale may really use this one-sided horn — however that may be — it would certainly be very convenient to him as a paper-folder in reading pamphlets. I have heard the Narwhale called the Tusked whale, the Horned whale, and the Unicorn whale. He is certainly a curious example of the Unicornism to be found in almost every kingdom of animate nature. From certain cloistered old authors I have gathered that this same sea-unicorn's horn was in ancient days regarded as the great antidote against poison, and as such, preparations of it brought immense prices. It was also distilled into volatile salts for fainting ladies, the same way that the horns of the male deer are made into hartshorn. Originally it was in itself considered an object of great curiosity. Black Letter (that is, old books printed in Gothic type) tells me that Sir Martin Frobisher, on his return from that voyage when Queen Bess gallantly waved her jeweled hand to him from a window of Greenwich Palace as his bold ship sailed down the Thames — "when Sir Martin returned from that voyage," says Black Letter, "on bended knees he presented to her highness a prodigious long horn of the Narwhale, which for a long period after hung in the castle at Windsor." An Irish author asserts that the Earl of Leicester, on bended knees, likewise presented to her highness another horn, belonging to a land beast of the unicorn nature.

The Narwhale looks very picturesque, rather like a leopard, with a milk-white base color dotted with round and oblong black spots. His oil is of excellent quality, clear and fine; but he has little of it, and is seldom hunted. He is found mostly in the circumpolar seas.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER IV (Killer). — Of this whale, the Nantucketer knows little with certainty, and the professional naturalist knows nothing at all. From what I have seen of him at a distance, I would say he is about the size of a grampus. He is very savage — a sort of Fiji fish. He sometimes seizes great Folio whales by the lip and hangs there like a leech until the mighty brute is worried to death. The Killer is never hunted. I have never heard what sort of oil he has. His name might be objected to on the grounds of vagueness. For we are all killers, on land and on sea — Bonapartes and sharks included.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER V (Thrasher). — This gentleman is famous for his tail, which he uses like a rod for whipping his enemies. He mounts the Folio whale's back and, as he swims, works his passage by flogging him — as some schoolmasters get through the world by a similar method. Even less is known about the Thrasher than the Killer. Both are outlaws, even in the lawless seas.
Thus ends BOOK II (Octavo), and begins BOOK III (Duodecimo).
DUODECIMOES. — These include the smaller whales: I. The Huzza Porpoise. II. The Algerine Porpoise. III. The Mealy-Mouthed Porpoise.

To those who have not happened to study the subject specially, it may possibly seem strange that fish not commonly exceeding four or five feet should be marshaled among WHALES — a word that, in the popular sense, always conveys an idea of hugeness. But the creatures listed above as Duodecimoes are infallibly whales, by the terms of my definition of what a whale is — that is, a spouting fish with a horizontal tail.

BOOK III (Duodecimo), CHAPTER 1 (Huzza Porpoise). — This is the common porpoise, found almost everywhere on the globe. The name is my own invention, since there is more than one kind of porpoise, and something has to be done to tell them apart. I call him that because he always swims in hilarious schools, which keep flinging themselves skyward on the open sea like caps thrown up in a Fourth-of-July crowd. Sailors usually greet their appearance with delight. Brimming with high spirits, they always come from the breezy waves to windward. They are the lads who always live before the wind. They're thought to be a lucky sign. If you yourself can keep from giving three cheers at the sight of these lively fish, then heaven help you; you haven't got the spirit of godly playfulness in you. A well-fed, plump Huzza Porpoise will give you one good gallon of good oil. But the fine, delicate fluid extracted from his jaws is extremely valuable. Jewelers and watchmakers are eager for it. Sailors put it on their whetstones. Porpoise meat is good eating, you know. It may never have occurred to you that a porpoise spouts. In fact, his spout is so small that it's not easy to make out. But the next time you get the chance, watch him, and you'll see the great Sperm whale himself in miniature.

BOOK III (Duodecimo), CHAPTER II (Algerine Porpoise). — A pirate. Very savage. He is only found, I think, in the Pacific. He is somewhat larger than the Huzza Porpoise but much the same in general build. Provoke him and he'll take on a shark. I've lowered the boats for him many times but have never yet seen him captured.

BOOK III (Duodecimo), CHAPTER III (Mealy-mouthed Porpoise). — The largest kind of Porpoise, and found only in the Pacific, so far as is known. The only English name by which he has so far been called is the fishermen's — Right-Whale Porpoise, from the fact that he is chiefly found near that Folio. In shape he differs somewhat from the Huzza Porpoise, being of a less rotund and jolly girth; indeed, he has quite a neat and gentlemanly figure. He has no fins on his back (most other porpoises have), he has a lovely tail, and sentimental Indian eyes of a hazel hue. But his mealy mouth spoils everything. Though his entire back, down to his side fins, is a deep sable, yet a boundary line called the "bright waist," as distinct as the mark on a ship's hull, streaks him from stem to stern with two separate colors, black above and white below. The white takes in part of his head and the whole of his mouth, which makes him look as if he had just escaped from a felonious visit to a meal-bag. A most mean and mealy aspect! His oil is much like that of the common porpoise.

Beyond the DUODECIMO, this system does not go, since the porpoise is the smallest of the whales. Above, you have all the notable Leviathans. But there is a rabble of uncertain, fleeting, half-mythical whales that I, as an American whaleman, know by reputation but not personally. I will list them by their forecastle names, since such a list may prove valuable to future researchers who may complete what I have only begun. If any of the following whales should be caught and identified, they can easily be added to this system according to their Folio, Octavo, or Duodecimo size: the Bottle-Nose Whale; the Junk Whale; the Pudding-Headed Whale; the Cape Whale; the Leading Whale; the Cannon Whale; the Scragg Whale; the Coppered Whale; the Elephant Whale; the Iceberg Whale; the Quog Whale; the Blue Whale; and so on. From Icelandic, Dutch, and old English sources, other lists of uncertain whales could be quoted, blessed with all manner of outlandish names. But I omit them as completely obsolete, and I can't help suspecting them of being mere sounds, full of Leviathanism, but signifying nothing.

Finally: it was stated at the outset that this system would not be perfected here and now. You can plainly see that I have kept my word. But I now leave my cetological system standing unfinished, even as the great Cathedral of Cologne was left, with the crane still standing atop the uncompleted tower. Small structures may be finished by their first architects. Grand ones, true ones, always leave the capstone to posterity. God keep me from ever completing anything. This whole book is but a draft — no, but the draft of a draft. Oh, Time, Strength, Cash, and Patience!

chapters.title: Chapter 33 — The Specksnyder
paragraphs: Concerning the officers of the whale ship, this seems as good a place as any to describe a small domestic peculiarity on board, arising from the existence of the harpooner class of officers — a class unknown, of course, in any other service but the whale fleet.

The great importance attached to the harpooner's profession is shown by the fact that originally, in the old Dutch Fishery two centuries and more ago, command of a whale ship was not entirely in the hands of the person now called the captain. It was divided between him and an officer called the Specksnyder. Literally, this word means Fat-Cutter, though in time it came to mean Chief Harpooner. In those days, the captain's authority was limited to navigation and the general management of the vessel, while over the whale-hunting department and everything related to it, the Specksnyder or Chief Harpooner reigned supreme. In the British Greenland Fishery, under the corrupted title of Specksioneer, this old Dutch post still exists, but with much reduced authority. At present he ranks simply as senior harpooner and is merely one of the captain's lesser subordinates. Nevertheless, since the success of a whaling voyage largely depends on the harpooners' performance, and since in the American Fishery the harpooner is not only an important officer in the boat but also, under certain circumstances like night watches on a whaling ground, has command of the ship's deck — the grand political principle of the sea demands that he should nominally live apart from the men before the mast and be in some way distinguished as their professional superior, though they always familiarly regard him as their social equal.

Now, the key distinction between officer and ordinary seaman at sea is this: the officer lives aft, the seaman lives forward. Hence, on whale ships and merchant vessels alike, the mates have their quarters with the captain. And on most American whalers, the harpooners are also housed in the aft part of the ship — meaning they eat their meals in the captain's cabin and sleep in a space that connects with it indirectly.

Though the long duration of a Southern whaling voyage (by far the longest of all voyages now or ever made by man), its peculiar perils, and the community of interest among a company all of whom, high or low, depend for their profits not on fixed wages but on their common luck, together with their common vigilance, courage, and hard work — though all these things do in some cases tend to produce a less rigorous discipline than on merchant ships generally, still, no matter how much like an old Mesopotamian family these whalemen may, in some primitive instances, live together, the punctilious externals of the quarter-deck, at least, are seldom materially relaxed, and in no instance done away with. Indeed, there are many Nantucket ships on which you will see the skipper parading his quarter-deck with an elated grandeur not surpassed in any military navy — no, extorting almost as much outward homage as if he wore the imperial purple, and not the shabbiest of pilot-cloth.

And although of all men the moody captain of the Pequod was the least inclined to that shallowest kind of pretension; and although the only homage he ever demanded was total, instant obedience; although he required nobody to take the shoes off his feet before stepping onto the quarter-deck; and although there were times when, because of peculiar circumstances connected with events to be described later, he addressed them in unusual terms, whether condescending, or in terrorem (meant to intimidate), or otherwise; still, even Captain Ahab was far from ignoring the paramount forms and customs of the sea.

Nor, perhaps, will it fail to be noticed in the end that behind those forms and customs, as it were, he sometimes masked himself, incidentally using them for other and more private ends than they were legitimately meant to serve. That certain sultanism of his brain, which had otherwise remained to a good degree unmanifested — through those forms that same sultanism became incarnate in an irresistible dictatorship. For whatever a man's intellectual superiority may be, it can never take on a practical, usable supremacy over other men without the help of some sort of external arts and entrenchments, which are always in themselves more or less paltry and base. It is this that forever keeps God's true princes of the Empire from the world's hustings, the platforms of public election, and leaves the highest honors that this air can give to those men who become famous more through their infinite inferiority to the choice hidden handful of the Divine Inert than through their undoubted superiority over the dead level of the mass. Such great virtue lurks in these small things, when extreme political superstitions invest them, that in some royal instances they have given potency even to idiot imbecility. But when, as in the case of Nicholas the Czar, the ringed crown of geographical empire encircles an imperial brain, then the plebeian herds crouch abased before the tremendous centralization. Nor will the tragic dramatist who would depict mortal indomitableness in its fullest sweep and direct swing ever forget a hint so incidentally important to his art as the one just alluded to.

But Ahab, my Captain, still moves before me in all his Nantucket grimness and shagginess; and in this episode touching on emperors and kings, I must not conceal that I have to do only with a poor old whale-hunter like him; and therefore all outward majestic trappings and housings are denied me. Oh, Ahab! Whatever is to be grand in you must be plucked from the skies, and dived for in the deep, and given features in the unbodied air!

chapters.title: Chapter 34 — The Cabin-Table
paragraphs: It is noon, and Dough-Boy, the steward, thrusts his pale bread-dough face from the cabin hatch to announce dinner to his lord and master. Ahab, sitting in the lee quarter-boat, has just been taking a reading of the sun and is now silently calculating the latitude on the smooth, medallion-shaped tablet reserved for this daily purpose on the upper part of his ivory leg. From his complete inattention to the news, you'd think moody Ahab hadn't heard his servant. But presently, catching hold of the mizzen shrouds, he swings himself to the deck and, in an even, unenthusiastic voice, says, "Dinner, Mr. Starbuck," and disappears into the cabin.

When the last echo of his sultan's step has faded and Starbuck, the first Emir, has every reason to believe he is seated, then Starbuck rouses from his stillness, takes a few turns along the deck, and after a grave peep into the binnacle (the compass housing), says with some touch of pleasantness, "Dinner, Mr. Stubb," and goes below. The second Emir lounges about the rigging a while, then slightly shakes the main brace, to see whether all is well with that important rope. He likewise takes up the old refrain and, with a quick "Dinner, Mr. Flask," follows his predecessors.

But the third Emir, now finding himself all alone on the quarter-deck, seems to feel freed from some odd restraint; for, tossing off all kinds of knowing winks in every direction and kicking off his shoes, he breaks into a quick but silent squall of a hornpipe right over the Grand Turk's head; and then, with a deft trick, tossing his cap up into the mizzentop to use as a shelf, he goes below, rollicking — at least as long as he stays visible from the deck — reversing all other processions by bringing up the rear with the music. But before stepping through the cabin doorway below, he stops, puts on a completely new face, and then independent, hilarious little Flask enters King Ahab's presence in the role of Abjectus, or the Slave.

It is not the least among the strange things bred by the intense artificiality of sea customs that, while on the open deck some officers will, when provoked, carry themselves boldly and defiantly enough toward their commander, yet, ten to one, let those very officers go down the next moment to their customary dinner in that same commander's cabin, and at once their inoffensive, not to say apologetic and humble, air toward him as he sits at the head of the table is marvelous, and sometimes most comical. Why this difference? A problem? Perhaps not. To have been Belshazzar, King of Babylon, and to have been Belshazzar not haughtily but courteously — in that there certainly must have been some touch of worldly grandeur. But the man who presides in a rightly regal and intelligent spirit over his own private dinner table of invited guests — that man's unchallenged power and dominion of personal influence for the time being, that man's royalty of state, surpasses Belshazzar's, for Belshazzar was not the greatest. Whoever has once had his friends to dinner has tasted what it is to be Caesar. It is a witchery of social czarship that there is no withstanding. Now, if on top of this you add the official supremacy of a ship's captain, then by inference you will arrive at the cause of that peculiarity of sea life just mentioned.

Over his ivory-inlaid table, Ahab presided like a mute, maned sea-lion on the white coral beach, surrounded by his warlike but still deferential cubs. Each officer waited to be served in his own proper turn. They were like little children before Ahab; and yet in Ahab there seemed not to lurk the smallest social arrogance. With one mind, their intent eyes all fastened on the old man's knife as he carved the chief dish before him. I do not suppose that for the world they would have profaned that moment with the slightest remark, even on so neutral a topic as the weather. No! And when, reaching out his knife and fork with the slice of beef locked between them, Ahab thereby motioned Starbuck's plate toward him, the mate received his meat as though receiving alms, and cut it tenderly, and started a little if the knife happened to graze the plate, and chewed it noiselessly, and swallowed it, not without caution. For, like the Coronation banquet at Frankfurt, where the German Emperor dines in profound state with the seven Imperial Electors, these cabin meals were somehow solemn meals, eaten in awful silence; and yet at table old Ahab did not forbid conversation; only he himself was silent. What a relief it was to choking Stubb when a rat made a sudden racket in the hold below. And poor little Flask — he was the youngest son and little boy of this weary family party. His were the shinbones of the salt beef; his would have been the drumsticks. For Flask to have presumed to help himself must have seemed to him the equivalent of larceny in the first degree. Had he helped himself at that table, doubtless he would never again have been able to hold his head up in this honest world; nevertheless, strange to say, Ahab never forbade him. And had Flask helped himself, the chances were that Ahab would never so much as have noticed it. Least of all did Flask presume to help himself to butter. Whether he thought the owners of the ship denied it to him on account of its clotting his clear, sunny complexion, or whether he reckoned that on so long a voyage in such marketless waters butter was at a premium, and therefore not for him, a subordinate — however it was, Flask, alas, was a butterless man!

Another thing: Flask was the last person down to dinner and the first one back up. Consider! This meant Flask's dinner was badly squeezed for time. Starbuck and Stubb both got a head start on him, yet they also had the privilege of lingering. If even Stubb, who ranks only one peg above Flask, happened to have a small appetite and showed signs of finishing his meal, then Flask had to hurry — he wouldn't get more than three mouthfuls that day, for it was against sacred custom for Stubb to leave the table before Flask. Therefore Flask once confided in private that ever since he had risen to the dignity of an officer, he had never known what it was to be anything other than hungry, more or less. What he ate didn't so much relieve his hunger as keep it alive forever. Peace and satisfaction, Flask thought, have departed from my stomach for good. I am an officer — but how I wish I could grab a bit of good old-fashioned beef in the forecastle, the way I used to as a common sailor. There's the fruit of promotion. There's the vanity of glory. There's the insanity of life! Besides, if any ordinary sailor on the Pequod had a grudge against Flask in his official capacity, all that sailor had to do for ample revenge was go aft at dinnertime and peek at Flask through the cabin skylight, sitting there silly and dumbfounded before awful Ahab.

Now, Ahab and his three mates formed what might be called the first table in the Pequod's cabin. After their departure, in reverse order of their arrival, the canvas tablecloth was cleared — or rather restored to some hasty order by the pale steward. Then the three harpooners were invited to the feast, being its residuary legatees — the heirs to whatever was left. They made a sort of temporary servants' hall of the high and mighty cabin.

In strange contrast to the hardly tolerable constraint and nameless invisible domineering of the captain's table was the entire carefree license and ease, the almost frantic democracy, of those inferior fellows the harpooners. While their masters, the mates, seemed afraid of the sound of the hinges of their own jaws, the harpooners chewed their food with such relish that there was a report to it. They dined like lords; they filled their bellies like Indian ships loading with spices all day. Such portentous appetites had Queequeg and Tashtego that, to fill the gaps left by the previous meal, the pale Dough-Boy often had to bring on a great baron of salt-junk (salt beef), seemingly quarried out of the solid ox. And if he was not lively about it, if he did not go with a nimble hop-skip-and-jump, then Tashtego had an ungentlemanly way of speeding him up by darting a fork at his back, harpoon-fashion. And once Daggoo, seized with a sudden humor, assisted Dough-Boy's memory by snatching him up bodily and thrusting his head into a great empty wooden trencher, while Tashtego, knife in hand, began laying out the circle preliminary to scalping him. He was naturally a very nervous, shuddering sort of little fellow, this bread-faced steward, the offspring of a bankrupt baker and a hospital nurse. And what with the standing spectacle of the black, terrifying Ahab and the periodic tumultuous visitations of these three savages, Dough-Boy's whole life was one continual lip-quiver. Usually, after seeing the harpooners furnished with everything they demanded, he would escape from their clutches into his little pantry next door, and fearfully peep out at them through the blinds of its door until it was all over.

It was a sight to see Queequeg seated opposite Tashtego, pitting his filed teeth against the Indian's; crosswise to them, Daggoo sat on the floor, for a bench would have brought his hearse-plumed head up against the low carlines (the beams under the deck overhead); at every motion of his colossal limbs he made the low cabin framework shake, as when an African elephant travels as a passenger in a ship. But for all this, the great negro was wonderfully abstemious, not to say dainty. It seemed hardly possible that by such comparatively small mouthfuls he could keep up the vitality spread through so broad, baronial, and superb a person. But doubtless this noble savage fed strong and drank deep of the abounding element of air, and through his dilated nostrils snuffed in the sublime life of the worlds. Not by beef or by bread are giants made or nourished. But Queequeg — he had a mortal, barbaric smack of the lip in eating, an ugly enough sound, so much so that the trembling Dough-Boy almost looked to see whether any teeth marks lurked in his own lean arms. And when he heard Tashtego singing out for him to show himself, so that his bones might be picked, the simple-witted steward all but shattered the crockery hanging around him in the pantry with his sudden fits of the palsy. Nor did the whetstones the harpooners carried in their pockets for their lances and other weapons — whetstones on which, at dinner, they would ostentatiously sharpen their knives — nor did that grating sound at all tend to calm poor Dough-Boy. How could he forget that in his Island days, Queequeg, for one, must certainly have been guilty of some murderous, convivial indiscretions? Alas, Dough-Boy! Hard fares the white waiter who waits on cannibals. Not a napkin should he carry on his arm, but a buckler. In good time, though, to his great delight, the three salt-sea warriors would rise and depart — to his credulous, fable-mongering ears, all their martial bones jingling in them at every step, like Moorish scimitars in scabbards.

But although these barbarians ate in the cabin and in name lived there, their habits were anything but sedentary, and so they were almost never in it except at mealtimes and just before bed, when they passed through on their way to their own particular quarters.

On this one point Ahab seemed no different from most American whaling captains, who, as a class, tend to think the ship's cabin belongs to them by right, and that anyone else is ever allowed in it only as a courtesy. So, in plain truth, the mates and harpooners of the Pequod could more accurately be said to have lived outside the cabin than in it. For when they did go in, it was rather the way a street door goes into a house: swinging inward for a moment, only to be swung back out the next, and living, permanently, in the open air. Not that they lost much by this; there was no companionship in the cabin; socially, Ahab was unapproachable. Though he was nominally counted in the census of Christendom, he was still a stranger to it. He lived in the world the way the last of the grizzly bears lived in settled Missouri. And just as, when spring and summer had gone, that wild Logan of the woods would bury himself in a hollow tree and live out the winter there, sucking his own paws, so in his harsh, howling old age Ahab's soul, shut up in the hollowed trunk of his body, fed there on the sullen paws of its gloom!

chapters.title: Chapter 35 — The Mast-Head
paragraphs: It was during the more pleasant weather that my first turn at the masthead came around, in due rotation with the other seamen.

On most American whalers, the mastheads are manned almost as soon as the ship leaves port, even though she may have fifteen thousand miles or more to sail before reaching her proper cruising ground. And if, after a three, four, or five-year voyage, she's heading home with anything unfilled — even an empty vial — then her mastheads stay manned to the last. Not until her skysail-poles, the very tops of her masts, sail in among the spires of the port does she give up the hope of catching one more whale.

Now, since the business of standing mastheads, ashore or afloat, is a very ancient and interesting one, let us enlarge on it here to some extent. I take it that the earliest masthead-standers were the old Egyptians, because in all my research I find none before them. For though their forebears, the builders of Babel, must doubtless have meant their tower to be the loftiest masthead in all Asia, or Africa either, yet since (before the final truck, the wooden cap at the very top of a mast, was put to it) that great stone mast of theirs may be said to have gone by the board in the dread gale of God's wrath, we cannot give these Babel builders priority over the Egyptians. And that the Egyptians were a nation of masthead-standers is an assertion based on the general belief among archaeologists that the first pyramids were founded for astronomical purposes — a theory singularly supported by the peculiar stair-like formation of all four sides of those buildings, by which, with prodigiously long liftings of their legs, those old astronomers used to climb to the apex and sing out for new stars, just as the lookouts of a modern ship sing out for a sail, or a whale just coming into sight. In Saint Stylites, the famous Christian hermit of old times, who built himself a lofty stone pillar in the desert and spent the whole latter part of his life on its summit, hoisting his food up from the ground with a tackle — in him we have a remarkable instance of a dauntless masthead-stander, who was not to be driven from his place by fogs or frosts, rain, hail, or sleet, but, valiantly facing everything out to the last, literally died at his post. Of modern masthead-standers we have only a lifeless set: mere stone, iron, and bronze men, who, though well able to face out a stiff gale, are still entirely incompetent at the business of singing out on discovering any strange sight. There is Napoleon, who stands with arms folded on top of the column of Vendome, some one hundred and fifty feet in the air, careless now who rules the decks below, whether Louis Philippe, Louis Blanc, or Louis the Devil. Great Washington, too, stands high aloft on his towering main-mast in Baltimore, and like one of Hercules' pillars, his column marks that point of human grandeur beyond which few mortals will go. Admiral Nelson, also, stands his masthead on a capstan of gun-metal in Trafalgar Square; and even when he is most obscured by that London smoke, there is still a token that a hidden hero is there; for where there is smoke, there must be fire. But neither great Washington, nor Napoleon, nor Nelson will answer a single hail from below, however madly they are invoked to help with their counsel the distracted decks they gaze down on — however it may be surmised that their spirits penetrate the thick haze of the future and see what shoals and what rocks must be avoided.

It may seem unjustified to link the masthead-standers of the land with those of the sea in any way, but that in truth it is not is plainly shown by a detail for which Obed Macy, the sole historian of Nantucket, is our source. Worthy Obed tells us that in the early days of the whale fishery, before ships were regularly sent out in pursuit, the islanders erected tall poles along the coast, to which lookouts climbed by means of nailed rungs, like chickens going up stairs in a henhouse. A few years ago, the same system was adopted by the bay whalemen of New Zealand, who, upon spotting whales, signaled the waiting boats near the beach. But this custom is now obsolete. So let us turn to the proper masthead: that of a whale ship at sea. The three mastheads are manned from sunrise to sunset, the sailors taking regular turns (as at the helm) and relieving each other every two hours. In the calm weather of the tropics, the masthead is exceedingly pleasant; no, to a dreamy, meditative man it is delightful. There you stand, a hundred feet above the silent decks, striding across the deep as if the masts were giant stilts. Beneath you and between your legs, so to speak, swim the largest monsters of the sea, just as ships once sailed between the boots of the famous Colossus of Rhodes. There you stand, lost in the infinite series of the sea, with nothing stirred but the waves. The hypnotized ship lazily rolls. The drowsy trade winds blow. Everything dissolves you into lethargy. For the most part, in this tropical whaling life, a sublime uneventfulness wraps around you. You hear no news. You read no newspapers. No extras with alarming reports of ordinary events trick you into unnecessary excitement. You hear of no family troubles or bankrupt investments or falling stocks. You never worry about what to have for dinner — all your meals for three years or more are snugly stowed in casks, and your menu is fixed.

On one of those southern whalers, on a long voyage of three or four years, as often happens, the hours you spend at the masthead add up to several whole months. And it's a great pity that the place where you spend so large a share of your entire natural life should be so sadly lacking in anything like cozy homeliness, or anything suited to breeding a comfortable sense of belonging to a spot, such as goes with a bed, a hammock, a hearse, a sentry box, a pulpit, a coach, or any of those other small, snug contraptions in which men shut themselves away for a time. Your usual perch is the top of the topgallant mast, where you stand on two thin parallel sticks (almost unique to whalemen) called the topgallant crosstrees. Up there, tossed about by the sea, the beginner feels roughly as cozy as he would standing on a bull's horns. Of course, in cold weather you can take your house aloft with you in the form of a watch-coat; but strictly speaking, the thickest watch-coat is no more a house than your bare body is.
