For just as the soul is glued inside its fleshly tabernacle, and can't move around freely in it, or even move out of it, without great risk of perishing (like an ignorant pilgrim crossing the snowy Alps in winter), so a watch-coat is not so much a house as a mere envelope, or an extra skin wrapped around you. You can't put a shelf or a chest of drawers inside your body, and neither can you make a handy closet out of your watch-coat.

On all this, it is much to be regretted that the mastheads of a southern whale ship are not provided with those enviable little tents or pulpits called crow's-nests, in which the lookouts of a Greenland whaler are protected from the inclement weather of the frozen seas. In the fireside narrative of Captain Sleet, titled "A Voyage among the Icebergs, in quest of the Greenland Whale, and incidentally for the re-discovery of the Lost Icelandic Colonies of Old Greenland" — in this admirable volume, all masthead-standers are furnished with a charmingly circumstantial account of the then recently invented crow's-nest of the Glacier, which was the name of Captain Sleet's good ship. He called it the Sleet's crow's-nest, in honor of himself, since he was the original inventor and patentee, and free from all ridiculous false delicacy; and he held that if we name our own children after ourselves (we fathers being the original inventors and patentees), we should likewise name after ourselves any other apparatus we may beget. In shape, the Sleet's crow's-nest is something like a large tierce or pipe (both big casks); it is open above, however, where it is fitted with a movable side-screen to keep to windward of your head in a hard gale. Since it is fixed on the top of the mast, you climb into it through a little trap-hatch in the bottom. On the after side, the side nearest the stern of the ship, is a comfortable seat, with a locker underneath for umbrellas, comforters, and coats. In front is a leather rack in which to keep your speaking trumpet, pipe, telescope, and other nautical conveniences. When Captain Sleet in person stood his masthead in this crow's-nest of his, he tells us that he always had a rifle with him (also fixed in the rack), together with a powder flask and shot, for the purpose of popping off the stray narwhales, or vagrant sea unicorns, infesting those waters; for you cannot shoot at them successfully from the deck, owing to the resistance of the water, but to shoot down on them is a very different thing. Now, it was plainly a labor of love for Captain Sleet to describe, as he does, all the little detailed conveniences of his crow's-nest. But though he enlarges on many of these, and though he treats us to a very scientific account of his experiments in this crow's-nest with a small compass he kept there to counteract the errors resulting from what is called the "local attraction" of all binnacle magnets — an error attributable to the horizontal nearness of the iron in the ship's planks, and, in the Glacier's case, perhaps to there having been so many broken-down blacksmiths among her crew — I say, though the Captain is very discreet and scientific here, yet for all his learned "binnacle deviations," "azimuth compass observations," and "approximate errors," he knows very well, Captain Sleet, that he was not so immersed in those profound magnetic meditations as not to be attracted now and then toward that well-replenished little case-bottle so nicely tucked in on one side of his crow's-nest, within easy reach of his hand. Though, on the whole, I greatly admire and even love the brave, the honest, and learned Captain, yet I take it very ill of him that he should so utterly ignore that case-bottle, seeing what a faithful friend and comforter it must have been while, with mittened fingers and hooded head, he was studying the mathematics up there in that bird's nest within three or four perches of the pole.

But if we southern whale-fishers aren't as snugly housed aloft as Captain Sleet and his Greenlandmen were, that disadvantage is greatly offset by the sharply contrasting serenity of those seductive seas where we mostly sail. For one, I used to lounge up the rigging quite leisurely, resting in the top for a chat with Queequeg or anyone else off duty I might find there. Then I'd climb a little higher, throw a lazy leg over the topsail yard, take a preliminary survey of the watery pastures, and at last reach my final destination.

Let me make a clean confession here and frankly admit that I kept a poor watch. With the problem of the universe revolving in my head, how could I — left completely alone at such a thought-provoking altitude — how could I take seriously my duty to observe all whale-ship standing orders: "Keep your weather eye open and sing out every time."

And let me here movingly warn you ship-owners of Nantucket! Beware of enlisting in your vigilant fisheries any lad with a lean brow and hollow eye, given to unseasonable meditation, who offers to ship with the Phaedon (Plato's dialogue on the immortality of the soul) instead of Bowditch (the standard navigation manual) in his head. Beware of such a one, I say: your whales must be seen before they can be killed, and this sunken-eyed young Platonist will tow you ten wakes around the world and never make you one pint of sperm the richer. Nor are these warnings at all unneeded. For nowadays the whale fishery provides an asylum for many romantic, melancholy, and absent-minded young men, disgusted with the gnawing cares of earth, and seeking sentiment in tar and blubber. Childe Harold not infrequently perches himself on the masthead of some luckless, disappointed whale ship, and in moody phrases exclaims:
"Roll on, thou deep and dark blue ocean, roll! Ten thousand blubber-hunters sweep over thee in vain."

Very often the captains of such ships scold these absent-minded young philosophers, criticizing them for not taking enough "interest" in the voyage — half-hinting that they are so hopelessly lost to all honorable ambition that they would secretly rather not see whales at all. But it's useless. These young Platonists have a theory that their vision is imperfect. They are nearsighted. What use, then, to strain their eyes? They've left their opera glasses at home.

"Why, you monkey," said a harpooner to one of these lads, "we've been cruising now hard on three years, and you haven't spotted a whale yet. Whales are as scarce as hen's teeth whenever you're up here." Perhaps they were. Or perhaps there might have been whole schools of them on the far horizon. But lulled into such an opium-like daze of vacant, unconscious daydreaming is this absent-minded youth — by the blending rhythm of waves and thoughts — that at last he loses his identity. He takes the mystic ocean at his feet for the visible image of that deep, blue, bottomless soul pervading all mankind and nature. Every strange, half-glimpsed, gliding, beautiful thing that escapes him, every dimly perceived rising fin of some unidentifiable form, seems to him the embodiment of those elusive thoughts that populate the soul by continually flitting through it. In this enchanted state, your spirit ebbs away to where it came from, becoming diffused through time and space, like Cranmer's sprinkled Pantheistic ashes, forming at last a part of every shore the round globe over.

There is no life in you now, except the rocking life given by a gently rolling ship — borrowed from the sea, and by the sea from the unfathomable tides of God. But while this sleep, this dream is upon you, move your foot or hand an inch — slip your grip even slightly — and your identity comes rushing back in horror. Over Descartian vortices you hover. And perhaps, at midday, in the fairest weather, with one half-strangled shriek you drop through that transparent air into the summer sea, never to rise again. Take heed, you Pantheists!

chapters.title: Chapter 36 — The Quarter-Deck
paragraphs: (Enter Ahab: Then, all.)

It was not long after the affair of the pipe that one morning shortly after breakfast, Ahab, as usual, climbed the cabin gangway to the deck. There most sea captains usually walk at that hour, the way country gentlemen take a turn in the garden after the same meal.

Soon his steady, ivory stride could be heard as he paced back and forth on his old rounds, over planks so familiar to his step that they were dented all over, like geological stones, with the distinctive marks of his walk. If you stared fixedly at his ribbed and dented brow, you would see still stranger footprints there — the footprints of his one sleepless, ever-pacing thought.

But on this particular occasion, those dents looked deeper, just as his nervous step that morning left a deeper mark. Ahab was so full of his thought that at every regular turn he made — now at the mainmast, now at the binnacle — you could almost see that thought turn inside him as he turned, and pace inside him as he paced. It possessed him so completely, in fact, that it all but seemed the inner mold of every outward movement.
"Do you notice him, Flask?" whispered Stubb. "The chick inside him is pecking at the shell. It'll be out soon."
The hours wore on — Ahab now shut up in his cabin, then pacing the deck again, with the same intense, fanatical purpose in his face.
The day was drawing to a close. Suddenly he stopped by the bulwarks, inserted his bone leg into the auger-hole there, and with one hand gripping a shroud, he ordered Starbuck to send everyone aft.
"Sir!" said the mate, astonished at an order seldom or never given on a ship except in some extraordinary situation.
"Send everybody aft," repeated Ahab. "Mastheads, there! Come down!"

When the entire ship's company was assembled and, with curious and somewhat uneasy faces, was watching him — for he looked not unlike the windward horizon when a storm is coming up — Ahab, after glancing quickly over the bulwarks and then darting his eyes among the crew, left his post. As though no one were near him, he resumed his heavy pacing across the deck. With bent head and half-slouched hat, he continued to pace, ignoring the wondering whispers among the men, until Stubb cautiously whispered to Flask that Ahab must have assembled them to witness some kind of walking performance. But this didn't last long. Pausing forcefully, he cried:
"What do you do when you see a whale, men?"
"Sing out for him!" was the instant answer from a score of voices in unison.
"Good!" cried Ahab, wild approval in his voice, as he watched the hearty excitement his unexpected question had so magnetically stirred in them.
"And what do you do next, men?"
"Lower away, and after him!"
"And what tune do you pull to, men?"
"A dead whale or a stove boat!"

Stranger and fiercer grew the glad, approving look on the old man's face with every shout. Meanwhile, the sailors began glancing curiously at each other, as if marveling at how they themselves had become so excited by such seemingly pointless questions.
But they were all eagerness again as Ahab, now half-revolving in his pivot-hole, one hand reaching high up a shroud and gripping it tightly, almost convulsively, addressed them:

"All you masthead-standers have already heard me give orders about a white whale. Look here! Do you see this Spanish gold ounce?" — holding up a broad, bright coin to the sun — "It's a sixteen-dollar piece, men. Do you see it? Mr. Starbuck, hand me that top-maul."

While the mate went for the hammer, Ahab, without speaking, slowly rubbed the gold piece against the skirts of his jacket, as if to heighten its shine. Without using any words, he hummed softly to himself, making a sound so strangely muffled and unclear that it seemed like the mechanical humming of the wheels of his vitality inside him.

Taking the top-maul from Starbuck, he advanced toward the mainmast with the hammer raised in one hand and the gold coin displayed in the other, and in a loud, raised voice he cried: "Whichever of you spots me a white-headed whale with a wrinkled brow and a crooked jaw — whichever of you spots me that white-headed whale with three holes punctured in his starboard fluke — look here, whichever of you spots me that same white whale, he shall have this gold ounce, my boys!"
"Hurrah! Hurrah!" cried the seamen, swinging their tarpaulin hats as they cheered the act of nailing the gold to the mast.
"It's a white whale, I say," Ahab continued, throwing down the hammer. "A white whale. Keep your eyes peeled for him, men. Watch for white water. If you see so much as a bubble, sing out."

All this time, Tashtego, Daggoo, and Queequeg had been watching with even more intense interest and surprise than the rest. At the mention of the wrinkled brow and crooked jaw, they had each started as if individually touched by some specific memory.
"Captain Ahab," said Tashtego, "that white whale must be the same one some call Moby Dick."
"Moby Dick?" shouted Ahab. "Do you know the white whale, then, Tash?"
"Does he spread his tail a little strangely, sir, before he dives?" said the Gay Header deliberately.
"And does he have an unusual spout, too," said Daggoo, "very bushy, even for a sperm whale, and very quick, Captain Ahab?"

"And he have one, two, three — oh! many many iron in him hide, too, Captain," cried Queequeg in his broken way, "all twiske-tee be-twisk, like him — him —" struggling for the word and screwing his hand round and round as if uncorking a bottle — "like him — him —"

"Corkscrew!" cried Ahab. "Yes, Queequeg, the harpoons lie all twisted and wrenched in him. Yes, Daggoo, his spout is a big one, like a whole sheaf of wheat, and white as a pile of our Nantucket wool after the great annual sheep-shearing. Yes, Tashtego, and he fans his tail like a split jib in a squall. Death and devils! Men, it is Moby Dick you have seen — Moby Dick — Moby Dick!"

"Captain Ahab," said Starbuck, who with Stubb and Flask had been watching his superior with growing surprise but now seemed struck by a thought that somewhat explained the wonder, "Captain Ahab, I have heard of Moby Dick — but it was not Moby Dick that took off your leg?"

"Who told you that?" cried Ahab. Then, pausing: "Yes, Starbuck. Yes, my hearties, all of you. It was Moby Dick that dismasted me. Moby Dick that brought me to this dead stump I stand on now. Yes, yes!" he shouted with a terrible, loud, animal sob, like that of a heart-stricken moose. "Yes, yes! It was that accursed white whale that razeed me — cut me down like a warship sheared of its upper deck — and made a poor peg-legged lubber of me forever and a day!" Then, throwing both arms wide, with measureless curses he shouted: "Yes, yes! And I'll chase him around the Cape of Good Hope, and around the Horn, and around the Norway Maelstrom, and around the flames of hell before I give him up. And this is what you have signed on for, men! To chase that white whale on both sides of land, and over all sides of earth, until he spouts black blood and rolls fin out. What do you say, men — will you splice hands on it now? I think you look brave."
"Yes! Yes!" shouted the harpooners and seamen, running closer to the excited old man. "A sharp eye for the white whale! A sharp lance for Moby Dick!"

"God bless you," he seemed to half sob and half shout. "God bless you, men. Steward! Go draw the great measure of grog. But what's this long face about, Mr. Starbuck? Won't you chase the white whale? Aren't you game for Moby Dick?"

"I'll face his crooked jaw, and the jaws of Death too, Captain Ahab, if it fairly comes in the way of the business we're here for. But I came here to hunt whales, not my commander's vengeance. How many barrels will your vengeance yield you, even if you get it, Captain Ahab? It won't fetch you much in our Nantucket market."

"Nantucket market! Ha! But come closer, Starbuck — you need to go a layer deeper. If money is to be the measure, man, and the accountants have computed their great counting-house, the globe, by girdling it with guineas, one to every three parts of an inch — then let me tell you that my vengeance will fetch a great premium here!"
"He strikes his chest," whispered Stubb. "What's that for? It seems to ring vast, but hollow."
"Vengeance on a dumb animal!" cried Starbuck. "That simply struck you from blindest instinct! Madness! To be enraged with a mindless creature, Captain Ahab, seems blasphemous."

"Listen again — the deeper layer. All visible things, man, are nothing but cardboard masks. But in each event — in the living act, the undeniable deed — there, some unknown but still reasoning thing puts forth the molded shape of its features from behind the unreasoning mask. If a man would strike, strike through the mask! How can the prisoner reach outside except by thrusting through the wall? To me, the white whale is that wall, shoved close against me. Sometimes I think there's nothing beyond it. But that's enough. He tasks me. He heaps me. I see in him outrageous strength, with an inscrutable malice giving it sinew. That inscrutable thing is chiefly what I hate. And whether the white whale is the agent or the principal, I will wreak that hate upon him. Don't talk to me of blasphemy, man — I'd strike the sun if it insulted me. For if the sun could do that, then I could do the other, since there is always a kind of fair play in this, with jealousy presiding over all creation. But not even that fair play is my master, man. Who is over me? Truth knows no boundaries. Take your eyes off me! More unbearable than a fiend's glare is a dull, stupid stare! So, so — you flush red and go pale. My heat has melted you into an angry glow. But listen, Starbuck — what is said in heat unsays itself. There are men from whom hot words are only a small indignity. I didn't mean to provoke you. Let it go. Look! See those Turkish cheeks of spotted tawny brown — living, breathing pictures painted by the sun. The pagan leopards — the heedless, unworshipping things that live and seek and give no reasons for the torrid life they feel! The crew, man, the crew! Aren't they one and all with Ahab in this matter of the whale? See Stubb — he laughs! See that Chilean — he snorts just thinking of it. Stand up against the general hurricane? Your one tossed sapling cannot, Starbuck! And what is it? Think about it. It's only helping to strike a fin — no great feat for Starbuck. What more is it? From this one poor hunt, then, the best lance out of all Nantucket will surely not hang back, when every common sailor has already grabbed a whetstone? Ah! Compulsions seize you — I see it! The wave lifts you! Speak — speak! Yes, yes! Your silence, then — that speaks for you. (Aside) Something shot from my flaring nostrils, and he has breathed it into his lungs. Starbuck is mine now. He cannot oppose me now without rebellion."
"God keep me! — keep us all!" murmured Starbuck, quietly.

But in his joy at the mate's enchanted, silent consent, Ahab did not hear his ominous prayer. Nor the low laugh from the hold. Nor the foreboding vibrations of the wind in the rigging. Nor the hollow flap of the sails against the masts, as for a moment their hearts sank in. For again Starbuck's downcast eyes lit up with the stubbornness of life. The subterranean laugh died away. The winds blew on. The sails filled out. The ship heaved and rolled as before. Ah, you warnings and omens! Why don't you stay when you come? But rather than warnings, you are predictions — you shadows! Yet not so much predictions from outside as confirmations of what was already inside. For with little to restrain us from without, the deepest necessities within our being still drive us on.
"The measure! The measure!" cried Ahab.

Receiving the brimming pewter mug and turning to the harpooners, he ordered them to produce their weapons. Then, lining them up before him near the capstan with their harpoons in hand, while his three mates stood at his side with their lances and the rest of the crew formed a circle around the group, he stood for a moment searching every man's face. Those wild eyes met his the way the bloodshot eyes of prairie wolves meet the eye of their leader before he rushes ahead of the pack on the trail of the buffalo — but alas, only to fall into the hidden trap of the Indian.

"Drink and pass!" he cried, handing the heavy, full flagon to the nearest seaman. "The crew alone drinks now. Pass it round! Short sips — long swallows, men. It's hot as Satan's hoof. Good, good — it goes round well. It spirals into you. It forks out at the serpent-snapping eye. Well done — nearly drained. That way it went, this way it comes. Hand it back — here's a hollow! Men, you are like the years: brimming life is gulped and gone. Steward, refill!"

"Listen now, my brave ones. I have gathered you all around this capstan. You mates, flank me with your lances. You harpooners, stand there with your irons. And you, stout sailors, ring me in, so I may in some fashion revive a noble custom of my fisherman fathers before me. O men, you will yet see that — Ha! Boy, back already? Bad pennies don't come back any sooner. Hand it here. Why, now, this pewter would have run brimming again if you weren't such a St. Vitus' imp — away with you, you shaking fever!"

"Advance, you mates! Cross your lances before me. Good! Let me touch the center." So saying, with extended arm he grasped the three level, radiating lances at their crossed center point. As he did so, he suddenly and nervously twitched them, meanwhile looking intently from Starbuck to Stubb, from Stubb to Flask. It seemed as though by some nameless, inner force of will, he wanted to shock into them the same fiery emotion stored in the Leyden jar of his own magnetic life. The three mates quailed before his strong, sustained, mystic presence. Stubb and Flask looked sideways away from him. The honest eye of Starbuck fell straight to the deck.

"In vain!" cried Ahab. "But maybe that's for the best. For if you three had once taken the full-forced shock, then my own electric thing might perhaps have drained out of me. Perhaps, too, it would have dropped you dead. Perhaps you don't need it. Lower lances! And now, you mates, I appoint you three cupbearers to my three pagan kinsmen there — those three most honorable gentlemen and noblemen, my valiant harpooners. You disdain the task? What — when the great Pope washes the feet of beggars, using his tiara for a water jug? Oh, my sweet cardinals! Your own condescension — that will bend you to it. I don't command you — you will it. Cut your lashings and draw the poles, you harpooners!"
Silently obeying the order, the three harpooners now stood holding the detached iron tips of their harpoons, about three feet long, barbs pointing up, before him.

"Don't stab me with that sharp steel! Tilt them — tilt them over! Don't you know the goblet end? Turn up the socket! Good, good. Now, you cupbearers, step forward. The irons! Take them. Hold them while I fill!" Then, slowly going from one officer to the next, he filled the harpoon sockets to the brim with the fiery liquor from the pewter.

"Now, three to three, you stand. Present the murderous chalices! Hand them over, you who are now partners in this unbreakable league. Ha! Starbuck! — but the deed is done! That ratifying sun now waits to set its seal on it. Drink, you harpooners! Drink and swear, you men who man the deadly whaleboat's bow — Death to Moby Dick! God hunt us all if we do not hunt Moby Dick to his death!" The long, barbed steel goblets were raised. To cries and curses against the white whale, the spirits were gulped down together with a hiss. Starbuck paled, turned, and shuddered. Once more, and finally, the refilled pewter went the rounds among the frenzied crew. Then, as he waved his free hand to them, they all dispersed, and Ahab retired to his cabin.

chapters.title: Chapter 37 — Sunset
paragraphs: The cabin, by the stern windows. Ahab sitting alone, gazing out.
I leave a white and troubled wake. Pale waters, paler cheeks, wherever I sail. The jealous waves swell sideways to swallow my track. Let them — but first I pass.

Out there, at the ever-brimming goblet's rim, the warm waves blush like wine. The golden brow plumbs the blue. The diver sun — slowly dived from noon — goes down. My soul mounts up! She tires of her endless hill. Is, then, the crown too heavy that I wear? This Iron Crown of Lombardy. Yet it is bright with many a gem. I, the wearer, cannot see its distant flashing — but I darkly feel that I wear something that dazzlingly confounds. It is iron — that I know — not gold. It is cracked, too — I feel it. The jagged edge chafes me so, my brain seems to beat against the solid metal. Yes, a steel skull, mine — the kind that needs no helmet in the most brain-battering fight!

Dry heat upon my brow? Oh! There was a time when the sunrise nobly stirred me and the sunset soothed. No more. This lovely light — it doesn't light me. All beauty is agony to me, since I can never enjoy it. Gifted with the high perception, I lack the low, enjoying power. Damned — most subtly and most cruelly! Damned in the midst of Paradise! Good night — good night! (Waving his hand, he moves from the window.)

It was not so hard a task. I expected to find at least one man stubborn, but my one geared circle fits into all their various wheels, and they revolve. Or, if you prefer, like so many anthills of gunpowder, they all stand before me — and I am their match. Oh, how hard! That to set others ablaze, the match itself must burn away! What I have dared, I have willed. And what I have willed, I will do! They think me mad — Starbuck does. But I am demonic. I am madness maddened! That wild madness that is calm only to comprehend itself! The prophecy said I would be dismembered — and yes! I lost this leg. I now prophesy that I will dismember my dismemberer. So let the prophet and the fulfiller be one. That's more than you great gods ever were. I laugh at you and hoot at you, you cricket-players, you boxers, you deaf Burkes and blinded Bendigoes! I will not say as schoolboys say to bullies: pick on someone your own size, don't pummel me! No — you've knocked me down, and I am up again. But you have run and hidden. Come out from behind your cotton bags! I have no long gun to reach you. Come, Ahab sends his compliments — come and see if you can swerve me. Swerve me? You cannot swerve me — or else you swerve yourselves! There, man has you. Swerve me? The path to my fixed purpose is laid with iron rails, and my soul is grooved to run on them. Over unsounded gorges, through the rifled hearts of mountains, under the beds of torrents, I rush unerringly! Nothing is an obstacle, nothing is an angle on the iron way!

chapters.title: Chapter 38 — Dusk
paragraphs: By the mainmast. Starbuck leaning against it.

My soul is more than matched — she's overpowered, and by a madman! What an unbearable sting, that sanity should lay down its arms on such a battlefield! But he drilled deep down and blasted all my reason out of me! I think I see his impious end, but I feel that I must help him reach it. Whether I will or not, the unspeakable thing has tied me to him, towing me with a cable I have no knife to cut. Horrible old man! "Who's above me?" he cries — yes, he would be a democrat to all above, but look how he lords it over all below! Oh! I can plainly see my miserable duty: to obey while rebelling, and worse still, to hate with a touch of pity! For in his eyes I read some terrible grief that would shrivel me up if I had it. Yet there is still hope. Time and tide flow wide. The hated whale has the whole round watery world to swim in, as a small goldfish has its glass globe. His heaven-insulting purpose — God may push it aside. I would take heart, if my heart were not like lead. But my whole clock has run down. My heart is the weight that controls everything, and I have no key to wind it again.
(A burst of revelry from the forecastle.)

Oh, God! To sail with such a heathen crew that have so little touch of human mothers in them! Whelped somewhere by the sharkish sea. The white whale is their demigorgon. Listen! Those infernal orgies! That revelry is forward. Notice the unbroken silence aft! It seems to me a picture of life. Out in front, through the sparkling sea, shoots the gay, embattled, bantering bow — but only to drag dark Ahab after it, where he broods inside his cabin at the stern, built over the dead water of the wake, and further on, hunted by its wolfish gurglings. The long howl thrills me through! Quiet, you revelers, and set the watch! Oh, life! It is in an hour like this, with the soul beaten down and held to knowledge — as wild, untamed creatures are forced to feed — oh, life! It is now that I feel the hidden horror in you! But it is not me! That horror is outside of me! And with the soft human feeling still in me, I will try to fight you, grim phantom futures! Stand by me, hold me, bind me, O you blessed influences!

chapters.title: Chapter 39 — First Night-Watch
paragraphs: Fore-Top.
(Stubb alone, mending a brace.)

Ha! Ha! Ha! Ha! Ahem! Let me clear my throat! I've been thinking about it ever since, and that ha, ha is the final conclusion. Why? Because a laugh is the wisest, easiest answer to everything that's strange. And come what may, one comfort always remains — that unfailing comfort is, it's all predestined. I didn't hear all his talk with Starbuck, but to my poor eye, Starbuck looked then something like the way I felt the other evening. You can be sure the old Mogul has got him, too. I caught on, I knew it — if I'd had the gift, I could easily have prophesied it — because when I clapped my eye on his skull, I saw it. Well, Stubb, wise Stubb — that's my title — well, Stubb, what of it, Stubb? Here's a carcass. I don't know all that may be coming, but whatever it is, I'll go to meet it laughing. What a mischievous leer lurks in all your horrors! I feel funny. Fa, la! Lirra, skirra! What's my juicy little pear at home doing now? Crying its eyes out? Giving a party for the latest harpooners to arrive, I'd wager, as cheerful as a frigate's pennant, and so am I — fa, la! Lirra, skirra! Oh —
We'll drink tonight with hearts as light, To love, as gay and fleeting As bubbles that swim on the beaker's brim, And break on the lips while meeting.
A brave song that — who calls? Mr. Starbuck? Yes, yes, sir — (Aside) he's my superior, and he has his too, if I'm not mistaken. — Yes, yes, sir, just finishing this job — coming.

chapters.title: Chapter 40 — Midnight, Forecastle
paragraphs: HARPOONERS AND SAILORS.
(The foresail rises and reveals the watch standing, lounging, leaning, and lying in various positions, all singing in chorus.)
Farewell and goodbye to you, Spanish ladies! Farewell and goodbye to you, ladies of Spain! Our captain's commanded —
1ST NANTUCKET SAILOR. Oh, boys, don't be sentimental — it's bad for the digestion! Take a tonic, follow me!
(Sings, and all follow.)

Our captain stood upon the deck, A spyglass in his hand, Surveying those gallant whales That blew at every strand. Oh, your tubs in your boats, my boys, And by your braces stand, And we'll have one of those fine whales, Hand, boys, over hand! So, be cheery, my lads! May your hearts never fail! While the bold harpooner is striking the whale!
MATE'S VOICE FROM THE QUARTER-DECK. Eight bells there, forward!

2ND NANTUCKET SAILOR. Stop the chorus! Eight bells there! Do you hear, bell-boy? Strike the bell eight, you Pip! You blackling! And let me call the watch. I've got the right kind of mouth for that — the hogshead mouth. So, so — (Thrusts his head down the hatch.) Star-bo-l-e-e-n-s, a-h-o-y! Eight bells there below! Tumble up!

DUTCH SAILOR. Great sleeping tonight, mate — a fat night for it. I notice this about our old Mogul's wine: it deadens some just as much as it livens up others. We sing, they sleep — yes, lying down there like the bottom tier of casks in the hold. At them again! Here, take this copper pump and hail them through it. Tell them to stop dreaming about their girls. Tell them it's the resurrection — they must give their last kiss and come to judgment. That's the way — that's it! Your throat hasn't been ruined by eating Amsterdam butter.

FRENCH SAILOR. Listen, boys! Let's have a jig or two before we anchor in Blanket Bay. What do you say? Here comes the other watch. Everybody on your feet! Pip! Little Pip! Come on with your tambourine!
PIP. (Sulky and sleepy.) Don't know where it is.

FRENCH SAILOR. Beat your belly, then, and flap your ears. Dance, men, I say! Merry's the word — hurrah! Damn me, won't you dance? Line up, Indian file, and gallop into the double-shuffle! Throw yourselves into it! Legs! Legs!
ICELAND SAILOR. I don't like your floor, mate — it's too springy for my taste. I'm used to ice floors. I'm sorry to throw cold water on the subject, but excuse me.
MALTESE SAILOR. Me too. Where are your girls? Who but a fool would take his own left hand in his right and say, 'How do you do?' Partners! I need partners!
SICILIAN SAILOR. That's right — girls and a green lawn! Then I'll dance with you — yes, I'll leap like a grasshopper!
LONG-ISLAND SAILOR. Well, well, you sulkers, there's plenty more of us. Hoe corn while you can, I say. All legs go to the harvest soon enough. Ah! Here comes the music — now for it!

AZORE SAILOR. (Climbing up and tossing the tambourine through the hatch.) Here you go, Pip — and there's the windlass post. Climb up! Now, boys! (Half of them dance to the tambourine; some go below; some sleep or lie among the coils of rigging. Plenty of cursing.)
AZORE SAILOR. (Dancing.) Go it, Pip! Bang it, bell-boy! Rig it, dig it, stig it, quig it, bell-boy! Make fireflies! Break the jinglers!
PIP. Jinglers, you say? There goes another one — fell off. I'm pounding it too hard.
CHINA SAILOR. Rattle your teeth, then, and keep pounding — make a pagoda of yourself.
FRENCH SAILOR. Wild and merry! Hold up your hoop, Pip, so I can jump through it! Split jibs! Tear yourselves!
TASHTEGO. (Quietly smoking.) That's a white man for you. He calls that fun. Humph! I'll save my sweat.

OLD MANX SAILOR. I wonder whether those cheerful lads realize what they're dancing over. 'I'll dance over your grave, I will' — that's the bitterest threat of your night-women, the ones who beat headwinds around corners. O Christ! To think of the green navies and the green-skulled crews! Well, well — maybe the whole world is a ball, as you scholars have it, and so it's only right to make one ballroom of it. Dance on, lads — you're young. I was once.
3RD NANTUCKET SAILOR. Break time! Whew! This is harder work than rowing after whales in a calm. Give us a puff, Tash.
(They stop dancing and gather in groups. Meanwhile, the sky darkens — the wind rises.)
LASCAR SAILOR. By Brahma! Boys, it'll be time to douse sail soon. The heaven-born, high-tide Ganges has turned to wind! You show your black brow, Seeva!

MALTESE SAILOR. (Reclining and shaking his cap.) It's the waves — the whitecaps are dancing now. They'll shake their tassels soon. If only all the waves were women — then I'd gladly go drown, and dance with them forever! There's nothing so sweet on earth — heaven itself can't match it — as those swift glances from warm, wild women's bosoms in the dance, when their arching arms hide such ripe, bursting grapes.

SICILIAN SAILOR. (Reclining.) Don't tell me about it! Listen, lad — fleet interlacings of the limbs — lithe swayings — coyings — flutterings! Lip! Heart! Hip! All graze: unceasing touch and go! Not a taste, mind you, or else satiety sets in. Eh, Pagan? (Nudging.)

TAHITIAN SAILOR. (Reclining on a mat.) Hail, holy nakedness of our dancing girls — the Heeva-Heeva! Ah, low-veiled, palm-crowned Tahiti! I still rest on your mat, but the soft earth has shifted! I saw you woven in the forest, my mat! Green the first day I carried you home; now worn and wilted. Ah me! Neither you nor I can bear the change! How would it be, then, if transplanted to that sky? Can I hear the roaring streams from Pirohitee's peak of spears, when they leap down the cliffs and drown the villages? — The blast! The blast! Up, spine, and face it! (Leaps to his feet.)
PORTUGUESE SAILOR. How the sea crashes against the hull! Stand by for reefing, lads! The winds are just crossing swords — soon they'll go lunging at each other.

DANISH SAILOR. Crack, crack, old ship! As long as you're cracking, you're holding! Well done! The mate keeps you to it firmly. He's no more afraid than the island fortress at Kattegat, built to fight the Baltic with storm-battered guns, crusted with sea salt!
4TH NANTUCKET SAILOR. He has his orders, mind you. I heard old Ahab tell him he must always kill a squall, the way you burst a waterspout with a pistol — fire your ship right into it!
ENGLISH SAILOR. Bloody hell, but that old man's a grand old fellow! We're the lads to hunt up his whale!
ALL. Yes! Yes!

OLD MANX SAILOR. How the three pines — the masts — shake! Pines are the hardest sort of tree to keep alive when moved to any other soil, and here there's none but the crew's cursed clay. Steady, helmsman! Steady. This is the sort of weather when brave hearts snap ashore, and keeled hulls split at sea. Our captain has his birthmark. Look there, boys — there's another one in the sky — lurid-like, you see, and all else pitch black.
DAGGOO. What of that? Whoever's afraid of black is afraid of me! I'm quarried out of it!

SPANISH SAILOR. (Aside.) He wants a fight, does he? The old grudge makes me touchy. (Stepping forward.) Yes, harpooner, your race is the undeniable dark side of mankind — devilishly dark, at that. No offense.
DAGGOO. (Grimly.) None.
ST. JAGO'S SAILOR. That Spaniard is either mad or drunk. But it can't be drink, or else in his one case our old Mogul's firewater is rather slow in working.
5TH NANTUCKET SAILOR. What's that I see — lightning? Yes.
SPANISH SAILOR. No. Daggoo showing his teeth.
DAGGOO. (Springing forward.) Swallow yours, runt! White skin, white liver!
SPANISH SAILOR. (Meeting him.) I'll carve you up! Big body, small soul!
ALL. A fight! A fight! A fight!
TASHTEGO. (Taking a puff.) A fight below and a fight aloft — gods and men, both brawlers! Humph!
BELFAST SAILOR. A fight! Arrah, a fight! The Virgin be blessed, a fight! Dive right in!
ENGLISH SAILOR. Fair play! Grab the Spaniard's knife! Make a ring, a ring!
OLD MANX SAILOR. Already formed — look! The ringed horizon. In that ring, Cain struck Abel. Sweet work, proper work! No? Then why, God, did you make the ring?
MATE'S VOICE FROM THE QUARTER-DECK. Hands to the halyards! Take in topgallant sails! Stand by to reef topsails!
ALL. The squall! The squall! Jump, my jollies! (They scatter.)

PIP. (Shrinking under the windlass.) Jollies? Lord help such jollies! Crish, crash! There goes the jib-stay! Blang-whang! God! Duck lower, Pip — here comes the royal yard! It's worse than being in the whirled woods on the last day of the year! Who'd go climbing after chestnuts now? But there they go, all cursing, and here I don't. Fine prospects to them — they're on the road to heaven. Hold on tight! Jiminy, what a squall! But those fellows there are worse yet — they are your white squalls, they are. White squalls? White whale, shh! Shh! Here I've heard all their talk just now, and the white whale — shh! Shh! — spoken of only once! And only this evening — it makes me jingle all over like my tambourine — that anaconda of an old man swore them in to hunt him! Oh, you big white God up there somewhere in that darkness, have mercy on this small black boy down here. Preserve him from all men who have no guts to feel fear!

chapters.title: Chapter 41 — Moby Dick
paragraphs: I, Ishmael, was one of that crew. My shouts had gone up with the rest. My oath had been welded with theirs. And I shouted louder and hammered my oath harder because of the dread in my soul. A wild, mystical, sympathetic feeling was in me. Ahab's unquenchable feud seemed like my own. With eager ears I learned the history of that murderous monster against whom I and all the others had sworn our oaths of violence and revenge.

For some time past, though only at intervals, the solitary, secluded White Whale had haunted those uncivilized seas mostly visited by the sperm whale hunters. But not all of them knew of his existence. Only a few, comparatively, had knowingly seen him, and the number who had actually and knowingly fought him was very small indeed. For many reasons — the large number of whale ships; the disorderly way they were scattered over the entire watery globe, many of them adventurously pushing their hunt along lonely latitudes, so that for a whole year or more at a stretch they might seldom or never meet a single sail of any sort that could tell them news; the extreme length of each voyage; the irregular times of sailing from home — all these, with other circumstances direct and indirect, had long prevented the specific news about Moby Dick as an individual from spreading through the whole worldwide whaling fleet. Several ships were reported to have encountered, at such and such a time or on such and such a meridian, a sperm whale of unusual size and malignity which, after doing great damage to its attackers, had completely escaped them; it could hardly be doubted — to some minds, I say, it was not an unfair assumption — that this whale must have been none other than Moby Dick. Yet since the sperm whale fishery had lately seen various and not infrequent instances of great ferocity, cunning, and malice in the whale under attack, those who by accident unknowingly fought Moby Dick were perhaps, for the most part, content to blame the peculiar terror he inspired more, as it were, on the dangers of the sperm whale fishery at large than on the individual cause. That, mostly, was how the disastrous encounter between Ahab and the whale had so far been popularly regarded.

As for those who had previously heard of the White Whale and then happened to see him — at first, almost every one of them had lowered for him as boldly and fearlessly as for any other sperm whale. But eventually, such catastrophes resulted from these attacks — not just sprained wrists and ankles, broken limbs, or devouring amputations, but fatalities of the deadliest kind — that these repeated, disastrous defeats, all piling their terrors onto Moby Dick, had gone far toward shaking the courage of many brave hunters who later heard the story of the White Whale.

Nor did wild rumors of all kinds fail to exaggerate the true accounts of these deadly encounters and make them still more horrifying. For not only do fantastic rumors naturally grow out of the very body of all surprising, terrible events, as a stricken tree gives birth to its fungi, but in life at sea, far more than on dry land, wild rumors abound wherever there is any adequate reality for them to cling to. And just as the sea surpasses the land in this respect, so the whale fishery surpasses every other kind of seafaring life in the wonder and fearfulness of the rumors that sometimes circulate there. For whalemen as a body are not exempt from the ignorance and superstition that all sailors inherit; but of all sailors, they are by far the most directly brought into contact with whatever is appallingly astonishing in the sea. Face to face they not only see its greatest marvels, but, hand to jaw, they fight them. Alone, in waters so remote that you could sail a thousand miles and pass a thousand shores without coming to a single chiseled hearthstone, or anything hospitable beneath that part of the sun — in such latitudes and longitudes, and pursuing such a calling as he does, the whaleman is wrapped in influences that all tend to make his imagination pregnant with many a mighty birth.

No wonder, then, that as the rumors of the White Whale kept gathering bulk from merely crossing the widest ocean spaces, they finally absorbed all manner of morbid hints and half-formed, fetal suggestions of supernatural forces, which in the end invested Moby Dick with new terrors borrowed from nothing that visibly appears. So in many cases he finally struck such a panic that, of those who had heard of the White Whale — through those rumors, at least — few of those hunters were willing to face the dangers of his jaw.

But there were still other, more vital practical influences at work. Even today, the original prestige of the sperm whale, as fearfully distinguished from all other species of leviathan, has not died out of the minds of whalemen as a body. There are those among them today who, though intelligent and brave enough to give battle to the Greenland or right whale, would perhaps — from lack of professional experience, or incompetence, or timidity — decline a contest with the sperm whale. At any rate, there are plenty of whalemen, especially among the whaling nations not sailing under the American flag, who have never met the sperm whale in battle, and whose only knowledge of the leviathan is limited to the ignoble monster originally hunted in the North. Seated on their hatches, these men will listen with a childlike fireside interest and awe to the wild, strange tales of southern whaling. And nowhere is the supreme tremendousness of the great sperm whale more deeply felt and understood than aboard the ships whose bows breast him.

And as if the now proven reality of his power had, in earlier legendary times, cast its shadow before it, we find some book naturalists — Olassen and Povelson — declaring the sperm whale not only to be a terror to every other creature in the sea but so incredibly ferocious as to be continually thirsting for human blood. Even as late as Cuvier's time, these or very similar impressions had not been erased. For in his Natural History, the Baron himself states that at the sight of the sperm whale, all fish (sharks included) are "struck with the most lively terrors," and "often in the precipitancy of their flight dash themselves against the rocks with such violence as to cause instantaneous death." And however much the general experience of the fishery may correct such reports, in their full terribleness — even down to Povelson's bloodthirsty detail — the superstitious belief in them is, in some turns of fortune in their calling, revived in the hunters' minds.

So, overawed by the rumors and portents concerning him, not a few of the fishermen recalled, in connection with Moby Dick, the earlier days of the sperm whale fishery, when it was often hard to persuade long-practiced right whalemen to embark on the perils of this new and daring warfare. Such men protested that although other leviathans might be pursued with hope of success, to chase and point a lance at such an apparition as the sperm whale was not for mortal man. To attempt it would inevitably mean being torn into a quick eternity. On this point, there are some remarkable documents that may be consulted.

Nevertheless, some there were who, even knowing all this, were ready to chase Moby Dick. And an even greater number, having only heard of him vaguely and at a distance, without specific details of any particular disaster and without the superstitious trappings, were tough enough not to flee from the fight if it came to them.

One of the wild ideas I mentioned, which eventually became linked with the White Whale in superstitious minds, was the eerie notion that Moby Dick was everywhere at once — that he had actually been encountered in opposite latitudes at the very same instant.

Nor, credulous as such minds must have been, was this idea altogether without some faint show of superstitious probability. For since the secrets of the ocean currents have never yet been revealed, even to the most learned research, the hidden ways of the sperm whale beneath the surface remain, in great part, unaccountable to his pursuers. From time to time they have given rise to the most curious and contradictory speculations, especially about the mystic means by which, after sounding to a great depth, he transports himself with such vast swiftness to the most widely distant points.

It is well known to both American and English whale ships, and was also placed on authoritative record years ago by Scoresby, that some whales captured far north in the Pacific have been found with the barbs of harpoons thrown in the Greenland seas still in their bodies. Nor can it be denied that in some of these cases it has been declared that the time between the two attacks could not have been very many days. Hence, by inference, some whalemen have believed that the Northwest Passage, so long a problem to man, was never a problem to the whale. So that here, in the real living experience of living men, the wonders told in old times of the inland Strello mountain in Portugal (near whose top there was said to be a lake in which the wrecks of ships floated up to the surface), and that still more wonderful story of the Arethusa fountain near Syracuse (whose waters were believed to have come from the Holy Land by an underground passage) — these fabulous tales are almost fully equaled by the realities of the whalemen.

Forced into familiarity with such wonders, then, and knowing that after repeated, fearless attacks the White Whale had escaped alive, it can hardly be surprising that some whalemen went still further in their superstitions. They declared Moby Dick not only everywhere at once but immortal (for immortality is only being everywhere in time). Though groves of spears should be planted in his flanks, he would still swim away unharmed. Or if indeed he should ever be made to spout thick blood, that sight would be only a ghastly deception. For again, in unbloodied waves hundreds of leagues away, his unstained spout would be seen once more.

But even stripped of these supernatural rumors, there was enough in the earthly reality and undeniable character of the monster to strike the imagination with extraordinary power. It was not so much his uncommon size that distinguished him from other sperm whales, but — as mentioned elsewhere — a peculiar snow-white, wrinkled forehead and a high, pyramid-shaped white hump. These were his prominent features, the marks by which, even in the limitless, uncharted seas, he revealed his identity at a great distance to those who knew him.

The rest of his body was so streaked, spotted, and marbled with the same ghostly hue that he had earned his distinctive name of the White Whale. A name literally justified by his vivid appearance when seen gliding at high noon through a dark blue sea, leaving a milky-way wake of creamy foam, all sparkling with golden gleams.

It was not his unusual size, nor his remarkable color, nor even his deformed lower jaw that invested the whale with such natural terror, but rather an unprecedented, intelligent malice that, according to specific accounts, he had displayed over and over in his attacks. Most of all, his treacherous retreats struck more fear than perhaps anything else. For when swimming ahead of his triumphant pursuers, showing every sign of alarm, he had been known several times to turn around suddenly and, bearing down on them, either smash their boats to splinters or drive them back in panic to their ship.

Several deaths had already attended his chase. Though similar disasters, however little talked about on shore, were by no means unusual in the fishery, in most cases the White Whale's ferocity seemed so infernal and premeditated that every maiming or death he caused was not wholly regarded as the work of an unintelligent agent.

Judge, then, what heights of inflamed, frantic fury the minds of his more desperate hunters were driven to when, among the splinters of chewed-up boats and the sinking limbs of torn-apart comrades, they swam out of the white curds of the whale's terrible wrath into the calm, infuriating sunlight, which went on smiling as if at a birth or a wedding.

His three boats stove in around him, and oars and men both whirling in the eddies, one captain had seized the line-knife from his broken bow and dashed at the whale like an Arkansas duelist at his enemy, blindly trying with a six-inch blade to reach the fathom-deep life of the whale. That captain was Ahab. And then it was that Moby Dick, suddenly sweeping his sickle-shaped lower jaw beneath him, reaped away Ahab's leg as a mower cuts a blade of grass in the field. No turbaned Turk, no hired Venetian or Malay, could have struck him with more apparent malice. There was little reason to doubt, then, that ever since that nearly fatal encounter, Ahab had nursed a wild vindictiveness against the whale — all the more deadly because in his frantic morbidness he at last came to identify with him not only all his bodily woes but all his intellectual and spiritual torments. The White Whale swam before him as the monomaniac incarnation of all those malicious forces that some deep men feel eating away inside them, until they are left living on with half a heart and half a lung. That intangible malignity which has existed from the beginning — to whose rule even modern Christians assign one half of the worlds, and which the ancient Ophites of the East revered in their statue devil — Ahab did not fall down and worship it as they did. Instead, deliriously transferring its idea to the hated white whale, he pitted himself, all mutilated, against it. All that most maddens and torments, all that stirs up the dregs of things, all truth with malice in it, all that cracks the sinews and cakes the brain, all the subtle demonisms of life and thought — all evil, to crazy Ahab, was visibly personified and made practically assailable in Moby Dick. He piled upon the whale's white hump the sum of all the general rage and hate felt by his whole race from Adam down. And then, as if his chest had been a mortar, he burst his hot heart's shell upon it.

It is not probable that this monomania in him arose at the precise moment of his bodily dismemberment. Then, in darting at the monster, knife in hand, he had only given way to a sudden, passionate, physical animosity. And when he received the stroke that tore him, he probably felt only the agonizing bodily laceration, and nothing more. Yet when, forced by this collision to turn toward home, Ahab and anguish lay stretched together in one hammock for long months of days and weeks, rounding in midwinter that dreary, howling Patagonian Cape — then it was that his torn body and gashed soul bled into one another, and, so mingling, made him mad. That it was only then, on the homeward voyage after the encounter, that the final monomania seized him seems all but certain from the fact that at intervals during the passage he was a raving lunatic. And though he had lost a leg, such vital strength still lurked in his Egyptian chest, further intensified by his delirium, that his mates were forced to lash him fast, even there, as he sailed, raving in his hammock. In a straitjacket he swung to the mad rocking of the gales. And when, running into more bearable latitudes, the ship floated across the tranquil tropics with mild studding sails spread, and to all appearances the old man's delirium seemed left behind him with the Cape Horn swells, and he came out of his dark den into the blessed light and air — even then, when he showed that firm, collected face, however pale, and gave his calm orders once again, and his mates thanked God the dreadful madness was now gone — even then, Ahab, in his hidden self, raved on. Human madness is often a cunning and most catlike thing. When you think it has fled, it may only have been transfigured into some still subtler form. Ahab's full lunacy did not subside but contracted and deepened, like the undiminished Hudson when that noble Northman flows narrowly but unfathomably through the Highland gorge. And just as in his narrow-flowing monomania not one jot of Ahab's broad madness had been left behind, so in that broad madness not one jot of his great natural intellect had perished. What had been the living agent now became the living instrument. If such a violent figure of speech may stand, his special lunacy stormed his general sanity and carried it, and turned all its concentrated cannon on its own mad target. So far from having lost his strength, Ahab, for that one end, now possessed a thousand times more power than he had ever sanely brought to bear on any one reasonable object.

This is much; yet Ahab's larger, darker, deeper part remains not even hinted at. But it is vain to popularize profundities, and all truth is profound. Winding far down from within the very heart of this spiked Hotel de Cluny where we now stand — however grand and wonderful, leave it now — take your way, you nobler, sadder souls, to those vast Roman halls of the Thermes (the ancient baths beneath it), where far below the fantastic towers of man's upper earth, his root of grandeur, his whole awful essence sits in bearded state: an antique buried beneath antiquities, and throned on torsos! So, with a broken throne, the great gods mock that captive king; so, like a Caryatid (a carved figure serving as a column), he sits patiently, holding up on his frozen brow the piled entablatures of ages. Wind your way down there, you prouder, sadder souls! Question that proud, sad king! A family likeness! Yes, he begat you, you young exiled royalties; and from your grim father alone will the old state secret come.

Now, in his heart, Ahab had some glimpse of this — namely: all my means are sane, my motive and my object mad. Yet without power to kill, change, or escape the fact, he also knew that he had long been deceiving mankind about it — and in some ways still was. But his deception was only subject to his awareness, not to his deliberate will. Nevertheless, he succeeded so well in it that when he stepped ashore on his ivory leg at last, no Nantucketer thought him anything other than naturally grief-stricken, and deeply so, by the terrible accident that had befallen him.

The reports of his undeniable delirium at sea were likewise popularly put down to a related cause. And so too was all the added moodiness that always afterward, right up to the day of sailing in the Pequod on the present voyage, sat brooding on his brow. And it is not so very unlikely that, far from doubting his fitness for another whaling voyage because of such dark symptoms, the calculating people of that prudent island were inclined to entertain the notion that for those very reasons he was all the better qualified and set on edge for a pursuit so full of rage and wildness as the bloody hunt of whales. Gnawed within and scorched without by the fixed, unrelenting fangs of some incurable idea — such a man, if he could be found, would seem the very man to dart his iron and lift his lance against the most appalling of all brutes. Or, if for any reason he were thought physically unfit for that, such a man would seem supremely qualified to cheer and howl his underlings on to the attack. But be all this as it may, this much is certain: with the mad secret of his unabated rage bolted up and locked inside him, Ahab had deliberately sailed on the present voyage with the one sole, all-consuming object of hunting the White Whale. Had any one of his old acquaintances on shore even half dreamed of what was lurking in him then, how quickly their aghast and righteous souls would have wrenched the ship from such a fiendish man! They were bent on profitable cruises, the profit to be counted down in dollars from the mint. He was intent on an audacious, implacable, and supernatural revenge.

Here, then, was this gray-headed, ungodly old man, chasing with curses a Job's whale around the world, at the head of a crew, too, made up chiefly of mongrel renegades, and castaways, and cannibals — a crew morally weakened as well by the helplessness of mere unaided virtue or right-mindedness in Starbuck, the invulnerable jollity of indifference and recklessness in Stubb, and the pervading mediocrity in Flask. Such a crew, so officered, seemed specially picked and packed by some infernal fate to help him to his monomaniac revenge. How it was that they responded so abundantly to the old man's fury — by what evil magic their souls were possessed, so that at times his hate seemed almost theirs, and the White Whale as much their unbearable enemy as his — how all this came to be — what the White Whale was to them, or how, to their unconscious understandings as well, in some dim, unsuspected way, he might have seemed the gliding great demon of the seas of life — to explain all this would be to dive deeper than Ishmael can go. The subterranean miner that works in all of us — how can anyone tell where his shaft leads by the ever-shifting, muffled sound of his pick? Who does not feel the irresistible arm drag? What skiff in tow of a seventy-four (a seventy-four-gun ship of the line) can stand still? For my part, I gave myself up to the abandon of the time and the place. But while still all in a rush to encounter the whale, I could see nothing in that brute but the deadliest ill.

chapters.title: Chapter 42 — The Whiteness of the Whale
paragraphs: What the white whale meant to Ahab has been hinted at. What he was to me, at times, remains unsaid.

Beyond the more obvious fears that Moby Dick could stir in any man's soul, there was another thought — or rather a vague, nameless horror about him — that sometimes overpowered everything else with its intensity. Yet it was so mystical, so nearly impossible to put into words, that I almost despair of making it comprehensible. It was the whiteness of the whale that appalled me above all things. But how can I hope to explain myself here? And yet, in some dim, fumbling way, explain myself I must, or all these chapters will have been for nothing.

In many natural objects, whiteness refines and enhances beauty, as if imparting some special virtue of its own — as in marbles, japonicas, and pearls. Various nations have in some way recognized a certain royal preeminence in this color. The barbaric, grand old kings of Pegu placed the title "Lord of the White Elephants" above all their other grandiloquent titles of dominion. The modern kings of Siam unfurled the same snow-white animal on their royal standard. The Hanoverian flag bore the single figure of a snow-white charger. The great Austrian Empire, Caesarian, heir to overlording Rome, took the same imperial hue for its imperial color. This preeminence applies to the human race itself, giving the white man ideal mastership over every dusky tribe. Beyond all this, whiteness has even been made a sign of gladness — among the Romans, a white stone marked a joyful day. In other human sympathies and symbols, this same color is made the emblem of many touching, noble things: the innocence of brides, the kindliness of old age. Among the Red Men of America, the gift of the white belt of wampum was the deepest pledge of honor. In many lands, whiteness represents the majesty of Justice in the judge's ermine, and adds to the daily grandeur of kings and queens drawn by milk-white steeds. Even in the higher mysteries of the most august religions, it has been made the symbol of divine spotlessness and power. The Persian fire worshippers held the white forked flame the holiest on the altar. In the Greek mythologies, great Jove himself was made incarnate in a snow-white bull. Among the noble Iroquois, the midwinter sacrifice of the sacred White Dog was by far the holiest festival of their theology — that spotless, faithful creature being held the purest envoy they could send to the Great Spirit with the yearly news of their own faithfulness. Directly from the Latin word for white, all Christian priests derive the name of one part of their sacred vestments — the alb, or tunic, worn beneath the cassock. Among the holy ceremonies of the Romish faith, white is specially used in celebrating the Passion of our Lord. In the Vision of St. John, white robes are given to the redeemed, and the twenty-four elders stand clothed in white before the great white throne, and the Holy One who sits there is white like wool. Yet for all these accumulated associations with whatever is sweet, honorable, and sublime, there still lurks something elusive in the innermost idea of this color that strikes more panic into the soul than the redness that frightens us in blood.

It is this elusive quality that causes the thought of whiteness, when separated from kinder associations and joined to any object terrible in itself, to heighten that terror to its furthest limits. Consider the white bear of the poles and the white shark of the tropics. What but their smooth, flaky whiteness makes them the transcendent horrors they are? It is that ghastly whiteness that gives such an abhorrent mildness, even more loathsome than terrifying, to the dumb gloating of their look. So that not even the fierce-fanged tiger in his heraldic coat can so stagger courage as the white-shrouded bear or shark.*

*With reference to the polar bear, it may possibly be argued by anyone who would like to go still deeper into this matter that it is not the whiteness, considered by itself, that heightens the intolerable hideousness of that beast. For, analyzed, that heightened hideousness, it might be said, only arises from the fact that the irresponsible ferociousness of the creature is dressed in the fleece of heavenly innocence and love; and so, by bringing together two such opposite emotions in our minds, the polar bear frightens us with so unnatural a contrast. But even assuming all this to be true, if it were not for the whiteness, you would not have that intensified terror.

As for the white shark, the white gliding ghostliness of that creature at rest, when seen in its ordinary moods, strangely matches the same quality in the polar quadruped. The French hit off this peculiarity most vividly in the name they give that fish. The Romish mass for the dead begins with "Requiem eternam" (eternal rest), from which "Requiem" names the mass itself and any other funeral music. Now, in allusion to the white, silent stillness of death in this shark, and the mild deadliness of his habits, the French call him Requin.

Think of the albatross. Where do those clouds of spiritual wonder and pale dread come from, in which that white phantom sails in every imagination? It was not Coleridge who first cast that spell, but God's great, unflattering poet laureate, Nature.*

*I remember the first albatross I ever saw. It was during a prolonged gale, in waters close to the Antarctic seas. From my morning watch below, I climbed up to the overclouded deck. There, dashed down upon the main hatches, I saw a regal, feathery thing of unspotted whiteness, with a hooked, Roman bill, sublime. At intervals it arched out its vast archangel wings, as if to embrace some holy ark. Wondrous flutterings and throbbings shook it. Though its body was unharmed, it uttered cries like some king's ghost in supernatural distress. Through its inexpressible, strange eyes, I thought I peered into secrets that took hold of God. Like Abraham before the angels, I bowed myself. The white thing was so white, its wings so wide, and in those forever-exiled waters I had lost the miserable, warping memories of traditions and of towns. Long I gazed at that prodigy of plumage. I cannot tell — I can only hint at — the things that darted through me then. But at last I came to myself, and turning, asked a sailor what bird this was. A goney, he replied. Goney! I had never heard that name before. Is it conceivable that this glorious thing is utterly unknown to men ashore? Never! But some time afterward I learned that "goney" was a seaman's name for the albatross. So by no possibility could Coleridge's wild Rhyme have had anything to do with those mystical impressions of mine when I saw that bird on our deck. For I had not then read the Rhyme, nor did I know the bird to be an albatross. Yet in saying this, I only indirectly polish a little brighter the noble merit of the poem and the poet.

I maintain, then, that the secret of the spell lurks chiefly in the bird's wondrous bodily whiteness. This truth is all the more evident from the fact that, by a contradiction in terms, there are birds called gray albatrosses. These I have often seen, but never with such emotions as when I beheld the Antarctic fowl.

But how had the mystic thing been caught? Don't breathe a word, and I will tell you: with a treacherous hook and line, as the bird floated on the sea. At last the Captain made a postman of it, tying a lettered leather tag around its neck with the ship's time and place, and then letting it escape. But I have no doubt that the leather tag, meant for man, was taken off in Heaven, when the white bird flew up to join the wing-folding, the invoking, and adoring cherubim!

Most famous in our Western annals and Indian traditions is the White Steed of the Prairies — a magnificent milk-white charger, large-eyed, small-headed, broad-chested, with the dignity of a thousand monarchs in his lofty, scornful bearing. He was the elected Xerxes of vast herds of wild horses, whose pastures in those days were fenced only by the Rocky Mountains and the Alleghenies. At their flaming head he trooped westward like that chosen star which every evening leads on the hosts of light. The flashing cascade of his mane and the curving comet of his tail decked him in trappings more resplendent than gold- and silver-beaters could have furnished. He was a most imperial and archangelic apparition of that unfallen western world, which to the eyes of the old trappers and hunters revived the glories of those primeval times when Adam walked majestic as a god, bluff-browed and fearless as this mighty steed. Whether marching among his aides and marshals at the front of countless columns that streamed endlessly over the plains like an Ohio, or whether, with his subjects browsing all around him to the horizon, he reviewed them at a gallop, his warm nostrils reddening through his cool milkiness — in whatever aspect he presented himself, he was always an object of trembling reverence and awe to the bravest Indians. Nor can it be questioned, from what stands on legendary record of this noble horse, that it was chiefly his spiritual whiteness that so clothed him with divineness; and that this divineness had something in it which, though commanding worship, at the same time enforced a certain nameless terror.
But there are other cases where whiteness loses all that added strange glory it possesses in the White Steed and the Albatross.

What is it about the albino man that so particularly repels and often shocks the eye, so that he is sometimes despised by his own family? It is the whiteness that covers him, the very thing expressed by his name. The albino is as well-built as other men — he has no real deformity — and yet this all-pervading whiteness makes him more strangely hideous than the ugliest abortion (a misshapen, monstrous birth). Why should this be?

Nor, in quite different aspects, does Nature, in her least tangible but no less malicious workings, fail to enlist this crowning attribute of the terrible among her forces. From its snowy appearance, the gauntleted ghost of the Southern Seas has been named the White Squall. Nor, in some historical cases, has the art of human malice left out so potent an ally. How wildly it heightens the effect of that passage in Froissart, when, masked in the snowy symbol of their faction, the desperate White Hoods of Ghent murder their bailiff in the marketplace!

In certain things, the common inherited experience of all humanity bears witness to the supernatural quality of this color. It can hardly be doubted that the one visible quality in the appearance of the dead that most horrifies the viewer is the marble paleness lingering there — as if that pallor were as much the mark of terror in the next world as it is of mortal fear in this one. From the pallor of the dead, we borrow the color of the shroud we wrap them in. Even in our superstitions we throw the same snowy cloak around our ghosts — all phantoms rise in a milk-white fog. And while these terrors grip us, let us add that even the king of terrors himself, as portrayed by the evangelist, rides on a pale horse.

Therefore, whatever grand or gracious thing a person may symbolize through whiteness in other moods, no one can deny that in its deepest, most idealized meaning, it summons a peculiar specter to the soul.

But though this point is settled beyond dispute, how can any mortal account for it? To analyze it would seem impossible. Can we, then, by citing some of those cases where this thing of whiteness — though for the time mostly or entirely stripped of all direct associations that might lend it anything fearful — is nevertheless found to work the same spell on us, however modified, hope to stumble upon some clue that leads us to the hidden cause we seek?

Let's try. But in a matter like this, subtlety speaks to subtlety, and without imagination nobody can follow anyone else into these halls. And though no doubt at least some of the imaginative impressions I am about to present have been shared by most people, perhaps few were fully aware of them at the time, and so they may not be able to call them up now.

Why does the bare mention of Whitsuntide (the church season of Pentecost), to the man of untrained imagination who happens to be only loosely acquainted with the particular character of the day, marshal in his fancy such long, dreary, speechless processions of slow-pacing pilgrims, downcast and hooded with new-fallen snow? Or why, to the unread, unsophisticated Protestant of the Middle American States, does the passing mention of a White Friar or a White Nun call up such an eyeless statue in the soul?

Or what is it — apart from the traditions of dungeoned warriors and kings, which will not wholly account for it — that makes the White Tower of London strike the imagination of an untraveled American so much more strongly than those other storied structures, its neighbors, the Byward Tower, or even the Bloody Tower? And those sublimer towers, the White Mountains of New Hampshire — why, in certain moods, does such a gigantic ghostliness come over the soul at the bare mention of that name, while the thought of Virginia's Blue Ridge is full of a soft, dewy, distant dreaminess? Or why, regardless of all latitudes and longitudes, does the name of the White Sea cast such a spectral spell over the imagination, while that of the Yellow Sea lulls us with mortal thoughts of long, lacquered, mild afternoons on the waves, followed by the gaudiest yet sleepiest of sunsets? Or, to choose a wholly insubstantial example, addressed purely to the imagination, why, in reading the old fairy tales of Central Europe, does "the tall pale man" of the Harz forests, whose changeless pallor glides without a rustle through the green of the groves — why is this phantom more terrible than all the whooping imps of the Blocksberg?

It is not entirely the memory of her cathedral-toppling earthquakes, nor the stampedes of her frantic seas, nor the tearlessness of arid skies that never rain, nor the sight of her wide field of leaning spires, wrenched copestones, and crosses all adroop (like the tilted yards of anchored fleets), and her suburban avenues of house-walls lying over upon one another like a tossed pack of cards — it is not these things alone that make tearless Lima the strangest, saddest city you can see. For Lima has taken the white veil, and there is a higher horror in this whiteness of her woe. Old as Pizarro, this whiteness keeps her ruins forever new. It does not admit the cheerful greenness of complete decay. It spreads over her broken ramparts the rigid pallor of a stroke that fixes its own distortions.

I know that to ordinary perception, whiteness is not admitted to be the prime agent in heightening the terror of things already terrible. Nor does the unimaginative mind find any terror in those sights whose awfulness, to another mind, consists almost entirely in this one quality — especially when displayed in any form approaching silence or universality. What I mean by these two statements may perhaps be clarified by the following examples.

First: The sailor, when approaching foreign coasts, if he hears the roar of breakers at night, snaps to alertness and feels just enough fear to sharpen all his senses. But under exactly the same conditions, let him be called from his hammock to see his ship sailing through a midnight sea of milky whiteness — as if herds of combed white bears were swimming around him from encircling headlands — and he feels a silent, superstitious dread. The shrouded phantom of the whitened waters is as horrible to him as a real ghost. In vain the sounding lead assures him he is still in deep water. Heart and helm both fail him. He never rests until blue water is beneath him again. Yet where is the sailor who will tell you, "Sir, it was not so much the fear of hitting hidden rocks as the fear of that hideous whiteness that shook me"?

Second: To the native Indian of Peru, the continual sight of the snow-howdahed Andes (their peaks capped with snow like the canopied seat on an elephant's back) conveys nothing of dread, except perhaps in merely imagining the eternal frozen desolation that reigns at such vast heights, and the natural thought of how fearful it would be to lose oneself in such inhuman solitudes. Much the same is true of the backwoodsman of the West, who views with comparative indifference a boundless prairie sheeted with driven snow, with no shadow of tree or twig to break the fixed trance of whiteness. Not so the sailor, beholding the scenery of the Antarctic seas, where at times, by some infernal sleight of hand in the powers of frost and air, he — shivering and half shipwrecked — instead of seeing rainbows that speak hope and comfort to his misery, sees what looks like a boundless churchyard grinning at him with its lean ice monuments and splintered crosses.
But you say: "I think this white-lead chapter about whiteness is just a white flag hung out by a cowardly soul. You are giving in to a fit of the blues, Ishmael."

Tell me, then — why does a strong young colt, born in some peaceful Vermont valley, far from all predators — why is it that on the sunniest day, if you shake a fresh buffalo hide behind him so he cannot even see it but only smells its wild animal musk — why will he bolt, snort, and paw the ground in frenzy with bulging eyes? He has no memory of being attacked by wild creatures in his green northern home. The strange muskiness cannot remind him of any past danger. What does this New England colt know of the black bison herds of distant Oregon?

Nothing. But here you see, even in a speechless animal, the instinct of knowing the demonic forces in the world. Though thousands of miles from Oregon, when he smells that savage musk, the charging, goring bison herds are as real to him as they are to the abandoned wild foal on the prairies, which at this very moment they may be trampling into dust.

So it is: the muffled rollings of a milky sea, the bleak rustlings of the festooned frosts of mountains, the desolate shiftings of the windrowed snows of prairies — all these are to Ishmael what the shaking of that buffalo robe is to the frightened colt!

Neither of us knows where the nameless things lie of which the mystic sign gives such hints; yet for me, as for the colt, those things must exist somewhere. Though in many ways this visible world seems to have been made in love, the invisible spheres were made in fright.

But we have not yet solved the spell of this whiteness or learned why it appeals with such power to the soul.
