And stranger still, far more ominous — why, as we have seen, it is at once the most meaningful symbol of spiritual things, the very veil of the Christian's God, and yet at the same time the intensifying agent in things most appalling to humanity.

Is it that by its indefiniteness it shadows forth the heartless voids and immensities of the universe, and so stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation when we gaze into the white depths of the Milky Way? Or is it that whiteness, in its essence, is not so much a color as the visible absence of color, and at the same time the concrete of all colors? Is it for these reasons that there is such a dumb blankness, full of meaning, in a wide landscape of snows — a colorless all-color of atheism from which we shrink? And when we consider that other theory of the natural philosophers, that all other earthly hues — every stately or lovely emblazoning, the sweet tinges of sunset skies and woods, yes, and the gilded velvets of butterflies, and the butterfly cheeks of young girls — all these are only subtle deceits, not actually inherent in substances, but only laid on from outside; so that all deified Nature absolutely paints like the harlot, whose allurements cover nothing but the charnel-house within; and when we go further and consider that the mystical cosmetic that produces every one of her hues, the great principle of light, forever remains white or colorless in itself, and if it acted upon matter without a medium, would touch all objects, even tulips and roses, with its own blank tinge — pondering all this, the palsied universe lies before us a leper. And like willful travelers in Lapland who refuse to wear colored and coloring glasses over their eyes, so the wretched infidel gazes himself blind at the monumental white shroud that wraps the whole prospect around him. And of all these things the albino whale was the symbol. Do you wonder, then, at the fiery hunt?

chapters.title: Chapter 43 — Hark!
paragraphs: "PSST! Did you hear that noise, Cabaco?"

It was the middle watch, in fair moonlight. The seamen were standing in a line stretching from one of the freshwater casks in the waist to the scuttlebutt (the drinking-water cask) near the taffrail. In this way they passed the buckets along to fill the scuttlebutt. Standing, for the most part, on the sacred ground of the quarter-deck, they were careful not to speak or shuffle their feet. From hand to hand the buckets went in the deepest silence, broken only by the occasional flap of a sail and the steady hum of the ceaselessly advancing keel.
It was in the middle of this calm that Archy, one of the line, whose station was near the after-hatches, whispered the words above to the man next to him, a Cholo.
"Psst! Did you hear that noise, Cabaco?"
"Take the bucket, will you, Archy? What noise do you mean?"
"There it is again — under the hatches — don't you hear it — a cough — it sounded like a cough."
"Cough be damned! Pass along that return bucket."
"There again — there it is! — it sounds like two or three sleepers turning over!"
"Caramba! Knock it off, shipmate, will you? It's the three soaked biscuits you ate for supper turning over inside you — nothing else. Watch the bucket!"
"Say what you want, shipmate. I've got sharp ears."
"Right, you're the one, aren't you, who heard the hum of the old Quaker lady's knitting needles fifty miles at sea from Nantucket. You're the one."

"Grin away. We'll see what turns up. Listen, Cabaco — there is somebody down in the after-hold who has not yet been seen on deck. And I suspect our old Mogul knows something about it too. I heard Stubb tell Flask, one morning watch, that there was something of that sort in the wind."
"Nonsense! The bucket!"

chapters.title: Chapter 44 — The Chart
paragraphs: If you had followed Captain Ahab down into his cabin after the squall that took place the night after that wild ratification of his purpose with the crew, you would have seen him go to a locker in the stern, bring out a large wrinkled roll of yellowish sea charts, and spread them before him on his bolted-down table. Then, sitting down before them, you would have seen him intently studying the various lines and shadings that met his eye, and with slow but steady pencil tracing additional courses over spaces that had been blank before. At intervals he would refer to stacks of old log-books beside him, in which were set down the seasons and places where, on various past voyages of various ships, sperm whales had been captured or seen.

While he worked this way, the heavy pewter lamp suspended in chains overhead rocked constantly with the ship's motion, throwing shifting gleams and shadows of lines across his wrinkled brow. It almost seemed that while he himself was marking out lines and courses on the wrinkled charts, some invisible pencil was also tracing lines and courses upon the deeply marked chart of his forehead.

But it was not only on this particular night that Ahab pondered over his charts alone in his cabin. Almost every night they were brought out. Almost every night some pencil marks were erased and others substituted. For with the charts of all four oceans spread before him, Ahab was threading a maze of currents and eddies, all with a view to the more certain accomplishment of that monomaniac thought of his soul.

Now, to anyone not fully acquainted with the ways of the leviathans, it might seem an absurdly hopeless task to seek out one solitary creature in the boundless oceans of this planet. But not so to Ahab. He knew the patterns of all tides and currents. By calculating the drifting of the sperm whale's food, and by recalling the regular, established seasons for hunting him in particular latitudes, he could arrive at reasonable estimates — almost approaching certainty — about the most timely day to be on this or that ground in search of his prey.

So well established, in fact, is the sperm whale's periodic return to given waters that many hunters believe that, if he could be closely observed and studied throughout the world — if the logs for a single voyage of the entire whale fleet were carefully compared — then the migrations of the sperm whale would be found as unvarying as those of the herring shoals or the flights of swallows. On this hint, attempts have been made to construct elaborate migratory charts of the sperm whale.*

*Since I wrote the above, the statement has been happily confirmed by an official circular issued by Lieutenant Maury of the National Observatory, Washington, on April 16th, 1851. That circular shows that exactly such a chart is now being completed, and parts of it are presented in the circular. "This chart divides the ocean into districts of five degrees of latitude by five degrees of longitude; perpendicularly through each of which districts are twelve columns for the twelve months; and horizontally through each of which districts are three lines; one to show the number of days that have been spent in each month in every district, and the two others to show the number of days in which whales, sperm or right, have been seen."

Besides, when making a passage from one feeding-ground to another, the sperm whales — guided by some infallible instinct, or rather, let us say, by secret intelligence from the Deity — mostly swim in what are called veins. They continue their way along a given ocean-line with such undeviating exactness that no ship ever sailed her course, by any chart, with one tenth of such marvelous precision. In these cases the direction taken by any one whale may be as straight as a surveyor's parallel, and his line of advance may be strictly confined to its own unavoidable, straight wake; yet the arbitrary vein in which he is said to swim at these times generally takes in some few miles of width (more or less, as the vein is presumed to expand or contract), but never more than can be swept by the eye from the whale-ship's mastheads as she glides cautiously along this magic zone. The upshot is that at particular seasons, within that breadth and along that path, migrating whales may be looked for with great confidence.

And so, not only at known times, upon well-known separate feeding-grounds, could Ahab hope to encounter his prey. Even in crossing the widest expanses of water between those grounds, he could, by his skill, so position and time himself along the way as to still have some prospect of a meeting.

There was a circumstance that at first glance seemed to entangle his delirious but still methodical scheme. But perhaps it did not in reality. Though the gregarious sperm whales have their regular seasons for particular grounds, you generally cannot conclude that the herds that haunted such-and-such a latitude or longitude this year, say, will turn out to be identically the same as those found there the season before — though there are peculiar and unquestionable cases where the contrary has proved true. In general, the same remark applies, only within narrower limits, to the solitaries and hermits among the mature, aged sperm whales. So although Moby Dick had in a former year been seen, for example, on what is called the Seychelle ground in the Indian Ocean, or in Volcano Bay on the Japanese coast, it did not follow that if the Pequod visited either of those spots at any later corresponding season, she would infallibly meet him there. The same was true of some other feeding-grounds where he had at times shown himself. But all these seemed only his casual stopping-places and ocean-inns, so to speak, not his places of long residence. And where Ahab's chances of achieving his object have been spoken of so far, the reference has only been to whatever wayside, preliminary, extra prospects were his before a particular fixed time or place was reached — when all possibilities would become probabilities, and, as Ahab fondly thought, every possibility the next thing to a certainty. That particular time and place were joined in the one technical phrase: the Season-on-the-Line (the Line being the equator). For there and then, for several consecutive years, Moby Dick had been periodically sighted, lingering in those waters for a while, just as the sun in its annual round loiters for a predicted interval in any one sign of the Zodiac. It was there, too, that most of the deadly encounters with the white whale had taken place; there the very waves were storied with his deeds; there also was that tragic spot where the monomaniac old man had found the awful motive for his vengeance. But with the cautious thoroughness and unresting vigilance with which Ahab threw his brooding soul into this unfaltering hunt, he would not allow himself to rest all his hopes on the one crowning fact just mentioned, however flattering it might be to those hopes; nor, in the sleeplessness of his vow, could he so calm his unquiet heart as to put off all searching in the meantime.

Now, the Pequod had sailed from Nantucket at the very beginning of the Season-on-the-Line. No possible effort could have enabled her commander to make the great passage southward, round Cape Horn, and then, running down sixty degrees of latitude, arrive in the equatorial Pacific in time to cruise there. Therefore he had to wait for the next season. Yet the premature hour of the Pequod's sailing had perhaps been correctly chosen by Ahab with a view to this very state of things. For an interval of three hundred and sixty-five days and nights lay before him — an interval which, instead of enduring it impatiently ashore, he would spend in a miscellaneous hunt, in case the White Whale, spending his vacation in seas far from his periodical feeding-grounds, should by chance turn up his wrinkled brow off the Persian Gulf, or in the Bengal Bay, or the China Seas, or in any other waters haunted by his race. So Monsoons, Pampas, Nor'-Westers, Harmattans, Trades — any wind but the Levanter and the Simoon — might blow Moby Dick into the devious zigzag world-circle of the Pequod's circumnavigating wake.

But granting all this, if you regard it discreetly and coolly, does it not seem a mad idea — that in the broad, boundless ocean one solitary whale, even if encountered, should be thought capable of being individually recognized by his hunter, like a white-bearded Mufti in the crowded thoroughfares of Constantinople? Yes. For the peculiar snow-white brow of Moby Dick, and his snow-white hump, could not fail to be unmistakable. And haven't I tallied the whale's marks, Ahab would mutter to himself, as, after poring over his charts until long after midnight, he would throw himself back in reverie — tallied him, and shall he escape? His broad fins are bored, and scalloped out like a lost sheep's ear! And here his mad mind would run on in a breathless race, until a weariness and faintness of pondering came over him, and he would seek to recover his strength in the open air of the deck. Ah, God! what trances of torment that man endures who is consumed with one unachieved, revengeful desire. He sleeps with clenched hands, and wakes with his own bloody nails in his palms.

Often, when he was driven from his hammock by exhausting and intolerably vivid dreams of the night — dreams which took up his own intense thoughts of the day and carried them on amid a clash of frenzies, whirling them round and round and round in his blazing brain until the very throbbing of his life-spot became unbearable anguish — and when, as was sometimes the case, these spiritual throes heaved his being up from its foundations, and a chasm seemed to open in him, from which forked flames and lightnings shot up, and accursed fiends beckoned him to leap down among them — when this hell within him yawned beneath him, a wild cry would be heard through the ship, and with glaring eyes Ahab would burst from his stateroom, as though escaping from a bed that was on fire. Yet these outbursts, perhaps, instead of being the irrepressible symptoms of some hidden weakness, or of fright at his own resolve, were only the plainest signs of its intensity. For at such times crazy Ahab, the scheming, unappeasably steadfast hunter of the white whale — this Ahab who had gone to his hammock — was not the agent that made him burst from it again in horror. That agent was the eternal, living principle, or soul, in him; and in sleep, being for the time separated from the characterizing mind, which at other times used it as its outer vehicle or agent, it spontaneously sought to escape from the scorching nearness of the frantic thing of which, for the time, it was no longer an integral part. But since the mind does not exist unless joined with the soul, it must have been that in Ahab's case, as he yielded up all his thoughts and fancies to his one supreme purpose, that purpose, by the sheer stubbornness of its own will, forced itself, against gods and devils, into a kind of self-assumed, independent being of its own. Indeed, it could grimly live and burn while the common vitality to which it was joined fled horror-stricken from the unbidden and unfathered birth. Therefore the tormented spirit that glared out of bodily eyes, when what seemed Ahab rushed from his room, was for the time only an emptied thing, a formless sleepwalking being — a ray of living light, to be sure, but without an object to color, and therefore a blankness in itself. God help you, old man, your thoughts have created a creature in you; and he whose intense thinking thus makes him a Prometheus — a vulture feeds upon that heart forever; that vulture the very creature he creates.

chapters.title: Chapter 45 — The Affidavit
paragraphs: As far as this book may have a narrative — and also because it indirectly touches on one or two very interesting and curious details of the habits of sperm whales — the foregoing chapter, in its earlier part, is as important as any to be found in this volume. But its leading matter needs to be enlarged upon still further, and more familiarly, in order to be properly understood, and also to remove any disbelief that a profound ignorance of the entire subject may produce in some minds as to the natural truth of the main points of this affair.

I do not care to do this part methodically, but will be content to make my point through separate examples of things practically or reliably known to me as a whaleman. From these examples, I trust, the conclusion I aim at will follow naturally.

First: I have personally known three instances where a whale, after receiving a harpoon, has made a complete escape and, after an interval (in one instance of three years), has been struck again by the same hand and killed — when the two irons, both marked with the same private cipher, have been taken from the body. In the instance where three years passed between the throwing of the two harpoons (and I think it may have been something more than that), the man who threw them happened in the interval to go in a trading ship on a voyage to Africa. He went ashore there, joined a discovery party, and made his way far into the interior, where he traveled for nearly two years, often endangered by serpents, savages, tigers, poisonous miasmas, and all the other common perils of wandering in the heart of unknown regions. Meanwhile the whale he had struck must also have been on its travels; no doubt it had circled the globe three times, brushing all the coasts of Africa with its flanks; but to no purpose. This man and this whale came together again, and the one vanquished the other. I say that I myself have known three instances like this: that is, in two of them I saw the whales struck, and after the second attack saw the two irons, with their respective marks cut in them, afterwards taken from the dead fish. In the three-year instance, it so happened that I was in the boat both times, first and last, and the last time I clearly recognized a peculiar sort of huge mole under the whale's eye which I had observed there three years before. I say three years, but I am pretty sure it was more than that. Here, then, are three instances whose truth I personally know; but I have heard of many other instances from people whose truthfulness in the matter there is no good reason to doubt.

Second: It is well known in the Sperm Whale Fishery, however ignorant the world ashore may be of it, that there have been several memorable historical cases where a particular whale in the ocean has been popularly recognizable at distant times and places. Why such a whale became marked in this way was not, entirely and originally, owing to bodily peculiarities distinguishing him from other whales; for however peculiar in that respect any chance whale may be, they soon put an end to his peculiarities by killing him and boiling him down into a peculiarly valuable oil. No: the reason was this — from the fatal experiences of the fishery, there hung about such a whale a terrible reputation for danger, as there did about the bandit Rinaldo Rinaldini, so much so that most fishermen were content to acknowledge him merely by touching their tarpaulin hats when they found him lounging near them on the sea, without trying to cultivate a closer acquaintance. Like some poor devils ashore who happen to know an irascible great man, they make distant, unobtrusive greetings to him in the street, for fear that if they pushed the acquaintance further they might get a summary thump for their presumption.

But each of these famous whales did more than enjoy great personal celebrity — no, call it ocean-wide renown; each was not only famous in life and immortal after death in forecastle stories, but was granted all the rights, privileges, and distinctions of a name, and had just as much of a name as Cambyses or Caesar. Wasn't it so, O Timor Tom! you famous leviathan, scarred like an iceberg, who lurked so long in the Eastern straits of that name, whose spout was often seen from the palm-lined beach of Ombay? Wasn't it so, O New Zealand Jack! you terror of all the cruisers that crossed their wakes near the Tattoo Land? Wasn't it so, O Morquan! King of Japan, whose tall jet, they say, sometimes took the shape of a snow-white cross against the sky? Wasn't it so, O Don Miguel! you Chilean whale, marked like an old tortoise with mystic hieroglyphics on your back! In plain prose, here are four whales as well known to students of Cetacean History as Marius or Sylla to the classical scholar.

But this is not all. New Zealand Tom and Don Miguel, after at various times causing great havoc among the boats of different ships, were finally hunted down, systematically pursued, and killed by valiant whaling captains who raised their anchors with that express purpose in mind — just as Captain Butler of old set out through the Narragansett Woods specifically to capture that notorious, murderous savage Annawon, the foremost warrior of the Indian King Philip.

I do not know where I can find a better place than right here to mention one or two other things which seem important to me, since in printed form they establish in all respects the reasonableness of the whole story of the White Whale, and especially of the catastrophe. For this is one of those disheartening cases where truth needs fully as much propping up as error. So ignorant are most landsmen of some of the plainest and most palpable wonders of the world that, without some hints about the plain facts, historical and otherwise, of the fishery, they might scoff at Moby Dick as a monstrous fable, or, still worse and more detestable, a hideous and intolerable allegory.

First: Though most men have some vague, flitting ideas of the general perils of the grand fishery, they have nothing like a fixed, vivid conception of those perils and of how often they recur. One reason, perhaps, is that not one in fifty of the actual disasters and accidental deaths in the fishery ever finds a public record at home, however brief and quickly forgotten that record may be. Do you suppose that that poor fellow there — who at this very moment, perhaps, caught by the whale-line off the coast of New Guinea, is being carried down to the bottom of the sea by the sounding leviathan — do you suppose that poor fellow's name will appear in the newspaper obituaries you will read tomorrow at breakfast? No: because the mails are very irregular between here and New Guinea. In fact, have you ever heard anything that could be called regular news, direct or indirect, from New Guinea? Yet I tell you that on one particular voyage I made to the Pacific, among many others we spoke — that is, hailed at sea — thirty different ships, every one of which had had a death by a whale, some of them more than one, and three that had each lost a boat's crew. For God's sake, be economical with your lamps and candles! There is not a gallon you burn that did not cost at least one drop of man's blood.

Second: People ashore have indeed some vague idea that a whale is an enormous creature of enormous power. But I have always found that when I have described to them some specific example of this twofold enormousness, they have pointedly complimented me on my facetiousness — when, I declare upon my soul, I was no more trying to be funny than Moses when he wrote the history of the plagues of Egypt.

But fortunately the particular point I am after here can be established on testimony entirely independent of my own. That point is this: the Sperm Whale is in some cases powerful enough, knowing enough, and judiciously malicious enough, with direct premeditation, to stave in, utterly destroy, and sink a large ship; and what is more, the Sperm Whale actually has done it.

First: In the year 1820 the ship Essex, Captain Pollard, of Nantucket, was cruising in the Pacific Ocean. One day she saw spouts, lowered her boats, and gave chase to a shoal of sperm whales. Before long several of the whales were wounded, when suddenly a very large whale, escaping from the boats, broke out of the shoal and bore straight down upon the ship. Dashing his forehead against her hull, he stove her in so badly that in less than "ten minutes" she settled down and fell over. Not a surviving plank of her has been seen since. After the most severe exposure, part of the crew reached land in their boats. When he had at last returned home, Captain Pollard sailed once more for the Pacific in command of another ship, but the gods shipwrecked him again on unknown rocks and breakers; for the second time his ship was utterly lost, and, at once forswearing the sea, he has never tempted it since. Captain Pollard lives in Nantucket to this day. I have seen Owen Chace, who was chief mate of the Essex at the time of the tragedy; I have read his plain and faithful narrative; I have talked with his son; and all this within a few miles of the scene of the catastrophe.*

*The following are extracts from Chace's narrative: "Every fact seemed to warrant me in concluding that it was anything but chance which directed his operations; he made two separate attacks upon the ship, at a short interval between them, both of which, according to their direction, were calculated to do us the most injury, by being made ahead, and thereby combining the speed of the two objects for the shock; to effect which, the exact maneuvers which he made were necessary. His aspect was most horrible, and such as indicated resentment and fury. He came directly from the shoal which we had just before entered, and in which we had struck three of his companions, as if fired with revenge for their sufferings." Again: "At all events, the whole circumstances taken together, all happening before my own eyes, and producing, at the time, impressions in my mind of decided, calculating mischief on the part of the whale (many of which impressions I cannot now recall), induce me to be satisfied that I am correct in my opinion."

Here are his reflections some while after leaving the ship, on a black night in an open boat, when he had almost given up hope of reaching any friendly shore. "The dark ocean and swelling waters were nothing; the fears of being swallowed up by some dreadful tempest, or dashed upon hidden rocks, with all the other ordinary subjects of fearful contemplation, seemed scarcely entitled to a moment's thought; the dismal looking wreck, and the horrid aspect and revenge of the whale, wholly engrossed my reflections, until day again made its appearance."
In another place — page 45 — he speaks of "the mysterious and mortal attack of the animal."

Second: The ship Union, also of Nantucket, was totally lost off the Azores in 1807 by a similar attack, but the authentic details of this catastrophe I have never happened to encounter, though from whale hunters I have now and then heard passing references to it.

Third: Some eighteen or twenty years ago Commodore J——, then commanding an American sloop-of-war of the first class, happened to be dining with a party of whaling captains on board a Nantucket ship in the harbor of Oahu, Sandwich Islands. When the conversation turned to whales, the Commodore was pleased to be skeptical about the amazing strength attributed to them by the professional gentlemen present. He flatly denied, for example, that any whale could strike his stout sloop-of-war hard enough to make her leak so much as a thimbleful. Very good; but there is more to come. Some weeks later the Commodore set sail in this impregnable craft for Valparaiso. But he was stopped on the way by a portly sperm whale, who asked for a few moments of confidential business with him. That business consisted of giving the Commodore's craft such a thwack that, with all his pumps going, he made straight for the nearest port to heave her down — tip her on her side — and repair her. I am not superstitious, but I consider the Commodore's interview with that whale providential. Was not Saul of Tarsus converted from unbelief by a similar fright? I tell you, the sperm whale will stand no nonsense.

I will now refer you to Langsdorff's Voyages for a small detail particularly interesting to me. Langsdorff, you should know, was attached to the Russian Admiral Krusenstern's famous Discovery Expedition at the beginning of the current century. Captain Langsdorff begins his seventeenth chapter thus:

"By the thirteenth of May our ship was ready to sail, and the next day we were out in the open sea, on our way to Ochotsh. The weather was very clear and fine, but so intolerably cold that we were obliged to keep on our fur clothing. For some days we had very little wind; it was not till the nineteenth that a brisk gale from the northwest sprang up. An uncommon large whale, the body of which was larger than the ship itself, lay almost at the surface of the water, but was not perceived by any one on board till the moment when the ship, which was in full sail, was almost upon him, so that it was impossible to prevent its striking against him. We were thus placed in the most imminent danger, as this gigantic creature, setting up its back, raised the ship three feet at least out of the water. The masts reeled, and the sails fell altogether, while we who were below all sprang instantly upon the deck, concluding that we had struck upon some rock; instead of this we saw the monster sailing off with the utmost gravity and solemnity. Captain D'Wolf applied immediately to the pumps to examine whether or not the vessel had received any damage from the shock, but we found that very happily it had escaped entirely uninjured."

Now, the Captain D'Wolf referred to here as commanding the ship in question is a New Englander who, after a long life of unusual adventures as a sea-captain, now lives in the village of Dorchester near Boston. I have the honor of being his nephew. I have questioned him particularly about this passage in Langsdorff. He confirms every word. The ship, however, was by no means a large one: a Russian craft built on the Siberian coast, and bought by my uncle after he had bartered away the vessel in which he sailed from home.

In the voyage of Lionel Wafer, one of ancient Dampier's old chums — that straightforward, manly book of old-fashioned adventure, so full of honest wonders — I found a small incident set down so like what I just quoted from Langsdorff that I cannot resist inserting it here as a supporting example, if one is needed.

Lionel, it seems, was headed for "John Ferdinando," as he calls what is now Juan Fernández. "In our way thither," he says, "about four o'clock in the morning, when we were about one hundred and fifty leagues from the Main of America, our ship felt a terrible shock, which put our men in such consternation that they could hardly tell where they were or what to think; but every one began to prepare for death. And, indeed, the shock was so sudden and violent, that we took it for granted the ship had struck against a rock; but when the amazement was a little over, we cast the lead, and sounded, but found no ground. * * * * * The suddenness of the shock made the guns leap in their carriages, and several of the men were shaken out of their hammocks. Captain Davis, who lay with his head on a gun, was thrown out of his cabin!" Lionel goes on to blame the shock on an earthquake, and seems to back up that explanation by stating that a great earthquake at roughly that time really did cause great damage along the Spanish mainland. But I wouldn't be very surprised if, in the darkness of that early morning hour, the shock was actually caused by an unseen whale butting the hull straight up from below.

I might go on with several more examples, known to me one way or another, of the great power and malice the sperm whale at times shows. In more than one instance he has been known not only to chase the attacking boats back to their ships, but to pursue the ship itself and hold out for a long time against all the lances hurled at him from its decks. The English ship Pusie Hall can tell a story on that score; and as for his strength, let me say that there have been cases where the lines attached to a running sperm whale have, in a calm, been transferred to the ship and made fast there, the whale towing her great hull through the water as a horse walks off with a cart. Again, it is very often observed that if the sperm whale, once struck, is given time to rally, he then acts not so often with blind rage as with willful, deliberate designs of destruction against his pursuers; and it says something eloquent about his character that, when attacked, he will often open his mouth and hold it in that dreadful gape for several minutes on end. But I must be content with only one more, concluding illustration — a remarkable and most significant one, from which you will not fail to see not only that the most marvelous event in this book is corroborated by plain facts of the present day, but that these marvels (like all marvels) are mere repetitions of the ages; so that for the millionth time we say amen with Solomon — truly, there is nothing new under the sun.

In the sixth century of the Christian era lived Procopius, a Christian magistrate of Constantinople, in the days when Justinian was Emperor and Belisarius was general. As many know, he wrote the history of his own times, a work of uncommon value in every way. By the best authorities, he has always been considered a most trustworthy and unsensational historian, except in one or two particulars that do not affect the matter I am about to mention.

Now, Procopius reports in this history of his that while he was prefect of Constantinople, a great sea-monster was caught in the nearby Propontis, or Sea of Marmora, after it had been wrecking ships in those waters, off and on, for more than fifty years. A fact recorded like this in serious history is hard to dispute, and there is no reason anyone should want to. The account does not say exactly what species the monster was. But because it destroyed ships, and for other reasons too, it must have been a whale — and I lean strongly toward a sperm whale. Let me explain why. For a long time I assumed the sperm whale had never been known in the Mediterranean or in the deep waters that connect with it. Even now I am sure those seas are not, and perhaps under the present order of things never can be, a place where he regularly gathers in herds. But recent research has shown me that in modern times the sperm whale has turned up in the Mediterranean in isolated cases. I have it on good authority that a Commodore Davis of the British navy found a sperm whale's skeleton on the Barbary coast. And since a warship passes easily through the Dardanelles, a sperm whale could take the same route out of the Mediterranean into the Propontis.

In the Propontis, as far as I can learn, none of that peculiar substance called brit — the food of the right whale — is to be found. But I have every reason to believe that the food of the sperm whale — squid or cuttlefish — lurks at the bottom of that sea, because large creatures of that sort, though by no means the largest, have been found at its surface. If, then, you properly put these statements together and reason on them a bit, you will clearly see that, according to all human reasoning, Procopius's sea-monster, which for half a century stove in the ships of a Roman Emperor, must in all probability have been a sperm whale.

chapters.title: Chapter 46 — Surmises
paragraphs: Though, consumed by the hot fire of his purpose, Ahab in all his thoughts and actions always had in view the ultimate capture of Moby Dick; though he seemed ready to sacrifice all mortal interests to that one passion; it may nevertheless have been that he was by nature and long habit far too wedded to a fiery whaleman's ways to give up altogether pursuing the ordinary business of the voyage alongside it. Or at least, if this was not so, there was no lack of other motives with much more influence on him. It would perhaps be too fine a point, even allowing for his monomania, to hint that his vindictiveness toward the White Whale might possibly have extended in some degree to all sperm whales, and that the more monsters he killed, the more he multiplied the chances that each whale he met afterward would prove to be the hated one he hunted. But if such a hypothesis is indeed open to objection, there were still further considerations which, though not so strictly in keeping with the wildness of his ruling passion, were by no means incapable of swaying him.

To accomplish his object Ahab had to use tools; and of all tools used in the shadow of the moon, men are the most apt to get out of order. He knew, for example, that however magnetic his ascendancy over Starbuck was in some respects, that ascendancy did not cover the whole spiritual man, any more than mere bodily superiority implies intellectual mastery; for to the purely spiritual, the intellectual stands only in a sort of bodily relation. Starbuck's body and Starbuck's coerced will were Ahab's, so long as Ahab kept his magnet at Starbuck's brain; still, he knew that for all this the chief mate in his soul abhorred his captain's quest, and if he could, would joyfully cut himself loose from it, or even thwart it. It might be a long time before the White Whale was seen. During that long interval Starbuck would always be liable to fall into open relapses of rebellion against his captain's leadership, unless some ordinary, prudential, circumstantial influences were brought to bear on him. Not only that, but the subtle insanity of Ahab concerning Moby Dick was nowhere more significantly shown than in his superlative sense and shrewdness in foreseeing that, for the present, the hunt should somehow be stripped of the strange imaginative impiety that naturally clothed it; that the full terror of the voyage must be kept back in the dim background (for few men's courage can hold out against long brooding unrelieved by action); and that when they stood their long night watches, his officers and men must have some nearer things to think about than Moby Dick. For however eagerly and impetuously the savage crew had hailed the announcement of his quest, all sailors of every sort are more or less capricious and unreliable — they live in the changing outer weather, and they breathe in its fickleness — and when they are kept at the pursuit of some remote and blank object, however much it promises life and passion in the end, it is above all necessary that temporary interests and occupations should intervene and hold them healthily suspended for the final dash.

Nor did Ahab forget another thing. In times of strong emotion mankind scorns all base considerations; but such times are fleeting. The permanent, constitutional condition of the manufactured man, thought Ahab, is sordidness. Granted that the White Whale fully stirs the hearts of this savage crew of mine, and, playing around their savageness, even breeds a certain generous knight-errantry in them — still, while they chase Moby Dick for the love of it, they must also have food for their more common, everyday appetites. For even the lofty, chivalric Crusaders of old were not content to cross two thousand miles of land to fight for their holy sepulchre without committing burglaries, picking pockets, and gaining other pious perks along the way. Had they been held strictly to their one final and romantic object, too many would have turned from that final and romantic object in disgust. I will not strip these men, thought Ahab, of all hope of cash — yes, cash. They may scorn cash now; but let some months go by with no prospect of it in view, and then this same dormant cash, suddenly mutinying in them, would soon cashier Ahab — dismiss him from his command.

There was yet another precautionary motive, more closely related to Ahab personally. Having revealed the prime but private purpose of the Pequod's voyage — impulsively, it is probable, and perhaps somewhat prematurely — Ahab was now fully aware that in doing so he had indirectly laid himself open to the unanswerable charge of usurpation; and with perfect impunity, both moral and legal, his crew, if they were so inclined and able to carry it out, could refuse all further obedience to him, and even take the command from him by force. Ahab must of course have been most anxious to protect himself from even the barest hint of a charge of usurpation, and from the possible consequences of such a suppressed feeling gaining ground. That protection could lie only in his own dominating brain and heart and hand, backed by a careful, closely calculating attention to every minute atmospheric influence to which his crew could possibly be subjected.

For all these reasons, and others perhaps too subtle to spell out here, Ahab plainly saw that he must still in good measure stay true to the natural, stated purpose of the Pequod's voyage — observe all customary practices, and not only that, but force himself to show all his well-known passionate interest in the general pursuit of his profession.

However that may be, his voice could now often be heard hailing the three mastheads, urging the men to keep a sharp lookout and to report even a porpoise. It did not take long for this vigilance to pay off.

chapters.title: Chapter 47 — The Mat-Maker
paragraphs: It was a cloudy, sultry afternoon. The seamen were lazily lounging about the decks or gazing vacantly over the rail into the lead-colored waters. Queequeg and I were quietly weaving what is called a sword-mat, to use as an additional lashing for our boat. So still and subdued was the whole scene, and yet somehow so full of anticipation, and such a spell of daydreaming lurked in the air, that each silent sailor seemed dissolved into his own invisible self.

I was Queequeg's attendant, or page, while he was busy at the mat. As I kept passing the filling, or woof, of marline back and forth between the long yarns of the warp, using my own hand as the shuttle, and as Queequeg, standing sideways, every now and then slid his heavy oaken sword between the threads and, idly looking off at the water, carelessly and unthinkingly drove every yarn home — I say, so strange a dreaminess reigned then over all the ship and all the sea, broken only by the intermittent dull sound of the sword, that it seemed as if this were the Loom of Time, and I myself a shuttle mechanically weaving and weaving away at the Fates. There lay the fixed threads of the warp, subject to only one single, ever-returning, unchanging vibration, and that vibration just enough to allow other threads to be interwoven crosswise with its own. This warp seemed necessity; and here, I thought, with my own hand I ply my own shuttle and weave my own destiny into these unalterable threads. Meanwhile Queequeg's impulsive, indifferent sword sometimes hit the woof slantwise, or crookedly, or strongly, or weakly, as the case might be, and by this difference in the concluding blow produced a corresponding contrast in the final look of the finished fabric. This savage's sword, I thought, which in the end shapes and fashions both warp and woof — this easy, indifferent sword must be chance — yes, chance, free will, and necessity, in no way incompatible, all working together, interwoven. The straight warp of necessity, not to be swerved from its ultimate course — its every alternating vibration, indeed, only tending toward that; free will, still free to ply her shuttle between given threads; and chance, though restrained in its play within the straight lines of necessity, and directed sideways in its motions by free will — though thus hemmed in by both, chance rules each of them by turns, and strikes the last, shaping blow at events.

We were weaving and weaving away like this when a sound made me start — a sound so strange, so drawn-out, so musically wild and unearthly, that the ball of free will fell from my hand, and I stood staring up at the clouds that voice had dropped from like a wing. High up in the crosstrees was that mad Gay Header, Tashtego. He was leaning eagerly forward, his hand stretched out like a wand, and in brief, sudden bursts he kept up his cries. Of course, that same sound was perhaps ringing out at that very moment all over the seas, from hundreds of whalemen's lookouts perched just as high; but few of those lungs could have given that familiar old cry such a marvelous cadence as Tashtego the Indian's did.

As he stood hovering over you, half-suspended in air, peering so wildly and eagerly toward the horizon, you would have thought him some prophet or seer beholding the shadows of Fate, and announcing their coming with those wild cries.
"There she blows! There! There! There! She blows! She blows!"
"Where away?"
"On the lee beam, about two miles off! A school of them!"
Instantly all was commotion.
The Sperm Whale blows as a clock ticks, with the same unwavering and reliable regularity. And by this the whalemen distinguish this fish from other species of his kind.
"There go flukes!" was now the cry from Tashtego, and the whales disappeared.
"Quick, steward!" cried Ahab. "Time! Time!"
Dough-Boy hurried below, glanced at the watch, and reported the exact minute to Ahab.

The ship was now kept away from the wind, and she went gently rolling before it. Since Tashtego reported that the whales had gone down heading to leeward, we confidently expected to see them again directly ahead of our bows. For that singular cunning the Sperm Whale at times shows — when, sounding (diving deep) with his head in one direction, he nevertheless mills round while hidden beneath the surface and swiftly swims off the opposite way — this deceitfulness of his could not be at work now; for there was no reason to suppose that the fish Tashtego had seen had been alarmed in any way, or indeed knew we were anywhere near. One of the men chosen as shipkeepers — that is, those not assigned to the boats — had by this time relieved the Indian at the mainmast head. The sailors at the fore and mizzen had come down; the line tubs were fixed in their places; the cranes were thrust out; the mainyard was backed; and the three boats swung over the sea like three samphire baskets over high cliffs. Outside the bulwarks their eager crews clung to the rail with one hand, while one foot was poised expectantly on the gunwale. That is how the long line of a man-of-war's men looks when they are about to throw themselves aboard an enemy's ship.

But at that critical moment a sudden shout went up that pulled every eye away from the whale. Startled, everyone stared at dark Ahab, who stood surrounded by five dusky phantoms that seemed to have just taken shape out of the air.

chapters.title: Chapter 48 — The First Lowering
paragraphs: The phantoms, for so they seemed at the time, were flitting on the other side of the deck, and with a noiseless swiftness were casting loose the tackles and bands of the boat that hung there. This boat had always been considered one of the spare boats, though technically it was called the captain's, because it hung from the starboard quarter. The figure that now stood by its bow was tall and dark, with one white tooth evilly protruding from his steel-like lips. A rumpled Chinese jacket of black cotton clothed him funereally, with wide black trousers of the same dark stuff. But strangely crowning all this blackness was a glistening white plaited turban — his own living hair, braided and coiled round and round upon his head. Less dark in appearance, the companions of this figure had that vivid, tiger-yellow complexion peculiar to some of the aboriginal natives of the Manila islands — a race notorious for a certain devilish subtlety, and supposed by some honest white sailors to be the paid spies and secret confidential agents, here on the water, of their lord the devil, whose counting-room they suppose to be elsewhere.
While the wondering ship's company were still staring at these strangers, Ahab cried out to the white-turbaned old man at their head, "All ready there, Fedallah?"
"Ready," was the half-hissed reply.
"Lower away then, do you hear?" he shouted across the deck. "Lower away there, I say."

Such was the thunder of his voice that, despite their amazement, the men sprang over the rail. The pulleys whirled round in the blocks. With a lurch, the three boats dropped into the sea. And with a deft, offhand daring unknown in any other profession, the sailors leaped like goats down the rolling ship's side into the tossing boats below.

They had hardly pulled out from under the ship's shelter when a fourth boat, coming from the windward side, pulled around under the stern and revealed the five strangers rowing Ahab, who stood erect in the stern and loudly ordered Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask to spread themselves widely so as to cover a large stretch of water. But with all their eyes riveted upon the dark Fedallah and his crew, the men in the other boats did not obey the command.
"Captain Ahab? —" said Starbuck.
"Spread yourselves," cried Ahab. "Give way, all four boats. You, Flask, pull out more to leeward!"

"Aye, aye, sir," cheerily cried little King-Post, sweeping his great steering oar around. "Lay back!" he called to his crew. "There! — there! — there again! There she blows right ahead, boys! — lay back!"
"Never mind those yellow fellows, Archy."
"Oh, I don't mind them, sir," said Archy. "I knew it all before. Didn't I hear them in the hold? And didn't I tell Cabaco here about it? What do you say, Cabaco? They are stowaways, Mr. Flask."

"Pull, pull, my fine hearts-alive; pull, my children; pull, my little ones," Stubb sighed to his crew in a slow, soothing drawl, some of them still showing signs of uneasiness. "Why don't you break your backbones, my boys? What is it you're staring at? Those chaps in that boat over there? Tut! They are only five more hands come to help us — never mind from where — the more the merrier. Pull, then, do pull; never mind the brimstone — devils are good enough fellows. So, so; there you are now; that's the stroke for a thousand pounds; that's the stroke to sweep the stakes! Hurrah for the gold cup of sperm oil, my heroes! Three cheers, men — all hearts alive! Easy, easy; don't be in a hurry — don't be in a hurry. Why don't you snap your oars, you rascals? Bite something, you dogs! So, so, so, then — softly, softly! That's it — that's it! Long and strong. Give way there, give way! The devil take you, you ragamuffin rapscallions; you're all asleep. Stop snoring, you sleepers, and pull. Pull, will you? Pull, can't you? Pull, won't you? Why in the name of gudgeons and ginger-cakes don't you pull? — pull and break something! Pull, till your eyes start out of your head! Here!" — whipping the sharp knife out of his belt — "every mother's son of you draw his knife, and pull with the blade between his teeth. That's it — that's it. Now you're doing something; that looks like it, my steel-bits. Start her — start her, my silver-spoons! Start her, marling-spikes!"

Stubb's opening address to his crew is given here in full because he had rather a peculiar way of talking to them in general, and especially in preaching the religion of rowing. But you must not suppose from this sample of his sermons that he ever flew into real rages with his congregation. Not at all — and that was his chief peculiarity. He would say the most terrible things to his crew in a tone so strangely mixed of fun and fury, with the fury seeming so calculated merely as a spice to the fun, that no oarsman could hear such odd invocations without pulling for dear life, and yet pulling for the mere joke of the thing. Besides, all the while he himself looked so easy and lazy, handled his steering-oar so loungingly, and yawned so broadly — open-mouthed at times — that the mere sight of such a yawning commander, by sheer force of contrast, worked like a charm upon the crew. Then again, Stubb was one of those odd sorts of humorists whose jollity is sometimes so curiously ambiguous as to put all their subordinates on guard when it comes to obeying them.
In obedience to a signal from Ahab, Starbuck was now pulling diagonally across Stubb's bow. When for a minute or so the two boats were fairly near each other, Stubb hailed the mate.
"Mr. Starbuck! Portside boat there, ahoy! A word with you, sir, if you please!"
"Hello!" returned Starbuck, turning not a single inch as he spoke, still earnestly but in whispers urging his crew, his face set like flint away from Stubb's.
"What do you think of those yellow fellows, sir?"

"Smuggled on board, somehow, before the ship sailed. (Strong, strong, boys!)" in a whisper to his crew, then speaking out loud again: "A sad business, Mr. Stubb! (Drive her, drive her, my lads!) But never mind, Mr. Stubb, all for the best. Let all your crew pull strong, come what may. (Spring, my men, spring!) There's hogsheads of sperm ahead, Mr. Stubb, and that's what you came for. (Pull, my boys!) Sperm, sperm's the game! This at least is duty — duty and profit hand in hand."

"Aye, aye, I thought as much," Stubb said to himself when the boats diverged. "As soon as I clapped eyes on them, I thought so. Aye, and that's what he went into the after-hold for so often, as Dough-Boy long suspected. They were hidden down there. The White Whale's at the bottom of it. Well, well, so be it! Can't be helped! All right! Give way, men! It isn't the White Whale today! Give way!"

Now, the arrival of these outlandish strangers at such a critical moment as the lowering of the boats had, not unreasonably, stirred a kind of superstitious amazement in some of the ship's company. But Archy's supposed discovery had got around among them some time before, and though nobody had believed it then, it had in some small measure prepared them for the event. It took the sharpest edge off their wonder; and so, what with all this and Stubb's confident way of accounting for the strangers' appearance, they were for the time freed from superstitious guessing — though the affair still left plenty of room for all kinds of wild conjectures about dark Ahab's exact part in the matter from the beginning. As for me, I silently recalled the mysterious shadows I had seen creeping on board the Pequod in the dim Nantucket dawn, as well as the cryptic hints of the unaccountable Elijah.

Meanwhile Ahab, out of hearing of his officers, having edged farthest to windward, was still ranging ahead of the other boats — a sign of how powerful a crew was pulling him. Those tiger-yellow creatures of his seemed all steel and whalebone. Like five trip-hammers they rose and fell with regular strokes of strength, which every so often shot the boat along the water like a horizontal burst boiler out of a Mississippi steamer. As for Fedallah, who was seen pulling the harpooner's oar, he had thrown aside his black jacket and bared his chest, the whole of his body above the gunwale sharply outlined against the alternating dips of the watery horizon; while at the other end of the boat Ahab, one arm thrown half backward into the air like a fencer's, as if to counterbalance any tendency to trip, was seen steadily managing his steering oar as he had in a thousand boat-lowerings before the White Whale tore him. All at once the outstretched arm made a peculiar motion and then stayed fixed, while the boat's five oars were seen peaked all at once. Boat and crew sat motionless on the sea. Instantly the three spread-out boats behind paused on their way. The whales had irregularly sunk bodily down into the blue, giving no sign of the movement that could be seen from a distance, though Ahab, being closer, had observed it.
"Every man look out along his oars!" cried Starbuck. "You, Queequeg, stand up!"

Nimbly springing up on the triangular raised box in the bow, the savage stood erect there, and with intensely eager eyes gazed off toward the spot where the chase had last been sighted. Likewise, on the extreme stern of the boat, where it was also built up into a triangular platform level with the gunwale, Starbuck himself was seen coolly and skillfully balancing himself against the jerking tosses of his chip of a craft, silently scanning the vast blue eye of the sea.

Not very far off, Flask's boat was also lying breathlessly still. Its commander was recklessly standing on top of the loggerhead, a stout sort of post rooted in the keel and rising some two feet above the level of the stern platform. It is used for catching turns with the whale line. Its top is no bigger than the palm of a man's hand, and standing on such a base as that, Flask seemed perched at the masthead of some ship that had sunk to all but her trucks, the caps at the very tops of her masts. But little King-Post was small and short, and at the same time little King-Post was full of a large and tall ambition, so that this loggerhead standpoint of his by no means satisfied King-Post.
"I can't see three waves off. Tip us up an oar there and let me climb on that."
Upon this, Daggoo, with either hand on the gunwale to steady himself, swiftly slid to the stern, and then straightening up, volunteered his lofty shoulders as a pedestal.
"Good a masthead as any, sir. Will you mount?"
"That I will, and thank you very much, my fine fellow. Only I wish you were fifty feet taller."

Whereupon, planting his feet firmly against two opposite planks of the boat, the gigantic negro stooped a little and offered his flat palm to Flask's foot; then, putting Flask's hand on his hearse-plumed head and telling him to spring just as he himself should toss, with one skillful fling he landed the little man high and dry on his shoulders. And here now stood Flask, Daggoo with one lifted arm giving him a breastband to lean against and steady himself by.

At any time it is a strange sight to the novice to see with what wonderful, unconscious habit of skill the whaleman will keep upright in his boat, even when pitched about by the most riotously perverse and cross-running seas. Stranger still to see him giddily perched on the loggerhead itself in such conditions. But the sight of little Flask mounted on gigantic Daggoo was more curious yet; for, holding himself up with a cool, indifferent, easy, unstudied, barbaric majesty, the noble negro rolled his fine form in harmony with every roll of the sea. On his broad back, flaxen-haired Flask seemed a snowflake. The bearer looked nobler than the rider. True, lively, tumultuous, showy little Flask would now and then stamp with impatience; but he did not add a single heave to the negro's lordly chest by it. So have I seen Passion and Vanity stamping on the living, magnanimous earth, but the earth did not alter her tides and her seasons for that.

Meanwhile Stubb, the third mate, showed no such far-gazing anxieties. The whales might have made one of their regular soundings (their long, deep dives), not a temporary dive from mere fright; and if that were the case, Stubb, as was apparently his habit in such cases, was determined to while away the dragging interval with his pipe. He drew it from his hatband, where he always wore it at a slant like a feather. He loaded it and rammed the tobacco home with the end of his thumb; but he had barely struck his match across the rough sandpaper of his hand when Tashtego, his harpooner, whose eyes had been turned to windward like two fixed stars, suddenly dropped like light from his upright stance to his seat, crying out in a quick frenzy of hurry, "Down, down all, and give way! — there they are!"

To a landsman, no whale, nor any sign of a herring, would have been visible at that moment — nothing but a troubled patch of greenish-white water, with thin, scattered puffs of vapor hovering over it and drifting diffusely off to leeward, like the confused spray blown from white rolling breakers. The air around suddenly vibrated and tingled, as it were, like the air over intensely heated plates of iron. Beneath this atmospheric waving and curling, and partly beneath a thin layer of water as well, the whales were swimming. Seen ahead of all the other signs, the puffs of vapor they spouted seemed their couriers running before them, their detached outriders flying ahead.

All four boats were now in keen pursuit of that one spot of troubled water and air. But it seemed ready to outrun them. It flew on and on, like a mass of merging bubbles swept down a swift stream from the hills.

"Pull, pull, my good boys," said Starbuck, in the lowest possible but most intensely concentrated whisper to his men. The sharp fixed glance from his eyes, aimed straight ahead of the bow, seemed almost like two visible needles in two unerring binnacle compasses. He did not say much to his crew, nor did they say anything to him. Only the silence of the boat was at intervals piercingly broken by one of his peculiar whispers — now harsh with command, now soft with pleading.

How different the loud little King-Post. "Sing out and say something, my hearties! Roar and pull, my thunderbolts! Beach me, beach me on their black backs, boys! Only do that for me, and I'll sign over my Martha's Vineyard plantation to you, boys — including wife and children, boys! Lay me on — lay me on! Oh Lord, Lord! I'll go stark, staring mad! See! See that white water!" And shouting like this, he pulled his hat from his head and stamped up and down on it; then, picking it up, he flicked it far off over the sea; and finally he took to rearing and plunging in the boat's stern like a crazed colt from the prairie.

"Look at that fellow now," Stubb drawled philosophically, following along at a short distance with his unlit pipe still mechanically clamped between his teeth. "He's got fits, that Flask has. Fits? Yes, give him fits — that's the very word — pitch fits into them. Merrily, merrily, hearts alive! Pudding for supper, you know — merry's the word. Pull, babes — pull, sucklings — pull, all. But what the devil are you hurrying about? Softly, softly, and steadily, my men. Only pull, and keep pulling. Nothing more. Crack all your backbones, and bite your knives in two — that's all. Take it easy — why don't you take it easy, I say, and burst all your livers and lungs!"

But what it was that inscrutable Ahab said to that tiger-yellow crew of his — those are words best left out here, for you live under the blessed light of the evangelical land. Only the infidel sharks in the audacious seas may listen to such words, when, with a tornado brow and eyes of red murder and foam-glued lips, Ahab leaped after his prey.

Meanwhile, all the boats tore on. Flask's repeated, specific references to "that whale," as he called the imaginary monster that he declared was constantly teasing his boat's bow with its tail — these references of his were at times so vivid and lifelike that they would make one or two of his men snatch a fearful look over their shoulders. But this was against all rules; for the oarsmen must put out their eyes and ram a skewer through their necks, custom declaring that in these critical moments they must have no organs but ears and no limbs but arms.

It was a sight full of quick wonder and awe! The vast swells of the all-powerful sea; the surging, hollow roar they made as they rolled along the eight gunwales, like gigantic bowls on a boundless bowling green; the brief, suspended agony of the boat as it tipped for an instant on the knife-like edge of the sharper waves, which almost seemed to threaten to cut it in two; the sudden deep plunge into the watery glens and hollows; the keen spurring and goading to reach the top of the opposite hill; the headlong, sled-like slide down its other side — all these, with the cries of the headsmen and harpooners and the shuddering gasps of the oarsmen, and the wondrous sight of the ivory Pequod bearing down on her boats with outstretched sails, like a wild hen after her screaming brood — all this was thrilling.

Not the raw recruit who marches straight from his wife's arms into the fever heat of his first battle; not the dead man's ghost meeting the first unknown phantom of the other world — neither of these feels stranger or stronger emotions than the man who finds himself, for the first time, rowing into the charmed, churned-up circle of a hunted sperm whale.

The dancing white water the chase churned up was growing more and more visible now, because the dull cloud-shadows thrown on the sea were getting darker. The jets of vapor had stopped blending together and slanted every which way, right and left; the whales seemed to be splitting their wakes apart. The boats spread farther from one another, Starbuck going after three whales that ran dead to leeward. We had our sail set now, and with the wind still rising we raced along, the boat tearing through the water so madly that the lee oars could hardly be worked fast enough to keep them from being ripped out of the rowlocks.
Soon we were running through a wide, drifting veil of mist. Neither ship nor boat to be seen.
"Give way, men," whispered Starbuck, drawing the sheet of his sail still further aft. "There is time to kill a fish yet before the squall comes. There's white water again! — close by! Spring!"

Soon after, two cries in quick succession on each side of us told us the other boats had struck fast. But they were hardly heard when, with a lightning-fast hissing whisper, Starbuck said: "Stand up!" and Queequeg, harpoon in hand, sprang to his feet.

Though not one of the oarsmen was facing the life-and-death danger so close ahead, yet with their eyes on the intense face of the mate in the stern of the boat, they knew the critical instant had come. They heard, too, an enormous wallowing sound, as of fifty elephants stirring in their bedding. Meanwhile the boat was still racing through the mist, the waves curling and hissing around us like the raised crests of enraged serpents.
"That's his hump. There, there, give it to him!" whispered Starbuck.

A short rushing sound leaped out of the boat — it was the darted iron of Queequeg. Then all in one welded commotion came an invisible push from behind, while forward the boat seemed to strike a ledge. The sail collapsed and exploded. A gush of scalding vapor shot up nearby. Something rolled and tumbled like an earthquake beneath us. The whole crew was half-suffocated as they were tossed helter-skelter into the white curdling cream of the squall. Squall, whale, and harpoon had all blended together. And the whale, merely grazed by the iron, escaped.

The boat was completely swamped but almost undamaged. We swam around it and gathered up the floating oars, lashed them across the gunwale, and scrambled back into our places. There we sat, knee-deep in the sea, with water over every rib and plank, so that to our eyes, gazing down, the boat hanging there in the water seemed like a coral boat that had grown up to us from the ocean floor.

The wind increased to a howl; the waves clashed their shields together; the whole squall roared, forked, and crackled around us like a white fire on the prairie, in which we were burning without being consumed — immortal in these jaws of death! In vain we hailed the other boats; you might as well roar to the live coals down the chimney of a blazing furnace as hail those boats in that storm. Meanwhile the driving spray, flying cloud, and mist grew darker with the shadows of night; no sign of the ship could be seen. The rising sea ruled out any attempt to bail out the boat. The oars were useless for rowing, and now served as life-preservers. So, cutting the lashing of the waterproof match keg, Starbuck, after many failures, managed to light the lamp in the lantern; then, fixing it on a waif pole (the flagged pole used to mark a killed whale), he handed it to Queequeg as the standard-bearer of this forlorn hope. There, then, he sat, holding up that feeble candle in the heart of that almighty forlornness. There, then, he sat, the sign and symbol of a man without faith, hopelessly holding up hope in the midst of despair.

Wet and drenched through, shivering with cold, having given up hope of either ship or boat, we raised our eyes as dawn broke. The mist still lay spread over the sea, and the empty lantern lay crushed in the bottom of the boat. Suddenly Queequeg leaped to his feet and cupped his hand to his ear. We all heard a faint creaking, like ropes and yards whose sound the storm had muffled until now. It came closer and closer; a huge, vague shape dimly parted the thick mist. In terror we all jumped into the sea as the ship finally loomed into view, bearing straight down on us, hardly more than her own length away.

From where we floated in the waves we saw the abandoned boat toss and gape for one instant under the ship's bows, like a chip of wood at the foot of a waterfall; then the huge hull rolled over it, and it vanished until it surfaced again, wallowing, astern. We swam for it again, were flung against it by the seas, and were finally picked up and brought safely on board. The other boats had cut loose from their fish before the squall reached them and had got back to the ship in good time. The ship had given us up for lost but was still cruising about, in case it might happen upon some sign of our death — an oar or a lance pole.

chapters.title: Chapter 49 — The Hyena
paragraphs: There are certain queer times and occasions in this strange, mixed affair we call life when a man takes this whole universe for a vast practical joke, though he only dimly sees the wit of it, and more than suspects that the joke is at nobody's expense but his own. Still, nothing gets him down, and nothing seems worth arguing about. He bolts down all events, all creeds and beliefs and persuasions, all hard things visible and invisible, no matter how knobby, as an ostrich with a powerful digestion gobbles down bullets and gun flints. And as for small difficulties and worries, prospects of sudden disaster, danger to life and limb — all these, and death itself, seem to him only sly, good-natured hits and jolly punches in the ribs from the unseen and unaccountable old joker. That odd, wayward sort of mood I am speaking of comes over a man only in some time of extreme trouble; it comes in the very midst of his earnestness, so that what a moment before might have seemed to him a thing of the greatest importance now seems only part of the general joke. There is nothing like the perils of whaling to breed this free-and-easy sort of genial, desperado philosophy; and it was with this that I now regarded the whole voyage of the Pequod, and the great White Whale that was its object.

"Queequeg," I said, when they had dragged me — the last man — to the deck, and I was still shaking myself in my jacket to fling off the water, "Queequeg, my fine friend, does this sort of thing happen often?" Without much emotion, though soaked through just like me, he gave me to understand that such things did often happen.

"Mr. Stubb," I said, turning to that worthy, who, buttoned up in his oil jacket, was now calmly smoking his pipe in the rain, "Mr. Stubb, I think I have heard you say that of all whalemen you ever met, our chief mate, Mr. Starbuck, is by far the most careful and prudent. I suppose, then, that going headlong at a running whale with your sail set in a foggy squall is the height of a whaleman's discretion?"
"Certainly. I've lowered for whales from a leaking ship in a gale off Cape Horn."

"Mr. Flask," I said, turning to little King-Post, who was standing close by, "you are experienced in these things, and I am not. Will you tell me whether it is an unbreakable law in this fishery, Mr. Flask, for an oarsman to break his own back pulling himself backward into death's jaws?"

"Can't you put it more simply?" said Flask. "Yes, that's the law. I'd like to see a boat's crew backing water up to a whale face-first. Ha, ha! The whale would give them squint for squint, mind that!"

Here, then, from three impartial witnesses, I had a deliberate statement of the whole case. Considering, therefore, that squalls, capsizings in the water, and the bivouacs on the deep that follow were matters of common occurrence in this kind of life; considering that at the supremely critical instant of going on to the whale I must hand my life over to the man who steered the boat — often a fellow who, at that very moment, in his impetuousness, is on the point of sinking the craft with his own frantic stamping; considering that the particular disaster to our own particular boat was chiefly to be blamed on Starbuck's driving on to his whale almost in the teeth of a squall, and considering that Starbuck, for all that, was famous for his great caution in the fishery; considering that I belonged to this uncommonly prudent Starbuck's boat; and finally, considering what a devil's chase I was caught up in, concerning the White Whale — taking all things together, I say, I thought I might as well go below and make a rough draft of my will. "Queequeg," I said, "come along; you shall be my lawyer, executor, and legatee."

It may seem odd that sailors, of all people, should be forever tinkering with their last wills and testaments, but nobody in the world enjoys that pastime more. This was the fourth time in my life at sea that I had done it. Once the ceremony was finished this time, I felt all the easier; a stone had been rolled away from my heart. What's more, every day I lived from then on would be as good as the days Lazarus lived after he was raised from the dead — a clear extra profit of however many months or weeks it might turn out to be. I had outlived myself; my death and burial were locked away in my chest. I looked around me calmly and contentedly, like a quiet ghost with a clear conscience sitting behind the bars of a snug family vault.
Now then, I thought, unconsciously rolling up my sleeves — here goes for a cool, collected dive at death and destruction, and the devil take the hindmost.

chapters.title: Chapter 50 — Ahab’s Boat and Crew. Fedallah
paragraphs: "Who would have thought it, Flask!" cried Stubb. "If I had only one leg, you wouldn't catch me in a boat — unless maybe to plug the drain-hole with my wooden toe. Oh! He's a wonderful old man!"

"I don't think it so strange, on that account," said Flask. "If his leg were off at the hip, now, that would be a different thing. That would disable him. But he has one knee, and a good part of the other left, you know."
"I don't know about that, little man. I've never yet seen him kneel."

Whale-wise people have often debated whether a whaling captain, given how vital his life is to the success of the voyage, has any right to risk that life in the dangers of the chase itself. In just the same way, Tamerlane's soldiers often argued, with tears in their eyes, whether that priceless life of his should be carried into the thick of the fighting.

But with Ahab the question took on a different angle. Considering that even with two legs a man is but a hobbling creature in times of danger — considering that the pursuit of whales is always conducted under great and extraordinary difficulties, and that every individual moment involves peril — under these circumstances, is it wise for any maimed man to enter a whale-boat in the hunt? As a general rule, the joint-owners of the Pequod must plainly have thought not.

Ahab knew well that although his friends at home would think little of his getting into a boat during certain comparatively harmless turns of the chase, for the sake of being near the action and giving his orders in person, yet for Captain Ahab to have a boat actually assigned to him as a regular headsman in the hunt — above all, for Captain Ahab to be supplied with five extra men as that boat's crew — he knew well that such generous notions never entered the heads of the owners of the Pequod. So he had not asked them for a boat's crew, nor had he in any way hinted at his wishes on that score. Nevertheless, he had taken private measures of his own in the whole matter. Until Cabaco's discovery was made public, the sailors had little foreseen it. To be sure, once they had been a little while out of port and all hands had finished the customary business of fitting out the whaleboats for service, Ahab was, some time after this, now and then found busying himself with making thole-pins (the pegs that hold the oars in place) with his own hands for what was thought to be one of the spare boats, and even carefully cutting the small wooden skewers that are pinned over the groove in the bow when the line is running out; when all this was noticed in him, and particularly his concern to have an extra layer of sheathing in the bottom of the boat, as if to make it better withstand the pointed pressure of his ivory limb; and also the anxiety he showed in shaping exactly the thigh-board, or clumsy cleat, as it is sometimes called — the horizontal piece in the boat's bow for bracing the knee against when darting or stabbing at the whale; when it was noticed how often he stood up in that boat with his single knee fixed in the semicircular hollow in the cleat, and with the carpenter's chisel gouged out a little here and straightened it a little there — all these things, I say, had stirred much interest and curiosity at the time. But almost everybody supposed that this particular care in preparation on Ahab's part could only be with a view to the final chase of Moby Dick, for he had already revealed his intention to hunt that mortal monster in person. But such a supposition by no means involved the faintest suspicion that any boat's crew would be assigned to that boat.

As for the lesser phantoms, whatever wonder was left about them soon faded, because on a whaler wonders never last long. Besides, every so often such unaccountable odds and ends of strange nations turn up from the unknown corners and ash-heaps of the earth to crew these floating outlaws, the whalers; and the ships themselves so often pick up such odd castaways, found drifting on the open sea on planks, scraps of wreckage, oars, whaleboats, canoes, Japanese junks blown off course, and who knows what else, that Beelzebub himself could climb up the side and go down into the cabin for a chat with the captain without stirring up any uncontrollable excitement in the forecastle.

But be all this as it may, it is certain that while the subordinate phantoms soon found their place among the crew — though still, as it were, somehow distinct from them — that hair-turbaned Fedallah remained a muffled mystery to the last. Where he came from, in a well-mannered world like this; by what unaccountable sort of tie he soon showed himself to be linked with Ahab's peculiar fortunes — indeed, so far as to have some sort of half-hinted influence; Heaven knows, it might even have been authority over him — all this nobody knew. But no one can keep up an air of indifference about Fedallah. He was such a creature as civilized, domestic people in the temperate zone see only in their dreams, and even then only dimly; but the like of him now and then glide among the unchanging Asiatic communities, especially the Oriental islands to the east of the continent — those isolated, immemorial, unalterable countries which even in these modern days still keep much of the ghostly aboriginal quality of earth's first generations, when the memory of the first man was a distinct recollection, and all men, his descendants, not knowing where he came from, eyed each other as real phantoms, and asked the sun and the moon why they were created and to what end; when, though according to Genesis the angels indeed consorted with the daughters of men, the devils also, add the uncanonical rabbis, indulged in earthly love affairs.

chapters.title: Chapter 51 — The Spirit-Spout
