The prow of the boat is partly intact and is drawn just balancing on the monster's spine; and standing in that prow, for one single flash of time too brief to measure, you see an oarsman, half hidden by the whale's furious, boiling spout, in the act of leaping as if from a cliff. The action of the whole scene is wonderfully good and true. The half-emptied line-tub floats on the whitened sea; the wooden shafts of the spilled harpoons bob slantwise in it; the heads of the swimming crew are scattered around the whale, their faces showing fright in contrasting ways; while in the black, stormy distance the ship is bearing down on the scene. You could find serious fault with the anatomical details of this whale, but let that go, since for the life of me I could not draw one as good.

In the second engraving, the boat is just drawing up beside the barnacled flank of a big Right Whale on the run, who rolls his black, weedy bulk through the sea like a mossy rockslide off the Patagonian cliffs. His jets stand straight up, full and black as soot, so that with so much smoke pouring from the chimney you would think a fine supper must be cooking in the great bowels below. Seabirds are pecking at the little crabs, shellfish, and other sea candies and macaroni that the Right Whale sometimes carries on his pestilent back. And all the while the thick-lipped leviathan is tearing through the deep, leaving tons of churning white curds in his wake and making the light boat rock in the swells like a skiff caught close to the paddle-wheels of an ocean steamer. So the foreground is all raging commotion; but behind it, in admirable artistic contrast, lies the glassy surface of a sea in a dead calm, the limp, unstarched sails of the helpless ship, and the inert mass of a dead whale — a conquered fortress — with the flag of capture hanging lazily from the whale-pole planted in his spout-hole.

Who Garnery the painter is, or was, I don't know. But I'd bet my life that he either knew his subject at first hand or was marvelously coached by some experienced whaleman. When it comes to painting action, the French are the lads. Go and look at all the paintings of Europe: where will you find such a gallery of living, breathing commotion on canvas as in that triumphal hall at Versailles, where the viewer fights his way pell-mell through one great battle of France after another; where every sword seems a flash of the Northern Lights, and armed kings and Emperors dash by one after another like a charge of crowned centaurs? These sea battle-pieces of Garnery are not wholly unworthy of a place in that gallery.

The natural French gift for catching the picturesque side of things seems especially evident in the paintings and engravings they have made of whaling scenes. With not a tenth of England's experience in the fishery, and not a thousandth of America's, they have still supplied both nations with the only finished sketches that can at all convey the real spirit of the whale hunt. English and American whale draftsmen mostly seem perfectly satisfied to give the mechanical outline of things, such as the whale's vacant profile — which, as far as picturesque effect goes, amounts to about the same as sketching the profile of a pyramid. Even Scoresby, the justly famous Right whaleman, after giving us a stiff full-length portrait of the Greenland whale and three or four delicate miniatures of narwhals and porpoises, treats us to a series of classic engravings of boat hooks, chopping knives, and grapnels; and with the microscopic diligence of a Leuwenhoeck (the pioneer of the microscope) he lays before a shivering world ninety-six facsimiles of magnified Arctic snow crystals. I mean no slight to the excellent voyager (I honor him as a veteran), but in so important a matter it was surely an oversight not to have gotten a sworn affidavit for every crystal, taken before a Greenland Justice of the Peace.

Besides those fine engravings after Garnery, there are two other French engravings worth noting, by someone who signs himself "H. Durand." One of them, though not exactly suited to our present purpose, still deserves mention for other reasons. It is a quiet noon scene among the islands of the Pacific: a French whaler anchored close inshore in a calm, lazily taking on water, the loosened sails of the ship and the long palm leaves behind her drooping together in the windless air. The effect is very fine, considering that it shows the hardy fishermen in one of their rare moments of oriental repose. The other engraving is a very different matter. The ship lies hove-to on the open sea, in the very heart of leviathan life, with a Right Whale alongside; the vessel (busy cutting-in) heels over toward the monster as if toward a wharf; and a boat, hastily pushing off from all this activity, is about to chase some whales in the distance. The harpoons and lances lie leveled and ready; three oarsmen are just stepping the mast into its hole; and a sudden roll of the sea has lifted the little craft half upright out of the water, like a rearing horse. From the ship, the smoke of the boiling whale's torments rises like the smoke over a village of smithies; and to windward, a black cloud rising with its promise of squalls and rain seems to spur on the excited seamen.

chapters.title: Chapter 57 — Of Whales in Paint; in Teeth; in Wood; in Sheet-Iron; in
paragraphs: Stone; in Mountains; in Stars.

On Tower Hill, as you head down to the London docks, you may have seen a crippled beggar (a kedger, as sailors call him) holding a painted board in front of him that shows the tragic scene in which he lost his leg. There are three whales and three boats, and one of the boats (supposed to hold the missing leg in all its original soundness) is being crunched in the jaws of the foremost whale. For the last ten years, they tell me, that man has held up that picture and shown off that stump to a disbelieving world. But now the time has come for him to be vindicated. His three whales are as good as any whales ever published in Wapping, at any rate, and his stump is as unquestionable a stump as any you'll find in the western clearings. Yet though he is forever mounted on that stump, the poor whaleman never makes a stump-speech; he just stands with downcast eyes, ruefully contemplating his own amputation.

Throughout the Pacific, and also in Nantucket, and New Bedford, and Sag Harbor, you will come across lively sketches of whales and whaling scenes, engraved by the fishermen themselves on Sperm Whale teeth, or on ladies' busks (corset stays) worked out of Right Whale bone, and other such skrimshander (scrimshaw) articles, as the whalemen call the numerous ingenious little objects they elaborately carve out of the rough material in their hours of ocean leisure. Some of them have little boxes of dentist-like tools, specially intended for the skrimshandering business. But in general they toil with their jackknives alone; and with that almost all-powerful tool of the sailor, they will turn out for you anything you please in the way of a mariner's fancy.

Long exile from Christendom and civilization inevitably returns a man to the condition God put him in — namely, what people call savagery. Your true whale-hunter is as much a savage as an Iroquois. I am a savage myself, loyal to no one but the King of the Cannibals, and ready to rebel against him at any moment.

Now, one of the peculiar characteristics of the savage in his domestic hours is his wonderful patience and industry. An ancient Hawaiian war-club or spear-paddle, in its full complexity and elaboration of carving, is as great a testament to human perseverance as a Latin dictionary. For with nothing but a bit of broken sea-shell or a shark's tooth, that miraculous intricacy of wooden net-work has been achieved. And it has cost steady years of steady work.

As with the Hawaiian savage, so with the white sailor-savage. With the same marvelous patience, and with the same single shark's tooth of his one poor jackknife, he will carve you a bit of bone sculpture — not quite as expertly made, but as densely packed in its maze-like design as the Greek savage Achilles's shield, and full of barbaric spirit and suggestion, as the prints of that fine old Dutch savage, Albert Durer.
Wooden whales — or whales cut in profile from small dark slabs of the noble South Sea war-wood — turn up often in the forecastles of American whalers. Some of them are made with great accuracy.

At some old gable-roofed country houses you will see brass whales hung by the tail as knockers on the roadside door. When the porter is sleepy, the anvil-headed whale would work best. But these knocking whales are seldom noteworthy as faithful likenesses. On the steeples of some old-fashioned churches you will see sheet-iron whales placed there as weather-vanes. But they are so high up, and besides are to all intents and purposes labeled "Hands off!" — so you cannot examine them closely enough to judge their merit.

In bony, ribbed regions of the earth, where masses of rock lie scattered in fantastic groups across the plain at the foot of high, broken cliffs, you will often find shapes that look like the petrified forms of Leviathan, half sunk in grass that breaks against them in a surf of green waves on a windy day.

Then again, in mountainous countries where the traveler is continually ringed by amphitheater-like heights, here and there from some lucky vantage point you will catch passing glimpses of the profiles of whales outlined along the undulating ridges. But you must be a thorough whaleman to see these sights; and not only that, but if you wish to return to such a sight again, you must be sure to take the exact intersecting latitude and longitude of your first standpoint; otherwise, so much a matter of chance are such observations of the hills, your precise earlier standpoint would require laborious rediscovery — like the Soloma Islands, which still remain unknown, though high-ruffed Mendanna once walked them and old Figuera chronicled them.

And when your subject lifts and expands your mind, you cannot help tracing great whales in the starry heavens, with boats chasing them — just as the Eastern nations, their minds long full of war, saw armies locked in battle among the clouds. So in the North I have chased Leviathan round and round the Pole, following the wheeling of the bright points that first outlined him for me. And under the blazing Antarctic skies I have boarded the Argo-Navis and joined the hunt for the starry Cetus far past the farthest reach of Hydrus and the Flying Fish.

With a frigate's anchors for my bridle-bits and bundles of harpoons for spurs, how I wish I could mount that whale and leap past the highest skies, to find out whether the fabled heavens, with all their countless tents, really lie camped beyond the reach of my mortal sight!

chapters.title: Chapter 58 — Brit
paragraphs: Steering northeast from the Crozets, we fell in with vast meadows of brit, the minute, yellow substance upon which the Right Whale largely feeds. For league upon league it undulated around us, so that we seemed to be sailing through boundless fields of ripe, golden wheat.

On the second day, numbers of Right Whales were seen, who — safe from the attack of a Sperm Whaler like the Pequod — with open jaws sluggishly swam through the brit. It clung to the fringing fibers of that wondrous Venetian blind in their mouths, and was in this way separated from the water that escaped at the lip.

Like mowers in the morning who move side by side, slowly and seethingly sweeping their scythes through the long wet grass of marshy meadows, these monsters swam along, making a strange, grassy, cutting sound and leaving endless swaths of blue behind them on the yellow sea.*

*That part of the sea known among whalemen as the "Brazil Banks" does not bear that name because of shallows and soundings there, as the Banks of Newfoundland do, but because of this remarkable meadow-like appearance, caused by the vast drifts of brit continually floating in those latitudes, where the Right Whale is often hunted.

But it was only the sound they made as they parted the brit that reminded one of mowers at all. Seen from the mastheads, especially when they paused and were still for a while, their vast black forms looked more like lifeless masses of rock than anything else. And as in the great hunting countries of India the stranger at a distance will sometimes pass elephants lying on the plains without knowing them for what they are, taking them for bare, blackened rises of the ground, so it often is with anyone who sees this species of the leviathans of the sea for the first time. And even when they are recognized at last, their immense size makes it very hard really to believe that such bulky masses of overgrowth can possibly be alive, in every part, with the same sort of life that lives in a dog or a horse.

Indeed, in other ways too, you can hardly feel about any creature of the deep the way you feel about those of the shore. Some old naturalists have held that every kind of land creature has its counterpart in the sea; and taking a broad, general view, that may well be so. But when you come down to particulars — where, for example, does the ocean offer a fish whose temperament matches the wise kindness of the dog? Only the accursed shark can be said, in any general way, to bear some comparison to him.

True, landsmen in general have always looked on the native inhabitants of the seas with feelings unspeakably unsociable and repellent. We know the sea to be an everlasting terra incognita, so much so that Columbus sailed over countless unknown worlds to discover his one superficial western one. By far the most terrible of all mortal disasters have, since time immemorial, struck down tens and hundreds of thousands of those who have gone to sea, without distinction. And a moment's thought will show that however much baby man may boast of his science and skill, and however much that science and skill may grow in a flattering future, the sea will go on insulting and murdering him forever and ever, to the crack of doom, and pulverizing the stateliest, stiffest frigate he can build. Yet for all that, the constant repetition of these very impressions has made man lose the sense of the sea's full awfulness that originally belongs to it.

The first boat we read of floated on an ocean that with Portuguese vengeance had drowned a whole world without leaving so much as a widow. That same ocean rolls now. That same ocean destroyed the wrecked ships of last year. Yes, foolish mortals — Noah's flood has not yet subsided. Two thirds of the fair world it still covers.

How do the sea and the land differ, that a miracle upon one is not a miracle upon the other? Supernatural terrors seized the Hebrews when under the feet of Korah and his company the living ground opened and swallowed them up forever. Yet not a modern sun ever sets without the living sea swallowing up ships and crews in precisely the same manner.

But the sea is not only the enemy of man, who is a stranger to it; it is also a fiend to its own offspring — worse than the Persian host who murdered his own guests, it does not spare even the creatures it has spawned itself. Like a savage tigress thrashing in the jungle who rolls over on her own cubs and smothers them, the sea dashes even the mightiest whales against the rocks and leaves them there beside the split wrecks of ships. No mercy, no power but its own, governs it. Panting and snorting like a mad warhorse that has lost its rider, the masterless ocean overruns the globe.

Consider the subtlety of the sea — how its most dreaded creatures glide under water, invisible for the most part, treacherously hidden beneath the loveliest shades of blue. Consider also the devilish brilliance and beauty of many of its most merciless species, like the elegantly shaped bodies of many kinds of sharks. Consider, once more, the universal cannibalism of the sea, all of whose creatures prey upon each other, waging eternal war since the world began.

Consider all this, and then turn to this green, gentle, and most docile earth. Consider them both — the sea and the land — and do you not find a strange parallel to something in yourself? For as this appalling ocean surrounds the green land, so in the soul of man there lies one island Tahiti, full of peace and joy, but surrounded by all the horrors of the half-known life. God keep you! Do not push off from that island — you can never return!

chapters.title: Chapter 59 — Squid
paragraphs: Slowly wading through the meadows of brit, the Pequod still held her course northeast toward the island of Java. A gentle breeze pushed her keel, so that in the surrounding calm her three tall tapering masts swayed mildly to the lazy wind, like three palm trees on a plain. And still, at wide intervals in the silvery night, the lonely, beckoning jet would be seen.

But one transparent blue morning, when a stillness almost supernatural spread over the sea — though with no stagnant calm about it — when the long burnished path of sunlight on the waters seemed a golden finger laid across them, commanding some secrecy, when the slippered waves whispered together as they softly ran on — in this profound hush of the visible world, a strange apparition was seen by Daggoo from the main-masthead.

In the distance, a great white mass lazily rose, and rising higher and higher, disentangling itself from the blue, at last gleamed before our bow like a snow-slide, freshly slipped from the hills. Thus glistening for a moment, it slowly sank. Then once more it arose and silently gleamed. It did not seem a whale — and yet, was this Moby Dick? thought Daggoo. Again the phantom went down, but reappearing once more, with a stiletto-like cry that startled every man from his drowse, the negro yelled out, "There! There again! There she breaches! Right ahead! The White Whale, the White Whale!"

At this the seamen rushed out to the yardarms, the way bees rush to the branches at swarming time. Ahab stood bareheaded on the bowsprit in the sweltering sun, one hand thrust far behind him, ready to signal his orders to the helmsman, and turned his eager gaze in the direction that Daggoo's outstretched, motionless arm was pointing from aloft.

Perhaps the drifting company of that one still, solitary jet had slowly worked on Ahab, so that he was now ready to link ideas of mildness and calm with the first sight of the particular whale he was hunting; or perhaps his eagerness got the better of him. Whichever it was, the moment he clearly made out the white mass, he gave orders, with quick intensity, to lower the boats.

The four boats were soon in the water, Ahab's in the lead, all pulling hard toward their prey. Soon the thing went down, and as we waited, oars raised, for it to reappear — look! — it slowly rose again in the very spot where it had sunk. Almost forgetting Moby Dick for the moment, we now stared at the most astonishing phenomenon the secret seas have yet revealed to mankind. A vast pulpy mass, furlongs long and wide, of a gleaming cream color, lay floating on the water, with countless long arms radiating from its center, curling and twisting like a nest of anacondas, as though groping blindly for any unlucky object within reach. It had no face or front that could be made out, no conceivable sign of either feeling or instinct; it simply rippled there on the waves, an unearthly, shapeless, chance-like apparition of life.

As with a low sucking sound it slowly disappeared again, Starbuck, still gazing at the agitated waters where it had sunk, exclaimed with a wild voice — "I would almost rather have seen Moby Dick and fought him than have seen you, white ghost!"
"What was it, sir?" said Flask.
"The great live squid, which, they say, few whale-ships have ever seen and returned to their ports to tell of it."
But Ahab said nothing. Turning his boat, he sailed back to the vessel. The rest silently followed.

Whatever superstitions sperm whalemen in general have attached to the sight of this object, one thing is certain: because a glimpse of it is so very rare, that fact alone has done much to give it an air of ill omen. It is seen so seldom that, although every one of them declares it the largest living thing in the ocean, very few have more than the haziest notions of its real nature and shape. Even so, they believe it provides the sperm whale with his only food. Other kinds of whales find their food above water, where men can watch them eating; but the spermaceti whale gets all his food in unknown zones below the surface, and what exactly it consists of can only be worked out by inference. Sometimes, when hard pressed, he will throw up what are thought to be the detached arms of the squid, some of them more than twenty and thirty feet long. The whalemen imagine that the monster these arms belonged to usually clings by them to the ocean floor, and that the sperm whale, unlike other species, has teeth so that he can attack it and tear it apart.

There seems some ground for imagining that the great Kraken of Bishop Pontoppodan may ultimately turn out to be a squid. The way the Bishop describes it — as alternately rising and sinking, with certain other details he provides — in all this, the two correspond. But much allowance must be made for the incredible size he assigns it.

By some naturalists who have vaguely heard rumors of the mysterious creature spoken of here, it is classed among the cuttlefish, to which, indeed, in certain outward respects it would seem to belong — but only as the Anak of the tribe — its biblical giant.

chapters.title: Chapter 60 — The Line
paragraphs: With reference to the whaling scene soon to be described, as well as for the better understanding of all similar scenes presented elsewhere, I must speak here of the magical, sometimes horrible whale-line.

The line originally used in the fishery was of the best hemp, only lightly treated with tar vapor, not saturated with tar as ordinary ropes are. For while tar, as ordinarily used, makes the hemp more pliable for the ropemaker, and also makes the rope itself more convenient for the sailor in common ship use, not only would the ordinary quantity stiffen the whale-line too much for the close coiling it must undergo; but, as most seamen are beginning to learn, tar in general by no means adds to a rope's durability or strength, however much compactness and gloss it may give it.

In recent years, Manila rope has in the American fishery almost entirely replaced hemp as a material for whale-lines. Though not as durable as hemp, it is stronger and far more soft and elastic. And I will add — since there is an aesthetics in all things — it is much more handsome and becoming to the boat than hemp. Hemp is a dusky, dark fellow, a sort of Indian; but Manila is like a golden-haired Circassian to look at.

The whale-line is only two-thirds of an inch thick. At first sight you would not think it as strong as it really is. By experiment, each of its fifty-one yarns will suspend a weight of one hundred and twenty pounds, so that the whole rope will bear a strain nearly equal to three tons. In length, the common sperm whale-line measures something over two hundred fathoms. Toward the stern of the boat it is spirally coiled away in the tub — not like the worm-pipe (the coiled tube) of a still, though, but so as to form one round, cheese-shaped mass of densely bedded "sheaves," or layers of concentric spirals, without any hollow except the "heart," the tiny vertical tube formed at the axis of the cheese. Since the least tangle or kink in the coiling would, as the line ran out, infallibly take off somebody's arm, leg, or entire body, the utmost care is taken in stowing the line in its tub. Some harpooners will spend almost an entire morning at this business, carrying the line high aloft and then reeving it downward through a block toward the tub, so as to free it of every possible wrinkle and twist in the act of coiling.

In the English boats two tubs are used instead of one, the same line being continuously coiled in both tubs. There is some advantage in this, because these twin tubs, being so small, fit more readily into the boat and do not strain it so much; whereas the American tub, nearly three feet in diameter and of proportionate depth, makes rather bulky freight for a craft whose planks are only half an inch thick; for the bottom of the whale-boat is like ice at the critical point, which will bear up a considerable weight if it is spread out, but not very much if it is concentrated. When the painted canvas cover is clapped on the American line-tub, the boat looks as if it were pulling off with a prodigious great wedding-cake to present to the whales.

Both ends of the line are exposed; the lower end finishes in an eye-splice, or loop, which comes up from the bottom against the side of the tub and hangs over its edge, completely free of everything. This arrangement of the lower end is necessary for two reasons. First: to make it easier to fasten to it an additional line from a neighboring boat, in case the struck whale should sound (dive) so deep as to threaten to carry off the entire line originally attached to the harpoon. In these instances the whale is, of course, passed like a mug of ale, as it were, from the one boat to the other; though the first boat always hovers close by to assist its partner. Second: this arrangement is indispensable for common safety's sake; for if the lower end of the line were in any way attached to the boat, and the whale were then to run the line out to the end almost in a single smoking minute, as he sometimes does, he would not stop there, for the doomed boat would infallibly be dragged down after him into the depths of the sea; and in that case no town-crier would ever find her again.

Before the boat is lowered for the chase, the upper end of the line is brought aft from the tub, taken around the loggerhead there (a stout wooden post in the stern), and then carried forward again along the whole length of the boat. It rests crosswise on the loom, or handle, of every man's oar, so that it bumps against his wrist as he rows, and it also runs between the men, who sit alternately at opposite gunwales, up to the leaded chocks, or grooves, in the sharp tip of the prow, where a wooden pin or skewer about the size of an ordinary quill keeps it from slipping out. From the chocks it hangs in a slight festoon over the bows and then comes back inside the boat. Some ten or twenty fathoms of it (called box-line) are coiled on the box in the bows, and from there it goes on to the gunwale a little farther aft, where it is fastened to the short-warp — the rope attached directly to the harpoon. Before that connection is made, though, the short-warp goes through various mystifications too tedious to describe.

Thus the whale-line folds the whole boat in its complicated coils, twisting and writhing around it in almost every direction. All the oarsmen are caught up in its perilous contortions, so that to the timid eye of the landsman they seem like Indian jugglers, with the deadliest snakes playfully draped around their limbs. No son of mortal woman can seat himself for the first time amid those hempen intricacies and, while straining his utmost at the oar, reflect that at any unknown instant the harpoon may be darted and all these horrible contortions be set in play like ringed lightning — no one can be placed like that without a shudder that makes the very marrow in his bones quiver like a shaken jelly. Yet habit — strange thing! what can habit not accomplish? — livelier sallies, merrier mirth, better jokes, and brighter repartee you never heard over your mahogany dinner table than you will hear over the half-inch white cedar of the whale-boat, when it is hung with hangman's nooses like this; and, like the six burghers of Calais before King Edward, the six men who make up the crew pull into the jaws of death with a halter around every neck, as you might say.

Perhaps a very little thought will now enable you to account for those repeated whaling disasters — some few of which are casually recorded — of this man or that man being taken out of the boat by the line and lost. For when the line is darting out, to be seated in the boat then is like being seated in the midst of the manifold whizzings of a steam-engine in full play, when every flying beam and shaft and wheel is grazing you. It is worse; for you cannot sit motionless in the heart of these perils, because the boat is rocking like a cradle, and you are pitched one way and the other without the slightest warning; and only by a certain self-adjusting buoyancy, and by willing and acting in the same instant, can you escape being made a Mazeppa of (like Byron's hero, lashed to a runaway horse) and carried off where the all-seeing sun himself could never pick you out.

Again: the deep calm that only seems to come before the storm and foretell it is perhaps more dreadful than the storm itself, since the calm is really just the wrapper and envelope of the storm, holding it inside, as the harmless-looking rifle holds the deadly powder, the ball, and the explosion. In the same way, the graceful repose of the line as it silently snakes around the oarsmen before it comes into actual play carries more real terror than any other part of this dangerous business. But why say more? All men live wrapped in whale-lines. All are born with nooses around their necks; but mortals only realize the silent, subtle, ever-present dangers of life when they are caught in the swift, sudden turn of death. And if you are a philosopher, then sitting in the whale-boat you would not feel one bit more terror at heart than if you were sitting by your evening fire with a poker, not a harpoon, beside you.

chapters.title: Chapter 61 — Stubb Kills a Whale
paragraphs: If Starbuck saw the apparition of the Squid as an omen, Queequeg saw it as something else entirely.
"When you see him squid," said the savage, honing his harpoon in the bow of his hoisted boat, "then you quick see him sperm whale."

The next day was exceedingly still and sultry, and with nothing special to occupy them, the Pequod's crew could hardly resist the spell of sleep brought on by such an empty sea. For this part of the Indian Ocean through which we were then voyaging is not what whalemen call a lively ground; that is, it offers fewer glimpses of porpoises, dolphins, flying fish, and other lively inhabitants of busier waters than the grounds off the Rio de la Plata, or the in-shore ground off Peru.

It was my turn to stand watch at the foremast-head, and with my shoulders leaning against the slack royal shrouds, I swayed lazily back and forth in what felt like enchanted air. No resolve could hold out against it. Losing all awareness in that dreamy mood, my soul finally left my body, though my body went on swaying as a pendulum does long after the force that set it moving has been removed.

Before I lost myself completely, I had noticed that the men at the main and mizzen mastheads were already drowsy. So in the end all three of us hung swinging lifelessly from the spars, and for every swing we made, the dozing helmsman below gave a nod. The waves, too, nodded their lazy crests; and across the wide trance of the sea, east nodded to west, and the sun over all.

Suddenly bubbles seemed to burst under my closed eyelids; my hands clamped onto the shrouds like vises; some unseen, merciful power saved me; with a jolt I came back to life. And there! Close under our lee, not forty fathoms away, a gigantic Sperm Whale lay rolling in the water like the overturned hull of a frigate, his broad, glossy back, the hue of an Ethiopian's, shining in the sun like a mirror. As he rocked lazily in the trough of the sea, calmly spouting his misty jet every now and then, the whale looked like a stout burgher smoking his pipe on a warm afternoon. But that pipe, poor whale, was your last. As if touched by some magician's wand, the drowsy ship and every sleeper aboard sprang awake at once; and more than twenty voices from every part of the vessel, together with the three cries from aloft, raised the familiar shout, while the great fish slowly and steadily spouted the sparkling brine into the air.
"Clear away the boats! Luff!" cried Ahab. And obeying his own order, he slammed the helm down before the helmsman could reach the spokes.

The crew's sudden shouts must have alarmed the whale, because before the boats were down he turned majestically and swam off to leeward — yet so steadily and calmly, raising so few ripples, that Ahab, thinking he might not be alarmed yet after all, ordered that no oar be used and that nobody speak above a whisper. So, sitting on the gunwales like Ontario Indians, we paddled along swiftly but silently; the calm made it impossible to set the noiseless sails. Soon, as we glided after him like this, the monster flipped his tail straight up forty feet into the air and then sank out of sight like a tower swallowed up.

"There go flukes!" was the cry — an announcement immediately followed by Stubb's producing his match and lighting his pipe, for now a breathing space was granted. After the full interval of his sounding (his deep dive) had passed, the whale rose again, and being now ahead of the smoker's boat, and much nearer to it than to any of the others, Stubb counted on the honor of the capture. It was obvious now that the whale had at last become aware of his pursuers. All cautious silence was therefore no longer of any use. Paddles were dropped, and oars came loudly into play. And still puffing at his pipe, Stubb cheered his crew on to the attack.
Yes, a mighty change had come over the fish. Fully alive to his danger, he was going "head out," his head projecting at a slant from the mad yeast he was brewing.*

*It will be seen elsewhere what a very light substance the entire interior of the sperm whale's enormous head consists of. Though apparently the most massive, it is by far the most buoyant part of him. So he raises it into the air with ease, and invariably does so when going at his utmost speed. Besides, such is the breadth of the upper part of the front of his head, and such the tapering, cutwater shape of the lower part, that by raising his head at a slant he may be said to transform himself from a bluff-bowed, sluggish galliot (a broad Dutch cargo boat) into a sharp-pointed New York pilot-boat.

"Start her, start her, my men! Don't hurry yourselves — take plenty of time — but start her; start her like thunderclaps, that's all," cried Stubb, sputtering out smoke as he spoke. "Start her, now; give them the long and strong stroke, Tashtego. Start her, Tash, my boy — start her, all; but keep cool, keep cool — cucumbers is the word — easy, easy — only start her like grim death and grinning devils, and raise the buried dead straight up out of their graves, boys — that's all. Start her!"

"Woo-hoo! Wa-hee!" screamed the Gay Header in reply, raising some old war-whoop to the skies, as every oarsman in the straining boat involuntarily lurched forward with the one tremendous leading stroke the eager Indian gave.
But his wild screams were answered by others equally wild. "Kee-hee! Kee-hee!" yelled Daggoo, straining forward and backward on his seat like a pacing tiger in his cage.

"Ka-la! Koo-loo!" howled Queequeg, as if smacking his lips over a mouthful of grenadier's steak. And so with oars and yells the keels cut the sea. Meanwhile, Stubb, keeping his place in the lead, still urged his men on to the attack, all the while puffing smoke from his mouth. Like desperadoes they tugged and strained, until the welcome cry was heard — "Stand up, Tashtego! — give it to him!" The harpoon was hurled. "Stern all!" The oarsmen backed water; at the same moment something went hot and hissing along every one of their wrists. It was the magical line. An instant before, Stubb had swiftly taken two extra turns with it around the loggerhead (the post in the stern around which the line is snubbed), from which, because of its increasingly rapid circling, a blue smoke of hemp now jetted up and mingled with the steady fumes from his pipe. As the line passed round and round the loggerhead, so also, just before reaching that point, it passed blisteringly through and through both of Stubb's hands, from which the hand-cloths — squares of quilted canvas sometimes worn at such times — had accidentally dropped. It was like holding an enemy's sharp two-edged sword by the blade, with that enemy all the time struggling to wrench it out of your grip.

"Wet the line! Wet the line!" cried Stubb to the tub oarsman (the one seated by the tub), who, snatching off his hat, dashed seawater into it.* More turns were taken, so that the line began to hold its place. The boat now flew through the boiling water like a shark all fins. Stubb and Tashtego here changed places — stem for stern — a staggering business indeed in that rocking commotion.

*Partly to show how indispensable this act is, it may be stated here that in the old Dutch fishery a mop was used to dash the running line with water; in many other ships, a wooden piggin, or bailer, is set aside for that purpose. Your hat, however, is the most convenient.

From the vibrating line stretching the entire length of the upper part of the boat, and from its now being tighter than a harpstring, you would have thought the craft had two keels — one cleaving the water, the other the air — as the boat churned on through both opposing elements at once. A continual cascade played at the bows; a ceaseless whirling eddy in her wake; and at the slightest motion from within, even of just a little finger, the vibrating, cracking craft tipped her spasmodic gunwale over into the sea. So they rushed on, each man clinging to his seat with all his might to keep from being tossed into the foam, and the tall form of Tashtego at the steering oar crouching almost double to bring down his center of gravity. Whole Atlantics and Pacifics seemed to pass as they shot on their way, until at last the whale somewhat slackened his flight.

"Haul in — haul in!" cried Stubb to the bowsman; and, facing round toward the whale, all hands began pulling the boat up to him while the boat was still being towed along. Soon drawing up alongside his flank, Stubb, firmly planting his knee in the clumsy cleat, darted dart after dart into the fleeing fish; at the word of command, the boat alternately backed away out of reach of the whale's horrible wallowing, and then drew up again for another throw.

Now the red tide poured from every side of the monster like brooks running downhill. His tortured body rolled not in brine but in blood, which bubbled and seethed for furlongs in their wake. The slanting sun, playing over this crimson pond in the sea, threw its reflection back into every face, so that the men all glowed at one another like red men. And all the while the whale's spout-hole shot out jet after jet of white smoke in agony, and the excited headsman's mouth shot out puff after furious puff; for after every dart Stubb hauled in his bent lance (by the line tied to it), straightened it again and again with a few quick blows against the gunwale, and then drove it into the whale again and again.

"Pull up — pull up!" he now cried to the bowsman, as the waning whale slackened in his wrath. "Pull up! — close to!" And the boat drew up along the fish's flank. Then, reaching far over the bow, Stubb slowly churned his long sharp lance into the fish, and kept it there, carefully churning and churning, as if cautiously feeling for some gold watch that the whale might have swallowed, and which he was afraid of breaking before he could hook it out. But that gold watch he sought was the innermost life of the fish. And now it is struck; for, starting from his trance into that unspeakable thing called his "flurry," the monster wallowed horribly in his blood and wrapped himself in impenetrable, mad, boiling spray, so that the endangered boat, instantly dropping astern, had a hard time struggling blindly out of that frenzied twilight into the clear air of the day.

And now, his flurry subsiding, the whale once more rolled into view, surging from side to side, spasmodically expanding and contracting his spout-hole with sharp, cracking, agonized breaths. At last, gush after gush of clotted red gore, as if it were the purple dregs of red wine, shot into the frightened air, and falling back again, ran dripping down his motionless flanks into the sea. His heart had burst!
"He's dead, Mr. Stubb," said Daggoo.
"Yes — both pipes smoked out!" And withdrawing his own pipe from his mouth, Stubb scattered the dead ashes over the water, and for a moment stood thoughtfully eyeing the vast corpse he had made.

chapters.title: Chapter 62 — The Dart
paragraphs: A word concerning an incident in the last chapter.

According to the invariable custom of the fishery, the whale-boat pushes off from the ship with the headsman, or whale-killer, as temporary steersman, and the harpooner, or whale-fastener, pulling the foremost oar, the one known as the harpooner-oar. Now it takes a strong, nervy arm to strike the first iron into the fish; for often, in what is called a long dart, the heavy implement has to be flung a distance of twenty or thirty feet. But however long and exhausting the chase, the harpooner is expected to pull his oar to the utmost all the while; indeed, he is expected to set the rest an example of superhuman activity, not only by incredible rowing, but by repeated loud and fearless shouts; and what it is to keep shouting at the top of your voice while every other muscle is strained and half wrenched out of place — that no one knows but those who have tried it. For my part, I cannot bawl very heartily and work very recklessly at one and the same time. In this straining, bawling state, then, with his back to the fish, the exhausted harpooner all at once hears the exciting cry — "Stand up, and give it to him!" He now has to drop and secure his oar, turn halfway round on his center, seize his harpoon from the crotch, and with what little strength may remain, try to pitch it somehow into the whale. No wonder, taking the whole fleet of whalemen together, that out of fifty fair chances for a dart, not five are successful; no wonder that so many luckless harpooners are madly cursed and demoted; no wonder that some of them actually burst their blood-vessels in the boat; no wonder that some sperm whalemen are gone four years with four barrels; no wonder that to many shipowners whaling is nothing but a losing business; for it is the harpooner who makes the voyage, and if you take the breath out of his body, how can you expect to find it there when it is most wanted!

Then again, if the dart hits home, at the second critical moment — when the whale starts to run — the boatheader and harpooner likewise start running fore and aft, putting themselves and everyone else in imminent danger. That is when they swap places, and the headsman, the chief officer of the little craft, takes his proper post in the bow.

Now, I don't care who says otherwise: all this is both foolish and unnecessary. The headsman should stay in the bow from start to finish. He should throw both the harpoon and the lance, and no rowing at all should be expected of him, except in circumstances any fisherman would recognize. I know this would sometimes cost a little speed in the chase; but the long experience of many whalemen of more than one nation has convinced me that in the great majority of failures in the fishery, the cause has by no means been so much the whale's speed as the harpooner's exhaustion that I described earlier.
To make the dart as effective as possible, the harpooners of this world must spring to their feet from rest, not from hard labor.

chapters.title: Chapter 63 — The Crotch
paragraphs: The branches grow out of the trunk, and the twigs out of the branches. In the same way, in productive subjects, the chapters grow.

The crotch mentioned on a previous page deserves a mention of its own. It is a notched stick of a peculiar shape, some two feet long, which is inserted upright into the starboard gunwale near the bow, to provide a rest for the wooden end of the harpoon, whose other, naked, barbed end projects at a slant from the prow. In this way the weapon is instantly at hand for its thrower, who snatches it up from its rest as readily as a backwoodsman swings his rifle down from the wall. It is customary to have two harpoons resting in the crotch, called respectively the first and second irons.

But these two harpoons, each by its own cord, are both connected with the line; the object being this: to dart them both, if possible, one instantly after the other into the same whale, so that if, in the coming drag, one should pull out, the other may still keep its hold. It is a doubling of the chances. But it very often happens that, owing to the instantaneous, violent, convulsive running of the whale on receiving the first iron, it becomes impossible for the harpooner, however lightning-quick his movements, to pitch the second iron into him. Nevertheless, since the second iron is already connected with the line, and the line is running, that weapon must at all events be tossed out of the boat in advance, somehow and somewhere; otherwise all hands would be in the most terrible danger. So in such cases it is tumbled into the water, the spare coils of box line (mentioned in a preceding chapter) making this feat, in most instances, prudently possible. But this critical act is not always free of the saddest and most fatal accidents.

Something else you should know: once the second iron has been thrown overboard, it turns into a dangling, sharp-edged menace, darting skittishly about both boat and whale, fouling the lines or slicing them, and causing a tremendous stir in every direction. And as a rule it cannot be secured again until the whale has been properly caught and is a corpse.

Consider, now, how it must be when four boats are all engaging one unusually strong, active, and knowing whale; when, owing to these qualities in him, as well as to the thousand coinciding accidents of such a daring enterprise, eight or ten loose second irons may be dangling about him at once. For, of course, each boat is supplied with several harpoons to bend on to the line should the first one be darted without effect and not recovered. All these particulars are faithfully set down here, as they will not fail to shed light on several most important, however intricate, passages in scenes to be painted later.

chapters.title: Chapter 64 — Stubb’s Supper
paragraphs: Stubb's whale had been killed some way off from the ship. There was a dead calm, so we formed a tandem of three boats and began the slow job of towing the trophy back to the Pequod. Hour after hour we eighteen men, with our thirty-six arms and one hundred and eighty thumbs and fingers, labored at that inert, sluggish corpse in the sea, and it seemed hardly to budge at all except at long intervals — plenty of proof of how enormous a mass we were moving. On the great canal of Hang-Ho, or whatever they call it, in China, four or five laborers on the towpath can haul a bulky loaded junk at a mile an hour; but this grand argosy of ours forged heavily along as if its hold were packed with pig-lead.

Darkness fell, but three lights hung up and down the Pequod's main-rigging dimly showed us the way; and as we drew nearer we saw Ahab lowering one of several more lanterns over the bulwarks. He looked blankly at the heaving whale for a moment, gave the usual orders for making it fast for the night, and then handed his lantern to a seaman and went off into the cabin, not coming forward again until morning.

Captain Ahab had shown his usual activity, if you can call it that, in directing the chase of this whale; but now that the creature was dead, some vague dissatisfaction, impatience, or despair seemed to be at work in him — as if the sight of that dead body reminded him that Moby Dick was still to be killed, and that even if a thousand other whales were brought to his ship, not one of them would bring his grand, monomaniac goal one jot closer. Soon, from the noise on the Pequod's decks, you would have thought all hands were getting ready to drop anchor in the deep; heavy chains are being dragged along the deck and shoved rattling out through the portholes. But those clanking links are meant to moor not the ship but the vast corpse itself. Tied by the head to the stern and by the tail to the bows, the whale now lies with its black hull close against the vessel's; and seen through the dark of night, which hid the spars and rigging overhead, the two — ship and whale — looked yoked together like colossal bullocks, one lying down while the other stands.*

*A little item may as well be told here. The strongest and most reliable hold the ship has on the whale when moored alongside is by the flukes, or tail; and since that part, from its greater density, is relatively heavier than any other (except the side-fins), its flexibility, even in death, makes it sink low beneath the surface, so that you cannot reach it by hand from the boat to put the chain around it. But this difficulty is ingeniously overcome: a small, strong line is prepared with a wooden float at its outer end and a weight in its middle, while the other end is made fast to the ship. By skillful management the wooden float is made to rise on the other side of the mass, so that, the line having now girdled the whale, the chain is easily made to follow; and being slipped along the body, it is at last locked fast around the smallest part of the tail, where it joins the broad flukes or lobes.

If moody Ahab was now all stillness, at least as far as could be known on deck, Stubb, his second mate, flushed with conquest, showed an unusual but still good-natured excitement. He was in such an unaccustomed bustle that the sober Starbuck, his official superior, quietly left the sole management of affairs to him for the time being. One small contributing cause of all this liveliness in Stubb was soon made strangely plain. Stubb was a high liver; he was somewhat intemperately fond of the whale as a thing flavorful to his palate.
"A steak, a steak, before I sleep! You, Daggoo! Overboard you go, and cut me one from his small!"

It should be known here that although these wild fishermen do not, as a general rule, follow the great military maxim of making the enemy pay the running expenses of the war (at least not before realizing the proceeds of the voyage), yet now and then you find some of these Nantucketers who have a genuine relish for that particular part of the Sperm Whale that Stubb named, which takes in the tapering end of the body.

Around midnight the steak was cut and cooked, and by the light of two sperm-oil lanterns Stubb stood up stoutly to his spermaceti supper at the capstan-head, as though the capstan were a sideboard. Nor was Stubb the only one feasting on whale meat that night. Thousands upon thousands of sharks, swarming around the dead leviathan, mixed their mumblings with his chewing as they feasted noisily on its fat. The few sleepers in their bunks below were often startled by the sharp slap of the sharks' tails against the hull, only a few inches from their hearts. If you peered over the side you could just make them out (having heard them first), wallowing in the sullen black water and rolling onto their backs as they scooped huge round chunks the size of a human head out of the whale. This particular feat of the shark seems almost miraculous. How they manage to gouge such symmetrical mouthfuls out of a surface that looks impossible to bite into remains part of the universal problem of all things. The mark they leave on the whale is best compared to the hollow a carpenter makes when countersinking for a screw.

Amid all the smoking horror and devilry of a sea-fight, sharks can be seen gazing longingly up at the ship's decks, like hungry dogs around a table where red meat is being carved, ready to gulp down every dead man thrown to them. While the valiant butchers at the deck-table are cannibally carving one another's live flesh with gilded, tasseled carving-knives, the sharks, with their jewel-hilted mouths, are carving away quarrelsomely under the table at the dead meat — and if you turned the whole affair upside down it would still be much the same thing, that is, a shocking, sharkish business all round. Sharks are also the unfailing outriders of every slave ship crossing the Atlantic, trotting methodically alongside, handy in case a parcel needs carrying somewhere or a dead slave needs a decent burial. And one or two other such cases could be listed, concerning the set times, places, and occasions when sharks gather most sociably and feast most hilariously. Yet there is no conceivable time or occasion when you will find them in such countless numbers, or in gayer and more jovial spirits, than around a dead sperm whale moored at night to a whaleship at sea. If you have never seen that sight, then hold off deciding whether devil-worship is proper and whether it is wise to keep on the good side of the devil.
But as yet Stubb paid no attention to the mumblings of the banquet going on so close to him, any more than the sharks noticed the smacking of his own gourmet lips.

"Cook, cook! — where's that old Fleece?" he cried at length, spreading his legs still wider as if to form a more secure base for his supper, and at the same time stabbing his fork into the dish as if it were a lance. "Cook, you cook! — sail this way, cook!"

The old black, in no great glee at having already been roused from his warm hammock at a most unseasonable hour, came shambling out of his galley. Like many old blacks, he had something wrong with his knee-pans, which he did not keep as well scoured as his other pans. This old Fleece, as they called him, came shuffling and limping along, propping up his step with his tongs, a clumsy pair made of straightened iron hoops. This old Ebony floundered forward and, as ordered, stopped dead on the far side of Stubb's sideboard. Then, with both hands folded in front of him and resting on his two-legged cane, he bent his arched back over still further, tilting his head to one side at the same time so as to bring his better ear into play.

"Cook," said Stubb, quickly lifting a rather reddish morsel to his mouth, "don't you think this steak is rather overdone? You've been beating this steak too much, cook; it's too tender. Don't I always say that to be good, a whale steak must be tough? There are those sharks now over the side — don't you see they prefer it tough and rare? What a racket they're kicking up! Cook, go and talk to them; tell them they are welcome to help themselves civilly, and in moderation, but they must keep quiet. Blast me if I can hear my own voice. Away, cook, and deliver my message. Here, take this lantern," snatching one from his sideboard; "now then, go and preach to them!"

Sullenly, old Fleece took the lantern he was offered and limped across the deck to the bulwarks. Then, holding his light low over the sea with one hand to get a good look at his congregation, he solemnly waved his tongs with the other, leaned far out over the side, and began to address the sharks in a mumbling voice, while Stubb crept softly up behind him and overheard everything that was said.

"Fellow-critters: I'se ordered here to say dat you must stop dat damn noise dere. You hear? Stop dat damn smackin' of de lip! Massa Stubb say dat you can fill your damn bellies up to de hatches, but by Gor! you must stop dat damn racket!"
"Cook," Stubb cut in here, with a sudden slap on the shoulder, "Cook! Why, damn your eyes, you mustn't swear that way when you're preaching. That's no way to convert sinners, cook!"
"Who dat? Den preach to him yourself," sullenly turning to go.
"No, cook. Go on, go on."
"Well, den, beloved fellow-critters:" —
"Right!" exclaimed Stubb approvingly. "Coax them into it. Try that." And Fleece continued.

"Though you is all sharks, and by natur' very voracious, yet I say to you, fellow-critters, dat dat voraciousness — 'top dat damn slappin' of de tail! How you tink to hear, s'pose you keep up such a damn slappin' and bitin' dere?"
"Cook," cried Stubb, grabbing him by the collar, "I won't have that swearing. Talk to them like a gentleman."
Once more the sermon proceeded.

"Your voraciousness, fellow-critters, I don't blame you so much for; dat is natur', and can't be helped; but to govern dat wicked natur', dat is de point. You is sharks, certain; but if you govern de shark in you, why den you be angel; for all angel is nothin' more dan de shark well governed. Now, look here, brethren, just try once to be civil, a-helpin' yourselves from dat whale. Don't be tearin' de blubber out of your neighbor's mouth, I say. Ain't one shark got as good a right as de other to dat whale? And, by Gor, none of you has de right to dat whale; dat whale belong to somebody else. I know some of you has very big mouth, bigger dan others; but den de big mouths sometimes has de small bellies; so dat de bigness of de mouth is not to swallow wid, but to bite off de blubber for de small fry of sharks, dat can't get into de crush to help demselves."
"Well done, old Fleece!" cried Stubb. "That's Christianity. Go on."

"No use goin' on; de damn villains will keep a-jostlin' and slappin' each other, Massa Stubb; dey don't hear one word; no use a-preachin' to such damn gluttons as you call 'em, till dere bellies is full, and dere bellies is bottomless; and when dey do get 'em full, dey won't hear you den; for den dey sink in de sea, go fast to sleep on de coral, and can't hear nothin' at all, no more, for ever and ever."
"Upon my soul, I am about of the same opinion. So give the benediction, Fleece, and I'll get back to my supper."
Upon this, Fleece, holding both hands over the fishy mob, raised his shrill voice and cried —
"Cussed fellow-critters! Kick up de damnedest row as ever you can; fill your damn bellies till dey bust — and den die."
"Now, cook," said Stubb, resuming his supper at the capstan, "stand just where you stood before, there, across from me, and pay particular attention."
"All 'tention," said Fleece, again stooping over his tongs in the desired position.
"Well," said Stubb, helping himself generously meanwhile, "I shall now go back to the subject of this steak. In the first place, how old are you, cook?"
"What dat do wid de steak?" said the old black, testily.
"Silence! How old are you, cook?"
"'Bout ninety, dey say," he muttered gloomily.

"And you have lived in this world close to one hundred years, cook, and don't know yet how to cook a whale steak?" — rapidly swallowing another mouthful at the last word, so that it seemed a continuation of the question. "Where were you born, cook?"
"'Hind de hatchway, in ferry-boat, goin' over de Roanoke."
"Born on a ferryboat! That's odd, too. But I want to know what country you were born in, cook!"
"Didn't I say de Roanoke country?" he cried sharply.
"No, you didn't, cook. But I'll tell you what I'm getting at, cook. You must go home and be born all over again. You don't know how to cook a whale steak yet."
"Bress my soul if I cook anoder one," he growled angrily, turning around to leave.

"Come back, cook — here, hand me those tongs — now take that bit of steak there, and tell me if you think that steak is cooked as it should be? Take it, I say" — holding the tongs toward him — "take it, and taste it."
Faintly smacking his withered lips over it for a moment, the old negro muttered, "Best cooked steak I ever taste; joosy, very joosy."
"Cook," said Stubb, squaring himself once more, "do you belong to the church?"
"Passed one once in Cape-Down," said the old man sullenly.

"And you have once in your life passed a holy church in Cape Town, where you no doubt overheard a holy parson addressing his listeners as his beloved fellow-creatures — have you, cook! And yet you come here and tell me such a dreadful lie as you just did, eh?" said Stubb. "Where do you expect to go, cook?"
"Go to bed very soon," he mumbled, half-turning as he spoke.
"Halt! Heave to! I mean when you die, cook. It's an awful question. Now what's your answer?"
"When dis old black man dies," said the negro slowly, changing his whole air and manner, "he hisself won't go nowhere; but some bressed angel will come and fetch him."
"Fetch him? How? In a coach and four, as they fetched Elijah? And fetch him where?"
"Up dere," said Fleece, holding his tongs straight over his head and keeping them there very solemnly.
"So you expect to go up to our main-top when you die, do you, cook? But don't you know that the higher you climb, the colder it gets? The main-top, eh?"
"Didn't say dat at all," said Fleece, sulking again.

"You said up there, didn't you? And now look for yourself and see where your tongs are pointing. But perhaps you expect to get into heaven by crawling through the lubber's hole (the opening through a mast's top platform that novice climbers use), cook; but no, no, cook, you don't get there unless you go the regular way, round by the rigging. It's a ticklish business, but it must be done, or else it's no go. But none of us are in heaven yet. Drop your tongs, cook, and hear my orders. Do you hear? Hold your hat in one hand, and clap the other on top of your heart when I'm giving my orders, cook. What! That your heart, there? — that's your gizzard! Aloft! Aloft! — that's it — now you have it. Hold it there now, and pay attention."
"All 'tention," said the old black, placing both hands as requested, vainly wriggling his grizzled head as if trying to get both ears in front at one and the same time.

"Well then, cook, you see, this whale steak of yours was so very bad that I've put it out of sight as fast as I could; you see that, don't you? Well, from now on, when you cook another whale steak for my private table here, the capstan, I'll tell you what to do so you don't spoil it by overcooking. Hold the steak in one hand and show a live coal to it with the other; once that's done, serve it up. Hear me? And tomorrow, cook, when we're cutting in the fish, make sure you're standing by to get the tips of his fins; have them pickled. As for the ends of the flukes, have them soused, cook. There, now you can go."
But Fleece had hardly gotten three steps away when he was called back.
"Cook, give me cutlets for supper tomorrow night during the mid-watch. Do you hear? Away you sail, then. — Wait! Stop! Make a bow before you go. — Hold on! Whale-balls for breakfast — don't forget."

"Wish, by Gor, whale eat him, 'stead of him eat whale. I'm bressed if he ain't more of shark dan Massa Shark hisself," muttered the old man, limping away; and with this sage outburst he went to his hammock.

chapters.title: Chapter 65 — The Whale as a Dish
paragraphs: That a mortal man should dine on the very creature that fuels his lamp, and, like Stubb, eat him by his own light, so to speak, seems so outlandish a thing that we have to look a little into its history and philosophy.

The records show that three centuries ago the Right Whale's tongue was prized as a great delicacy in France, where it fetched high prices. They also show that in the time of Henry VIII a certain court cook won a handsome reward for inventing an admirable sauce to go with barbecued porpoises, which, you will remember, are a species of whale. Porpoises, in fact, are still thought fine eating today. The meat is rolled into balls about the size of billiard balls, and when well seasoned and spiced it could pass for turtle-balls or veal balls. The old monks of Dunfermline loved them. The crown had given them a large grant of porpoises.

The fact is that, among his hunters at least, the whale would be considered a noble dish by all hands, were there not so much of him; but when you come to sit down before a meat-pie nearly one hundred feet long, it takes away your appetite. Only the most unprejudiced of men, like Stubb, eat cooked whale nowadays; but the Eskimos are not so fastidious. We all know how they live on whales, and keep rare old vintages of prime old train oil. Zogranda, one of their most famous doctors, recommends strips of blubber for infants, as being exceedingly juicy and nourishing. And this reminds me of certain Englishmen who long ago were accidentally left behind in Greenland by a whaling vessel: these men actually lived for several months on the moldy scraps of whales that had been left ashore after the blubber was tried out (boiled down for oil). Among the Dutch whalemen these scraps are called "fritters," which, indeed, they greatly resemble, being brown and crisp, and smelling something like old Amsterdam housewives' doughnuts, or oly-cooks, when fresh. They look so edible that the most self-denying stranger can hardly keep his hands off them.

But what further lowers the whale as a civilized dish is his exceeding richness. He is the great prize ox of the sea, too fat to be delicately good. Look at his hump, which would be as fine eating as the buffalo's (which is prized as a rare dish), were it not such a solid pyramid of fat. But the spermaceti itself — how bland and creamy that is, like the transparent, half-jellied white meat of a coconut in the third month of its growth; yet far too rich to serve as a substitute for butter. Nevertheless, many whalemen have a way of absorbing it into some other substance and then eating it. In the long try-watches of the night it is a common thing for the seamen to dip their ship's biscuit into the huge oil-pots and let it fry there a while. I have made many a good supper that way.

With a small Sperm Whale, the brains are considered a fine dish. The casket of the skull is broken into with an axe, and the two plump, whitish lobes are drawn out (looking exactly like two large puddings); they are then mixed with flour and cooked into a most delectable mess, in flavor somewhat like calves' head, which is quite a dish among some epicures; and everyone knows that some young bucks among the epicures, by continually dining on calves' brains, by and by come to have a little brains of their own, enough to tell a calf's head from their own heads — which, indeed, takes uncommon discrimination. And that is why a young buck with an intelligent-looking calf's head before him is somehow one of the saddest sights you can see. The head looks at him in a sort of reproachful way, with an "Et tu, Brute!" expression.

Perhaps it is not entirely because the whale is so extremely oily that landsmen seem to find the idea of eating him abhorrent. That seems to stem, somehow, from the point already made: that a man should eat a freshly murdered creature of the sea, and eat it by its own light at that. But no doubt the first man who ever murdered an ox was regarded as a murderer; perhaps they hanged him; and if oxen had put him on trial, they certainly would have — and he certainly deserved it, if any murderer does. Go to the meat market on a Saturday night and look at the crowds of live bipeds gazing up at the long rows of dead quadrupeds. Doesn't that sight knock a tooth out of the cannibal's jaw? Cannibals? Who isn't a cannibal? I tell you, it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the Fijian who salted a lean missionary down in his cellar to see him through a coming famine — more tolerable for that provident Fijian, I say — than for you, civilized and enlightened gourmand, who nail geese to the ground and feast on their bloated livers in your pâté de foie gras.

But Stubb eats the whale by its own light, does he? And that adds insult to injury, does it? Take a look at your knife handle there, my civilized and enlightened gourmand, as you dine on that roast beef. What is the handle made of? What else but the bones of the brother of the very ox you are eating? And what do you pick your teeth with after polishing off that fat goose? A feather from the same bird. And what quill did the Secretary of the Society for the Suppression of Cruelty to Ganders use to pen his official circulars? Only in the last month or two has that society passed a resolution to use nothing but steel pens.

chapters.title: Chapter 66 — The Shark Massacre
paragraphs: When, in the Southern Fishery, a captured Sperm Whale is brought alongside late at night after long and weary toil, it is not, as a general rule at least, customary to proceed at once to the business of cutting him in. For that business is an exceedingly laborious one; it is not very soon completed, and it requires all hands to set about it. Therefore the common practice is to take in all sail, lash the helm alee, and then send everyone below to his hammock until daylight — with the provision that until then anchor-watches shall be kept; that is, the crew in rotation, two by two, each pair for an hour, shall come up on deck to see that all goes well.

But sometimes, especially on the Line (the Equator) in the Pacific, this plan will not answer at all, because such incalculable hosts of sharks gather around the moored carcass that if it were left so for, say, six hours at a stretch, little more than the skeleton would be visible by morning. In most other parts of the ocean, however, where these fish are not so abundant, their wondrous voracity can at times be considerably reduced by vigorously stirring them up with sharp whaling-spades — a procedure which, nevertheless, in some instances only seems to tickle them into still greater activity. But it was not so in the present case with the Pequod's sharks; though, to be sure, any man unused to such sights who had looked over her side that night would almost have thought the whole round sea was one huge cheese, and those sharks the maggots in it.

All the same, when Stubb set the anchor-watch after finishing his supper, and Queequeg and a forecastle seaman came on deck to keep it, the sharks were thrown into no small uproar. The two men at once hung the cutting stages over the side and lowered three lanterns, which threw long gleams of light across the murky water; then, darting their long whaling-spades, they kept up a ceaseless murdering of the sharks,* driving the keen steel deep into their skulls, which seemed to be their only vital spot. But in the foaming confusion of that tangled, struggling mass, the marksmen could not always hit their target, and this revealed fresh evidence of the enemy's incredible ferocity. The sharks snapped viciously not only at one another's spilled entrails but, bending round like flexible bows, at their own, until those entrails seemed to be swallowed over and over by the same mouth, only to pass out again the opposite way through the gaping wound. Nor was that all. It was dangerous to meddle with the corpses and ghosts of these creatures. A kind of generic or Pantheistic vitality seemed to linger in their very joints and bones after what might be called their individual life had gone. One of these sharks, killed and hauled on deck for its skin, nearly took poor Queequeg's hand off when he tried to shut the dead lid of its murderous jaw.

*The whaling-spade used for cutting-in is made of the very best steel; it is about the size of a man's spread hand, and in general shape corresponds to the garden tool it is named after, except that its sides are perfectly flat and its upper end considerably narrower than the lower. This weapon is always kept as sharp as possible, and when in use it is honed now and then, just like a razor. A stiff pole, from twenty to thirty feet long, is fitted into its socket as a handle.
"Queequeg no care what god made him shark," said the savage, agonizingly lifting his hand up and down. "Whether Fiji god or Nantucket god — but the god that made shark must be one damn Indian."

chapters.title: Chapter 67 — Cutting In
paragraphs: It was a Saturday night, and such a Sabbath as followed! By their very profession, all whalemen are breakers of the Sabbath. The ivory Pequod was turned into what seemed a slaughterhouse. Every sailor was a butcher. You would have thought we were sacrificing ten thousand red oxen to the sea gods.

In the first place, the enormous cutting tackles were hoisted up to the main-top. Among other ponderous things, they include a cluster of blocks generally painted green, which no single man can possibly lift; and this vast bunch of grapes was firmly lashed to the lower masthead, the strongest point anywhere above a ship's deck. The end of the hawser-like rope winding through these intricacies was then led to the windlass, and the huge lower block of the tackles was swung over the whale; to this block the great blubber hook, weighing some one hundred pounds, was attached. And now, suspended over the side on stages (planks slung from the ship as platforms), Starbuck and Stubb, the mates, armed with their long spades, began cutting a hole in the body for the insertion of the hook, just above the nearer of the two side-fins. This done, a broad, semicircular line is cut around the hole, the hook is inserted, and the main body of the crew, striking up a wild chorus, now begin heaving in one dense crowd at the windlass. Instantly the entire ship careens over on her side; every bolt in her starts like the nail-heads of an old house in frosty weather; she trembles, quivers, and nods her frightened mastheads to the sky. More and more she leans over to the whale, while every gasping heave of the windlass is answered by a helping heave from the waves; till at last a swift, startling snap is heard; with a great swash the ship rolls upward and backward from the whale, and the triumphant tackle rises into sight, dragging after it the loosened semicircular end of the first strip of blubber. Now, as the blubber envelops the whale precisely as the rind does an orange, so it is stripped off the body precisely as an orange is sometimes peeled — in a spiral. For the strain constantly kept up by the windlass keeps the whale rolling over and over in the water, and the blubber peels off in one even strip along the line called the "scarf," which is cut at the same time by the spades of Starbuck and Stubb, the mates; and just as fast as it is peeled off, and indeed by that very act, it is hoisted higher and higher aloft, until its upper end grazes the main-top. The men at the windlass then stop heaving, and for a moment or two the prodigious, blood-dripping mass sways to and fro as if let down from the sky, and everyone present must take good care to dodge it when it swings, or it may box his ears and pitch him headlong overboard.

One of the harpooners standing by now steps forward with a long, sharp weapon called a boarding-sword, waits for his moment, and deftly cuts a sizable hole in the lower part of the swinging mass. The end of the second of the two great alternating tackles is then hooked into this hole to keep a grip on the blubber and prepare for what comes next. Then this accomplished swordsman warns everyone to stand clear, makes one more scientific lunge at the mass, and with a few desperate, sidelong, slashing strokes cuts it clean in two. The short lower part stays fast, while the long upper strip, called a blanket-piece, swings free, ready to be lowered. The heavers forward now strike up their song again. While one tackle peels and hoists a second strip off the whale, the other is slowly eased off, and down goes the first strip through the main hatchway directly below, into a bare parlor called the blubber-room. In this twilight room a number of nimble hands keep coiling away the long blanket-piece as though it were a great living heap of braided snakes. And so the work goes on: the two tackles hoisting and lowering together; whale and windlass both heaving, the heavers singing, the blubber-room gentlemen coiling, the mates scarfing, the ship straining, and everyone swearing now and then to ease the general friction.

chapters.title: Chapter 68 — The Blanket
paragraphs: I have paid no small attention to that much-disputed subject, the skin of the whale. I have argued about it with seasoned whalemen at sea and with learned naturalists on land. My original opinion has not changed — but it is only an opinion.

The question is this: what is the whale's skin, and where is it? You already know what his blubber is. It has roughly the texture of firm, close-grained beef, only tougher, more elastic and more compact, and it runs from eight or ten to twelve and fifteen inches thick.

Now, however absurd it may seem at first to speak of any creature's skin as being of that sort of consistency and thickness, in point of fact these are no arguments against such a presumption; because you cannot raise any other dense enveloping layer from the whale's body except that same blubber; and the outermost enveloping layer of any animal, if reasonably dense, what can that be but the skin? True, from the unmarred dead body of the whale you may scrape off with your hand an infinitely thin, transparent substance, somewhat like the thinnest shreds of isinglass (a clear gelatin made from fish bladders), only it is almost as flexible and soft as satin — that is, before it is dried, when it not only contracts and thickens but becomes rather hard and brittle. I have several such dried bits, which I use as bookmarks in my whale-books. It is transparent, as I said before; and laying it on the printed page, I have sometimes amused myself by imagining that it had a magnifying effect. At any rate, it is pleasant to read about whales through their own spectacles, as you might say. But what I am driving at here is this. That same infinitely thin, isinglass substance, which, I admit, covers the entire body of the whale, is not so much to be regarded as the skin of the creature as the skin of the skin, so to speak; for it would be simply ridiculous to say that the proper skin of the tremendous whale is thinner and more tender than the skin of a newborn child. But no more of this.

Assuming the blubber to be the skin of the whale: when this skin, as in the case of a very large Sperm Whale, will yield the bulk of one hundred barrels of oil; and when you consider that, in quantity, or rather weight, that oil in its pressed-out state is only three-quarters, and not the entire substance, of the coat — you may get some idea from this of the enormousness of that living mass, a mere part of whose mere covering yields such a lake of liquid as that. Reckoning ten barrels to the ton, you have ten tons for the net weight of only three-quarters of the stuff of the whale's skin.

In life, the visible surface of the Sperm Whale is not the least among the many marvels he presents. Almost invariably it is obliquely crossed and re-crossed all over with countless straight marks in thick array, something like those in the finest Italian line engravings. But these marks do not seem to be impressed upon the isinglass substance mentioned above; rather, they seem to be seen through it, as if they were engraved upon the body itself. Nor is this all. In some instances, to the quick, observant eye, those linear marks, as in a real engraving, only provide the ground for quite other drawings. These are hieroglyphical; that is, if you call those mysterious ciphers on the walls of pyramids hieroglyphics, then that is the proper word to use here. Remembering well the hieroglyphics on one Sperm Whale in particular, I was much struck by a plate showing the old Indian characters chiseled on the famous hieroglyphic palisades on the banks of the Upper Mississippi.
