Like those mystic rocks, too, the mystic-marked whale remains undecipherable. This allusion to the Indian rocks reminds me of another thing. Besides all the other phenomena that the exterior of the Sperm Whale presents, he quite often shows his back, and more especially his flanks, with the regular linear pattern largely effaced by numerous rough scratches, altogether irregular and random in appearance. I should say that those New England rocks on the sea-coast which Agassiz imagines to bear the marks of violent scraping contact with vast floating icebergs — I should say that those rocks must resemble the Sperm Whale not a little in this respect. It also seems to me that such scratches in the whale are probably made by hostile contact with other whales; for I have noticed them most in the large, full-grown bulls of the species.

A word or two more about this matter of the skin or blubber of the whale. It has already been said that it is stripped from him in long pieces, called blanket-pieces. Like most sea terms, this one is very apt and meaningful. For the whale is indeed wrapped up in his blubber as in a real blanket or bedspread — or, better still, an Indian poncho slipped over his head and hanging down around his extremity. It is because of this cozy blanketing of his body that the whale is able to keep himself comfortable in all weathers, in all seas, times, and tides. What would become of a Greenland whale, say, in those shuddering, icy seas of the North, if he were not supplied with his cozy overcoat? True, other fish are found to be exceedingly lively in those Hyperborean waters; but these, mind you, are your cold-blooded, lungless fish, whose very bellies are refrigerators; creatures that warm themselves in the lee of an iceberg, as a traveler in winter would bask before an inn fire; whereas, like man, the whale has lungs and warm blood. Freeze his blood, and he dies. How wonderful it is, then — unless it is explained — that this great monster, to whom bodily warmth is as indispensable as it is to man; how wonderful that he should be found at home, immersed to his lips for life in those Arctic waters! — where, when seamen fall overboard, they are sometimes found months afterward, frozen upright into the hearts of fields of ice, as a fly is found glued in amber. But it is more surprising still to know, as has been proved by experiment, that the blood of a Polar whale is warmer than that of a Borneo negro in summer.

It certainly seems to me that here we see the rare virtue of a strong individual vitality, the rare virtue of thick walls, and the rare virtue of roominess within. Oh, man! Admire the whale and take him as your model! You, too, stay warm in the ice. You, too, live in this world without being of it. Stay cool at the equator; keep your blood flowing at the Pole. Like the great dome of St. Peter's, and like the great whale, keep, O man, a temperature of your own in every season.
But how easy it is to teach these fine things, and how hopeless! How few buildings have a dome like St. Peter's! How few creatures are as vast as the whale!

chapters.title: Chapter 69 — The Funeral
paragraphs: "Haul in the chains! Let the carcass go astern!"

The vast tackles have now done their duty. The peeled white body of the beheaded whale gleams like a marble tomb; though changed in color, it has not visibly lost anything in bulk. It is still colossal. Slowly it floats farther and farther away, the water around it torn and splashed by the insatiable sharks, and the air above harassed by rapacious flights of screaming birds, whose beaks are like so many insulting daggers in the whale. The vast white headless phantom floats farther and farther from the ship, and with every rod that it floats, what seem square roods of sharks and cubic roods of birds swell the murderous din. For hours and hours that hideous sight can be seen from the almost motionless ship. Beneath the unclouded, mild blue sky, upon the fair face of the pleasant sea, carried along by the joyous breezes, that great mass of death floats on and on, till it is lost in infinite perspectives.

What a doleful and mocking funeral this is! The sea-vultures all in pious mourning, the air-sharks all correctly dressed in black or speckled. Few of them, I suspect, would have lifted a finger for the whale in life, had he happened to need it; but at the banquet of his funeral they pounce with the greatest piety. Oh, the horrible vultureism of the earth, from which not even the mightiest whale is exempt!

Nor is this the end. Desecrated as the body is, a vengeful ghost survives and hovers over it to frighten. Sighted from afar by some timid warship or blundering discovery-vessel — when the distance hides the swarming birds but still shows the white mass floating in the sun, and the white spray heaving high against it — straightaway the whale's harmless corpse is set down in the log with trembling fingers: "Shoals, rocks, and breakers hereabouts: beware!" And for years afterward, perhaps, ships avoid the place, leaping over it as silly sheep leap over empty air, because their leader originally leaped there when a stick was held up. There's your law of precedents; there's your usefulness of traditions; there's the story of your stubborn survival of old beliefs never grounded on the earth, and now not even hovering in the air! There's orthodoxy!
So while the great whale's living body may have been a real terror to his enemies, once he is dead his ghost becomes a powerless panic to a whole world.
Do you believe in ghosts, my friend? There are other ghosts besides the Cock-Lane one (the famous London ghost hoax of 1762), and men far deeper than Doctor Johnson believe in them.

chapters.title: Chapter 70 — The Sphynx
paragraphs: It should not have been omitted that before the body of the leviathan was completely stripped, he was beheaded. Now, the beheading of the Sperm Whale is a scientific anatomical feat upon which experienced whale surgeons very much pride themselves — and not without reason.

Consider that the whale has nothing that can properly be called a neck; on the contrary, where his head and body seem to join, there, in that very place, is the thickest part of him. Remember, too, that the surgeon must operate from above, with some eight or ten feet between him and his subject, and that subject almost hidden in a discolored, rolling, and often tumultuous and bursting sea. Bear in mind also that under these unfavorable circumstances he has to cut many feet deep into the flesh; and in that underground fashion, without getting so much as a single peep into the ever-contracting gash he is making, he must skillfully steer clear of all the neighboring, forbidden parts, and divide the spine exactly at a critical point close to where it enters the skull. Don't you marvel, then, at Stubb's boast that he needed only ten minutes to behead a sperm whale?

When first severed, the head is dropped astern and held there by a cable until the body is stripped. That done, if it belongs to a small whale, it is hoisted on deck to be dealt with at leisure. But with a full-grown leviathan this is impossible; for the sperm whale's head makes up nearly one third of his entire bulk, and to suspend such a burden completely, even by the immense tackles of a whaler, would be as futile as trying to weigh a Dutch barn in jewelers' scales.

The Pequod's whale having been beheaded and the body stripped, the head was hoisted against the ship's side — about halfway out of the sea, so that it might still be largely buoyed up by its native element. And there, with the strained vessel leaning steeply over toward it because of the enormous downward drag from the lower masthead, and every yard-arm on that side sticking out like a crane over the waves — there that blood-dripping head hung at the Pequod's waist like the giant Holofernes's from the girdle of Judith.

By the time this last job was done it was noon, and the seamen went below for their dinner. Silence settled over the deck, so noisy a moment before and now deserted. An intense copper calm, like a universal yellow lotus, was unfolding more and more of its silent, boundless leaves across the sea.

A short time passed, and up into this silence came Ahab, alone, from his cabin. Taking a few turns on the quarter-deck, he paused to gaze over the side; then, slowly climbing into the main-chains, he took Stubb's long spade — still lying there after the whale's beheading — and, striking it into the lower part of the half-suspended mass, he placed its other end like a crutch under one arm, and so stood leaning over, his eyes intently fixed on this head.

It was a black and hooded head; and hanging there in the midst of so intense a calm, it seemed like the Sphynx's in the desert. "Speak, you vast and venerable head," muttered Ahab, "you who, though you have no beard, yet here and there look hoary with mosses; speak, mighty head, and tell us the secret thing that is in you. Of all divers, you have dived the deepest. That head upon which the upper sun now gleams has moved among this world's foundations. Where unrecorded names and navies rust, and untold hopes and anchors rot; where in her murderous hold this frigate earth is ballasted with the bones of millions of the drowned; there, in that awful water-land, there was your most familiar home. You have been where diving-bell or diver never went; you have slept by many a sailor's side, where sleepless mothers would give their lives to lay them down. You saw the locked lovers when they leaped from their flaming ship; heart to heart they sank beneath the exulting wave; true to each other, when heaven seemed false to them. You saw the murdered mate when pirates tossed him from the midnight deck; for hours he fell into the deeper midnight of the insatiable maw; and his murderers still sailed on unharmed — while swift lightning shattered the neighboring ship that would have carried a righteous husband to outstretched, longing arms. O head! you have seen enough to split the planets and make an infidel of Abraham, and not one syllable is yours!"
"Sail ho!" cried a triumphant voice from the main-masthead.

"Aye? Well now, that's cheering," cried Ahab, suddenly straightening up, while whole thunderclouds swept aside from his brow. "That lively cry upon this deadly calm might almost convert a better man. — Where away?"
"Three points on the starboard bow, sir, and bringing down her breeze to us!"

"Better and better, man. If only St. Paul would come along that way now, and bring his breeze to my breezelessness! O Nature, and O soul of man! how far beyond all words are your linked analogies! Not the smallest atom stirs or lives on matter without having its cunning duplicate in mind."

chapters.title: Chapter 71 — The Jeroboam’s Story
paragraphs: Ship and breeze blew on hand in hand; but the breeze was faster than the ship, and before long the Pequod began to rock.

Before long, the spyglass showed from the stranger's boats and manned mastheads that she was a whale-ship. But she was so far to windward, and moving past so quickly, apparently on her way to some other ground, that the Pequod had no hope of reaching her. So the signal was hoisted to see what answer would come.

It should be said here that, like the vessels of navies, the ships of the American Whale Fleet each have a private signal; all these signals are collected in a book, with the names of the respective vessels attached, and every captain is provided with it. By this means the whale captains are able to recognize each other on the ocean, even at considerable distances and with no small ease.

The Pequod's signal was at last answered by the stranger's hoisting her own, which proved the ship to be the Jeroboam of Nantucket. Squaring her yards, she bore down, came up abeam under the Pequod's lee, and lowered a boat. It soon drew near; but as the side-ladder was being rigged by Starbuck's order to accommodate the visiting captain, the stranger in question waved his hand from his boat's stern to show that this was entirely unnecessary. It turned out that the Jeroboam had a malignant epidemic on board, and that Mayhew, her captain, was afraid of infecting the Pequod's company. For although he himself and his boat's crew remained uninfected, and although his ship was half a rifle-shot away, with an incorruptible sea and air rolling and flowing between, he nevertheless conscientiously kept to the timid quarantine of the land, and flatly refused to come into direct contact with the Pequod.

But this by no means prevented all communication. Keeping a gap of a few yards between itself and the ship, the Jeroboam's boat, by occasional use of its oars, managed to keep parallel to the Pequod as she heavily forged through the sea (for by this time it was blowing very fresh), with her main-topsail aback; though, indeed, at times the sudden onset of a large rolling wave would push the boat some way ahead, but it would soon be skillfully brought back to its proper position. Subject to this and other such interruptions now and then, a conversation was kept up between the two parties — though at intervals it was broken by still another interruption of a very different sort.

Pulling an oar in the Jeroboam's boat was a man of singular appearance, even in that wild whaling life where the whole is made up of nothing but remarkable individuals. He was a small, short, youngish man, sprinkled all over his face with freckles, and wearing an abundance of yellow hair. A long-skirted coat of cabalistic cut, of a faded walnut color, enveloped him; its overlapping sleeves were rolled up at his wrists. A deep, settled, fanatic delirium was in his eyes.

As soon as this figure had first been sighted, Stubb had exclaimed — "That's him! that's him! — the long-togged scaramouch the Town-Ho's company told us of!" Stubb was referring here to a strange story told about the Jeroboam, and a certain man among her crew, some time before, when the Pequod spoke the Town-Ho. According to this account, and what was learned afterward, it seemed that the scaramouch in question had gained a remarkable hold over almost everybody in the Jeroboam. His story was this:

He had originally been raised among the crazy society of Neskyeuna Shakers, where he had been a great prophet; in their cracked, secret meetings he had several times descended from heaven by way of a trap-door, announcing the speedy opening of the seventh vial, which he carried in his vest-pocket — but which, instead of containing gunpowder, was supposed to be charged with laudanum. A strange, apostolic whim having seized him, he had left Neskyeuna for Nantucket, where, with that cunning peculiar to craziness, he put on a steady, common-sense exterior and offered himself as a green-hand candidate for the Jeroboam's whaling voyage. They took him on; but the moment the ship was out of sight of land, his insanity broke out in a flood. He announced himself as the archangel Gabriel, and ordered the captain to jump overboard. He published his manifesto, in which he proclaimed himself the deliverer of the isles of the sea and vicar-general of all Oceanica. The unflinching earnestness with which he declared these things — the dark, daring play of his sleepless, excited imagination, and all the preternatural terrors of real delirium — combined to invest this Gabriel, in the minds of most of the ignorant crew, with an atmosphere of sacredness. Moreover, they were afraid of him. As such a man, however, was not of much practical use in the ship, especially as he refused to work except when he pleased, the unbelieving captain would gladly have been rid of him; but on learning that the captain intended to land him at the first convenient port, the archangel at once opened all his seals and vials — devoting the ship and all hands to unconditional damnation if this intention was carried out. So strongly did he work upon his disciples among the crew that at last they went to the captain in a body and told him that if Gabriel was sent from the ship, not a man of them would remain. He was therefore forced to give up his plan. Nor would they allow Gabriel to be mistreated in any way, whatever he might say or do; so that it came about that Gabriel had the complete freedom of the ship. The consequence of all this was that the archangel cared little or nothing for the captain and mates; and since the epidemic had broken out, he was more high-handed than ever, declaring that the plague, as he called it, was at his sole command, and that it would not be stopped except at his good pleasure. The sailors, mostly poor devils, cringed, and some of them fawned before him; following his instructions, they sometimes paid him personal homage, as to a god. Such things may seem incredible; but, however astonishing, they are true. Nor is the history of fanatics half so striking for the measureless self-deception of the fanatic himself as for his measureless power of deceiving and bedeviling so many others. But it is time to return to the Pequod.
"I'm not afraid of your epidemic, man," said Ahab from the bulwarks to Captain Mayhew, who stood in the boat's stern. "Come on board."
But now Gabriel started to his feet.
"Think, think of the fevers, yellow and bilious! Beware of the horrible plague!"
"Gabriel! Gabriel!" cried Captain Mayhew. "You must either —" But that instant a headlong wave shot the boat far ahead, and its noise drowned all speech.
"Have you seen the White Whale?" demanded Ahab, when the boat drifted back.
"Think, think of your whale-boat, stoven and sunk! Beware of the horrible tail!"

"I tell you again, Gabriel, that —" But once more the boat shot ahead as if fiends were dragging it. For some moments no one spoke, while a series of riotous waves rolled past — waves that, in one of the sea's occasional whims, were tumbling the boat rather than lifting it. Meanwhile the hoisted sperm whale's head was jolting about violently, and Gabriel could be seen eyeing it with rather more alarm than his archangel nature seemed to justify.

When this interlude was over, Captain Mayhew began a dark story about Moby Dick — not, however, without frequent interruptions from Gabriel whenever his name was mentioned, and from the crazy sea that seemed to be in league with him.

It seemed that the Jeroboam had not long left home when, on speaking a whale-ship, her people were reliably informed of the existence of Moby Dick and the havoc he had made. Greedily drinking in this news, Gabriel solemnly warned the captain against attacking the White Whale in case the monster should be seen; in his gibbering insanity he declared the White Whale to be no less a being than the Shaker God incarnate, the Shakers accepting the Bible. But when, a year or two afterward, Moby Dick was fairly sighted from the mastheads, Macey, the chief mate, burned with eagerness to encounter him; and the captain himself being not unwilling to give him the chance, despite all the archangel's denunciations and warnings, Macey succeeded in persuading five men to man his boat. With them he pushed off; and after much weary pulling, and many perilous, unsuccessful attacks, he at last succeeded in getting one iron fast. Meanwhile Gabriel, climbing to the main-royal masthead, was tossing one arm in frantic gestures and hurling forth prophecies of swift doom upon the sacrilegious attackers of his divinity. Now, while Macey the mate was standing up in his boat's bow, and with all the reckless energy of his tribe was venting his wild exclamations at the whale and trying to get a fair chance for his poised lance — look! a broad white shadow rose from the sea, and by its quick, fanning motion for the moment knocked the breath out of the oarsmen's bodies. The next instant the luckless mate, so full of furious life, was struck bodily into the air, and, making a long arc in his descent, fell into the sea about fifty yards away. Not a chip of the boat was harmed, nor a hair of any oarsman's head; but the mate sank forever.

It is worth adding here, in parentheses, that among the fatal accidents of the Sperm-Whale Fishery, this kind is perhaps nearly as common as any. Sometimes nothing is hurt except the man who is wiped out this way; more often the bow of the boat is knocked off, or the thigh-board where the headsman (the officer commanding the boat) stands is torn loose and goes along with the body. But strangest of all is the fact that more than once, when the body has been recovered, not a single mark of violence could be found on it — and the man stone dead.

From the ship the whole disaster, including Macey's falling body, was clearly visible. With a piercing shriek — "The vial! the vial!" — Gabriel called the terrified crew off from any further pursuit of the whale. This terrible event gave the archangel still more influence, because his gullible disciples believed he had predicted this very thing, rather than merely making a general prophecy, which anyone could have done, and so happened to hit one of the many targets its wide margin allowed. He became a nameless terror to the ship.

When Mayhew had finished his story, Ahab put such questions to him that the stranger captain could not help asking whether he intended to hunt the White Whale, if the opportunity came. To which Ahab answered — "Aye." Immediately, then, Gabriel once more started to his feet, glaring at the old man, and vehemently exclaimed, with downward-pointing finger — "Think, think of the blasphemer — dead, and down there! — beware of the blasphemer's end!"
Ahab stolidly turned aside, then said to Mayhew, "Captain, I have just remembered my letter-bag. There is a letter for one of your officers, if I'm not mistaken. Starbuck, look through the bag."

Every whale-ship carries out a good number of letters for various other ships, and whether they reach the people they are addressed to depends purely on the chance of meeting those ships somewhere in the four oceans. So most letters never arrive; and many are received only when they are two or three years old or more.

Soon Starbuck returned with a letter in his hand. It was badly creased, damp, and covered with a dull, spotted green mold from being kept in a dark locker in the cabin. Of such a letter, Death himself might well have been the postman.

"Can't you read it?" cried Ahab. "Give it to me, man. Aye, aye, it's but a dim scrawl — what's this?" As he was studying it out, Starbuck took a long cutting-spade pole, and with his knife slightly split the end, to insert the letter there, and in that way hand it to the boat without its having to come any closer to the ship.
Meanwhile, Ahab holding the letter, muttered, "Mr. Har — yes, Mr. Harry — a woman's handwriting — the man's wife, I'll wager — aye — Mr. Harry Macey, Ship Jeroboam — why, it's Macey, and he's dead!"
"Poor fellow! Poor fellow! And from his wife," sighed Mayhew. "But let me have it."
"No, keep it yourself," cried Gabriel to Ahab. "You are soon going that way."

"Curses strangle you!" yelled Ahab. "Captain Mayhew, stand by now to receive it." And taking the fatal letter from Starbuck's hands, he caught it in the slit of the pole and reached it out toward the boat. But as he did so, the oarsmen, expecting it, stopped rowing; the boat drifted a little toward the ship's stern; so that, as if by magic, the letter suddenly came level with Gabriel's eager hand. He clutched it in an instant, seized the boat-knife, and, impaling the letter on it, sent it, thus loaded, back into the ship. It fell at Ahab's feet. Then Gabriel shrieked out to his comrades to pull hard on their oars, and in that manner the mutinous boat rapidly shot away from the Pequod.
After this interlude, as the seamen went back to work on the whale's jacket, many strange things were hinted about this wild affair.

chapters.title: Chapter 72 — The Monkey-Rope
paragraphs: In the tumultuous business of cutting-in and attending to a whale, there is much running back and forth among the crew. Now hands are wanted here, and then again hands are wanted there. There is no staying in any one place; for at one and the same time everything has to be done everywhere. It is much the same with anyone who tries to describe the scene. We must now retrace our steps a little. It was mentioned that, on first breaking ground in the whale's back, the blubber-hook was inserted into the original hole cut there by the spades of the mates. But how did so clumsy and weighty a mass as that hook get fixed in that hole? It was put there by my particular friend Queequeg, whose duty it was, as harpooner, to go down onto the monster's back for that special purpose. But in very many cases circumstances require the harpooner to remain on the whale until the whole flensing, or stripping, operation is finished. The whale, mind you, lies almost entirely submerged, except for the parts being worked on. So down there, some ten feet below the level of the deck, the poor harpooner flounders about, half on the whale and half in the water, as the vast mass revolves like a treadmill beneath him. On the occasion in question, Queequeg appeared in Highland costume — a shirt and socks — in which, to my eyes at least, he looked uncommonly well; and no one had a better chance to observe him, as will soon be seen.

As the savage's bowsman — that is, the man who pulled the bow-oar in his boat (the second from the front) — it was my cheerful job to look after him while he did his hard-scrabble scrambling on the dead whale's back. You have seen Italian organ-grinder boys holding a dancing ape on a long cord. In just the same way, from the ship's steep side, I held Queequeg down there in the sea by what the fishery technically calls a monkey-rope, fastened to a strong strip of canvas belted around his waist.

It was a comically dangerous business for both of us. For before we go any further, I should explain that the monkey-rope was fastened at both ends: to Queequeg's broad canvas belt and to my narrow leather one. So for better or worse, the two of us were, for the time being, married; and if poor Queequeg sank never to rise again, both custom and honor required that the cord not be cut, but that it drag me down after him. In short, we were joined by a stretched-out Siamese ligature. Queequeg was my own inseparable twin brother, and there was no way for me to escape the dangerous liabilities that the hempen bond carried with it.

So strongly and metaphysically did I conceive of my situation then that, while earnestly watching his motions, I seemed distinctly to perceive that my own individuality was now merged in a joint-stock company of two; that my free will had received a mortal wound; and that another's mistake or misfortune might plunge innocent me into undeserved disaster and death. Therefore, I saw that here was a sort of interregnum in Providence; for its even-handed fairness never could have allowed so gross an injustice. And yet, still further pondering — while I jerked him now and then from between the whale and the ship, which threatened to jam him — still further pondering, I say, I saw that this situation of mine was the precise situation of every mortal that breathes; only, in most cases, he, one way or another, has this Siamese connection with a plurality of other mortals. If your banker breaks, you snap; if your apothecary by mistake sends you poison in your pills, you die. True, you may say that by exceeding caution you may possibly escape these and the countless other evil chances of life. But however carefully I handled Queequeg's monkey-rope, sometimes he jerked it so that I came very near sliding overboard. Nor could I possibly forget that, whatever I did, I had the management of only one end of it.*

*Every whaler has a monkey-rope; but only on the Pequod were the monkey and his holder ever tied together. This improvement on the usual practice was introduced by no less a man than Stubb, to give the endangered harpooner the firmest possible guarantee that whoever held his monkey-rope would be faithful and alert.

I have hinted that I often had to jerk poor Queequeg out from between the whale and the ship, where he would sometimes fall because of the ceaseless rolling and swaying of both. But that was not the only crushing danger he faced. Not at all put off by the slaughter inflicted on them during the night, the sharks, now drawn afresh and more keenly by the blood that had been pent up until then and was starting to flow from the carcass — those rabid creatures swarmed around it like bees in a hive.

And right in among those sharks was Queequeg, often shoving them aside with his floundering feet. That would be quite unbelievable, except that when the shark, which will otherwise eat almost anything, is drawn by prey like a dead whale, it will seldom touch a man.

Still, you can well believe that since the sharks have such a greedy finger in the pie, it is considered only sensible to keep a close watch on them. So, besides the monkey-rope, with which I now and then jerked the poor fellow away when he got too close to the jaws of some especially ferocious-looking shark, he had yet another protection. Hanging over the side in one of the stages, Tashtego and Daggoo kept waving a pair of sharp whale-spades over his head and killed as many sharks as they could reach. This was, to be sure, very unselfish and kind of them. They wanted Queequeg's greatest happiness, I admit; but in their hasty zeal to help him, and because he and the sharks were sometimes half hidden in the blood-clouded water, those careless spades of theirs came closer to cutting off a leg than a tail. But poor Queequeg, I suppose, straining and gasping there with that great iron hook — poor Queequeg, I suppose, just prayed to his Yojo and put his life in the hands of his gods.

Well, well, my dear comrade and twin brother, I thought, as I hauled in the rope and then let it out with every swell of the sea — what does it matter, after all? Aren't you the precious image of each and every one of us men in this whaling world? That unfathomed ocean you gasp in is Life; those sharks are your enemies; those spades, your friends; and between sharks and spades you are in a sorry pickle and peril, poor lad.

But courage! There is good cheer in store for you, Queequeg. For now, as with blue lips and bloodshot eyes the exhausted savage at last climbs up the chains and stands all dripping and involuntarily trembling over the side, the steward comes forward and, with a kindly, consoling glance, hands him — what? Some hot cognac? No! He hands him — ye gods! — he hands him a cup of lukewarm ginger and water!

"Ginger? Do I smell ginger?" Stubb asked suspiciously, coming near. "Yes, this must be ginger," peering into the as yet untasted cup. Then, standing as if in disbelief for a while, he calmly walked toward the astonished steward, slowly saying, "Ginger? ginger? And will you have the goodness to tell me, Mr. Dough-Boy, where the virtue of ginger lies? Ginger! Is ginger the sort of fuel you use, Dough-Boy, to kindle a fire in this shivering cannibal? Ginger! — what the devil is ginger? Sea-coal? Firewood? — lucifer matches? — tinder? — gunpowder? — what the devil is ginger, I say, that you offer this cup to our poor Queequeg here?"

"There is some sneaking Temperance Society movement behind this business," he suddenly added, now approaching Starbuck, who had just come from forward. "Will you look at that little can, sir? Smell it, if you please." Then, watching the mate's face, he added, "The steward, Mr. Starbuck, had the nerve to offer that calomel and jalap to Queequeg there, just this instant off the whale. Is the steward an apothecary, sir? And may I ask whether this is the sort of bitters with which he blows the life back into a half-drowned man?"
"I trust not," said Starbuck. "It is poor stuff enough."

"Aye, aye, steward," cried Stubb. "We'll teach you to drug a harpooner! None of your apothecary's medicine here! You want to poison us, do you? You've got life insurance on us and want to murder us all and pocket the money, do you?"
"It was not me," cried Dough-Boy. "It was Aunt Charity that brought the ginger on board, and told me never to give the harpooners any spirits, but only this ginger-jub — so she called it."

"Ginger-jub! You gingerly rascal! Take that! And run along with you to the lockers, and get something better. I hope I do no wrong, Mr. Starbuck. It is the captain's orders — grog for the harpooner on a whale."
"Enough," replied Starbuck. "Only don't hit him again, but —"
"Oh, I never hurt when I hit, except when I hit a whale or something of that sort. And this fellow's a weasel. What were you about to say, sir?"
"Only this: go down with him, and get what you want yourself."

Stubb came back with a dark flask in one hand and a kind of tea-caddy in the other. The flask held strong liquor and was passed to Queequeg; the caddy was Aunt Charity's present, and that was generously handed over to the waves.

chapters.title: Chapter 73 — Stubb and Flask kill a Right Whale; and Then Have a Talk
paragraphs: over Him.

Keep in mind that all this while a Sperm Whale's enormous head has been hanging from the Pequod's side. But we must leave it hanging there a while longer, until we get a chance to deal with it. Other matters are pressing just now, and the best we can do for the head at present is to pray to heaven that the tackles hold.

Now, during the past night and morning, the Pequod had gradually drifted into a sea which, by its occasional patches of yellow brit, gave unusual signs that Right Whales were near — a species of the Leviathan that few supposed to be lurking anywhere nearby at this particular time. And though all hands commonly disdained the capture of those inferior creatures; and though the Pequod was not commissioned to cruise for them at all; and though she had passed numbers of them near the Crozets without lowering a boat — yet now that a Sperm Whale had been brought alongside and beheaded, to everyone's surprise the announcement was made that a Right Whale should be captured that day, if the opportunity arose.

We did not have long to wait. Tall spouts were sighted to leeward, and two boats, Stubb's and Flask's, were sent after them. They pulled farther and farther off until the men at the masthead could barely see them. Then suddenly, far away, they saw a great heap of churning white water, and soon word came down from aloft that one or both boats must be fast. After a while the boats came into plain view, being dragged straight toward the ship by the whale that had them in tow. The monster came so close to the hull that at first he seemed to mean it harm; but then, within three rods of the planking, he suddenly plunged down in a whirlpool and vanished completely, as if diving under the keel. "Cut, cut!" the ship shouted to the boats, which for an instant looked certain to be smashed against the vessel's side. But since they still had plenty of line in the tubs and the whale was not sounding very fast, they paid out rope freely while rowing with all their strength to get ahead of the ship. For a few minutes things were extremely critical: as they let out the taut line in one direction and worked their oars in another, the opposing pulls threatened to drag them under. Yet all they needed to gain was a few feet. They kept at it until they gained them — and at that instant a swift tremor ran like lightning along the keel, as the strained line, scraping along beneath the ship, suddenly surfaced under her bows, snapping and quivering and shaking off its drips so that they fell like bits of broken glass on the water; the whale also came up into sight beyond, and once again the boats were free to fly. But the worn-out whale slowed down and, blindly changing course, swung around the ship's stern with the two boats in tow, so that they made a full circle.

Meanwhile, they hauled more and more on their lines, till, closely flanking him on both sides, Stubb answered Flask lance for lance; and so round and round the Pequod the battle went, while the multitudes of sharks that had been swimming around the Sperm Whale's body rushed to the fresh blood that was spilled, thirstily drinking at every new gash, as the eager Israelites drank at the new fountains that burst from the smitten rock.
At last his spout thickened, and with a horrible roll and a vomit he turned over onto his back, a corpse.
While the two headsmen were busy tying cords to his flukes and otherwise getting the great mass ready to tow, the two of them fell into conversation.
"I wonder what the old man wants with this lump of foul lard," said Stubb, somewhat disgusted at the thought of dealing with such a lowly leviathan.

"Wants with it?" said Flask, coiling some spare line in the boat's bow. "Did you never hear that the ship which even once has a Sperm Whale's head hoisted on her starboard side, and at the same time a Right Whale's on the port side — did you never hear, Stubb, that that ship can never afterward capsize?"
"Why not?"

"I don't know, but I heard that yellowish ghost of a Fedallah saying so, and he seems to know all about ships' charms. But I sometimes think he'll charm the ship to no good in the end. I don't half like that fellow, Stubb. Did you ever notice how that tusk of his is sort of carved into a snake's head, Stubb?"

"Sink him! I never look at him at all. But if I ever get the chance on a dark night, with him standing close by the bulwarks and nobody around — look down there, Flask" — pointing into the sea with a peculiar motion of both hands — "yes, I will! Flask, I take that Fedallah for the devil in disguise. Do you believe that cock-and-bull story about him being stowed away on board? He's the devil, I tell you. The reason you don't see his tail is that he tucks it up out of sight; he carries it coiled up in his pocket, I guess. Blast him! Now that I think of it, he's always asking for oakum to stuff into the toes of his boots."
"He sleeps in his boots, doesn't he? He hasn't got any hammock, but I've seen him lie at night in a coil of rigging."
"No doubt — and it's because of his cursed tail. He coils it down, do you see, in the eye of the rigging."
"What's the old man have so much to do with him for?"
"Striking up a swap or a bargain, I suppose."
"Bargain? — about what?"

"Why, do you see, the old man is dead set on that White Whale, and the devil there is trying to come around him and get him to swap away his silver watch, or his soul, or something of that sort, and then he'll deliver Moby Dick."
"Nonsense! Stubb, you are joking. How can Fedallah do that?"

"I don't know, Flask, but the devil is a curious fellow, and a wicked one, I tell you. Why, they say he went sauntering into the old flagship once, switching his tail about, devilish easy and gentlemanlike, and asking if the old governor was at home. Well, he was at home, and asked the devil what he wanted. The devil, switching his hoofs, up and says, 'I want John.' 'What for?' says the old governor. 'What business is that of yours?' says the devil, getting mad — 'I want to use him.' 'Take him,' says the governor — and by the Lord, Flask, if the devil didn't give John the Asiatic cholera before he was through with him, I'll eat this whale in one mouthful. But look sharp — aren't you all ready there? Well, then, pull ahead, and let's get the whale alongside."
"I think I remember some story like the one you were telling," said Flask, when at last the two boats were slowly advancing with their burden toward the ship. "But I can't remember where I heard it."
"Three Spaniards? Adventures of those three bloody-minded soldiers? Did you read it there, Flask? I guess you did?"
"No — never saw such a book. Heard of it, though. But now, tell me, Stubb — do you suppose that devil you were speaking of just now was the same you say is now on board the Pequod?"

"Am I the same man who helped kill this whale? Doesn't the devil live forever? Whoever heard of the devil dying? Did you ever see a parson in mourning for the devil? And if the devil has a latchkey to let himself into the admiral's cabin, don't you think he can crawl through a porthole? Tell me that, Mr. Flask?"
"How old do you suppose Fedallah is, Stubb?"

"Do you see that mainmast there?" pointing to the ship. "Well, that's the figure one. Now take all the hoops in the Pequod's hold, and string them along in a row with that mast, for zeros, do you see? Well, that wouldn't even begin to be Fedallah's age. Not all the coopers in creation could show hoops enough to make zeros enough."

"But see here, Stubb, I thought you boasted a little just now that you meant to give Fedallah a toss in the sea if you got a good chance. Now, if he's as old as all those hoops of yours come to, and if he's going to live forever, what good will it do to pitch him overboard — tell me that?"
"Give him a good ducking, anyway."
"But he'd crawl back."
"Duck him again, and keep ducking him."
"Suppose he should take it into his head to duck you, though — yes, and drown you — what then?"

"I'd like to see him try it. I'd give him such a pair of black eyes he wouldn't dare show his face in the admiral's cabin again for a good long while, let alone down in the orlop there, where he lives, or around here on the upper decks, where he sneaks about so much. Damn the devil, Flask — so you think I'm afraid of the devil? Who's afraid of him, except the old governor, who doesn't dare catch him and clap him in double-darbies — double handcuffs — as he deserves, but lets him go around kidnapping people? Yes, and he even signed a bond with him that he'd roast for him all the people the devil kidnapped. There's a governor for you!"
"Do you suppose Fedallah wants to kidnap Captain Ahab?"

"Do I think so? You'll find out before long, Flask. But from now on I'm going to keep a sharp lookout on him, and if I see anything very suspicious going on, I'll just grab him by the scruff of the neck and say — Look here, Beelzebub, don't you do it. And if he makes any fuss, by the Lord, I'll reach into his pocket for his tail, take it to the capstan, and give it such a wrench and heave that it snaps clean off at the stump — do you see? And then, I rather guess, when he finds himself docked in that odd way, he'll slink off without even the poor satisfaction of feeling his tail between his legs."
"And what will you do with the tail, Stubb?"
"Do with it? Sell it for an ox whip when we get home — what else?"
"Now, do you mean what you say, and have been saying all along, Stubb?"
"Mean or not mean, here we are at the ship."
The boats were now hailed to tow the whale on the port side, where fluke chains and other gear were already prepared for securing him.
"Didn't I tell you so?" said Flask. "Yes, you'll soon see this right whale's head hoisted up opposite that sperm whale's."

In good time, Flask's saying proved true. As before, the Pequod had leaned steeply over toward the sperm whale's head; now, by the counterweight of both heads, she regained her even keel — though sorely strained, you may well believe. So, when on one side you hoist in Locke's head, you go over that way; but now, on the other side, hoist in Kant's and you come back again — but in very poor shape. Thus some minds forever keep trimming boat. Oh, you foolish ones! Throw all these thunder-heads overboard, and then you will float light and right.

When the body of a right whale is brought alongside the ship to be dealt with, the same preliminary steps usually take place as with a sperm whale; the difference is that the sperm whale's head is cut off whole, whereas the right whale's lips and tongue are removed separately and hoisted on deck, together with all the familiar black bone (the baleen, or whalebone) attached to what is called the crown-piece. But in this case nothing of the kind had been done. Both carcasses had drifted astern, and the ship, weighed down with heads, looked rather like a mule carrying a pair of overloaded panniers.

Meanwhile, Fedallah was calmly eyeing the right whale's head, and every now and then glancing from the deep wrinkles there to the lines in his own hand. And Ahab happened to stand so that the Parsee occupied his shadow; while, if the Parsee's shadow was there at all, it seemed only to blend with and lengthen Ahab's. As the crew toiled on, Laplandish speculations were bandied about among them concerning all these passing things.

chapters.title: Chapter 74 — The Sperm Whale’s Head—Contrasted View
paragraphs: Here, now, are two great whales, laying their heads together. Let us join them and lay our own together.

Of the grand order of folio leviathans, the Sperm Whale and the Right Whale are by far the most remarkable. They are the only whales that man hunts regularly. To the Nantucketer they represent the two extremes among all the known kinds of whale. Since the outward difference between them shows mainly in their heads, and since a head of each is hanging from the Pequod's side at this very moment, and since we can move freely from one to the other simply by stepping across the deck — where, I'd like to know, could you find a better chance to study practical cetology than here?

In the first place, you are struck by the general contrast between these heads. Both are massive enough, heaven knows; but there is a certain mathematical symmetry in the Sperm Whale's that the Right Whale's sadly lacks. There is more character in the Sperm Whale's head. As you look at it, you find yourself involuntarily granting him an immense superiority in pervading dignity. In the present instance, too, this dignity is heightened by the pepper-and-salt color of his head at the summit, a sign of advanced age and long experience. In short, he is what the fishermen technically call a "gray-headed whale."

Let us now note what is least dissimilar in these heads — namely, the two most important organs: the eye and the ear. Far back on the side of the head, and low down, near the angle of either whale's jaw, if you search carefully, you will at last see a lashless eye, which you would think belonged to a young colt — it is so disproportionately small.

Now, from this peculiar sideways position of the whale's eyes, it is plain that he can never see an object that is exactly ahead, any more than one that is exactly astern. In a word, the position of the whale's eyes corresponds to that of a man's ears; and you may imagine for yourself how it would go with you if you surveyed objects sideways through your ears. You would find that you could command only some thirty degrees of vision forward of the straight side-line of sight, and about thirty more behind it. If your bitterest enemy were walking straight toward you in broad daylight with a dagger raised, you would not be able to see him, any more than if he were creeping up on you from behind. In a word, you would have two backs, so to speak; but at the same time also two fronts (side fronts): for what is it that makes the front of a man — what, indeed, but his eyes?

Moreover, in most other animals that I can now think of, the eyes are so placed as to blend their visual power imperceptibly, producing one picture for the brain and not two. But the peculiar position of the whale's eyes, effectively divided as they are by many cubic feet of solid head, which towers between them like a great mountain separating two lakes in valleys, must of course wholly separate the impressions that each independent organ conveys. The whale, therefore, must see one distinct picture on this side and another distinct picture on that side, while all between must be profound darkness and nothingness to him. Man, in effect, may be said to look out on the world from a sentry-box with two joined sashes for his window. But in the whale these two sashes are set in separately, making two distinct windows, but sadly impairing the view. This peculiarity of the whale's eyes is something always to be borne in mind in the fishery, and to be remembered by the reader in some later scenes.

A curious and most puzzling question might be raised about this matter of the Leviathan's vision. But I must be content with a hint. So long as a man's eyes are open in the light, the act of seeing is involuntary; that is, he cannot help mechanically seeing whatever objects are in front of him. Nevertheless, anyone's experience will teach him that, though he can take in an undiscriminating sweep of things at one glance, it is quite impossible for him to examine any two things attentively and completely — however large or however small — at one and the same instant of time, even if they lie side by side and touch each other. But if you now separate these two objects and surround each with a circle of profound darkness, then, in order to see one of them in such a way as to bring your mind to bear on it, you will utterly shut the other out of your consciousness at that moment. How is it, then, with the whale? True, both his eyes, in themselves, must act simultaneously; but is his brain so much more comprehensive, combining and subtle than man's that he can at the same moment attentively examine two distinct prospects, one on one side of him and the other in exactly the opposite direction? If he can, then it is as marvelous a thing in him as if a man were able to work through the proofs of two distinct problems in Euclid simultaneously. Nor, strictly investigated, is there anything incongruous in this comparison.

It may be only an idle whim, but it has always seemed to me that the extraordinary wavering movements some whales display when beset by three or four boats, and the timidity and liability to odd frights so common in such whales — that all this, I think, comes indirectly from the helpless perplexity of will in which their divided and diametrically opposite powers of vision must involve them.

But the whale's ear is every bit as curious as his eye. If you know nothing at all about the species, you could search these two heads for hours without ever finding that organ. The ear has no outer flap at all, and the hole itself is so wonderfully small that you could hardly push a quill into it. It sits a little behind the eye. Where their ears are concerned, there is one important difference to note between the sperm whale and the right whale: the sperm whale's ear opens to the outside, while the right whale's is completely and smoothly covered with a membrane, so that it cannot be seen from outside at all.

Is it not curious that so vast a being as the whale should see the world through so small an eye, and hear the thunder through an ear smaller than a hare's? But if his eyes were as broad as the lens of Herschel's great telescope, and his ears as capacious as the porches of cathedrals, would that make him any longer of sight, or any sharper of hearing? Not at all. Why, then, do you try to "enlarge" your mind? Make it subtler.

Let us now, with whatever levers and steam-engines we have at hand, tip the sperm whale's head over so that it lies bottom up; then, climbing a ladder to the summit, take a peep down the mouth; and if the body were not now completely separated from it, we might go down with a lantern into the great Kentucky Mammoth Cave of his stomach. But let us hold on here by this tooth and look about us where we are. What a really beautiful and chaste-looking mouth! From floor to ceiling it is lined, or rather papered, with a glistening white membrane, glossy as bridal satin.

But step outside now and look at this ominous lower jaw, which looks like the long narrow lid of an enormous snuffbox, hinged at one end instead of along one side. If you pry it up over your head so that its rows of teeth show, it looks like a fearsome portcullis — and that, sadly, is just what it proves to be for many a poor soul in the fishery, when these spikes come down on him with impaling force. But it is far more terrible to see when, fathoms down in the sea, you spot some sulky whale hanging there motionless, his huge jaw, some fifteen feet long, dangling straight down at right angles to his body, for all the world like a ship's jib-boom. This whale is not dead; he is just discouraged — out of sorts, perhaps; hypochondriac; and so limp that the hinges of his jaw have gone slack, leaving him in that awkward predicament, a disgrace to his whole tribe, who, no doubt, must be wishing lockjaw on him.

In most cases this lower jaw — being easily unhinged by a practiced hand — is detached and hoisted on deck for the purpose of extracting the ivory teeth and furnishing a supply of that hard white whalebone with which the fishermen fashion all sorts of curious articles, including canes, umbrella-sticks, and handles for riding-whips.

The jaw is hauled on board with a long, weary hoist, like an anchor; and when the right time comes — a few days after the other work — Queequeg, Daggoo, and Tashtego, all skilled dentists, are put to pulling teeth. Queequeg lances the gums with a sharp cutting-spade; then the jaw is lashed down to ringbolts, a tackle is rigged from aloft, and they drag out the teeth the way Michigan oxen drag old oak stumps out of wild woodland. Usually there are forty-two teeth in all; in old whales they are much worn down but not decayed, and not filled in our artificial way either. Afterward the jaw is sawn into slabs and stacked away like joists for building houses.

chapters.title: Chapter 75 — The Right Whale’s Head—Contrasted View
paragraphs: Now let's cross the deck and take a good long look at the Right Whale's head.

As in general shape the noble Sperm Whale's head may be compared to a Roman war-chariot (especially in front, where it is so broadly rounded), so, seen broadly, the Right Whale's head bears a rather inelegant resemblance to a gigantic galliot-toed shoe, its toe rounded like the bow of a Dutch galliot. Two hundred years ago an old Dutch voyager likened its shape to that of a shoemaker's last. And in this same last or shoe, that old woman of the nursery tale, with her swarming brood, might very comfortably be housed, she and all her children.

But as you get closer to this great head, it takes on different appearances depending on where you stand. If you stand on top of it and look at these two F-shaped spout-holes, you would think the whole head was an enormous bass-viol and these spiracles the holes in its sounding-board. Then again, if you fix your eye on this strange crested, comb-like crust on top of the mass — this green, barnacled growth that the Greenlanders call the Right Whale's "crown" and the Southern whalemen its "bonnet" — if you look only at this, you would take the head for the trunk of some huge oak with a bird's nest in its fork. At any rate, when you watch those live crabs nesting here on the bonnet, that idea is almost bound to occur to you — unless, of course, your imagination has latched onto the technical term "crown" that it also goes by. In that case you will find it very interesting to think that this mighty monster is really a crowned king of the sea, whose green crown has been assembled for him in this marvelous way. But if this whale is a king, he is a very sulky-looking fellow to grace a diadem. Look at that drooping lower lip! What an enormous sulk and pout! A sulk and pout that measures, by carpenter's rule, about twenty feet long and five feet deep — a sulk and pout that will give you some 500 gallons of oil and more.

A great pity, now, that this unfortunate whale should be hare-lipped. The cleft is about a foot across. Probably the mother, during an important interval, was sailing down the Peruvian coast when earthquakes made the beach gape. Over this lip, as over a slippery threshold, we now slide into the mouth. Upon my word, if I were at Mackinaw, I should take this for the inside of an Indian wigwam. Good Lord! Is this the road that Jonah went? The roof is about twelve feet high, and runs up to a pretty sharp angle, as if there were a regular ridge-pole there; while these ribbed, arched, hairy sides present us with those wondrous, half-vertical, scimitar-shaped slats of whalebone, say three hundred on a side, which, hanging down from the upper part of the head or crown bone, form those Venetian blinds that have been briefly mentioned elsewhere. The edges of these bones are fringed with hairy fibers, through which the Right Whale strains the water, and in whose tangles he keeps back the small fish when he goes open-mouthed through the seas of brit at feeding time. In the central blinds of bone, as they stand in their natural order, there are certain curious marks, curves, hollows and ridges, by which some whalemen calculate the creature's age, as the age of an oak is reckoned by its circular rings. Though the certainty of this test is far from demonstrable, it has the flavor of probability by analogy. At any rate, if we accept it, we must grant the Right Whale a far greater age than will seem reasonable at first glance.

In old times, the most curious fancies seem to have prevailed about these blinds. One voyager in Purchas calls them the wondrous "whiskers" inside the whale's mouth;* another, "hogs' bristles"; a third old gentleman in Hackluyt uses the following elegant language, with "chop" for jaw: "There are about two hundred and fifty fins growing on each side of his upper chop, which arch over his tongue on each side of his mouth."

*This reminds us that the Right Whale really does have a sort of whisker — or rather a mustache — made up of a few scattered white hairs on the upper part of the outer end of the lower jaw. These tufts sometimes lend his otherwise solemn face a rather bandit-like look.

As everyone knows, these same "hogs' bristles," "fins," "whiskers," "blinds," or whatever you please, supply the ladies with their busks and other stiffening contrivances. But in this respect the demand has long been declining. It was in Queen Anne's time that the bone was in its glory, the farthingale (a hooped petticoat) being then all the fashion. And as those ancient ladies moved about gaily, though in the jaws of the whale, as you might say, so, in a shower, with the same thoughtlessness, do we nowadays run under the same jaws for protection; the umbrella being a tent spread over the same bone.

But forget about blinds and whiskers for a moment now, and, standing inside the Right Whale's mouth, take a fresh look around you. With all these colonnades of bone arranged so neatly around you, wouldn't you think you were inside the great Haarlem organ, gazing at its thousand pipes? As a carpet for the organ, we have a rug of the softest Turkey weave — the tongue, which is stuck, so to speak, to the floor of the mouth. It is very fat and tender and tends to tear apart when it is hoisted on deck. As for this particular tongue in front of us, at a quick glance I'd call it a six-barreler — that is, it will yield about that much oil.

By now you must clearly see the truth of what I began with: that the Sperm Whale and the Right Whale have almost completely different heads. To sum up, then: the Right Whale's head has no great well of sperm, no ivory teeth at all, and no long, slender lower jawbone like the Sperm Whale's. The Sperm Whale, for his part, has none of those bony blinds, no huge lower lip, and hardly any tongue to speak of. And again, the Right Whale has two external spout-holes, while the Sperm Whale has only one.
Take your last look now at these venerable hooded heads while they still lie side by side; one will soon sink into the sea with no record kept, and the other will not be far behind.

Can you make out the expression on the Sperm Whale's head there? It is the one he died with, except that some of the longer wrinkles in his forehead now seem to have faded. To me his broad brow seems full of a prairie-like calm, born of a speculative indifference to death. But look at the other head's expression. See that astonishing lower lip, pressed by chance against the ship's side so that it hugs the jaw tightly. Doesn't this whole head seem to express an enormous practical resolve in the face of death? I take this Right Whale to have been a Stoic; the Sperm Whale, a Platonist, who might have taken up Spinoza in his later years.

chapters.title: Chapter 76 — The Battering-Ram
paragraphs: Before leaving the Sperm Whale's head for now, I would have you, as a sensible physiologist, simply — and particularly — take note of its front, in all its compact concentration. I would have you examine it now with the single aim of forming for yourself some unexaggerated, intelligent estimate of whatever battering-ram power may be lodged there. This is a vital point, for you must either settle this matter to your own satisfaction, or remain forever an unbeliever about one of the most appalling, but no less true, events to be found perhaps anywhere in all recorded history.

You observe that in the ordinary swimming position of the Sperm Whale, the front of his head presents an almost entirely vertical surface to the water. You observe that the lower part of that front slopes considerably backward, so as to leave more room for the long socket that receives the boom-like lower jaw. You observe that the mouth is entirely under the head, much as though your own mouth were entirely under your chin. Moreover, you observe that the whale has no external nose, and that what nose he has — his spout hole — is on the top of his head; you observe that his eyes and ears are at the sides of his head, nearly one third of his entire length back from the front. So you must by now have realized that the front of the Sperm Whale's head is a dead, blind wall, without a single organ or tender projection of any kind whatsoever. Furthermore, you must now consider that only in the extreme, lower, backward-sloping part of the front of the head is there the slightest trace of bone, and that not until you get nearly twenty feet back from the forehead do you come to the full development of the skull. So this whole enormous boneless mass is like one wad. Finally, although, as will soon be revealed, its contents partly consist of the most delicate oil, you must now be told the nature of the substance that so impregnably encases all that apparent delicacy. Earlier I described to you how the blubber wraps the body of the whale as the rind wraps an orange. It is just the same with the head, but with this difference: around the head this envelope, though not so thick, has a boneless toughness that no one who has not handled it can imagine. The most sharply pointed harpoon, the keenest lance thrown by the strongest human arm, bounces off it powerlessly. It is as though the forehead of the Sperm Whale were paved with horses' hoofs. I do not think that any sensation lurks in it.

Think of another thing, too. When two large, loaded Indiamen — big merchant ships of the India trade — happen to crowd and crush toward each other in the docks, what do the sailors do? They do not hang between them, at the point where they will touch, any merely hard substance, like iron or wood. No, they hold there a large, round wad of tow (coarse flax or hemp fiber) and cork, wrapped in the thickest and toughest of ox-hide. That wad bravely and without injury takes the squeeze that would have snapped all their oak handspikes and iron crowbars. By itself this is enough to illustrate the obvious fact I am driving at. But in addition to this, it has occurred to me as a hypothesis that, since ordinary fish have what is called a swimming bladder, which they can swell or shrink at will; and since the Sperm Whale, as far as I know, has no such equipment; considering, too, the otherwise unaccountable way in which he sometimes sinks his head completely beneath the surface, and at other times swims with it raised high out of the water; considering the unobstructed elasticity of its envelope; considering the unique interior of his head — it has occurred to me as a hypothesis, I say, that those mystical, lung-celled honeycombs in there may possibly have some hitherto unknown and unsuspected connection with the outer air, so that they can be swelled and shrunk by the atmosphere. If this is so, imagine the irresistible force of that might, when the most impalpable and destructive of all the elements contributes to it.

Now, notice this. Driving this dead, impregnable, uninjurable wall unerringly forward, and this most buoyant thing inside it, there swims behind it all a mass of tremendous life, which can only be properly measured the way piled wood is — by the cord; and all of it obeys a single will, as the smallest insect does. So when I later describe to you in detail all the special powers and concentrations of force lurking everywhere in this vast monster, and show you some of his lesser feats of head-smashing, I trust you will have given up all ignorant disbelief and be ready to stand by this: that even if the Sperm Whale smashed a passage through the Isthmus of Darien, in Panama, and mixed the Atlantic with the Pacific, you would not raise one hair of your eyebrow. For unless you acknowledge the whale, you are only a provincial and a sentimentalist in Truth. But clear Truth is something only salamander giants can face; how small, then, are the chances for the provincials? What happened to the feeble youth who lifted the veil of the dread goddess at Lais?

chapters.title: Chapter 77 — The Great Heidelburgh Tun
paragraphs: Now comes the baling of the case. But to understand it properly, you must know something of the curious internal structure of the thing being operated upon.

Regarding the Sperm Whale's head as a solid oblong, you may divide it sideways, along an inclined plane, into two quoins,* of which the lower is the bony structure forming the skull and jaws, and the upper an oily mass entirely free of bones, its broad forward end forming the expanded, vertical, apparent forehead of the whale. At the middle of the forehead, subdivide this upper quoin horizontally, and you then have two almost equal parts, which were already naturally divided by an internal wall of a thick, tendinous substance.

*Quoin is not a Euclidean term. It belongs to pure nautical mathematics. I am not aware that it has been defined before. A quoin is a solid which differs from a wedge in having its sharp end formed by the steep slant of one side, instead of by both sides tapering toward each other.

The lower subdivided part, called the junk, is one immense honeycomb of oil, formed throughout its whole extent by tough, elastic white fibers crossing and recrossing into ten thousand infiltrated cells. The upper part, known as the Case, may be regarded as the great Heidelburgh Tun of the Sperm Whale, after the famous giant wine-cask of that name. And as that famous great cask is mystically carved in front, so the whale's vast pleated forehead forms countless strange devices for the emblematic adornment of his wondrous tun. Moreover, as the Tun of Heidelburgh was always kept filled with the most excellent of the wines of the Rhine valleys, so the tun of the whale contains by far the most precious of all his oily vintages; namely, the highly prized spermaceti, in its absolutely pure, limpid and fragrant state. Nor is this precious substance found unmixed in any other part of the creature. Though in life it remains perfectly fluid, yet on exposure to the air after death it soon begins to solidify, sending out beautiful crystalline shoots, as when the first thin, delicate ice is just forming in water. A large whale's case generally yields about five hundred gallons of sperm, though, owing to unavoidable circumstances, a good deal of it is spilled, leaks and dribbles away, or is otherwise irretrievably lost in the ticklish business of securing what you can.

I don't know what fine and costly material lined the inside of the Heidelburgh Tun, but in sheer richness that lining could never have matched the silky, pearl-colored membrane, like the lining of an elegant fur-trimmed cloak, that forms the inner surface of the Sperm Whale's case.

It will have been seen that the Heidelburgh Tun of the Sperm Whale takes in the whole length of the entire top of the head; and since — as has been set out elsewhere — the head takes up one third of the whole length of the creature, then, putting that length at eighty feet for a good-sized whale, you have more than twenty-six feet for the depth of the tun when it is hoisted lengthwise, up and down, against a ship's side.

Since, in beheading the whale, the operator's instrument is brought close to the spot where an entrance is later forced into the spermaceti magazine, he has to be uncommonly careful, lest a careless, untimely stroke should invade the sanctuary and wastefully let out its invaluable contents. It is this beheaded end of the head, too, that is at last raised out of the water and held in that position by the enormous cutting tackles, whose hempen combinations, on one side, make quite a wilderness of ropes in that quarter.
Thus much being said, attend now, I ask you, to that marvelous and — in this particular instance — almost fatal operation whereby the Sperm Whale's great Heidelburgh Tun is tapped.

chapters.title: Chapter 78 — Cistern and Buckets
paragraphs: Nimble as a cat, Tashtego climbs aloft and, without changing his upright posture, runs straight out along the overhanging main-yard-arm to the point where it projects exactly over the hoisted Tun. He has taken with him a light tackle called a whip, consisting of only two parts running through a single-sheaved block (a pulley with a single wheel). Securing this block so that it hangs down from the yard-arm, he swings one end of the rope until it is caught and firmly held by a hand on deck. Then, hand over hand, down the other part, the Indian drops through the air until he deftly lands on the summit of the head. There — still raised high above the rest of the company, to whom he calls out in lively fashion — he seems some Turkish Muezzin calling the good people to prayer from the top of a tower. A short-handled sharp spade is sent up to him, and he diligently searches for the proper place to begin breaking into the Tun. In this business he goes very carefully, like a treasure-hunter in some old house, sounding the walls to find where the gold is walled in. By the time this cautious search is over, a stout iron-bound bucket, exactly like a well-bucket, has been attached to one end of the whip, while the other end, stretched across the deck, is held there by two or three alert hands. These now hoist the bucket within reach of the Indian, to whom someone else has handed up a very long pole. Inserting this pole into the bucket, Tashtego guides the bucket down into the Tun until it entirely disappears; then, when he gives the word to the seamen at the whip, up comes the bucket again, all bubbling like a dairymaid's pail of new milk. Carefully lowered from its height, the brimming bucket is caught by a hand appointed for the purpose and quickly emptied into a large tub. Then it goes back up aloft and through the same round again, until the deep cistern will yield no more. Toward the end, Tashtego has to ram his long pole harder and harder, and deeper and deeper into the Tun, until some twenty feet of the pole have gone down.

Now, the people of the Pequod had been baling for some time in this way, and several tubs had been filled with the fragrant sperm, when all at once a strange accident happened. Whether it was that Tashtego, that wild Indian, was so heedless and reckless as to let go for a moment his one-handed hold on the great cabled tackles holding up the head; or whether the place where he stood was so treacherous and oozy; or whether the Evil One himself would have it happen so, without stating his particular reasons — how exactly it was, there is no telling now; but suddenly, as the eightieth or ninetieth bucket came suckingly up — my God! poor Tashtego — like the twin bucket that goes down as the other comes up in a real well, dropped head first down into this great Tun of Heidelburgh, and with a horrible oily gurgling went clean out of sight!

"Man overboard!" cried Daggoo, who, amid the general dismay, was the first to come to his senses. "Swing the bucket this way!" And he put one foot into it, the better to secure his slippery handhold on the whip itself, and the hoisters ran him high up to the top of the head, almost before Tashtego could have reached its bottom inside. Meanwhile, there was a terrible tumult. Looking over the side, they saw the head, lifeless until then, throbbing and heaving just below the surface of the sea, as if at that moment seized by some momentous idea; whereas it was only the poor Indian unconsciously revealing by those struggles the perilous depth to which he had sunk.

At this instant, while Daggoo, on the summit of the head, was clearing the whip — which had somehow got fouled in the great cutting tackles — a sharp cracking noise was heard; and to the unspeakable horror of all, one of the two enormous hooks holding up the head tore out, and with a vast vibration the enormous mass swung sideways, until the drunken ship reeled and shook as if struck by an iceberg. The one remaining hook, on which the entire strain now depended, seemed every instant on the point of giving way — an event made still more likely by the violent motions of the head.

"Come down, come down!" yelled the seamen to Daggoo. But with one hand holding on to the heavy tackles, so that if the head should drop he would still remain suspended, the negro, having cleared the foul line, rammed the bucket down into the now collapsed well, meaning that the buried harpooner should grasp it and so be hauled out.
"In heaven's name, man," cried Stubb, "are you ramming home a cartridge there? — Stop! How will that help him — jamming that iron-bound bucket on top of his head? Stop, will you!"
"Stand clear of the tackle!" cried a voice like the bursting of a rocket.

Almost in the same instant, with a thunder-boom, the enormous mass dropped into the sea, like Niagara's Table Rock into the whirlpool; the suddenly relieved hull rolled away from it so far that the glittering copper sheathing far down her side came into view; and all caught their breath as Daggoo, half swinging — now over the sailors' heads, and now over the water — was dimly seen through a thick mist of spray, clinging to the dangling tackles, while poor, buried-alive Tashtego was sinking utterly down to the bottom of the sea! But hardly had the blinding vapor cleared away when a naked figure with a boarding-sword in his hand was seen for one swift moment hovering over the bulwarks. The next, a loud splash announced that my brave Queequeg had dived to the rescue. Everyone rushed together to the side, and every eye counted every ripple, as moment followed moment and no sign of either the sinker or the diver could be seen. Some hands now jumped into a boat alongside and pushed a little way off from the ship.

"Ha! Ha!" cried Daggoo all at once, from his now quiet, swinging perch overhead. And looking further off from the side, we saw an arm thrust upright from the blue waves — a sight as strange as an arm thrust forth from the grass over a grave.

"Both! Both! — it is both!" cried Daggoo again with a joyful shout. And soon after, Queequeg was seen boldly striking out with one hand, and with the other clutching the long hair of the Indian. Drawn into the waiting boat, they were quickly brought to the deck. But Tashtego was long in coming to, and Queequeg did not look very well either.

Now, how had this noble rescue been accomplished? Why, diving after the slowly descending head, Queequeg, with his keen sword, had made side lunges near its bottom, so as to cut a large hole there; then, dropping his sword, he had thrust his long arm far inward and upward, and so hauled out poor Tash by the head. He declared that when he first reached in for him, a leg was presented; but, knowing well that that was not as it ought to be, and might cause great trouble, he had thrust back the leg, and by a deft heave and toss had turned the Indian a somersault; so that at the next try he came out in the good old way — head first. As for the great head itself, that was doing as well as could be expected.

And so, thanks to Queequeg's courage and great skill in obstetrics, the deliverance — or rather, the delivery — of Tashtego was successfully carried out, and in the face of the most awkward and seemingly hopeless obstacles, too. It is a lesson not to be forgotten. Midwifery should be taught alongside fencing and boxing, riding and rowing.

I know that this strange adventure of the Gay Header's will be sure to seem incredible to some landsmen, though they themselves may have seen or heard of someone falling into a cistern ashore — an accident which happens not infrequently, and with much less reason, too, than the Indian's, considering the extreme slipperiness of the rim of the Sperm Whale's well.

But perhaps it may be shrewdly objected: how is this? We thought the tissued, infiltrated head of the Sperm Whale was the lightest and most corklike part of him; and yet you make it sink in an element of far greater specific gravity than itself. We have you there. Not at all — I have you; for at the time poor Tash fell in, the case had been nearly emptied of its lighter contents, leaving little but the dense tendinous wall of the well — a double-welded, hammered substance, as I have said before, much heavier than sea water, a lump of which sinks in it almost like lead. But in this instance the tendency of this substance to sink rapidly was materially counteracted by the other parts of the head that remained attached to it, so that it sank very slowly and deliberately indeed, giving Queequeg a fair chance to perform his agile obstetrics on the run, as you might say. Yes, it was a running delivery, so it was.

Now, had Tashtego perished in that head, it would have been a very precious perishing: smothered in the very whitest and daintiest of fragrant spermaceti; coffined, hearsed and entombed in the secret inner chamber and sanctum sanctorum of the whale. Only one sweeter end comes readily to mind — the delicious death of an Ohio honey-hunter, who, seeking honey in the fork of a hollow tree, found such a great store of it that, as he leaned too far over, it sucked him in, so that he died embalmed. How many, do you think, have likewise fallen into Plato's honey head, and sweetly perished there?

chapters.title: Chapter 79 — The Prairie
paragraphs: To scan the lines of his face, or feel the bumps on the head of this Leviathan — this is something no physiognomist or phrenologist, no reader of character from the face or from the skull, has yet undertaken. Such an enterprise would seem about as hopeful as for Lavater to have scrutinized the wrinkles on the Rock of Gibraltar, or for Gall to have climbed a ladder and felt over the Dome of the Pantheon. Still, in that famous work of his, Lavater not only treats of the various faces of men, but also attentively studies the faces of horses, birds, serpents and fish, and dwells in detail on the changes of expression to be seen in them. Nor have Gall and his disciple Spurzheim failed to throw out some hints about the phrenological characteristics of beings other than man. Therefore, though I am poorly qualified to be a pioneer in applying these two semi-sciences to the whale, I will do my best. I try all things; I achieve what I can.

Regarded physiognomically, the Sperm Whale is an anomalous creature. He has no proper nose.
