And since the nose is the central and most conspicuous of the features, and since it perhaps most modifies and finally controls their combined expression, it would seem that its entire absence, as an external appendage, must very largely affect the whale's countenance. For as in landscape gardening a spire, cupola, monument or tower of some sort is thought almost indispensable to complete the scene, so no face can be physiognomically in keeping without the raised, open-work belfry of the nose. Knock the nose off Phidias's marble Jove, and what a sorry remainder! Nevertheless, Leviathan is of so mighty a magnitude, and all his proportions are so stately, that the same deficiency which would be hideous in the sculptured Jove is no blemish at all in him. No, it is an added grandeur. A nose on the whale would have been impertinent. As you sail round his vast head in your jolly-boat on your physiognomical voyage, your noble conceptions of him are never insulted by the reflection that he has a nose to be pulled — a pestilent notion that so often insists on intruding even when you look at the mightiest royal beadle on his throne.
In certain respects, perhaps the most imposing view of the Sperm Whale's physiognomy is the full front of his head. Seen from this angle, he is sublime.

In thought, a fine human brow is like the East when troubled with the morning. In the repose of the pasture, the curled brow of the bull has a touch of the grand in it. When the elephant pushes heavy cannon up mountain passes, his brow is majestic. Human or animal, the mystical brow is like that great golden seal affixed by the German emperors to their decrees. It signifies — "God: done this day by my hand." But in most creatures, and even in man himself, the brow is very often a mere strip of alpine land lying along the snow line. Few are the foreheads which, like Shakespeare's or Melancthon's, rise so high and come down so low that the eyes themselves seem clear, eternal, tideless mountain lakes; and in the forehead's wrinkles above them you seem to track the antlered thoughts coming down there to drink, as Highland hunters track the deer's prints in the snow. But in the great Sperm Whale, this high and mighty godlike dignity inherent in the brow is so immensely amplified that, gazing on it in that full front view, you feel the Deity and the dread powers more forcibly than in looking at any other object in living nature. For you see no one point precisely; not one distinct feature is revealed; no nose, eyes, ears or mouth; no face — he has none, properly speaking; nothing but that one broad firmament of a forehead, pleated with riddles, dumbly lowering with the doom of boats, and ships, and men. Nor does this wondrous brow diminish in profile, though viewed that way its grandeur does not overpower you so much. In profile you plainly see that horizontal, half-moon-shaped hollow in the middle of the forehead which, in man, is Lavater's mark of genius.

But how? Genius in the Sperm Whale? Has the Sperm Whale ever written a book or made a speech? No, his great genius is declared in his doing nothing in particular to prove it. It is declared, moreover, in his pyramid-like silence. And this reminds me that had the great Sperm Whale been known to the young Orient World, he would have been deified by the childlike thoughts of its magi. They deified the crocodile of the Nile because the crocodile is tongueless; and the Sperm Whale has no tongue, or at least it is so exceedingly small that it cannot be thrust out. If hereafter any highly cultured, poetical nation shall lure back to their birthright the merry May-day gods of old, and enthrone them, living, once more in the now egotistical sky, on the now unhaunted hill, then be sure that, raised to Jove's high seat, the great Sperm Whale shall lord it there.

Champollion deciphered the wrinkled granite hieroglyphics. But there is no Champollion to decipher the Egypt of every man's and every creature's face. Physiognomy, like every other human science, is nothing but a passing fable. So if Sir William Jones, who could read thirty languages, could not read the deeper and subtler meanings in the simplest peasant's face, how can unlettered Ishmael hope to read the awe-inspiring Chaldee of the Sperm Whale's brow? All I do is set that brow before you. Read it if you can.

chapters.title: Chapter 80 — The Nut
paragraphs: If, in his features, the Sperm Whale is a Sphinx, then to the phrenologist his brain looks like that geometrical circle which can never be squared.

In the full-grown creature the skull will measure at least twenty feet in length. Unhinge the lower jaw, and the side view of this skull is like the side of a moderately inclined plane resting throughout on a level base. But in life — as we have seen elsewhere — this inclined plane is filled up at an angle, and almost squared off, by the enormous mass of the junk and sperm lying on top of it. At the high end the skull forms a crater to bed that part of the mass; while under the long floor of this crater — in another cavity seldom more than ten inches long and as many deep — lies the mere handful of this monster's brain. In life the brain is at least twenty feet from his apparent forehead; it is hidden away behind its vast outworks, like the innermost citadel within the enlarged fortifications of Quebec. It is secreted in him like a choice casket, so much so that I have known some whalemen who flatly deny that the Sperm Whale has any other brain than that palpable semblance of one formed by the cubic yards of his sperm magazine. Given its strange folds, courses and convolutions, they think it more in keeping with the idea of his general might to regard that mystic part of him as the seat of his intelligence.

Plainly, then, from the phrenologist's point of view, the head of this Leviathan, while the creature is alive and whole, is a complete illusion. As for his real brain, you can neither see any sign of it then nor feel any. Like all mighty things, the whale shows a false brow to the ordinary world.

If you clear his skull of its spermy heaps and then look at its back end from behind — which is the high end — you will be struck by how much it resembles a human skull seen in the same position and from the same angle. In fact, put this reversed skull (scaled down to human size) on a plate among men's skulls, and you would unthinkingly mix it up with them; and noticing the hollows on one part of its top, you would say in phrenological terms: This man had no self-esteem and no veneration. And from those negatives, taken together with the positive fact of his enormous bulk and power, you can best form the truest, if not the most cheerful, idea of what the loftiest power is.

But if, from the comparative dimensions of the whale's actual brain, you think it incapable of being adequately charted, then I have another idea for you. If you look attentively at almost any quadruped's spine, you will be struck by the resemblance of its vertebrae to a strung necklace of dwarfed skulls, all bearing a rudimentary resemblance to the skull proper. It is a German notion that the vertebrae are absolutely undeveloped skulls. But I take it that the Germans were not the first men to perceive the curious external resemblance. A foreign friend once pointed it out to me in the skeleton of an enemy he had killed, with whose vertebrae he was inlaying the beaked prow of his canoe in a sort of bas-relief. Now, I consider that the phrenologists have left out an important thing in not pushing their investigations from the cerebellum through the spinal canal. For I believe that much of a man's character will be found indicated in his backbone. I would rather feel your spine than your skull, whoever you are. A thin joist of a spine never yet held up a full and noble soul. I rejoice in my spine, as in the firm, audacious staff of that flag which I fling half out to the world.

Apply this spinal branch of phrenology to the Sperm Whale. His skull cavity runs straight into the first neck vertebra, and in that vertebra the bottom of the spinal canal measures ten inches across and eight high, in a triangular shape with its base at the bottom. As the canal passes through the rest of the vertebrae it narrows, but for a good distance it stays very roomy. Now, naturally, this canal is filled with much the same strangely fibrous substance as the brain — the spinal cord — and connects directly with the brain. What's more, for many feet after leaving the brain's cavity, the spinal cord keeps its full thickness, nearly equal to that of the brain. Given all this, would it be unreasonable to survey and chart the whale's spine phrenologically? For seen this way, the wonderful relative smallness of his actual brain is more than made up for by the wonderful relative size of his spinal cord.

But leaving this hint to have whatever effect it may on the phrenologists, I would simply adopt the spinal theory for a moment with regard to the Sperm Whale's hump. This majestic hump, unless I am mistaken, rises over one of the larger vertebrae, and so is, in a way, its outer convex mold. Judging by its position, then, I would call this high hump the Sperm Whale's organ of firmness, or indomitableness. And you will yet have cause to learn that the great monster is indomitable.

chapters.title: Chapter 81 — The Pequod Meets The Virgin
paragraphs: The fated day arrived, and we duly met the ship Jungfrau, captained by Derick De Deer, out of Bremen.

The Dutch and Germans, once the greatest whaling peoples in the world, are now among the least; but now and then, at very wide intervals of latitude and longitude, you still come across their flag in the Pacific.

For some reason, the Jungfrau seemed quite eager to pay her respects. While still some distance from the Pequod, she rounded to and dropped a boat, and her captain was rowed toward us, standing impatiently in the bow instead of the stern.
"What has he got in his hand there?" cried Starbuck, pointing to something the German was waving. "Impossible! A lamp-feeder!"

"Not that," said Stubb. "No, no, it's a coffee-pot, Mr. Starbuck. He's coming over to make us our coffee, that German. Don't you see that big tin can beside him? That's his boiling water. Oh, he's all right, that German."
"Go on with you," cried Flask. "It's a lamp-feeder and an oil-can. He's out of oil and has come begging."

However curious it may seem for an oil-ship to be borrowing oil on the whaling-ground, and however much it may turn on its head the old proverb about carrying coals to Newcastle, sometimes such a thing really happens. And in the present case, Captain Derick De Deer was indeed carrying a lamp-feeder, just as Flask had said.

As he climbed onto the deck, Ahab abruptly confronted him, paying no attention to what he held. But in his broken English, the German quickly showed his complete ignorance of the White Whale. He immediately turned the conversation to his lamp-feeder and oil-can, remarking that he had to turn into his hammock at night in total darkness. His last drop of Bremen oil was gone, and not a single flying-fish had been captured to make up the difference. He finished by hinting that his ship was indeed what the Fishery technically calls a clean one — that is, an empty one — well deserving the name of Jungfrau, or the Virgin.

His needs supplied, Derick departed. But he had not yet reached his ship when whales were spotted almost simultaneously from the mastheads of both vessels. Derick was so eager for the chase that without pausing to put his oil-can and lamp-feeder aboard, he swung his boat around and went after the great lamp-feeders themselves.

Now, since the whales had surfaced to leeward, Derick and the other three German boats that soon followed him had a considerable head start on the Pequod's boats. There were eight whales, an average pod. Aware of their danger, they were swimming abreast at great speed straight before the wind, rubbing their flanks as closely as a team of horses in harness. They left a great, wide wake behind them, as though continually unrolling a vast parchment upon the sea.

Far behind in this rapid wake swam a huge, humped old bull. His comparatively slow progress and the unusual yellowish growths covering him made him seem afflicted with jaundice or some other infirmity. Whether this whale belonged to the pod ahead was questionable, for it is not customary for such ancient leviathans to be social. Nevertheless, he stuck to their wake, though their backwater must have slowed him, because the white foam at his broad muzzle was broken and choppy, like the swell formed when two opposing currents meet. His spout was short, slow, and labored — coming forth with a choking sort of gush and spending itself in torn shreds, followed by strange subterranean rumblings inside him that seemed to find their exit at his other buried end, causing the waters behind him to bubble up.

"Who's got some paregoric?" said Stubb. "He has the stomach-ache, I'm afraid. Lord, think of having half an acre of stomach-ache! Contrary winds are holding a mad Christmas inside him, boys. It's the first foul wind I ever knew to blow from astern. But look — did a whale ever yaw like that before? He must have lost his tiller."

As an overloaded East Indiaman bearing down the Hindostan coast with a deck-load of frightened horses careens, buries, rolls, and wallows on her way, so did this old whale heave his aged bulk. Now and then, partly turning over on his cumbersome rib-ends, he exposed the cause of his unsteady wake: the unnatural stump of his starboard fin. Whether he had lost that fin in battle or had been born without it was hard to say.
"Only wait a bit, old chap, and I'll give you a sling for that wounded arm," cried cruel Flask, pointing to the whale-line near him.
"Watch he doesn't sling you with it," cried Starbuck. "Give way, or the German will have him."

With single purpose, all the rival boats were pointed toward this one whale. Not only was he the largest and therefore the most valuable, but he was nearest to them. The other whales were swimming with such great speed as to almost defy pursuit for the time being. At this point, the Pequod's boats had shot past the three German boats that launched last. But from the great head start he had, Derick's boat still led the chase, though his foreign rivals closed in with every moment. The only thing they feared was that, being already so close to the whale, he would manage to dart his iron before they could completely overtake and pass him. As for Derick, he seemed quite confident this would be the case, and occasionally shook his lamp-feeder at the other boats with a mocking gesture.

"The ungracious and ungrateful dog!" cried Starbuck. "He mocks and taunts me with the very charity box I filled for him not five minutes ago!" Then in his old intense whisper: "Give way, greyhounds! Dog to it!"

"I tell you what it is, men," cried Stubb to his crew. "It's against my religion to get mad. But I'd like to eat that villainous German. Pull — won't you? Are you going to let that rascal beat you? Do you love brandy? A hogshead of brandy, then, to the best man. Come, why don't some of you burst a blood-vessel? Who's been dropping an anchor overboard? We don't budge an inch — we're dead in the water. Look, there's grass growing on the boat's bottom, and by the Lord, the mast is budding. This won't do, boys. Look at that German! The short and long of it is, men — will you spit fire or not?"

"Oh, see the foam he makes!" cried Flask, dancing up and down. "What a hump! Oh, do pile on the muscle — he lies like a log! Oh, my lads, do spring! Flapjacks and clams for supper, you know, my lads — baked clams and muffins! Oh, do, do spring! He's a hundred-barrel whale! Don't lose him now — don't, oh, don't! See that German! Oh, won't you pull for your pudding, my lads? Such a prize! Such a beauty! Don't you love spermaceti? There goes three thousand dollars, men! A bank! A whole bank! The Bank of England! Oh, do, do, do! What's that German about now?"

At this moment Derick was in the act of pitching his lamp-feeder at the advancing boats, and also his oil-can — perhaps with the double purpose of slowing his rivals' progress while accelerating his own through the backward momentum of the throw.

"The unmannerly Dutch dogger!" cried Stubb. "Pull now, men, like fifty thousand battleship-loads of red-haired devils. What do you say, Tashtego — are you the man to snap your spine in twenty-two pieces for the honor of old Gay Head? What do you say?"
"I say, pull like god-damn," cried the Indian.

Fiercely but evenly spurred on by the German's taunts, the Pequod's three boats now began ranging almost abreast, and in that formation they steadily closed the gap. In that fine, loose, gallant stance of the headsman drawing near to his prey, the three mates stood up proudly, occasionally urging on the rear oarsman with an exhilarating cry: "There she slides now! Hurrah for the white-ash breeze! Down with the German! Sail over him!"

But Derick had such a decisive head start that despite all their courage, he would have won this race — had not righteous judgment descended upon him in the form of a crab that caught the blade of his middle oarsman. While this clumsy fellow was struggling to free his oar, and while Derick's boat was nearly capsizing as he thundered at his men in a mighty rage — that was the moment for Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask. With a shout, they surged forward and ranged up diagonally on the German's quarter. An instant more, and all four boats were in the whale's immediate wake, while stretching from them on both sides was the foaming swell the whale created.

It was a terrific, most pitiable, and maddening sight. The whale was now going head out, sending his spout before him in a continual tormented jet, while his one poor fin beat his side in an agony of fright. Now to this side, now to that, he swerved in his faltering flight. At every wave he broke, he either spasmodically sank into the sea or rolled sideways, lifting his one beating fin toward the sky. I have seen a bird with a clipped wing making frightened broken circles in the air, vainly trying to escape piratical hawks. But the bird has a voice, and with plaintive cries makes known her fear. Yet the fear of this vast dumb creature of the sea was chained up and enchanted in him. He had no voice except that choking respiration through his blowhole, and this made the sight of him unspeakably pitiable — while still, in his amazing bulk, his portcullis jaw, and his omnipotent tail, there was enough to terrify the bravest man who pitied him.

Seeing now that only a few more moments would give the Pequod's boats the advantage, and rather than be cheated of his prey, Derick chose to risk what must have seemed to him an unusually long throw before his last chance escaped forever.

But no sooner did his harpooner stand up for the strike than all three tigers — Queequeg, Tashtego, Daggoo — instinctively sprang to their feet. Standing in a diagonal row, they simultaneously aimed their barbs and darted over the head of the German harpooner. Their three Nantucket irons entered the whale. Blinding vapors of foam and white fire! The three boats, in the first fury of the whale's headlong rush, bumped the German's aside with such force that both Derick and his baffled harpooner were spilled out and sailed over by the three flying keels.

"Don't be afraid, my butter-boxes," cried Stubb, casting a passing glance at them as he shot by. "You'll be picked up presently — all right. I saw some sharks astern — St. Bernard's dogs, you know — they relieve distressed travelers. Hurrah! This is the way to sail now. Every keel a sunbeam! Hurrah! Here we go like three tin kettles at the tail of a mad cougar! This puts me in mind of being fastened to an elephant in a carriage on a plain — makes the wheel-spokes fly, boys, when you fasten to him that way. And there's danger of being pitched out, too, when you hit a hill. Hurrah! This is the way a fellow feels when he's going to Davy Jones — all a rush down an endless slope! Hurrah! This whale carries the everlasting mail!"

But the monster's run was brief. Giving a sudden gasp, he plunged straight down. With a grating rush, the three lines flew around the loggerheads with such force as to gouge deep grooves into them. The harpooners were so afraid this rapid sounding would soon exhaust the lines that they used all their skill to catch repeated smoking turns with the rope to hold on. At last — owing to the perpendicular strain from the lead-lined chocks of the boats, where the three ropes went straight down into the blue — the gunwales of the bows were almost level with the water, while the three sterns tilted high in the air. When the whale stopped sounding, they remained in that position for a time, afraid to let out more line, though the situation was precarious. Boats have been pulled down and lost this way, yet it is this "holding on" — this hooking up of the whale from the back by the sharp barbs in his living flesh — that often torments the Leviathan into rising again to meet the sharp lance of his enemies. Yet the peril aside, it is doubtful whether this is always the best course. It is reasonable to assume that the longer the wounded whale stays underwater, the more he is exhausted. Because of the enormous surface area of a full-grown sperm whale — something less than two thousand square feet — the pressure of the water is immense. We all know what an astonishing atmospheric weight we ourselves bear, even here above ground in the air. How vast, then, the burden of a whale, bearing on his back a column of two hundred fathoms of ocean! It must at least equal the weight of fifty atmospheres. One whaleman has estimated it at the weight of twenty warships, with all their guns, stores, and men on board.

As the three boats lay there on that gently rolling sea, gazing down into its eternal blue noon — and as not a single groan or cry, not so much as a ripple or a bubble, came up from its depths — what landsman would have thought that beneath all that silence and peace, the greatest monster of the seas was writhing and wrenching in agony! Not eight inches of perpendicular rope were visible at the bows. Can it be believed that by three such thin threads the great Leviathan was suspended like the weight of an eight-day clock? Suspended? And from what? From three bits of board. Is this the creature of whom it was once so triumphantly said: "Can you fill his skin with barbed irons? Or his head with fish-spears? The sword of him that strikes at him cannot hold; the spear, the dart, nor the coat of mail. He regards iron as straw; the arrow cannot make him flee; darts are counted as stubble; he laughs at the shaking of a spear!" This the creature? This he? Oh, that prophecies should go unfulfilled! For with the strength of a thousand thighs in his tail, Leviathan had run his head under the mountains of the sea to hide from the Pequod's fish-spears!

In that sloping afternoon sunlight, the shadows that the three boats cast beneath the surface must have been long enough and broad enough to shade half of Xerxes' army. Who can tell how terrifying those huge phantoms must have been, flitting over the wounded whale's head!

"Stand by, men — he stirs," cried Starbuck, as the three lines suddenly vibrated in the water, conducting upward to them like magnetic wires the life-and-death throbs of the whale. Every oarsman felt them in his seat. The next moment, largely relieved from the downward strain at the bows, the boats gave a sudden bounce upward, like a small ice field when a dense herd of polar bears is scared off it into the sea.
"Haul in! Haul in!" cried Starbuck again. "He's rising."

The lines, of which hardly an instant before not a hand's breadth could have been gained, were now flung back in long, quick coils, dripping, into the boats. Soon the whale broke the surface within two ship-lengths of the hunters.

His movements clearly showed his extreme exhaustion. In most land animals, there are certain valves in their veins that, when the animal is wounded, at least partly shut off the blood flow in certain directions. Not so with the whale. One of his peculiarities is a completely non-valvular blood-vessel structure, so that when pierced by even so small a point as a harpoon, a deadly drain begins at once upon his whole arterial system. When this is worsened by the extraordinary water pressure at great depth below the surface, his life may be said to pour from him in constant streams. Yet so vast is the quantity of blood in him, and so distant and numerous its interior sources, that he will keep bleeding for a considerable period — even as a river will flow during a drought whose source lies in the hidden springs of far-off hills. Even now, when the boats closed on this whale and dangerously drew over his swaying flukes, and the lances were thrust into him, they were followed by steady jets from the new wounds, which kept continually playing, while the natural spout-hole in his head only sent its frightened moisture into the air at intervals, however rapid. From this last vent no blood yet came, because no vital part had been struck. His life, as they significantly call it, was untouched.

As the boats now more closely surrounded him, the whole upper part of his body, including much that is normally submerged, was plainly revealed. His eyes — or rather the places where his eyes had been — were visible. As strange, misshapen growths gather in the knotholes of the noblest oaks when they lie fallen, so from the spots where the whale's eyes had once been, there now protruded blind bulbs, horribly pitiable to see. But pity there was none. For all his old age, his one arm, and his blind eyes, he must die and be murdered — in order to light the gay weddings and other celebrations of men, and also to illuminate the solemn churches that preach unconditional harmlessness of all toward all. Still rolling in his blood, at last he partly revealed a strangely discolored lump or swelling, the size of a bushel, low on his flank.
"A nice spot," cried Flask. "Just let me prick him there once."
"Hold off!" cried Starbuck. "There's no need of that!"

But humane Starbuck was too late. The instant the dart struck, an ulcerous jet shot from that cruel wound. Goaded by it into more than bearable agony, the whale — now spouting thick blood — blindly charged the boats with swift fury, spattering them and their exulting crews all over with showers of gore, capsizing Flask's boat and damaging the bows. It was his death stroke. For by this time, so drained was he from blood loss that he helplessly rolled away from the wreck he had made, lay panting on his side, and impotently flapped his stumped fin. Then over and over he slowly revolved like a dying world, turned up the white secrets of his belly, lay like a log, and died. It was most pitiable, that last expiring spout. As when unseen hands gradually draw the water from some mighty fountain, and with half-stifled, melancholy gurglings the spray-column lowers and lowers to the ground — so fell the last long dying spout of the whale.

Soon, while the crews waited for the ship to arrive, the body showed signs of sinking with all its treasures untouched. Immediately, by Starbuck's orders, lines were secured to it at different points, so that before long every boat served as a buoy, with the sunken whale suspended a few inches beneath them by the ropes. By very careful management, when the ship drew near, the whale was transferred to her side and strongly secured there by the stiffest fluke-chains. For it was clear that unless artificially held up, the body would sink at once to the bottom.

It happened that almost upon the first cut into him with the spade, the entire length of a corroded harpoon was found embedded in his flesh, on the lower part of the lump described before. But since the stumps of harpoons are frequently found in the dead bodies of captured whales, with the flesh perfectly healed around them and no sign of their location, there must have been some other unknown reason to explain the ulceration. But still more curious was the fact that a stone lance-head was found in him, not far from the buried iron, with the flesh perfectly firm around it. Who had thrown that stone lance? And when? It might have been hurled by some Northwest Indian long before America was discovered.

What other marvels might have been dug out of this monstrous cabinet there is no telling. But a sudden stop was put to further discoveries when the ship was dragged over sideways toward the sea to a most unusual degree, owing to the body's enormously increasing tendency to sink. However, Starbuck, who was in charge, hung on to it to the last — hung on so stubbornly, in fact, that when at length the ship would have capsized if she had kept locking arms with the body, and the command was given to break clear, the strain upon the timber-heads to which the fluke-chains and cables were fastened was so immense that it was impossible to cast them off. Meanwhile, everything in the Pequod was tilted at an angle. To cross to the other side of the deck was like walking up the steep gabled roof of a house. The ship groaned and gasped. Many of the ivory inlays in her bulwarks and cabins were popped from their places by the unnatural dislocation. In vain, handspikes and crowbars were brought to bear upon the immovable fluke-chains to pry them loose from the timber-heads. And the whale had now settled so low that the submerged ends could not be reached at all, while every moment whole tons of weight seemed to be added to the sinking mass, and the ship seemed on the point of going over.

"Hold on, hold on, won't you?" cried Stubb to the body. "Don't be in such a devil of a hurry to sink! By thunder, men, we must do something or we're done for. No use prying there. Stop it, I say, with your handspikes, and one of you run for a prayer book and a pen-knife and cut the big chains."

"Knife? Aye, aye," cried Queequeg, and seizing the carpenter's heavy hatchet, he leaned out of a porthole and, steel against iron, began slashing at the largest fluke-chains. But only a few strokes, full of sparks, were needed before the tremendous strain did the rest. With a terrific snap, every fastening broke loose. The ship righted. The carcass sank.

Now, this occasional inevitable sinking of the recently killed sperm whale is a very curious thing. No fisherman has yet adequately explained it. Usually the dead sperm whale floats with great buoyancy, its side or belly considerably elevated above the surface. If the only whales that sank this way were old, meager, broken-hearted creatures, with their pads of fat diminished and all their bones heavy and rheumatic, then you might reasonably argue that this sinking is caused by an uncommon density in the whale, resulting from this lack of buoyant matter in him. But it is not so. For young whales in the peak of health, swelling with noble aspirations, prematurely cut off in the warm flush and springtime of life with all their panting fat about them — even these strong, buoyant heroes sometimes sink.

It should be said, however, that the Sperm Whale is far less prone to this than any other species. Where one Sperm Whale goes down, twenty Right Whales do. This difference is no doubt largely due to the greater quantity of bone in the Right Whale. His Venetian blinds alone — the slatted baleen in his mouth — sometimes weigh more than a ton, and from this burden the Sperm Whale is wholly free. But there are instances where, after many hours or several days, the sunken whale rises again, more buoyant than in life. The reason is obvious. Gases are generated inside him. He swells to prodigious size and becomes a sort of animal balloon. A warship could hardly keep him under then. In the shore whaling, in the shallows among the bays of New Zealand, when a Right Whale shows signs of sinking, they fasten buoys to him with plenty of rope, so that when the body has gone down, they know where to look for it when it rises again.

It was not long after the sinking of the body that a cry was heard from the Pequod's mastheads, announcing that the Jungfrau was again lowering her boats — though the only spout in sight was that of a fin-back, a species of whale that is impossible to capture because of its incredible swimming speed. Nevertheless, the fin-back's spout is so similar to the sperm whale's that unskilled fishermen often mistake it. And so Derick and all his men were now in valiant chase of this uncatchable brute. The Virgin, crowding on all sail, followed after her four young boats, and they all disappeared far to leeward, still in bold, hopeful pursuit.
Oh! Many are the fin-backs, and many are the Dericks, my friend.

chapters.title: Chapter 82 — The Honor and Glory of Whaling
paragraphs: There are some enterprises in which a careful disorderliness is the true method.

The more I dive into this matter of whaling, and the further I push my research up to its very source, the more I am impressed by its great honor and antiquity. And especially when I find so many great demigods and heroes, and prophets of every sort, who one way or another have brought it distinction, I am carried away by the thought that I myself belong, even if only in a humble rank, to a brotherhood so emblazoned with glory.

The gallant Perseus, a son of Jupiter, was the first whaleman; and to the eternal honor of our calling, let it be said that the first whale our brotherhood ever attacked was not killed for any sordid motive. Those were the knightly days of our profession, when we took up arms only to rescue the distressed, and not to fill men's lamp-feeders. Everyone knows the fine story of Perseus and Andromeda: how the lovely Andromeda, a king's daughter, was tied to a rock on the seacoast, and just as Leviathan was in the very act of carrying her off, Perseus, the prince of whalemen, fearlessly advanced, harpooned the monster, and rescued and married the maiden. It was an admirable, artful feat, and one the best harpooners of today rarely achieve, since this Leviathan was killed with the very first throw. And let no one doubt this Arkite story; for in ancient Joppa, now Jaffa, on the Syrian coast, there stood for many ages, in one of the pagan temples, the vast skeleton of a whale, which the city's legends and all its inhabitants declared to be the very bones of the monster Perseus killed. When the Romans took Joppa, that same skeleton was carried to Italy in triumph. What seems most remarkable and suggestively important in this story is this: it was from Joppa that Jonah set sail.

Related to the adventure of Perseus and Andromeda — indeed, some suppose it was indirectly derived from it — is the famous story of St. George and the Dragon. That dragon, I maintain, was a whale; for in many old chronicles whales and dragons are strangely jumbled together and often stand in for each other. "You are like a lion of the waters, and like a dragon of the sea," says Ezekiel — plainly meaning a whale; in fact, some versions of the Bible use that very word. Besides, it would take a great deal from the glory of the exploit if St. George had merely met a crawling reptile of the land, instead of doing battle with the great monster of the deep. Any man can kill a snake, but only a Perseus, a St. George, a Nantucket Coffin has the heart to march boldly up to a whale.

Don't let the modern paintings of this scene mislead us. It is true that the creature this valiant whaleman of old fought is vaguely shown in a griffin-like shape, and that the battle is pictured on land, with the saint on horseback. But consider the great ignorance of those times, when artists did not know the true form of the whale; consider that, as in Perseus's case, St. George's whale may have crawled up out of the sea onto the beach; and consider that the animal St. George rode might have been only a large seal, or sea-horse. With all this in mind, it will not seem altogether inconsistent with the sacred legend and the most ancient drawings of the scene to hold that this so-called dragon was none other than the great Leviathan himself. In fact, set before the strict and piercing truth, this whole story will fare like Dagon, that fish, flesh, and fowl idol of the Philistines: when he was set up before the ark of Israel, his horse's head and both the palms of his hands fell off him, and only the stump, the fishy part of him, remained. So, then, one of our own noble stamp — a whaleman, no less — is the guardian patron of England; and by rights, we Nantucket harpooners should be enrolled in the most noble Order of St. George. And therefore let the knights of that honorable company (none of whom, I venture to say, has ever had anything to do with a whale, as their great patron did) — let them never look down on a Nantucketer, since even in our woolen frocks and tarred trousers we are far better entitled to St. George's decoration than they are.

Whether to admit Hercules among us or not was something I long remained doubtful about. For although, according to the Greek myths, that ancient Crockett and Kit Carson — that brawny doer of joyful good deeds — was swallowed down and thrown up again by a whale, it is still debatable whether that strictly makes him a whaleman. Nowhere does it appear that he ever actually harpooned his fish, unless, indeed, from the inside. Nevertheless, he may be considered a sort of involuntary whaleman; at any rate, the whale caught him, even if he didn't catch the whale. I claim him as one of our clan.

But by the best contradictory authorities, this Greek story of Hercules and the whale is considered to derive from the still more ancient Hebrew story of Jonah and the whale, and vice versa. Certainly they are very similar. If I claim the demigod, then why not the prophet?

Nor do heroes, saints, demigods, and prophets alone make up the whole roll of our order. Our grand master is still to be named; for like the royal kings of old, we trace the headwaters of our brotherhood to nothing less than the great gods themselves. That wondrous Eastern story must now be retold from the Shaster, the Hindu scriptures, which give us the dread Vishnoo, one of the three persons in the godhead of the Hindus — give us this divine Vishnoo himself for our Lord; Vishnoo, who, by the first of his ten earthly incarnations, has forever set apart and sanctified the whale. When Brahma, or the God of Gods, says the Shaster, resolved to re-create the world after one of its periodic dissolutions, he gave birth to Vishnoo to preside over the work. But the Vedas, or mystical books — which Vishnoo apparently had to read before beginning the creation, and which therefore must have contained something in the way of practical hints to young architects — these Vedas were lying at the bottom of the waters. So Vishnoo became incarnate in a whale, and, sounding down in him to the uttermost depths, rescued the sacred volumes. Wasn't this Vishnoo a whaleman, then, just as a man who rides a horse is called a horseman?
Perseus, St. George, Hercules, Jonah, and Vishnoo! There's a membership roll for you! What club but the whaleman's can be headed like that?

chapters.title: Chapter 83 — Jonah Historically Regarded
paragraphs: The last chapter mentioned the historical story of Jonah and the whale. Now, some Nantucketers are rather suspicious of this historical story of Jonah and the whale. But then, there were some skeptical Greeks and Romans who broke ranks with the orthodox pagans of their day and doubted, just as much, the story of Hercules and the whale and that of Arion and the dolphin; and yet their doubts did not make those traditions the slightest bit less factual, for all that.

One old Sag-Harbor whaleman's chief reason for questioning the Hebrew story was this. He had one of those quaint old-fashioned Bibles decorated with curious, unscientific engravings, one of which showed Jonah's whale with two spouts in his head — a peculiarity true only of one species of Leviathan (the Right Whale and the varieties of that order), of which the fishermen have this saying: "A penny roll would choke him"; his swallow is so very small. But Bishop Jebb has an answer to this ready in advance. It is not necessary, the Bishop hints, to think of Jonah as entombed in the whale's belly, but rather as temporarily lodged in some part of his mouth. And this seems reasonable enough of the good Bishop. For truly, the Right Whale's mouth would hold a couple of whist-tables and comfortably seat all the players. Possibly, too, Jonah might have tucked himself away in a hollow tooth; but, on second thought, the Right Whale has no teeth.

Another reason Sag-Harbor (he went by that name) gave for his lack of faith in this matter of the prophet was something vaguely to do with the imprisoned body and the whale's gastric juices. But this objection likewise falls to the ground, because a German biblical interpreter supposes that Jonah must have taken refuge in the floating body of a whale that was already dead — just as the French soldiers in the Russian campaign turned their dead horses into tents and crawled inside them. Besides, other continental commentators have guessed that when Jonah was thrown overboard from the Joppa ship, he promptly escaped to another vessel close by, some vessel with a whale for a figurehead; and, I would add, possibly called "The Whale," just as some craft nowadays are christened the "Shark," the "Gull," or the "Eagle." Nor has there been any shortage of learned interpreters who have held that the whale mentioned in the book of Jonah simply meant a life-preserver — an inflated bag of wind — which the endangered prophet swam to, and so was saved from a watery death. Poor Sag-Harbor, then, seems beaten on every side. But he had still another reason for his lack of faith. It was this, if I remember right: Jonah was swallowed by the whale in the Mediterranean Sea, and after three days he was vomited up somewhere within three days' journey of Nineveh, a city on the Tigris, which is very much more than three days' journey from the nearest point of the Mediterranean coast. How is that?

But was there no other way for the whale to land the prophet that close to Nineveh? There was. He could have carried him around by way of the Cape of Good Hope. But leaving aside the voyage through the whole length of the Mediterranean and another up the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, such a theory would mean sailing right around Africa in three days — to say nothing of the fact that the Tigris, near where Nineveh stood, is too shallow for any whale to swim in. Besides, the idea of Jonah rounding the Cape of Good Hope at such an early date would rob Bartholomew Diaz, its reputed discoverer, of the honor of finding that great headland, and so make modern history a liar.

But all these foolish arguments of old Sag-Harbor only showed his foolish pride of reason — a thing all the more blameworthy in him, since he had little learning beyond what he had picked up from the sun and the sea. I say it only shows his foolish, impious pride, and his abominable, devilish rebellion against the reverend clergy. For a Portuguese Catholic priest put forward this very idea of Jonah's going to Nineveh by way of the Cape of Good Hope as a remarkable magnifying of the general miracle. And so it was. Besides, to this day the highly enlightened Turks devoutly believe in the historical story of Jonah. And some three centuries ago, an English traveler in old Harris's Voyages tells of a Turkish mosque built in honor of Jonah, in which there was a miraculous lamp that burned without any oil.

chapters.title: Chapter 84 — Pitchpoling
paragraphs: To make them run easily and swiftly, the axles of carriages are anointed; and for much the same purpose, some whalers perform a similar operation on their boats — they grease the bottom. Nor can it be doubted that, since such a procedure can do no harm, it may possibly be of no small advantage, considering that oil and water are hostile, that oil is a sliding thing, and that the object in view is to make the boat slide bravely along. Queequeg believed strongly in anointing his boat, and one morning, not long after the German ship Jungfrau disappeared, he took more than his usual pains over it, crawling under its bottom where it hung over the side and rubbing in the grease as though he were diligently trying to raise a crop of hair on the craft's bald keel. He seemed to be acting on some particular premonition. Nor did what followed prove it unfounded.
Toward noon whales were sighted; but as soon as the ship sailed down on them, they turned and fled in headlong haste — a disordered flight, like that of Cleopatra's barges from Actium.

Nevertheless, the boats gave chase, and Stubb's was in the lead. With great effort, Tashtego at last managed to plant one iron; but the stricken whale, without sounding at all, kept up his horizontal flight, even faster than before. Such unbroken strain on the planted iron must sooner or later inevitably pull it out. It became essential to lance the fleeing whale, or be content to lose him. But hauling the boat up to his flank was impossible; he swam so fast and furiously. What was left, then?

Of all the wondrous devices and skills, the sleights of hand and countless subtleties that the veteran whaleman is so often driven to, none surpass that fine maneuver with the lance called pitchpoling. Neither small sword nor broadsword, in all its drills, can boast anything like it. It is indispensable only with a whale that is a stubborn runner; its great feature and fact is the wonderful distance to which the long lance is accurately thrown from a violently rocking, jerking boat racing ahead at full speed. Steel and wood included, the whole spear is some ten or twelve feet long; the shaft is much slighter than the harpoon's, and of a lighter material too — pine. It is fitted with a small rope of considerable length, called a warp, by which it can be hauled back to the hand after the throw.

But before going further, it is important to mention here that although the harpoon may be pitchpoled in the same way as the lance, it is seldom done; and when it is, it succeeds still less often, because of the harpoon's greater weight and shorter length compared with the lance, which in practice become serious drawbacks. As a general rule, therefore, you must first get fast to a whale before any pitchpoling comes into play.

Look now at Stubb — a man whose humorous, deliberate coolness and composure in the direst emergencies made him especially fit to excel at pitchpoling. Look at him: he stands upright in the tossing bow of the flying boat; wrapped in fleecy foam, the towing whale is forty feet ahead. Handling the long lance lightly, glancing two or three times along its length to see that it is exactly straight, Stubb, whistling, gathers up the coil of the warp in one hand, so as to keep its free end in his grip and leave the rest unobstructed. Then, holding the lance squarely in front of the middle of his waistband, he levels it at the whale; and, keeping it trained on him, he steadily presses down the butt-end in his hand, thereby raising the point until the weapon stands neatly balanced on his palm, fifteen feet in the air. He reminds you a little of a juggler balancing a long staff on his chin. The next moment, with a rapid, nameless impulse, the bright steel spans the foaming distance in a superb, lofty arc and quivers in the whale's life-spot. Instead of sparkling water, he now spouts red blood.

"That drove the spigot out of him!" cried Stubb. "It's the immortal Fourth of July; all fountains must run wine today! If only it were old Orleans whiskey, or old Ohio, or unspeakable old Monongahela! Then, Tashtego, lad, I'd have you hold a mug to the jet, and we'd drink a round from it! Yes, truly, my hearties, we'd brew choice punch in the spread of his spout-hole there, and from that live punch-bowl drink down the living stuff."

Again and again, to such playful talk, the deft throw is repeated, the spear returning to its master like a greyhound held on a skillful leash. The agonized whale goes into his flurry, the convulsion of his death; the towline is slackened, and the pitchpoler, dropping astern, folds his hands and silently watches the monster die.

chapters.title: Chapter 85 — The Fountain
paragraphs: That for six thousand years — and no one knows how many millions of ages before — the great whales should have been spouting all over the sea, sprinkling and misting the gardens of the deep as if with so many watering-cans and misting-pots; and that for some centuries now, thousands of hunters should have been close by the whale's fountain, watching these sprinklings and spoutings — that all this should be so, and yet that down to this blessed minute (fifteen and a quarter minutes past one in the afternoon of this sixteenth day of December, A.D. 1851) it should still remain an open question whether these spoutings are, after all, really water or nothing but vapor — this is surely a remarkable thing.

Let us, then, look into this matter, along with some interesting related points. Everyone knows that, by the peculiar ingenuity of their gills, the finny tribes in general breathe the air that is always mixed into the element they swim in; so a herring or a cod might live a century without once raising its head above the surface. But because of his distinctive internal structure, which gives him real lungs like a human being's, the whale can live only by breathing the free air of the open atmosphere. Hence his need to visit the upper world at regular intervals. But he cannot breathe through his mouth at all, for in his ordinary posture the Sperm Whale's mouth is buried at least eight feet below the surface; and, what is more, his windpipe has no connection with his mouth. No, he breathes through his spiracle, or blowhole, alone; and this is on the top of his head.

If I say that in any creature breathing is only a function indispensable to life, in that it draws from the air a certain element which, once brought into contact with the blood, gives the blood its life-giving principle, I don't think I shall be wrong — though I may be using some unnecessary scientific words. Assume it, and it follows that if all the blood in a man could be aerated with one breath, he might then seal up his nostrils and not take another for a considerable time. That is to say, he would then live without breathing. Strange as it may seem, this is exactly the case with the whale, who systematically lives, at intervals, his full hour and more (when at the bottom) without drawing a single breath or inhaling so much as a particle of air in any way; for remember, he has no gills. How is this? Between his ribs and on each side of his spine he is supplied with a remarkable, intricate Cretan labyrinth of vermicelli-like vessels, and when he leaves the surface these vessels are completely swollen with oxygenated blood. So for an hour or more, a thousand fathoms down in the sea, he carries a surplus stock of vitality in him, just as the camel crossing the waterless desert carries a surplus supply of drink for future use in its four supplementary stomachs. The anatomical fact of this labyrinth is indisputable; and that the supposition founded on it is reasonable and true seems all the more convincing to me when I consider that leviathan's otherwise inexplicable stubbornness in "having his spoutings out," as the fishermen put it. This is what I mean. If undisturbed, the Sperm Whale, on rising to the surface, will stay there for a length of time exactly the same as on all his other undisturbed risings. Say he stays eleven minutes and jets seventy times — that is, takes seventy breaths; then whenever he rises again, he is sure to take his seventy breaths over again, to the minute. Now, if after he has taken a few breaths you alarm him so that he sounds, he will keep dodging back up to make good his regular allowance of air. And not until those seventy breaths are counted out will he finally go down to stay out his full term below. Notice, however, that these rates differ from one whale to another; but in any one whale they are the same. Now, why should the whale insist like this on having his spoutings out, unless it is to refill his reservoir of air before descending for good? How obvious it is, too, that this necessity of rising exposes the whale to all the fatal hazards of the chase. For neither hook nor net could catch this vast leviathan when he is sailing a thousand fathoms beneath the sunlight. So it is not so much your skill, O hunter, as these great necessities that win you the victory!

In man, breathing goes on incessantly — one breath serving for only two or three heartbeats; so whatever other business he has to attend to, waking or sleeping, breathe he must, or die he will. But the Sperm Whale breathes only about one-seventh of his time — his Sunday, so to speak.

It has been said that the whale breathes only through his spout-hole. If it could truthfully be added that his spouts are mixed with water, then I think we would have the reason why his sense of smell seems wiped out in him; for the only thing about him that at all corresponds to a nose is that same spout-hole, and being so clogged with two elements, it could hardly be expected to have the power of smelling. But because of the mystery of the spout — whether it is water or whether it is vapor — no absolute certainty can yet be reached on this point. It is certain, nevertheless, that the Sperm Whale has no proper organs of smell. But what does he want them for? There are no roses, no violets, no cologne in the sea.

Furthermore, since his windpipe opens only into the tube of his spouting canal, and since that long canal — like the grand Erie Canal — is fitted with a sort of locks (which open and shut) to keep air in below or keep water out above, the whale has no voice; unless you insult him by saying that when he rumbles so strangely, he is talking through his nose. But then again, what has the whale to say? I have seldom known any profound being that had anything to say to this world, unless forced to stammer out something to earn a living. Oh, how lucky that the world is such an excellent listener!

Now, the Sperm Whale's spouting canal, meant chiefly as it is for carrying air, runs for several feet horizontally just beneath the upper surface of his head, and a little to one side; this curious canal is very much like a gas-pipe laid down on one side of a city street. But the question comes back whether this gas-pipe is also a water-pipe; in other words, whether the Sperm Whale's spout is merely the vapor of the exhaled breath, or whether that exhaled breath is mixed with water taken in at the mouth and discharged through the spiracle. It is certain that the mouth connects indirectly with the spouting canal; but it cannot be proved that this is for the purpose of discharging water through the spiracle. For the greatest need to do so would seem to arise when he accidentally takes in water while feeding. But the Sperm Whale's food is far beneath the surface, and there he cannot spout even if he wanted to. Besides, if you watch him very closely and time him with your watch, you will find that, when he is undisturbed, there is an unvarying rhythm between the timing of his jets and his ordinary periods of breathing.

But why bother anyone with all this reasoning about it? Just say it plainly! You have seen him spout, so tell us what the spout is. Can't you tell water from air? My dear sir, in this world these plain things are not so easy to settle. I have always found the plain things the most tangled of all. And as for this whale spout, you could almost stand in it and still not be sure exactly what it is.

The central body of it is hidden in the snowy, sparkling mist that envelops it; and how can you tell for certain whether any water falls from it, when, whenever you are near enough to a whale to get a close view of his spout, he is always in a tremendous commotion, with the water cascading all around him? And if at such times you thought you really saw drops of moisture in the spout, how do you know that they are not merely condensed from its vapor? Or how do you know that they are not those very drops lying on the surface of the spout-hole fissure, which is countersunk into the top of the whale's head? For even when he is swimming tranquilly through the midday sea in a calm, with his raised hump as sun-dried as a dromedary's in the desert — even then the whale always carries a small basin of water on his head, just as under a blazing sun you will sometimes see a hollow in a rock filled up with rain.

Nor is it at all wise for the hunter to be too curious about the precise nature of the whale's spout. It won't do for him to go peering into it and putting his face in it. You cannot go to this fountain with your pitcher, fill it, and carry it away. For even slight contact with the outer, vapory shreds of the jet, which will often happen, makes your skin smart feverishly from the acrid sting of the stuff that touches it. And I know a man who came into still closer contact with the spout — whether with some scientific object in view or otherwise, I cannot say — and the skin peeled off his cheek and arm. So among whalemen the spout is considered poisonous; they try to avoid it. Another thing: I have heard it said, and I don't much doubt it, that if the jet is spouted straight into your eyes, it will blind you. The wisest thing the investigator can do, then, it seems to me, is to leave this deadly spout alone.

Still, we can form a hypothesis, even if we cannot prove and establish it. My hypothesis is this: that the spout is nothing but mist. And besides other reasons, I am driven to this conclusion by considerations of the great inherent dignity and sublimity of the Sperm Whale. I consider him no common, shallow being, since it is an undisputed fact that he is never found on soundings — in water shallow enough to reach bottom with a lead line — or near shores; all other whales sometimes are. He is both ponderous and profound. And I am convinced that from the heads of all ponderous, profound beings, such as Plato, Pyrrho, the Devil, Jupiter, Dante, and so on, there always rises a certain half-visible steam while they are thinking deep thoughts. While I was composing a little treatise on Eternity, I had the curiosity to set a mirror in front of me; and before long I saw reflected there a curious, intricate worming and rippling in the air over my head. The invariable dampness of my hair while I am plunged in deep thought, after six cups of hot tea in my thin-shingled attic on an August noon — this seems a further argument for the above supposition.

And how grandly it lifts our idea of the mighty, misty monster to see him sailing solemnly through a calm tropical sea, his vast, gentle head overhung by a canopy of vapor produced by his incommunicable thoughts — and that vapor, as you will sometimes see, glorified by a rainbow, as if Heaven itself had set its seal on his thinking. For, you see, rainbows do not come to clear air; they light up only vapor. And in the same way, through all the thick mists of dim doubt in my mind, divine intuitions shoot every now and then, lighting up my fog with a heavenly ray. And I thank God for it; for everyone has doubts, and many deny, but few who have doubts or denials have intuitions along with them. Doubts about all things earthly and intuitions of some things heavenly — this combination makes neither believer nor infidel, but makes a man who looks on both with an even eye.

chapters.title: Chapter 86 — The Tail
paragraphs: Other poets have sung the praises of the soft eye of the antelope and the lovely plumage of the bird that never lands. Less heavenly, I celebrate a tail.

If you reckon the largest sperm whale's tail to begin at the point of the trunk where it tapers to about the girth of a man, it covers an area on its upper surface alone of at least fifty square feet. The compact round root expands into two broad, firm, flat palms or flukes, gradually thinning to less than an inch in thickness. At the junction, these flukes slightly overlap, then recede sideways from each other like wings, leaving a wide gap between them. In no living thing are the lines of beauty more exquisitely defined than in the crescent borders of these flukes. At full expansion in a full-grown whale, the tail will considerably exceed twenty feet across.

The entire structure seems a dense, webbed bed of welded sinews. But cut into it and you find three distinct layers: upper, middle, and lower. The fibers in the upper and lower layers are long and horizontal. Those in the middle are very short, running crosswise between the outer layers. This three-part structure, as much as anything else, gives the tail its power. To the student of old Roman walls, the middle layer will offer a curious parallel to the thin course of tiles always alternating with stone in those wonderful ancient ruins, which undoubtedly contribute so much to the masonry's great strength.

But as if this vast local power in the sinewy tail were not enough, the whole bulk of the leviathan is knit over with a warp and woof of muscular fibers and filaments. These pass on either side of the loins and run down into the flukes, blending with them seamlessly and greatly adding to their might. So in the tail, the combined, measureless force of the whole whale seems concentrated to a point. If annihilation could occur to matter, this would be the thing to do it.

Nor does this amazing strength at all cripple the graceful flexibility of its motions, where an infantlike ease undulates through a titanic power. On the contrary, those motions derive their most fearsome beauty from it. Real strength never impairs beauty or harmony but often bestows it. In everything impressively beautiful, strength has much to do with the magic. Take away the tied tendons that everywhere seem bursting from the marble in the carved Hercules, and its charm would be gone. When devout Eckerman lifted the linen sheet from Goethe's naked corpse, he was overwhelmed by the massive chest, which seemed like a Roman triumphal arch. When Angelo — Michelangelo — paints even God the Father in human form, notice the robustness there. And whatever they may reveal of divine love in the Son, those soft, curled, hermaphroditic Italian paintings in which his image has been most successfully embodied — so destitute of all brawniness — hint nothing of any power but the merely negative, feminine one of submission and endurance, which by all accounts form the peculiar practical virtues of his teachings.

Such is the subtle elasticity of the organ I describe that whether wielded in sport, in earnest, or in anger, whatever its mood, its movements are invariably marked by exceeding grace. No fairy's arm can surpass it.
Five great motions are peculiar to it. First, when used as a fin for propulsion. Second, when used as a club in battle. Third, in sweeping. Fourth, in lob-tailing. Fifth, in peaking flukes.

First: Being horizontal in position, the Leviathan's tail acts differently from the tails of all other sea creatures. It never wriggles. In man or fish, wriggling is a sign of inferiority. To the whale, his tail is his sole means of propulsion. Coiled forward like a scroll beneath the body and then rapidly sprung backward — this is what gives that singular darting, leaping motion to the monster when swimming furiously. His side fins serve only to steer.

Second: It is somewhat significant that while one sperm whale fights another only with his head and jaw, in his conflicts with man he chiefly and contemptuously uses his tail. In striking at a boat, he swiftly curves his flukes away from it, and the blow is delivered only by the recoil. If made in the unobstructed air, especially if it descends on its mark, the stroke is simply irresistible. No ribs of man or boat can withstand it. Your only salvation lies in dodging it. But if it comes sideways through the water, then partly owing to the light buoyancy of the whaleboat and the springiness of its materials, a cracked rib or a smashed plank or two — a sort of stitch in the side — is generally the worst of it. These underwater side-blows are so common in the fishery that they are considered child's play. Someone strips off a shirt, and the hole is plugged.

Third: I cannot prove it, but it seems to me that in the whale the sense of touch is concentrated in the tail. In this respect, there is a delicacy in it matched only by the daintiness of the elephant's trunk. This sensitivity is chiefly shown in the action of sweeping, when with maidenly gentleness the whale slowly moves his immense flukes from side to side upon the surface of the sea. And if he feels but a sailor's whisker — woe to that sailor, whiskers and all. What tenderness there is in that preliminary touch! Had this tail any grasping power, I should think of Darmonodes' elephant that so frequented the flower market and with low bows presented bouquets to young ladies, then caressed their waists. On more accounts than one, it is a pity the whale does not possess this grasping ability. For I have heard of yet another elephant that, when wounded in a fight, curved its trunk around and extracted the dart.

Fourth: Coming upon the whale unawares in the fancied security of the middle of solitary seas, you find him unbent from the vast dignity of his bulk, and kittenlike, he plays on the ocean as if it were a hearth. But still you see his power in his play. The broad palms of his tail are flipped high into the air, then brought smiting down upon the surface — the thunderous concussion resounding for miles. You would almost think a cannon had been fired. And if you noticed the light wreath of vapor from the blowhole at his other end, you would think that was the smoke from the touch-hole.

Fifth: In his normal floating posture, the leviathan's flukes lie considerably below the level of his back, completely out of sight beneath the surface. But when he is about to plunge into the depths, his entire flukes and at least thirty feet of his body are tossed erect in the air, remaining there vibrating a moment before they shoot downward out of view. Except for the sublime breach — to be described elsewhere — this peaking of the whale's flukes is perhaps the grandest sight in all of living nature. Out of the bottomless deep, the gigantic tail seems to be spasmodically grasping at the highest heaven. So in dreams, I have seen majestic Satan thrusting forth his tormented colossal claw from the flaming Baltic of Hell. But in gazing at such scenes, it all depends on your mood. If you are in the Dantean frame, devils will come to mind. If in that of Isaiah, archangels. Standing at the masthead of my ship during a sunrise that crimsoned sky and sea, I once saw a large herd of whales in the east, all heading toward the sun, and for a moment vibrating in concert with peaked flukes. As it seemed to me then, such a grand embodiment of adoration of the gods was never seen, even in Persia, the home of fire worshippers. As Ptolemy Philopater testified of the African elephant, I then testified of the whale, pronouncing him the most devout of all beings. For according to King Juba, the military elephants of antiquity often hailed the morning with their trunks uplifted in the most profound silence.

The casual comparison in this chapter between the whale and the elephant — so far as some aspects of the tail of the one and the trunk of the other are concerned — should not suggest those two opposite organs are equal, much less the creatures they belong to. For as the mightiest elephant is only a terrier to Leviathan, so compared with Leviathan's tail, the elephant's trunk is only the stalk of a lily. The most dreadful blow from the elephant's trunk would be as the playful tap of a fan compared with the measureless crush and crash of the sperm whale's ponderous flukes, which have repeatedly hurled entire boats, one after the other, with all their oars and crews into the air, much as an Indian juggler tosses his balls.*

*Any comparison of overall bulk between the whale and the elephant is absurd, since in that respect the elephant stands to the whale roughly as a dog stands to the elephant; still, there is no lack of curious resemblances between them, and one of these is the spout. Everyone knows that the elephant will often suck water or dust up into his trunk and then raise it and shoot it out in a stream.

The more I consider this mighty tail, the more I deplore my inability to express it. At times there are gestures in it that, though they would well grace the hand of man, remain wholly inexplicable. In an extensive herd, so remarkable, at times, are these mystic gestures that I have heard hunters declare them akin to Freemason signs and symbols — that the whale, by these methods, was intelligently conversing with the world. Nor is that all: there are other motions of the whale's body as a whole, full of strangeness and unaccountable to his most experienced pursuer. However I dissect him, then, I only go skin deep. I do not know him, and never will. But if I cannot even understand the tail of this whale, how can I understand his head? Still less can I comprehend his face, when he has none. You shall see my back parts, my tail, he seems to say, but my face shall not be seen. But I cannot fully make out his back parts either. And hint what he will about his face — I say again he has no face.

chapters.title: Chapter 87 — The Grand Armada
paragraphs: The long and narrow peninsula of Malacca, extending southeast from the territories of Burma, forms the most southerly point of all Asia. In a continuous line from that peninsula stretch the long islands of Sumatra, Java, Bali, and Timor. These, with many others, form a vast mole, or rampart, lengthwise connecting Asia with Australia and dividing the long unbroken Indian Ocean from the densely studded eastern archipelagoes. This rampart is pierced by several sally-ports for the convenience of ships and whales, the most prominent being the Straits of Sunda and Malacca. By the Straits of Sunda, chiefly, vessels bound to China from the west emerge into the China seas.

The narrow Straits of Sunda separate Sumatra from Java. Set halfway along that vast wall of islands and buttressed by the bold green headland sailors call Java Head, they correspond rather closely to the central gate into some huge walled empire. And considering the endless wealth of spices, silks, jewels, gold, and ivory with which the thousand islands of that oriental sea are stocked, it seems a meaningful arrangement of nature that the very shape of the land should give such treasures at least the look — however ineffective — of being guarded against the all-grasping western world. The shores of the Straits of Sunda have none of those domineering fortresses that guard the entrances to the Mediterranean, the Baltic, and the Propontis (the Sea of Marmara). Unlike the Danes, these Orientals do not demand the servile salute of lowered topsails from the endless procession of ships running before the wind that for centuries, night and day, have passed between Sumatra and Java loaded with the costliest cargoes of the east. But though they freely forgo a ceremony like this, they by no means give up their claim to more substantial tribute.

Time out of mind, the piratical proas (swift sailing craft) of the Malays, lurking among the low, shaded coves and islets of Sumatra, have sallied out upon the vessels sailing through the straits, fiercely demanding tribute at spear-point. Though the boldness of these corsairs has of late been somewhat checked by the repeated bloody punishments they have received at the hands of European warships, even now we occasionally hear of English and American vessels that have been ruthlessly boarded and plundered in those waters.

With a fair, fresh wind, the Pequod was now drawing near to these straits. Ahab intended to pass through them into the Java Sea, and thence, cruising northward over waters known to be frequented here and there by the sperm whale, sweep inshore by the Philippine Islands and reach the far coast of Japan in time for the great whaling season there. By this route, the circumnavigating Pequod would sweep almost all the known sperm whale cruising grounds of the world before descending upon the equator in the Pacific — where Ahab, though everywhere else frustrated in his pursuit, firmly counted on giving battle to Moby Dick in the sea he was most known to frequent, at a season when he might most reasonably be expected to haunt it.

But what now? In this globe-girdling quest, does Ahab touch no land? Does his crew drink air? Surely he will stop for water. No. For a long time now, the circus-running sun has raced within his fiery ring and needs no sustenance but what is in himself. So with Ahab. Notice this, too, about the whaler. While other ships are loaded down with foreign goods to be transferred to distant wharves, the world-wandering whale-ship carries no cargo but herself and her crew, their weapons and their wants. She has a whole lake's contents bottled in her ample hold. She is ballasted with useful things, not entirely with useless pig-lead and ballast iron. She carries years' worth of water in her. Clear old prime Nantucket water, which, when three years at sea, the Nantucketer in the Pacific prefers to drink over the brackish fluid rafted off only yesterday in casks from Peruvian or Indian streams. Hence it is that while other ships may have gone to China from New York and back again, touching at a score of ports, the whale-ship in all that time may not have sighted one grain of soil — her crew having seen no man but floating seamen like themselves. So that if you brought them the news that another flood had come, they would only answer: "Well, boys, here's the ark!"

Now, as many sperm whales had been captured off the western coast of Java, near the Straits of Sunda, and since most of the surrounding waters were generally recognized by fishermen as an excellent cruising ground, the Pequod's lookouts were repeatedly hailed and warned to stay wide awake as she gained upon Java Head. But though the green palmy cliffs of the land soon loomed on the starboard bow, and with delighted nostrils the fresh cinnamon was sniffed in the air, yet not a single spout was sighted. Almost giving up all thought of finding any whales in these parts, the ship had nearly entered the straits when the customary cheering cry was heard from aloft, and before long a spectacle of singular magnificence greeted us.

But here it must be noted that owing to the relentless activity with which sperm whales have lately been hunted over all four oceans, they now frequently gather in extensive herds, instead of almost invariably sailing in small, separate groups as in former times. Sometimes these herds embrace so great a multitude that it would almost seem as if numerous nations of them had sworn a solemn league and covenant for mutual assistance and protection. To this gathering of sperm whales into such immense caravans may be attributed the fact that even in the best cruising grounds, you may now sometimes sail for weeks and months without being greeted by a single spout — and then be suddenly confronted by what sometimes seems thousands upon thousands.

Broad on both bows, at a distance of two or three miles, forming a great semicircle that embraced one half of the level horizon, a continuous chain of whale-spouts was playing and sparkling in the noonday air. Unlike the straight perpendicular twin-jets of the right whale, which divide at the top and fall over in two branches like the cleft, drooping boughs of a willow, the single forward-slanting spout of the sperm whale presents a thick curled bush of white mist, continually rising and falling away to leeward.

Seen from the Pequod's deck as she would rise on a high hill of the sea, this host of vapory spouts, individually curling up into the air and viewed through a blending atmosphere of bluish haze, looked like the thousand cheerful chimneys of some dense city, glimpsed on a balmy autumn morning by some horseman on a hill.

As marching armies approaching an unfriendly mountain pass accelerate their march, all eagerness to put that perilous passage behind them and once more expand in comparative safety upon the plain — even so did this vast fleet of whales now seem hurrying forward through the straits, gradually contracting the wings of their semicircle and swimming on in one solid but still crescent-shaped formation.

Crowding on all sail, the Pequod pressed after them. The harpooners handled their weapons and cheered loudly from the bows of their still-suspended boats. If the wind only held, they had little doubt that, once chased through these Straits of Sunda, the vast host would only spread out into the eastern seas to see not a few of their number captured. And who could tell whether, in that gathered caravan, Moby Dick himself might not be temporarily swimming, like the worshipped white elephant in a Siamese coronation procession! So with studding-sail piled on studding-sail, we sailed along, driving these leviathans before us — when suddenly, the voice of Tashtego was heard, loudly directing attention to something in our wake.

Corresponding to the crescent ahead of us, we saw another behind us. It seemed formed of detached white vapors, rising and falling somewhat like whale-spouts, only they did not fully come and go but constantly hovered without quite disappearing. Leveling his glass at this sight, Ahab quickly spun in his pivot-hole, crying: "Aloft there, and rig whips and buckets to wet the sails! Malays, sir, and after us!"

Apparently having lurked too long behind the headlands, waiting until the Pequod had fairly entered the straits, these rascally Asiatics were now in hot pursuit to make up for their overcautious delay. But when the swift Pequod, with a fresh leading wind, was herself in hot chase — how very kind of these tawny philanthropists to help speed her on to her own chosen pursuit, serving as mere riding-crops and spurs to her. Some such thought seemed to be Ahab's as he paced the deck with glass under arm, in his forward turn beholding the monsters he chased and in his after turn the bloodthirsty pirates who were chasing him, the chaser. And when he glanced upon the green walls of the watery passage through which the ship was sailing, and considered that through that gate lay the route to his vengeance, and saw how through that same gate he was now both chasing and being chased to his deadly end — and not only that, but a herd of remorseless wild pirates and inhuman atheistical devils were infernally cheering him on with their curses — when all these thoughts had passed through his brain, Ahab's brow was left gaunt and furrowed, like a black sand beach after some stormy tide has been gnawing it without being able to drag the firm thing from its place.

But thoughts like these troubled very few of the reckless crew. When, after steadily dropping the pirates astern, the Pequod at last shot past the vivid green Cockatoo Point on the Sumatra side, emerging upon the broad waters beyond, the harpooners seemed more grieved that the swift whales had been gaining on the ship than glad that the ship had so victoriously gained upon the Malays.
