But still driving on in the whales' wake, at length they seemed to slow their speed. Gradually the ship neared them. The wind dying away, word was passed to launch the boats. But no sooner did the herd — by some presumed wonderful instinct of the sperm whale — become aware of the three boats coming after them, though still a mile behind, than they rallied again. Forming in close ranks and battalions, so that their spouts all looked like flashing lines of stacked bayonets, they moved on with redoubled speed.

Stripped to our shirts and drawers, we sprang to the oars. After several hours' pulling, we were almost ready to give up the chase when a general pausing commotion among the whales gave encouraging signs that they were now at last under the influence of that strange paralysis of indecision which, when fishermen see it in a whale, they say he is gallied. The compact martial columns in which they had been rapidly and steadily swimming now broke apart in one measureless rout. Like King Porus's elephants in the Indian battle with Alexander, they seemed going mad with panic. Expanding in vast irregular circles in all directions, swimming aimlessly this way and that, they plainly showed their distracted terror by their short, thick spoutings. This was still more strangely shown by those among them who, completely paralyzed as it were, helplessly floated like waterlogged dismasted ships on the sea. Had these leviathans been but a flock of simple sheep pursued over a pasture by three fierce wolves, they could not possibly have shown such excessive dismay. But this occasional timidity is characteristic of almost all herding creatures. Though banding together in tens of thousands, the lion-maned buffaloes of the West have fled before a solitary horseman. Witness, too, all human beings — how when herded together in the sheepfold of a theater pit, they will at the slightest alarm of fire rush helter-skelter for the exits, crowding, trampling, jamming, and mercilessly crushing each other to death. So it is best to withhold any amazement at the strangely gallied whales before us, for there is no folly of the beasts of the earth which is not infinitely outdone by the madness of men.

Though many of the whales, as has been said, were in violent motion, as a whole the herd neither advanced nor retreated but collectively remained in one place. As is customary in such cases, the boats separated at once, each making for some lone whale on the outskirts of the shoal. In about three minutes, Queequeg's harpoon was flung. The stricken whale darted blinding spray in our faces, then ran away with us like light, steering straight for the heart of the herd. Though such a move by a harpooned whale is by no means unprecedented and indeed is almost always expected to some degree, it presents one of the more dangerous episodes of the fishery. For as the swift monster drags you deeper and deeper into the frantic shoal, you bid farewell to cautious living and exist only in a delirious throb.

As, blind and deaf, the whale plunged forward, as if by sheer speed to rid himself of the iron leech fastened to him — as we tore a white gash in the sea, menaced on all sides by the crazed creatures rushing to and fro around us — our beset boat was like a ship mobbed by icebergs in a tempest, striving to steer through their complicated channels and straits, not knowing at what moment it might be locked in and crushed.

But not a bit daunted, Queequeg steered us manfully — now sheering off from this monster directly across our route, now edging away from that one whose colossal flukes were suspended overhead — while all the time Starbuck stood in the bow, lance in hand, pricking aside whatever whales he could reach with short thrusts, for there was no time for long ones. Nor were the oarsmen quite idle, though their usual duty was now entirely suspended. They chiefly attended to the shouting part of the business. "Out of the way, Commodore!" cried one to a great dromedary of a whale that suddenly rose bodily to the surface and for an instant threatened to swamp us. "Hard down with your tail, there!" cried a second to another that, close to our gunwale, seemed calmly cooling himself with his own fan-like extremity.

All whaleboats carry certain curious devices, originally invented by the Nantucket Indians, called druggs. Two thick squares of wood of equal size are stoutly clenched together so that they cross each other's grain at right angles. A line of considerable length is then attached to the middle of this block, and the other end of the line, being looped, can in a moment be fastened to a harpoon. It is chiefly among gallied whales that this drugg is used. For then, more whales are close around you than you can possibly chase at one time. But sperm whales are not encountered every day, so while you can, you must kill all you can. And if you cannot kill them all at once, you must wound them so that they can be killed afterward at your leisure. Hence it is that at times like these the drugg comes into play. Our boat was furnished with three of them. The first and second were successfully thrown, and we saw the whales staggering off, fettered by the enormous sideways resistance of the towing drugg. They were hobbled like criminals with ball and chain. But when we flung the third, the clumsy wooden block, as it was being tossed overboard, caught under one of the boat's seats and in an instant tore it out and carried it away, dumping the oarsman into the boat's bottom as the seat slid from under him. On both sides the sea poured in at the damaged planks, but we stuffed two or three pairs of drawers and shirts in, and so stopped the leaks for the time being.

It would have been nearly impossible to throw these drugged harpoons had our whale's pace not greatly slowed as we advanced into the herd. Moreover, as we went still further from the circumference of commotion, the chaos seemed to be waning. So when at last the jerking harpoon pulled free and the towing whale vanished sideways, we glided with the tapering force of his parting momentum between two whales into the innermost heart of the shoal — as if from some mountain torrent we had slid into a serene valley lake. Here the storms in the roaring glens between the outermost whales were heard but not felt. In this central expanse, the sea presented that smooth satin-like surface called a sleek, produced by the subtle moisture thrown off by the whale in his quieter moods. Yes, we were now in that enchanted calm which they say lurks at the heart of every commotion. And still in the distracted distance we saw the tumults of the outer concentric circles — successive pods of whales, eight or ten in each, swiftly going round and round like multiplied teams of horses in a ring, so closely shoulder to shoulder that a titanic circus-rider might easily have arched over the middle ones and ridden round on their backs. Owing to the density of the whales reposing more immediately around the trapped center of the herd, no possible chance of escape was presently offered to us. We had to watch for a breach in the living wall that hemmed us in — the wall that had only admitted us in order to shut us up. Keeping to the center of the lake, we were occasionally visited by small, tame cows and calves: the women and children of this routed host.

Now, including the occasional wide intervals between the revolving outer circles and the spaces between the various pods in any one of those circles, the entire area taken up by the whole multitude at this point must have contained at least two or three square miles. At any rate — though such a measurement at such a time might be deceptive — spouts could be seen from our low boat that seemed to play up almost from the rim of the horizon. I mention this because these smaller whales, now and then visiting our becalmed boat from the margin of the lake, showed a wondrous fearlessness and confidence, or else a still, spellbound panic that was impossible not to marvel at — whether because the cows and calves had, as it were, been purposely locked up in this innermost fold, and the wide extent of the herd had so far prevented them from learning the precise cause of its stopping, or possibly because they were so young, unsophisticated, and in every way innocent and inexperienced — however it may have been. Like household dogs, they came snuffling round us, right up to our gunwales and touching them, until it almost seemed that some enchantment had suddenly domesticated them. Queequeg patted their foreheads. Starbuck scratched their backs with his lance, though, fearful of the consequences, he refrained from darting it for the time.

But far beneath this wondrous world upon the surface, another and still stranger world met our eyes as we gazed over the side. For suspended in those watery vaults floated the forms of nursing mother whales, and those that by their enormous girth seemed shortly to become mothers. The lake, as I have hinted, was to a considerable depth exceedingly transparent. And as human infants while suckling will calmly and fixedly gaze away from the breast, as if leading two different lives at the same time — while yet drawing mortal nourishment, still spiritually feasting upon some unearthly memory — even so did the young of these whales seem to look up toward us, but not at us, as if we were but a bit of Gulfweed in their newborn sight. Floating on their sides, the mothers also seemed quietly eyeing us. One of these little infants, that from certain signs seemed hardly a day old, might have measured some fourteen feet in length and six feet around. He was a little frisky, though his body seemed scarcely recovered from the irksome position it had so recently occupied in the maternal reticule — the womb pictured as a lady's drawstring bag — where, tail to head and all ready for the final spring, the unborn whale lies bent like a Tartar's bow. The delicate side-fins and the palms of his flukes still freshly retained the plaited, crumpled appearance of a baby's ears newly arrived from foreign parts.
"Line! Line!" cried Queequeg, looking over the gunwale. "Him fast! Him fast! Who line him? Who struck? Two whale — one big, one little!"
"What ails you, man?" cried Starbuck.
"Look here," said Queequeg, pointing down.

Just as a harpooned whale, having run out hundreds of fathoms of rope from the tub, floats up again after a deep dive and shows the slack, curling line rising buoyantly and spiraling up into the air — so now Starbuck saw long coils of Madame Leviathan's umbilical cord, by which the young cub still seemed tethered to its mother. Quite often, in the swift ups and downs of the chase, this natural line, loose at the mother's end, gets tangled with the hemp one, and the cub is caught that way. Some of the sea's subtlest secrets seemed to be revealed to us in this enchanted pond. We saw young Leviathan romances in the deep.*

*The sperm whale, like all other species of Leviathan but unlike most other fish, breeds indiscriminately at all seasons. After a gestation that may probably be set at nine months, it produces but one at a time, though in some few known instances giving birth to an Esau and Jacob — twins — a contingency provided for in suckling by two teats, curiously situated one on each side of the anus, though the breasts themselves extend upward from that point. When by chance these precious parts in a nursing whale are cut by the hunter's lance, the mother's pouring milk and blood, rivaling each other, discolor the sea for rods around. The milk is very sweet and rich. It has been tasted by man, and it might go well with strawberries. When overflowing with mutual esteem, the whales salute more hominum — in the manner of human beings.

And so, though surrounded by circle upon circle of terrors and frights, these inscrutable creatures at the center freely and fearlessly went about all their peaceful concerns — indeed, they serenely reveled in dalliance and delight. But just so, amid the tornadoed Atlantic of my being, I myself still forever frolic at the center in mute calm; and while ponderous planets of unwaning woe revolve around me, deep down and deep inland there I still bathe in an eternal mildness of joy.

Meanwhile, as we lay entranced, the occasional sudden frantic scenes in the distance showed the activity of the other boats, still engaged in drugging the whales on the frontier of the host, or possibly carrying on the war within the first circle, where there was room enough and some convenient retreats. But the sight of the enraged drugged whales now and then blindly darting to and fro across the circles was nothing to what at last met our eyes. It is sometimes the custom, when fast to a whale more than usually powerful and alert, to try to hamstring him, as it were, by severing or maiming his gigantic tail-tendon. This is done by throwing a short-handled cutting-spade with a rope attached for hauling it back. A whale wounded in this way — as we afterward learned — but not effectively, as it seemed, had broken away from the boat, carrying along with him half of the harpoon line. In the extraordinary agony of the wound, he was now dashing among the revolving circles like the lone mounted desperado Arnold at the Battle of Saratoga, carrying dismay wherever he went.

But agonizing as this whale's wound was, and appalling a spectacle in itself, the peculiar horror he seemed to inspire in the rest of the herd was owing to a cause which at first the intervening distance hid from us. But at length we saw that by one of the unimaginable accidents of the fishery, this whale had become entangled in the harpoon line he towed. He had also run off with the cutting-spade in him. While the free end of the rope attached to that weapon had permanently caught in the coils of the harpoon line wound around his tail, the cutting-spade itself had worked loose from his flesh. So, tormented to madness, he was now churning through the water, violently flailing with his flexible tail and tossing the keen spade about him, wounding and killing his own companions.

This terrific sight seemed to rouse the whole herd from their frozen fright. First, the whales forming the margin of our lake began to crowd a little and jostle against each other, as if lifted by half-spent waves from afar. Then the lake itself began faintly to heave and swell. The submarine nurseries and bridal chambers vanished. In tighter and tighter orbits, the whales in the more central circles began to swim in thickening clusters. Yes, the long calm was departing. A low advancing hum was soon heard. And then, like the tumultuous masses of block-ice when the great river Hudson breaks up in spring, the entire host of whales came tumbling upon their inner center, as if to pile themselves up in one common mountain. Instantly Starbuck and Queequeg changed places, Starbuck taking the stern.

"Oars! Oars!" he intensely whispered, seizing the helm. "Grip your oars and clench your souls now! My God, men, stand by! Shove him off, Queequeg — the whale there! Prick him! Hit him! Stand up — stand up, and stay so! Spring, men — pull, men! Never mind their backs — scrape them! Scrape away!"

The boat was now all but jammed between two vast black bulks, leaving a narrow Dardanelles between their long bodies. But by desperate effort we at last shot into a temporary opening, then pulled hard, earnestly watching for another way out. After many similar narrow escapes, we at last swiftly glided into what had just been one of the outer circles but was now crossed by random whales, all violently making for the center. This lucky escape was cheaply purchased by the loss of Queequeg's hat, which, while he stood in the bow pricking the fleeing whales, was snatched clean from his head by the air-current made by the sudden tossing of a pair of broad flukes close by.

Riotous and disordered as the universal commotion now was, it soon resolved itself into what seemed a systematic movement. Having clumped together at last in one dense body, the whales renewed their forward flight with increased speed. Further pursuit was useless, but the boats still lingered in their wake to pick up whatever drugged whales might be dropped behind, and also to secure one that Flask had killed and waifed. The waif is a pennoned pole (a pole carrying a small flag), two or three of which are carried by every boat. When additional prey is at hand, these are inserted upright into the floating body of a dead whale, both to mark its place on the sea and as a token of prior possession, should the boats of any other ship draw near.

The result of this hunt was somewhat illustrative of that wise saying in the fishery: the more whales, the less fish. Of all the drugged whales, only one was captured. The rest managed to escape for the time, but only to be taken, as will later be seen, by some other vessel than the Pequod.

chapters.title: Chapter 88 — Schools and Schoolmasters
paragraphs: The previous chapter gave an account of an immense body or herd of sperm whales, and it also gave the probable cause of those vast gatherings.

Now, though such great bodies are at times encountered, as has been seen, even today small separate bands are occasionally observed, ranging from twenty to fifty individuals each. Such bands are known as schools. They are generally of two sorts: those composed almost entirely of females, and those mustering none but young, vigorous males — or bulls, as they are familiarly called.

In gallant attendance upon the school of females, you invariably see a male of full-grown size, but not old, who upon any alarm shows his chivalry by falling to the rear and covering the flight of his ladies. In truth, this gentleman is a luxurious Ottoman, swimming about the watery world, surrounded by all the comforts and pleasures of the harem. The contrast between this Ottoman and his concubines is striking, because while he is always of the largest leviathanic proportions, the ladies, even at full growth, are not more than one-third the bulk of an average-sized male. They are comparatively delicate, indeed — I daresay not exceeding half a dozen yards around the waist. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that on the whole they are hereditarily entitled to plumpness.

It is very curious to watch this harem and its lord on their lazy rambles. Like people of fashion, they are always on the move, in leisurely pursuit of variety. You meet them on the Line (the equator) just in time for the full bloom of the Equatorial feeding season, perhaps just back from summering in the Northern seas, and so sparing themselves all of summer's unpleasant fatigue and heat. After lounging up and down the promenade of the Equator for a while, they set off for Oriental waters ahead of the cool season there, and so escape the year's other extreme of temperature.

When serenely traveling on one of these journeys, if any strange suspicious sights are seen, the lord whale keeps a wary eye on his interesting family. Should any rudely bold young Leviathan happen that way and presume to draw confidentially close to one of the ladies — with what prodigious fury the Bashaw (the pasha) assails him and chases him away! A fine state of affairs indeed, if unprincipled young rakes like him are to be permitted to invade the sanctity of domestic bliss. Though do what the Bashaw will, he cannot keep the most notorious Lothario out of his bed, for alas, all fish bed in common. As on shore, the ladies often cause the most terrible duels among their rival admirers. Just so with the whales, who sometimes come to deadly battle, and all for love. They fence with their long lower jaws, sometimes locking them together and striving for supremacy like elks that interlock their antlers in war. Not a few are captured bearing the deep scars of these encounters: furrowed heads, broken teeth, scalloped fins, and in some instances wrenched and dislocated mouths.

But suppose the invader of domestic bliss takes himself away at the first rush of the harem's lord. Then it is very amusing to watch that lord. Gently he insinuates his vast bulk among them again and revels there awhile, still in tantalizing proximity to young Lothario, like pious Solomon devoutly worshipping among his thousand concubines. If other whales are in sight, the fishermen will seldom give chase to one of these Grand Turks, for these Grand Turks are too lavish with their strength, and hence their oil-yield is small. As for the sons and daughters they beget, those sons and daughters must take care of themselves — at least with only the mother's help. For like certain other omnivorous roving lovers that might be named, the lord whale has no taste for the nursery, however much for the bower. And so, being a great traveler, he leaves his anonymous babies all over the world, every baby an exotic. In good time, nevertheless, as the ardor of youth declines — as years and gloom increase, as reflection lends her solemn pauses — in short, as a general weariness overtakes the sated Turk, a love of ease and virtue replaces the love of maidens. Our Ottoman enters upon the impotent, repentant, lecturing stage of life, forswears and disbands the harem, and grown to an exemplary, sulky old soul, goes about all alone among the meridians and parallels saying his prayers and warning each young Leviathan from his amorous errors.

Now, as the harem of whales is called by the fishermen a school, so is the lord and master of that school technically known as the schoolmaster. It is therefore not in strict character — however admirably satirical — that after going to school himself, he should then go abroad teaching not what he learned there but the folly of it. His title of schoolmaster would very naturally seem derived from the name of the harem itself. But some have guessed that the man who first gave this name to this sort of Ottoman whale must have read the memoirs of Vidocq (the French criminal turned police detective), and informed himself what sort of country schoolmaster that famous Frenchman was in his younger days, and what was the nature of those secret lessons he taught some of his pupils.

The same seclusion and isolation to which the schoolmaster whale retreats in his advancing years is true of all aged sperm whales. Almost universally, a lone whale — as a solitary Leviathan is called — proves to be an ancient one. Like the venerable moss-bearded Daniel Boone, he will have no one near him but Nature herself. And her he takes to wife in the wilderness of waters — and the best of wives she is, though she keeps so many moody secrets.

The schools composed of nothing but young, vigorous males, previously mentioned, offer a strong contrast to the harem schools. For while those female whales are characteristically timid, the young males — or forty-barrel-bulls, as they call them — are by far the most combative of all Leviathans and proverbially the most dangerous to encounter, excepting those wondrous gray-headed, grizzled whales sometimes met, who will fight you like grim fiends exasperated by a gout sent as punishment.

The forty-barrel-bull schools are larger than the harem schools. Like a mob of young college men, they are full of fight, fun, and wickedness, tumbling round the world at such a reckless, rollicking rate that no prudent insurance man would cover them any more than he would a riotous student at Yale or Harvard. They soon outgrow this wildness, though, and when about three-quarters grown, they break up and separately go about in quest of settlements — that is, harems.

Another difference between the male and female schools is still more characteristic of the sexes. Say you strike a forty-barrel-bull: poor devil! All his comrades abandon him. But strike a member of the harem school, and her companions swim around her with every sign of concern, sometimes lingering so near and so long as to fall prey themselves.

chapters.title: Chapter 89 — Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish
paragraphs: The mention of the waif and waif-poles in the chapter before last calls for some account of the laws and regulations of the whale fishery, of which the waif may be considered the grand symbol and badge.

It frequently happens that when several ships are cruising together, a whale may be struck by one vessel, then escape, and finally be killed and captured by another. And within this general situation are many minor variations, all sharing this one feature. For example: after a weary and perilous chase and capture of a whale, the body may break loose from the ship in a violent storm and drift far to leeward, only to be retaken by a second whaler who, in a calm, snugly tows it alongside without risk of life or line. Thus the most maddening and violent disputes would often arise between fishermen, were there not some written or unwritten, universal, undisputed law applicable to all cases.

Perhaps the only formal whaling code ever enacted by a legislature was Holland's, decreed by the States-General in A.D. 1695. But although no other nation has ever had a written whaling law, American fishermen have acted as their own lawmakers and lawyers in this matter. They have devised a system that for concise completeness outdoes Justinian's Pandects and the By-laws of the Chinese Society for the Suppression of Meddling with other People's Business. Yes, these laws are so short they could be engraved on a Queen Anne's farthing, or on the barb of a harpoon, and worn around the neck.
I. A Fast-Fish belongs to the party fast to it.
II. A Loose-Fish is fair game for anybody who can soonest catch it.
But what causes trouble with this masterful code is the admirable brevity of it, which requires a vast volume of commentary to explain it.

First: What is a Fast-Fish? Alive or dead, a fish is technically fast when it is connected with an occupied ship or boat by any medium at all controllable by the occupant or occupants — a mast, an oar, a nine-inch cable, a telegraph wire, or a strand of cobweb, it is all the same. Likewise, a fish is technically fast when it bears a waif or any other recognized symbol of possession, so long as the party waifing it plainly shows both its ability to take the fish alongside at any time, and its intention to do so.

These are the learned commentaries. But the commentaries of the whalemen themselves sometimes consist of hard words and harder knocks — the Coke-upon-Littleton (the standard English law textbook) of the fist. True, among the more upright and honorable whalemen, allowances are always made for special cases where it would be an outrageous moral injustice for one party to claim possession of a whale previously chased or killed by another. But others are by no means so scrupulous.

Some fifty years ago there was a curious case of whale-trover (a suit to recover the value of goods wrongfully taken) litigated in England. The plaintiffs stated that after a hard chase of a whale in the northern seas, and when indeed they (the plaintiffs) had succeeded in harpooning the fish, they were at last, through peril of their lives, obliged to abandon not only their lines but their boat itself. Eventually the defendants — the crew of another ship — came up with the whale, struck, killed, seized, and finally appropriated it before the very eyes of the plaintiffs. And when those defendants were confronted, their captain snapped his fingers in the plaintiffs' faces and assured them that by way of a doxology (a closing hymn of praise) to the deed he had done, he would now retain their line, harpoons, and boat, which had remained attached to the whale at the time of the seizure. So the plaintiffs sued for the recovery of the value of their whale, line, harpoons, and boat.

Mr. Erskine represented the defendants; Lord Ellenborough was the judge. In the course of the defense, the witty Erskine illustrated his point by referring to a recent crim. con. case (a suit for adultery), in which a gentleman had tried in vain to curb his wife's vicious ways and had finally abandoned her on the seas of life; but years later, regretting that step, he sued to get her back. Erskine had been on the other side, and he had argued then that although the gentleman had originally harpooned the lady, and once had her fast, and had only abandoned her at last because of the terrible strain of her plunging viciousness, abandon her he nevertheless did, so that she became a loose-fish; and therefore when a later gentleman harpooned her again, the lady became that later gentleman's property, together with any harpoon that might be found sticking in her.
Now in the present case, Erskine argued that the whale and the lady each served to illustrate the other.

These arguments and counter-arguments being duly heard, the very learned judge officially decided as follows: As for the boat, he awarded it to the plaintiffs, because they had merely abandoned it to save their lives. But with regard to the disputed whale, harpoons, and line, they belonged to the defendants — the whale because it was a Loose-Fish at the time of the final capture, and the harpoons and line because when the fish made off with them, it (the fish) acquired property in those articles, and hence anybody who afterward took the fish had a right to them. Now the defendants afterward took the fish; therefore, the aforesaid articles were theirs.

An ordinary man looking at this decision of the very learned judge might possibly object to it. But plowed down to the bedrock of the matter, the two great principles laid down in the twin whaling laws previously quoted — applied and explained by Lord Ellenborough in the above-cited case — these two laws touching Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish will, on reflection, be found the fundamentals of all human law. For notwithstanding its complicated decorative sculpture, the Temple of the Law, like the Temple of the Philistines, has but two pillars to stand on.

Is it not a saying on everyone's lips that possession is half the law — regardless of how the thing came into possession? But often possession is the whole of the law. What are the bodies and souls of Russian serfs and Republican slaves but Fast-Fish, of which possession is the whole of the law? What to the greedy landlord is the widow's last mite but a Fast-Fish? What is yonder undetected villain's marble mansion with a door-plate for a waif — what is that but a Fast-Fish? What is the ruinous discount that Mordecai the broker gets from poor Woebegone the bankrupt, on a loan to keep Woebegone's family from starving — what is that ruinous discount but a Fast-Fish? What is the Archbishop of Savesoul's income of £100,000, seized from the meager bread and cheese of hundreds of thousands of broken-backed laborers, all sure of heaven without any of Savesoul's help — what is that globular £100,000 but a Fast-Fish? What are the Duke of Dunder's hereditary towns and hamlets but Fast-Fish? What to that mighty harpooner John Bull is poor Ireland but a Fast-Fish? What to that apostolic lancer Brother Jonathan (the United States) is Texas but a Fast-Fish? And concerning all these, is not Possession the whole of the law?
But if the doctrine of Fast-Fish applies fairly generally, the related doctrine of Loose-Fish applies more widely still. It holds everywhere, internationally and universally.

What was America in 1492 but a Loose-Fish, in which Columbus planted the Spanish standard by way of waifing it (flagging it as claimed) for his royal master and mistress? What was Poland to the Czar? What was Greece to the Turk? What was India to England? And what will Mexico finally be to the United States? Loose-Fish, all of them.

What are the Rights of Man and the Liberties of the World but Loose-Fish? What are all men's minds and opinions but Loose-Fish? What is the principle of religious belief in them but a Loose-Fish? To the showy, smuggling wordmongers, what are the thoughts of thinkers but Loose-Fish? What is the great globe itself but a Loose-Fish? And what are you, reader, but a Loose-Fish — and a Fast-Fish, too?

chapters.title: Chapter 90 — Heads or Tails
paragraphs: "De balena vero sufficit, si rex habeat caput, et regina caudam." — Bracton, l. 3, c. 3.

Latin from the books of the Laws of England, which, read in context, means that of all whales caught by anyone on the coast of that country, the King, as Honorary Grand Harpooner, must get the head, and the Queen must respectfully be given the tail. With a whale, this division is a lot like cutting an apple in half: nothing is left over in between. Now, since this law, in a modified form, is still in force in England today, and since it presents in several ways a strange exception to the general law of Fast and Loose-Fish, it gets a chapter of its own here — on the same courteous principle that leads the English railways to go to the expense of a separate car reserved especially for royalty. First, as a curious proof that the law just mentioned is still in force, let me put before you something that happened within the last two years.

It seems that some honest sailors of Dover, or Sandwich, or some one of the Cinque Ports, had after a hard chase succeeded in killing and beaching a fine whale which they had originally spotted far off from the shore. Now the Cinque Ports are partially or somehow under the jurisdiction of a sort of policeman or beadle (a minor parish officer) called a Lord Warden. He holds the office directly from the crown, I believe, and all the royal revenues from the Cinque Port territories become his by assignment. Some writers call this office a sinecure. But not so. Because the Lord Warden is busily employed at times in pocketing his perquisites — which are his chiefly by virtue of that same pocketing of them.

Now when these poor sun-burnt sailors, barefoot and with their trousers rolled high up on their eel-like legs, had wearily hauled their fat fish high and dry, promising themselves a good £150 from the precious oil and bone — and in their imaginations already sipping fine tea with their wives and good ale with their friends, upon the strength of their respective shares — up steps a very learned and most Christian and charitable gentleman, with a copy of Blackstone under his arm. Laying it upon the whale's head, he says: "Hands off! This fish, my masters, is a Fast-Fish. I seize it as the Lord Warden's." Upon this, the poor sailors in their respectful consternation — so truly English — knowing not what to say, fell to vigorously scratching their heads all round, meanwhile ruefully glancing from the whale to the stranger. But that did nothing to mend the matter or soften the hard heart of the learned gentleman with his copy of Blackstone. At length one of them, after long scratching about for his ideas, made bold to speak:
"Please, sir, who is the Lord Warden?"
"The Duke."
"But the Duke had nothing to do with taking this fish?"
"It is his."
"We have been at great trouble and peril and some expense, and is all that to go to the Duke's benefit — we getting nothing at all for our pains but our blisters?"
"It is his."
"Is the Duke so very poor as to be forced to this desperate way of getting a livelihood?"
"It is his."
"I meant to help support my old bedridden mother with part of my share of this whale."
"It is his."
"Won't the Duke be content with a quarter or a half?"
"It is his."

In short, the whale was seized and sold, and his Grace the Duke of Wellington got the money. Feeling that, seen in certain lights, the case might just possibly, and in some small degree, be considered rather a hard one under the circumstances, an honest clergyman of the town wrote his Grace a respectful note, begging him to give the case of those unlucky sailors his full consideration. To this my Lord Duke replied, in substance (both letters were published), that he had already done so, and had received the money, and would be obliged to the reverend gentleman if in future he (the reverend gentleman) would kindly refrain from meddling with other people's business. Is this the still-militant old man who stands at the corners of the three kingdoms, forcing alms out of beggars on every side?

It is easy to see that in this case the Duke's claimed right to the whale was one delegated to him by the Sovereign. So we have to ask on what principle the Sovereign holds that right in the first place. The law itself has already been stated. But Plowdon gives us the reason for it. According to Plowdon, a whale caught this way belongs to the King and Queen "because of its superior excellence." And the soundest commentators have always considered this a compelling argument in such matters.
But why should the King get the head and the Queen the tail? Give us a reason for that, you lawyers!

In his treatise on "Queen-Gold," or Queen's pin-money, an old King's Bench author, one William Prynne, writes thus: "The tail is the Queen's, that the Queen's wardrobe may be supplied with whalebone." Now this was written at a time when the black limber bone of the Greenland or right whale was widely used in ladies' bodices. But this same bone is not in the tail; it is in the head — which is a sad mistake for a learned lawyer like Prynne. But is the Queen a mermaid, to be presented with a tail? An allegorical meaning may lurk here.

English legal writers name two royal fish — the whale and the sturgeon — both of them royal property within certain limits, and in name supplying the tenth branch of the crown's ordinary revenue. I am not aware that any other author has touched on the matter, but it seems to me by inference that the sturgeon must be divided the same way as the whale, the King getting that fish's peculiarly dense and elastic head — which, taken symbolically, may possibly rest, humorously, on some supposed kinship. And so there seems to be a reason for everything, even in law.

chapters.title: Chapter 91 — The Pequod Meets The Rose-Bud
paragraphs: "In vain it was to rake for Ambergris in the paunch of this Leviathan, insufferable stench denying not inquiry." — Sir T. Browne, V.E.

It was a week or two after the last whaling scene I described, as we were sailing slowly over a sleepy, hazy midday sea, that the many noses on the Pequod's deck turned out to be sharper lookouts than the three pairs of eyes aloft. A strange and none too pleasant smell could be smelled on the sea.
"I'll bet something now," said Stubb, "that somewhere nearby are some of those drugged whales we tickled the other day. I thought they'd turn belly-up before long."

Presently, the haze ahead slid aside, and there in the distance lay a ship whose furled sails indicated that some sort of whale must be alongside. As we glided nearer, the stranger showed French colors from her peak. And by the eddying cloud of vulture sea-birds that circled, hovered, and swooped around her, it was plain that the whale alongside must be what the fishermen call a blasted whale — that is, a whale that has died unmolested on the sea and so floated as an unclaimed corpse. You can well imagine what an unsavory odor such a mass must give off — worse than an Assyrian city in the plague, when the living cannot bury the dead. So intolerable is it considered by some that no greed could persuade them to moor alongside it. Yet there are those who will still do it, notwithstanding the fact that the oil obtained from such subjects is of very inferior quality, and by no means of the nature of attar of roses.

As we drew still closer on the dying breeze, we saw that the Frenchman had a second whale alongside, and this one seemed even more of a nosegay than the first. In fact, it proved to be one of those puzzling whales that seem to shrivel and die of some enormous dyspepsia, or indigestion, leaving their dead bodies almost completely bankrupt of anything like oil. All the same, we shall see in due course that no knowing fisherman will ever turn up his nose at a whale like this, however much he may avoid blasted whales in general.
The Pequod had now swept so close to the stranger that Stubb swore he recognized his cutting spade-pole entangled in the lines knotted around the tail of one of these whales.

"There's a pretty fellow now," he banteringly laughed, standing in the ship's bow. "There's a jackal for you! I well know that these Crappoes of Frenchmen are but poor devils in the fishery — sometimes lowering their boats for breakers, mistaking them for sperm whale spouts. Yes, and sometimes sailing from their port with their hold full of boxes of tallow candles and cases of snuffers, foreseeing that all the oil they'll get won't be enough to dip the captain's wick into. Aye, we all know these things. But look here, here's a Crappo that is content with our leavings — the drugged whale there, I mean. Aye, and content too with scraping the dry bones of that other precious fish he has there. Poor devil! I say, pass round a hat, someone, and let's make him a present of a little oil for dear charity's sake. For what oil he'll get from that drugged whale there wouldn't be fit to burn in a jail — no, not in a condemned cell. And as for the other whale, why, I'll agree to get more oil by chopping up and boiling out these three masts of ours than he'll get from that bundle of bones. Though, now that I think of it, it may contain something worth a good deal more than oil. Yes — ambergris. I wonder now if our old man has thought of that. It's worth trying. Yes, I'm for it." And so saying he started for the quarter-deck.

By this time the faint breeze had become a complete calm, so that like it or not, the Pequod was now fairly trapped in the smell, with no hope of escaping unless the wind picked up again. Coming out of the cabin, Stubb called his boat's crew and pulled off for the stranger. Drawing across her bow, he saw that in accordance with the fanciful French taste, the upper part of her stem-piece was carved in the likeness of a huge drooping stalk, was painted green, and for thorns had copper spikes projecting from it here and there — the whole terminating in a symmetrical folded bulb of a bright red color. Upon her headboards, in large gilt letters, he read "Bouton de Rose" — Rose-button, or Rose-bud. And this was the romantic name of this aromatic ship.
Though Stubb did not understand the "Bouton" part of the inscription, the word "rose" and the bulbous figurehead put together sufficiently explained the whole to him.
"A wooden rose-bud, eh?" he cried with his hand to his nose. "That will do very well. But how like all creation it smells!"
Now in order to communicate directly with the people on deck, he had to pull around the bow to the starboard side, and thus come close to the blasted whale and talk over it.
Arriving at this spot, with one hand still to his nose, he bawled: "Bouton-de-Rose, ahoy! Are there any of you Bouton-de-Roses that speak English?"
"Yes," replied a Guernseyman from the bulwarks, who turned out to be the chief mate.
"Well then, my Bouton-de-Rose-bud, have you seen the White Whale?"
"What whale?"
"The White Whale — a sperm whale — Moby Dick. Have you seen him?"
"Never heard of such a whale. Cachalot Blanche! White Whale — no."
"Very good, then. Goodbye now, and I'll call again in a minute."

Then, pulling quickly back toward the Pequod and seeing Ahab leaning on the quarter-deck rail waiting for his report, he cupped his two hands into a trumpet and shouted, "No, sir! No!" At that, Ahab withdrew, and Stubb went back to the Frenchman.
He now saw that the Guernseyman, who had just climbed into the chains and was working with a cutting-spade, had his nose slung up in a kind of bag.
"What's the matter with your nose there?" said Stubb. "Broken it?"
"I wish it was broken, or that I didn't have any nose at all!" answered the Guernseyman, who did not seem to relish the job he was at very much. "But what are you holding yours for?"
"Oh, nothing! It's a wax nose — I have to hold it on. Fine day, isn't it? Air rather garden-like, I should say. Throw us a bunch of posies, will you, Bouton-de-Rose?"
"What in the devil's name do you want here?" roared the Guernseyman, flying into a sudden rage.

"Oh, keep cool — cool? Yes, that's the word! Why don't you pack those whales in ice while you're working at them? But joking aside, though — do you know, Rose-bud, that it's all nonsense trying to get any oil out of such whales? As for that dried-up one there, he hasn't a gill of oil in his whole carcass."

"I know that well enough. But, d'you see, the Captain here won't believe it. This is his first voyage — he was a Cologne manufacturer before. But come aboard, and maybe he'll believe you, if he won't believe me. And so I'll get out of this dirty mess."

"Anything to oblige you, my sweet and pleasant fellow," Stubb answered, and with that he was soon up on deck. A strange scene met him there. The sailors, in tasseled caps of red worsted, were getting the heavy tackles ready for the whales. But they worked rather slowly and talked very fast, and seemed in anything but a good mood. All their noses pointed upward from their faces like so many jib-booms. Every so often a couple of them would drop their work and run up to the masthead for some fresh air. Some, fearing they would catch the plague, dipped oakum in coal tar and held it to their nostrils from time to time. Others had snapped the stems of their pipes off almost at the bowl and were puffing hard on tobacco smoke, so that it kept their noses constantly full.

Stubb was struck by a shower of outcries and curses coming from the captain's round-house aft. Looking in that direction, he saw a fiery face thrust from behind the door, which was held slightly open from within. This was the tormented surgeon, who, after protesting in vain against the day's proceedings, had retreated to the captain's round-house ("cabinet," he called it) to avoid the pestilence — but still could not help yelling out his pleas and objections from time to time.

Noting all this, Stubb saw his opportunity. Turning to the Guernseyman, he had a little chat with him, during which the mate expressed his contempt for his captain as a conceited fool who had brought them all into so stinking and unprofitable a mess. Sounding him carefully, Stubb further perceived that the Guernseyman had not the slightest suspicion concerning the ambergris. He therefore kept quiet on that subject, but otherwise was quite frank and friendly with him, so that the two quickly hatched a little plan for both outwitting and mocking the captain, without his at all suspecting their true intentions. According to this plan, the Guernseyman, under cover of being an interpreter, was to tell the captain whatever he pleased, but as if it came from Stubb. And as for Stubb, he was to utter whatever nonsense came to mind during the interview.

By now their intended victim had come out of his cabin. He was a small, dark man, rather delicate-looking for a sea captain, though he did have large whiskers and a mustache; and he wore a red cotton-velvet vest with watch-seals at his side. The Guernseyman now introduced Stubb politely to this gentleman, and at once made a show of acting as interpreter between them.
"What shall I say to him first?" said he.
"Why," said Stubb, eyeing the velvet vest and the watch and seals, "you might as well start by telling him he looks kind of babyish to me, though I don't claim to be a judge."

"He says, Monsieur," said the Guernseyman in French, turning to his captain, "that only yesterday his ship spoke a vessel whose captain and chief mate, with six sailors, had all died of a fever caught from a blasted whale they had brought alongside."
Upon this the captain started, and eagerly wanted to know more.
"What now?" said the Guernseyman to Stubb.

"Why, since he takes it so easily, tell him that now I've eyed him carefully, I'm quite certain that he's no more fit to command a whale-ship than a St. Jago monkey. In fact, tell him from me he's a baboon."
"He vows and declares, Monsieur, that the other whale, the dried one, is far more deadly than the blasted one. In short, Monsieur, he begs us, as we value our lives, to cut loose from these fish."
At once the captain ran forward and shouted to his crew to stop hoisting the cutting-tackles and to cast off immediately the cables and chains that held the whales to the ship.
"What now?" said the Guernseyman, when the captain had returned to them.
"Why, let me see. Yes, you may as well tell him now that — that — in fact, tell him I've diddled him, and" — aside to himself — "perhaps somebody else."
"He says, Monsieur, that he's very happy to have been of any service to us."
Hearing this, the captain declared that they were the grateful parties — meaning himself and the mate — and concluded by inviting Stubb down to his cabin to drink a bottle of Bordeaux.
"He wants you to take a glass of wine with him," said the interpreter.
"Thank him heartily, but tell him it's against my principles to drink with the man I've diddled. In fact, tell him I must go."

"He says, Monsieur, that his principles won't allow him to drink. But that if Monsieur wants to live another day to drink, then Monsieur had best drop all four boats and pull the ship away from these whales, for it's so calm they won't drift."

By this time Stubb was over the side, and getting into his boat, he hailed the Guernseyman to this effect: that having a long tow-line in his boat, he would do what he could to help them by pulling out the lighter whale from the ship's side. While the Frenchman's boats were engaged in towing the ship one way, Stubb benevolently towed his whale the other way, ostentatiously letting out an unusually long tow-line.

Soon a breeze came up. Stubb made a show of casting off from the whale; the Frenchman hoisted his boats and quickly drew away, while the Pequod slipped in between him and Stubb's whale. At that, Stubb rowed swiftly to the floating body, hailed the Pequod to let them know what he meant to do, and at once set about reaping the fruit of his unrighteous cunning. Grabbing his sharp boat-spade, he began digging a hole in the body a little behind the side fin. You would almost have thought he was digging a cellar out there in the sea; and when his spade finally struck the gaunt ribs, it was like turning up old Roman tiles and pottery buried in fat English loam. His boat's crew were all wildly excited, eagerly helping their chief and looking as anxious as gold prospectors.

And all the while countless birds were diving and ducking and screaming and yelling and fighting around them. Stubb was starting to look disappointed, especially as the horrible nosegay grew stronger, when suddenly, from the very heart of this plague, a faint stream of perfume came stealing out. It ran through the tide of foul smells without being swallowed up by it, the way one river will flow into another and then run alongside it for a while without mixing at all.
"I have it! I have it!" cried Stubb with delight, striking something in the underground regions. "A purse! A purse!"

Dropping his spade, he plunged both hands in and pulled out handfuls of something that looked like ripe Windsor soap or rich, mottled old cheese, very oily and savory besides. You could easily dent it with your thumb; its color is somewhere between yellow and ash. And this, my good friends, is ambergris, worth a gold guinea an ounce to any druggist. About six handfuls were recovered; more was unavoidably lost in the sea, and still more might perhaps have been saved if impatient Ahab had not loudly ordered Stubb to stop and come aboard, or else the ship would say goodbye to them.

chapters.title: Chapter 92 — Ambergris
paragraphs: Now this ambergris is a very curious substance, and it was so important as an article of trade that in 1791 a certain Nantucket-born Captain Coffin was questioned about it at the bar of the English House of Commons. At that time, and in fact until fairly recently, the exact origin of ambergris was, like that of amber itself, a puzzle to scholars. The word ambergris is simply the French compound for "gray amber," yet the two substances are entirely different. Amber is sometimes found on the seashore, but it is also dug up from soil far inland, whereas ambergris is found only at sea. Amber, moreover, is hard, transparent, brittle and odorless, and it is used for pipe mouthpieces, beads and ornaments. Ambergris is soft and waxy, and so intensely fragrant and spicy that it is widely used in perfume, in pastilles, fine candles, hair powders and pomade. The Turks cook with it, and they also carry it to Mecca for the same purpose that frankincense is carried to St. Peter's in Rome. Some wine merchants drop a few grains into claret to flavor it.

Who would think, then, that such fine ladies and gentlemen should treat themselves to an essence found in the inglorious bowels of a sick whale! Yet so it is. By some, ambergris is supposed to be the cause of the whale's indigestion, and by others the effect. How to cure such indigestion would be hard to say, unless by administering three or four boatloads of Brandreth's pills (a popular patent laxative) and then running out of harm's way, as laborers do when blasting rocks.

I forgot to mention that we found some hard, round, bony plates in this ambergris. At first Stubb thought they might be buttons off sailors' trousers, but it later turned out that they were just pieces of small squid bones that had been embalmed in it that way.

Now that the incorruption of this most fragrant ambergris should be found in the heart of such decay — is this nothing? Think of that saying of St. Paul in Corinthians, about corruption and incorruption: how we are sown in dishonor but raised in glory. And likewise call to mind that saying of Paracelsus about what it is that makes the best musk. Also do not forget the strange fact that of all foul-smelling things, Cologne water, in its earliest manufacturing stages, is the worst.

I would like to end the chapter on that appeal, but I can't, because I am anxious to answer a charge often made against whalemen — one that some already prejudiced minds might think is indirectly confirmed by what I have said about the Frenchman's two whales. Elsewhere in this book I have disproved the slander that whaling is a sloppy, dirty business from start to finish. But there is another charge to rebut. People hint that all whales always smell bad. So where did this hateful stigma come from?

I believe it is plainly traceable to the first arrival of the Greenland whaling ships in London, more than two centuries ago. Because those whalemen did not then, and do not now, render their oil at sea as the southern ships have always done. Instead, cutting up the fresh blubber in small bits, they thrust it through the bungholes of large casks and carry it home that way — the shortness of the season in those icy seas and the sudden, violent storms to which they are exposed forbidding any other course. The consequence is that upon breaking into the hold and unloading one of these whale cemeteries in the Greenland dock, a stench is released somewhat similar to that rising from excavating an old city graveyard for the foundations of a lying-in (maternity) hospital.

I partly suspect also that this wicked charge against whalers may likewise be attributed to the existence on the coast of Greenland, in former times, of a Dutch village called Schmerenburgh or Smeerenberg — which latter name is the one used by the learned Fogo Von Slack in his great work on Smells, a textbook on that subject. As its name implies (smeer, fat; berg, to put up), this village was founded to provide a place for the blubber of the Dutch whale fleet to be rendered without being taken home to Holland. It was a collection of furnaces, fat-kettles, and oil sheds, and when the works were in full operation, they certainly gave off no very pleasant odor. But all this is quite different with a South Sea sperm whaler. In a voyage of perhaps four years, after completely filling her hold with oil, she does not perhaps spend fifty days in the business of boiling out. And in the state that it is casked, the oil is nearly scentless. The truth is that, living or dead, if but decently treated, whales as a species are by no means foul-smelling creatures. Nor can whalemen be detected, as the people of the Middle Ages claimed to detect a Jew in the company, by the nose. Nor indeed can the whale possibly be otherwise than fragrant, when, as a general thing, he enjoys such excellent health — taking abundant exercise, always out of doors, though, it is true, seldom in the open air. I say that the motion of a sperm whale's flukes above water gives off a perfume, as when a musk-scented lady rustles her dress in a warm parlor. What then shall I liken the sperm whale to for fragrance, considering his magnitude? Must it not be to that famous elephant, with jeweled tusks and redolent with myrrh, which was led out of an Indian town to do honor to Alexander the Great?

chapters.title: Chapter 93 — The Castaway
paragraphs: It was only some few days after encountering the Frenchman that a most significant event befell the most insignificant of the Pequod's crew — an event most lamentable, and which ended in providing the sometimes madly merry and predestined craft with a living and ever-accompanying prophecy of whatever shattered fate might prove her own.

Now, on a whale-ship, not everyone goes in the boats. Some few hands are held back as ship-keepers, whose job it is to work the vessel while the boats are chasing the whale. As a general thing, these ship-keepers are as hardy as the men in the boats' crews. But if there happens to be an unduly slender, clumsy, or timid fellow on the ship, that fellow is certain to be made a ship-keeper. It was so on the Pequod with the little negro nicknamed Pippin — Pip, for short. Poor Pip! You have heard of him before. You must remember his tambourine on that dramatic midnight, so gloomy-jolly.

In outward appearance, Pip and Dough-Boy made a match, like a black pony and a white one, of equal size though different color, driven together as one eccentric team. But while hapless Dough-Boy was by nature dull and sluggish in his wits, Pip, though over tender-hearted, was at bottom very bright, with that pleasant, warm, jolly brightness peculiar to his tribe — a tribe who ever enjoy all holidays and festivities with finer, freer relish than any other race. For blacks, the year's calendar should show nothing but three hundred and sixty-five Fourth of Julys and New Year's Days. Nor smile while I write that this little black boy was brilliant, for even blackness has its brilliance: behold that lustrous ebony, paneled in kings' cabinets. But Pip loved life and all life's peaceful securities, so that the panic-striking business in which he had somehow become entangled had most sadly dimmed his brightness — though, as will soon be seen, what was thus temporarily subdued in him was destined in the end to be luridly illuminated by strange wild fires, that falsely showed him off to ten times the natural luster with which, in his native Tolland County in Connecticut, he had once enlivened many a fiddler's dance on the green and, at melodious twilight, with his gay ha-ha! had turned the round horizon into one star-belled tambourine. So, though in the clear light of day a pure diamond drop suspended against a blue-veined neck will glow with healthy beauty, yet when the cunning jeweler would show you the diamond in its most impressive luster, he lays it against a gloomy background and then lights it up not by the sun but by some unnatural gas. Then come those fiery blazes, infernally superb. Then the evil-blazing diamond, once the divinest symbol of the crystal skies, looks like some crown-jewel stolen from the King of Hell. But let us get to the story.
It came to pass that in the ambergris affair, Stubb's rear oarsman happened to sprain his hand so badly as to be temporarily disabled. And so Pip was put in his place.

The first time Stubb lowered with him, Pip showed much nervousness. But happily, that time he escaped close contact with the whale, and therefore came off not altogether badly — though Stubb, observing him, afterward took care to urge him to nurture his courage to the utmost, for he might often find it necessary.

Now upon the second lowering, the boat paddled up to the whale. As the fish received the darted harpoon, it gave its customary jolt, which happened in this instance to be right under poor Pip's seat. The involuntary shock of the moment caused him to leap, paddle in hand, out of the boat — and in such a way that part of the slack whale-line came against his chest, so that he carried it overboard with him and became entangled in it when he plunged into the water. That instant the struck whale started on a fierce run. The line swiftly straightened, and — presto! — poor Pip came foaming up to the chocks of the boat, remorselessly dragged there by the line, which had taken several turns around his chest and neck.

Tashtego stood in the bow. He was full of the fire of the hunt. He hated Pip for a coward. Snatching the boat-knife from its sheath, he held its sharp edge over the line, and turning toward Stubb, cried: "Cut?" Meanwhile, Pip's blue, choking face plainly pleaded: Do, for God's sake! All passed in a flash. In less than half a minute, the whole thing happened.
"Damn him, cut!" roared Stubb. And so the whale was lost and Pip was saved.

As soon as he recovered himself, the poor little negro was assailed by yells and curses from the crew. Calmly letting these irregular damnations blow over, Stubb then in a plain, businesslike, but still half-humorous manner, cursed Pip officially. And that done, unofficially gave him much wholesome advice. The substance was: Never jump from a boat, Pip, except — but all the rest was indefinite, as the soundest advice ever is. Now, in general, "Stick to the boat" is the true motto in whaling. But cases will sometimes arise when "Leap from the boat" is still better. Moreover, as if realizing at last that if he gave Pip fully conscientious advice, he would be leaving him too wide a margin to jump in for the future, Stubb suddenly dropped all counsel and concluded with a flat command: "Stick to the boat, Pip, or by the Lord, I won't pick you up if you jump. Mind that. We can't afford to lose whales because of the likes of you. A whale would sell for thirty times what you would, Pip, in Alabama. Bear that in mind, and don't jump anymore." By this, perhaps, Stubb indirectly hinted that though man loved his fellow, yet man is a money-making animal, a tendency that too often interferes with his kindness.

But we are all in the hands of the Gods, and Pip jumped again. It was under very similar circumstances to the first time, but now he did not carry the line overboard with him. And so when the whale started to run, Pip was left behind on the sea, like a hurried traveler's trunk. Alas! Stubb was but too true to his word. It was a beautiful, bountiful, blue day. The spangled sea was calm and cool, stretching flatly away on all sides to the horizon, like gold-beater's skin hammered out to the extreme. Bobbing up and down in that sea, Pip's ebony head showed like a head of cloves. No boat-knife was lifted when he fell so rapidly astern. Stubb's inexorable back was turned upon him, and the whale was winged. In three minutes, a whole mile of shoreless ocean lay between Pip and Stubb. Out from the center of the sea, poor Pip turned his crisp, curling, black head to the sun — itself another lonely castaway, though the loftiest and the brightest.

Now in calm weather, to swim in the open ocean is as easy for the practiced swimmer as to ride in a spring-carriage on shore. But the awful loneliness is intolerable. The intense concentration of self in the middle of such a heartless immensity — my God! Who can tell it? Notice how, when sailors in a dead calm bathe in the open sea — notice how closely they hug their ship and only coast along her sides.

But had Stubb really abandoned the poor little negro to his fate? No — he did not mean to, at least. Because there were two boats in his wake, and he supposed, no doubt, that they would quickly come up to Pip and pick him up. Though, indeed, such consideration toward oarsmen endangered through their own timidity is not always shown by the hunters in similar cases. And such cases occur not infrequently. Almost invariably in the fishery, a coward, so called, is marked with the same ruthless contempt peculiar to military navies and armies.

But it so happened that those boats, without seeing Pip, suddenly spotted whales close to them on one side, turned, and gave chase. And Stubb's boat was now so far away, and he and all his crew so intent upon their whale, that Pip's ringed horizon began to expand around him miserably. By the merest chance, the ship itself at last rescued him. But from that hour the little negro went about the deck an idiot — such, at least, they said he was. The sea had mockingly kept his finite body up but drowned the infinite of his soul. Not drowned entirely, though. Rather carried down alive to wondrous depths, where strange shapes of the unwarped primal world glided to and fro before his passive eyes. And the miser-merman, Wisdom, revealed his hoarded heaps. And among the joyous, heartless, ever-youthful eternities, Pip saw the multitudinous, God-omnipresent coral insects that out of the firmament of waters heaved the colossal orbs. He saw God's foot upon the treadle of the loom, and spoke it. And therefore his shipmates called him mad. So man's insanity is heaven's sense. And wandering from all mortal reason, man comes at last to that celestial thought which, to reason, is absurd and frantic — and, weal or woe, feels then uncompromised, indifferent as his God.
For the rest, do not blame Stubb too harshly. The thing is common in that fishery. And in the sequel of the narrative, it will be seen what similar abandonment befell me.

chapters.title: Chapter 94 — A Squeeze of the Hand
paragraphs: Stubb's whale, bought at such a high price, was brought alongside the Pequod in due course, and all the cutting and hoisting operations described earlier were carried out in the usual way, right down to bailing out the Heidelburgh Tun, or Case.

While some were occupied with this latter duty, others were employed in dragging away the larger tubs as soon as they were filled with sperm. And when the proper time arrived, this same sperm was carefully processed before going to the try-works, of which more later.

The sperm had cooled and crystallized so much that when I sat down with several others in front of a large Constantine's bath of it, I found it had oddly set into lumps, which rolled about here and there in the liquid. Our job was to squeeze these lumps back into fluid. A sweet, oily duty! No wonder this sperm was such a popular cosmetic in the old days. What a cleanser! What a sweetener! What a softener! What a delicious soother! After my hands had been in it just a few minutes, my fingers felt like eels and began, so to speak, to snake and spiral.

As I sat there at my ease, cross-legged on the deck — after the bitter exertion at the windlass, under a blue tranquil sky, the ship under lazy sail and gliding so serenely along — as I bathed my hands among those soft, gentle globules of infiltrated tissue, woven almost within the hour, as they richly broke to my fingers and discharged all their richness, like fully ripe grapes their wine, as I breathed in that uncontaminated aroma, literally and truly like the smell of spring violets — I declare to you that for the time I lived as in a musky meadow. I forgot all about our horrible oath. In that inexpressible sperm, I washed my hands and my heart of it. I almost began to credit the old Paracelsan superstition that sperm is of rare virtue in calming the heat of anger. While bathing in that bath, I felt divinely free from all ill-will, or irritation, or malice of any sort whatsoever.

Squeeze! Squeeze! Squeeze! All the morning long I squeezed that sperm till I myself almost melted into it. I squeezed that sperm till a strange sort of madness came over me, and I found myself unwittingly squeezing my co-workers' hands in it, mistaking their hands for the gentle globules. Such an overflowing, affectionate, friendly, loving feeling did this work beget that at last I was continually squeezing their hands and looking up into their eyes sentimentally — as much as to say: Oh, my dear fellow beings, why should we any longer harbor any social bitterness, or know the slightest ill-humor or envy! Come, let us squeeze hands all round. No, let us all squeeze ourselves into each other. Let us squeeze ourselves universally into the very milk and sperm of kindness.

If only I could go on squeezing that sperm forever! Long, repeated experience has taught me that in every case a man must eventually lower, or at least relocate, his notion of the happiness he can reach — placing it not in the intellect or the imagination at all, but in the wife, the heart, the bed, the table, the saddle, the fireside, the country. Now that I have seen all this, I am ready to squeeze case for all eternity. In thoughts of the visions of the night, I saw long rows of angels in paradise, each with his hands in a jar of spermaceti.
Now, while speaking of sperm, it is fitting to mention other things related to it in the business of preparing the sperm whale for the try-works.

First there is what is called white-horse, which comes from the tapering part of the fish and from the thicker parts of his flukes. It is tough with congealed tendons — a wad of muscle — but it still holds some oil. Once it has been cut from the whale, the white-horse is first chopped into oblong pieces small enough to carry, before it goes to the mincer. These look a lot like blocks of Berkshire marble.

Plum-pudding is the name given to certain scraps of the whale's flesh that stick here and there to the blanket of blubber and often share a good deal of its oiliness. It is a most refreshing, festive, beautiful thing to look at. As the name suggests, it has an extremely rich, mottled color: a streaky snow-white and golden ground dotted with spots of the deepest crimson and purple. It is plums of ruby set in pictures of citron. Against all reason, it is hard to stop yourself from eating it. I admit that I once slipped behind the foremast to taste some. It tasted rather as I imagine a royal cutlet from the thigh of Louis le Gros might have tasted — supposing he had been killed on the first day after the venison season, and that this particular venison season had coincided with an unusually fine vintage in the vineyards of Champagne.

There is another substance, a very singular one, which turns up in the course of this business, but which I find very difficult to adequately describe. It is called slobgollion — a name original with the whalemen, and the substance itself is just as original. It is an indescribably oozy, stringy affair, most frequently found in the tubs of sperm after a prolonged squeezing and subsequent decanting. I hold it to be the wondrously thin, ruptured membranes of the case, fused together.

Gurry, as it is called, is strictly a right whalemen's term, though the sperm whalers sometimes use it in passing. It means the dark, sticky substance scraped off the back of the Greenland or right whale, and a great deal of it ends up covering the decks of those inferior souls who hunt that ignoble Leviathan.

Nippers. Strictly, this word is not native to the whale's vocabulary. But as applied by whalemen, it becomes so. A whaleman's nipper is a short, firm strip of tendinous stuff cut from the tapering part of Leviathan's tail. It averages an inch in thickness and is otherwise about the size of the iron part of a hoe. Moved edgewise along the oily deck, it works like a leather squeegee, and by nameless coaxings, as if by magic, it lures along with it all impurities.

But to learn all about these obscure matters, your best course is to go straight down into the blubber-room and have a long talk with its inmates. This place has previously been mentioned as the receptacle for the blanket-pieces when stripped and hoisted from the whale. When the time comes to cut up its contents, this room becomes a scene of terror to all newcomers, especially at night. On one side, lit by a dull lantern, a space has been cleared for the workmen. They generally go in pairs — a pike-and-gaff man and a spademan. The whaling-pike is similar to a frigate's boarding-weapon of the same name. The gaff is something like a boat-hook. With his gaff, the gaffman hooks onto a sheet of blubber and tries to hold it from slipping as the ship pitches and lurches about. Meanwhile, the spademan stands on the sheet itself, chopping it perpendicularly into portable horse-pieces. This spade is as sharp as a whetstone can make it. The spademan's feet are shoeless. The thing he stands on will sometimes irresistibly slide away from him like a sled. If he cuts off one of his own toes, or one of his assistants', would you be very much surprised? Toes are scarce among veteran blubber-room men.

chapters.title: Chapter 95 — The Cassock
paragraphs: Had you stepped aboard the Pequod at a certain point in this post-mortem of the whale and strolled forward near the windlass, I am quite sure you would have studied with no small curiosity a very strange, puzzling object lying lengthwise in the lee scuppers. Not the wondrous cistern in the whale's huge head; not the wonder of his unhinged lower jaw; not the miracle of his symmetrical tail — none of these would so surprise you as half a glimpse of that unaccountable cone, longer than a Kentuckian is tall, nearly a foot in diameter at the base, and jet-black as Yojo, the ebony idol of Queequeg. And an idol, indeed, it is — or rather, in old times, its likeness was. Such an idol as that found in the secret groves of Queen Maachah in Judea, and for worshipping which King Asa, her son, deposed her, destroyed the idol, and burnt it as an abomination at the brook Kedron, as darkly set forth in the fifteenth chapter of the First Book of Kings.

Look at the sailor called the mincer, who now comes along and, assisted by two helpers, heavily shoulders the grandissimus, as the mariners call it, and with bowed shoulders staggers off with it as if he were a grenadier carrying a dead comrade from the field. Laying it upon the forecastle deck, he proceeds to remove its dark skin cylindrically, as an African hunter skins a boa. This done, he turns the skin inside out like a trouser leg, gives it a good stretching so as almost to double its diameter, and at last hangs it, well spread, in the rigging to dry. Before long it is taken down. Removing some three feet from the pointed end and then cutting two slits for armholes at the other end, he lengthwise slips himself bodily into it. The mincer now stands before you invested in the full canonicals (the clerical vestments) of his calling. As it has for all his order from time immemorial, this investiture alone will adequately protect him while employed in the peculiar functions of his office.

That office consists in mincing the horse-pieces of blubber for the pots — an operation conducted at a curious wooden horse planted endwise against the bulwarks, with a capacious tub beneath it into which the minced pieces drop, fast as the sheets from a rapt orator's desk. Arrayed in decent black, occupying a conspicuous pulpit, intent on Bible leaves — what a candidate for an archbishopric, what a lad for a Pope, this mincer!*

*Bible leaves! Bible leaves! This is the invariable cry from the mates to the mincer. It commands him to be careful and cut his work into the thinnest possible slices, inasmuch as by doing so the business of boiling out the oil is much accelerated and its quantity considerably increased, besides perhaps improving it in quality.

chapters.title: Chapter 96 — The Try-Works
paragraphs: Besides her hoisted boats, an American whaler is outwardly distinguished by her try-works. She presents the curious anomaly of the most solid masonry joined with oak and hemp to constitute the completed ship. It is as if a brick kiln were transported from an open field to her planks.

The try-works stand between the foremast and the mainmast, where the deck has the most room. The timbers underneath are specially strong, built to carry the weight of an almost solid block of brick and mortar about ten feet by eight and five feet high. The foundation does not go through the deck; instead, the masonry is bolted firmly to the surface by heavy iron knees that brace it on every side and screw it down to the timbers. Its sides are cased in wood, and its top is completely covered by a large, sloping, battened hatch. Take off this hatch and you uncover the great try-pots. There are two of them, and each holds several barrels. When they are not in use, they are kept remarkably clean. Sometimes they are polished with soapstone and sand until the insides shine like silver punch-bowls. On night watches some cynical old sailors will crawl into them and curl up there for a nap. While the pots are being polished — one man in each, side by side — plenty of confidential talk passes back and forth over the iron rims. It is also a place for deep mathematical thought. It was in the Pequod's left-hand try-pot, with the soapstone busily circling around me, that the remarkable fact first struck me, indirectly, that in geometry all bodies sliding along the cycloid, my soapstone for example, will descend from any point in exactly the same time.

Take the fire-board off the front of the try-works and you expose the bare masonry on that side, pierced by the two iron mouths of the furnaces, directly below the pots. These mouths have heavy iron doors. A shallow tank running under the whole enclosed base of the works keeps the fierce heat of the fire from passing into the deck. A funnel fitted at the back keeps this tank topped up with water as fast as it evaporates. There are no outside chimneys; the flues open straight out of the back wall. And here let us go back for a moment.
It was about nine o'clock at night that the Pequod's try-works were first fired up on this present voyage. It fell to Stubb to oversee the business.

"All ready there? Off hatch, then, and start her. You, cook, light the works." That was easy, since the carpenter had been stuffing his shavings into the furnace all through the voyage. It should be said here that on a whaling voyage the first fire in the try-works has to be fed with wood for a while. After that no wood is used, except to get the regular fuel burning quickly. The point is this: once it has been tried out, the crisp, shriveled blubber, now called scraps or fritters, still holds a good deal of its oil. These fritters feed the flames. Like a bloated, burning martyr, or a misanthrope consuming himself, the whale, once lit, supplies his own fuel and burns with his own body. If only he would consume his own smoke too! For his smoke is horrible to breathe, and breathe it you must; not only that, you must live in it for the time being. It has an unspeakable, wild, Hindu smell, the kind that may hang around funeral pyres. It smells like the left wing of the day of judgment; it is an argument for the pit.

By midnight the works were going full blast. We had cast off the carcass and set sail; the wind was rising, and the darkness over the wild ocean was intense.
