But the fierce flames licked that darkness up as they shot out in forks from the sooty flues every so often, lighting every high rope in the rigging as if with the famous Greek fire. The burning ship drove on, as though she had been sent without mercy on some errand of vengeance. In just this way the brigs of the bold Hydriote Canaris, loaded with pitch and sulfur, came out of their harbors at midnight with broad sheets of flame for sails, bore down on the Turkish frigates, and wrapped them in fire.

With the hatch lifted off the top of the works, there was now a wide hearth in front of them. On it stood the Tartarean shapes of the pagan harpooners, who are always the stokers on a whale-ship. With huge pronged poles they tossed hissing masses of blubber into the scalding pots or stirred up the fires underneath, until the flames shot out of the doors like curling snakes and snapped at their feet. The smoke rolled away in sullen heaps. Every time the ship pitched, the boiling oil pitched with her, as if it longed to leap into their faces. Across from the mouth of the works, on the far side of the wide wooden hearth, was the windlass, which served as a sea-going sofa. The watch lounged there when they had nothing else to do, staring into the red heat of the fire until their eyes felt scorched in their heads. Their tawny faces, now thick with grime from smoke and sweat, their matted beards, and by contrast the barbaric brilliance of their teeth were all strangely lit up by the flickering blaze of the works. As they told each other their unholy adventures, tales of terror in words of mirth; as their uncivilized laughter forked up out of them like the flames from the furnace; as the harpooners gestured wildly back and forth in front of them with their huge pronged forks and dippers; as the wind howled on, and the sea leaped, and the ship groaned and dove, and yet steadily drove her red hell farther and farther into the blackness of the sea and the night, and scornfully champed the white bone in her mouth, and spat viciously all around her; then the rushing Pequod, loaded with savages and freighted with fire, burning a corpse and plunging into that blackness of darkness, seemed the physical counterpart of her monomaniac commander's soul.

So it seemed to me as I stood at her helm, and for long hours silently guided the way of this fire-ship on the sea. Wrapped in darkness myself for that interval, I only the better saw the redness, the madness, the ghastliness of others. The continual sight of the fiendish shapes before me, capering half in smoke and half in fire, at last bred kindred visions in my soul, as soon as I began to yield to that unaccountable drowsiness that always came over me at a midnight helm.

But that night in particular something strange happened to me, something I have never been able to explain. I jerked awake from a brief sleep on my feet, horribly aware that something was fatally wrong. The jawbone tiller was hitting my side, where I had been leaning against it; in my ears was the low hum of sails just starting to shake in the wind. I thought my eyes were open, and I was half aware of putting my fingers to the lids and mechanically stretching them even wider. Yet in spite of all this I could see no compass in front of me to steer by, though it seemed only a minute since I had been watching the card in the light of the steady binnacle lamp. There seemed to be nothing ahead of me but a jet-black gloom, made ghastly now and then by flashes of red. My strongest impression was that whatever swift, rushing thing I was standing on was not so much heading for any harbor ahead as fleeing from every harbor behind. A stark, bewildered feeling, like death, came over me. My hands clutched the tiller convulsively, but with the crazy idea that the tiller had somehow, by some enchantment, been turned upside down. My God! What is the matter with me? I thought. And then I saw it: in my brief sleep I had turned around and was facing the ship's stern, with my back to her bow and the compass. In an instant I turned back, just in time to keep the vessel from flying up into the wind and very likely capsizing. How glad and how grateful I was to be free of this unnatural hallucination of the night, and of the fatal danger of being brought by the lee!

Do not look too long in the face of the fire, O man! Never dream with your hand on the helm! Do not turn your back to the compass; heed the first hint of the hitching tiller; do not believe the artificial fire when its redness makes all things look ghastly. Tomorrow, in the natural sun, the skies will be bright; those who glared like devils in the forking flames, the morning will show in far different, at least gentler, relief — the glorious, golden, glad sun, the only true lamp — all others but liars!

Nevertheless, the sun does not hide Virginia's Dismal Swamp, nor Rome's accursed Campagna, nor the wide Sahara, nor all the millions of miles of deserts and of griefs beneath the moon. The sun does not hide the ocean, which is the dark side of this earth, and which is two-thirds of this earth. So therefore, that mortal man who has more of joy than sorrow in him — that mortal man cannot be true — not true, or undeveloped. With books the same. The truest of all men was the Man of Sorrows, and the truest of all books is Solomon's, and Ecclesiastes is the fine hammered steel of woe. "All is vanity." ALL. This willful world has not yet grasped unchristian Solomon's wisdom. But he who dodges hospitals and jails and walks fast crossing graveyards and would rather talk of operas than hell — who calls Cowper, Young, Pascal, Rousseau poor devils, all of them sick men, and throughout a carefree lifetime swears by Rabelais as supremely wise and therefore jolly — not that man is fitted to sit down on tombstones and break the green damp mold with the unfathomably wondrous Solomon.

But even Solomon, he says, "the man that wandereth out of the way of understanding shall remain" — that is, even while he is still alive — "in the congregation of the dead." So do not surrender yourself to fire, or it may turn you upside down and deaden you, as it did me for a time. There is a wisdom that is woe, but there is a woe that is madness. And in some souls there is a Catskill eagle that can dive down into the blackest gorges and just as well soar out of them again and vanish into the sunny spaces. And even if he flies forever inside the gorge, that gorge is in the mountains, so that even at the bottom of his lowest swoop the mountain eagle is still higher than other birds on the plain, even when they soar.

chapters.title: Chapter 97 — The Lamp
paragraphs: If you had gone down from the Pequod's try-works to the Pequod's forecastle, where the off-duty watch lay asleep, you would almost have thought for one moment that you were standing in some lit-up shrine of sainted kings and counselors. There they lay in their three-cornered oak vaults, each sailor a carved silence, with a score of lamps flashing on his hooded eyes.

In merchant ships, oil for the sailor is more scarce than the milk of queens. To dress in the dark, eat in the dark, and stumble in darkness to his bed — this is his usual lot. But the whaleman, as he seeks the food of light, so he lives in light. He makes his bunk an Aladdin's lamp and lies down in it, so that in the blackest night the ship's dark hull still houses an illumination.

See with what perfect freedom the whaleman takes his handful of lamps — often only old bottles and vials, though — to the copper cooler at the try-works and refills them there, as mugs of ale at a vat. He burns, too, the purest of oil, in its unprocessed and therefore untainted state — a fluid unknown to solar, lunar, or astral lamps on shore. It is sweet as early grass butter in April. He goes and hunts for his oil, so as to be sure of its freshness and genuineness, even as the traveler on the prairie hunts up his own supper of game.

chapters.title: Chapter 98 — Stowing Down and Clearing Up
paragraphs: I have already told how the great leviathan is sighted far off from the masthead; how he is chased across the watery moors and slaughtered in the valleys of the deep; how he is then towed alongside and beheaded; how (on the same principle that gave the headsman of old the clothes his victim was executed in) his great padded overcoat becomes the property of his executioner; and how, in due course, he is sentenced to the pots, where, like Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, his spermaceti, oil and bone pass through the fire unharmed. What remains, to close the last chapter of this part of the account, is to recite — to sing, if I may — the romantic business of drawing off his oil into the casks and stowing them down in the hold. There leviathan goes back once more to his native depths, gliding along under the surface as before — but, alas, never again to rise and blow.

While still warm, the oil, like hot punch, is received into the six-barrel casks. And while perhaps the ship is pitching and rolling this way and that in the midnight sea, the enormous casks are rolled around and upended, sometimes perilously scooting across the slippery deck like so many landslides, till at last they are wrestled into place and secured. And all around the hoops, rap, rap, go as many hammers as can play upon them, for now, by virtue of his office, every sailor is a cooper.

Finally, once the last pint is in the cask and everything has cooled, the great hatches are opened up, the ship's bowels are laid bare, and down go the casks to their final resting place in the sea. When that is done, the hatches are put back and sealed airtight, like a closet that has been walled up.

In the sperm fishery, this is perhaps one of the most remarkable incidents in all the business of whaling. One day the planks stream with torrents of blood and oil. On the sacred quarter-deck, enormous masses of the whale's head are profanely piled. Great rusty casks lie about, as in a brewery yard. The smoke from the try-works has blackened all the bulwarks. The sailors go about coated with grease. The entire ship seems the great leviathan himself. And on all hands the noise is deafening.

But a day or two later, you look about you and prick your ears on this same ship. And were it not for the telltale boats and try-works, you would all but swear you trod some silent merchant vessel with a most scrupulously neat commander. The unprocessed sperm oil possesses a singularly cleansing virtue. This is the reason why the decks never look so white as just after what they call an affair of oil. Besides, from the ashes of the burned scraps of the whale, a potent lye is readily made. And whenever any stickiness from the whale's back remains clinging to the side, that lye quickly eliminates it. Hands go diligently along the bulwarks, and with buckets of water and rags restore them to their full tidiness. The soot is brushed from the lower rigging. All the numerous tools that have been in use are likewise faithfully cleaned and put away. The great hatch is scrubbed and placed upon the try-works, completely hiding the pots. Every cask is out of sight. All tackles are coiled in unseen nooks. And when, by the combined and simultaneous industry of almost the entire ship's company, the whole of this conscientious duty is at last concluded, then the crew themselves proceed to their own washing, change their clothes from top to toe, and finally emerge onto the immaculate deck, fresh and all aglow, as bridegrooms newly leaped from the finest Dutch linen.

Now, with elated step, they pace the planks in twos and threes, and humorously discuss parlors, sofas, carpets, and fine fabrics. They propose to carpet the deck; think of having curtains from the top; raise no objection to taking tea by moonlight on the terrace of the forecastle. To hint to such perfumed mariners of oil, and bone, and blubber would be little short of audacity. They do not know the thing you distantly allude to. Away, and bring us napkins!

But look: aloft there, at the three mastheads, stand three men intent on spotting more whales, which, if caught, will infallibly again soil the old oaken furniture and drop at least one small grease-spot somewhere. Yes — and many is the time when, after the severest uninterrupted labors that know no night, continuing straight through for ninety-six hours, when from the boat where they have swollen their wrists with all-day rowing on the equator, they only step to the deck to carry vast chains and heave the heavy windlass and cut and slash — yes, and in their very sweating to be smoked and burned anew by the combined fires of the equatorial sun and the equatorial try-works — when, on the heels of all this, they have finally roused themselves to clean the ship and make a spotless dairy room of it — many is the time the poor fellows, just buttoning the necks of their clean shirts, are startled by the cry of "There she blows!" And away they fly to fight another whale and go through the whole weary thing again. Oh, my friends, but this is man-killing! Yet this is life. For hardly have we mortals by long toiling extracted from this world's vast bulk its small but valuable sperm, and then with weary patience cleaned ourselves from its defilements and learned to live here in clean tabernacles of the soul — hardly is this done when: There she blows! The ghost is spouted up, and away we sail to fight some other world and go through young life's old routine again.

Oh, the metempsychosis — the transmigration of souls! Oh, Pythagoras, who died in bright Greece two thousand years ago, so good, so wise, so mild — I sailed with you along the Peruvian coast last voyage, and, foolish as I am, taught you, a green simple boy, how to splice a rope!

chapters.title: Chapter 99 — The Doubloon
paragraphs: It has already been told how Ahab was in the habit of pacing his quarter-deck, taking regular turns between the binnacle and the mainmast. But in the multitude of other things requiring narration, it has not been added how sometimes in these walks, when most sunk in his mood, he would pause at each spot in turn and stand there strangely eyeing the particular object before him. When he halted before the binnacle, with his gaze fastened on the pointed needle in the compass, that glance shot like a javelin with the pointed intensity of his purpose. And when, resuming his walk, he again paused before the mainmast — then, as the same riveted gaze fastened upon the riveted gold coin there, he still wore the same expression of nailed firmness, only touched with a certain wild longing, if not hopefulness.

But one morning, as he turned to pass the doubloon, he seemed freshly drawn to the strange figures and inscriptions stamped on it, as though he were only now beginning to read into them, in his own monomaniac way, whatever meaning might be hidden there. And some meaning is hidden in all things; otherwise all things are worth very little, and the round world itself is nothing but an empty zero, good only for selling by the cartload, the way they sell off hills around Boston, to fill in some swamp in the Milky Way.

Now this doubloon was of the purest virgin gold, dug somewhere out of the heart of splendid hills from which the headwaters of many a Pactolus (the gold-bearing river of legend) flow east and west over golden sands. And though it was now nailed among rusty iron bolts and copper spikes green with verdigris, it still kept its Quito glow, untouched and unstained by any filth. It had been placed among a ruthless crew, ruthless hands passed it every hour, and all night long it was wrapped in thick darkness that could have hidden any thief creeping up on it; yet every sunrise found the doubloon where the last sunset had left it. For it was set apart and made sacred for one awe-inspiring purpose, and however reckless their sailor ways, the sailors one and all revered it as the white whale's talisman. Sometimes they talked it over during the weary night watch, wondering who would end up with it, and whether he would live to spend it.

Now those noble golden coins of South America are like medals of the sun and tropic tokens. Here palms, alpacas, and volcanoes; sun's disks and stars; ecliptics, horns of plenty, and rich banners waving are stamped in lavish profusion — so that the precious gold seems almost to gain an added preciousness and enhancing glory by passing through those fancy mints, so Spanishly poetic.

As it happened, the Pequod's doubloon was an unusually rich example of such things. Around its rim ran the letters REPUBLICA DEL ECUADOR: QUITO. So this bright coin came from a country set in the middle of the world, right under the great equator and named after it, and it had been minted halfway up the Andes, in a climate that never wanes and knows no autumn. Inside the ring of letters you could see the figures of three Andean peaks: a flame rising from one, a tower on another, and on the third a crowing rooster. Arching over them all was a section of the divided zodiac, each sign marked with its usual cabalistic symbols, and the keystone sun entering the equinoctial point at Libra.
Before this equatorial coin, Ahab, not unobserved by others, was now pausing.

"There is always something egotistical in mountaintops and towers and every other grand and lofty thing. Look here — three peaks as proud as Lucifer. The firm tower, that is Ahab; the volcano, that is Ahab; the brave, the fearless and victorious bird, that too is Ahab. They are all Ahab. And this round gold is only the image of the rounder globe, which, like a magician's glass, reflects back to each and every man in turn nothing but his own mysterious self. Great pains, small gains for those who ask the world to solve them; it cannot solve itself. It strikes me now that this coined sun has a ruddy face. But look! Yes, he is entering the sign of storms, the equinox! And only six months ago he rolled out of the last equinox, at Aries! From storm to storm! So be it, then. Born in labor, it is fitting that man should live in pain and die in agony! So be it, then! Here is solid stuff for woe to work on. So be it, then."

"No fairy fingers can have pressed this gold; devil's claws must have left their marks on it since yesterday," Starbuck murmured to himself, leaning against the bulwarks. "The old man seems to be reading Belshazzar's terrible writing on the wall. I have never looked at the coin closely. He has gone below; let me read it. A dark valley between three mighty peaks that dwell in heaven and almost seem the Trinity, in some faint earthly symbol. So in this valley of Death God surrounds us, and above all our gloom the sun of Righteousness still shines as a beacon and a hope. If we look down, the dark valley shows us her moldy soil; but if we look up, the bright sun meets our eyes halfway to cheer us. Yet, oh, the great sun does not stay put; and if at midnight we would gladly snatch some sweet comfort from him, we look for him in vain! This coin speaks wisely, gently, truly, but still sadly to me. I will leave it, for fear Truth may shake me falsely."

"There now's the old Mogul," Stubb mused to himself by the try-works. "He's been studying it; and there goes Starbuck from the same, and both with faces which I should say might be somewhere within nine fathoms long. And all from looking at a piece of gold, which, did I have it now on Negro Hill or in Corlaer's Hook, I'd not look at it very long before spending it. Humph! In my poor, insignificant opinion, I regard this as queer. I have seen doubloons before in my voyages — your doubloons of old Spain, your doubloons of Peru, your doubloons of Chile, your doubloons of Bolivia, your doubloons of Popayan; with plenty of gold moidores and pistoles and joes and half joes and quarter joes. What then should there be in this doubloon of the Equator that is so killing wonderful? By Golconda! Let me read it once. Hello! Here's signs and wonders truly! That, now, is what old Bowditch in his Epitome calls the zodiac, and what my almanac below calls ditto. I'll get the almanac, and as I have heard devils can be raised with Daboll's arithmetic, I'll try my hand at raising a meaning out of these queer curves here with the Massachusetts calendar. Here's the book. Let's see now. Signs and wonders — and the sun, he's always among them. Hmm, hmm, hmm; here they are — here they go — all alive: Aries, or the Ram; Taurus, or the Bull; and Jimimi! here's Gemini himself, or the Twins. Well, the sun wheels among them. Aye, here on the coin he's just crossing the threshold between two of twelve sitting-rooms all in a ring. Book! You lie there; the fact is, you books must know your places. You'll do to give us the bare words and facts, but we come in to supply the thoughts. That's my small experience, so far as the Massachusetts calendar, and Bowditch's navigator, and Daboll's arithmetic go. Signs and wonders, eh? Pity if there is nothing wonderful in signs and significant in wonders! There's a clue somewhere; wait a bit; hush — hark! By Jove, I have it! Look you, Doubloon, your zodiac here is the life of man in one round chapter; and now I'll read it off straight out of the book. Come, Almanac! To begin: there's Aries, or the Ram — lecherous dog, he begets us; then Taurus, or the Bull — he bumps us the first thing; then Gemini, or the Twins — that is, Virtue and Vice; we try to reach Virtue, when lo! comes Cancer the Crab and drags us back; and here, going from Virtue, Leo, a roaring Lion, lies in the path — he gives a few fierce bites and surly swats with his paw; we escape and hail Virgo, the Virgin! That's our first love; we marry and think to be happy forever, when pop comes Libra, or the Scales — happiness weighed and found wanting; and while we are very sad about that, Lord! how we suddenly jump as Scorpio, or the Scorpion, stings us in the rear; we are treating the wound when whang come the arrows all round; Sagittarius, or the Archer, is amusing himself. As we pluck out the shafts, stand aside! Here's the battering-ram, Capricornus, or the Goat; full tilt he comes rushing and headlong we are tossed; when Aquarius, or the Water-bearer, pours out his whole flood and drowns us; and to wind up with Pisces, or the Fishes, we sleep. There's a sermon now, written in high heaven, and the sun goes through it every year and yet comes out of it all alive and hearty. Jollily he, aloft there, wheels through toil and trouble; and so, down here, does jolly Stubb. Oh, jolly's the word forever! Farewell, Doubloon! But wait; here comes little King-Post; dodge round the try-works now and let's hear what he'll have to say. There; he's before it; he'll come out with something presently. So, so — he's beginning."

"I see nothing here but a round thing made of gold, and whoever raises a certain whale, this round thing belongs to him. So what's all this staring been about? It is worth sixteen dollars — that's true. And at two cents the cigar, that's nine hundred and sixty cigars. I won't smoke dirty pipes like Stubb, but I like cigars, and here's nine hundred and sixty of them. So here goes Flask aloft to spot them out."

"Shall I call that wise or foolish now? If it is really wise, it has a foolish look to it; yet if it is really foolish, then it has a sort of wiseish look to it. But hold on; here comes our old Manxman — the old hearse-driver, he must have been, that is, before he took to the sea. He luffs up before the doubloon — hello, and goes round on the other side of the mast. Why, there's a horseshoe nailed on that side. And now he's back again. What does that mean? Hark! He's muttering — voice like an old worn-out coffee-mill. Prick up your ears and listen!"

"If the White Whale is raised, it must be in a month and a day, when the sun stands in some one of these signs. I've studied signs and know their marks; they were taught me forty years ago by the old witch in Copenhagen. Now, in what sign will the sun then be? The horseshoe sign — for there it is, right opposite the gold. And what's the horseshoe sign? The lion is the horseshoe sign — the roaring and devouring lion. Ship, old ship! My old head shakes to think of you."

"There's another reading now; but still one text. All sorts of men in one kind of world, you see. Dodge again! Here comes Queequeg — all tattooing — looks like the signs of the zodiac himself. What says the Cannibal? As I live, he's comparing notes; looking at his thigh bone; thinks the sun is in the thigh, or in the calf, or in the bowels, I suppose, as the old women talk Surgeon's Astronomy in the backwoods. And by Jove, he's found something there near his thigh — I guess it's Sagittarius, or the Archer. No — he doesn't know what to make of the doubloon; he takes it for an old button off some king's trousers. But aside again! Here comes that ghost-devil Fedallah; tail coiled out of sight as usual, oakum in the toes of his shoes as usual. What does he say with that look of his? Ah, he only makes a sign to the sign and bows himself; there is a sun on the coin — fire-worshipper, depend upon it. Ho! More and more. This way comes Pip — poor boy! Would that he had died, or I! He's half horrible to me. He too has been watching all of these interpreters — myself included — and look now, he comes to read with that unearthly idiot face. Stand away again and hear him. Hark!"
"I look, you look, he looks; we look, ye look, they look."
"Upon my soul, he's been studying Murray's Grammar! Improving his mind, poor fellow! But what's that he says now — hush!"
"I look, you look, he looks; we look, ye look, they look."
"Why, he's getting it by heart — hush! Again."
"I look, you look, he looks; we look, ye look, they look."
"Well, that's funny."

"And I, you, and he; and we, ye, and they are all bats; and I'm a crow, especially when I stand atop of this pine tree here. Caw! Caw! Caw! Caw! Caw! Caw! Ain't I a crow? And where's the scarecrow? There he stands — two bones stuck into a pair of old trousers, and two more poked into the sleeves of an old jacket."

"Wonder if he means me? Complimentary! Poor lad! I could go hang myself. Anyway, for the present, I'll quit Pip's company. I can stand the rest, for they have plain wits; but he's too crazy-witty for my sanity. So, so, I leave him muttering."

"Here's the ship's navel, this doubloon here, and they are all on fire to unscrew it. But unscrew your navel, and what's the consequence? Then again, if it stays here, that is ugly too, for when anything's nailed to the mast it's a sign that things grow desperate. Ha, ha! Old Ahab! The White Whale — he'll nail you! This is a pine tree. My father, in old Tolland County, cut down a pine tree once and found a silver ring grown over in it — some old darkey's wedding ring. How did it get there? And so they'll say in the resurrection, when they come to fish up this old mast and find a doubloon lodged in it, with bedded oysters for the shaggy bark. Oh, the gold! The precious, precious gold! The green miser'll hoard you soon! Hush! Hush! God goes among the worlds blackberrying. Cook! Ho, cook! And cook us! Jenny! Hey, hey, hey, hey, hey, Jenny, Jenny! And get your hoecake done!"

chapters.title: Chapter 100 — Leg and Arm
paragraphs: The Pequod, of Nantucket, Meets the Samuel Enderby, of London.
"Ship, ahoy! Have you seen the White Whale?"

Ahab shouted this as he hailed yet another ship, this one flying English colors and bearing down under the stern. The old man stood in his hoisted quarter-boat with the trumpet to his mouth, his ivory leg in plain view of the stranger captain, who was lounging casually in the bow of his own boat. He was a deeply tanned, burly, good-natured, handsome man of about sixty, dressed in a roomy short jacket that hung around him in folds of blue pilot-cloth; one empty sleeve of it streamed out behind him like the embroidered sleeve of a hussar's cloak.
"Have you seen the White Whale?"
"Do you see this?" He pulled it out from the folds that had hidden it and held up a white arm made of sperm whale bone, ending in a wooden head like a mallet.
"Man my boat!" cried Ahab, impetuously tossing about the oars near him. "Stand by to lower!"

In less than a minute Ahab and his crew, still sitting in their little boat, had been lowered to the water, and they were soon alongside the stranger. But now an odd problem came up. In the excitement of the moment Ahab had forgotten that since losing his leg he had never once boarded any ship at sea except his own, and even then always by means of a clever and very handy mechanical device found only on the Pequod, which could not be rigged up and fitted on another vessel at a moment's notice. Now, it is not at all easy for anyone except people who do it almost every hour, like whalemen, to climb up a ship's side from a boat on the open sea, because the great swells lift the boat high up toward the bulwarks one moment and in the next instant drop it halfway down to the keelson. So, with one leg gone, and the strange ship naturally having none of that thoughtful invention, Ahab found himself miserably reduced to a clumsy landsman again, staring hopelessly at the shifting, uncertain height he could hardly hope to climb.

I may have hinted before that almost every small mishap that came his way as an indirect result of his unlucky injury irritated or infuriated Ahab. This time all of that was made worse by the sight of the strange ship's two officers leaning over the side next to the upright ladder of nailed-on cleats and swinging a pair of prettily decorated man-ropes toward him; at first it did not seem to occur to them that a one-legged man would be too crippled to use their sea-banisters. But this awkward moment lasted only a minute, because the strange captain saw at a glance how things stood and called out, "I see, I see! Stop hauling there! Jump to it, boys, and swing over the cutting-tackle."

As good luck would have it, they had had a whale alongside a day or two before, and the great tackles were still aloft, and the massive curved blubber-hook, now clean and dry, was still attached to the end. This was quickly lowered to Ahab, who at once understanding everything, slid his solitary thigh into the curve of the hook — it was like sitting in the fluke of an anchor, or the crotch of an apple tree — and then giving the word, held himself fast while also helping to hoist his own weight by pulling hand-over-hand upon one of the running parts of the tackle. Soon he was carefully swung inside the high bulwarks and gently landed upon the capstan head. With his ivory arm frankly thrust forth in welcome, the other captain advanced, and Ahab, putting out his ivory leg and crossing the ivory arm — like two swordfish blades — cried out in his walrus way: "Aye, aye, hearty! Let us shake bones together! An arm and a leg! An arm that never can shrink, d'you see, and a leg that never can run. Where did you see the White Whale? How long ago?"

"The White Whale," said the Englishman, pointing his ivory arm toward the east and taking a rueful sight along it as if it had been a telescope, "there I saw him, on the Line (the equator), last season."
"And he took that arm off, did he?" asked Ahab, now sliding down from the capstan and resting on the Englishman's shoulder as he did so.
"Aye, he was the cause of it, at least. And that leg, too?"
"Spin me the yarn," said Ahab. "How was it?"

"It was the first time in my life I had ever cruised on the Line," the Englishman began. "I didn't know anything about the White Whale back then. Well, one day we lowered for a pod of four or five whales, and my boat got fast to one of them. He was a real circus horse, too, going round and round in circles, so that the only way my boat's crew could keep her level was by all sitting with their backsides on the outer gunwale. Then all of a sudden a great bouncing whale comes breaching up from the bottom of the sea, with a milky-white head and hump, all crow's-feet and wrinkles."
"It was he, it was he!" cried Ahab, suddenly letting out his suspended breath.
"And harpoons sticking in near his starboard fin."
"Aye, aye — they were mine — my irons," cried Ahab, exultantly — "but go on!"

"Give me a chance, then," said the Englishman, good-humoredly. "Well, this old great-grandfather, with the white head and hump, runs all foaming into the pod and goes to snapping furiously at my fast-line!"
"Aye, I see! Wanted to part it — free the fast-fish — an old trick — I know him."

"How it was exactly," continued the one-armed commander, "I do not know. But in biting the line, it got foul of his teeth, caught there somehow. But we didn't know it then, so that when we afterward pulled on the line, bounce we came plump onto his hump! — instead of the other whale's, that went off to windward, all fluking. Seeing how matters stood, and what a noble great whale it was — the noblest and biggest I ever saw, sir, in my life — I resolved to capture him, despite the boiling rage he seemed to be in. And thinking the tangled line would get loose, or the tooth it was caught on might pull free — for I have a devil of a boat's crew for a pull on a whale-line — seeing all this, I say, I jumped into my first mate's boat. Mr. Mounttop's here — by the way, Captain: Mounttop; Mounttop: the Captain. As I was saying, I jumped into Mounttop's boat, which was gunwale to gunwale with mine then, and snatching the first harpoon, let this old great-grandfather have it. But Lord, look you, sir — hearts and souls alive, man — the next instant, in a flash, I was blind as a bat — both eyes out — all befogged and bedeadened with black foam, the whale's tail looming straight up out of it, perpendicular in the air like a marble steeple. No use backing off then. But as I was groping at midday with a blinding sun, all crown-jewels — as I was groping, I say, after the second iron to toss it overboard — down comes the tail like a Lima tower, cutting my boat in two, leaving each half in splinters. And, flukes first, the white hump backed through the wreck as though it was all chips. We all struck out. To escape his terrible flailing, I seized hold of my harpoon-pole sticking in him and for a moment clung to that like a sucker-fish. But a breaking wave dashed me off, and at the same instant the fish, taking one good dart forward, went down like a flash. And the barb of that cursed second iron, towing along near me, caught me here" — clapping his hand just below his shoulder — "yes, caught me just here, I say, and bore me down to Hell's flames, I was thinking. When — when — all of a sudden, thank the good God, the barb ripped its way along the flesh — clear along the whole length of my arm — came out near my wrist, and up I floated. And that gentleman there will tell you the rest. By the way, Captain: Dr. Bunger, ship's surgeon; Bunger, my lad: the Captain. Now, Bunger boy, spin your part of the yarn."

The professional gentleman being pointed out so casually had been standing near them the whole time, with nothing in particular to show his gentleman's rank on board. His face was extremely round but serious. He wore a faded blue woolen frock, or shirt, and patched trousers, and until now he had been dividing his attention between a marlinspike in one hand and a pill-box in the other, now and then throwing a critical glance at the ivory limbs of the two crippled captains. But when his superior introduced him to Ahab, he bowed politely and went straight off to do what his captain had asked.
"It was a shockingly bad wound," began the whale-surgeon, "and taking my advice, Captain Boomer here stood our old Sammy —"
"Samuel Enderby is the name of my ship," interrupted the one-armed captain, addressing Ahab. "Go on, boy."

"Stood our old Sammy off to the northward, to get out of the blazing hot weather there on the Line. But it was no use — I did all I could; sat up with him nights; was very severe with him about his diet —"

"Oh, very severe!" chimed in the patient himself. Then suddenly changing his tone: "Drinking hot rum toddies with me every night till he couldn't see to put on the bandages, and sending me to bed, half-drunk, about three o'clock in the morning. Oh, you stars! He sat up with me indeed, and was very severe with my diet. Oh, a great watcher and very dietetically severe is Dr. Bunger. — Bunger, you dog, laugh out! Why don't you? You know you're a precious jolly rascal. — But push ahead, boy. I'd rather be killed by you than kept alive by any other man."

"My captain, you must have by now perceived, respected sir" — said the unflappable, pious-looking Bunger, slightly bowing to Ahab — "is inclined to be humorous at times. He spins us many clever things of that sort. But I may as well say — en passant, as the French remark — that I myself — that is to say, Jack Bunger, late of the reverend clergy — am a strict total abstinence man. I never drink —"
"Water!" cried the captain. "He never drinks it. It gives him a sort of fits. Fresh water throws him into the hydrophobia. But go on — go on with the arm story."

"Yes, I may as well," said the surgeon, coolly. "I was about to observe, sir, before Captain Boomer's humorous interruption, that despite my best and severest efforts, the wound kept getting worse and worse. The truth was, sir, it was as ugly a gaping wound as surgeon ever saw — more than two feet and several inches long. I measured it with the lead line. In short, it turned black. I knew what was threatened, and off it came. But I had no hand in shipping that ivory arm there" — pointing at it with the marlinspike — "that thing is against all rule. That is the captain's work, not mine. He ordered the carpenter to make it. He had that club-hammer there put on the end to knock someone's brains out with, I suppose, as he tried mine once. He flies into diabolical rages sometimes. Do you see this dent, sir?" — removing his hat and brushing aside his hair, exposing a bowl-like cavity in his skull, but which bore not the slightest scar or any token of ever having been a wound — "Well, the captain there will tell you how that came to be. He knows."

"No, I don't," said the captain, "but his mother did; he was born with it. Oh, you solemn rogue, you — you Bunger! Was there ever such another Bunger in the watery world? Bunger, when you die, you ought to die in pickle, you dog. You should be preserved for future ages, you rascal."
"What happened to the White Whale?" Ahab shouted now; up to this point he had been listening impatiently to this byplay between the two Englishmen.

"Oh!" cried the one-armed captain. "Oh, yes! Well, after he sounded, we didn't see him again for some time. In fact, as I hinted before, I didn't then know what whale it was that had served me such a trick, till some time afterward, when coming back to the Line, we heard about Moby Dick — as some call him — and then I knew it was he."
"Did you cross his wake again?"
"Twice."
"But could not fasten?"
"Didn't want to try. Ain't one limb enough? What should I do without this other arm? And I'm thinking Moby Dick doesn't bite so much as he swallows."

"Well, then," Bunger broke in, "give him your left arm as bait to get back the right. Do you know, gentlemen" — bowing very gravely and with mathematical precision to each captain in turn — "do you know, gentlemen, that Divine Providence has built the whale's digestive organs so mysteriously that he cannot possibly digest even a man's arm completely? And he knows it, too. So what you take for the White Whale's malice is only his clumsiness. He never intends to swallow a single limb; he only means to scare you with feints. But sometimes he is like the old juggler, once a patient of mine in Ceylon, who used to pretend to swallow jackknives, and one day actually let one slip down inside him for real. There it stayed for a year or more, until I gave him an emetic and he threw it up in little tacks, you see. There was no possible way for him to digest that jackknife and fully absorb it into his general bodily system. Yes, Captain Boomer, if you are quick enough about it, and are willing to pawn one arm for the privilege of giving the other a decent burial, why, in that case the arm is yours. Just let the whale have another go at you soon, that's all."

"No, thank you, Bunger," said the English captain. "He's welcome to the arm he has, since I can't help it and didn't know him then. But not to another one. No more White Whales for me. I've lowered for him once, and that has satisfied me. There would be great glory in killing him, I know that, and there is a shipload of precious sperm in him. But hark you, he's best let alone. Don't you think so, Captain?" — glancing at the ivory leg.

"He is. But he will still be hunted, for all that. The accursed thing that is best let alone is not always the thing that least allures. He's all a magnet! How long since you saw him last? Which way heading?"

"Bless my soul, and curse the foul fiend's," cried Bunger, stooping and walking round Ahab, and like a dog strangely sniffing, "this man's blood — bring the thermometer! — it's at the boiling point! His pulse makes these planks beat! Sir!" — taking a lancet from his pocket and drawing near to Ahab's arm.
"Back off!" roared Ahab, dashing him against the bulwarks. "Man the boat! Which way heading?"
"Good God!" cried the English captain, to whom the question was put. "What's the matter? He was heading east, I think. Is your captain crazy?" whispering to Fedallah.

But Fedallah put a finger to his lips and slid over the bulwarks to take the boat's steering oar, while Ahab swung the cutting-tackle over to himself and ordered the ship's sailors to get ready to lower.

A moment later he was standing in the stern of the boat, and the Manila men were jumping to their oars. The English captain called after him, but it was no use. Ahab stood upright, his back to the stranger ship and his face set like flint toward his own, until they came alongside the Pequod.

chapters.title: Chapter 101 — The Decanter
paragraphs: Before the English ship fades from sight, let it be set down here that she hailed from London and was named after the late Samuel Enderby, merchant of that city, the founder of the famous whaling house of Enderby & Sons — a house which, in my poor whaleman's opinion, comes not far behind the united royal houses of the Tudors and Bourbons in terms of real historical interest. How long before the year 1775 this great whaling house existed, my numerous fish-documents do not make clear. But in that year it fitted out the first English ships that ever regularly hunted the sperm whale — though for some twenty years before that, ever since 1726, our valiant Coffins and Maceys of Nantucket and the Vineyard had in large fleets pursued that Leviathan, but only in the North and South Atlantic, not elsewhere. Let it be distinctly recorded here that the Nantucketers were the first among mankind to harpoon with civilized steel the great sperm whale, and that for half a century they were the only people of the whole globe who did so.

In 1778, a fine ship, the Amelia, fitted out for the express purpose and at the sole expense of the vigorous Enderbys, boldly rounded Cape Horn and was the first among the nations to lower a whaleboat of any sort in the great South Sea. The voyage was a skillful and lucky one, and returning to her berth with a full hold of precious sperm, the Amelia's example was soon followed by other ships, English and American, and thus the vast sperm whale grounds of the Pacific were thrown open. But not content with this good deed, the tireless house bestirred itself again. It was Samuel and all his sons — how many, only their mother knows — under whose immediate sponsorship, and partly, I think, at whose expense, the British government was induced to send the sloop-of-war Rattler on a whaling voyage of discovery into the South Sea. Commanded by a naval post-captain, the Rattler made a rattling voyage of it and did some service — how much does not appear. But this is not all. In 1819, the same house fitted out a discovery whale-ship of their own to go on a tasting cruise to the remote waters of Japan. That ship — well called the Syren — made a noble experimental cruise, and it was thus that the great Japanese whaling ground first became generally known. The Syren on this famous voyage was commanded by a Captain Coffin, a Nantucketer.

So all honor to the Enderbies, whose firm, I believe, is still in business today — though the original Samuel has no doubt long since slipped his cable and sailed for the great South Sea of the other world.

The ship named for him deserved the honor; she was very fast and a noble vessel in every way. I went aboard her once at midnight somewhere off the coast of Patagonia and drank good flip down in the forecastle. It was a fine gam we had, and they were all good sports — every soul on board. May they have a short life and a jolly death. And that fine gam I had — long, long after old Ahab set his ivory heel on her planks — brings back to me the noble, solid, Saxon hospitality of that ship. May my parson forget me and the devil remember me if I ever lose sight of it. Flip? Did I say we had flip? Yes, and we flipped it down at ten gallons an hour. And when the squall hit (it's squally down there off Patagonia) and all hands, visitors included, were called to reef topsails, we were so top-heavy that we had to hoist each other aloft in bowlines. Not knowing what we were doing, we furled the tails of our jackets into the sails, so that we hung there, reefed tight in the howling gale, a warning to all drunken sailors. Still, the masts didn't go overboard, and eventually we scrambled down, so sober that we had to pass the flip around again — though the savage salt spray bursting down the forecastle hatch watered it down and pickled it rather too much for my taste.

The beef was fine — tough but with body in it. They said it was bull-beef; others, that it was dromedary beef. But I do not know for certain which it was. They had dumplings too — small but substantial, symmetrically globular, and indestructible dumplings. I fancied that you could feel them and roll them about inside you after they were swallowed. If you stooped over too far forward, you risked their pitching out of you like billiard balls. The bread — but that couldn't be helped; besides, it was an anti-scorbutic (a guard against scurvy); in short, the bread contained the only fresh fare they had. But the forecastle was not very bright, and it was very easy to step into a dark corner when you ate it. But all in all, taking her from truck to helm, considering the dimensions of the cook's boilers, including his own live parchment boilers — fore and aft, I say, the Samuel Enderby was a jolly ship: of good food and plenty, fine flip and strong, crack fellows all, and capital from boot heels to hat-band.

But why was it, do you think, that the Samuel Enderby and some other English whalers I know of — not all, though — were such famously hospitable ships, that passed round the beef and the bread and the can and the joke, and were not soon weary of eating, drinking, and laughing? I will tell you. The overflowing good cheer of these English whalers is a matter for historical research. Nor have I been at all sparing of historical whale research when it has seemed needed.

The English were preceded in the whale fishery by the Dutch, Zealanders, and Danes, from whom they inherited many terms still used in the fishery, and — what is even more important — their fat old traditions of plenty to eat and drink. For as a general thing, the English merchant ship stints her crew, but not so the English whaler. Hence, among the English, this tradition of whaling good cheer is not normal and natural but incidental and particular, and therefore must have some special origin, which is here pointed out and will be further explained.

During my research into the Leviathanic histories, I stumbled upon an ancient Dutch volume which, by the musty whaling smell of it, I knew must be about whalers. The title was "Dan Coopman," so I concluded that this must be the invaluable memoirs of some Amsterdam cooper in the fishery, as every whale-ship must carry its cooper. I was supported in this belief by seeing that it was written by one "Fitz Swackhammer." But my friend Dr. Snodhead, a very learned man, professor of Low Dutch and High German at the college of Santa Claus and St. Pott's, to whom I handed the work for translation, giving him a box of sperm candles for his trouble — this same Dr. Snodhead, as soon as he saw the book, assured me that "Dan Coopman" did not mean "The Cooper" but "The Merchant." In short, this ancient and learned Low Dutch book treated of the commerce of Holland, and among other subjects contained a very interesting account of its whale fishery. And in this chapter, headed "Smeer," or "Fat," I found a long, detailed list of the provisions for the larders and cellars of 180 Dutch whalers. From which list, as translated by Dr. Snodhead, I copy the following:

400,000 pounds of beef. 60,000 pounds of Friesland pork. 150,000 pounds of stockfish. 550,000 pounds of biscuit. 72,000 pounds of soft bread. 2,800 firkins (small casks) of butter. 20,000 pounds of Texel and Leyden cheese. 144,000 pounds of cheese (probably of lower quality). 550 ankers (casks) of Geneva gin. 10,800 barrels of beer.
Most statistical tables make for bone-dry reading. That is not true here, though, where the reader gets drenched in whole pipes, barrels, quarts and gills of good gin and good cheer.

At the time I spent three days carefully digesting all this beer, beef and bread, and along the way it happened to give me many profound thoughts that could be applied in a transcendental and Platonic sense. I also drew up some supplementary tables of my own on the probable amount of stockfish, and so on, eaten by every Low Dutch harpooner in that old Greenland and Spitsbergen whale fishery. To begin with, the amount of butter and of Texel and Leyden cheese they ate seems astonishing. I put it down, though, to their naturally oily natures, which were made oilier still by their line of work, and especially by their hunting their game in those frozen polar seas, right on the coasts of the Eskimo country, where the sociable natives drink each other's health in brimming glasses of train oil.

The amount of beer is also very large: 10,800 barrels. Now, those polar fisheries could only be worked during the short summer of that climate, so the whole cruise of one of these Dutch whalemen, including the short trip to and from the Spitsbergen sea, did not run much beyond three months, let's say. Counting 30 men for each of the 180 ships in their fleet, we get 5,400 Low Dutch seamen in all. So, I say, we have exactly two barrels of beer per man as a twelve weeks' ration, not counting his fair share of those 550 ankers of gin. Now, whether these gin-and-beer harpooners, as tipsy as you might imagine them to have been, were the right sort of men to stand up in the bow of a boat and take good aim at fleeing whales seems rather unlikely. Yet they did aim at them, and hit them, too. But remember, this was very far north, where beer suits the constitution well. On the equator, in our southern fishery, beer would tend to make the harpooner drowsy at the masthead and sozzled in his boat, and Nantucket and New Bedford might suffer heavy losses.

But that's enough of that. I have said enough to show that the old Dutch whalers of two or three centuries ago lived well, and that the English whalers have not ignored such an excellent example. For, as they say, when you are cruising in an empty ship, if you can't get anything better out of the world, at least get a good dinner out of it. And that empties the decanter.

chapters.title: Chapter 102 — A Bower in the Arsacides
paragraphs: Up to now, in describing the sperm whale, I have mostly dwelt on the marvels of his outer appearance, or else, separately and in detail, on a few features of his inner structure. But for a large, thorough, sweeping understanding of him, I must now unbutton him still further: untie the laces of his hose, unbuckle his garters, unfasten the hooks and eyes of the joints of his innermost bones, and set him before you in his final state — that is to say, in his unconditional skeleton.

But what now, Ishmael? How is it that you, a mere oarsman in the fishery, claim to know anything about the underground parts of the whale? Did learned Stubb, mounted on your capstan, deliver lectures on the anatomy of the Cetacea, and with the help of the windlass hold up a specimen rib for exhibition? Explain yourself, Ishmael. Can you land a full-grown whale on your deck for examination, the way a cook dishes up a roast pig? Surely not. Up to now you have been a true witness, Ishmael; but be careful how you seize a privilege that belongs to Jonah alone — the privilege of discoursing on the joists and beams, the rafters, ridgepole, sleepers and underpinnings that make up the framework of leviathan, and, likely enough, on the tallow-vats, dairy-rooms, pantries and cheese-rooms in his bowels.

I confess that since Jonah, few whalemen have got very far beneath the skin of the adult whale. Nevertheless, I have been blessed with a chance to dissect him in miniature. On a ship I once belonged to, a small cub sperm whale was hoisted bodily onto the deck for his poke, or bag, to make sheaths for the barbs of the harpoons and for the heads of the lances. Do you think I let that chance go by without using my boat-hatchet and jackknife, breaking the seal and reading all the contents of that young cub?

As for my exact knowledge of the leviathan's bones at their gigantic, fully grown size, I owe that rare knowledge to my late royal friend Tranquo, king of Tranque, one of the Arsacides. Years ago, when I was serving on the trading ship Dey of Algiers and we called at Tranque, the lord of Tranque invited me to spend part of the Arsacidean holidays with him at his secluded palm villa at Pupella, a seaside glen not far from his capital, which our sailors called Bamboo-Town.

Among many other fine qualities, my royal friend Tranquo had a devout love for all matters of barbaric curios, and had gathered together in Pupella whatever rare things the more ingenious of his people could invent: chiefly carved woods of wonderful design, chiseled shells, inlaid spears, costly paddles, aromatic canoes — and all these set out among whatever natural wonders the wonder-laden, tribute-paying waves had cast up on his shores.

The most important of these was a great Sperm Whale that had been found dead and stranded after an unusually long, raging gale, with his head against a coconut tree whose drooping tufts of feathery leaves looked like his green spout. When the huge body had finally been stripped of its fathom-deep wrappings and the bones had dried to dust in the sun, the skeleton was carefully carried up the Pupella glen, where a grand temple of lordly palms now gave it shelter.

The ribs were hung with trophies; the vertebrae were carved with Arsacidean chronicles in strange hieroglyphics; in the skull, the priests kept an aromatic flame always burning, so that the mystic head again sent forth its vapory spout; while, hung from a bough, the terrible lower jaw swung over all the worshippers, like the sword hung by a hair that so terrified Damocles.

It was a wondrous sight. The wood was as green as the mosses of the Icy Glen; the trees stood high and haughty, feeling their living sap; the busy earth beneath was like a weaver's loom with a gorgeous carpet on it, the ground-vine tendrils forming its warp and woof and the living flowers its figures. All the trees with all their laden branches, all the shrubs and ferns and grasses, the message-carrying air — all these were unceasingly active. Through the lacework of the leaves, the great sun seemed a flying shuttle weaving the tireless greenery. Oh, busy weaver! Unseen weaver! Pause! One word! Where does the fabric flow? What palace will it adorn? Why all this ceaseless toil? Speak, weaver! Stop your hand! Just one single word with you! No — the shuttle flies; the figures float out of the loom; the carpet, rushing like a flood, slides away forever. The weaver-god weaves, and that weaving deafens him so that he hears no mortal voice; and that humming deafens us too, who look on at the loom; and only when we escape it shall we hear the thousand voices that speak through it. For it is just the same in all material factories. The spoken words that cannot be heard among the flying spindles are plainly heard outside the walls, bursting from the open windows. That is how villainies have been found out. Ah, mortal! Then be careful; for so, in all this din of the great world's loom, your most secret thoughts may be overheard far away.

There, in the green, restlessly living loom of that Arsacidean wood, the great, white, worshipped skeleton lay lounging — a gigantic idler! And yet, as the green warp and weft, forever being woven, mingled and hummed around him, the mighty idler seemed to be the cunning weaver himself, though he was all woven over with the vines, putting on greener and fresher growth every month, and was himself only a skeleton. Life wrapped Death; Death was a trellis for Life; the grim god married youthful Life and fathered curly-headed glories on her.

When I visited this wonderful whale with royal Tranquo and saw that its skull had been made an altar, with artificial smoke rising from the place where the real spout had come out, I was surprised that the king should treat a chapel as a collector's piece. He laughed. But I was more surprised that the priests swore that smoky spout of his was genuine. I paced back and forth in front of the skeleton, pushed the vines aside, broke in through the ribs, and, unwinding a ball of Arsacidean twine behind me, wandered and circled for a long time among its many winding, shady colonnades and arbors. But my line soon ran out, and following it back, I came out through the opening where I had gone in. I saw nothing living inside; there was nothing there but bones.

Cutting myself a green measuring-rod, I once more dove within the skeleton. From their arrow-slit in the skull, the priests saw me taking the height of the final rib. "What's this!" they shouted. "You dare to measure this god of ours! That's for us to do." "Aye, priests — well, how long do you make him, then?" But here a fierce argument broke out among them concerning feet and inches; they cracked each other's heads with their yardsticks — the great skull echoed — and seizing that lucky chance, I quickly completed my own measurements.

These measurements I now propose to set before you. But first let it be recorded that in this matter I am not free to state any imaginary measurement I please, because there are skeleton authorities you can consult to test my accuracy. There is a Leviathanic Museum, I am told, in Hull, England, one of that country's whaling ports, where they have some fine specimens of fin-backs and other whales. Likewise, I have heard that in the museum of Manchester, in New Hampshire, they have what the proprietors call "the only perfect specimen of a Greenland or River Whale in the United States." Moreover, at a place in Yorkshire, England, by the name of Burton Constable, a certain Sir Clifford Constable owns the skeleton of a sperm whale, but of moderate size, by no means of the full-grown magnitude of my friend King Tranquo's.

In both cases, the stranded whales to which these two skeletons belonged were originally claimed by their owners on similar grounds: King Tranquo seized his because he wanted it, and Sir Clifford because he was lord of the manors of those parts. Sir Clifford's whale has been articulated throughout, so that, like a great chest of drawers, you can open and shut him in all his bony cavities — spread out his ribs like a gigantic fan — and swing all day on his lower jaw. Locks are to be put on some of his trap-doors and shutters, and a footman will show future visitors around with a bunch of keys at his side. Sir Clifford is thinking of charging twopence for a peep at the whispering gallery in the spinal column, threepence to hear the echo in the hollow of his cerebellum, and sixpence for the unrivaled view from his forehead.

The measurements of the skeleton that I am about to record are copied word for word from my right arm, where I had them tattooed, since in my wild wanderings at the time there was no other safe way to keep such valuable figures. But I was short of space, and I wanted the rest of my body — or whatever parts of it were still untattooed — to stay a blank page for a poem I was writing then, so I did not bother with the odd inches. Nor, in fact, should inches come into any measurement of the whale that suits him.

chapters.title: Chapter 103 — Measurement of The Whale’s Skeleton
paragraphs: First of all, I want to give you a detailed, plain account of how big this leviathan is when alive, since we are about to show his skeleton briefly. That account may be useful here.

According to a careful calculation I have made, partly based upon Captain Scoresby's estimate of seventy tons for the largest sized Greenland whale of sixty feet in length, a sperm whale of the largest magnitude, between eighty-five and ninety feet in length and something less than forty feet in its fullest circumference, will weigh at least ninety tons. So that, reckoning thirteen men to a ton, he would considerably outweigh the combined population of a whole village of eleven hundred inhabitants.
Don't you think, then, that brains, like yoked cattle, should be put to this leviathan, to make him budge at all in any landsman's imagination?

I have already shown you, in various ways, his skull, spout-hole, jaw, teeth, tail, forehead, fins and several other parts, so now I will simply point out what is most interesting in the general mass of his bones once they are laid bare. But the colossal skull makes up so very large a share of the whole length of the skeleton, and it is by far the most complicated part, and nothing about it will be repeated in this chapter; so you must be sure to keep it in your mind, or under your arm, as we go on. Otherwise you will not get a complete idea of the overall structure we are about to look at.

In length, the sperm whale's skeleton at Tranque measured seventy-two feet. So that when fully fleshed out and extended in life, he must have been ninety feet long, for in the whale the skeleton loses about one-fifth in length compared with the living body. Of this seventy-two feet, his skull and jaw comprised some twenty feet, leaving about fifty feet of plain backbone. Attached to this backbone, for something less than a third of its length, was the mighty circular basket of ribs that once enclosed his vital organs.

To me this vast chest with its ivory ribs, and the long, plain spine running far away from it in a straight line, looked a good deal like the hull of a great ship just laid down on the stocks, when only about twenty of her bare bow-ribs have been set in place and the keel, for the moment, is otherwise just a long, unconnected timber.

There were ten ribs on each side. The first, counting from the neck, was nearly six feet long. The second, third and fourth each got longer in turn, up to the high point of the fifth, one of the middle ribs, which measured eight feet and a few inches. From there the remaining ribs grew shorter, until the tenth and last spanned only five feet and a few inches. Their thickness was generally in proportion to their length. The middle ribs had the greatest curve. On some of the Arsacides, ribs like these are used as beams to lay footbridges across small streams.

Looking at these ribs, I was struck once again by the point this book has made in so many ways: the whale's skeleton is by no means a mold of his body as it is when clothed in flesh. The largest of the Tranque ribs, one of the middle ones, sat in the part of the fish that is deepest in life. Now, the greatest depth of this particular whale's body, fully clothed, must have been at least sixteen feet, while the matching rib measured only a little over eight. So this rib gave only half a true idea of how big that part was in the living animal. What's more, for some distance along where I now saw only a bare spine, all of it had once been wrapped in tons of extra bulk in the form of flesh, muscle, blood and bowels. Furthermore, in place of the broad fins I saw here only a few jumbled joints, and in place of the heavy, majestic, but boneless flukes, nothing at all!

How vain and foolish, then, I thought, for timid, untraveled man to try to comprehend this wondrous whale rightly by merely poring over his dead, shrunken skeleton, stretched in this peaceful wood. No. Only in the heart of the quickest perils, only when within the swirling of his angry flukes, only on the profound unbounded sea, can the fully living whale be truly found out.

But the spine. For that, the best way to consider it is with a crane, to pile its bones high up on end. No speedy enterprise. But now that it's done, it looks much like Pompey's Pillar, the ancient column at Alexandria.

There are forty-odd vertebrae altogether, and in the skeleton they are not locked together. Most of them lie like the great knobbed blocks of a Gothic spire, forming solid layers of heavy masonry. The largest, one in the middle, is a little under three feet wide and more than four feet deep. The smallest, where the spine narrows into the tail, is only two inches wide and looks rather like a white billiard ball. I was told there had been even smaller ones, but some little cannibal urchins, the priest's children, had stolen them to play marbles with, and they were lost. So we see that the spine of even the hugest living thing tapers off in the end into simple child's play.

chapters.title: Chapter 104 — The Fossil Whale
paragraphs: With his mighty bulk, the whale offers a most congenial theme on which to enlarge, amplify, and generally expand. Even if you wanted to, you could not compress him. By rights he should only be treated in imperial folio, the largest size of book. Not to count over again his furlongs from spout-hole to tail and the yards he measures around the waist — only think of the gigantic coils of his intestines, where they lie in him like great cables and hawsers coiled away on the underground orlop-deck of a ship of the line.

Since I have undertaken to manhandle this Leviathan, I must prove myself omnisciently exhaustive in the enterprise — not overlooking the tiniest seminal germs of his blood, and spinning him out to the last coil of his bowels. Having already described him in most of his present habitat and anatomical peculiarities, it now remains to magnify him from an archaeological, fossiliferous, and antediluvian point of view. Applied to any other creature than the Leviathan — to an ant or a flea — such portly terms might fairly be judged unjustifiably grandiloquent. But when Leviathan is the text, the case is different. I am glad to stagger into this undertaking under the weightiest words in the dictionary. And let it be said here that whenever it has been convenient to consult one in the course of these dissertations, I have always used a huge quarto edition of Johnson, bought expressly for that purpose, because that famous lexicographer's uncommon personal bulk made him better fitted to compile a dictionary for a whale author like me.

We often hear of writers who rise and swell along with their subject, even when it may seem an ordinary one. So what about me, writing about this Leviathan? Without my meaning it, my handwriting grows into poster capitals. Give me a condor's quill! Give me Vesuvius' crater for an inkwell! Friends, hold my arms! For the mere act of writing down my thoughts about this Leviathan wears me out and makes me faint, they reach out so widely and take in so much, as if they would include the whole circle of the sciences, and all the generations of whales and men and mastodons, past, present and to come, along with all the turning panoramas of empire on earth and across the whole universe, not leaving out its suburbs. That is how much a large, generous theme can magnify a writer! We swell to its size. To produce a mighty book, you must choose a mighty theme. No great and lasting book can ever be written about the flea, though plenty of people have tried.

Before taking up the subject of fossil whales, I present my credentials as a geologist by stating that in my odd moments I have been a stonemason, and also a great digger of ditches, canals and wells, wine-vaults, cellars, and cisterns of all sorts. Likewise, by way of preliminary, I want to remind the reader that while in the earlier geological strata are found the fossils of monsters now almost completely extinct, the later relics discovered in what are called the Tertiary formations seem to be connecting links, or at any rate intervening links, between those creatures from before recorded time and the ones whose remote descendants are said to have entered the Ark. All the fossil whales discovered so far belong to the Tertiary period, which is the last one before the surface formations. And though none of them exactly matches any known species of the present time, they are still similar enough to them in general respects to justify their being ranked as Cetacean fossils.

Detached, broken fossils of pre-Adamite whales — fragments of their bones and skeletons — have been found at various intervals within the past thirty years at the base of the Alps, in Lombardy, in France, in England, in Scotland, and in the states of Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama. Among the more curious of these remains is part of a skull which in 1779 was dug up in the Rue Dauphine in Paris, a short street opening almost directly on the palace of the Tuileries; and bones dug up while excavating the great docks of Antwerp in Napoleon's time. Cuvier pronounced these fragments to have belonged to some utterly unknown Leviathanic species.

But by far the most wonderful of all Cetacean remains was the nearly complete, enormous skeleton of an extinct monster found in 1842 on Judge Creagh's plantation in Alabama. The awestruck, credulous slaves who lived nearby took it for the bones of one of the fallen angels. The Alabama doctors declared it a huge reptile and gave it the name Basilosaurus. But when some sample bones were taken across the sea to Owen, the English anatomist, this supposed reptile turned out to be a whale, though of a species now gone. That is a telling example of the fact this book has repeated again and again: the whale's skeleton gives very little clue to the shape of his body when fully clothed in flesh. So Owen renamed the monster Zeuglodon, and in his paper read before the London Geological Society he declared it, in substance, one of the most extraordinary creatures that the changes of the globe have wiped out of existence.

When I stand among these mighty Leviathan skeletons, skulls, tusks, jaws, ribs, and vertebrae — all showing partial resemblances to the existing breeds of sea-monsters, but at the same time bearing similar likenesses to the annihilated Leviathans from before recorded time, their incalculable elders — I am carried back as if by a flood to that wondrous period before time itself can be said to have begun; for time began with man. Here Saturn's gray chaos rolls over me, and I catch dim, shuddering glimpses of those polar eternities when wedged bastions of ice pressed hard on what are now the Tropics, and in all the 25,000 miles of this world's circumference not a hand's breadth of habitable land was visible. Then the whole world was the whale's; and, king of creation, he left his wake along the present lines of the Andes and the Himalayas. Who can show a pedigree like Leviathan? Ahab's harpoon had shed older blood than Pharaoh's. Methuselah seems a schoolboy. I look around to shake hands with Shem. I am horror-struck at this existence of the unspeakable terrors of the whale — older than Moses, without a source — terrors which, having been before all time, must of necessity go on existing after all human ages are over.

But this Leviathan has not only left his pre-Adamite traces in the stereotype plates of nature, and bequeathed his ancient bust to limestone and marl; on Egyptian tablets too, so old that they seem almost fossils themselves, we find the unmistakable print of his fin. In a room of the great temple of Denderah, some fifty years ago, there was discovered on the granite ceiling a sculptured and painted planisphere, a map of the heavens, crowded with centaurs, griffins, and dolphins, like the grotesque figures on the celestial globes of the moderns. Gliding among them, old Leviathan swam as in days of old; he was there, swimming in that planisphere, centuries before Solomon was in his cradle.
Nor must I leave out another strange testimony to the antiquity of the whale, in his own bony, after-the-Flood reality, as recorded by the venerable John Leo, the old Barbary traveler.

"Not far from the seaside, they have a Temple, the rafters and beams of which are made of whale-bones; for whales of a monstrous size are often cast up dead on that shore. The common people imagine that by a secret power bestowed by God on the Temple, no whale can pass it without immediate death. But the truth of the matter is that on either side of the Temple there are rocks that shoot two miles into the sea and wound the whales when they come upon them. They keep a whale's rib of an incredible length as a miracle, which, lying on the ground with its convex side uppermost, makes an arch whose top cannot be reached by a man on a camel's back. This rib (says John Leo) is said to have lain there a hundred years before I saw it. Their historians affirm that a prophet who prophesied of Mahomet came from this Temple, and some do not hesitate to assert that the Prophet Jonas was cast out by the whale at the base of the Temple."
In this African Temple of the Whale I leave you, reader; and if you are a Nantucketer and a whaleman, you will silently worship there.

chapters.title: Chapter 105 — Does the Whale’s Magnitude Diminish?—Will He Perish?
paragraphs: Inasmuch, then, as this Leviathan comes floundering down upon us from the headwaters of the Eternities, it is fair to ask whether, in the long course of his generations, he may have shrunk from the original bulk of his ancestors.

But when we look into it, we find that today's whales are not only bigger than those whose fossil remains turn up in the Tertiary system (which covers a distinct geological period before man), but that among the whales found in that Tertiary system, the ones from its later formations are larger than the ones from its earlier formations.

The largest by far of all the pre-Adamite whales dug up so far is the Alabama one mentioned in the last chapter, and its skeleton was under seventy feet long. Yet we have already seen that the tape measure gives seventy-two feet for the skeleton of a large modern whale. And whalemen have told me that Sperm Whales nearly a hundred feet long at the time of capture have been taken.
But may it not be that while the whales of the present hour are an advance in size upon those of all previous geological periods, they have degenerated since Adam's time?

We certainly must conclude so, if we are to believe the accounts of gentlemen like Pliny and the ancient naturalists in general. For Pliny tells us of whales whose living bulk covered acres, and Aldrovandus of others that were eight hundred feet long — whales the size of ropewalks and Thames Tunnels! And even in the time of Banks and Solander, Cooke's naturalists, we find a Danish member of the Academy of Sciences recording certain Iceland Whales (reydan-siskur, or Wrinkled Bellies) as one hundred and twenty yards long, that is, three hundred and sixty feet. And Lacépède, the French naturalist, in his detailed history of whales, right at the start of his work (page 3), gives the Right Whale as one hundred meters, or three hundred and twenty-eight feet. And this work came out as recently as A.D. 1825.

But will any whaleman believe these stories? No. The whale of today is as big as his ancestors in Pliny's time. And if I ever go where Pliny is, I, a whaleman (more of one than he was), will make bold to tell him so. Because when the Egyptian mummies buried thousands of years before Pliny was even born do not measure as much in their coffins as a modern Kentuckian in his socks; and when the cattle and other animals carved on the oldest Egyptian and Nineveh tablets, by the relative proportions in which they are drawn, just as plainly prove that the high-bred, stall-fed prize cattle of Smithfield not only equal but far exceed in size the fattest of Pharaoh's fat cattle — then, in the face of all this, I cannot understand how of all animals the whale alone should have degenerated, and I will not admit it.

But yet another question remains, one often debated by the more learned Nantucketers. Given the almost all-seeing lookouts at the mastheads of the whale-ships, now pushing even through Bering Strait and into the remotest secret drawers and lockers of the world, and the thousand harpoons and lances darted along all the continental coasts, the disputed point is whether Leviathan can long endure so wide a chase and so remorseless a slaughter; whether he must not at last be exterminated from the waters, and the last whale, like the last man, smoke his last pipe and then himself evaporate in the final puff.

If you compare the humped herds of whales with the humped herds of buffalo that, less than forty years ago, covered the prairies of Illinois and Missouri in their tens of thousands, shaking their iron manes and scowling with their thunder-clotted brows over the sites of what are now crowded river cities, where the polite broker now sells you land at a dollar an inch, that comparison would seem to offer an unanswerable argument that the hunted whale cannot escape rapid extinction.

But you have to look at this question from every angle. It is true that only a short time ago — less than a full lifetime — the buffalo of Illinois outnumbered the people of London today; that now not a single horn or hoof of them is left anywhere in that region; and that the cause of this astonishing extermination was the spear of man. Even so, the very different nature of the whale hunt absolutely rules out so inglorious an end for the Leviathan. Forty men in one ship who hunt Sperm Whales for forty-eight months think they have done extremely well, and thank God, if they finally bring home the oil of forty fish. By contrast, in the days of the old Canadian and Indian hunters and trappers of the West, when the far west (in whose sunset suns still rise) was an untouched wilderness, the same number of men in moccasins, over the same number of months, riding horses instead of sailing ships, would have killed not forty buffalo but forty thousand and more — a fact that could be backed up with statistics if necessary.

Nor, rightly considered, does it seem to be any argument for the gradual extinction of the sperm whale, for example, that in former years (the latter part of the last century, say) these Leviathans were met in small pods much more often than at present, and that as a result the voyages were not so long and were also much more profitable.
