Because, as has been noted elsewhere, those whales, influenced by some considerations of safety, now swim the seas in immense caravans, so that to a large degree the scattered solitaries, yokes, pods, and schools of other days are now gathered into vast but widely separated, infrequent armies. That is all. And equally mistaken seems the idea that because the so-called whale-bone whales no longer haunt many grounds that once abounded with them, that species too must be declining. For they are only being driven from promontory to cape; and if one coast is no longer enlivened with their spouts, then, you may be sure, some other and remoter shore has very recently been startled by the unfamiliar spectacle.

Furthermore, these last-mentioned Leviathans have two firm fortresses which, in all human probability, will remain forever impregnable. And as the frosty Swiss, when their valleys were invaded, retreated to their mountains, so, hunted from the savannas and glades of the middle seas, the whale-bone whales can at last take refuge in their polar citadels, and diving under the ultimate glassy barriers and walls there, come up among icy fields and floes, and in a charmed circle of everlasting December defy all pursuit by man.

But as perhaps fifty of these whale-bone whales are harpooned for every one cachalot, or sperm whale, some philosophers of the forecastle have concluded that this positive slaughter has already very seriously thinned their battalions. But though for some time past a number of these whales, no fewer than 13,000, have been killed every year on the northwest coast by the Americans alone, there are considerations which make even this fact of little or no weight as an opposing argument in this matter.

Natural as it is to be somewhat skeptical concerning the abundance of the more enormous creatures of the globe, yet what shall we say to Harto, the historian of Goa, when he tells us that at one hunt the King of Siam took 4,000 elephants; that in those regions elephants are as numerous as droves of cattle in temperate climates? And if these elephants, which have now been hunted for thousands of years by Semiramis, by Porus, by Hannibal, and by all the successive monarchs of the East — if they still survive there in great numbers, there seems no reason to doubt that the great whale may far more easily outlast all hunting, since he has a pasture to roam in that is precisely twice as large as all Asia, both Americas, Europe and Africa, New Holland, and all the islands of the sea combined.

Moreover, we have to consider that since whales are thought to live a very long time, probably reaching a hundred years or more, several separate adult generations must be alive at any one time. We can quickly get some idea of what that means if we imagine all the graveyards, cemeteries and family vaults in creation giving up the living bodies of all the men, women and children who were alive seventy-five years ago, and then add that countless multitude to the present human population of the globe.

For all these reasons, then, we consider the whale immortal in his species, however perishable as an individual. He swam the seas before the continents broke water; he once swam over the site of the Tuileries, and Windsor Castle, and the Kremlin. In Noah's flood he despised Noah's Ark; and if the world is ever to be flooded again, like the Netherlands, to kill off its rats, the eternal whale will still survive, and rearing up on the topmost crest of the equatorial flood, spout his frothing defiance to the skies.

chapters.title: Chapter 106 — Ahab’s Leg
paragraphs: The hasty manner in which Captain Ahab had left the Samuel Enderby of London had not been without some small violence to his own person. He had landed with such energy upon a thwart of his boat that his ivory leg had received a half-splintering shock. And when, after gaining his own deck and his own pivot-hole there, he so vehemently wheeled round with an urgent command to the steersman — it was, as ever, something about his not steering firmly enough — then the already shaken ivory received such an additional twist and wrench that, though it still remained intact and to all appearances strong, Ahab did not consider it entirely trustworthy.

And indeed it seemed hardly surprising that, for all his pervading, mad recklessness, Ahab did at times pay careful attention to the condition of that dead bone on which he partly stood. For not very long before the Pequod sailed from Nantucket, he had been found one night lying face-down on the ground, unconscious: by some unknown and seemingly inexplicable, unimaginable accident, his ivory limb had been so violently displaced that it had struck him like a stake and all but pierced his groin; and only with extreme difficulty was the agonizing wound entirely healed.

Nor, at the time, had it failed to enter his monomaniac mind that all the anguish of that present suffering was nothing but the direct result of an earlier woe. And he seemed to see all too plainly that just as the most poisonous reptile of the marsh perpetuates its kind as inevitably as the sweetest songbird of the grove, so, equally with every happiness, all miserable events naturally beget their like. Yes, more than equally, thought Ahab, since both the ancestry and the descendants of Grief reach further than the ancestry and descendants of Joy. For, leaving aside this point — that it is an inference from certain church teachings that while some natural pleasures here will have no children born to them in the other world, but, on the contrary, will be followed by the joy-childlessness of all hell's despair, some guilty mortal miseries will still fruitfully beget for themselves an eternally growing brood of griefs beyond the grave — leaving that aside entirely, there still seems to be an inequality in the deeper analysis of the thing. For, thought Ahab, while even the highest earthly happiness always has a certain meaningless pettiness lurking in it, all heart-woes have at bottom a mystic significance, and in some men an archangelic grandeur; and careful tracing-out of them does not contradict the obvious conclusion. To trace the family trees of these high mortal miseries leads us at last among the sourceless first-born lines of the gods; so that, in the face of all the glad, haymaking suns and the soft, cymbal-clashing round harvest moons, we must give in to this: that the gods themselves are not forever glad. The ineradicable, sad birthmark on the brow of man is only the stamp of sorrow in those who signed it.

Unwittingly here a secret has been divulged which perhaps might more properly have been disclosed before, in due order. Along with many other particulars concerning Ahab, it had always remained a mystery to some why, for a certain period both before and after the sailing of the Pequod, he had hidden himself away with such grand-lama-like seclusion, and for that one interval sought speechless refuge, as it were, among the marble senate of the dead. Captain Peleg's rumored reason for this seemed by no means adequate, though indeed, where all Ahab's deeper nature was concerned, every revelation partook more of significant darkness than of explanatory light. But in the end it all came out — this one matter did, at least. That dreadful mishap was at the bottom of his temporary seclusion. And not only this, but to that ever-shrinking, dwindling circle ashore who, for any reason, possessed the privilege of a less prohibited approach to him — to that timid circle the above-hinted accident, remaining as it did moodily unexplained by Ahab, invested itself with terrors not entirely unrelated to the land of spirits and of wails. So that, through their concern for him, they had all conspired, so far as they could, to hush up the knowledge of this thing from others. And hence it was that not till a considerable time had passed did it come to light upon the Pequod's decks.

But be all this as it may; whether or not the unseen, ambiguous council in the air, or the vindictive princes and potentates of fire, have anything to do with earthly Ahab, in this present matter of his leg he took plain, practical steps: he called the carpenter.

And when that functionary appeared before him, he ordered him to set about making a new leg without delay, and directed the mates to see that he was supplied with all the studs and joists of jaw-ivory (sperm whale) accumulated so far on the voyage, so that a careful selection of the stoutest, clearest-grained stuff could be made. This done, the carpenter received orders to have the leg finished that night, and to provide all the fittings for it, independent of those belonging to the distrusted one in use. Moreover, the ship's forge was ordered to be hoisted out of its temporary idleness in the hold; and, to speed things up, the blacksmith was commanded to begin at once forging whatever iron contrivances might be needed.

chapters.title: Chapter 107 — The Carpenter
paragraphs: Seat yourself like a sultan among the moons of Saturn and take high, abstract man alone; and he seems a wonder, a grandeur, and a woe. But from the same point, take mankind in mass, and for the most part they seem a mob of unnecessary duplicates, both contemporary and hereditary. But humble as he was, and far from furnishing an example of the high, humane abstraction, the Pequod's carpenter was no duplicate. Hence he now comes in person on this stage.

Like all sea-going ship's carpenters, and especially those on whaling vessels, he was, to a certain offhand, practical extent, experienced in many trades and callings alongside his own, the carpenter's trade being the ancient, branching trunk of all those many handicrafts that have more or less to do with wood as a supporting material. But beyond this general remark, which applies to him as well, this carpenter of the Pequod was singularly capable in the thousand nameless mechanical emergencies that keep arising in a large ship on a three- or four-year voyage in uncivilized, far-distant seas. For not to speak of his readiness in ordinary duties — repairing stove boats and sprung spars, reshaping clumsy-bladed oars, setting bull's-eyes (thick glass deck-lights) into the deck or new tree-nails into the side planks, and other miscellaneous matters more directly belonging to his special business — he was also unhesitatingly expert in all sorts of conflicting abilities, both useful and whimsical.

The one grand stage where he performed all his manifold roles was his vice-bench: a long, crude, heavy table furnished with several vises of different sizes, both of iron and of wood. At all times except when whales were alongside, this bench was securely lashed crosswise against the rear of the try-works.

A belaying pin turns out to be too large to go easily into its hole: the carpenter claps it into one of his ever-ready vises and at once files it smaller. A lost land-bird of strange plumage strays on board and is made a captive: out of clean-shaved rods of right-whale bone and crossbeams of sperm whale ivory, the carpenter makes a pagoda-looking cage for it. An oarsman sprains his wrist: the carpenter concocts a soothing lotion. Stubb longed for vermilion stars to be painted on the blade of every one of his oars: screwing each oar into his big wooden vise, the carpenter symmetrically supplies the constellation. A sailor takes a fancy to wear shark-bone earrings: the carpenter drills his ears. Another has a toothache: the carpenter whips out his pincers and, slapping one hand on his bench, tells him to sit there; but the poor fellow flinches uncontrollably before the operation is done; so, whirling round the handle of his wooden vise, the carpenter signals him to clamp his jaw in that, if he wants the tooth drawn.

So this carpenter was prepared at all points, and equally indifferent and without respect in all. Teeth he counted as bits of ivory; heads he regarded as nothing but top-blocks; men themselves he lightly took for capstans. Now, being so variously accomplished over so wide a field, and with such lively expertness too, all this would seem to argue some uncommon quickness of intelligence. But not exactly. For this man was remarkable above all for a certain impersonal stolidity, as it were — impersonal, I say, because it so shaded off into the surrounding infinity of things that it seemed one with the general stolidity visible in the whole world, which, while ceaselessly active in countless ways, still eternally holds its peace and ignores you, though you dig foundations for cathedrals. Yet this half-horrible stolidity in him, which seemed to involve an all-branching heartlessness too, was oddly mixed at times with an old, crutch-like, antediluvian, wheezing humor, streaked now and then with a certain grizzled wit, such as might have served to pass the time during the midnight watch on the bearded forecastle of Noah's ark. Was it that this old carpenter had been a lifelong wanderer, whose much rolling to and fro had not only gathered no moss but, what is more, had rubbed off whatever small outward attachments might originally have belonged to him? He was a stripped abstraction; an unbroken whole number; as uncompromised as a newborn baby; living without any deliberate reference to this world or the next. You might almost say that this strange uncompromisedness in him involved a sort of unintelligence; for in his numerous trades he did not seem to work so much by reason or by instinct, or simply because he had been taught to, or by any mixture of all these, even or uneven, but merely by a kind of deaf-and-dumb, spontaneous, literal process. He was a pure manipulator, a worker with the hands; his brain, if he had ever had one, must have oozed early on into the muscles of his fingers. He was like one of those unreasoning but still highly useful Sheffield contrivances, multum in parvo (much in little), which have the outside — though a little swollen — of a common pocketknife, but contain not only blades of various sizes but also screwdrivers, corkscrews, tweezers, awls, pens, rulers, nail-files, and countersinks. So if his superiors wanted to use the carpenter as a screwdriver, all they had to do was open that part of him, and the screw was fast; or if as tweezers, pick him up by the legs, and there they were.

Yet, as previously hinted, this all-tooled, open-and-shut carpenter was, after all, no mere machine or automaton. If he did not have a common soul in him, he had a subtle something that somehow did its duty in an odd way. What that was — whether an essence of quicksilver or a few drops of smelling salts — there is no telling. But there it was, and there it had resided for now some sixty years or more. And this it was, this same unaccountable, cunning life-principle in him, that kept him a great part of the time talking to himself; but only like an unreasoning wheel, which also hummingly talks to itself; or rather, his body was a sentry-box and this self-talker on guard there, and talking all the time to keep himself awake.

chapters.title: Chapter 108 — Ahab and the Carpenter
paragraphs: The Deck — First Night Watch.

(The carpenter stands at his vise-bench, filing away busily by the light of two lanterns at the ivory shaft for the leg, which is clamped tight in the vise. Slabs of ivory, leather straps, pads, screws and all kinds of tools lie scattered over the bench. Farther forward the red flame of the forge can be seen, where the blacksmith is working.)

Drat the file, and drat the bone! What should be soft is hard, and what should be hard is soft. That's how it goes for us who file old jaws and shinbones. Let's try another. Aye, now, this works better (sneezes). Hello, this bone dust is (sneezes) — why it's (sneezes) — yes it's (sneezes) — bless my soul, it won't let me speak! This is what an old fellow gets now for working in dead lumber. Saw a live tree and you don't get this dust; amputate a live bone and you don't get it (sneezes). Come, come, you old Smut, there, lend a hand, and let's have that ferrule and buckle-screw; I'll be ready for them in a minute. Lucky now (sneezes) there's no knee-joint to make; that might puzzle me a little; but a mere shinbone — why, it's as easy as making hop-poles; only I'd like to put a good finish on it. Time, time; if I only had the time, I could turn him out as neat a leg now as ever (sneezes) scraped to a lady in a parlor. Those buckskin legs and calves I've seen in shop windows wouldn't compare at all. They soak up water, they do; and of course they get rheumatic and have to be doctored (sneezes) with washes and lotions, just like live legs. There; before I saw it off, now, I must call his old Mogulship and see whether the length will be all right; too short, if anything, I guess. Ha! That's the heel; we're in luck; here he comes, or it's somebody else, that's certain.
AHAB (advancing). (During the ensuing scene, the carpenter continues sneezing at times.)
Well, man-maker!
Just in time, sir. If it suits the captain, I'll mark the length now. Let me measure you, sir.

Measured for a leg! Good. Well, it's not the first time. Get to it! There; keep your finger on it. This is a strong vise you have here, carpenter; let me feel its grip once. So, so; it does pinch some.
Oh, sir, it will break bones — beware, beware!
Don't worry; I like a good grip. I like to feel something in this slippery world that can hold on, man. What's Prometheus up to over there? The blacksmith, I mean — what's he doing?
He must be forging the buckle-screw, sir, now.
Right. It's a partnership; he supplies the muscle part. He makes a fierce red flame there!
Aye, sir; he must have the white heat for this kind of fine work.

Mm. So he must. It strikes me now as deeply significant that the old Greek Prometheus, who made men, so they say, should have been a blacksmith and brought them to life with fire; for whatever is made in fire must rightly belong to fire, and so hell is likely. Look how the soot flies! This must be the leftover stuff the Greek made the Africans from. Carpenter, when he's finished with that buckle, tell him to forge a pair of steel shoulder blades; there's a peddler on board with a crushing pack.
Sir?

Wait. While Prometheus is at it, I'll order a complete man, made to a pattern I like. Item one: fifty feet tall in his socks. Next, a chest built on the model of the Thames Tunnel. Next, legs with roots on them, so he stays in one place. Next, arms three feet thick at the wrist. No heart at all, a brass forehead, and about a quarter of an acre of fine brains. And let me see — shall I order eyes that look outward? No, but put a skylight on top of his head to light up the inside. There, take the order and be off.
Now what is he talking about, and who is he talking to, I'd like to know? Should I keep standing here? (aside)
It is poor architecture to make a blind dome; here's one. No, no, no; I must have a lantern.
Ho, ho! That's it, hey? Here are two, sir; one will do for me.
What are you thrusting that thief-catcher into my face for, man? Forced light is worse than pointed pistols.
I thought, sir, that you spoke to the carpenter.
Carpenter? Why, that's — but no; a very tidy, and, I may say, an extremely gentlemanlike sort of business you are in here, carpenter; or would you rather work in clay?
Sir? Clay? Clay, sir? That's mud; we leave clay to ditchers, sir.
The fellow's impious! What are you sneezing about?
Bone is rather dusty, sir.
Take the hint, then; and when you are dead, never bury yourself under living people's noses.
Sir? Oh! Ah! I guess so; yes — oh, dear!

Look here, carpenter, I daresay you call yourself a right good workmanlike workman, eh? Well, then, will it speak thoroughly well for your work if, when I come to mount this leg you make, I shall nevertheless feel another leg in the same identical place with it; that is, carpenter, my old lost leg; the flesh and blood one, I mean. Can you not drive that old Adam away?

Well, sir, I'm starting to understand a little now. Yes, I've heard something curious about that, sir: that a dismasted man never quite loses the feeling of his old spar, and it still pricks him now and then. May I humbly ask if that's really true, sir?

It is, man. Look, put your living leg here, in the spot where mine used to be. There — now the eye sees only one distinct leg, but the soul sees two. Where you feel tingling life, there, exactly there, right down to a hair, I feel it too. Is that a riddle?
I should humbly call it a puzzler, sir.

Hush, then. How do you know that some entire, living, thinking thing may not be standing invisibly, and without mingling with you, exactly where you are standing now; aye, and standing there in spite of you? In your most solitary hours, then, don't you fear eavesdroppers? Hold on, don't speak! And if I still feel the sting of my crushed leg, though it has now been dissolved so long, then why might you not, carpenter, feel the fiery pains of hell forever, and without a body? Hah!
Good Lord! Honestly, sir, if it comes to that, I'll have to work out my sums again; I think I forgot to carry a small figure, sir.
Look here, pudding-heads should never grant premises. How long before the leg is done?
Perhaps an hour, sir.

Bungle away at it, then, and bring it to me when it's done (turns to go). Oh, Life! Here I stand, as proud as a Greek god, and yet I am in debt to this blockhead for a bone to stand on! A curse on this mortal web of everyone owing everyone, which will never let us be rid of ledgers. I want to be as free as air, and here I am written down in the whole world's account books. I am so rich that I could have matched the wealthiest Praetorians bid for bid when they auctioned off the Roman empire (which was the world's); and yet I owe for the very flesh of the tongue I brag with. By heaven! I'll get a crucible, climb in, and melt myself down into one small, compact vertebra. So.
CARPENTER (resuming his work).

Well, well, well! Stubb knows him best of all, and Stubb always says he's queer; says nothing but that one sufficient little word queer; he's queer, says Stubb; he's queer — queer, queer; and keeps dinning it into Mr. Starbuck all the time — queer, sir, queer, queer, very queer. And here's his leg! Yes, now that I think of it, here's his bedfellow! Has a stick of whale's jawbone for a wife! And this is his leg; he'll stand on this. What was that now about one leg standing in three places, and all three places standing in one hell — how was that? Oh! I don't wonder he looked so scornful at me! I'm sort of strange-thoughted sometimes, they say; but that's only haphazard-like. Then, a short little old body like me should never try to wade out into deep waters with tall, heron-built captains; the water chucks you under the chin pretty quick, and there's a great cry for lifeboats. And here's the heron's leg! Long and slim, sure enough! Now, for most folks one pair of legs lasts a lifetime, and that must be because they use them mercifully, the way a tender-hearted old lady uses her roly-poly old coach-horses. But Ahab — oh, he's a hard driver. Look, he's driven one leg to death and lamed the other for life, like a spavined horse, and now wears out bone legs by the cord. Hello, there, you Smut! Lend a hand there with those screws, and let's finish it before the resurrection fellow comes calling with his horn for all legs, true or false, the way brewery-men go round collecting old beer barrels to fill them up again. What a leg this is! It looks like a real live leg, filed down to nothing but the core; he'll be standing on this tomorrow; he'll be taking altitudes on it. Hello! I almost forgot the little oval slate, smoothed ivory, where he figures up the latitude. So, so; chisel, file, and sandpaper, now!

chapters.title: Chapter 109 — Ahab and Starbuck in the Cabin
paragraphs: As usual, they were pumping out the ship the next morning, and, surprisingly, a fair amount of oil came up with the water; the casks down below must have sprung a bad leak. Everyone was very worried, and Starbuck went down to the cabin to report this bad news.*

*In sperm-whalers with any considerable quantity of oil on board, it is a regular twice-weekly duty to run a hose into the hold and drench the casks with sea-water, which is afterward removed at varying intervals by the ship's pumps. In this way the aim is to keep the casks damp and tight; while from the changed character of the water pumped out, the sailors readily detect any serious leakage in the precious cargo.

By now the Pequod was approaching Formosa and the Bashee Isles from the south and west; between them runs one of the tropical passages out of the China seas into the Pacific. So Starbuck found Ahab with a general chart of the eastern archipelagoes spread out in front of him, along with a separate one showing the long eastern coasts of the Japanese islands of Nippon, Matsumae and Shikoku. The wondrous old man, with his back to the gangway door, his snow-white new ivory leg braced against the screwed-down leg of his table and a long jackknife like a pruning-hook in his hand, was frowning and tracing out his old courses again.
"Who's there?" hearing the footstep at the door, but not turning round to it. "On deck! Begone!"
"Captain Ahab is mistaken; it is I. The oil in the hold is leaking, sir. We must hoist the Burtons (the hoisting tackles) and break out the hold."
"Hoist the Burtons and break out? Now that we are nearing Japan — heave to here for a week to tinker a parcel of old hoops?"
"It's either that, sir, or lose more oil in one day than we can make up in a year. Something we sail twenty thousand miles to get is worth saving, sir."
"So it is, so it is; if we get it."
"I was speaking of the oil in the hold, sir."

"And I wasn't speaking or thinking of that at all. Get out! Let it leak! I'm all leaks myself. Yes! Leaks within leaks! Not only full of leaky casks, but those leaky casks are in a leaky ship; and that's a far worse fix than the Pequod's, man. Yet I don't stop to plug my leak, for who can find it down in the deep-loaded hull? And even if it were found, how could anyone hope to plug it in this life's howling gale? Starbuck! I won't have the Burtons hoisted."
"What will the owners say, sir?"

"Let the owners stand on Nantucket beach and outyell the typhoons. What does Ahab care? Owners, owners? You are always prattling to me, Starbuck, about those miserly owners, as if the owners were my conscience. But look here, the only real owner of anything is its commander; and listen, my conscience is in this ship's keel. On deck!"

"Captain Ahab," said the mate, flushing as he stepped farther into the cabin. His boldness was so oddly respectful and careful that it seemed not only to be trying in every way to avoid showing itself outwardly in the slightest, but inwardly as well to be more than half unsure of itself. "A better man than I am might well overlook in you what he would be quick enough to resent in a younger man — yes, and in a happier one, Captain Ahab."
"Devils! Do you then so much as dare to think critically of me? On deck!"
"No, sir, not yet; I do beg you. And I do dare, sir — to be patient! Shall we not understand each other better than we have till now, Captain Ahab?"

Ahab seized a loaded musket from the rack — forming part of most South Sea vessels' cabin furniture — and pointing it toward Starbuck, exclaimed: "There is one God that is Lord over the earth, and one Captain that is lord over the Pequod. On deck!"

For an instant in the flashing eyes of the mate, and his fiery cheeks, you would have almost thought that he had really received the blast of the leveled barrel. But, mastering his emotion, he half-calmly rose, and as he left the cabin, paused for an instant and said: "You have outraged, not insulted me, sir; but for that I ask you not to beware of Starbuck — you would only laugh; but let Ahab beware of Ahab. Beware of yourself, old man."

"He grows brave but nevertheless obeys; that's a most careful bravery!" murmured Ahab, as Starbuck disappeared. "What's that he said — Ahab beware of Ahab — there's something there!" Then, unconsciously using the musket for a walking stick, with an iron brow he paced to and fro in the little cabin; but presently the thick furrows of his forehead relaxed, and returning the gun to the rack, he went to the deck.

"You are only too good a fellow, Starbuck," he said quietly to the mate; then, raising his voice to the crew: "Furl the topgallant-sails, and close-reef the topsails, fore and aft; back the main-yard; hoist the Burton, and break out in the main-hold."

It would perhaps be useless to guess exactly why Ahab acted this way toward Starbuck. It may have been a flash of honesty in him; or mere prudent policy which, under the circumstances, sternly forbade the slightest sign of open disaffection, however fleeting, in the important chief officer of his ship. However it was, his orders were carried out; and the Burtons were hoisted.

chapters.title: Chapter 110 — Queequeg in His Coffin
paragraphs: When they searched, they found that the casks most recently lowered into the hold were perfectly sound, and that the leak must be farther off. So, since the weather was calm, they broke out deeper and deeper, disturbing the slumbers of the huge ground-tier butts and sending those gigantic moles up from that black midnight into the daylight above. They went so deep, and the lowest puncheons looked so ancient, corroded and weedy, that you almost expected to find next some moldy cornerstone cask containing coins of Captain Noah, along with copies of the posted placards that vainly warned the infatuated old world about the flood. Tierce after tierce of water, and bread, and beef, too, and shooks of staves (bundled staves for making casks), and iron bundles of hoops, were hoisted out, until at last the piled decks were hard to get about on; and the hollow hull echoed underfoot, as if you were treading over empty catacombs, and reeled and rolled in the sea like a demijohn with nothing but air for freight. The ship was as top-heavy as a dinnerless student with all of Aristotle in his head. It was just as well that the Typhoons did not visit them then.
Now it was at this time that my poor pagan companion and close bosom friend, Queequeg, was seized with a fever, which brought him near to his endless end.

Let it be said that in this vocation of whaling, sinecures are unknown; dignity and danger go hand in hand; until you become captain, the higher you rise, the harder you toil. So it was with poor Queequeg, who, as harpooner, must not only face all the rage of the living whale, but — as we have seen elsewhere — mount his dead back in a rolling sea; and finally go down into the gloom of the hold and, sweating bitterly all day in that underground confinement, resolutely manhandle the clumsiest casks and see to their stowage. In short, among whalemen, the harpooners are the holders, as they are called.

Poor Queequeg! When the ship was about half disemboweled, you should have stooped over the hatchway and peered down at him there, where, stripped to his woolen drawers, the tattooed savage was crawling about amid that dampness and slime like a green spotted lizard at the bottom of a well. And a well, or an icehouse, it somehow proved to be for him, poor pagan; for there, strange to say, for all the heat of his sweating, he caught a terrible chill which turned into a fever, and at last, after some days' suffering, laid him in his hammock, close to the very sill of the door of death. How he wasted and wasted away in those few long, lingering days, until there seemed little left of him but his frame and his tattooing. But as everything else in him thinned, and his cheekbones grew sharper, his eyes nevertheless seemed to grow fuller and fuller; they took on a strange softness of luster, and looked out at you mildly but deeply from his sickness, a wondrous testimony to that immortal health in him which could not die or be weakened. And like circles on the water, which expand as they grow fainter, his eyes seemed rounding and rounding, like the rings of Eternity. An awe that cannot be named would steal over you as you sat beside this waning savage and saw things in his face as strange as any seen by those who stood by when Zoroaster died. For whatever is truly wondrous and fearful in man has never yet been put into words or books. And the approach of Death, which levels all alike, impresses all alike with a last revelation, which only an author returned from the dead could adequately tell. So that — let us say it again — no dying Chaldee or Greek had higher and holier thoughts than those whose mysterious shadows you saw creeping over the face of poor Queequeg, as he lay quietly in his swaying hammock, and the rolling sea seemed to be gently rocking him to his final rest, and the ocean's invisible flood-tide lifted him higher and higher toward his destined heaven.

Every man in the crew gave him up for lost; and as for Queequeg himself, what he thought of his condition was forcibly shown by a curious favor he asked. He called one of the men to him in the gray morning watch, just as day was breaking, and, taking his hand, said that while in Nantucket he had happened to see certain little canoes of dark wood, like the rich war-wood of his native island; and on inquiring, he had learned that all whalemen who died in Nantucket were laid in those same dark canoes, and that the idea of being laid out that way had greatly pleased him. For it was not unlike the custom of his own people, who, after embalming a dead warrior, stretched him out in his canoe and so left him to be floated away to the starry archipelagoes; for not only do they believe that the stars are islands, but that far beyond all visible horizons their own mild, uncontinented seas flow together with the blue heavens, and so form the white breakers of the Milky Way. He added that he shuddered at the thought of being buried in his hammock, according to the usual custom at sea, tossed like something vile to the death-devouring sharks. No: he wanted a canoe like those of Nantucket, all the more congenial to him as a whaleman because, like a whaleboat, these coffin-canoes had no keel — though that meant uncertain steering, and a great deal of leeway down the dim ages.

Now, when this strange circumstance was made known aft, the carpenter was at once ordered to do Queequeg's bidding, whatever it might involve. There was some heathenish, coffin-colored old lumber aboard, which, on a long voyage some time before, had been cut from the aboriginal groves of the Lackaday islands, and it was recommended that the coffin be made from these dark planks. No sooner had the carpenter been told of the order than he took his rule and, with all the indifferent promptness of his character, went straight into the forecastle and took Queequeg's measure with great accuracy, regularly marking Queequeg's person with chalk as he shifted the rule.
"Ah! poor fellow! he'll have to die now," exclaimed the Long Island sailor.

Going to his vise-bench, the carpenter, for convenience' sake and general reference, now measured off on it, by transfer, the exact length the coffin was to be, and then made the record permanent by cutting two notches at its ends. This done, he marshaled the planks and his tools, and set to work.
Once the last nail had been driven in and the lid properly planed and fitted, he swung the coffin easily onto his shoulder and carried it forward, asking whether they were ready for it up there yet.

Queequeg overheard the indignant, half-joking shouts with which the men on deck started to chase the coffin away, and, to everyone's dismay, he ordered it brought to him at once. There was no refusing him, since some dying men are the most tyrannical of all mortals; and surely, since they will soon trouble us so little forever after, the poor fellows ought to be humored.

Leaning out of his hammock, Queequeg studied the coffin closely for a long time. Then he asked for his harpoon, had the wooden shaft taken out of it, and had the iron part laid in the coffin together with one of the paddles from his boat. Next, again at his own request, biscuits were lined up around the inside walls; a flask of fresh water was set at the head, and at the foot a small bag of woody earth scraped up from the hold. A piece of sailcloth was rolled up for a pillow, and then Queequeg begged to be lifted into his final bed so that he could test how comfortable it was, if it was comfortable at all. He lay still for a few minutes, then told someone to go to his bag and bring out his little god, Yojo. Then he crossed his arms on his chest with Yojo between them and asked for the coffin lid (he called it the hatch) to be put over him. The head section folded back on a leather hinge, and there lay Queequeg in his coffin with hardly anything showing but his calm face. "Rarmai" (it will do; it is easy), he murmured at last, and signaled to be put back in his hammock.
But before this was done, Pip, who had been slyly hovering nearby all this while, came close to him where he lay and, with soft sobs, took him by the hand, holding his tambourine in the other.

"Poor rover! Will you never be done with all this weary roving? Where are you going now? But if the currents carry you to those sweet Antilles where the beaches are beaten only by water-lilies, will you do one little errand for me? Seek out one Pip, who's been missing a long time now: I think he's in those far Antilles. If you find him, then comfort him, for he must be very sad; for look! he's left his tambourine behind — I found it. Rig-a-dig, dig, dig! Now, Queequeg, die; and I'll beat you your dying march."

"I have heard," murmured Starbuck, gazing down the scuttle, "that in violent fevers men wholly without learning have talked in ancient languages; and that when the mystery is looked into, it always turns out that in their wholly forgotten childhood those ancient languages had really been spoken in their hearing by some lofty scholars. So, in my fond faith, poor Pip, in this strange sweetness of his lunacy, brings heavenly vouchers of all our heavenly homes. Where did he learn that, if not there? — Listen! He's speaking again: but more wildly now."

"Form up two by two! Let's make a General of him! Ho, where's his harpoon? Lay it across here. — Rig-a-dig, dig, dig! Hurrah! Oh, for a gamecock now to sit on his head and crow! Queequeg dies game! — mind you that; Queequeg dies game! — take good note of that; Queequeg dies game! I say; game, game, game! But base little Pip, he died a coward; died all a-shiver — shame on Pip! Listen; if you find Pip, tell all the Antilles he's a runaway; a coward, a coward, a coward! Tell them he jumped from a whaleboat! I'd never beat my tambourine over base Pip, and hail him General, if he were dying here once more. No, no! Shame on all cowards — shame on them! Let them go drown like Pip, who jumped from a whaleboat. Shame! Shame!"
Through all of this Queequeg lay with his eyes shut, as if he were dreaming. Pip was led away, and the sick man was put back in his hammock.

But now that he had apparently made every preparation for death, now that his coffin had proved a good fit, Queequeg suddenly rallied; soon there seemed no need for the carpenter's box. And then, when some expressed their delighted surprise, he said, in substance, that the cause of his sudden recovery was this: at a critical moment he had just remembered a little duty ashore that he was leaving undone, and so had changed his mind about dying; he could not die yet, he declared. They asked him, then, whether living or dying was a matter of his own sovereign will and pleasure. He answered, certainly. In a word, it was Queequeg's notion that if a man made up his mind to live, mere sickness could not kill him: nothing but a whale, or a gale, or some violent, ungovernable, unintelligent destroyer of that sort.

Now, there is this noteworthy difference between savage and civilized: while a sick civilized man may take six months to recover, generally speaking a sick savage is almost half-well again in a day. So in good time my Queequeg gained strength; and at length, after sitting on the windlass for a few idle days (but eating with a vigorous appetite), he suddenly leaped to his feet, threw out his arms and legs, gave himself a good stretch, yawned a little, and then, springing into the head of his hoisted boat and poising a harpoon, declared himself fit for a fight.

With a wild whimsicality, he now used his coffin as a sea-chest; and emptying his canvas bag of clothes into it, he set them in order there. He spent many spare hours carving the lid with all kinds of grotesque figures and drawings; and it seemed that in this way he was trying, in his rough fashion, to copy parts of the twisted tattooing on his body. And this tattooing had been the work of a departed prophet and seer of his island, who, by those hieroglyphic marks, had written out on his body a complete theory of the heavens and the earth, and a mystical treatise on the art of attaining truth; so that Queequeg in his own proper person was a riddle to unfold, a wondrous work in one volume, but one whose mysteries not even he himself could read, though his own living heart beat against them; and these mysteries were therefore destined in the end to molder away with the living parchment on which they were inscribed, and so remain unsolved to the last. And it must have been this thought that prompted Ahab's wild exclamation when, one morning, he turned away from surveying poor Queequeg — "Oh, devilish tantalization of the gods!"

chapters.title: Chapter 111 — The Pacific
paragraphs: As we glided past the Bashee isles, we emerged at last upon the great South Sea. Were it not for other things, I could have greeted my dear Pacific with uncounted thanks, for now the long prayer of my youth was answered: that serene ocean rolled eastward from me a thousand leagues of blue.

There is some sweet mystery about this sea — no one knows quite what — whose gently awesome stirrings seem to speak of some hidden soul beneath — like those fabled heavings of the Ephesian sod over the buried Evangelist St. John. And it is fitting that over these sea-pastures, wide-rolling watery prairies and Potters' Fields of all four continents, the waves should rise and fall, and ebb and flow unceasingly; for here millions of mixed shades and shadows, drowned dreams, sleepwalkings, reveries — all that we call lives and souls — lie dreaming, dreaming, still; tossing like sleepers in their beds; the ever-rolling waves made so only by their restlessness.

To any meditative Magian rover, this serene Pacific, once seen, must forever after be the sea of his adoption. It rolls the midmost waters of the world, the Indian Ocean and the Atlantic being only its arms. The same waves wash the breakwaters of the newly built Californian towns, planted only yesterday by the most recent race of men, and bathe the faded but still gorgeous skirts of Asiatic lands older than Abraham; while between them all float milky ways of coral islands, and low-lying, endless, unknown archipelagoes, and impenetrable Japans. Thus this mysterious, divine Pacific girdles the world's whole bulk; makes all coasts one bay to it; seems the tide-beating heart of the earth. Lifted by those eternal swells, you cannot help but acknowledge the seductive god, bowing your head to Pan.

But few thoughts of Pan stirred Ahab's brain as, standing like an iron statue at his accustomed place beside the mizzen rigging, with one nostril he unthinkingly sniffed the sugary musk from the Bashee isles (in whose sweet woods mild lovers must be walking), and with the other consciously breathed in the salt breath of the newfound sea — that sea in which the hated White Whale must even then be swimming. Launched at last upon these almost final waters, and gliding toward the Japanese cruising ground, the old man's purpose intensified. His firm lips met like the lips of a vise; the Delta of his forehead's veins swelled like overloaded brooks; even in his sleep, his ringing cry ran through the vaulted hull: "Stern all! The White Whale spouts thick blood!"

chapters.title: Chapter 112 — The Blacksmith
paragraphs: Taking advantage of the mild, summer-cool weather that now reigned in these latitudes, and in preparation for the especially active pursuits expected shortly, Perth, the begrimed, blistered old blacksmith, had not moved his portable forge back to the hold after finishing his share of the work on Ahab's leg, but kept it on deck, lashed fast to ringbolts by the foremast; for he was now almost constantly called on by the headsmen, and harpooners, and bowsmen to do some little job for them — altering, or repairing, or reshaping their various weapons and boat gear. Often he would be surrounded by an eager circle, all waiting to be served, holding boat-spades, pike-heads, harpoons and lances, and jealously watching his every sooty movement as he toiled. Nevertheless, this old man's was a patient hammer wielded by a patient arm. No murmur, no impatience, no petulance came from him. Silent, slow and solemn, bowing his chronically broken back still further, he toiled away as if toil were life itself, and the heavy beating of his hammer the heavy beating of his heart. And so it was. — Most miserable!

The old man walked in an odd way, with a slight lurch in his step that looked painful, and early in the voyage this had made the sailors curious. They had kept pestering him with questions until he finally gave in, and so now everyone knew the shameful story of his miserable fate.

Out late, and not innocently, one bitter winter midnight on the road between two country towns, the blacksmith, half-stupefied, felt the deadly numbness stealing over him, and took refuge in a leaning, dilapidated barn. The outcome was the loss of the ends of both his feet. From this revelation, piece by piece, there at last emerged the four acts of gladness, and the one long fifth act of grief, its catastrophe not yet reached, of his life's drama.

He was an old man who, at the age of nearly sixty, had belatedly encountered that thing called, in the technical language of sorrow, ruin. He had been a craftsman of famed excellence, with plenty to do; he owned a house and garden, embraced a youthful, daughter-like, loving wife and three merry, rosy-cheeked children, and every Sunday went to a cheerful-looking church planted in a grove. But one night, under cover of darkness, and further concealed in a most cunning disguise, a desperate burglar slid into his happy home and robbed them all of everything. And darker still to tell, it was the blacksmith himself who unknowingly led this burglar into the heart of his family. It was the Bottle Conjuror! When that fatal cork was drawn, out flew the fiend and shriveled up his home. Now, for prudent, most wise and economical reasons, the blacksmith's shop was in the basement of his house, but with a separate entrance of its own; so the young, loving, healthy wife had always listened — with no unhappy nervousness, but with vigorous pleasure — to the stout ringing of her young-armed old husband's hammer, whose echoes, muffled by passing through the floors and walls, came up to her, not unsweetly, in her nursery; and so, to stout Labor's iron lullaby, the blacksmith's infants were rocked to sleep.

Oh, woe on woe! Oh, Death, why can you not sometimes come in time? Had you taken this old blacksmith to yourself before his full ruin came upon him, then the young widow would have had a delicious grief, and her orphans a truly venerable, legendary father to dream of in their later years; and all of them a care-killing sufficiency to live on. But Death plucked down some virtuous elder brother, on whose whistling daily toil alone hung the responsibilities of some other family, and left the worse-than-useless old man standing, until the hideous rot of life should make him easier to harvest.

Why tell all of it? Every day the blows of the hammer in the basement came farther apart, and every day each blow was fainter than the one before. The wife sat frozen at the window, her eyes tearless and glittering as she stared into the weeping faces of her children. The bellows fell still; the forge clogged with cinders; the house was sold; the mother sank down into the long grass of the churchyard; twice her children followed her there; and the old man, without house or family, staggered off as a tramp in mourning crape, with no one to respect his sorrows, his gray head mocked by flaxen curls!

Death seems the only desirable sequel for a career like this; but Death is only a launching into the region of the strange Untried; it is only the first greeting to the possibilities of the immense Remote, the Wild, the Watery, the Unshored. Therefore, to the death-longing eyes of such men, who still have left in them some inward scruples against suicide, the all-contributed and all-receptive ocean alluringly spreads out his whole plain of unimaginable, captivating terrors and wonderful, new-life adventures; and from the hearts of infinite Pacifics the thousand mermaids sing to them: "Come to us, broken-hearted; here is another life without the guilt of dying in between; here are supernatural wonders, without dying for them. Come to us! Bury yourself in a life which, to your landed world, now equally abhorred and abhorring, is more oblivious than death. Come to us! You too, put up your gravestone within the churchyard, and come to us, till we marry you!"
Listening to these voices, East and West, at early sunrise and at nightfall, the blacksmith's soul answered: Aye, I come! And so Perth went a-whaling.

chapters.title: Chapter 113 — The Forge
paragraphs: With matted beard, and wrapped in a bristling sharkskin apron, Perth was standing about midday between his forge and anvil, the anvil set on an ironwood log, with one hand holding a pike-head in the coals and the other at his forge's lungs, the bellows, when Captain Ahab came along, carrying in his hand a small, rusty-looking leather bag. While still a little distance from the forge, moody Ahab paused; until at last Perth, drawing his iron out of the fire, began hammering it on the anvil — the red mass sending off sparks in thick hovering flights, some of which flew close to Ahab.
"Are these your Mother Carey's chickens, Perth? They are always flying in your wake; birds of good omen, too, but not to all — look here, they burn; but you — you live among them without a scorch."
"Because I am scorched all over, Captain Ahab," answered Perth, resting for a moment on his hammer; "I am past scorching; not easily can you scorch a scar."

"Well, well; no more. Your shrunken voice sounds too calmly, sanely woeful to me. In no Paradise myself, I am impatient of all misery in others that is not mad. You should go mad, blacksmith; say, why don't you go mad? How can you endure without being mad? Do the heavens yet hate you, that you cannot go mad? What were you making there?"
"Welding an old pike-head, sir; there were seams and dents in it."
"And can you make it all smooth again, blacksmith, after such hard usage as it had?"
"I think so, sir."
"And I suppose you can smooth almost any seams and dents; never mind how hard the metal, blacksmith?"
"Aye, sir, I think I can; all seams and dents but one."

"Look here, then," cried Ahab, passionately advancing, and leaning with both hands on Perth's shoulders; "look here — here — can you smooth out a seam like this, blacksmith?" sweeping one hand across his furrowed brow; "if you could, blacksmith, I would gladly lay my head upon your anvil, and feel your heaviest hammer between my eyes. Answer! Can you smooth this seam?"
"Oh! That is the one, sir! Did I not say all seams and dents but one?"

"Aye, blacksmith, it is the one; aye, man, it is unsmoothable; for though you only see it here in my flesh, it has worked down into the bone of my skull — that is all wrinkles! But away with child's play; no more gaffs and pikes today. Look here!" jingling the leather bag as if it were full of gold coins. "I, too, want a harpoon made; one that a thousand yoke of fiends could not pull apart, Perth; something that will stick in a whale like his own fin-bone. There's the stuff," flinging the pouch upon the anvil. "Look, blacksmith, these are the gathered nail-stubs of the steel shoes of racing horses."
"Horseshoe stubs, sir? Why, Captain Ahab, you have here, then, the best and stubbornest stuff we blacksmiths ever work."

"I know it, old man. These stubs will weld together like glue made from the melted bones of murderers. Quick! Forge me the harpoon. First make me twelve rods for its shank; then wind and twist and hammer the twelve together like the yarns and strands of a towline. Quick! I'll blow the fire."

When at last the twelve rods were made, Ahab tried them, one by one, by spiraling them with his own hand round a long, heavy iron bolt. "A flaw!" rejecting the last one. "Work that over again, Perth."

When that was done, Perth was about to start welding the twelve into one, but Ahab stopped him and said he would weld his own iron. So Ahab hammered away on the anvil with steady, gasping grunts, while Perth handed him the glowing rods one after another and the hard-driven forge sent up its fierce, straight flame. Meanwhile the Parsee passed by without a word and bent his head toward the fire, as though calling down some curse or some blessing on the work. But when Ahab looked up, he slipped away to one side.

"What's that bunch of lucifer matches dodging about there for?" muttered Stubb, looking on from the forecastle. "That Parsee smells fire like a fuse; and smells of it himself, like a hot musket's powder-pan."
Finally the shank, now one complete rod, got its last heating; and when Perth plunged it, all hissing, into the nearby cask of water to temper it, the scalding steam shot up into Ahab's bent face.
"Would you brand me, Perth?" wincing for a moment with the pain; "have I been but forging my own branding-iron, then?"
"God forbid, not that; and yet I am afraid of something, Captain Ahab. Isn't this harpoon meant for the White Whale?"
"For the white fiend! But now for the barbs; you must make them yourself, man. Here are my razors — the best of steel; here, and make the barbs sharp as the needle-sleet of the Icy Sea."
For a moment the old blacksmith looked at the razors as if he would prefer not to use them.
"Take them, man, I have no need for them; for I now neither shave, eat, nor pray till — but here — to work!"

At last the steel was hammered into the shape of an arrowhead, and once Perth had welded it to the shank, it soon formed the point of the iron. As the blacksmith was about to give the barbs a final heating before tempering them, he called to Ahab to set the water-cask close by.

"No, no — no water for that; I want it of the true death-temper. Ahoy, there! Tashtego, Queequeg, Daggoo! What do you say, pagans! Will you give me as much blood as will cover this barb?" holding it high up. A cluster of dark nods replied: Yes. Three punctures were made in the heathen flesh, and the White Whale's barbs were then tempered.

"Ego non baptizo te in nomine patris, sed in nomine diaboli!" (I do not baptize you in the name of the father, but in the name of the devil!) deliriously howled Ahab, as the malignant iron scorchingly devoured the baptismal blood.

Next, Ahab gathered up the spare poles from below, picked one of hickory with the bark still on it, and fitted its end into the socket of the iron. Then a coil of new tow-line was unwound, and several fathoms of it were led to the windlass and pulled very taut. Ahab pressed his foot down on it until the rope hummed like a harp-string; then, bending eagerly over it and finding no broken strands, he exclaimed, "Good! Now for the seizings."

At one end the rope was unstranded, and the separate spread yarns were all braided and woven round the socket of the harpoon; the pole was then driven hard up into the socket; from the lower end the rope was traced halfway along the pole's length and firmly secured there with intertwistings of twine. This done, pole, iron and rope — like the Three Fates — remained inseparable, and Ahab moodily stalked away with the weapon, the sound of his ivory leg and the sound of the hickory pole both ringing hollowly along every plank. But before he entered his cabin, a light, unnatural, half-bantering, yet most piteous sound was heard. Oh, Pip! Your wretched laugh, your idle but unresting eye, all your strange mummery blended, not without meaning, with the black tragedy of the melancholy ship, and mocked it!

chapters.title: Chapter 114 — The Gilder
paragraphs: Pushing deeper and deeper into the heart of the Japanese cruising ground, the Pequod was soon in a constant bustle with the fishery. Often, in mild, pleasant weather, the crew spent twelve, fifteen, eighteen and twenty hours at a stretch in the boats, steadily rowing, sailing or paddling after the whales, or, for a spell of sixty or seventy minutes, waiting calmly for them to surface — though they had little success for all their trouble.

At such times, under a softened sun, afloat all day upon smooth, slow-heaving swells, seated in his boat as light as a birch canoe, and so sociably mingling with the soft waves themselves that, like hearthstone cats, they purr against the gunwale — these are the times of dreamy quietude, when beholding the tranquil beauty and brilliance of the ocean's skin, one forgets the tiger heart that pants beneath it; and would not willingly remember that this velvet paw but conceals a merciless fang.

At such times the wanderer in his whaleboat quietly feels a certain filial, trusting, land-like feeling toward the sea, and looks on it as so much flowery earth. The distant ship, with only the tops of her masts showing, seems to struggle forward not through high rolling waves but through the tall grass of a rolling prairie — the way the western emigrants' horses show only their pricked-up ears while their hidden bodies wade far and wide through the astonishing greenery.

The long-drawn virgin valleys; the mild blue hillsides; as the hush, the hum steals over these, you would almost swear that play-weary children lie sleeping in these solitudes, in some glad springtime, when the flowers of the woods are plucked. And all this mixes with your most mystic mood; so that fact and fancy, half-way meeting, interpenetrate and form one seamless whole.

Nor did such soothing scenes, however temporary, fail to have at least an equally temporary effect on Ahab. But if these secret golden keys did seem to open his own secret golden treasuries within him, his breath upon them proved only tarnishing.

Oh, grassy glades! Oh, endless landscapes of everlasting spring in the soul! In you — though you have long been parched by the dead drought of our earthy life — in you men can still roll like young horses in fresh morning clover, and for a few fleeting moments feel the cool dew of immortal life on them. I wish to God these blessed calms would last. But the mingled and mingling threads of life are woven warp and woof: calms crossed by storms, a storm for every calm. There is no steady progress in this life that never doubles back; we do not climb through fixed stages and then rest at the last one. We pass through infancy's unconscious spell, boyhood's unthinking faith, adolescence's doubt (the common fate), then skepticism, then disbelief, and come to rest at last in manhood's brooding repose of If. But once we have gone through it all, we go round the circle again, and are infants, boys and men, and Ifs, forever. Where is the final harbor, from which we will never cast off again? In what ecstatic ether does the world sail, the one that even the weariest will never tire of? Where is the foundling's father hidden? Our souls are like those orphans whose unmarried mothers die giving birth to them: the secret of who our father is lies in their grave, and we must go there to learn it.
That same day, too, Starbuck, gazing far down from the side of his boat into the same golden sea, murmured quietly:

"Loveliness unfathomable, as ever lover saw in his young bride's eye! Do not tell me of your teeth-tiered sharks and your kidnapping cannibal ways. Let faith oust fact; let fancy oust memory; I look deep down and do believe."
And Stubb, fish-like, with sparkling scales, leaped up in that same golden light:
"I'm Stubb, and Stubb has a history; but right here Stubb swears that he has always been jolly!"

chapters.title: Chapter 115 — The Pequod Meets The Bachelor
paragraphs: And jolly enough they were, the sights and sounds that came sweeping down before the wind a few weeks after Ahab's harpoon had been welded.

It was a Nantucket ship, the Bachelor, which had just squeezed in her last cask of oil and bolted down her bulging hatches. Now, decked out in cheerful holiday finery, she was sailing joyfully — if a little boastfully — around among the widely scattered ships on the ground before turning her prow for home.

The three men at her mastheads wore long streamers of narrow red bunting on their hats; from the stern a whaleboat was hung, bottom down; and hanging captive from the bowsprit was the long lower jaw of the last whale they had killed. Signals, ensigns and jacks of all colors were flying from her rigging on every side. Lashed sideways in each of her three basketed tops were two barrels of sperm; above them, in her topmast crosstrees, you saw slender breakers (small casks) of the same precious fluid; and nailed to her main truck, the cap at the very top of the mainmast, was a brass lamp.

It was learned afterward that the Bachelor had had the most astonishing success — all the more remarkable because many other ships cruising the same seas had gone whole months without taking a single fish. She had not only given away barrels of beef and bread to make room for the far more valuable sperm, but had also traded for extra casks from the ships she met, and these were stowed along the deck and in the captain's and officers' staterooms. Even the cabin table had been broken up for kindling, and those who ate in the cabin took their meals off the broad head of an oil-butt lashed to the floor as a centerpiece. In the forecastle, the sailors had actually caulked and tarred their sea chests and filled them. It was added, as a joke, that the cook had fitted a lid on his largest boiler and filled it; that the steward had plugged his spare coffee-pot and filled it; that the harpooners had capped the sockets of their irons and filled them; that in fact everything was filled with sperm except the captain's trouser pockets, and those he kept free to thrust his hands into, as smug evidence of his complete satisfaction.

As this happy ship of good fortune bore down on the gloomy Pequod, the barbaric boom of enormous drums came from her forecastle. As she came closer still, a crowd of her men could be seen standing around her huge try-pots, which had been covered with the parchment-like poke, or stomach skin, of the black fish, and which roared loudly at every blow of the crew's clenched fists. On the quarter-deck the mates and harpooners were dancing with the olive-skinned girls who had run off with them from the Polynesian Isles, while three Long Island negroes, perched in a decorated boat hung high and firmly secured between the foremast and mainmast, led the riotous jig with glittering fiddle-bows of whale ivory. Meanwhile others of the crew were noisily busy tearing apart the brickwork of the try-works, from which the huge pots had been taken out. You would almost have thought they were pulling down the cursed Bastille, such wild cries they let out as the now useless brick and mortar went hurtling into the sea.

Lord and master of the whole scene, the captain stood upright on the ship's raised quarter-deck, where the entire joyful spectacle played out in full view before him, and seemed to have been staged solely for his own amusement.

And Ahab, he too was standing on his quarter-deck, shaggy and black, with a stubborn gloom; and as the two ships crossed each other's wakes — one all celebrations for things past, the other all forebodings for things to come — their two captains in themselves embodied the whole striking contrast of the scene.
"Come aboard, come aboard!" cried the gay Bachelor's commander, lifting a glass and a bottle in the air.
"Have you seen the White Whale?" gritted Ahab in reply.
"No; only heard of him; but don't believe in him at all," said the other good-humoredly. "Come aboard!"
"You are too damned jolly. Sail on. Have you lost any men?"

"Not enough to speak of — two islanders, that's all; but come aboard, old hearty, come along. I'll soon take that black from your brow. Come along, will you — merry's the play — a full ship and homeward-bound."

"How wondrously familiar a fool is!" muttered Ahab; then aloud: "You are a full ship and homeward-bound, you say; well, then, call me an empty ship, and outward-bound. So go your ways, and I will mine. Forward there! Set all sail, and keep her to the wind!"

So, while one ship ran cheerfully before the breeze, the other fought stubbornly against it, and the two vessels parted. The Pequod's crew watched the retreating Bachelor with grave, lingering looks, but the Bachelor's men, caught up in their lively celebration, paid no attention to their gaze. And as Ahab leaned over the taffrail and watched the homeward-bound ship, he took a small vial of sand from his pocket; then, looking from the ship to the vial, he seemed to be bringing two distant associations together, for that vial held Nantucket soundings.

chapters.title: Chapter 116 — The Dying Whale
paragraphs: It happens often enough in this life that when fortune's favorites sail close by us on the right side, we, though we were drooping before, catch something of their rushing breeze and joyfully feel our slack sails fill out. So it seemed with the Pequod. On the day after she met the cheerful Bachelor, whales were sighted and four were killed, one of them by Ahab.

It was far into the afternoon; and when all the spearings of the crimson fight were done, and, floating in the lovely sunset sea and sky, sun and whale both silently died together — then such sweetness and such plaintiveness, such wreathing prayers, curled up into that rosy air that it almost seemed as if, far over from the deep green convent valleys of the Manila isles, the Spanish land-breeze, wantonly turned sailor, had gone to sea freighted with these vesper hymns.

Soothed again, but only soothed to deeper gloom, Ahab, who had backed off from the whale, sat intently watching its final wanings from the now tranquil boat. For that strange spectacle observable in all sperm whales dying — the turning sunward of the head, and so expiring — that strange spectacle, seen on such a placid evening, somehow conveyed to Ahab a wondrousness unknown before.

"He turns and turns himself to it — how slowly, but how steadfastly, his homage-rendering and invoking brow, with his last dying motions. He too worships fire; most faithful, broad, baronial vassal of the sun! Oh, that these too-favoring eyes should see these too-favoring sights. Look! Here, far water-locked; beyond all hum of human weal or woe; in these most candid and impartial seas; where no rocks furnish tablets for traditions; where for long Chinese ages the billows have still rolled on speechless and unspoken to, like stars that shine upon the Niger's unknown source — here, too, life dies sunward full of faith; but see! No sooner dead than death whirls round the corpse, and it heads some other way.

"Oh, you dark Hindu half of nature, who have built your separate throne of drowned bones somewhere in the heart of these unverdured seas; you are an infidel, you queen, and too truly you speak to me in the wide-slaughtering Typhoon, and the hushed burial of its after-calm. Nor has this whale of yours turned his dying head sunward, and then gone round again, without a lesson to me.

"Oh, trebly hooped and welded hip of power! Oh, high aspiring, rainbowed jet! The one strives, the other jets, all in vain! In vain, oh whale, do you seek intercession with the all-quickening sun, that only calls forth life but does not give it again. Yet you, darker half, rock me with a prouder, if a darker faith. All your unnamable imminglings float beneath me here; I am buoyed by breaths of once living things, exhaled as air, but water now.

"Then hail, forever hail, O sea, in whose eternal tossing the wild bird finds its only rest. I was born of earth, yet nursed by the sea; though hill and valley mothered me, you rolling waves are my foster-brothers!"

chapters.title: Chapter 117 — The Whale Watch
paragraphs: The four whales killed that evening had died wide apart; one far to windward, one less distant to leeward, one ahead, one astern. These last three were brought alongside before nightfall; but the windward one could not be reached till morning; and the boat that had killed it lay by its side all night. And that boat was Ahab's.

The waif-pole, the pole planted to mark a dead whale, was thrust upright into the dead whale's spout-hole; and the lantern hanging from its top cast a troubled flickering glare upon the black, glossy back, and far out upon the midnight waves, which gently chafed the whale's broad flank, like soft surf upon a beach.

Ahab and all his boat's crew seemed asleep but the Parsee; who, crouching in the bow, sat watching the sharks that spectrally played round the whale and tapped the light cedar planks with their tails. A sound like the moaning of unforgiven ghosts of Gomorrah, in squadrons over Asphaltites (the Dead Sea), ran shuddering through the air.

Starting from his slumbers, Ahab found himself face to face with the Parsee; and hooped round by the gloom of the night, they seemed the last men in a flooded world. "I have dreamed it again," he said.
"The hearses? Haven't I told you, old man, that you can have neither hearse nor coffin?"
"And who that dies on the sea is ever hearsed?"

"But I said, old man, that before you could die on this voyage, two hearses must truly be seen by you on the sea; the first not made by mortal hands; and the visible wood of the last one must be grown in America."
"Aye, aye! A strange sight that, Parsee: a hearse and its plumes floating over the ocean with the waves for the pallbearers. Ha! Such a sight we shall not soon see."
"Believe it or not, you cannot die until it is seen, old man."
"And what was that saying about yourself?"
"Even if it comes to the last, I shall still go before you, your pilot."

"And when you are so gone before — if that ever happens — then before I can follow, you must still appear to me, to pilot me still? Was it not so? Well, then, if I believed all you say, oh my pilot, I have here two pledges that I shall yet slay Moby Dick and survive it."
"Take another pledge, old man," said the Parsee, as his eyes lit up like fireflies in the gloom — "Hemp only can kill you."
"The gallows, you mean. I am immortal then, on land and on sea," cried Ahab, with a laugh of derision. "Immortal on land and on sea!"
Once more both fell silent, as if they were one man. The gray dawn came, the sleeping crew got up from the bottom of the boat, and before noon the dead whale had been brought to the ship.

chapters.title: Chapter 118 — The Quadrant
paragraphs: The season for the Line, the equator, finally came close. Every day, whenever Ahab came up from his cabin and looked aloft, the watchful helmsman would make a show of handling his spokes, and the eager sailors would hurry to the braces and stand there with every eye fixed on the nailed doubloon, impatient for the order to point the ship's prow toward the equator. In due time the order came. It was nearly high noon, and Ahab, seated in the bow of his boat, hoisted high, was about to take his usual daily sighting of the sun to find his latitude.

Now, in that Japanese sea, the days in summer are floods of brilliance. That unblinkingly vivid Japanese sun seems the blazing focus of the glassy ocean's immeasurable burning-glass. The sky looks lacquered; there are no clouds; the horizon floats; and this nakedness of unrelieved radiance is like the unbearable splendors of God's throne. It was well that Ahab's quadrant, the instrument for measuring the sun's height, was fitted with colored glasses through which to sight that solar fire. So, swinging his seated body to the roll of the ship, and with his astrological-looking instrument to his eye, he held that posture for some moments to catch the exact instant when the sun should reach its precise meridian. Meanwhile, as his whole attention was absorbed, the Parsee was kneeling beneath him on the ship's deck, and with his face thrown up like Ahab's, was eyeing the same sun with him; only his eyelids half hooded his eyes, and his wild face was subdued to an earthly passionlessness. At length the desired observation was taken; and with his pencil on his ivory leg, Ahab soon calculated what his latitude must be at that precise instant. Then, falling into a moment's reverie, he looked up again toward the sun and murmured to himself: "You sea-mark! You high and mighty Pilot! You tell me truly where I am now — but can you cast the least hint of where I shall be? Or can you tell where some other thing besides me is living this moment? Where is Moby Dick? This instant you must be eyeing him. These eyes of mine look into the very eye that is even now beholding him; aye, and into the eye that is even now equally beholding the objects on the unknown, far side of you, you sun!"

Then, gazing at his quadrant and handling one after another its many cabalistic contrivances, he pondered again, and muttered: "Foolish toy! Babies' plaything of haughty Admirals, and Commodores, and Captains; the world brags of you, of your cunning and might; but what, after all, can you do, except tell the poor, pitiful point where you yourself happen to be on this wide planet, and the hand that holds you — no! not one jot more! You cannot tell where one drop of water or one grain of sand will be tomorrow noon; and yet with your impotence you insult the sun! Science! Curse you, you vain toy; and cursed be all the things that cast man's eyes aloft to that heaven whose live vividness only scorches him, as these old eyes are even now scorched with your light, O sun! By nature, the glances of man's eyes are level with this earth's horizon; not shot from the crown of his head, as if God had meant him to gaze on his firmament. Curse you, you quadrant!" dashing it to the deck. "No longer will I guide my earthly way by you; the level ship's compass, and the level dead-reckoning, by log and by line — it is these that shall guide me, and show me my place on the sea. Aye," stepping down from the boat to the deck, "thus I trample on you, you paltry thing that feebly points on high; thus I split and destroy you!"

As the frantic old man thus spoke and thus trampled with his live and dead feet, a sneering triumph that seemed meant for Ahab, and a fatalistic despair that seemed meant for himself — these passed over the mute, motionless Parsee's face. Unobserved he rose and glided away; while, awestruck by the aspect of their commander, the sailors clustered together on the forecastle, until Ahab, pacing the deck in agitation, shouted out: "To the braces! Up helm! — square in!"

In an instant the yards swung around, and as the ship half-spun on her heel, her three graceful masts, firmly seated and standing upright on her long ribbed hull, looked like the three Horatii pirouetting on a single horse strong enough to carry them all.
Standing between the knightheads (the timbers on either side of the bowsprit), Starbuck watched the Pequod's tumultuous way, and Ahab's also, as he went lurching along the deck.

"I have sat by a thick coal fire and watched it glowing, full of its tormented, flaming life, and I have seen it fade at last, down, down, to the dumbest dust. Old man of the oceans! Of all this fiery life of yours, what will finally be left but one little heap of ashes!"

"Aye," cried Stubb, "but sea-coal ashes — mind you that, Mr. Starbuck — sea-coal, not your common charcoal. Well, well; I heard Ahab mutter, 'Here someone thrusts these cards into these old hands of mine; swears that I must play them, and no others.' And damn me, Ahab, but you act right; live in the game, and die in it!"

chapters.title: Chapter 119 — The Candles
paragraphs: It is the warmest climates that nurse the cruelest fangs: the tiger of Bengal crouches in spiced groves of never-fading green. It is the most dazzling skies that carry the deadliest thunders in their basket: gorgeous Cuba knows tornadoes that never swept tame northern lands. So, too, it is that in these resplendent Japanese seas the mariner meets the most terrible of all storms, the Typhoon. It will sometimes burst out of that cloudless sky like a bomb exploding on a dazed and sleepy town.

Toward evening of that day, the Pequod had her canvas torn away and, bare-poled, was left to fight a typhoon which had struck her directly ahead. When darkness came on, sky and sea roared and split with the thunder and blazed with the lightning that showed the disabled masts fluttering here and there with the rags which the first fury of the storm had left for its after-sport.

Holding on to a shroud, Starbuck was standing on the quarter-deck, glancing aloft at every flash of lightning to see what further disaster might have befallen the intricate rigging there, while Stubb and Flask were directing the men in hoisting the boats higher and lashing them more firmly. But all their efforts seemed in vain. Though hoisted to the very top of the cranes, the windward quarter boat (Ahab's) did not escape. A great rolling sea, dashing high against the reeling ship's tall, teetering side, stove in the boat's bottom at the stern, and left it again, dripping through like a sieve.

"Bad work, bad work, Mr. Starbuck," said Stubb, looking at the wreck, "but the sea will have its way. Stubb, for one, can't fight it. You see, Mr. Starbuck, a wave has such a great long start before it leaps — all round the world it runs, and then comes the spring! But as for me, all the start I have to meet it is just across the deck here. But never mind; it's all in fun, so the old song says —" (Sings.)
Oh! jolly is the gale, / And a joker is the whale, / A-flourishing his tail — / Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
The scud all a-flying, / That's his flip only foaming; / When he stirs in the spicing — / Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
Thunder splits the ships, / But he only smacks his lips, / A-tasting of this flip — / Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
"Enough, Stubb," cried Starbuck, "let the Typhoon sing, and strike his harp here in our rigging; but if you are a brave man you will hold your peace."

"But I'm not a brave man; I never said I was a brave man; I'm a coward, and I sing to keep my spirits up. And I'll tell you how it is, Mr. Starbuck: the only way to stop my singing in this world is to cut my throat. And when that's done, ten to one I'll sing you the doxology to wind up with."
"Madman! Look through my eyes if you have none of your own."
"What! How can you see better on a dark night than anybody else, never mind how foolish?"
