"Here!" cried Starbuck, seizing Stubb by the shoulder and pointing his hand toward the weather bow. "Don't you see that the gale comes from the east, the very course Ahab is to run for Moby Dick? The very course he swung to at noon today? Now look at his boat there; where is it stove? In the stern-sheets, man, where he always stands — his stand-point is stove, man! Now jump overboard and sing away, if you must!"
"I don't half understand you; what's in the wind?"

"Yes, yes, round the Cape of Good Hope is the shortest way to Nantucket," mused Starbuck suddenly, paying no attention to Stubb's question. "This gale that now hammers at us to stave us in — we can turn it into a fair wind that will drive us toward home. Over there, to windward, all is blackness of doom; but to leeward, homeward — I see it lightens up there; but not with the lightning."
Just then, in one of the spells of deep darkness that followed the flashes, a voice was heard beside him, and almost at the same moment a volley of thunderclaps rolled overhead.
"Who's there?"
"Old Thunder!" said Ahab, groping his way along the bulwarks to his pivot-hole; but suddenly finding his path made plain by angled lances of fire.

Now, just as the lightning rod on a spire ashore is meant to carry the dangerous fluid off into the soil, so the similar rod that some ships at sea carry to each mast is meant to conduct it into the water. But this conductor must reach down to a considerable depth, so that its end may avoid all contact with the hull; and, moreover, if it were kept towing there all the time, it would be liable to many mishaps, besides interfering more than a little with some of the rigging and more or less slowing the vessel's way through the water. Because of all this, the lower parts of a ship's lightning-rods are not always overboard; they are generally made in long slender links, so that they can more readily be hauled up into the chains (the ledges outside the hull where the shrouds are fastened), or thrown down into the sea, as occasion requires.

"The rods! The rods!" cried Starbuck to the crew, suddenly warned to vigilance by the vivid lightning that had just been darting like torches to light Ahab to his post. "Are they overboard? Drop them over, fore and aft. Quick!"

"Stop!" cried Ahab; "let's have fair play here, though we are the weaker side. Yet I'll contribute to raise rods on the Himalayas and Andes, that all the world may be secured; but away with privileges! Let them be, sir."
"Look aloft!" cried Starbuck. "The corpusants! The corpusants!"

The tips of all the yardarms were lit with a pale fire — the corpusants, or St. Elmo's fire. Each of the three tall masts, touched at every three-pronged end of its lightning-rod with three tapering white flames, burned silently in that sulfurous air like three gigantic wax candles before an altar.

"Blast the boat! Let it go!" cried Stubb at this instant, as a washing sea heaved up under his own little craft, so that its gunwale violently jammed his hand as he was passing a lashing. "Blast it!" But slipping backward on the deck, his uplifted eyes caught the flames; and immediately shifting his tone, he cried: "The corpusants have mercy on us all!"

To sailors, oaths are everyday words; they will swear in the trance of the calm and in the teeth of the tempest; they will hurl curses from the topsail-yard-arms when most they teeter over a seething sea; but in all my voyaging, seldom have I heard a common oath when God's burning finger has been laid on the ship — when His Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin — the writing on Belshazzar's wall — has been woven into the shrouds and the cordage.

While this pale fire burned aloft, the spellbound crew said little. They stood in one thick cluster on the forecastle, all their eyes gleaming in that pale phosphorescence like a distant constellation of stars. Outlined against the ghostly light, the gigantic jet-black negro, Daggoo, loomed up to three times his real height and seemed to be the black cloud the thunder had come from. Tashtego's parted lips showed his shark-white teeth, which gleamed strangely as if they too had been tipped with corpusants; and, lit up by the unnatural light, Queequeg's tattoos burned on his body like Satanic blue flames.

At last the whole scene faded along with the pale fire aloft, and once more the Pequod and every soul on her decks were wrapped in a pall. A moment or two went by; then Starbuck, going forward, bumped into someone. It was Stubb. "What do you think now, man? I heard your cry; it wasn't the same as in the song."

"No, no, it wasn't; I said the corpusants have mercy on us all; and I hope they will, still. But do they only have mercy on long faces? Have they no sympathy for a laugh? And look, Mr. Starbuck — but it's too dark to look. Hear me, then: I take that mast-head flame we saw for a sign of good luck; for those masts are rooted in a hold that is going to be chock-full of sperm-oil, d'you see; and so, all that sperm will work up into the masts, like sap in a tree. Yes, our three masts will yet be as three sperm candles — that's the good promise we saw."

At that moment Starbuck caught sight of Stubb's face slowly beginning to glimmer into view. Glancing upward, he cried: "See! See!" And once more the high tapering flames were beheld with what seemed redoubled otherworldliness in their pallor.
"The corpusants have mercy on us all," cried Stubb again.

At the foot of the mainmast, right under the doubloon and the flame, the Parsee knelt in front of Ahab, but with his head bowed away from him. Close by, a number of seamen who had just been securing a spar up in the arched, overhanging rigging were caught and held by the glare; they now huddled together and hung there like a cluster of numbed wasps from a drooping orchard twig. Others stood rooted to the deck in various spellbound poses, like the standing, stepping or running skeletons at Herculaneum; but every eye was turned upward.

"Aye, aye, men!" cried Ahab. "Look up at it; mark it well; the white flame only lights the way to the White Whale! Hand me those mainmast links there; I want to feel this pulse, and let mine beat against it — blood against fire! So."

Then, turning — with the last link still gripped in his left hand — he set his foot on the Parsee, and with his eyes fixed upward and his right arm flung high, he stood upright before the towering three-pronged trinity of flames.

"Oh! You clear spirit of clear fire, whom I once worshipped on these seas as a Persian, until in the sacramental act I was so burned by you that to this hour I bear the scar — I know you now, you clear spirit, and I know now that the right way to worship you is defiance. You will be kind to neither love nor reverence; and even for hate you can only kill; and all are killed. It is no fearless fool who faces you now. I acknowledge your speechless, placeless power; but to the last gasp of my earthquake life I will dispute its unconditional, unintegral mastery in me. In the midst of the personified impersonal, a personality stands here. Though only a point at best — wherever I came from, wherever I go — yet while I live on earth, the queenly personality lives in me and feels her royal rights. But war is pain, and hate is woe. Come in your lowest form of love, and I will kneel and kiss you; but at your highest, come as mere supernal power, and though you launch navies of fully laden worlds, there is something in here that still remains indifferent. Oh, you clear spirit, you made me out of your fire, and like a true child of fire, I breathe it back to you."
[Sudden, repeated flashes of lightning; the nine flames shoot up lengthwise to three times their former height; Ahab, like the rest, shuts his eyes, pressing his right hand hard over them.]

"I acknowledge your speechless, placeless power; didn't I say so? Nor was it wrung out of me; nor do I drop these links now. You can blind; but then I can grope. You can consume; but then I can be ashes. Take the homage of these poor eyes, and shutter-hands. I would not take it. The lightning flashes through my skull; my eyeballs ache and ache; my whole beaten brain seems beheaded, and rolling on some stunning ground. Oh, oh! Blindfolded, I will still talk to you. Light though you are, you leap out of darkness; but I am darkness leaping out of light, leaping out of you! The javelins stop; open, eyes; do you see, or not? There burn the flames! Oh, you magnanimous one! Now I do glory in my genealogy. But you are only my fiery father; my sweet mother I do not know. Oh, cruel! What have you done with her? There lies my puzzle; but yours is greater. You do not know how you came to be, and so you call yourself unbegotten; you certainly do not know your beginning, and so you call yourself unbegun. I know something of myself that you do not know of yourself, oh you omnipotent. There is some unsuffusing thing beyond you, you clear spirit, to whom all your eternity is only time, all your creativeness mechanical. Through you, your flaming self, my scorched eyes dimly see it. Oh, you foundling fire, you hermit immemorial, you too have your incommunicable riddle, your unshared grief. Here again, with haughty agony, I read my sire. Leap! Leap up, and lick the sky! I leap with you; I burn with you; I long to be welded with you; defiantly I worship you!"
"The boat! The boat!" cried Starbuck, "look at your boat, old man!"

Ahab's harpoon, the one forged in Perth's fire, was still lashed firmly in its conspicuous crotch, so that it stuck out beyond the bow of his whaleboat. But the sea that had stove in the boat's bottom had knocked off the loose leather sheath, and from the sharp steel barb there now streamed a level flame of pale, forked fire. As the silent harpoon burned there like a serpent's tongue, Starbuck seized Ahab by the arm. "God, God is against you, old man; hold back! This is an evil voyage! Badly begun, badly continued. Let me square the yards while we still can, old man, and make a fair wind of it for home, and go on a better voyage than this."

Hearing Starbuck, the panic-stricken crew ran to the braces at once — though not a single sail was left aloft. For the moment they seemed to share all the horrified mate's thoughts, and they raised a half-mutinous shout. But Ahab flung the rattling lightning links down on the deck, snatched up the burning harpoon, and waved it among them like a torch, swearing he would run it through the first sailor who so much as cast loose a rope's end. Petrified by his look, and shrinking still more from the fiery dart in his hand, the men fell back in dismay, and Ahab spoke again:

"Every oath you swore to hunt the White Whale binds you as tightly as mine binds me; and heart, soul and body, lungs and life, old Ahab is bound. And so that you may know what tune this heart beats to — look here: this is how I blow out the last fear!" And with a single blast of breath he put out the flame.

As in the hurricane that sweeps the plain, men flee the neighborhood of some lone, gigantic elm, whose very height and strength only make it all the more unsafe, because all the more a target for thunderbolts; so at those last words of Ahab's, many of the sailors did run from him in a terror of dismay.

chapters.title: Chapter 120 — The Deck Towards the End of the First Night Watch
paragraphs: Ahab standing by the helm. Starbuck approaching him.
"We have to send down the main-topsail yard, sir. The band is working loose, and half the strands of the lee lift have parted. Should I strike it, sir?"
"Strike nothing; lash it. If I had sky-sail poles, I'd sway them up now."
"Sir! — in God's name! — sir?"
"Well."
"The anchors are working, sir. Shall I get them inboard?"

"Strike nothing and stir nothing, but lash everything down. The wind is rising, but it hasn't reached my tablelands yet. Quick, see to it. — By masts and keels! He takes me for the hunchbacked skipper of some little coasting smack. Send down my main-topsail yard! Ho, you gluepots! The loftiest trucks were made for the wildest winds, and this brain-truck of mine is sailing now among the scudding clouds. Should I strike that? Oh, only cowards send down their brain-trucks in a storm. What a hullabaloo up there! I'd almost take it for the sublime, if I didn't know that colic is a noisy illness. Oh, take some medicine, take some medicine!"

chapters.title: Chapter 121 — Midnight.—The Forecastle Bulwarks
paragraphs: Stubb and Flask mounted on them, and passing additional lashings over the anchors hanging there.

"No, Stubb; you can pound that knot there as much as you like, but you'll never pound into me what you were just saying. And how long is it since you said exactly the opposite? Didn't you once say that any ship Ahab sails in ought to pay something extra on its insurance, just as if it were loaded with powder barrels aft and boxes of lucifer matches forward? Hold on, now; didn't you say that?"

"Well, suppose I did? What then? I've partly changed my flesh since that time; why not my mind? Besides, supposing we really are loaded with powder barrels aft and lucifer matches forward — how the devil could the matches catch fire in this drenching spray here? Why, my little man, you have pretty red hair, but you couldn't catch fire now. Shake yourself; you're Aquarius, the Water-bearer, Flask; a man might fill pitchers at your coat collar. Don't you see, then, that for these extra risks the Marine Insurance companies have extra guarantees? Here are hydrants, Flask. But listen again, and I'll answer you the other thing. First take your leg off the crown of the anchor here, though, so I can pass the rope; now listen. What's the mighty difference between holding a mast's lightning-rod in the storm and standing close by a mast that hasn't got any lightning-rod at all in a storm? Don't you see, you timber-head, that no harm can come to the holder of the rod unless the mast is struck first? What are you talking about, then? Not one ship in a hundred carries rods, and Ahab — yes, man, and all of us — were in no more danger then, in my poor opinion, than all the crews in ten thousand ships now sailing the seas. Why, you King-Post, you, I suppose you would have every man in the world go about with a small lightning-rod running up the corner of his hat, like a militia officer's skewered feather, and trailing behind like his sash. Why don't you be sensible, Flask? It's easy to be sensible; why don't you, then? Any man with half an eye can be sensible."
"I don't know that, Stubb. You sometimes find it rather hard."

"Yes, when a fellow's soaked through, it's hard to be sensible, that's a fact. And I'm just about drenched by this spray. Never mind; catch the turn there and pass it. It seems to me we're lashing these anchors down now as if they were never going to be used again. Tying up these two anchors here, Flask, is like tying a man's hands behind his back. And what big, generous hands they are, to be sure. These are your iron fists, eh? And what a grip they have, too! I wonder, Flask, whether the world is anchored anywhere; if she is, though, she swings on an uncommonly long cable. There, hammer that knot down, and we're finished. There; next to setting foot on land, landing on deck is the most satisfying thing. Say, just wring out my jacket tails for me, will you? Thanks. They laugh at long-togs so, Flask; but it seems to me a long-tailed coat ought always to be worn in every storm at sea. The tails, tapering down like that, carry the water off, you see. Same with cocked hats; the cocks make gutters at the gable-ends, Flask. No more monkey-jackets and tarpaulin hats for me; I must climb into a swallow-tail coat and jam on a beaver hat; there. Hallo! Whew! There goes my tarpaulin overboard! Lord, Lord, that the winds that come from heaven should have such bad manners! This is a nasty night, lad."

chapters.title: Chapter 122 — Midnight Aloft.—Thunder and Lightning
paragraphs: The main-top-sail yard. Tashtego passing new lashings around it.
"Um, um, um. Stop that thunder! Plenty too much thunder up here. What's the use of thunder? Um, um, um. We don't want thunder; we want rum; give us a glass of rum. Um, um, um!"

chapters.title: Chapter 123 — The Musket
paragraphs: During the most violent shocks of the Typhoon, the man at the Pequod's jawbone tiller had several times been flung reeling to the deck by its spasmodic motions, even though preventer tackles had been attached to it; for they were kept slack, because some play in the tiller was indispensable.

In a severe gale like this, while the ship is only a shuttlecock tossed by the blast, it is by no means uncommon to see the needles in the compasses, at intervals, go round and round. It was so with the Pequod's; at almost every shock the helmsman had noticed the whirling speed with which they spun round on the cards; it is a sight that hardly anyone can watch without some sort of unaccustomed emotion.

Some hours after midnight, the Typhoon abated so much that through the strenuous efforts of Starbuck and Stubb — one engaged forward and the other aft — the shattered remnants of the jib and fore and main-topsails were cut adrift from the spars, and went whirling away to leeward like the feathers of an albatross, which are sometimes cast to the winds when that storm-tossed bird is on the wing.

The three corresponding new sails were now bent and reefed, and a storm-trysail was set farther aft, so that the ship soon went through the water with some precision again; and the course — for the present, east-southeast — which he was to steer, if practicable, was once more given to the helmsman. For during the violence of the gale he had steered only according to its shifts. But as he was now bringing the ship as near her course as possible, watching the compass meanwhile — look! a good sign! — the wind seemed to be coming round astern; yes, the foul breeze had turned fair!

Instantly the yards were squared, to the lively song of "Ho! the fair wind! oh-ye-ho, cheerly men!" — the crew singing for joy that so promising an event should so soon have proved false the evil omens that preceded it.

In compliance with the standing order of his commander — to report immediately, at any of the twenty-four hours, any decided change in the affairs of the deck — Starbuck had no sooner trimmed the yards to the breeze, however reluctantly and gloomily, than he mechanically went below to inform Captain Ahab of the circumstance.

Before knocking at his stateroom, he involuntarily paused in front of it for a moment. The cabin lamp — taking long swings this way and that — was burning fitfully, and casting fitful shadows on the old man's bolted door, a thin one, with fixed blinds set in it in place of upper panels. The isolated, underground seclusion of the cabin made a certain humming silence reign there, though it was hooped round by all the roar of the elements. The loaded muskets in the rack were shiningly revealed, standing upright against the forward bulkhead. Starbuck was an honest, upright man; but out of Starbuck's heart, at the instant he saw the muskets, there strangely arose an evil thought — but so blended with its neutral or good accompaniments that for the moment he hardly recognized it for what it was.

"He would have shot me once," he murmured. "Yes, there's the very musket he pointed at me — that one with the studded stock. Let me touch it — lift it. Strange, that I, who have handled so many deadly lances, strange that I should shake so now. Loaded? I must see. Yes, yes; and powder in the pan — that's not good. Better spill it? Wait. I'll cure myself of this. I'll hold the musket boldly while I think. I come to report a fair wind to him. But fair how? Fair for death and doom — that's fair for Moby Dick. It's a fair wind that's only fair for that accursed fish. The very barrel he pointed at me! — the very one; this one — I hold it here; he would have killed me with the very thing I'm handling now. Yes, and he would gladly kill all his crew. Doesn't he say he will not strike his spars to any gale? Hasn't he smashed his heavenly quadrant? And in these same dangerous seas, doesn't he grope his way by mere dead reckoning of the error-ridden log? And in this very Typhoon, didn't he swear that he would have no lightning-rods? But shall this crazed old man be meekly allowed to drag a whole ship's company down to doom with him? Yes, it would make him the willful murderer of thirty men and more, if this ship comes to any deadly harm; and my soul swears this ship will come to deadly harm if Ahab has his way. If, then, he were this instant — put aside, that crime would not be his. Ha! Is he muttering in his sleep? Yes, just there — in there, he's sleeping. Sleeping? Yes, but still alive, and soon awake again. I can't stand against you, then, old man. Not reasoning, not protest, not pleading will you listen to; you scorn all this. Flat obedience to your own flat commands — that is all you breathe. Yes, and you say the men have vowed your vow; you say all of us are Ahabs. Great God forbid! But is there no other way? No lawful way? Make him a prisoner to be taken home? What! Hope to wrest this old man's living power from his own living hands? Only a fool would try it. Say he were even tied hand and foot; knotted all over with ropes and hawsers; chained down to ring-bolts on this cabin floor; he would be more hideous than a caged tiger then. I could not endure the sight; could not possibly escape his howlings; all comfort, sleep itself, priceless reason would leave me on the long, intolerable voyage. What, then, remains? The land is hundreds of leagues away, and locked-up Japan the nearest. I stand alone here on an open sea, with two oceans and a whole continent between me and the law. Yes, yes, that's how it is. Is heaven a murderer when its lightning strikes a would-be murderer in his bed, burning sheets and skin together like tinder? And would I be a murderer, then, if —" and slowly, stealthily, half looking sideways, he placed the loaded musket's end against the door.

"On this level, Ahab's hammock swings inside; his head this way. A touch, and Starbuck may survive to hug his wife and child again. Oh Mary! Mary! — boy! boy! boy! But if I don't wake you to death, old man, who can tell to what unsounded depths Starbuck's body may sink a week from today, with all the crew! Great God, where are You? Shall I? Shall I? — The wind has gone down and shifted, sir; the fore and main topsails are reefed and set; she heads her course."
"Stern all! Oh Moby Dick, I clutch your heart at last!"
These were the sounds that now came hurtling out of the old man's tormented sleep, as if Starbuck's voice had made the long-mute dream speak.

The musket, still leveled, shook against the panel like a drunkard's arm; Starbuck seemed to be wrestling with an angel. But he turned away from the door, put the death-tube back in its rack, and left.
"He's too sound asleep, Mr. Stubb; go down, and wake him, and tell him. I must see to the deck here. You know what to say."

chapters.title: Chapter 124 — The Needle
paragraphs: The next morning the sea, not yet calmed, rolled in long, slow swells of enormous bulk, and, surging along in the Pequod's gurgling wake, pushed her forward like the outspread palms of giants. The strong, steady breeze blew so abundantly that sky and air seemed like vast billowing sails; the whole world boomed along before the wind. Muffled in the full morning light, the sun could not be seen, and was known only by the spread-out intensity of the place where he stood, where his bayonet rays moved forward in stacks. Heraldic splendors, as of crowned Babylonian kings and queens, reigned over everything. The sea was like a crucible of molten gold, bubbling and leaping with light and heat.

Keeping a spellbound silence for a long time, Ahab stood apart. Every time the teetering ship dipped her bowsprit low, he turned to look at the bright rays of the sun stretching out ahead; and when she sank deep by the stern, he turned around and saw where the sun stood behind them, and how the same yellow rays were blending with his unswerving wake.

"Ha, ha, my ship! You might well be taken now for the sea-chariot of the sun. Ho, ho! All you nations before my prow, I bring the sun to you! Yoke on the further billows; hallo! A tandem, I drive the sea!"
But, suddenly pulled up short by some contrary thought, he hurried to the helm and asked hoarsely which way the ship was heading.
"East-southeast, sir," said the frightened steersman.
"You lie!" striking him with his clenched fist. "Heading east at this hour in the morning, and the sun astern?"
At this everyone was dumbfounded; for somehow the phenomenon Ahab had just noticed had escaped everyone else — though its very glaring obviousness must have been the reason.

Thrusting his head halfway into the binnacle, Ahab caught one glimpse of the compasses; his uplifted arm slowly fell; for a moment he almost seemed to stagger. Standing behind him, Starbuck looked, and — behold! — the two compasses pointed east, and the Pequod was just as unerringly going west.

But before the first wild alarm could get abroad among the crew, the old man with a rigid laugh exclaimed: "I have it! It has happened before. Mr. Starbuck, last night's thunder turned our compasses — that's all. You've heard of such a thing before now, I take it."
"Aye; but it has never happened to me before, sir," said the pale mate gloomily.

Here it must be said that accidents like this have occurred in more than one case to ships in violent storms. The magnetic energy, as developed in the mariner's needle, is, as everyone knows, essentially one with the electricity seen in the heavens; so it is not much to be wondered at that such things should happen. In instances where the lightning has actually struck the vessel, so as to knock down some of the spars and rigging, the effect on the needle has at times been still more fatal: all its loadstone power has been destroyed, so that the formerly magnetic steel was of no more use than an old wife's knitting needle. But in either case, the needle never again recovers by itself the original power thus marred or lost; and if the binnacle compasses are affected, the same fate reaches all the others that may be in the ship, even if the lowest one were set into the kelson, the timber running along the keel inside the hold.

Standing deliberately in front of the binnacle and eyeing the turned-around compasses, the old man now took the exact bearing of the sun with the edge of his outstretched hand. Satisfied that the needles were exactly reversed, he shouted orders for the ship's course to be changed to match. The yards were put hard up, and once again the Pequod drove her undaunted bows into the opposing wind, for the supposedly fair one had only been fooling her.

Meanwhile, whatever his own secret thoughts were, Starbuck said nothing, but quietly issued all the necessary orders; while Stubb and Flask — who in some small degree seemed then to be sharing his feelings — likewise went along without a murmur. As for the men, though some of them rumbled low, their fear of Ahab was greater than their fear of Fate. But as ever before, the pagan harpooners remained almost wholly unimpressed; or if impressed, it was only with a certain magnetism shot into their kindred hearts from inflexible Ahab's.

For a while the old man paced the deck, lost in rolling daydreams. But happening to slip with his ivory heel, he caught sight of the crushed copper sight-tubes of the quadrant he had smashed on the deck the day before.

"You poor, proud heaven-gazer and sun's pilot! Yesterday I wrecked you, and today the compasses would gladly have wrecked me. So, so. But Ahab is lord over the level loadstone yet. Mr. Starbuck — a lance without a pole; a top-maul, and the smallest of the sail-maker's needles. Quick!"

Contributing, perhaps, to the impulse behind what he was now about to do were certain prudent motives, whose object might have been to revive the spirits of his crew by a stroke of his subtle skill, in a matter so wondrous as that of the inverted compasses. Besides, the old man well knew that to steer by reversed needles, though clumsily workable, was not a thing superstitious sailors would let pass without some shuddering and forebodings of evil.

"Men," he said, turning steadily to face the crew as the mate handed him the things he had asked for, "my men, the thunder has turned old Ahab's needles; but from this bit of steel Ahab can make one of his own that will point as true as any."
As he said this, the sailors exchanged shamefaced glances of slavish wonder, and waited with fascinated eyes for whatever magic might come next. But Starbuck looked away.

With a blow from the top-maul Ahab knocked off the steel head of the lance, and then, handing the mate the long iron rod that remained, told him to hold it upright without letting it touch the deck. Then, after repeatedly striking the upper end of this iron rod with the maul, he placed the blunted needle endwise on top of it and hammered that, less strongly, several times, the mate still holding the rod as before. Then, going through some small strange motions with it — whether necessary to the magnetizing of the steel, or merely meant to increase the awe of the crew, is uncertain — he called for linen thread; and moving to the binnacle, he slipped out the two reversed needles there and hung the sail-needle horizontally by its middle over one of the compass-cards. At first the steel went round and round, quivering and vibrating at either end; but at last it settled into its place, and Ahab, who had been intently watching for this result, stepped openly back from the binnacle and, pointing his outstretched arm toward it, exclaimed: "Look for yourselves, and see if Ahab is not lord of the level loadstone! The sun is east, and that compass swears it!"
One after another they peered in — for only their own eyes could convince men as ignorant as they were — and one after another they crept away.
Then you could see Ahab in all his fatal pride, in those fiery eyes full of scorn and triumph.

chapters.title: Chapter 125 — The Log and Line
paragraphs: Though the fated Pequod had now been afloat so long on this voyage, the log and line — a wooden float paid out astern from a reel on a line, to measure the ship's speed — had very seldom been used. Owing to a confident reliance on other means of determining the vessel's position, some merchantmen, and many whalemen, especially when cruising, wholly neglect to heave the log; though at the same time, and often more for form's sake than anything else, they regularly put down on the customary slate the course steered by the ship, as well as the presumed average rate of progress every hour. It had been so with the Pequod. The wooden reel and the angular log attached to it hung, long untouched, just beneath the railing of the after bulwarks. Rain and spray had dampened it; sun and wind had warped it; all the elements had combined to rot a thing that hung so idly. But, heedless of all this, his mood seized Ahab as he happened to glance at the reel, not many hours after the magnet scene; and he remembered that his quadrant was no more, and recalled his frantic oath about the level log and line. The ship was sailing with a plunging motion; astern, the billows rolled in riots.
"Forward, there! Heave the log!"
Two seamen came. The golden-hued Tahitian and the grizzled Manxman. "Take the reel, one of you; I'll heave."
They went toward the far end of the stern, on the ship's lee side, where the deck, tilted by the slanting force of the wind, was now almost dipping into the creamy sea that rushed past alongside.

The Manxman took the reel and held it up high by the handles sticking out at each end of the spindle the spool of line turned on; he stood like that, with the angular log hanging down, until Ahab came up to him.

Ahab stood in front of him and was lightly unwinding some thirty or forty turns to make a preliminary hand-coil for tossing overboard, when the old Manxman, who was watching both him and the line intently, ventured to speak.
"Sir, I mistrust it; this line looks far gone. Long heat and wet have spoiled it."
"It will hold, old gentleman. Long heat and wet — have they spoiled you? You seem to hold. Or, truer perhaps, life holds you; not you it."
"I hold the spool, sir. But just as my captain says. With these gray hairs of mine, it's not worth while disputing, especially with a superior who'll never confess."
"What's that? There now's a patched professor in Queen Nature's granite-founded College; but I think he's too subservient. Where were you born?"
"In the little rocky Isle of Man, sir."
"Excellent! You've hit the world by that."
"I don't know, sir, but I was born there."

"In the Isle of Man, eh? Well, taken the other way, it's good. Here's a man from Man; a man born in once-independent Man, and now unmanned of Man; which is sucked in — by what? Up with the reel! In the end the dead, blind wall butts every questioning head. Up with it! There."

The log was heaved. The loose coils rapidly straightened out in a long dragging line astern, and then instantly the reel began to whirl. In turn, as the log was jerkingly raised and lowered by the rolling waves, its towing resistance caused the old reelman to stagger strangely.
"Hold hard!"
Snap! The line, strained too far, sagged down in a single long loop; the tugging log was gone.

"I smash the quadrant, the thunder reverses the needles, and now the mad sea snaps the log-line. But Ahab can mend everything. Haul in here, Tahitian; reel up, Manxman. And listen: get the carpenter to make another log, and you mend the line. See to it."

"There he goes now; to him nothing has happened; but to me it feels as if the skewer is working loose from the middle of the world. Haul in, haul in, Tahitian! These lines go out whole and whirling, and come back broken and dragging slow. Ha, Pip? Come to help, eh, Pip?"

"Pip? Who are you calling Pip? Pip jumped from the whale-boat. Pip's missing. Let's see now if you haven't fished him up here, fisherman. It drags hard; I guess he's holding on. Jerk him, Tahiti! Jerk him off; we haul in no cowards here. Ho! There's his arm just breaking water. A hatchet! A hatchet! Cut it off — we haul in no cowards here. Captain Ahab! Sir, sir! Here's Pip, trying to get on board again."
"Peace, you crazy loon," cried the Manxman, seizing him by the arm. "Away from the quarter-deck!"
"The greater idiot always scolds the lesser," muttered Ahab, advancing. "Hands off that holiness! Where did you say Pip was, boy?"
"Astern there, sir, astern! Look! Look!"
"And who are you, boy? I don't see my reflection in the vacant pupils of your eyes. Oh God! That man should be a thing for immortal souls to sieve through! Who are you, boy?"

"Bell-boy, sir; ship's crier; ding, dong, ding! Pip! Pip! Pip! One hundred pounds of clay reward for Pip; five feet high — looks cowardly — quickest known by that! Ding, dong, ding! Who's seen Pip the coward?"

"There can be no hearts above the snow-line. Oh, you frozen heavens! Look down here. You begot this luckless child, and have abandoned him, you creative libertines. Here, boy; Ahab's cabin shall be Pip's home henceforth, while Ahab lives. You touch my inmost center, boy; you are tied to me by cords woven of my heart-strings. Come, let's go down."

"What's this? Here's velvet shark-skin," gazing intently at Ahab's hand and feeling it. "Ah, now, if poor Pip had only felt so kind a thing as this, maybe he'd never have been lost! This seems to me, sir, like a man-rope, something weak souls can hold on to. Oh, sir, let old Perth come now and rivet these two hands together, the black one with the white, for I won't let this go."

"Oh, boy, nor will I let go of you, unless by holding on I should drag you to worse horrors than are here. Come, then, to my cabin. Look, you believers in gods all goodness and in man all ill — look, you! See the omniscient gods oblivious of suffering man; and man, though idiotic and not knowing what he does, yet full of the sweet things of love and gratitude. Come! I feel prouder leading you by your black hand than if I grasped an Emperor's!"

"There go two daft ones now," muttered the old Manxman. "One daft with strength, the other daft with weakness. But here's the end of the rotten line — all dripping, too. Mend it, eh? I think we had best have a new line altogether. I'll see Mr. Stubb about it."

chapters.title: Chapter 126 — The Life-Buoy
paragraphs: Steering now southeastward by Ahab's leveled steel, and with her progress determined solely by Ahab's level log and line, the Pequod held on her path toward the Equator. Making so long a passage through such unfrequented waters, sighting no ships, and before long pushed sideways by unvarying trade winds over monotonously mild waves — all these seemed the strange calm things that come before some riotous and desperate scene.

At last, as the ship neared the outskirts, so to speak, of the Equatorial fishing-ground, and was sailing past a cluster of rocky islets in the deep darkness before dawn, the watch — then headed by Flask — was startled by a cry so plaintively wild and unearthly — like the half-formed wailing of the ghosts of all Herod's murdered Innocents — that every one of them started out of his daydreams, and for some moments they stood, or sat, or leaned, all listening as if transfixed, like the carved Roman slave, for as long as that wild cry could still be heard. The Christian or civilized part of the crew said it was mermaids, and shuddered; but the pagan harpooners were not frightened. Yet the gray Manxman — the oldest sailor of them all — declared that the wild, thrilling sounds they heard were the voices of men newly drowned in the sea.

Ahab, below in his hammock, heard nothing about this until gray dawn, when he came on deck. Then Flask told him the story, not without hinting at dark meanings. He gave a hollow laugh and explained the wonder like this.

Those rocky islands the ship had passed were home to great numbers of seals, and some young seals that had lost their mothers, or some mothers that had lost their young, must have surfaced near the ship and kept company with her, crying and sobbing with that human-like wail of theirs. But this only disturbed some of the men all the more, because most sailors have a very superstitious feeling about seals, which comes not only from their strange cries when in distress but also from the human look of their round heads and half-intelligent faces as they rise peering out of the water alongside. At sea, under certain conditions, seals have more than once been taken for men.

But the crew's forebodings were destined to receive a most plausible confirmation that morning, in the fate of one of their own. At sunrise this man went from his hammock to his post at the fore-masthead; and whether he was not yet even half awake (for sailors sometimes go aloft while still between sleeping and waking) — whether that was the case with this man, there is now no way of knowing. But however that may be, he had not been long at his perch when a cry was heard — a cry and a rushing sound — and looking up, they saw a falling phantom in the air; and looking down, a little tossing heap of white bubbles in the blue of the sea.

The life-buoy — a long slender cask — was dropped from the stern, where it always hung obedient to a cunning spring; but no hand rose to seize it, and the sun had beaten on this cask so long that it had shrunk, so that it slowly filled, and the parched wood also filled at every pore; and the studded, iron-bound cask followed the sailor to the bottom, as if to give him his pillow, though in truth only a hard one.

And so the first man of the Pequod to climb the mast to look out for the White Whale, on the White Whale's own special ground — that man was swallowed up by the deep. But few, perhaps, thought of that at the time. In fact, in a sense, they were not saddened by this event, at least not as an omen; for they saw it not as a sign of evil to come but as the fulfillment of an evil already foretold. They declared that now they knew why they had heard those wild shrieks the night before. But once again the old Manxman said no.

The lost life-buoy now had to be replaced, and Starbuck was told to see to it. But no cask light enough could be found; and in the feverish eagerness of what seemed to be the approaching crisis of the voyage, all hands were impatient with any work except what bore directly on its final end, whatever that might turn out to be. So they were about to leave the ship's stern without a buoy, when Queequeg, by certain strange signs and innuendoes, hinted a hint about his coffin.
"A life-buoy of a coffin!" cried Starbuck, starting.
"Rather queer, that, I should say," said Stubb.
"It will make a good enough one," said Flask. "The carpenter here can arrange it easily."
"Bring it up; there's nothing else for it," said Starbuck, after a melancholy pause. "Rig it, carpenter; do not look at me so — the coffin, I mean. Do you hear me? Rig it."
"Shall I nail down the lid, then, sir?" moving his hand as if holding a hammer.
"Aye."
"And shall I caulk the seams, sir?" moving his hand as with a caulking-iron.
"Aye."
"And then shall I pay it over with pitch, sir?" moving his hand as if holding a pitch-pot.
"Away! What possesses you? Make a life-buoy of the coffin, and no more. Mr. Stubb, Mr. Flask, come forward with me."

"He goes off in a huff. The whole thing he can stand; it's the parts he balks at. Now, I don't like this. I make a leg for Captain Ahab, and he wears it like a gentleman; but I make a bandbox for Queequeg, and he won't put his head in it. Are all my pains over that coffin to go for nothing? And now I'm ordered to make a life-buoy out of it. It's like turning an old coat inside out; I'm going to bring the flesh to the other side now. I don't like this patching sort of business — I don't like it at all; it's undignified; it's not my place. Let tinkers' brats do the tinkering; we're above them. I like to take on nothing but clean, virgin, fair-and-square mathematical jobs, something that properly begins at the beginning, is at the middle when it's halfway, and comes to an end at the finish; not a cobbler's job, that's at an end in the middle and at the beginning at the end. It's an old woman's trick to be handing out cobbling jobs. Lord! what a fondness all old women have for tinkers. I know an old woman of sixty-five who once ran off with a bald-headed young tinker. And that's why I never would work for lonely old widow women ashore, when I kept my job-shop on the Vineyard; they might have taken it into their lonely old heads to run off with me. But heigh-ho! there are no caps at sea but snow-caps. Let me see. Nail down the lid; caulk the seams; pay it over with pitch; batten them down tight, and hang it by the snap-spring over the ship's stern. Were such things ever done with a coffin before? Some superstitious old carpenters, now, would let themselves be tied up in the rigging before they'd do the job. But I'm made of knotty Aroostook hemlock; I don't budge. Cruppered with a coffin! Sailing around with a graveyard tray! But never mind. We woodworkers make bridal bedsteads and card-tables as well as coffins and hearses. We work by the month, or by the job, or for the profit; it's not for us to ask the why and wherefore of our work, unless it's too confounded cobbling, and then we drop it if we can. Hem! I'll do the job tenderly now. I'll have — let's see — how many are in the ship's company, all told? But I've forgotten. Anyway, I'll have thirty separate life-lines with Turk's-head knots, each three feet long, hanging all around the coffin. Then, if the hull goes down, there'll be thirty lively fellows all fighting over one coffin, a sight not seen very often under the sun! Come, hammer, caulking-iron, pitch-pot and marlinspike! Let's get to it."

chapters.title: Chapter 127 — The Deck
paragraphs: The coffin lies on two line-tubs between the vise-bench and the open hatchway; the Carpenter is caulking its seams, the strand of twisted oakum slowly unwinding from a large roll of it tucked into the front of his smock. Ahab comes slowly from the cabin-gangway and hears Pip following him.
"Back, lad; I'll be with you again soon. He goes! This hand of mine does not do my bidding more kindly than that boy does. — Middle aisle of a church! What's here?"
"Life-buoy, sir. Mr. Starbuck's orders. Oh, look, sir! Beware the hatchway!"
"Thank you, man. Your coffin lies handy to the vault."
"Sir? The hatchway? Oh! So it does, sir, so it does."
"Aren't you the leg-maker? Look, didn't this stump come from your shop?"
"I believe it did, sir; does the ferrule stand, sir?"
"Well enough. But aren't you also the undertaker?"
"Aye, sir; I patched this thing together as a coffin for Queequeg, but now they've set me to turning it into something else."

"Then tell me: aren't you an arrant, all-grasping, intermeddling, monopolizing, heathenish old scamp, to be one day making legs, and the next day coffins to clap them in, and yet again life-buoys out of those same coffins? You are as unprincipled as the gods, and as much of a jack-of-all-trades."
"But I do not mean anything, sir. I do as I do."

"The gods again. Listen, don't you ever sing while working on a coffin? The Titans, they say, hummed snatches of song when chipping out the craters for volcanoes; and the grave-digger in the play sings, spade in hand. Don't you ever?"

"Sing, sir? Do I sing? Oh, I'm indifferent enough for that, sir; but the reason the grave-digger made music must have been that there was none in his spade, sir. The caulking mallet, though, is full of it. Listen to it."

"Aye, and that's because the lid there is a sounding-board; and what makes the sounding-board in all things is this — there's nothing beneath. And yet a coffin with a body in it rings pretty much the same, carpenter. Have you ever helped carry a bier, and heard the coffin knock against the churchyard gate, going in?"
"Faith, sir, I've —"
"Faith? What's that?"
"Why, faith, sir, it's only a sort of exclamation-like — that's all, sir."
"Um, um; go on."
"I was about to say, sir, that —"
"Are you a silk-worm? Do you spin your own shroud out of yourself? Look at your bosom! Be quick! and get these traps out of sight."

"He goes aft. That was sudden, now; but squalls come sudden in hot latitudes. I've heard that the Isle of Albemarle, one of the Galapagos, is cut by the Equator right in the middle. Seems to me some sort of Equator cuts that old man, too, right in his middle. He's always under the Line — fiery hot, I tell you! He's looking this way — come, oakum; quick. Here we go again. This wooden mallet is the cork, and I'm the professor of musical glasses — tap, tap!"
(Ahab to himself.)

"There's a sight! There's a sound! The gray-headed woodpecker tapping the hollow tree! The blind and the dumb might well be envied now. Look! That thing rests on two line-tubs full of tow-lines. A most malicious joker, that fellow. Rat-tat! So man's seconds tick! Oh, how immaterial all materials are! What real things are there, except weightless thoughts? Here now is the very dreaded symbol of grim death, turned by mere chance into the expressive sign of help and hope for life in the greatest danger. A life-buoy made of a coffin! Does it go further? Can it be that, in some spiritual sense, the coffin is after all only an immortality-preserver? I'll think about that. But no. I am so far gone into the dark side of the earth that its other side, the theoretical bright one, seems only an uncertain twilight to me. Will you never be done, Carpenter, with that cursed sound? I'm going below; don't let me see that thing here when I come back. Now then, Pip, we'll talk this over; I suck the most wondrous philosophies out of you! Some unknown channels from the unknown worlds must empty into you!"

chapters.title: Chapter 128 — The Pequod Meets The Rachel
paragraphs: Next day, a large ship, the Rachel, was sighted bearing straight down on the Pequod, all her spars thickly clustered with men. At the time the Pequod was making good speed through the water; but as the broad-winged stranger shot close to her from windward, her boastful sails all fell slack together like empty bladders that have burst, and all life fled from the stricken hull.
"Bad news; she brings bad news," muttered the old Manxman. But before her commander, who stood up in his boat with his trumpet to his mouth — before he could hail hopefully, Ahab's voice was heard.
"Have you seen the White Whale?"
"Aye, yesterday. Have you seen a whale-boat adrift?"

Throttling his joy, Ahab answered no to this unexpected question, and would then gladly have boarded the stranger, when the stranger's captain himself, having stopped his vessel, was seen climbing down her side. A few sharp pulls at the oars, and his boat-hook soon gripped the Pequod's main-chains, and he sprang onto the deck. Ahab immediately recognized him as a Nantucketer he knew. But no formal greeting was exchanged.
"Where was he? — not killed! — not killed!" cried Ahab, pressing close to him. "How did it happen?"

It seemed that rather late on the previous afternoon, three of the stranger's boats had been engaged with a shoal of whales that had led them some four or five miles from the ship; and while they were still in swift chase to windward, the white hump and head of Moby Dick had suddenly loomed up out of the water, not very far to leeward. At that, the fourth rigged boat — a reserve one — had been instantly lowered to give chase. After a keen sail before the wind, this fourth boat — the swiftest-keeled of all — seemed to have succeeded in fastening to him; at least, as far as the man at the mast-head could tell anything about it. In the distance he saw the boat shrunk to a dot; then a swift gleam of bubbling white water; and after that, nothing more. From this it was concluded that the stricken whale must have run away with his pursuers for some indefinite distance, as often happens. There was some apprehension, but as yet no real alarm. The recall signals were hoisted in the rigging; darkness came on; and since the ship had to pick up her three boats far to windward before going in search of the fourth in exactly the opposite direction, she had not only been forced to leave that boat to its fate until nearly midnight, but for the time being to increase her distance from it. But once the rest of her crew were at last safe aboard, she crowded on all sail — studding-sail on studding-sail — after the missing boat, lighting a fire in her try-pots as a beacon, with every other man aloft on the lookout. But though she then sailed far enough to reach the presumed spot where the missing men were last seen; though she then stopped to lower her spare boats to row all around her; and, finding nothing, had dashed on again, stopped again, and lowered her boats again; and though she had kept doing this until daylight — still not the least glimpse of the missing keel had been seen.

Having told the story, the stranger captain at once went on to reveal why he had boarded the Pequod. He wanted her to join his own ship in the search, the two of them sailing over the sea some four or five miles apart, on parallel lines, and so sweeping a double horizon, as it were.

"I will wager something now," whispered Stubb to Flask, "that someone in that missing boat went off wearing that captain's best coat; maybe his watch — he's so cursed anxious to get it back. Who ever heard of two pious whale-ships cruising after one missing whale-boat in the height of the whaling season? See, Flask, only see how pale he looks — pale in the very buttons of his eyes — look — it wasn't the coat — it must have been the —"

"My boy, my own boy is among them. For God's sake — I beg you, I implore you" — so the stranger captain now cried out to Ahab, who until then had received his plea with nothing but ice. "Let me charter your ship for forty-eight hours — I will gladly pay for it, and pay handsomely — if there is no other way — for forty-eight hours only — only that — you must, oh, you must, and you shall do this thing."
"His son!" cried Stubb, "oh, it's his son he's lost! I take back the coat and watch — what does Ahab say? We must save that boy."
"He's drowned with the rest of them, last night," said the old Manx sailor standing behind them. "I heard; all of you heard their spirits."

Now, as it soon turned out, what made this incident of the Rachel's all the more melancholy was that not only was one of the captain's sons among the missing boat's crew, but among the crews of the other boats — which had at the same time been separated from the ship in the other direction during the dark confusion of the chase — there had been yet another son. So for a time the wretched father was plunged to the very bottom of the cruelest perplexity, which was only resolved for him when his chief mate instinctively adopted a whale-ship's ordinary procedure in such emergencies: when caught between endangered but divided boats, always pick up the majority first. But the captain, for some unknown reason of temperament, had refrained from mentioning all this, and not until Ahab's iciness forced him to it did he speak of his one still-missing boy — a little lad, only twelve years old, whose father, with the earnest but untroubled boldness of a Nantucketer's paternal love, had sought this early to initiate him into the perils and wonders of a calling that had been, almost from time immemorial, the destiny of all his race. Nor is it uncommon for Nantucket captains to send a son of such tender age away from them, on a long three or four years' voyage in some ship other than their own, so that the boy's first knowledge of a whaleman's career will not be weakened by any chance display of a father's natural but ill-timed favoritism, or undue anxiety and concern.
Meanwhile the stranger was still begging his poor favor of Ahab; and Ahab still stood like an anvil, taking every blow without the least quiver of his own.

"I will not go," said the stranger, "until you say yes to me. Do to me as you would have me do to you in the same case. For you, too, have a boy, Captain Ahab — though only a child, and nestling safely at home now — a child of your old age, too. Yes, yes, you relent; I see it — run, run, men, now, and stand by to square in the yards."

"Avast," cried Ahab — "don't touch a rope-yarn"; then, in a voice that drew out and shaped every word — "Captain Gardiner, I will not do it. Even now I am losing time. Good-bye, good-bye. God bless you, man, and may I forgive myself, but I must go. Mr. Starbuck, look at the binnacle watch, and three minutes from this very instant warn off all strangers; then brace forward again, and let the ship sail as before."

Turning hurriedly, with his face averted, he went down into his cabin, leaving the stranger captain transfixed at this unconditional and utter rejection of so earnest a plea. But starting out of his trance, Gardiner silently hurried to the side, more fell than stepped into his boat, and returned to his ship.

Soon the two ships' wakes parted; and as long as the strange vessel stayed in view, she was seen to yaw this way and that toward every dark spot on the sea, however small. This way and that her yards were swung round; to starboard and to larboard she kept tacking; now she beat against a head sea, and now it pushed her before it; while all the while her masts and yards were thickly clustered with men, like three tall cherry trees when the boys are up among the boughs picking cherries.

But from her still faltering course and her winding, sorrowful path, you could plainly see that this ship, weeping spray as she went, still had not been comforted. She was Rachel, weeping for her children, because they were not.

chapters.title: Chapter 129 — The Cabin
paragraphs: (Ahab moving to go on deck; Pip catches him by the hand to follow.)

"Lad, lad, I tell you that you must not follow Ahab now. The hour is coming when Ahab would not scare you from him, yet would not have you by him. There is something in you, poor lad, that I feel is too much of a cure for my malady. Like cures like; and for this hunt, my malady becomes my most desired health. Stay down here, where they will serve you as if you were the captain. Aye, lad, you shall sit here in my own screwed chair; you must be another screw to it."
"No, no, no! You don't have a whole body, sir; just use poor me for your one lost leg; only tread on me, sir; I ask no more, so long as I remain a part of you."
"Oh! in spite of a million villains, this makes me a bigot in the fadeless fidelity of man! — and a black! and crazy! — but I think like-cures-like applies to him too; he grows so sane again."

"They tell me, sir, that Stubb once abandoned poor little Pip, whose drowned bones now show white, for all the blackness of his living skin. But I will never abandon you, sir, the way Stubb did him. Sir, I have to go with you."
"If you talk to me like this much more, Ahab's purpose will turn keel-up in him. I tell you no; it cannot be."
"Oh good master, master, master!"

"Weep like that, and I will murder you! Take care, for Ahab too is mad. Listen, and you will often hear my ivory foot upon the deck, and still know that I am there. And now I leave you. Your hand! — Met! You are as true, lad, as the circumference to its center. So: God forever bless you; and if it comes to that — God forever save you, come what may."
(Ahab goes; Pip steps one step forward.)

"He stood here this very instant; I stand in his air — but I'm alone. Now if even poor Pip were here I could endure it, but he's missing. Pip! Pip! Ding, dong, ding! Who's seen Pip? He must be up here; let's try the door. What? Neither lock, nor bolt, nor bar; and yet there's no opening it. It must be the spell; he told me to stay here. Yes, and told me this screwed chair was mine. Here, then, I'll sit myself down, against the transom, in the ship's full middle, all her keel and her three masts before me. Here, our old sailors say, in their black seventy-fours (warships of seventy-four guns) great admirals sometimes sit at table and lord it over rows of captains and lieutenants. Ha! What's this? Epaulets! epaulets! The epaulets all come crowding! Pass round the decanters; glad to see you; fill up, monsieurs! What an odd feeling, now, when a black boy's host to white men with gold lace on their coats! — Monsieurs, have you seen one Pip? — a little negro lad, five feet high, hang-dog look, and cowardly! Jumped from a whale-boat once — seen him? No! Well then, fill up again, captains, and let's drink shame upon all cowards! I name no names. Shame upon them! Put one foot upon the table. Shame upon all cowards. — Hush! Up there, I hear ivory — Oh, master! master! I am down-hearted indeed when you walk over me. But here I'll stay, though this stern strikes rocks, and they bulge through, and oysters come to join me."

chapters.title: Chapter 130 — The Hat
paragraphs: And now that, at the proper time and place, after so long and wide a preliminary cruise, Ahab — all other whaling waters swept — seemed to have chased his foe into a fold of the ocean, to slay him there the more securely; now that he found himself close to the very latitude and longitude where his tormenting wound had been inflicted; now that a vessel had been hailed which, only the day before, had actually encountered Moby Dick; and now that all his successive meetings with various ships had, in their contrasting ways, combined to show the demonic indifference with which the white whale tore his hunters, whether sinning or sinned against — now there lurked something in the old man's eyes that feeble souls could hardly bear to see. Like the never-setting polar star, which through the long, six-month arctic night keeps up its piercing, steady, central gaze, Ahab's purpose now gleamed fixedly down upon the constant midnight of the gloomy crew. It so dominated them that all their forebodings, doubts, misgivings and fears were forced to hide beneath their souls, and not sprout a single blade or leaf.

In this foreshadowing interval, too, all humor, forced or natural, vanished. Stubb no longer tried to raise a smile; Starbuck no longer tried to check one. Joy and sorrow, hope and fear alike seemed ground to the finest dust, and powdered for the time in the clamped mortar of Ahab's iron soul. Like machines, they moved dumbly about the deck, always aware that the old man's despot eye was on them.

But had you studied him closely in his more secret, private hours, when he thought no eye but one was on him, you would have seen that just as Ahab's eyes awed the crew's, the inscrutable Parsee's glance awed his — or at least, somehow, in some wild way, affected it at times. Such an added, gliding strangeness now began to surround the thin Fedallah, and such ceaseless shudderings shook him, that the men eyed him doubtfully, half uncertain, it seemed, whether he really was a mortal substance or else a tremulous shadow cast upon the deck by some unseen being's body. And that shadow was always hovering there. For not even by night had Fedallah ever been known for certain to sleep or go below. He would stand still for hours, but he never sat or leaned; his wan but wondrous eyes said plainly — We two watchmen never rest.

Nor could the sailors now step onto the deck at any time, night or day, without finding Ahab there before them — either standing in his pivot-hole, or pacing the planks exactly between two unvarying limits, the main-mast and the mizen; or else they saw him standing in the cabin-scuttle, his living foot advanced upon the deck as if to take a step, his hat slouched heavily over his eyes. So however motionless he stood, and however many days and nights were added on in which he had not swung in his hammock, still, hidden beneath that slouching hat, they could never tell for certain whether, for all this, his eyes were actually closed at times, or whether he was still intently watching them — no matter that he stood like that in the scuttle for a whole hour at a stretch, and the unheeded night-damp gathered in beads of dew on that stone-carved coat and hat. The clothes the night had wet, the next day's sunshine dried on him; and so, day after day and night after night, he no longer went below the planks; whatever he wanted from the cabin, he sent for.

He ate in the same open air — that is, his only two meals, breakfast and dinner; supper he never touched. Nor did he reap his beard, which grew darkly, all gnarled, like the unearthed roots of blown-over trees, which still grow idly on at the naked base though they have perished in the green growth above. But though his whole life had now become one watch on deck, and though the Parsee's mystic watch was as unbroken as his own, these two never seemed to speak — one man to the other — except when, at long intervals, some passing, unimportant matter made it necessary. Though such a potent spell seemed secretly to join the two, openly, and to the awe-struck crew, they seemed as far apart as the poles. If by day they happened to speak one word, by night both were dumb men, as far as the slightest exchange of words went. At times, for the longest hours, without a single hail, they stood far apart in the starlight, Ahab in his scuttle, the Parsee by the mainmast, but still gazing fixedly at each other — as if in the Parsee Ahab saw his forethrown shadow, and in Ahab the Parsee saw his abandoned substance.

And yet, somehow, Ahab — in his own proper self, as he was daily, hourly and every instant commandingly revealed to his subordinates — Ahab seemed an independent lord, and the Parsee only his slave. Then again, both seemed yoked together, with an unseen tyrant driving them: the lean shadow alongside the solid rib. For whatever this Parsee might be, all rib and keel was solid Ahab.

At the first faintest glimmering of dawn, his iron voice was heard from aft — "Man the mast-heads!" — and all through the day, until after sunset and after twilight, the same voice was heard every hour, at the striking of the helmsman's bell — "What do you see? — sharp! sharp!"

But when three or four days had slipped by since meeting the children-seeking Rachel, and still no spout had been seen, the monomaniac old man seemed to distrust his crew's loyalty — at least, that of nearly all of them except the Pagan harpooners. He even seemed to suspect that Stubb and Flask might willingly overlook the sight he was seeking. But if these suspicions really were his, he shrewdly refrained from putting them into words, however much his actions might seem to hint at them.

"I will have the first sight of the whale myself," he said. "Aye! Ahab must have the doubloon!" And with his own hands he rigged a nest of basketed bowlines; and sending a man aloft with a single-sheaved block to fasten to the main-mast head, he took the two ends of the rope rove down through it; and attaching one to his basket, he prepared a belaying pin for the other end, so as to fasten it at the rail. This done, with that end still in his hand and standing beside the pin, he looked round at his crew, sweeping from one to another, letting his glance rest long on Daggoo, Queequeg and Tashtego, but avoiding Fedallah; and then, settling his firm, trusting eye on the chief mate, he said — "Take the rope, sir — I give it into your hands, Starbuck." Then, settling himself in the basket, he gave the word for them to hoist him to his perch, Starbuck being the one who finally made the rope fast, and who afterwards stood near it. And so, with one hand clinging round the royal mast, Ahab gazed out over the sea for miles and miles — ahead, astern, this side and that — within the wide, expanded circle commanded from so great a height.

When a sailor at sea, working with his hands at some high, almost isolated spot in the rigging that happens to offer no foothold, is hoisted up to that spot and held there by the rope, the rope's fastened end on deck is always given in strict charge to one particular man, who has the special watch of it. This is because, in such a wilderness of running rigging, whose various relations aloft cannot always be told with certainty from what can be seen of them on deck, and when the deck-ends of these ropes are being cast off from their fastenings every few minutes, it would be only a natural fatality if, without a constant watchman, the hoisted sailor were cast adrift through some carelessness of the crew and fell swooping down into the sea. So Ahab's proceedings in this matter were not unusual. The only strange thing about them seemed to be that Starbuck — almost the only man who had ever ventured to oppose him with anything even slightly approaching decisiveness, and one of those, too, whose faithfulness on the lookout he had seemed somewhat to doubt — it was strange that this was the very man he should choose as his watchman, freely placing his whole life in the hands of a man he otherwise distrusted.

Now, the first time Ahab was perched aloft, before he had been there ten minutes, one of those savage red-billed sea-hawks that so often fly annoyingly close around the manned mast-heads of whalemen in these latitudes — one of these birds came wheeling and screaming round his head in a maze of untrackably swift circlings. Then it shot a thousand feet straight up into the air, then spiraled downward, and went eddying round his head again.

But with his gaze fixed on the dim and distant horizon, Ahab seemed not to notice this wild bird; nor, indeed, would anyone else have noticed it much, since it was no uncommon occurrence; only now, almost the least heedful eye seemed to see some sort of cunning meaning in almost every sight.

"Your hat, your hat, sir!" the Sicilian seaman suddenly cried. He was posted at the mizzen-masthead and stood directly behind Ahab, though somewhat below his level, with a deep gulf of air between them.
But the dark wing was already before the old man's eyes, the long hooked beak at his head; and with a scream the black hawk shot away with his prize.

An eagle flew three times around Tarquin's head, lifting off his cap and then putting it back, and at that Tanaquil, his wife, declared that Tarquin would be king of Rome. But it was only because the cap was put back that the omen was counted good. Ahab's hat was never restored; the wild hawk flew on and on with it, far ahead of the prow, and at last disappeared; while from the point where it disappeared, a tiny black spot was dimly seen falling from that vast height into the sea.

chapters.title: Chapter 131 — The Pequod Meets The Delight
paragraphs: The intense Pequod sailed on; the rolling waves and days went by; the life-buoy coffin still swung lightly; and another ship, most miserably misnamed the Delight, was sighted. As she drew near, all eyes were fixed on her broad beams, called shears, which in some whaling ships cross the quarter-deck at a height of eight or nine feet, serving to carry the spare, unrigged or disabled boats.

On the stranger's shears could be seen the shattered white ribs and a few splintered planks of what had once been a whale-boat; but you could now see through this wreck as plainly as you see through the peeled, half-unhinged, bleaching skeleton of a horse.
"Have you seen the White Whale?"
"Look!" the hollow-cheeked captain answered from his taffrail, and pointed his trumpet at the wreck.
"Have you killed him?"
"The harpoon that will ever do that is not yet forged," answered the other, glancing sadly at a rounded hammock on the deck, whose gathered sides some silent sailors were busy sewing together.

"Not forged!" — and snatching Perth's leveled iron from the crotch, Ahab held it out, exclaiming — "Look here, Nantucketer; here in this hand I hold his death! These barbs are tempered in blood, and tempered by lightning; and I swear to temper them a third time in that hot place behind the fin, where the White Whale most feels his accursed life!"

"Then God keep you, old man — do you see that?" — pointing to the hammock — "I am burying only one of five stout men who were alive only yesterday but were dead before night. Only that one do I bury; the rest were buried before they died; you sail upon their tomb." Then, turning to his crew — "Are you ready there? Place the plank on the rail, then, and lift the body; so, then — Oh! God" — advancing toward the hammock with uplifted hands — "may the resurrection and the life —"
"Brace forward! Up helm!" cried Ahab like lightning to his men.

But the suddenly started Pequod was not quick enough to escape the sound of the splash the corpse soon made as it struck the sea; not quick enough, indeed, to keep some of the flying bubbles from perhaps sprinkling her hull with their ghostly baptism.
As Ahab now glided away from the dejected Delight, the strange life-buoy hanging at the Pequod's stern stood out in sharp relief.
"Ha! Over there! Look over there, men!" cried a foreboding voice in her wake. "In vain, oh you strangers, do you flee our sad burial; you only turn your taffrail to us to show us your coffin!"

chapters.title: Chapter 132 — The Symphony
paragraphs: It was a clear, steel-blue day. In that all-pervading blue, the firmaments of air and sea could hardly be told apart; except that the thoughtful air was transparently pure and soft, with a woman's look, while the strong, manlike sea heaved with long, powerful, lingering swells, like Samson's chest as he sleeps.

High overhead, the snow-white wings of small, unspeckled birds glided this way and that; these were the gentle thoughts of the feminine air. But far down in the bottomless blue, mighty leviathans, swordfish and sharks rushed back and forth through the depths; and these were the strong, troubled, murderous thinkings of the masculine sea.
But though the two contrasted so within, without, the contrast was only in shades and shadows; those two seemed one — it was only the sex, as it were, that distinguished them.

High above, like a royal czar and king, the sun seemed to be giving this gentle air in marriage to this bold, rolling sea, as a bride is given to a groom. And at the encircling line of the horizon, a soft, trembling motion — seen most of all here at the equator — showed the fond, throbbing trust and the loving fears with which the poor bride gave away her bosom.

Bound up and twisted, gnarled and knotted with wrinkles, haggardly firm and unyielding, his eyes glowing like coals that still glow in the ashes of ruin, Ahab stood forth without tottering in the clear morning, lifting the splintered helmet of his brow to heaven's fair, girlish forehead.

Oh, immortal infancy and innocence of the azure! Invisible winged creatures that frolic all around us! Sweet childhood of air and sky! How oblivious you were of old Ahab's close-coiled woe! But just so have I seen little Miriam and Martha, laughing-eyed elves, heedlessly frolicking around their old father, playing with the circle of singed locks that grew on the edge of that burnt-out crater of his brain.

Crossing the deck slowly from the scuttle, Ahab leaned over the side and watched how his shadow in the water sank deeper and deeper before his eyes the harder he tried to see into the depths. But the lovely fragrances of that enchanted air did at last seem to drive away, for a moment, the cankerous thing in his soul. That glad, happy air, that winning sky, did at last stroke and caress him; the stepmother world, so long cruel — forbidding — now threw loving arms around his stubborn neck, and seemed to sob over him with joy, as if over someone whom, however willful and wayward, she could still find it in her heart to save and to bless. From under his slouched hat Ahab dropped a tear into the sea; and the whole Pacific held no wealth to match that one tiny drop.

Starbuck saw the old man — saw how heavily he leaned over the side; and in his own true heart he seemed to hear the boundless sobbing that crept out from the center of the calm all around. Taking care not to touch him or be noticed by him, he nevertheless came close to him and stood there.
Ahab turned.
"Starbuck!"
"Sir."

"Oh, Starbuck! It is a mild, mild wind, and a mild-looking sky. On such a day — very much such a sweetness as this — I struck my first whale — a boy-harpooner of eighteen! Forty — forty — forty years ago! — ago! Forty years of continual whaling! Forty years of privation, and peril, and storm-time! Forty years on the pitiless sea! For forty years Ahab has forsaken the peaceful land, for forty years to make war on the horrors of the deep! Aye and yes, Starbuck, out of those forty years I have not spent three ashore. When I think of this life I have led — the desolation of solitude it has been; the masoned, walled town of a captain's exclusiveness, which lets in so little sympathy from the green country outside — oh, weariness! heaviness! Guinea-coast slavery of solitary command! — when I think of all this, only half-suspected, not so keenly known to me before — and how for forty years I have fed on dry salted fare, fit emblem of the dry nourishment of my soil! — while the poorest landsman has had fresh fruit to his daily hand, and broken the world's fresh bread against my moldy crusts — away, whole oceans away, from that young girl-wife I married when I was past fifty, and sailed for Cape Horn the next day, leaving only one dent in my marriage pillow — wife? wife? — rather a widow with her husband alive! Aye, I widowed that poor girl when I married her, Starbuck; and then the madness, the frenzy, the boiling blood and the smoking brow with which, for a thousand lowerings, old Ahab has furiously, foamingly chased his prey — more a demon than a man! — aye, aye! what a forty years' fool — fool — old fool, old Ahab has been! Why this strife of the chase? Why weary and palsy the arm at the oar, and the iron, and the lance? How is Ahab the richer or better now? Look. Oh, Starbuck! is it not hard that, with this weary load I bear, one poor leg should have been snatched from under me? Here, brush this old hair aside; it blinds me, so that I seem to weep. Locks so gray never grew except out of some ashes! But do I look very old, so very, very old, Starbuck? I feel deadly faint, bowed and humped, as though I were Adam, staggering beneath the piled-up centuries since Paradise. God! God! God! — crack my heart! — stave in my brain! — mockery! mockery! bitter, biting mockery of gray hairs, have I lived enough joy to wear you, and to seem and feel so intolerably old? Close! stand close to me, Starbuck; let me look into a human eye; it is better than to gaze into sea or sky; better than to gaze upon God. By the green land; by the bright hearth-stone! this is the magic glass, man; I see my wife and my child in your eye. No, no; stay on board, on board! — do not lower when I do, when branded Ahab gives chase to Moby Dick. That hazard shall not be yours. No, no! not with the far-away home I see in that eye!"

"Oh, my Captain! my Captain! noble soul! grand old heart, after all! Why should anyone give chase to that hated fish? Away with me! Let us fly these deadly waters! Let us go home! Wife and child, too, are Starbuck's — wife and child of his brotherly, sisterly, play-fellow youth; just as yours, sir, are the wife and child of your loving, longing, paternal old age! Away! Let us away! — let me alter the course this instant! How cheerily, how hilariously, O my Captain, we would bowl along on our way to see old Nantucket again! I think, sir, they have some such mild blue days, just like this one, in Nantucket."

"They have, they have. I have seen them — on some summer days, in the morning. About this time — yes, he's having his noon nap now — the boy wakes up full of life and sits up in bed, and his mother tells him about me, about cannibal old me; how I'm away out on the deep, but will still come back to dance him again."

"It's my Mary, my Mary herself! She promised that every morning my boy would be carried up the hill to catch the first glimpse of his father's sail! Yes, yes! No more! It's settled! We head for Nantucket! Come, my Captain, work out the course, and let's be off! Look, look! The boy's face at the window! The boy's hand on the hill!"
But Ahab looked away; he shook like a blighted fruit tree and dropped his last, charred apple to the ground.

"What is it, what nameless, inscrutable, unearthly thing is it; what deceitful, hidden lord and master, what cruel, remorseless emperor commands me, so that against all natural loves and longings I keep pushing and crowding and jamming myself on all the time, recklessly making me ready to do what in my own proper, natural heart I would not dare so much as to dare? Is Ahab, Ahab? Is it I, God, or who, that lifts this arm? But if the great sun does not move by himself, but is like an errand-boy in heaven; and if not one single star can revolve except by some invisible power; how then can this one small heart beat, this one small brain think thoughts, unless God does that beating, does that thinking, does that living, and not I? By heaven, man, we are turned round and round in this world like that windlass over there, and Fate is the handspike. And all the while, look! that smiling sky, and this unsounded sea! Look! See that albacore there! Who put it into him to chase that flying-fish and sink his fangs in it? Where do murderers go, man? Who is to pass sentence, when the judge himself is dragged before the bar?
