But it is a mild, mild wind, and a mild-looking sky; and the air smells now as if it blew from a faraway meadow; they have been making hay somewhere under the slopes of the Andes, Starbuck, and the mowers are sleeping in the new-mown hay. Sleeping? Aye, however hard we toil, we all sleep in the field at last. Sleep? Aye, and rust amid the green, like last year's scythes thrown down and left in the half-cut rows — Starbuck!"
But blanched to a corpse's hue with despair, the mate had stolen away.
Ahab crossed the deck to look over the other side, but started at the sight of two fixed eyes reflected in the water there. Fedallah was leaning, motionless, over the same rail.

chapters.title: Chapter 133 — The Chase—First Day
paragraphs: That night, during the middle watch, when the old man — as he did from time to time — stepped out of the scuttle where he had been leaning and went to his pivot-hole, he suddenly thrust his face out fiercely and sniffed the sea air, the way a clever ship's dog will when the ship draws near some savage island. He declared that a whale must be close. Soon the whole watch could smell that peculiar odor which the living sperm whale sometimes gives off to a great distance; and no sailor was surprised when Ahab, after checking the compass, then the dog-vane, and then fixing the exact bearing of the smell as nearly as he could, quickly ordered the ship's course altered slightly and the sail shortened.

The shrewd thinking behind these movements was sufficiently proved at daybreak by the sight of a long slick on the sea directly and lengthwise ahead, smooth as oil, and resembling, in the pleated watery wrinkles bordering it, the polished metallic marks of some swift tidal rip at the mouth of a deep, rapid stream.
"Man the mastheads! Call all hands!"

Thundering on the forecastle deck with the butts of three clubbed handspikes, Daggoo woke the sleepers with such Judgment-Day claps that they seemed to be breathed out of the scuttle, so instantly did they appear, clothes in hand.
"What do you see?" cried Ahab, flattening his face to the sky.
"Nothing, nothing, sir!" was the sound hailing down in reply.
"Topgallant sails! Stunsails! Aloft and alow, and on both sides!"

All sail being set, he now cast loose the life-line, reserved for swaying him up to the main royal-masthead; and in a few moments they were hoisting him there. He was only two-thirds of the way aloft, peering ahead through the horizontal vacancy between the main-topsail and topgallant-sail, when he raised a gull-like cry in the air. "There she blows! — there she blows! A hump like a snow-hill! It is Moby Dick!"

Fired by the cry, which the three lookouts seemed to take up at the same moment, the men on deck rushed into the rigging to see the famous whale they had been pursuing so long. Ahab had now reached his final perch, some feet above the other lookouts, with Tashtego standing just below him on the cap of the topgallant-mast, so that the Indian's head was almost level with Ahab's heel. From this height the whale could now be seen a mile or so ahead, showing his high, sparkling hump at every roll of the sea and regularly jetting his silent spout into the air. To the credulous sailors it seemed the same silent spout they had seen so long ago in the moonlit Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
"And did none of you see it before?" cried Ahab, hailing the perched men all around him.
"I saw him almost that same instant, sir, that Captain Ahab did, and I cried out," said Tashtego.

"Not the same instant; not the same — no, the doubloon is mine; Fate kept the doubloon for me. Only I; none of you could have raised the White Whale first. There she blows! — there she blows! — there she blows! There again! — there again!" he cried, in long-drawn, lingering, measured tones, keeping time with the gradual lengthening of the whale's visible jets. "He's going to sound! In stunsails! Down topgallant-sails! Stand by three boats. Mr. Starbuck, remember, stay on board and keep the ship. Helm there! Luff, luff a point! So; steady, man, steady! There go flukes! No, no; only black water! All ready the boats there? Stand by, stand by! Lower me, Mr. Starbuck; lower, lower — quick, quicker!" And he slid through the air to the deck.
"He is heading straight to leeward, sir," cried Stubb, "right away from us; cannot have seen the ship yet."
"Be quiet, man! Stand by the braces! Hard down the helm! — brace up! Shiver her! — shiver her! So; well that! Boats, boats!"

Soon all the boats except Starbuck's were lowered; all the boat-sails were set and all the paddles working, and they shot to leeward with rippling speed, Ahab leading the charge. A pale, deathly glimmer lit up Fedallah's sunken eyes; a hideous movement gnawed at his mouth.

Like noiseless nautilus shells, their light prows sped through the sea; but they closed on the foe only slowly. As they came nearer, the ocean grew smoother still; it seemed to be drawing a carpet over its waves; it seemed a noon meadow, so serenely did it spread. At length the breathless hunter came so close to his seemingly unsuspecting prey that the whale's entire dazzling hump was plainly visible, sliding along the sea as if it were a thing apart, and ringed all the while by a revolving circle of the finest, fleecy, greenish foam. Beyond it he saw the vast, intricate wrinkles of the slightly projecting head. Ahead of the whale, far out on the soft waters patterned like a Turkish rug, went the glistening white shadow of his broad, milky forehead, with a musical rippling playfully keeping the shadow company; behind, the blue waters flowed in turn into the moving valley of his steady wake; and on either side bright bubbles rose and danced along beside him. But these were broken again by the light toes of hundreds of gay sea-birds softly feathering the sea between their fitful flights; and like some flagstaff rising from the painted hull of an argosy, the tall but shattered pole of a recent lance stuck up from the white whale's back; and every so often one of the cloud of soft-toed birds, hovering and skimming to and fro like a canopy over the fish, would silently perch and rock on this pole, its long tail feathers streaming like pennons.

A gentle joyousness — a mighty mildness of repose in swiftness — clothed the gliding whale. Not the white bull Jupiter, swimming away with the ravished Europa clinging to his graceful horns, his lovely, leering eyes turned sideways on the girl, rippling with smooth, bewitching speed straight for the bridal bower in Crete — not Jove, not that great majesty Supreme! — surpassed the glorified White Whale as he swam so divinely.

On each soft side — in step with the parted swell that, once it left him, flowed so far and wide away — on each bright side, the whale gave off enticements. No wonder there had been some among the hunters who, carried away and allured beyond words by all this serenity, had ventured to attack it, only to find, fatally, that this quietude was nothing but the garment of tornadoes. Yet calm, enticing calm, oh whale! You glide on before all who see you for the first time, no matter how many in that same way you may have tricked and destroyed before.

And so, through the calm serenity of the tropical sea, among waves whose hand-clapping was held back by overwhelming rapture, Moby Dick moved on, still keeping the full terrors of his submerged trunk out of sight and completely hiding the twisted hideousness of his jaw. But soon the front of him slowly rose out of the water; for an instant his whole marble-like body formed a high arch, like Virginia's Natural Bridge; and, waving his bannered flukes in the air in warning, the grand god revealed himself, sounded, and disappeared. Hovering, pausing and dipping on the wing, the white seabirds lingered longingly over the churning pool he left behind.
With oars peaked, blades raised clear of the water, and paddles down, the sheets of their sails adrift, the three boats now silently floated, awaiting Moby Dick's reappearance.

"An hour," said Ahab, standing rooted in the stern of his boat; and he gazed past the place where the whale had been, toward the dim blue spaces and wide, wooing emptiness to leeward. It lasted only an instant; for his eyes again seemed to whirl around in his head as he swept the circle of water. The breeze was freshening now; the sea began to swell.
"The birds! — the birds!" cried Tashtego.

In long Indian file, like herons taking wing, the white birds were now all flying toward Ahab's boat; and when they were within a few yards they began fluttering over the water there, wheeling round and round with joyous, expectant cries. Their vision was keener than man's; Ahab could find no sign in the sea. But suddenly, as he peered down and down into its depths, far down he saw a white living spot no bigger than a white weasel rising with wonderful speed and growing larger as it rose, until it turned, and then two long crooked rows of white, glistening teeth were plainly revealed, floating up from the unfathomable bottom. It was Moby Dick's open mouth and scrolled jaw, his vast, shadowed bulk still half blending with the blue of the sea. The glittering mouth yawned beneath the boat like a marble tomb with its door open; and with one sidelong sweep of his steering oar, Ahab whirled the boat aside from this tremendous apparition. Then, calling on Fedallah to change places with him, he went forward to the bow, seized Perth's harpoon, and ordered his crew to grip their oars and stand ready to back the boat astern.

Now, because the boat had been spun round on its axis in time, its bow was made to face the whale's head in advance, while the head was still under water. But as if he saw through this stratagem, Moby Dick, with that malicious intelligence ascribed to him, shifted himself sideways in an instant, as it were, shooting his pleated head lengthwise beneath the boat.

Through and through — through every plank and every rib — a thrill ran for an instant, as the whale, lying obliquely on his back in the manner of a biting shark, slowly and sensitively took the bows fully into his mouth, so that the long, narrow, scrolled lower jaw curled high up into the open air, and one of the teeth caught in a rowlock. The bluish pearl-white of the inside of the jaw was within six inches of Ahab's head, and reached higher than that. In this position the White Whale now shook the slight cedar boat as a mildly cruel cat shakes her mouse. Fedallah gazed with unastonished eyes and crossed his arms; but the tiger-yellow crew were tumbling over each other's heads to reach the farthest end of the stern.

And now the two springy gunwales were bending in and out as the whale toyed with the doomed boat in this devilish way; his body was submerged beneath the boat, so he could not be darted at from the bow, for the bow was almost inside him, as it were; and the other boats had involuntarily paused, as before a sudden crisis impossible to withstand. It was then that the monomaniac Ahab, furious at being so tantalizingly close to his foe — a closeness that put him, fully alive and helpless, in the very jaws he hated — frenzied by all this, seized the long bone with his bare hands and wildly strove to wrench it loose from its grip. As he strove in vain, the jaw slipped from him; the frail gunwales bent in, collapsed, and snapped, as both jaws, like enormous shears, slid further aft, bit the boat completely in two, and locked themselves shut again in the sea, midway between the two floating wrecks. These drifted apart, their broken ends drooping, the crew at the stern-wreck clinging to the gunwales and struggling to hold on to the oars in order to lash them across.

At that opening moment, before the boat was snapped, Ahab had been the first to see the whale's intent, from the crafty lifting of his head — a movement that loosened his hold for the time — and at that moment his hand made one final effort to push the boat out of the bite. But the boat, only slipping further into the whale's mouth and tilting sideways as it slipped, had shaken off his hold on the jaw and spilled him out as he leaned into the push; and so he fell flat on his face upon the sea.

Rippling away from his prey, Moby Dick now lay a little distance off, thrusting his oblong white head vertically up and down in the billows while slowly revolving his whole spindle-shaped body; so that whenever his vast wrinkled forehead rose — some twenty feet or more out of the water — the swells, now rising, broke dazzlingly against it with all their merging waves, vindictively tossing their shattered spray still higher into the air.* So, in a gale, the Channel billows, only half baffled, recoil from the base of the Eddystone lighthouse only to leap triumphantly over its summit with their scud.

*This motion is peculiar to the sperm whale. It gets its name (pitchpoling) because it is likened to the preliminary up-and-down poise of the whale-lance in the exercise called pitchpoling, described earlier. By this motion the whale must best and most comprehensively view whatever objects may be encircling him.

But soon, returning to a horizontal position, Moby Dick swam swiftly round and round the wrecked crew, churning the water sideways in his vengeful wake, as if whipping himself up to yet another and deadlier attack. The sight of the splintered boat seemed to madden him, as the blood of grapes and mulberries, cast before Antiochus's elephants in the book of Maccabees, maddened them. Meanwhile Ahab was half smothered in the foam of the whale's insolent tail, and too much of a cripple to swim — though he could still keep afloat, even in the heart of a whirlpool like that — and helpless Ahab's head could be seen like a tossed bubble that the slightest chance shock might burst. From the broken-off stern of the boat Fedallah watched him with mild indifference; the clinging crew at the other drifting end could not help him; it was more than enough for them to look after themselves. For the White Whale's aspect as he revolved was so appalling, and the ever-tightening circles he made were so swift, like a planet's, that he seemed to be swooping horizontally upon them. And though the other boats, unharmed, still hovered close by, they dared not pull into the eddy to strike, for fear that would be the signal for the instant destruction of the endangered castaways, Ahab and all; nor in that case could they themselves hope to escape. So, with straining eyes, they stayed on the outer edge of the dreadful zone, whose center had now become the old man's head.

Meanwhile, from the beginning all this had been seen from the ship's mastheads; and squaring her yards, she had borne down upon the scene; and was now so near that Ahab in the water hailed her! "Sail on the" — but that moment a breaking sea dashed on him from Moby Dick, and overwhelmed him for the time. But struggling out of it again, and chancing to rise on a towering crest, he shouted: "Sail on the whale! Drive him off!"
The Pequod's bows were pointed at them; breaking up the charmed circle, she succeeded in separating the white whale from his victim. As he swam sullenly away, the boats flew to the rescue.

Ahab was dragged into Stubb's boat with bloodshot, blinded eyes, the white brine caking in his wrinkles; and the long tension of his bodily strength cracked, and helplessly he yielded to his body's doom: for a time, lying all crushed in the bottom of Stubb's boat, like one trodden underfoot by herds of elephants. Far inland, nameless wails came from him, like desolate sounds from out of ravines.

But the very intensity of his physical collapse only made it the shorter. Within the span of an instant, great hearts sometimes condense into one deep pang the sum total of those shallow pains that are mercifully spread through the whole lives of feebler men. And so such hearts, though brief in each single suffering, still, if the gods decree it, pile up in their lifetime a whole age of woe, made up entirely of instantaneous intensities; for even in their centers, mere points though these are, those noble natures contain the entire circumferences of inferior souls.
"The harpoon," said Ahab, half-rising and draggingly leaning on one bent arm — "is it safe?"
"Aye, sir, for it was not darted; this is it," said Stubb, showing it.
"Lay it before me; any missing men?"
"One, two, three, four, five; there were five oars, sir, and here are five men."

"That's good. Help me, man; I wish to stand. So, so, I see him! There! There! Going to leeward still; what a leaping spout! — Hands off from me! The eternal sap runs up in Ahab's bones again! Set the sail; out oars; the helm!"

It often happens that when a boat is stove, its crew, once picked up by another boat, help to work that second boat; and the chase is then continued with what are called double-banked oars. So it was now. But the added power of the boat did not match the added power of the whale, for he seemed to have treble-banked every fin, swimming at a speed that plainly showed that if the chase were pushed on now, under these circumstances, it would prove an indefinitely prolonged one, if not a hopeless one; nor could any crew endure such unbroken, intense straining at the oar for so long a period — a thing barely bearable even for one brief spell. The ship itself, then, as sometimes happens, offered the most promising way of overtaking the chase in the meantime. Accordingly, the boats now made for her and were soon swayed up to their cranes — the two parts of the wrecked boat having already been secured by her — and then, hoisting everything up to her side, piling her canvas high, and stretching it out sideways with stunsails like the double-jointed wings of an albatross, the Pequod bore down in Moby Dick's leeward wake. At the familiar, regular intervals, the whale's glittering spout was duly announced from the manned mastheads; and whenever he was reported as just gone down, Ahab would note the time, and then, pacing the deck binnacle-watch in hand, the moment the last second of the allotted hour ran out, his voice was heard: "Whose is the doubloon now? Do you see him?" And if the reply was "No, sir!" he at once ordered them to hoist him to his perch. In this way the day wore on; Ahab now aloft and motionless, now pacing the planks without rest.

As he walked like this, making no sound except to hail the men aloft or to tell them to hoist a sail still higher or spread one still wider — pacing back and forth like this beneath his slouched hat — at every turn he passed his own wrecked boat, which had been dropped onto the quarter-deck and lay there upside down, broken bow to shattered stern. At last he stopped in front of it; and just as fresh troops of clouds will sometimes sail across a sky that is already overcast, so some such added gloom now crept over the old man's face.

Stubb saw him stop; and perhaps meaning — though not vainly — to show that his own courage was undiminished, and so keep a brave place in his Captain's thoughts, he stepped forward and, eyeing the wreck, exclaimed, "The thistle the ass refused; it pricked his mouth too sharply, sir; ha! ha!"

"What soulless thing is this that laughs in front of a wreck? Man, man! If I did not know you to be as brave as fearless fire (and as mechanical), I could swear you were a coward. Neither groan nor laugh should be heard in front of a wreck."
"Aye, sir," said Starbuck, drawing near, "it is a solemn sight; an omen, and an ill one."

"Omen? Omen? — the dictionary! If the gods mean to speak outright to man, they will honorably speak outright; not shake their heads and give an old wives' dark hint. — Begone! You two are the opposite poles of one thing; Starbuck is Stubb reversed, and Stubb is Starbuck; and you two are all mankind; and Ahab stands alone among the millions of the peopled earth, with neither gods nor men for his neighbors! Cold, cold — I shiver! — What now? Aloft there! Do you see him? Sing out for every spout, even if he spouts ten times a second!"
The day was nearly done; only the hem of its golden robe was rustling. Soon it was almost dark, but the lookout men still remained at their posts.
"Can't see the spout now, sir; too dark," cried a voice from the air.
"How heading when last seen?"
"As before, sir — straight to leeward."

"Good! He will travel slower now that it's night. Down royals and topgallant stunsails, Mr. Starbuck. We must not run over him before morning; he's making a passage now, and may heave to for a while. Helm there! Keep her full before the wind! — Aloft! Come down! — Mr. Stubb, send a fresh hand to the fore-masthead, and see that it's manned till morning." Then, advancing toward the doubloon on the mainmast: "Men, this gold is mine, for I earned it; but I shall let it stay here till the White Whale is dead; and then, whichever of you first raises him on the day he is killed, this gold is that man's; and if on that day I raise him again myself, then ten times its sum shall be divided among all of you! Away now! — the deck is yours, sir!"
Saying this, he stationed himself halfway inside the scuttle, pulled his hat down low, and stood there until dawn, except when he roused himself now and then to see how the night was going.

chapters.title: Chapter 134 — The Chase—Second Day
paragraphs: At daybreak, the three mastheads were promptly manned again.
"Do you see him?" cried Ahab, after allowing a little time for the light to spread.
"See nothing, sir."
"Turn up all hands and make sail! He travels faster than I thought — the topgallant sails! — aye, they should have been kept on her all night. But no matter — he's only resting for the rush."

Let it be said here that this persistent pursuit of one particular whale, kept up through day into night and through night into day, is by no means unheard of in the South Sea fishery. For such is the wonderful skill, the foresight born of experience, and the unshakable confidence acquired by some great natural geniuses among the Nantucket captains, that from simply observing a whale when last sighted they will, under certain given circumstances, predict pretty accurately both the direction in which he will keep swimming for a while out of sight, and his probable rate of progress during that time. In these cases the whale-fisherman does somewhat as a pilot does when he is about to lose sight of a coast whose general trend he knows well, and which he wants to return to shortly, but at some further point: just as this pilot stands by his compass and takes the exact bearing of the cape now in view, so as to be surer of hitting the remote, unseen headland he will eventually reach, so the fisherman stands at his compass with the whale; for after the creature has been chased and carefully marked through several hours of daylight, then, when night hides the fish, its future wake through the darkness is almost as settled in the hunter's shrewd mind as the pilot's coast is in his. So, to this hunter's wondrous skill, a wake — that proverbially fleeting thing written in water — is for all desired purposes nearly as reliable as the steadfast land. And just as the mighty iron Leviathan of the modern railway is so familiarly known in its every pace that men, watches in hand, time his rate as doctors time a baby's pulse, and say casually that the up train or the down train will reach such and such a spot at such and such an hour, so, almost, there are occasions when these Nantucketers time that other Leviathan of the deep by the observed humor of his speed, and say to themselves that so many hours from now this whale will have gone two hundred miles, and will have about reached this or that degree of latitude or longitude. But for this sharpness to succeed at all in the end, the wind and the sea must be the whaleman's allies; for what use at the moment to the becalmed or windbound sailor is the skill that assures him he is exactly ninety-three leagues and a quarter from his port? Many further subtle points concerning the chase of whales can be inferred from these statements.
The ship tore on, leaving a furrow in the sea like the one a stray cannonball makes when it turns plowshare and furrows up the level field.

"By salt and hemp!" cried Stubb, "but this swift motion of the deck creeps up one's legs and tingles at the heart. This ship and I are two brave fellows! — Ha, ha! Someone pick me up and launch me spine-first on the sea — for, by live-oaks! my spine's a keel. Ha, ha! We go the gait that leaves no dust behind!"
"There she blows — she blows! — she blows! — right ahead!" was now the cry from the masthead.

"Aye, aye!" cried Stubb. "I knew it — you can't escape — blow on and split your spout, O whale! The mad fiend himself is after you! Blow your trumpet — blister your lungs! — Ahab will dam off your blood, as a miller shuts his watergate on the stream!"

And Stubb was only speaking for nearly the whole crew. The frenzies of the chase had by now worked them up into a bubbling ferment, like old wine fermenting anew. Whatever pale fears and forebodings some of them might have felt before, these were now not only kept out of sight by their growing awe of Ahab, but broken up and routed on all sides, like timid prairie hares scattering before the bounding bison. The hand of Fate had snatched all their souls; and by the stirring dangers of the day before, the torment of the past night's suspense, and the fixed, unfearing, blind, reckless way their wild ship went plunging toward its flying target — by all these things their hearts were bowled along. The wind that swelled their sails into great bellies and rushed the vessel on with arms as invisible as they were irresistible seemed the symbol of that unseen power which so enslaved them to the race.

They were one man, not thirty. For just as the one ship that held them all, though it was put together from all sorts of contrasting things — oak, and maple, and pine; iron, and pitch, and hemp — yet had all these running into one another in the single solid hull, which shot on its way both balanced and steered by the long central keel, so all the individualities of the crew — this man's courage, that man's fear, guilt and guiltiness — all these varieties were welded into oneness, and all were directed toward that fatal goal which Ahab, their one lord and keel, pointed to.

The rigging was alive. The mastheads, like the tops of tall palms, sprouted outspreading tufts of arms and legs. Clinging to a spar with one hand, some reached out the other with impatient waves; others, shading their eyes from the vivid sunlight, sat far out on the rocking yards; every spar bore its full crop of mortals, ready and ripe for their fate. Ah! how they still strove through that infinite blueness to seek out the thing that might destroy them!

"Why don't you sing out for him, if you see him?" cried Ahab, when some minutes had passed since the first cry and no more had been heard. "Sway me up, men; you have been deceived. Moby Dick does not cast one odd jet that way and then disappear."

It was just so; in their headlong eagerness the men had mistaken something else for the whale's spout, as the event itself soon proved; for hardly had Ahab reached his perch, hardly was the rope made fast to its pin on deck, when he struck the keynote for an orchestra that made the air vibrate as if with the combined discharge of rifles. The triumphant shout of thirty buckskin lungs was heard as — much nearer the ship than the place of the imaginary jet, less than a mile ahead — Moby Dick burst bodily into view! For the White Whale now revealed his nearness not by any calm and lazy spouting, not by the peaceful gush of that mystic fountain in his head, but by the far more wondrous phenomenon of breaching. Rising at his utmost speed from the farthest depths, the Sperm Whale in this way booms his entire bulk into the pure element of air, and, piling up a mountain of dazzling foam, shows where he is to a distance of seven miles and more. At such moments the torn, enraged waves he shakes off seem to be his mane; in some cases this breaching is his act of defiance.

"There she breaches! There she breaches!" was the cry, as in his immeasurable bravado the White Whale tossed himself salmon-like to Heaven. Seen so suddenly in the blue plain of the sea, and set off against the still bluer edge of the sky, the spray he raised glittered and glared unbearably for the moment, like a glacier; and it stood there, gradually fading and fading from its first sparkling intensity to the dim mistiness of a shower advancing up a valley.
"Aye, breach your last to the sun, Moby Dick!" cried Ahab. "Your hour and your harpoon are at hand! — Down! Down, all of you, but one man at the fore. The boats! — stand by!"

Ignoring the tedious rope-ladders of the shrouds, the men slid to the deck like shooting stars by the lone backstays and halyards, while Ahab, less dartingly but still rapidly, was lowered from his perch.
"Lower away," he cried, as soon as he had reached his boat — a spare one, rigged the afternoon before. "Mr. Starbuck, the ship is yours — keep away from the boats, but keep near them. Lower, all!"

As if to strike quick terror into them — being by this time the first to attack — Moby Dick had turned and was now coming for the three crews. Ahab's boat was in the center; and cheering his men on, he told them he would take the whale head-and-head — that is, pull straight up to his forehead — which is not an uncommon thing; for within a certain distance such a course keeps the coming attack out of the whale's sideways vision. But before that close range was reached, and while all three boats were still as plain to his eye as the ship's three masts, the White Whale, churning himself into a furious speed, rushed among the boats almost in an instant, as it were, with open jaws and lashing tail, and offered appalling battle on every side; and heedless of the irons darted at him from every boat, he seemed intent only on annihilating each separate plank those boats were made of. But skillfully maneuvered, wheeling ceaselessly like trained war-horses on the field, the boats evaded him for a while, though at times only by a plank's breadth; while all the time Ahab's unearthly war cry tore every other cry but his to shreds.

But at last, in his untraceable twists and turns, the White Whale so crossed and recrossed, and in a thousand ways so tangled the slack of the three lines now fast to him, that they shortened and, of themselves, hauled the doomed boats toward the irons planted in him; though now for a moment the whale drew a little aside, as if to rally for a more tremendous charge. Seizing that chance, Ahab first paid out more line, and then began rapidly hauling and jerking it in again — hoping that way to clear it of some snarls — when look! — a sight more savage than the embattled teeth of sharks!

Caught and twisted — corkscrewed in the tangles of the line — loose harpoons and lances, with all their bristling barbs and points, came flashing and dripping up to the chocks in the bow of Ahab's boat. Only one thing could be done. Seizing the boat-knife, he reached with precise care within — through — and then out beyond — the rays of steel; dragged in the line beyond them, passed it inboard to the bowsman, and then, cutting the rope twice near the chocks, dropped the intercepted bundle of steel into the sea, and was all fast again. At that instant the White Whale made a sudden rush among the remaining tangles of the other lines; by doing so he irresistibly dragged the more entangled boats of Stubb and Flask toward his flukes, dashed them together like two husks rolling on a surf-beaten beach, and then, diving down into the sea, disappeared in a boiling maelstrom, in which, for a while, the fragrant cedar chips of the wrecks danced round and round like grated nutmeg in a swiftly stirred bowl of punch.

While the two crews were still circling in the water, reaching out after the revolving line-tubs, oars, and other floating gear; while little Flask, slanting, bobbed up and down like an empty vial, twitching his legs upward to escape the dreaded jaws of sharks; and Stubb was lustily singing out for someone to ladle him up; and while the old man's line — now parting — allowed him to pull into the creamy pool to rescue whom he could — in that wild simultaneous rush of a thousand massed perils, Ahab's still unstruck boat seemed drawn up toward Heaven by invisible wires, as, arrow-like, shooting straight up out of the sea, the White Whale dashed his broad forehead against its bottom and sent it turning over and over into the air, until it fell again, gunwale downward, and Ahab and his men struggled out from under it like seals from a seaside cave.

The whale's first upward momentum — changing its direction as he struck the surface — carried him along it, without his willing it, to a little distance from the center of the destruction he had made; and with his back to it he now lay for a moment, slowly feeling from side to side with his flukes; and whenever a stray oar, a bit of plank, or the least chip or crumb of the boats touched his skin, his tail swiftly drew back and came sideways, smiting the sea. But soon, as if satisfied that his work for that time was done, he pushed his pleated forehead through the ocean and, trailing the intertangled lines after him, continued on his way to leeward at a traveler's steady pace.

As before, the watchful ship had seen the whole fight and again came bearing down to the rescue; lowering a boat, she picked up the floating sailors, tubs, oars, and whatever else could be caught hold of, and landed them safely on her decks. Some sprained shoulders, wrists, and ankles; livid bruises; wrenched harpoons and lances; hopeless tangles of rope; shattered oars and planks — all these were there; but no fatal or even serious harm seemed to have come to anyone. As with Fedallah the day before, Ahab was now found grimly clinging to his boat's broken half, which made a comparatively easy float; nor did this mishap exhaust him as much as the previous day's had.

But when he was helped onto the deck, all eyes were fixed on him; for instead of standing by himself he still hung half his weight on the shoulder of Starbuck, who had so far been the first to help him. His ivory leg had been snapped off, leaving only one short, sharp splinter.
"Aye, aye, Starbuck, it's sweet to lean sometimes, whoever the leaner may be; and I wish old Ahab had leaned more often than he has."
"The ferrule has not held, sir," said the carpenter, now coming up; "I put good work into that leg."
"But no bones broken, sir, I hope," said Stubb with true concern.

"Aye! And all splintered to pieces, Stubb! — do you see it? — But even with a broken bone, old Ahab is untouched; and I count no living bone of mine one jot more me than this dead one that's lost. Neither white whale, nor man, nor fiend can so much as graze old Ahab in his own proper and inaccessible being. Can any lead touch that floor down there, any mast scrape that roof up there? — Aloft there! Which way?"
"Dead to leeward, sir."
"Up helm, then; pile on the sail again, shipkeepers! Down with the rest of the spare boats and rig them — Mr. Starbuck, away, and muster the boats' crews."
"Let me first help you toward the bulwarks, sir."
"Oh, oh, oh! How this splinter gores me now! Cursed fate! That the unconquerable captain in the soul should have such a cowardly mate!"
"Sir?"

"My body, man, not you. Give me something for a cane — there, that shattered lance will do. Muster the men. Surely I have not seen him yet. By heaven, it cannot be! — missing? — quick! Call them all."
The old man's half-spoken thought was true. When the company was mustered, the Parsee was not there.
"The Parsee!" cried Stubb — "he must have been caught in — "
"May the black vomit wrench you! — run, all of you, above, below, cabin, forecastle — find him — not gone — not gone!"
But they quickly came back to him with the news that the Parsee was nowhere to be found.
"Aye, sir," said Stubb — "caught among the tangles of your line — I thought I saw him dragging under."

"My line! My line? Gone? — gone? What does that little word mean? — What death-knell rings in it, that old Ahab shakes as if he were the belfry? The harpoon, too! — toss over the litter there — do you see it? — the forged iron, men, the white whale's — no, no, no — blistered fool! this hand did dart it! — it's in the fish! — Aloft there! Keep him nailed — quick! — all hands to the rigging of the boats — collect the oars — harpooners! the irons, the irons! — hoist the royals higher — a pull on all the sheets! — helm there! Steady, steady for your life! I'll girdle the unmeasured globe ten times; yes, and dive straight through it, but I'll slay him yet!"

"Great God! Show yourself, if only for one single instant," cried Starbuck; "never, never will you capture him, old man — in Jesus' name, no more of this; it's worse than devil's madness. Two days chased; twice stove to splinters; your very leg snatched from under you once more; your evil shadow gone — all good angels mobbing you with warnings — what more do you want? — Shall we keep chasing this murderous fish till he swamps the last man? Shall we be dragged by him to the bottom of the sea? Shall we be towed by him to the infernal world? Oh, oh — it is impiety and blasphemy to hunt him any more!"

"Starbuck, lately I've felt strangely moved toward you, ever since that hour when we both saw — you know what — in one another's eyes. But in this matter of the whale, let the front of your face be to me as the palm of this hand — a lipless, featureless blank. Ahab is forever Ahab, man. This whole act is immutably decreed. You and I rehearsed it a billion years before this ocean rolled. Fool! I am the Fates' lieutenant; I act under orders. See to it, underling, that you obey mine. — Stand round me, men. You see an old man cut down to the stump, leaning on a shattered lance, propped up on a lonely foot. That is Ahab — his body's part; but Ahab's soul's a centipede that moves on a hundred legs. I feel strained, half stranded, like ropes that tow dismasted frigates in a gale; and I may look so. But before I break, you'll hear me crack; and till you hear that — know that Ahab's hawser tows his purpose yet. Do you believe, men, in the things called omens? Then laugh aloud, and cry encore! For before they drown, drowning things will rise twice to the surface; then rise again, to sink forevermore. So with Moby Dick — two days he's floated — tomorrow will be the third. Aye, men, he'll rise once more — but only to spout his last! Do you feel brave, men, brave?"
"As fearless fire," cried Stubb.

"And as mechanical," muttered Ahab. Then, as the men went forward, he muttered on: "The things called omens! And yesterday I talked the same way to Starbuck there, about my broken boat. Oh! how valiantly I try to drive out of others' hearts what's clinched so fast in mine! — The Parsee — the Parsee! — gone, gone? And he was to go before — but still was to be seen again before I could perish — how's that? — There's a riddle now that might baffle all the lawyers, backed by the ghosts of the whole line of judges — it pecks my brain like a hawk's beak. I — I will solve it, though!"
When dusk came down, the whale was still in sight to leeward.

So once more the sail was shortened, and everything passed nearly as on the night before; except that the sound of hammers and the hum of the grindstone were heard until nearly daylight, as the men toiled by lantern light at the complete and careful rigging of the spare boats and the sharpening of their fresh weapons for the next day. Meanwhile, out of the broken keel of Ahab's wrecked boat the carpenter made him another leg; while, still as on the night before, Ahab stood slouched and fixed within his scuttle, his hidden, heliotrope glance — sun-seeking, like the flower — turned back ahead of time on its dial, set due east for the earliest sun.

chapters.title: Chapter 135 — The Chase.—Third Day
paragraphs: The third morning dawned fair and fresh, and once again the lone night-watchman at the fore-masthead was relieved by crowds of daytime lookouts, who dotted every mast and nearly every spar.
"Do you see him?" cried Ahab; but the whale was not yet in sight.

"In his infallible wake, though; just follow that wake, that's all. Helm there; steady, as you go and have been going. What a lovely day again! If it were a new-made world, made for a summer-house for the angels, and this morning the first of its throwing open to them, a fairer day could not dawn upon that world. Here's food for thought, if Ahab had time to think; but Ahab never thinks; he only feels, feels, feels; and that is tingling enough for mortal man! To think is audacity. God alone has that right and privilege. Thinking is, or ought to be, a coolness and a calmness; and our poor hearts throb, and our poor brains beat, too much for that. And yet I've sometimes thought my brain was very calm — frozen calm, this old skull cracks so, like a glass whose contents have turned to ice and shivered it. And still this hair is growing now; growing this moment, and heat must breed it; but no, it's like that sort of common grass that will grow anywhere, between the earthy clefts of Greenland ice or in Vesuvius lava. How the wild winds blow it; they whip it about me as the torn shreds of split sails lash the tossed ship they cling to. A vile wind that has no doubt blown before this through prison corridors and cells, and hospital wards, and aired them out, and now comes blowing here as innocent as fleeces. Away with it! — it's tainted. If I were the wind, I'd blow no more on such a wicked, miserable world. I'd crawl off somewhere to a cave, and slink there. And yet the wind is a noble and heroic thing! Who ever conquered it? In every fight it has the last and bitterest blow. Run tilting at it, and you only run through it. Ha! a coward wind that strikes stark-naked men, but will not stand to receive a single blow. Even Ahab is a braver thing — a nobler thing than that. If only the wind had a body now; but all the things that most exasperate and outrage mortal man, all these things are bodiless — but bodiless only as objects, not as agents. There's a most special, a most cunning, oh, a most malicious difference! And yet, I say again, and swear it now, that there's something all glorious and gracious in the wind. These warm Trade Winds, at least, that blow straight on in the clear heavens, in strong and steadfast, vigorous mildness, and do not veer from their mark, however the baser currents of the sea may turn and tack, and the mightiest Mississippis of the land rush and swerve about, uncertain where to go at last. And by the eternal Poles! these same Trades that blow my good ship on so directly — these Trades, or something like them — something as unchangeable, and just as strong, blow my keeled soul along! To it! Aloft there! What do you see?"
"Nothing, sir."

"Nothing! And noon at hand! The doubloon goes begging! Look at the sun! Aye, aye, it must be so. I've oversailed him. How? Did he get the start? Aye, he's chasing me now — not I chasing him; that's bad; I might have known it, too. Fool! The lines — the harpoons he's towing. Aye, aye, I ran past him last night. About! About! Come down, all of you, except the regular lookouts! Man the braces!"

Because of the way she had been steering, the wind had been somewhat on the Pequod's quarter; so now, pointed in the reverse direction, the braced ship sailed close to the wind as she churned up again the cream of her own white wake.

"Against the wind he now steers for the open jaw," murmured Starbuck to himself, as he coiled the newly hauled main-brace on the rail. "God keep us, but already my bones feel damp inside me, and they wet my flesh from within. I fear that I disobey my God in obeying him!"
"Stand by to sway me up!" cried Ahab, advancing to the hempen basket. "We should meet him soon."
"Aye, aye, sir," and at once Starbuck did Ahab's bidding, and once more Ahab swung on high.

A whole hour now passed, beaten out like gold into ages. Time itself now held long breaths in keen suspense. But at last, some three points off the weather bow, Ahab sighted the spout again, and instantly three shrieks went up from the three mastheads, as if tongues of fire had voiced them.

"Forehead to forehead I meet you, this third time, Moby Dick! On deck there! — brace sharper up; crowd her into the wind's eye. He's too far off to lower yet, Mr. Starbuck. The sails shake! Stand over that helmsman with a top-maul! So, so; he travels fast, and I must go down. But let me have one more good round look aloft here at the sea; there's time for that. An old, old sight, and yet somehow so young; aye, and not changed a wink since I first saw it, a boy, from the sand-hills of Nantucket! The same! — the same! — the same to Noah as to me. There's a soft shower to leeward. Such lovely leewardings! They must lead somewhere — to something other than common land, more palmy than the palms. Leeward! The white whale goes that way; look to windward, then; the better if the bitterer quarter. But good-bye, good-bye, old masthead! What's this? — green? Aye, tiny mosses in these warped cracks. No such green weather-stains on Ahab's head! There's the difference now between man's old age and matter's. But aye, old mast, we both grow old together; sound in our hulls, though, are we not, my ship? Aye, minus a leg, that's all. By heaven, this dead wood has the better of my live flesh every way. I can't compare with it; and I've known some ships made of dead trees outlast the lives of men made of the most vital stuff of vital fathers. What's that he said? He should still go before me, my pilot, and yet be seen again? But where? Will I have eyes at the bottom of the sea, supposing I go down those endless stairs? And all night I've been sailing away from him, wherever he sank to. Aye, aye, like many more, you told dire truth about yourself, O Parsee; but, Ahab, there your shot fell short. Good-bye, masthead — keep a good eye on the whale while I'm gone. We'll talk tomorrow — no, tonight, when the white whale lies down there, tied by head and tail."
He gave the order, and, still looking all around him, was lowered steadily through the split blue air to the deck.

In due time the boats were lowered; but as Ahab, standing in the stern of his boat, hovered just at the point of descending, he waved to the mate — who held one of the tackle-ropes on deck — and told him to pause.
"Starbuck!"
"Sir?"
"For the third time my soul's ship sets out on this voyage, Starbuck."
"Aye, sir, you will have it so."
"Some ships sail from their ports and are missing ever afterward, Starbuck!"
"Truth, sir: saddest truth."
"Some men die at ebb tide; some at low water; some at the full of the flood; — and I feel now like a billow that's all one crested comb, Starbuck. I am old; — shake hands with me, man."
Their hands met; their eyes fastened; Starbuck's tears were the glue.
"Oh, my captain, my captain! — noble heart — don't go — don't go! — see, it's a brave man that weeps; how great, then, the agony of the pleading!"
"Lower away!" cried Ahab, tossing the mate's arm from him. "Stand by the crew!"
In an instant the boat was pulling round close under the stern.
"The sharks! The sharks!" cried a voice from the low cabin window there. "O master, my master, come back!"
But Ahab heard nothing, for just then his own voice was raised high; and the boat sprang on.

Yet the voice spoke true; for he had scarcely pushed off from the ship when numbers of sharks, seemingly rising out of the dark waters beneath the hull, snapped maliciously at the oar blades every time they dipped into the water, and in this way kept the boat company with their bites. It is a thing that not uncommonly happens to whaleboats in those swarming seas, the sharks at times apparently following them with the same foresight with which vultures hover over the banners of marching regiments in the east. But these were the first sharks the Pequod had observed since the White Whale was first sighted; and whether it was that Ahab's crew were all such tiger-yellow barbarians, and their flesh therefore more musky to the sharks' senses — a thing sometimes well known to affect them — however it was, they seemed to follow that one boat without molesting the others.

"Heart of wrought steel!" murmured Starbuck, gazing over the side and following the receding boat with his eyes — "can you still ring boldly to that sight? — lowering your keel among ravening sharks, and followed by them, open-mouthed, to the chase; and this the critical third day? — For when three days flow together in one continuous, intense pursuit, be sure the first is the morning, the second the noon, and the third the evening and the end of that thing — whatever that end may be. Oh, my God! what is this that shoots through me and leaves me so deadly calm, yet expectant — fixed at the top of a shudder! Future things swim before me, as in empty outlines and skeletons; all the past has somehow grown dim. Mary, girl! you fade in pale glories behind me; boy! I seem to see nothing of you but your eyes, grown wondrous blue. The strangest problems of life seem to be clearing; but clouds sweep between — Is my journey's end coming? My legs feel faint, like those of a man who has been on foot all day. Feel your heart — does it still beat? Stir yourself, Starbuck! — stave it off — move, move! Speak aloud! — Masthead there! Do you see my boy's hand on the hill? — Crazed; — aloft there! — keep your keenest eye on the boats — mark the whale well! — Ho! again! — drive off that hawk! See! he pecks — he tears the vane" — pointing to the red flag flying at the main-truck, the cap at the very top of the mainmast — "Ha! he soars away with it! — Where's the old man now? Do you see that sight, oh Ahab! — shudder, shudder!"

The boats had not gone very far when, by a signal from the mastheads — an arm pointed downward — Ahab knew that the whale had sounded; but meaning to be near him at his next rising, he held on his way a little to one side of the vessel, the spellbound crew keeping the deepest silence as the head-on waves hammered and hammered against the opposing bow.
"Drive, drive in your nails, oh you waves! Drive them in to their very heads! You only strike a thing without a lid; and no coffin and no hearse can be mine — and only hemp can kill me! Ha! ha!"

Suddenly the waters around them slowly swelled in broad circles; then quickly heaved up, as if sliding sideways off a submerged iceberg swiftly rising to the surface. A low rumbling sound was heard, a hum from under the earth; and then all held their breath, as, draggled with trailing ropes and harpoons and lances, a vast form shot lengthwise, but slantwise, from the sea. Shrouded in a thin, drooping veil of mist, it hovered for a moment in the rainbowed air, and then fell swamping back into the deep. Crushed thirty feet upward, the waters flashed for an instant like heaps of fountains, then sank brokenly in a shower of flakes, leaving the circling surface creamed like new milk round the marble trunk of the whale.

"Give way!" cried Ahab to the oarsmen, and the boats darted forward to the attack; but, maddened by yesterday's fresh irons corroding in him, Moby Dick seemed possessed by all the angels that fell from heaven at once. The wide tiers of welded tendons spreading over his broad white forehead beneath the transparent skin looked knitted together, as he came on head first, churning his tail among the boats, and once more flailed them apart, spilling the irons and lances out of the two mates' boats and smashing in one side of the upper part of their bows, but leaving Ahab's almost without a scar.

While Daggoo and Queequeg were stopping up the strained planks, and as the whale, swimming out from them, turned and showed one entire flank as he shot past them again, at that moment a quick cry went up. Lashed round and round to the fish's back, pinned in the turns upon turns in which the whale had wound the coils of the lines around himself during the past night, the half-torn body of the Parsee was seen, his black garments frayed to shreds, his bulging eyes turned full upon old Ahab.
The harpoon dropped from his hand.

"Fooled, fooled!" — drawing in a long, lean breath — "Aye, Parsee! I see you again. — Aye, and you go before; and this — this, then — is the hearse that you promised. But I hold you to the last letter of your word. Where is the second hearse? Away, mates, to the ship! Those boats are useless now; repair them if you can in time, and return to me; if not, Ahab is enough to die — Down, men! The first thing that so much as offers to jump from this boat I stand in, that thing I harpoon. You are not other men, but my arms and my legs; so obey me. — Where's the whale? Gone down again?"

But he looked too near the boat; for, as if bent on escaping with the corpse he carried, and as if the particular place of the last encounter had been only a stage in his voyage to leeward, Moby Dick was now again swimming steadily forward, and had almost passed the ship — which so far had been sailing in the opposite direction to him, though for the present her headway had been stopped. He seemed to be swimming at his utmost speed, and now intent only on pursuing his own straight path in the sea.
"Oh! Ahab," cried Starbuck, "it is not too late, even now, the third day, to stop. See! Moby Dick does not seek you. It is you, you, that madly seek him!"

Setting sail to the rising wind, the lonely boat was driven swiftly to leeward by both oars and canvas. And at last, as Ahab was sliding past the vessel, so near that he could plainly make out Starbuck's face as he leaned over the rail, he hailed him to turn the vessel about and follow him, not too swiftly, at a judicious interval. Glancing upward, he saw Tashtego, Queequeg, and Daggoo eagerly climbing to the three mastheads, while the oarsmen were rocking in the two staved boats, which had just been hoisted to the side, busily at work repairing them. One after another, through the portholes, as he sped by, he also caught flying glimpses of Stubb and Flask busying themselves on deck among bundles of new irons and lances. As he saw all this, as he heard the hammers in the broken boats, far different hammers seemed to be driving a nail into his heart. But he rallied. And now, noticing that the vane or flag was gone from the main-masthead, he shouted to Tashtego, who had just reached that perch, to come down again for another flag, and a hammer and nails, and so nail it to the mast.

Whether he was worn out by the three days' running chase and by the drag of the knotted tangle he carried, or whether it was some hidden deceitfulness and malice in him — whichever was true, the White Whale's speed now began, as it seemed from the boat so rapidly nearing him once more, to slacken; though indeed the whale's last start had not been so long a one as before. And still, as Ahab glided over the waves, the pitiless sharks went with him, and stuck so doggedly to the boat, and bit so continually at the plying oars, that the blades became jagged and crunched, and left small splinters in the sea at almost every dip.
"Pay them no heed! Those teeth only give your oars new rowlocks. Pull on! The shark's jaw is a better rest than the yielding water."
"But at every bite, sir, the thin blades grow smaller and smaller!"

"They will last long enough! Pull on! — But who can tell," he muttered, "whether these sharks swim to feast on the whale or on Ahab? — But pull on! Aye, all alive now — we're nearing him. The helm! Take the helm! Let me pass" — and with that, two of the oarsmen helped him forward to the bow of the still-flying boat.

At length, as the boat was cast to one side and ran along level with the White Whale's flank, he seemed strangely unaware of its approach — as the whale sometimes will be — and Ahab was right inside the smoky mountain of mist which, thrown off from the whale's spout, curled around his great Monadnock hump. He was that close to him when, with his body arched back and both arms raised high lengthwise to the poise, he darted his fierce iron, and his far fiercer curse, into the hated whale. As both steel and curse sank in to the socket, as if sucked into a morass, Moby Dick writhed sideways, rolled his near flank convulsively against the bow, and, without staving a hole in it, tipped the boat over so suddenly that, if it had not been for the raised part of the gunwale he then clung to, Ahab would once more have been thrown into the sea. As it was, three of the oarsmen — who had not known beforehand the exact instant of the dart, and were therefore unprepared for its effects — were flung out; but they fell in such a way that in an instant two of them clutched the gunwale again and, rising to its level on a combing wave, hurled themselves bodily back inboard; the third man dropped helplessly astern, but was still afloat and swimming.

Almost at the same moment, with a mighty act of will and a swiftness that came instantly, all at once, the White Whale darted through the weltering sea. But when Ahab called to the steersman to take new turns with the line and hold it so, and ordered the crew to turn round on their seats and tow the boat up to the mark, the moment the treacherous line felt that double strain and tug, it snapped in the empty air!
"What breaks in me? Some sinew cracks! — it's whole again; oars! oars! Burst in upon him!"

Hearing the tremendous rush of the sea-crashing boat, the whale wheeled round to present his blank forehead at bay; but in that turn, catching sight of the black hull of the ship drawing near, seemingly seeing in it the source of all his persecutions, taking it — it may be — for a larger and nobler foe, he suddenly bore down on its advancing prow, clashing his jaws amid fiery showers of foam.
Ahab staggered; his hand struck his forehead. "I'm growing blind; hands! stretch out before me so that I may still grope my way. Is it night?"
"The whale! The ship!" cried the cringing oarsmen.

"Oars! oars! Slope downward to your depths, O sea, so that before it is forever too late, Ahab may slide this last, last time upon his mark! I see: the ship! the ship! Dash on, my men! Will you not save my ship?"

But as the oarsmen violently forced their boat through the sledgehammering seas, the bow-ends of two planks that the whale had already struck burst through, and almost in an instant the temporarily disabled boat lay nearly level with the waves, its half-wading, splashing crew trying hard to stop the gap and bail out the pouring water.

Meanwhile, for that one instant of watching, Tashtego's masthead hammer stayed suspended in his hand; and the red flag, half wrapping him like a plaid, then streamed straight out from him, like his own forward-flowing heart; while Starbuck and Stubb, standing on the bowsprit below, caught sight of the oncoming monster just as soon as he did.

"The whale, the whale! Up helm, up helm! Oh, all you sweet powers of air, hold me close now! Let not Starbuck die, if die he must, in a woman's fainting fit. Up helm, I say — you fools, the jaw! the jaw! Is this the end of all my bursting prayers? all my lifelong fidelities? Oh, Ahab, Ahab, behold your work. Steady! helmsman, steady. No, no! Up helm again! He turns to meet us! Oh, his unappeasable brow drives on toward one whose duty tells him he cannot depart. My God, stand by me now!"

"Don't stand by me, but stand under me, whoever you are that will now help Stubb; for Stubb, too, sticks here. I grin at you, you grinning whale! Who ever helped Stubb, or kept Stubb awake, but Stubb's own unwinking eye? And now poor Stubb goes to bed on a mattress that is all too soft; I wish it were stuffed with brushwood! I grin at you, you grinning whale! Look here, sun, moon, and stars! I call you assassins of as good a fellow as ever spouted up his ghost. For all that, I would still clink glasses with you, if you would only hand the cup! Oh, oh! oh, oh! you grinning whale, but there'll be plenty of gulping soon! Why don't you fly, O Ahab! For me, off with shoes and jacket for it; let Stubb die in his drawers! A most moldy and oversalted death, though — cherries! cherries! cherries! Oh, Flask, for one red cherry before we die!"
"Cherries? I only wish that we were where they grow. Oh, Stubb, I hope my poor mother has drawn my part-pay before now; if not, few coppers will come to her now, for the voyage is up."

From the ship's bows nearly all the seamen now hung idle, hammers, bits of plank, lances, and harpoons still mechanically held in their hands, just as they had rushed from their various jobs; all their spellbound eyes were fixed on the whale, which, strangely swinging his predestinating head from side to side, sent a broad band of spreading, semicircular foam before him as he rushed. Retribution, swift vengeance, eternal malice were in his whole aspect, and in spite of all that mortal man could do, the solid white buttress of his forehead struck the ship's starboard bow, till men and timbers reeled. Some fell flat on their faces. Like dislodged trucks, the heads of the harpooners aloft shook on their bull-like necks. Through the breach they heard the waters pour, like mountain torrents down a flume.
"The ship! The hearse! — the second hearse!" cried Ahab from the boat. "Its wood could only be American!"

Diving beneath the settling ship, the whale ran quivering along its keel; but, turning under water, he shot swiftly to the surface again, far off the other bow, but within a few yards of Ahab's boat, where for a time he lay still.

"I turn my body from the sun. What ho, Tashtego! Let me hear your hammer. Oh! you three unsurrendered spires of mine; you uncracked keel; and only god-bullied hull; you firm deck, and haughty helm, and Pole-pointed prow — death-glorious ship! must you then perish, and without me? Am I cut off from the last fond pride of the meanest shipwrecked captains? Oh, lonely death on lonely life! Oh, now I feel my topmost greatness lies in my topmost grief. Ho, ho! from all your farthest bounds, pour in now, you bold billows of my whole bygone life, and top this one piled comber of my death! Toward you I roll, you all-destroying but unconquering whale; to the last I grapple with you; from hell's heart I stab at you; for hate's sake I spit my last breath at you. Sink all coffins and all hearses to one common pool! and since neither can be mine, let me then be towed to pieces, while still chasing you, though tied to you, you damned whale! Thus, I give up the spear!"

The harpoon was thrown; the wounded whale shot forward; the line ran through the grooves with igniting speed — and fouled. Ahab bent down to clear it; he did clear it; but the flying loop caught him around the neck, and as silently as Turkish mutes strangle their victim with the bowstring, he was jerked out of the boat before the crew knew he was gone. The next instant the heavy eye-splice at the very end of the rope flew out of the completely empty tub, knocked down an oarsman, and, hitting the sea, vanished into its depths.

For an instant the entranced boat's crew stood still; then turned. "The ship? Great God, where is the ship?" Soon, through dim, bewildering mediums, they saw her sidelong fading phantom, as in the gaseous Fata Morgana mirage, only the uppermost masts out of the water; while, fixed by infatuation, or fidelity, or fate to their once lofty perches, the pagan harpooners still kept their sinking lookouts on the sea. And now concentric circles seized the lone boat itself, and all its crew, and each floating oar, and every lance-pole, and, spinning animate and inanimate all round and round in one vortex, carried the smallest chip of the Pequod out of sight.

But as the last floods poured, mingling, over the sunken head of the Indian at the mainmast, leaving a few inches of the upright spar still visible, together with long streaming yards of the flag, which calmly rippled, with ironic coincidence, over the destroying billows they almost touched — at that instant a red arm and a hammer hovered, raised backward in the open air, in the act of nailing the flag faster and yet faster to the sinking spar. A sky-hawk that had tauntingly followed the main-truck downward from its natural home among the stars, pecking at the flag and harassing Tashtego there, now happened to put its broad fluttering wing between the hammer and the wood; and at the same moment, feeling that ethereal thrill, the submerged savage below, in his death-gasp, kept his hammer frozen there; and so the bird of heaven, with archangelic shrieks, his imperial beak thrust upward, and his whole captive form folded in the flag of Ahab, went down with his ship, which, like Satan, would not sink to hell until she had dragged a living part of heaven along with her and helmeted herself with it.

Now little birds flew screaming over the gulf, which still gaped open; a sullen white surf beat against its steep sides; then everything collapsed, and the great shroud of the sea rolled on as it had rolled five thousand years ago.

chapters.title: Epilogue — The Drama's Done
paragraphs: "AND I ONLY AM ESCAPED ALONE TO TELL THEE" — Job.
The drama's done. Why then does anyone step forth here? Because one did survive the wreck.

It happened that after the Parsee disappeared, I was the one the Fates appointed to take the place of Ahab's bowsman, when that bowsman took over the vacant post; and I was the same man who, on the last day, when the three men were thrown out of the rocking boat, was dropped astern. So, floating on the edge of the scene that followed, and in full view of it, I was drawn, though slowly, toward the closing vortex when the half-spent suction of the sunken ship reached me. By the time I reached it, it had settled into a creamy pool. Then round and round I went, like another Ixion, always drawing closer to the button-like black bubble at the center of that slowly wheeling circle. At last, when I reached that vital center, the black bubble burst upward; and now, set free by its ingenious spring and rising with great force because of its great buoyancy, the coffin life-buoy shot lengthwise out of the sea, fell over, and floated beside me. Kept afloat by that coffin for almost a whole day and night, I drifted on a soft, dirge-like sea. The sharks glided by without harming me, as if they had padlocks on their mouths; the savage sea-hawks sailed with their beaks sheathed. On the second day a sail drew near, nearer, and picked me up at last. It was the Rachel, cruising her winding course, who in retracing her search after her missing children found only another orphan.
